Clumsy game feels a lot like doing your taxes.  It has a lot of love poured into it, and the artistry is pretty evident.  Why is it such a chore to play?
It's turn-based, for one.  I'm playing it on a computer, however - it is hard to imagine why I am taking turns.  That is for postal chess games.
It has squares, for another.  Why not hexes, or no "spots" at all?
There are too many different commodities to track:  supplies, "intel", scientists, engineers, soldiers, many types of inventory.  There is a world map where you click on something and a world of spam is unleashed on you:  some VIP needs rescuing in Kamchatka, some VIP needs whacking in Peoria, a kitten is stuck in a tree in Irkutsk.
Some menacing guy from the Hair Club for Men is constantly trying to Skype me, and I have no idea whether he's even wearing pants.  And to top it all off, I'm supposed to save Earth by driving around the Globe in a flying minivan like a Soccer Mom?  It's just too much to ask.
This is flash game, very easy and very fun.

I tried all of them, and of all the gamedev sims this one hits the mark. It's got nice visuals, and building your studio adds a lot more depth than just making game after game and upgrading like the others. What I like about this game is the growth potential- you start as a one-man studio and can end up a large publisher, complete with production facilities- and you can buy out your competitors. Basically a lot more to do, but everything is still kept simple and, er, manageable.
Also the devs showed exemplary Early Access behavior, showering us with updates and improving an already playable game on a fairly constant basis.
There are a lot of management-type games coming out lately, I wrote this review with the hope that this one gets the attention it deserves. If you want a game dev sim, this is the one; for business sim fans, check it out too. it's worth a look for sure.

Fallout 4 is very hit and miss. I think the graphics are slick, the gunplay is fun, and the new "live action" VATS deal is cool. But, the story is weak, the dialogue options have been butchered, the characters are boring, the role-playing elements have been watered down, the soundtrack is just recycled from Fallout 3 w/ a few new good songs and several annoying ones, and the DLC is a RIPOFF!!! The DLC seems so lazy, which does not compliment a game that feels overall uninspired compared to its predecessors. There's basically two-and-a-half story-based DLC's for FO4; Automatron, Far Harbor, and Nuka World. Automatron is just a few extra quests, Far Harbor is just FO3's Point Lookout all over again with an annoying puzzle thing towards the end of it that nearly ruins the whole DLC, and finally Nuka World is just okay. All of the other DLC is for the stupid settlement creation which sucks. I'd recommend this game for no more than $30 and no one needs the Season Pass. Just get Far Habor, Automatron, and Nuka World on a sale.

I've played this game awhile back in early 2015. Game was boring and basically P2W. There wasn't much to do, because upgrades were really freaking expensive, and to progress you needed to do hours of mindless grinding for Mastery Rank (MR) just to get a class coin in order unlock a new class. Chaos Chests were only purchasable through actual money or else costs thousands of flux on the market. I stopped playing because I reached a point where I can't progress F2P anymore. I had to purchase to progress. So I quitted then from disappointment.
Today, I came back to a new Trove. I was happy to see that Trion Worlds brought this game towards a more F2P direction. The community didn't change. Still the friendly type who would definitely reply. Unlike other RPGs where you don't get replies at all from global chat, I love Trove because of the community. Though there are salty ones or those who insult you for no reason, it's a rare sight.
Also there's lots of events going on now, and you can craft classes now. You don't P2W anymore, but you pay to advance much faster. Lots of contents added to this game. Back then it was pretty boring for the first 20 MRs because you couldn't do anything before that. But now MRs aren't a massive factor for newbies in early game, because they can do Shadow Towers with around 500 PR - it got a lot easier too. I'm also glad that this game has gone more friendly towards new players. Prices of Penta, Quad, Thrice, Twice souls have drastically decreased. In my days in the early 2015s, Pentas were 50k flux each. Today it's as low as 6k flux. Chaos Chests now drop in dungeons and you can easily get at least 10 a day from dungeons. Also the weekly contests give generous rewards - Daily Loot Chests. If you don't feel like grinding you can join up to 5 clubs and chat with the players (in global as well), or build up your own cornerstone ! I'm very much happier to spend time on this game now.
The cons of this game however, rich players are manipulating the market, which is a pretty bad thing. Prices are fluctuating because of those rich selfish players. Market is terribly volatile. Times like these I take a break from the game until the markets stabilize. Also the server ping fluctuates terribly. As a player from SEA region, I hope they put up a SEA server. I've heard of complains from the UK players as well where they disconnect more often than I do. If there's one thing bad, is that Trion Worlds haven't changed the quality of their game servers since I played back then. When the ping spikes I get off the game for an hour then it will be fine after that. However, the challenges they made such as the flying and coin collection depends on their servers to ping what you've collect. So you'd usually have a hard time with it when the ping spikes.
Game is fine overall. I'd give it a solid 8/10. I'm loving it. A little edgy on some aspects, but there's room for improvement. You would hear people complaining how too many items are untradeable (i.e Dragon Coins, Shadow Keys, Moon Keys), but in my opinion Trion Worlds did it because they want you as a player to experience some challenges in the game instead of being able to buy your way through. This is pretty much an action RPG version of Minecraft. My support goes out to the Trove developers. This game has a very huge potential, completely unique. I'm proud of the direction they're heading. Though, I apologize I'm not the kind of player to spend money on this game.

I really enjoy this game.
I love space sims and sci-fi stuff in general, and I'm also a big fan of crafting sandbox games like Minecraft and Terraria, so I was pretty excited when I found this game.
The gameplay is pretty similar to terraria, except the worlds are smaller, but you can fly to other planets, so that's not an issue at all. The crafting works well and the space travel is well done.
Lately, I've been enjoying the multiplayer side of things over the LAN. The server is really easy to set up over the LAN, since you don't have to mess with router configurations or anything. My only complaint with the multiplayer is that there's no way to fight the other players, at least not that I know of.
In recent updates, they've added more quest stuff and missions and things like that if you like a more structured RPG. I like the open endedness of it, so I like that the missions aren't necessary to enjoy the game. You do have to complete a few missions to get your ship fully up and running to jump between systems, but that adds to the experience of the game.

Overall, this game's been pretty great for me, a free-to-play player of Trove. You've got a couple of the vital elelments in a great mmo like WOW with the added bonus of Minecraft-Style building in pretty much any environment. Hwoever for me, this game has been frustrating lately. The developers have recently added a new system to buy classes with in-game resources instead of credits or cubits, but it is not designed for the end-game players like ScythePlays, Underrated, or Lordfafy. Since the devs have made so many compromising changes in the past that haven't benefitted new players, many have quit, leaving end-gamers as the majority in the Trove community. This new patch will probably make some of their most faithful end-gamers quit... At the moment, however, I recommend this game to anyone who has at least an afternoon to sink into this game and see how you feel about it. WARNING: Grinding is the main form of gameplay unfortunately, so to get your character to a high level you'll have to sink about 50-100 hours into this game depending on how effecient you are... Anyways, hope this review helped some of the potential Trove players decide what they'll play.

Town of Salem is a very fascinating game of deception. You will never play the same game twice, and the roles are each very diverse and unique. Play time can vary greatly depending on how well each player preforms their role, this means a game can end in seconds or will drag out for up to half an hour. My only complaints are that you cannot add symbols and numbers to your name while in-game, and that certain classes can be over-powered, and others are quite underpowered. It also takes a long time to understand all the rules of the game, so i would suggest looking over the wiki, then playing classic mode until you feel like you understand the complexity of this game. Do not let that deter you from purchasing this game, it is a lot of fun, and is a great game to play with your friends.

Utterly beautiful in it's simplicity. I picked this up on for next to nothing and boy did it impress!

Brilliant voice acting
Super super interesting way to implement difficulty settings.
Endearing weapons
The only thing I was disappointed in was a certain skill you get near the end of the game. The skill itself was fun. The much too short period of time you get to use it for isn't. The segment you use it in is easily the worst part of the game as well. That's an incredibly minor nitpick in the grand scheme of the game.

Having a well-built plot, an excellent narrator and a colorful cultural setting, Baston revolves around a magnificent, post-apocalyptic world with a vast variety, presented by it's fascinating 2-dimentional, hand-drawn graphics. The atmosphere of the game is further enhanced by it's oriental and quite fitting soundtrack (written by Darren Korb).
The gameplay itself is not so challenging, although it can be made so. The main fighting gameplay is based upon and inspired by some retro-era games. The player may choose between a dozen of weapons, each with it's unique manner of play. Other than that, the presence of the ability to upgrade weapons makes them even more customizable, depending on the player's desires.
Bastion is certainly among the best games I've ever played and I base this upon every aspect of the game (I could even call it a masterpiece), so I would definitely recommend it to anyone!

Finished the game on hard/intense(including secret bosses/All code reds)
Berseria takes place around 1000 years before Zestiria, so if you want to play in order, this should be first, even tho it was released after.
Now for the review, i came into this game not expecting much because unfortunately Zestiria was lackluster in many areas, however i was pleasantly surprised when i found out that those areas were all, imo, fixed.
The story is more captivating, the characters are all likable and have their own reasons for their adventure, theyre not some mindless addons like the malak were in Zestiria and i think the idea that theyre only together because of their own individual wishes really helps with that. The villain also is better, at the start he might seem like your average villain but as you proceed on the story and learn more about him, you'll learn he is just like the "heroes", someone after his own wishes, the idea of individualism is strong in Berseria.
The combat, one of the things that has always drawn me to Tales, thankfully turned out to be amazing in this game, combos here actually matter, alongside proper management of Souls, If you have more souls, your chances of being stunned/hit by a status effect are bigger(both which cause you to lose a soul) but it also means you can use break souls/bigger combos, it's an interesting trade-off and on intense it made me have to juggle my soul-count constantly, specially because Break souls are the main source of healing outside of items as Healing artes are weaker in this tales.
The world is smaller, but interesting enough that you won't get bored, they made the areas smaller but more straight to the objective of getting from point A to B, all while filling them with items to collect along the way, making them not feel empty like Zestiria's world where they had huge areas, but it was incredibly boring to walk through those.
The weakest point of the game, yet not a bad one, was the soundtrack, while it's not a bad one, it didn't leave any impact on me except for few tracks, one of which was a Zestiria one, so i guess i wouldn't count it for Berseria, however, Magilou's theme is absolutely amazing.
Nothing is perfect unfortunately, the way BAMCO is taking with DLC is not nice, tales games used to give you all costumes ingame all while showing you funny events or sidequests, it made doing those fun and rewarding, in Berseria, costumes are all behind either some lame minigames(slash card which is very luck based and the nightmare of the restaurant minigame, which isnt as bad as the previous ones, but still awful in the last 2 levels) or behind DLC, which is unfortunate, but i guess thats the way games are going to be nowadays.
Lastly, regarding the port, it was a great port, it runs smoothly and i've had almost no problems with the game itself, the only one i had was fixed in the most recent patch(the AI problem), so if you are worried about performance, this is safe on that side.
Overall i'd definitely recommend it to RPG/JRPG fans, the DLC thing is a bummer, but at least theyre not locking actual gameplay content(story/bosses) behind it.

This is a pretty solid game. A clever streamlined parody of LoZ with heavier focus on puzzles.
Thematically it's a parody of classic top down Legend of Zelda. It has pretty funny writing, and I like the style. A lot of games with a similar silly aesthetic are also kinda gross, but this one thankfully isn't.
On the gameplay front it's very streamlined. For instance, to view signs or have your character comment on things, you just walk up to them. No pressing an interact button is needed, and it doesn't make you stop moving to read it. There are multiple routes you can take, but no backtracking is needed. As posted on a sign outside a dungeon: "Dear adventurer: for your convenience, there are no items or chests you can miss in the dungeons." And there are no keys you have to find in one room and take halfway across the dungeon to use in another room you saw earlier. The overworld is another story, though. There are several optional one-room mini dungeons scattered about, and a few of them you do have to come back later to clear.

I just finished a playthrough of WotC, and decided I’d write up a quick review to share my thoughts. Overall, the expansion is a great edition to the base game. The Chosen, who are the new boss-type enemies added, are a fantastic edition to the game. Each Chosen is different, requiring players to vary up their strategy against each enemy. As well as this, the ability for them to capture and interrogate soldiers is a solid edition.
As well as this, the expansion added in three new resistance factions, with a new hero/class type to go along with each faction. Each of the new soldier types are fantastic, with each offering a unique way of playing. Interestingly, it is quite difficult to obtain multiple of a hero unit, for example more than one Templar soldier, which I feel is good decision by the developers. If players were permitted to have a full six-man squad of the new units, I could imagine the balance would go out of wack.
Other cool additions include the bonding system, which allows two soldiers to form a bond, giving them access to special abilities that include an ability to both fire at a target within the same action, or given a bond-mate a free action point. The covert action system is also pretty neat, allowing the player to send soldiers out on missions, with a wide variety of potential rewards. During these actions, there is a potential for a soldier to be injured or captured, which forces the player to weigh the potential risks and rewards of a cover action. Lastly, the new enemy type, the lost, as well as missions associated to them are a good change of pace to the standard mission types.
Another feature added that I loved was the propaganda feature, which allows players to create unique posters of their soldiers, which can later show up in missions. Whilst the options can be somewhat limited in certain areas, overall, the mechanic is amazing.
Lastly, the new maps and areas added in are neat. In the base game, a lot of the locations could feel repetitive after a while. Whilst the maps were random, the environment was very similar. The new areas added in, like subways and sewer tunnels, add a spice of variety, which always helps.
The only negative thing I want to share is regarding the story with the templars. Without going into spoilers, it feels clear to me that a decent amount of effort was put into the story between the Skirmishers and the Reapers. But the Templars feel kind of just slid in.
Overall though, I enjoyed the expansion. The amount of content added in is staggering, with the vast majority of that content being a joy to play.
TL;DR - The expansion is a fantastic addition to the base game, and well worth the price.

There are still some pretty hefty issues in the current game version (the most notable being the random AI "freeze" that occassionally happens shortly after starting a new game, but this is afterall a pre-alpha product and is being improved upon by a team of highly dedicated developers.

One of my favourite games of all time.  If the part of Garry's Mod that you liked was the building part, or if you ever played Garry's Mod and were all like "Man, I wish it was easier to make awesome vehicles", this game.  The storyline barely makes any sense, but it is hilarious.  Don't go into it thinking "OH MAN WHERE'S MY PERFECT PHYSICS" or "GAAAAAAWD GUYS THIS PLOT DOESN'T EVEN MAKE SENSE".  It doesn't need to.  It's not supposed to.  It's fun.  It's just fun.  That's all it's suposed to be.  Build random things, play with the bizarre locals, have a few hours of laughs and giggles, then put it down.  You won't play this every day, and you won't ponder over the story and its depth for days to come.  You won't.  You just won't.  But it will let you have fun for a few hours, and it will teach you that sometimes replayability or depth just aren't necessary for a game.
If you go in demanding these things and ignoring what Cargo! is trying to show you, you will be let down.  If you listen to Cargo!, and embrace what it's trying to give you, you'll truly come out better and happier for it.

Fallout 4 is the long awaited sequel to Fallout 3, which is, in my mind, a reboot of the Fallout franchise.  Now I played all of the Fallout games.  I picked up Fallout 1 (loved) in the store back in 97, then I eagerly bought the sequel in 98 (loved).  Played Fallout Tactics (ok), even bough the turd Fallout: Brotherhood of Steel for my Xbox (sucked).  I was a rabid fan of the old Fallout franchise, and though I had some fun on the fresh take in Fallout 3, the story, I felt, was lack luster and not true to the Fallout genre.  The same exact thing I will claim happened in this title, Fallout 4.  Everything from the story, to the horrible DLC, reeks of a corporate sellout and recycled content that utterly destroys immersion.
Graphically speaking, Fallout 4 is a decent shooter RPG.  The sound and visuals, along with the combat are good, for the most part.  However, the Elderscrolls engine is outdated, graphics and loadings screens.  Even with the acquisition of the RAGE engine, which had limited implementation in Fallout 4, the game still looked and felt like a desert Skyrim with guns, with an incredible amount of loading screens.  It takes a great deal of mods to update the game to look closer to modern shooter titles, however, transitioning from different parts of the game world is designed for console, so loading screens aplenty.
The sounds in Fallout are average.  The elderscrolls engine has never been a ground breaker on sound design, so once again, players are left with the option of keeping sub-standard weapon and explosion audio, or relying on mods.
The modding community on nexusmods is fantastic.  The mods make Fallout 4 enjoyable, as vanilla Fallout 4 feels like a lot of things are missing.  I again want to criticize Bethesda for its involvement in paid mods.  It didn't learn the first time when the player community mutinied against Bethesda for trying to rip off modders and players by forcing the user to pay for mods.  Bethesda still pulled the trigger on a mod store that is built in to the game, whether you like it or not.  Leave it to the modders at nexusmods to maintain a mod that kills the Bethesda store in your game.
Now for the story.  I just couldn't get into the shoes of the main character.  Now I am a veteran with a wife and kids, but this dude just isn't me.  The old Fallout 1 and 2 seemed like I could customize a character completely from scratch, and take on the world however I wanted.  I could be evil, I could be a slaver, I could be a thief, a raider, murderer, jigalo, child killer, or a do gooder.  I could wander the wastes until the people I was supposed to save died for reasons, or I could blunder right into the final boss from out the starting gate.  Fallout 1&2 was all about player choice.  Fallout 3 and 4 are not.  In F4, you pick either the male combat veteran, or the female lawyer.  You can customize your stats however you like, but the characters are fully voiced, and the scenes are rather limited on dialogue choices.  It's generally locked into 4 categories, Question, Hostile, Nice, and Funny.  There are some speech and skill checks during dialogue, and they are color coded like a highlighter, so it's obvious you will pass or fail based on your character skill.
Add in the magic quest arrow so you never get lost or stuck, and the dumbed down dialogue and scripted out story feels like it was designed for console♥♥♥♥♥♥♥playing a movie game.  Without spoiling the story too much, some of the quest characters are plain annoying.  They are also immortal, so good luck killing them.  That's a big turn off for me right there.  Fallout 1 and 2 has no immortal characters.  Everyone is fair game, including children.  Some of the quest stories in this game are fun, but the main quest line and a great deal of the content, including the horrible DLC's are cliche, dull, or not immersive.  There are entire parts of this game that has meaningless content that I just want to skip, but cannot, because the story is linear and forces me to do these meaningless things.  For example, the minutemen.  I should not be limited to Preston Garvey, I should be able to form my own militia, or raider group, to fulfill the independent faction requirement.  Anyways, I felt trapped in another man's shoes, and not free to make my own choices.
That leads me to radiant quests.  Once again, Bethesda is recycling its radiant quest system from its earlier titles.  It's literally a pick a random location, add a random item to get, or random boss to kill.  The radiant system also applies to conquering settlements.  You are often tasked with rather annoying rescue missions or raider cleanse missions that require a great deal of walking, in order to liberate towns.  The content is cookie cutter and gets boring.  Several factions offer radiant quests.  I typically avoid the nonsense.
I picked up the season pass for this game and have been totally unimpressed with the lack of effort put into the quests for the DLC.  The voice acting and stories are garbage.  A lot of the DLCs feel like The Sims stuff packs.  It's just paid addons that don't really enhance the game all that much.
Voice acting.  Remember the voice actors from Oblivion?  Ever feel like those voices in Fallout 3 sounded familiar?  How about Skyrim, you notice some repeat characters?  Ah, Fallout 4...the king of using the same fricken voice actors for most generic NPCs and even major story characters.  I'm absolutely sick of hearing Joan Allen in every Bethesda title.  This is another penny pinching move by Bethesda, keep billing the same actors and reuse as much dialogue as possible.  It just kills my immersion when I hear a character and immediately recall a similarly voiced, even looking character from another game / genre.  Delphine from Skyrim is Desdemona in F4, fortunately, she was killable in the latter.
Town building: This was fun for a time, but the vanilla town construction was rather limited.  You can't build exactly where or what you want all the time, and you have to rely on console trickery to move pieces just right.  Mods help in this category.  In fact, mods and this game mode are why I spent so long playing Fallout 4.  Town building in Fallout 4 is pointless, but fun.  There are no real benefits to building a cool settlement.  It has zero impact on the main story, and there is no impact on regular settlements laden with NPCs.  IE, no diplomacy or trade options.  It's basically an empty feature that Todd Howard pitched as some latest and greatest cool thing they are doing in Fallout.
So in summary, I am not recommending this title because Bethesda is no longer capable of breaking new grounds.  They are recycling the same crap with each new release, half assing new game content, and are focused entirely on marketing and profit margins.  Once upon a time, Bethesda was making really cool and original games.  Now its lawyers do all the heavy lifting.  After this title, I believe I am finished with the Fallout franchise and the Elder Scrolls series.  Perhaps I will pick up the newer titles when the development cycles are completed, all DLC are released, cool mods are made, and the title with all addons is on sale for a bargain price.  I just feel taken advantage of everytime I buy Bethesda software, and the only real joy is user made content, which Bethesda is trying to cash in on, and will likely not allow in its future titles unless they can get money for it.

As an avid dinosaur lover, it disappoints me to no end to see how bare bones this game is. I was hoping that combat wouldn't be as simplistic as it would be in the isle, given that its contemporary possesses a far larger selection of playable dinosaurs, but nope, as of its current state, saurian is about as shallow as a drying puddle.
As a baby, any animal that is slightly larger than you can apparently reduce your bones to jelly with a single nip. While I don't mind the fact that you have to play as a vulnerable infant at the start of your journey, I am not cool with playing as an animal made of paper mache. Sure I can buy a crocodile mangling me within seconds if it got its jaws on me, its absolutely infuriating when a marginally larger acheroraptor drops you with a tap of its jaw. This game is supposed to strive for realism, yet there is little to no feeling of impact when animals enter conflict with one another in this game. When I attacked a acheroraptor, I expected to get bowled over and mauled, but instead I got slapped down like an underleved RPG character taking on a boss would.
This dissapointing combat system might be slightly more tolerable if it weren't for the fact that the only prey you can realistically hunt as an infant, barring exploitation of a the terrible ai, are tiny lizards, that are at least from my experience, litterally less common than eight ton t.rexes. So far, the only times I've been able to eat are when a t.rex randomly murders a pachy and walks away from the corpse without taking a single bite of it.
I realize that the devs put a lot of effort into making this game, but maybe instead of paying painstaking detail to recreating realistic flora at least 95 percent of people won't appreciate, more time could have been spent working on ai, combat, and adding more prey species for the early game.
I'll stick around just cause I am obsessed dinosaurs too much, but unless you share a similar devoted passion, this game would appeal to almost no one in its current form.

*No spoilers* - Edit: Finished the game.
This is hands down one of the best rpg's I've played and also one of my favorites. I'd really like to see this franchise do well and grow with sequels.
I'll start with saying I never played any other Tales game. But I've played other rpg's and this has the best battle system I've ever played, and it was really fun. The soulbreak mechanic was really fun, and the item dismantling/enhancments were a cool feature. I'd like to see them take it a step further with character equipment. It was cool seeing all the different types of weapons like the cards for Laphicete or the dolls for Maggie, and the daggers for Roku ect.
The story is awesome. I love the fact that its darker and it isn't predictable either. It has a really good story that captures you and emerses you into the world of Berseria. The characters are all really charming, some lovable and some not so much because they're evil. The cutscenes are awesome, and I'd love to see more of (the opening before the main menu for example was awesome). The soundtrack is good...a good soundtrack will always make games like these take off in my opinion.
I loved the artwork and design, everything from characters to places. I'd like to see more artistic detail put into the world in all aspects of the game (comparing to the art design of cities like FFIX) but overall they've done a really good job. I was really impressed with navigation through the game and how this developed.
I really enjoyed the length of the game, and it was important for me that it wasn't too short. I'd rather it be as long as possible. I'd like to see maybe more sidequests...I'm happy they included minigames in. I also like the fact that you can set the difficulty yourself at any time in the game and it can be more rewarding if its harder...having that flexibility to decide as an option is awesome. The game never made me want to stop playing.
Lastly, I was really excited that they added more content/dlc's into a game that already has a lot of content which was really refreshing to see. Sadly I beat it so fast, I think there's going to be more coming our way....Overall this was my first experience with a Tales game, and I'm happy to say it exceeded my expectations. I'm just sad its over. And I might give it another play through. I hope there's way more to come!

I am probably not far enough into the game to give a proper review, but so far I love this game. The story is dark and emotional (especially compared to Zestiria), and has great characters. JRPGs I typically find to have a lot of grinding, which is one thing I HATE about any RPG, but in Tales of Berseria I (so far) have not felt like I have to do any grinding. Yes, obviously there will be plenty of combat (which is more or less the same as Zestiria, except you can now freely move the camera), but you can avoid some of it and (again, so far) never feel like you have to back track and kill monsters over and over to level up. And unlike in many other RPGS, you feel like you are constantly progressing the story, as opposed to games like Elder Scrolls or Fallout, where most of your time is spent exploring and doing mostly meaningless side quests (those are still great games though). As far as the PC port goes, Tales of Berseria is excellent. While the Tales of Symphonia port was filled with technical issues (I haven't played it yet, but everyone seems to say the same thing about it), Berseria constantly runs at 60 FPS (you can change the cap between 30 and 60), and besides my controller (Xbox One controller) randomly stopping working while in game a couple times (unplugging and plugging back in normally fixed it), I have not had any crashes or bugs of any kind. There are a decent amount of graphics options, nothing mind blowing, but not a dissapointing lack of. Graphically, the game looks pretty nice with it's anime art style, and sometimes the environment looks beautiful, but when when you get up close to some things it will look a little ugly here and there.

I bought this game during the last Steam Summer Sale, and frankly, the fact that I paid anything at all for this rudimentary 'Zelda' parody makes me feel ripped off.
'Ittle Dew' is a 2D overhead adventure game designed as a blatantly-obvious homage to 'A Link to the Past'. Maybe "homage" is the wrong word, since many aesthetic elements are lifted straight from 'ALTTP'. A fact evident just by looking at 'Ittle Dew's' protagonist. It's a wonder Nintendo never sued.
While 'A Link to the Past' was a classic, fun, robust game that could hook first-time adventurers for dozens of hours, though, the world of 'Ittle Dew' is strangely barren. There's pretty much no story to speak of, zero character development. Combat is uninspired and suffers from hit detection issues when using certain weapons. Add to that, I managed to complete the game with every collectible in 7 hours on my first playthrough (that's IN SPITE of challening the secret extra cave). No multiplayer or DLC to extend the game's replay value either.
Funny thing is, 'Ittle Dew' seems to know it's lame, as the title is replete with self-aware, self-deprecating humor. So in summary:
Pros:
- Handrawn art style beautiful in its simplicity
- Ocassionally funny, self-aware dialogue
Cons:
- Obscenely short length
- No replay value (beyond a few Achievements)
- No plot
- Overeliance on block puzzles
- Hit detection issues
Conclusion: 'Ittle Dew' started out as a free game made using 'Game Maker', and that's how it should've stayed. Even if it has its charms, there's just too little content to justify paying $9.99 for.

An absolute blast, I loved every second. That said, everyone here has already sung its praises. I like to talk about game scripts and writing. So if you're looking for a full review, everyone else here has got a pretty good handle on what's good and bad about the game. I wanna talk about its writing.
Played it just coming off of Yooka Laylee, which had one of the worst scripts I've ever encountered in a game, but Ittle Dew is comparably comedic, childish and meta-oriented, with 4th-wall breaking jokes coming out of sardonic, goofy characters. The degree to which Ittle Dew trounces Yooka Laylee in its execution, however, is startling.
Ittle Dew's writing has three things going for it that make the script not just lovable and silly, but exceptional:
-A clever Double Act
-Unobtrusiveness
-A well-thought out balance of cynicism and heart.
A good Double Act is always based on the chemistry between two disparate characters. Abbott and Costello: A no-nonsense straight-man and a clowny, intentionally-frustrating goof. The reason they bounce off each other is because they can create increasing comedic energy from the simple act of interaction.
Straight man says a baseline for Goof to comment upon, which straight-man replies to with frustration, which goof replies to with knowing snark and back and forth, a consistent volley of energy that takes a decent amount of time to grow old because neither of characters ever venture into 'unlikeable'.
This disparate natures of Ittle and Tippsie are naive, curious energy and sarcastic, exhausted wit. Ittle can respond with curiosity, to which Tippsie responds with cynical resentment, to which Ittle responds with frustrated surprise, to which Tippsie responds with sarcastic acknowledgement, which is a funny volley over and over again, and because they're both characters who are, if not fleshed out, then at least well-established and full of interesting, fun characteristics.
As for unobtrusiveness: Ittle Dew's dialogue has a habit of appearing when a new enemy or concept is introduced and right before boss battles. Exceptions are rare. This means that dialogue only appears distinctly at moments when more information would be desirable and, very importantly, only while the game is continuing to be interesting. In the middle of a slow area, where frustration is high and concentration/patience is important, there is a 0% chance of dialogue interrupting anything or presenting itself as a time-waster.
Lastly: the game is very meta, but never at its own expense. It's a game who's storyline is "We've arrived on Video Game Island, I wonder what's in store for us", and while it makes a few cracks at typical genre conventions, it never accuses itself of not being fun (something that Yooka Laylee did fairly and unfortunately often), it takes as gospel the fact that the player has shown up to have fun and has a love for the genre, and thus mirrors the player's enthusiasm by taking loving jabs and a genuine enthusiasm for the premise and world and gameplay.
The ending is character-oriented, which may seem like a weird choice in a plot that's essentially non-existent, until you realize that without the formality of plot, the things we've grown to love over the game's runtime are the gameplay itself and the characters who were enjoying it.
It's a delightful game with a delightful story and it doesn't need to be any more than that. Hearty recommend.

Con:
Graphic, would have prefered good 2D-Art to bad 3D-Art
counterintuative UI, menus are unnecessarily split in two
repetitive combat, you have to dump a lot of skill points into your skills just to get more options than melee and ranged. The enemies are not very varied either.
Hitpoints are basically just another ressource you have to manage and combat is just a constant drain of said ressource and the only difference is how far you can go until your characters actually risk dying.
Getting ressources is largely limited to picking a location fighting the same enemies 10 times and if you still have enough hp you can fight another 10 harder recoulered enemies and hope they drop enough of what you need.
Crafting is very limited. One low quality item for each equipment slot and weapon type and a high quality counterpart.
The permadeath/save system is annoying: the game only saves at the beginning of the day. So if you are in the middle of a day and have to go do something else or your computer acts up you have to redo the whole day or end a day early just to save and quit. Their are better ways out there to make sure your players don't cheat the permadeath.
Quest(at least early on) are a nuisance that just interrupt your ressource gathering ( I need food so I want to go to the woods with 2 specific companions. No NPC x wants me to go to the highway for 3 encounters and then call it a day. And you have to go alone or with a companion you wanted to use for jobs today.
The rouguelike elements really don't fit a game like this. You get "medals" by completing achievements (kill 10 of enemy x)  you can use to buy stat boosts and unlock new character (you start with a weapon and a skill point in a skill instead without those). But since you end up doing the same thing all over again it's like you just wasted your time with the previous tries. I repeatetly killed myself on purpose(you can't end a game) just so I could save some time and get a better start.

XCOM is one of my favorite games and XCOM2 for sure is a very good game. The community is huge (over 13 000 people played the game while i wrote this review). I can't speak about the WOTC Add-On since I don't own it.
What is good?
+ Story
+ Visual impressive
+ A lot of different types of enemies with different attacking patterns and abilities
+ A lot of high quality animated video cutszenes
+ Maps are randomly generated ( I never played on one and the same map twice, except the last level)
+ the game doesn't drag on unneccesarily
+ Customization is very detaild.
What is bad? (Note: I describe what is weaker in this game that was better in the predecessor.)

- no clever base management is needed. (Excavate a slot and buy a new part of your base when you have resources for it. That's it. You don't need to pay attention to adjacency boni.
-The squad size is 4 in the beginning and can get up to 6. (same in XCOM enemy unknown but I wished for a bigger squad size).
- Development of your base or contacting all resistance cells isn't a must have to finish the game. Get the Shadow chamber stuff researched and you're good to go for the last mission. ( The game shoots itself in the foot with that, non of my soldiers could deploy psionic powers yet and I finished the game.
- The game crashes a lot. It crashes when you customize, It crashes in the aftermission video sequence, it crashes while in battle. It crashes that much that the crash report shown starts with "Hello Commander, your game crashed ..." I was confused whether this is part of the new XCOM experience or why do they call me commander on a crashreprot?
- There is no aerial battle mode anymore. It's been cut from the game completely. :(
- The abilities of the unites don't work together as good as they did in XCOM Enemy unknown. (Personal opinion)
All in all the game is good but the predecessor is better. In my eyes at least.

I have played this game since the Open-Beta, and I wish I knew I was able to connect Glyph with Steam in the past so this review can be taken in a more "Experienced" matter by having WAY more hours on it.
First off, the start of the game. In my experiences, it was basically a tutorial in a regular world with other players, but Trove at the present time has now made this private world to teach combat before things like mining, building, etc. The controls have just a little bit of a League of Legends feel (and yes I've played it, just on a friend's computer). Then we go to first impressions of the graphics. It's supposed to be another one of those "block games", so I have to admit I was unimpressed at first. Also, to anyone that says this is another Minecraft, you're literally an imbecile, the fact that a.) you've never played it, or b.) you've played it, but not all the way to where you can actually point out the things you think are negative about it. When I had the feel to attempt the game, it was actually alright. It was VERY laggy for me at first, but it became better when I played it constantly.
Now, the general "gameplay". Controls are pretty much easy to master. It's just your simple WASD with other keys that bring up things like the Marketplace. When you're a beginner, you're usually exploring stuff such as new biomes when you go to the new adventure worlds (after the Master Adventure World, it is the same biomes unless it is something like UBER-04 in which they added new worlds for specifically gems that they added). You also explore Trove's features like different classes, currency system, mastery, wings, fishing, and more that I could go in depth, but this isn't really a damn tutorial. Then when you play it for a while, you start getting into the difficult things like getting the right gear and focusing on stats. Trust me when I say this, you will need patience for this. I've played for a while with sort of long breaks at some parts and I only have 1 radiant weapon. And now that they added gems, you will also be hunting for the best ones you can get. You can purchase things for real money, but the majority of it is useless. The only reason I bought stuff is whenever there are sales. Now here comes the "combat" part. First off, shadow tower. This used to be only the Shadow Arena in Open-Beta that you find in Uber Worlds, but stuff changes. I would also talk about the early days of shadow tower, but I should probably focus on the one now. For every two levels of the Shadow Tower in every difficulty, your character, or "class" (classes act like separate characters/save files) needs to have a certain Power Rank, which depends on the equipment you have. For example, to go to the Spike Walker level on Normal Shadow Tower, you'll need a Power Rank of 500. In Ultra, it is 5000 to get the rewards. Then there's dungeons in the regular adventure worlds. It is basically a repeated process of getting loot for this. Enter, slay the boss, get the loot, go to the next one. For classes, I would recommend just exploring them yourself when going into the game so you can choose which class suites you the best (I main Chloromancer). Exploring classes was easier in the past since classes had the cost of only Cubits, but was techincally made pay to play (unlock in this case) due to only buying it with Credits. However, the game decides to give 2 free class coins to every new player, so don't worry about paying up front. I know there's PvP, but it is mostly just Capture the Flag against other players. Now the sandbox part of it. Although it requires somewhat more time and crafting than other games, players can create many great and "cool" things, like pixel art and music (they create these with noteblocks that activate when you step on them). In fact, one of my used to be active clubs had this fully finished instrumental songs with only the noteblocks the game provides.
Finally, players in general. Overall, other players are pretty chill and kind. In fact, some people stream and give away things for free like Balefire Wings Codes. They also offered advice which helps me a lot due to major updates compared to open-beta making me feel like a 69 year old man.
If you have read all of this, then thank you for spending time looking at this review for Trove and I hope this inspired you to either try it out or get you into it/back into it.

I enjoyed both of the reboot XCOM games, but after War of the Chosen, I cannot bring myself to recommend the game. War of the Chosen really brought home one of the biggest issues I have had with the game.
All a matter of price charged to content available. It keeps coming across as a hollow experience
War of the Chosen is a good example of the problem. It has good ideas in it, but they are not fleshed out enough to make it worth the price.
Take the Chosen, the core of War of the Chosen, apart from their appearances in the regular missions and their stronghold mission, you barely interact with them, and the mission to find them are boringly passive....Just wait for a few days to pass? So much more could have been done with them, Finding out who they were, how they became the Chosen, some history behind their weapons. There was so much wasted potential in the Chosen. Which is a shame, their design was interesting and the voice actors do a good job in giving them some life.
The factions are a similiar case. Interesting design, interesting abilities but the interactions with them as so passive , no story missions beyond the first one...Worse for the Templar who get no real introduction like the Reapers and the Skirmishers. Nothing is learnt about the origin of the factions, or about their leaders, which again is a shame because the brief snippets of voice acting you get for them is rather good.
The large amounts of passive downtime one gets during the game could really be one of its biggest flaws, so much time is spent on the Geoscape, just scanning little bits and pieces. I am sure some of that passive time could have been given over to a bit more story.
The same applies to The Lost, The Alien Rulers. Wasted potential.
Honestly, the only one I was too disappointed by was Shen's Last Gift, but even that was a case of wasted potential.
The biggest issue, in the end, is the price. £35 for DLC, when nothing provided in it altered the game play in any radical fashion, some nice new ways to vary the missions up a little, but so much of it was just adding more aspects that required you to wait.
Wait until  it comes down in price..£15 maybe....but beyond that, I cannot recommend it.
And, while I doubt anyone for Firaxis really reads these reviews, if someone is, please, reconsider your DLC practices for any future XCOM games, these games are good at their core, but the lack lustre DLC really does lower the overall quality.

After years of bad dinosaur game after bad dinosaur game... I am so happy that I can finally say that this game is enjoyable...
Now it's not perfect, it is incredibly clunky and poorly optimized, as well as that the AI is incredibly dumb... And yet it is still a fun game to play.
Some things that I really like about this game is the focus on realism while still striving to be a fun and enjoyable experience, far too many devs only go for one of these and the game can often suffer as a result.
Another thing is the music of this game is great, one momment it can be peaceful and relaxing and then the next you feel like you are playing a horror game.
This game is in a very early state and that is quite obvious, but what sets this aside from a couple other dinosaur survival games, is that they didn't use that as an excuse to release with actually nothing to do gameplay wise like another dinosaur game I had the displeasure of playing... Saurian actually has gameplay and goals to achieve, the most obvious goal is to survive and make it to adulthood, but there are also other things you could do such as try to get the achievents.
And finally I can say I do recommend this game, and as long as the devs keep at it I can see this becoming a great game.

It was a while before I could figure out what genre this game belongs in, it's frequently dubbed an Action-Adventure, RPG and Indie (in no way a genre) game, you know, the non-categories that it's easy to shove games into. Well it finally dawned on me. Bastion is a Hack & Slash game, and a damn good one. You progressively unlock and upgrade different weapons and  customize  the protagainist with one of many different possible loadouts and proceed to rip through many different enemy types with good varied AI. It's linear but rewards exploration, difficult but accessible, stylistically restricted but still grandeur. That's a description of a good Hack & Slash like God of War or Devil May Cry.
So the gameplay is solid. However, one couldn't possibly look at Bastion without noticing the narrative. It's not so much the concept for the game's story but its execution that's so good. The whole thing is implimented with the use of a brilliant naration and practically nothing else. The narrator, my favourite description of whom is Zero Punctuation's 'disturbingly sexy', comments on almost everything you do. Even the protagainist's thoughts are simply stated by the narrator. It's an odd, but pretty unique method and, combined with the music, just gives the game one of the best 'vibe's you'll ever come across.
Overall, very few faults, there are perhaps too many weapons, and there's a choice system that's a little annoying though it's barely present. It hardly matters though, they're vastly compensated for. The game is great, no question. Definitely worth playing.

First and foremost, this is a really fun game. It's got great atmosphere, music, story. You'll have a good time running through the game once, staying intrigued with the new areas and the narrator giving a running commentary. The option to play it casually makes it viable for most gamers.
The difficulty curve isn't that amazing, as it starts out relatively easy and just gets easier as you get access to better equipment. You could artificially make it harder by not upgrading and using sub-optimal weapons, but that's a decision neither to the game's credit nor detriment.
What really brings down the rating, and which is something you'll get annoyed by, is the sometimes lackluster controls. You'll encounter jumping enemies who make it look like you can roll under them, but you'll take damage from the air beneath them even though they'll dodge the same shots going under them. There's also an issue with defending in this game, as it's the same button as locking onto enemies. This is a problem as you'll sometimes lock on to the wrong enemy, causing your character to turn around and take damage from the shots you intended to block, waste your shots in the wrong direction and make you miss reflecting blows.
The controls are a major cause for frustration throughout the game, but for me, the upsides outweigh that downside. I'd recommend this game when it's on sale, as well as when you're looking for a solid story that's not epic, but well told and immersive.

This is probably my favorite game.  Despite it being about 2 years old at this point, it is still my go-to game and one I come back to time and time again.  Fallout 4 is a post-apocalyptic open world game that is completely addictive.  What I love about it is that it's a non-linear game that you can play so many different ways...  You could literally just explore and loot, complete quests, pick fights or sneak around them, build settlements and suits, collect and craft things, turn people into allies and enemies and so much more.  It makes the gameplay diverse enough that you don't get bored playing.  The aesthetic is this unique blend of futuristic and 1950s, which becomes it's own flavor of familiar. There are mixed reviews about the graphics, but I love that they weren't too over-the-top - not only does it go well with the retro feel of the game, but you don't have to deal with slow loading scenes and get to just play the game.  Instead they focused on things like character personalities and adding little easter eggs, like the quirky radio channels you can tune into.  I honestly can't say there is much I disliked realistically.  Mostly just little quirks with things like the default key configuration which can be customized.  Bottom line is it's the perfect game for someone who like flexibility and diversity in gameplay.

Solved a lot of the issues I had with Zestiria.  Battle camera is back to just being usual levels of Tales-janky rather than completely uncontrollable, characters are much more likable and less vapid, and world design is more detailed.  Not everying is great, though.  The dungeons are so far (five hours in) pretty bland, caves with different color palettes.  Performance is better, with a capped 60 fps mode, but it's a stuttery, poorly framepaced 60 fps on a 1070!
Having really been on a Nier kick lately, I appreciate the story for setting us as kind of the villains (like Nier, although perhaps less genocidal).  You're basically fighting the guys that have been the first thing to go even remotely right for the world.  I wouldn't call them good guys, not when they're fine with using magical children as mini suicide bombers to defeat their enemies, but they're about the only thing the world has representing stability, and we're setting out to destroy it.  It's an interesting predicament, because they're easy enemies to hate, but the game also does a pretty good job of illustrating all they've accomplished, and all the collateral damage our quest is going to cause.  Suffice it to say I'm looking forward to seeing more.
Would I recommend it?  Yeah, if the story looks interesting to you.  This is a genuinely competent addition to the series.  Use the mod on the forums to help with the framepacing issues, though, since BN is too incompetent to fix their own issues.

Ittle Dew is a top-down puzzle game with light action elements.  The game's main castle is non-linear, and depending on where you go, you can get money, which you use to obtain one of three pieces of equipment.  The equipment can be used to advance further, get more equipment, and so on.  The non-linear design guarantees that everyone can approach the game in a variety of ways.  This brings a surprising amount of replayability to what would otherwise be a linear game.
The primary focus of the gameplay is in the puzzling.  The puzzles are well thought-out, and even if you know you have the right equipment to solve a particular room, it can require a clever approach and out of the box thinking to advance.  Most of them use elements of sliding block puzzling, but thanks to the unique elements of the game, they feel like much more.
The humor is great as well.  While the game is excellent from its level design and puzzles, the humor is the cherry on top that makes it a masterpiece.  The sound and art contribute to the theme, and I can't possibly recommend this game enough.
If you want puzzles, this game will scratch that itch.  If you want action, while it has some of that, it's not going to put up that much of a challenge.  Either way, pick it up.  You will be surprised that more games aren't like this one.

An example of how solid core gameplay can be tainted by the game's presentation.
Intrusion 2 is a run-and-gun game channeling the likes of Contra, Metal Slug, and countless flash games on Newgrounds. The grab here is that most of the trappings in a level have physics to them, from the crates to suspended logs, that you can manipulate to your advantage.

Sounds like a solid idea on paper, but the first problem in the execution here is that the object physics do more harm than good. Their primary use is to shield you from fire, which is practically a requirement for survival in the second boss fight. Unfortunately, you have very little means of manipulating objects. You can only walk towards an object to push it, and shoot it to give it a little more momentum if needed. Crates and the like make effectivive means of cover, but only in a "heat-of-the-moment" kind of way. You could never plan out your own crate protection fort because you don't have enough control over objects to plan something like that. All of these moveable crates, as well as debris from defeated mechanical enemies,  start to pile up and have a tendency to block off ammo pickups or a paths.
Throughout the game you can pilot other means of transport. There's an oversized wolf, a gunner mech, and a similar-looking mech but with a sword and claw that can grab and shoot things. The wolf controls are easily the worst in the game, featuring the inability to turn around fast and sudden stops for seemingly no reason. The mechs controls are more adequate and it does feel slightly empowering when you pilot them.
The game's sound design is flaccid. The levels' music is quick to loop and there's only the bare minimum for sound effects. The ninja-type enemies in one level had their own sound effect, but every other enemy is silent. Voice effects would have helped craft a unique personality to the mech enemies in the game. The soundtrack ramps up during boss fights, but the dearth of sound effects gives off a sense of emptiness.
The game ran sluggishly in full-screen mode. Only when I switched to windowed mode did it run at 30 fps, which it is apparently locked at. I'm not someone who thinks anything under 60 fps is unplayable but I find it odd that a game in such a face-pasted genre would restrict itself to 30 fps.
Overall, the game is okay. It's a decent challenge and can produce some intense moments. Unfortunately, rather than top the likes of Metal Slug, it just makes me want to go play that instead.

Note: This review is focused on me reviewing the game itself, not the marketing, not the developers, just the game in it's definitely not a game for everybody, it can be boring, repetitive, and sometimes downright frustrating, but when it is not those things is when it shines the most. The feeling of exploring a planet you know nobody has been to before, or even the rarer instance of finding a planet someone else has traversed, and seeing the things they have lovingly named after their favorite parts of human anatomy can feel absolutely wonderful. Finding a beautiful, lush, tropical planet is a great reminder of how amazing this game can look, not to mention that the music system is very well done.
Blockade 3D is a very relaxing game about exploration and survival in a procedurally generated universe, and that is what it accomplishes (Granted the survival in the current state is pretty trivial). Early on, the game is very grindy, and exploration can be annoying until you learn how to manage your inventory, along with learning what is and is not important.
Now, at present, the game still has plenty of problems. If you plan on buying the game, I recommend waiting until Hello Games releases a couple more patches to smooth out more of the performance issues some players are having, and if you are expecting a lot of things to DO, you should probably wait until more content is added later down the road.
I am still enjoying the game after over 60 hours of playing, and after reaching the center, and expect to continue to do so with future updates and content. The modding community for this game seems to have potential to do a lot with this game, and I look forward to watching the progress of that as well.
If I had to rate this game, I would give it a 7/10 : Not for everyone

Welcome to my review on The Walking Dead
*Background*

The game is based off on the television and comic books of the same name, The Walking Dead. Though, the game may exist in the same universe as its other counter parts, the game follows another set of characters surviving in the disaster that is the game's universe. Our main character is Lee, a convicted fella going to jail after murdering a senater for reasons unknown until playing the game. He takes care of a young girl he found while finding help, Clementine. The game revolves around the decisions you made in episodic format and you can only trust who you think are you're friends. With the decisions, you have to live with it and having a girl around you to protect, thats gonna be a hard choice. But you can always expect this kind of gameplay with the creators of the game, Talltele Games, with how detailed they are with their dialouge. TallTele Games made a great effort and making me want to buy the second or even third game when I'm done with finishing the game.
*Gameplay*
The gameplay is all about the dialouge and the choices you made during the storyline that could change how the game plays for your playthrough. Their would be a lot of dialogue during the entire story and talking to your other fellow survivors is the key to who woud lives, dies or be an ally to you during the last episode. The dialogue is very important to how it plays and even the littiliest of choices has a big impact on the story, like if you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off someone by your opinions and then later on they're still be mad about what you said. The biggest of decisions are always told to you at the end of the episode and you can see what percentage of people sided with you on your decisions. The biggest decisions tells you what happens and how your characters can adapt to your decisions, TellTale Games did a great job on the dialogue and how it effects your playthrough. The other gameplay is point-and-click, its how you do certain actions and can react to fast pace actions when it occurs. Both of these gameplays help bring this game to life and it makes me feel like I have a big part into the sayings of what happens to the characters. They are the big engines that keep this game going and I'm a proud passenger of that engine.
*Story*
Our main character is Lee, an African man being brought in to jail after murding a senator for reasons explain in the game. After some nice chat with a police officer, they get hit by a Walker and crazing down at the side of the freeway. Lee wakes up hours later and find himself in the car as the officer's body lay motionless on the ground. Finding a way out and killing the officer's animated corpse later, Lee try to find help in a house he happens to be at their backyard after jumping the fence like a criminal. He looks around the insides of the house while hearing the phone machine goes, Lee founds a Walkie-Talkie and becomes the guardian of a little child name Clementine, after killing her dead babysitter. This game is rather fantastic for the limitations of the engine. It really does a lot with a little, and that's one of the biggest advantages to this game. It innovates with so little.

Half-Life put first person shooters in the limelight. Sure, this game is by no means the first of its kind. There were plenty of FPS games before, and there will be plenty that come after. But few will reach to the standards of quality set by this game. This game came out in 1998, and it just goes to show how prophetic this game is that it still holds up a decade plus later. Few games could even dream of being relevant a few years later, with how fast things are moving now.

Any run of the mill FPS game can rattle off the industry standard arsenal; the bad guys, the bombs, the grenade throwing shotgun blasting yehaw games that we've all played a thousand times by this point. It takes serious effort to innovate. Do anything new and exciting. By this point, we've seen so much of the same. You know what would really be super? To look at a game made in a time when these rules were still being written. You didn't need fancy particle effects, slowdown bullet time, or any of the gratuitous garbage you would see in any dime a dozen unity project.

Half-Life is a simple game about escaping Black Mesa. That's it. You play as a dude with a crowbar and a suit of armor. It's just so hard to express how engrossing this game is, especially after a few hours of gameplay. Its easy to forget that you're essentially walking down hallways, jumping across rooms with one entrance and one exit, and fighting the same enemies. Its just, the game executes everything to well that none of it's limitations matter. Barney is every security guard? Doesn't matter. Don't know where to go? Doesn't matter. The graphics aren't that impressive anymore? Doesn't matter. You can honestly forgive a lot solely on how amazingly smooth the gameplay is. It's rock solid except for the spare few times I got stuck in a wall or crashed the game. For a game this large, that's an achievement.

This game is nowhere near perfect. Not even close. I think an argument can be made that the silent protagonist trite can be traced all the way back to the grand daddy himself. I think my only other major complaint is that the game starts to drag it's feet in maybe the last hour of gameplay. Right up to the final boss. The muddy textures don't do the game a lot of favors when they're stretched and repeated. Nor does the level design at that point. It's a bit of slow down in what otherwise is an amazing experience.

This is a classic. I'm glad to have played it. Not only that, but I recommend anyone who is mildly interested in FPS games to try it out. It's the great grand dad of them all. It just does so much perfectly.

I enjoyed both of the reboot XCOM games, but after War of the Chosen, I cannot bring myself to recommend the game. War of the Chosen really brought home one of the biggest issues I have had with the game.
All a matter of price charged to content available. It keeps coming across as a hollow experience
War of the Chosen is a good example of the problem. It has good ideas in it, but they are not fleshed out enough to make it worth the price.
Take the Chosen, the core of War of the Chosen, apart from their appearances in the regular missions and their stronghold mission, you barely interact with them, and the mission to find them are boringly passive....Just wait for a few days to pass? So much more could have been done with them, Finding out who they were, how they became the Chosen, some history behind their weapons. There was so much wasted potential in the Chosen. Which is a shame, their design was interesting and the voice actors do a good job in giving them some life.
The factions are a similiar case. Interesting design, interesting abilities but the interactions with them as so passive , no story missions beyond the first one...Worse for the Templar who get no real introduction like the Reapers and the Skirmishers. Nothing is learnt about the origin of the factions, or about their leaders, which again is a shame because the brief snippets of voice acting you get for them is rather good.
The large amounts of passive downtime one gets during the game could really be one of its biggest flaws, so much time is spent on the Geoscape, just scanning little bits and pieces. I am sure some of that passive time could have been given over to a bit more story.
The same applies to The Lost, The Alien Rulers. Wasted potential.
Honestly, the only one I was too disappointed by was Shen's Last Gift, but even that was a case of wasted potential.
The biggest issue, in the end, is the price. £35 for DLC, when nothing provided in it altered the game play in any radical fashion, some nice new ways to vary the missions up a little, but so much of it was just adding more aspects that required you to wait.
Wait until  it comes down in price..£15 maybe....but beyond that, I cannot recommend it.
And, while I doubt anyone for Firaxis really reads these reviews, if someone is, please, reconsider your DLC practices for any future XCOM games, these games are good at their core, but the lack lustre DLC really does lower the overall quality.

I need to preface this by stating that I can -only- reccomend purchasing this if your intent is to wait for the game to be completed and treat it as a preoder, because as it stands the game is virtually unplayable. I have enough respect for the developers and their passion to create an accurate look on how dinosaurs should and deserve to be protrayed that I'm holding off giving it a negative review. With that out of the way, time for the actual review of the current state of the game.
In Saurian, you currently join the game as a male or female infant raptor, and must grow up to survive. On paper this sounds like it could be fun, but unfortunately it doesn't have enough content or real depth to be enjoyable. As a hatchling your parents and siblings will either completely ignore you or try to kill you, so your only gameplay is hunting lizards, which are rare enough to make most of the time spent in this state wandering in search of them. While the game does have a prey tracking mechanic, it can only be used at extremely close ranges and as such only helps if you are already near a target as opposed to looking for one.
As you get older, you can hunt an additional two or three animals and that's it. The amount of dinosaurs in game is quite small right now, you get a T.rex, Triceratops, Pachycephalosaurus, two types of raptors and while they don't technically count a croc and a lizard. The larger species predominantly ignore you so in a way I feel like they should have focused more on species that you could interact with as the first playable.
I wouldn't mind the lack of variety if the AI was engaging, but frankly it's terrible. It might be better than say, Ark, but it's deeply troubling when a game that had immersive AI has a major selling point has AI that is so basic. AI predominatly stands in one place and occasionaly moves to a new place slightly to the left. Eating and drinking are extremely rare behaviors for ai, and they almost never interact with each other. Raptors and herbivorous Pachycephalosaurs have no problem being two feet from each other, and T.rex and Triceratops generally don't seem to perceive each other. In the rare case that AI does interact with each other, it's not very interesting because one always one shots the other; if a rex and a trike fight one always instantly kills the other. I understand that so early on they might not have unique combat systems or animations yet but it would be far more exciting to see an actual fight between dinosaurs.
As you get older you really don't change much other than visually. Genders don't have a meaning yet and again outside of hunting there is nothing to do. Hunting itself is not very enjoyable because, as said earlier, combat is largely one sided. As a raptor anything smaller than a pachy is an easy kill, and a pachy is still an easy kill unless it can turn fast enough to hit you, at which case it one or two shots you. Calling it hunting also seems a poor choice when the AI do not run away outside of the lizard; they ignore you until you start the fight with the exception of the T.rex which will sometimes call out when it detects you.
It has to be said that the game's performance is awful; While my computer is not the most recent model it can run most games on high or very high at good FPS, but even on very low this game runs at less than 30 fps if nothing is going on. If a fight starts or the area is foliage heavy, it goes to maybe 5-15. Saurian's graphics really aren't that great at the moment so I am not sure the cause of this.
Lastly, while the game devs clearly care about the project it's only been updated twice since release about a month and a half ago or so, and one of those was just to fix major bugs like falling through the ground and launch crashes which frankly had no right being present on release, even for an early access game given the amount of testers were avaliable.
That's not to say the game is -terrible-. The music is great and I love the idea and concept, and as I said before the developers clearly care about the project and I have faith that they will improve, and I have no problem with spending the money I did to ensure it's development.
If you love dinosaurs I reccomend buying as a pre-order, but the game as it stands at the moment the review was written is nearly unplayable due to terrible performance, bugs, poor ai systems, and lack of overall content and gameplay features.

After more than 500 hours of gameplay, I could not decide as to whether or not I like this game. Even now, I still ponder whether or not Fallout 4 could be considered a positive addition to the series, especially coming into Fallout 4 as someone who loved the older games, 3, and NV.
Gunplay is great, there are tons of weapons to choose from which consist of small firearms, explosives, large weapons, melee weapons, and energy weapons. There is a large assortment of satisfying guns to choose from, and it would take alot of time to get bored with every weapon. Each one comes with a nice selection of weapon modifications, including scopes, silencers, and magazines. of course, we had this feature in Fallout: New Vegas too- but what sets this game and NV apart, is the fact that you could take one weapon such as a Plasma rifle, and turn it into a new weapon with a completely different use, like a Plasma flamer. I thought this idea was ingenius, and it should have been expanded upon more. The same goes for Armor, though Armor modifications are a bit more limited- they offer new ways of making your life easier in the commonwealth, such as increased carry weight, damage resistance, and other such benefits.
Settlement building at times, is a bit annoying with the large restrictions on where you can, or where you can't place objects. It almost feels like there are invisible forcefields around each object, making it impossible to place another object close to something you've already built. This becomes quite apparent when building walls using the game's junk walls- there will be gaps all over the place, which may bother some players like me who like to spend alot of time in their settlements. To make settlement building more enjoyable, I would recommend Sim Settlements. An amazing mod, which has been hailed as what settlement building should have been in this game.
This brings me onto my biggest issue with Fallout 4. There is a sense of laziness from Bethesda when it comes to game-breaking bugs, crashes, and stability. The UI is awkward, and many features outside of crafting feel unpolished. Much of the lore in the previous games feels ignored also, resulting in many hardcore fans who enjoy such things to be upset at Bethesda. Many people have cited "who needs polish when we have modders?" as being one of Bethesda's new taglines, and it honestly does feel like Bethesda is relying more and more on it's modding community to make their games better.
I can honestly say, that without the modding community- this game would feel quite bland and dull. Which is one of the reasons I do not recommend this game. If you plan to use mods, then you will have a blast- but I must insist that Bethesda should move away from this mentality, and look towards overhauling their engine and polishing their games more. This is why I cannot give this game a positive review, as without mods- this game feels like a big step down from Fallout: New Vegas, and Fallout 3, especially if you're going in expecting a fantastic RPG.
Creation club woes, we all have opinions on Bethesda's new paid mods. I am of the opinion that no matter what Bethesda brands them, they are indeed just paid mods still. I was actually a supporter of paid mods at first, intent on them being a great way for us to have epic, large scale quest lines, new lands, and incredible amor sets made by Fallout's extremely dedicated fanbase. However, this did not become a reality, as most of the paid mods on offer are of low quality, and certainly not worth the price of admission. Of course, there is the argument that one is not forced to purchase these mods- however, that will not stop people having an opinion on them. And my general opinion is negative, not because I have to spend money, but because the items on sale are poor as previously stated, I was also hoping for more lore-friendly additions to creation club, and was not particularly impressed when I came to learn that Bethesda spent development time creating the Doom Marine armor, and the BFG.
Personally, I would have liked to have seen large scale DLC-sized quest mods, such as Far Harbor, or perhaps weapons and armor packs- consisting of many sets of weapons and armor. I feel that would be far more worth it.
