There are two responses I get, without fail, every time I try to get someone new to play this game. "I don't like the art style," or "I've seen the Escapist Arcade version - NO THANKS."  I'm guilty of both of these myself.  But if there's one thing I need to stress before even getting started on this review, it's that the Escapist Arcade version is NOT Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition. For the love of god, PLEASE do not think it is.  If you've suffered the misfortune of seeing some of the Escapist Arcade content, just erase it from your mind and start fresh.  They butchered it - there's really no other way to put it.  They cut gameplay, changed the dialogue to fit a MUCH younger and apparently far less intelligent audience (almost insultingly so), gave the characters RIDICULOUS voices, and pretty much watered down the game as a whole.  The mobile version has done a much better job so far from what I've seen, but regardless, playing this on Steam, in its original Japanese form with subtitles, is really the way to go.
As for the art style, it's true, it's completely different from almost anything else I've seen.  Much more "cartoonish" and maybe not what you'd expect from a video game.  Despite that, you end up loving it.  I wouldn't even say that you have to "get used to it" because it's not something that detracts from the rest of the game in any way.  It didn't even take me five minutes before I was thoroughly enjoying it and seeing it as a fresh, new style, exciting almost and unlike anything I'd experienced before.  Now, some 90 minutes later, I can't remember ever NOT liking it, or even why I would have.
Especially now with Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition being played in high definition, the art is crisp, clean, colorful - VERY sharp and wonderful to look at.
Now that we've got those two points out of the way... (minor spoilers below)
Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition is actually one of the best games I've ever played, PC/console or otherwise.  The plot is pretty basic at first.  You have just set out on your own to find the legendary treasure 'hat' and become a man with a hat, and you're looking for more hats to fall from the sky.  You'll find yourself falling in love with each and every new hat as you find them.  They're all extremely well developed, with interesting backgrounds and unique, fun personalities.  They form one very quirky collection that's always defining new fashion styles and somehow getting your character into trouble as they strive to achieve their dreams.  Each main hat story arc introduces new minor characters as well, and they're just as much fun and easy to fall in love with as the first hat.  Not one character is left out or feels like they're there for no reason.  Every hat has a purpose and adds to the storyline, and one of the really cool things about Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition is that these 'purposes' often resurface at later points in the game.  No detail is left untouched, and you'll seriously be amazed by the way Yahtzee's presence threads together plots and characters and blends all their stories perfectly the more the game progresses.
The plot itself, though fairly straightforward at first like I said, quickly evolves into something HUGE.  Much of the beginning of the game is dedicated to gathering hats and letting you get to know them, though it's definitely never lacking in action, but once you fall in love with Hat-Chan after an emotionally wrenching section of Wonderful Headgear Romance, you're swept up in adventure after adventure and following some of the most fantastic sections you'll ever play.  The battles and fights are well-paced, with the final boss fight almost always being completely EPIC.  But even through the action, Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition never quite loses it's lighthearted, humorous edge.  The game is sprinkled with PLENTY of funny moments, never too many and never too few.  There's always a wonderful balance of action and humor.
Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition also has its fair share of heart-wrenching moments that I referenced earlier, which may take you by surprise!  There are some EXTREMELY powerful scenes and gameplay sections that kind of blindside you and leave you wondering when you became quite so emotionally attached to certain characters or other things.  I've definitely found myself near tears or actually crying at more than one point.  Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition has it all - amazing characters, the never-ending yet never TOO over-the-top humor, exciting battles, fun adventures, heartbreaking moments with quick to follow touching moments.  And underneath everything, there's always the theme of friendship and teamwork, of working to reach your dreams and helping those closest to you achieve theirs, of growing and maturing as a person and discovering the power within yourself to overcome obstacles of any sort, of just BEING THERE for the rest of your hats when they need you - of being ace pilot Jake Starbone.
In a word, Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition is perfect.  And perhaps I'm just biased, being an obviously OBSESSED fan at this point, haha, but what can I say?  It's been on Steam for almost two years so far at time of writing this review and not ONCE have I wondered or hoped that it would start to reach an end.  It is, simply put, amazing.
So why should you play Zero Punctuation: Hatfall - Hatters Gonna Hat Edition?
Because you're missing out on one hell of a fantastic gaming experience if you don't at least give it a try.

All though the basic premise behind this game is interesting, the actual delivery is let down by some frustrating controls. Mainly the use of the camera to create platforms, which you need to complete the levels. The taking and placing of these platforms is often finnicky and imprecise. And that is using a controller. Using K&M the mechanic often won't work at all, or only after multiple presses.
And even when it does work the controls feel floaty and impresice. So if you don't have a controller, do n ot buy this as it is more frustration than fun.
However even if you do have a controller, the overall empty feel of the game, the imprecise mechanics and the decent if samey art makes this one to pick up on a sale only or if your a hardcore pixel art platformer fan. If you're not, then there are far better pixel art platformers on steam to introduce to the genre.

Tales of Berseria is a great game. It may start slow, but it quickly reminded me why i'm so addicted to the Tales series, the loveable characters and the fun interactions between them. Listening to every dialogue is a blast, every character has it's own feelings and personality, there are many funny moments, happy moments and yes, some sad ones too. I found the plot properly written and interesting compared to the previous installment, Zestiria.
While the combat is great and the machines work for the most part, it does get very repetitive and even tedious at some point. But then again, that's where the story and characters come in. Despite the game's repetitive nature, it never felt like a "chore", the story drives the player from start to finish, every battle feels like it has a purpose. The story development is steady and while the game might just be a bit too long (took me about 45 to 50 hours), the story never really loses it's pacing.
Yes, Tales of Berseria does have it's fair share of flaws, as you can already see in other reviews around here, like the somewhat lacking level design and the repetitive gameplay. But overall, it was a very fun adventure, an experience, and a one that I won't be forgetting anytime soon.
Highly recommended to anyone who likes RPG's with grindy combat and fun story, even for that who never played a Tales game before, it's a fine place to start.

I'm a sucker for games like this, business management sims.  This is hands down the deepest of the bunch.  I have played Game Dev Tycoon, and while that game is fun, it's very simple.  Also, my biggest pet peeve with GDT was that, absent mods, the popularity of the systems was easy to anticipate.  The nintendo-like console would succeed, the dreamcast-like console would fail, the same topics and genres went well together.
Mad Games Tycoon fixes this problem by giving you an option for randomizing the popularity different platforms and topic/genre combinations.  This means that every play through can be completely unique.  I love the engine optimization, and that you can sell your engine and actually make money off it.  I love the fact that I get to choose the layout of my office, hire as many people I want, the game is great.
To give an example of depth, when you get big enough, you can start producing your own games.  This isn't as simple as choosing self-produce.  You have to have a production room and buy production machines to make the games.  Then you have to have a storage room to store the copies.  Then you have to choose how many copies of the game you are going to produce.  You don't want to produce too many, cause then you'll have huge stacks of the game sitting on shelves, but if you don't produce enough, you won't be able to meet demand and you'll be losing money.  You have to watch the sales of the game and watch the amount of copies of the game you have on hand, so if supply starts running low, you have to produce more.
This is just one example of the complexity and depth of this game.  I love it.  It's my new addiction.

A masterful parody of the 2D Legend of Zelda games, ittle Dew (lowercase i) takes the well-known item-based puzzle solving of the series and polishes it to a mirror shine, wrapped up in a cheerful and smoothly-animated art style, while layering on enjoyable helpings of wry wit as it pokes fun at traditional video game conventions.  Who keeps putting hearts into rocks, anyways?
ittle Dew never wastes time and is built as tight as a drum.  There’s no sprawling overworld, no overly dramatic plot, and no tedious filler; it gets in, delivers the puzzles, and gets out before wearing out its welcome.  The game is comprised of three short item dungeons (which can be completed in any order), a dozen or so optional puzzle rooms, and a central non-linear castle that is revisited multiple times as the player gains more items.  A first run through the game is a casual five hours (more if going for all the secrets), and optional second-run challenges are also available for the minimalist and speedrunning players.
The puzzles are a masterwork in this game, relying only on simple tasks (i.e. push a block onto a button) with simple rules (i.e. ice blocks slide until they hit something) that are easy to understand but take careful planning to execute.  Puzzles squeeze every bit of use out of all the items and mechanics presented; rarely will a player encounter the same type of puzzle twice, keeping the game fresh and interesting.  However, a warning:  while the game does give vague hints, some of the more complex item mechanics are never explicitly explained, occasionally leading to seemingly impossible tasks until trial and error leads to a eureka moment.  Fortunately, the worst of these are confined to the Master Dungeon, an optional end-game challenge for people who LIKE impossible tasks.
If any nitpick could be made of the game, it would be that the enemies just feel sort of “there”; a necessary construct of the game’s Legend of Zelda roots, but ultimately little more than an annoyance that detract from the puzzle-solving focus of the game.  Common baddies move slowly, deal low damage, and are easily dispatched, while the three item dungeon bosses are largely uninspired, requiring simple puzzles to be solved while dodging their predictable attacks.  The final boss fortunately bucks this trend and is a frantic and satisfying exclamation point to the game.

Preface: Be advised that this is not a "Zelda clone", but it does fall into the "puzzle dungeon" genre. It leans heavily into complex single-room puzzles with minimal combat. Contrast this with: Zelda's simpler, but multi-room puzzles, with casual-but-competent combat; and Darksiders' more refined combat and more focus on platforming.
Novel and fresh take on an abused and neglected genre.
Some highlights of particularly strong game design:
* Each puzzle feels fresh. Particularly impressive given the amount of them
* Comedic elements are light and witty, without trying to steal focus from the experience
* Difficulty curve is smooth, with a good pacing of optional mini-puzzles along a parallel difficulty curve
* At end of game, meaningful replay value in the form of multiple "low %" completion routes are made clear to the player
* Optional end-dungeon "Master Cave" adds a new level of complexity to the fundamentals
* Game intentionally avoids putting rewards in places that can be missed
* No meaningful padding or filler, all content is quickly reachable from the center of the world
* Death (though an extremely rare occurence as hazards are not the focus of the game) is not punishing, and just throws the player back at the start of the current room with minimal delay
* I'll say it: better puzzle and dungeon design than any Zelda game. Puzzle elements are clearly identifiable, and multi-room puzzles are EXTREMELY rare (and when present, are simply that a room transition is one-way, which is always reasonably obvious)
Some nitpicks to improve on:
* Zelda Link to the Past has a superior melee attack, in that it hits in a wide arc. Ittle Dew's feels clunky in comparison. Thankfully, combat is not a focus for the vast majority of the game. But...
* Final boss has a very "twitch action-game" phase when compared to the rest of the game, and thus unfairly gates players to completion by requiring a skillset they didn't sign up for, and the game didn't ramp them up to
* "Master Cave" boss is devoid of puzzle elements entirely, and REALLY feels out of place in the game as a result
I would consider this game to be mandatory reference material for all developers in the "puzzle dungeon" genre.

This is definitely my top favourite tycoon game. I've played this many a time into the early morning. The devs have actively been updating the game fairly often throughout early access and it's just gotten better and better.
It's kind of a cross between Hospital Tycoon and Game Dev Tycoon. GDT is still one of the better game dev games out there and I enjoyed that but find that MGT just has so much more to offer.
You start out in a garage in the early 80's and slowly build up your game dev business. You can move into bigger buildings, research numerous topics and techs. You can build consoles, develop game dev kits, games, do programming or game dev contracts, and/or publish games. When you have enough money, you can also start buying out other game companies. I really enjoy that there are various ways to build your business although I usually end up with creating dev kits, then moving on to a combination of production or game dev.

It's fun, addictive, high replay value, has a large number of topics and techs to research. Highly recommended if you like management games, and if you liked GDT, then this is that but so much more. Highly recommended.
Also just a big thank you to Eggcode for a great game and all the effort you put into it.

Not kidding, this is the best naval action game published so far.
I have discovered this game on Kickstarter a long time ago.
All backers were invited to play the alpha, which I joined since the first day.
I followed the game through it's development.
Of course the alpha versions of the game were a bit buggy but the testers have pretty much gotten rid of every bug in the game.
This is not a realistic game, the development was focussed on gameplay.
When joining a server you can choose a team (if not unbalanced).
Within that team you can choose a crew to be part of.
Every crew votes a captain.
The captain takes the wheel and controls the ship and sails.
The rest of the crew has to do tasks like:
Repairing the ship, using the hammer, fixing the holes in the ship.
Hoaling supplies, going to the back of the ship to get a crate, bringing it towards the ammo boxes near the cannons.
Reloading a cannon, put gunpowder in the cannon, put a round shot in there, ram it with the rod.
Firing cannons, using the ignition stick, wait for the ship to line up and light the fuse.
Repairing the sails, climbing the nets on the side, using the hammer to patch the holes in the sails.
Shooting anti sail cannons, slowing down the enemy ship by aiming at it's sails.
Shooting swivel guns, a gun with low penetration and a little difficult to aim but it makes one shot kills.
Boarding, prepare your muskets, pistols and swords, as soon as the enemy ship is nearby or within swimming distance, board the ship and kill everyone repairing the ship.
Currently the game offers 2 ships:
The hoy, which is a smaller ship for about 7-9 players with 4 cannons on each side, the hoy turns quickly and sails fast.
The galleon is the bigger ship that requires at least 7 players to have an advantage on a hoy, the ship has 8 cannons on each side (16 both sides), 2 bow chasers and 2 stern cannons. Being a little slower than the hoy, it can deal a lot of damage.
The game has a few game modes:
Hoy vs Hoy: 8 players fight 8 players on a hoy, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink the ship to win.
Galleon vs Galleon: A 15 players fight 15 players on a galleon, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink the ship to win.
2 Hoy vs 2 Hoy: 2 hoys with 8 players on each team, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink enough ships to win.
2 Galleon vs 2 Galleon: 2 galleons with 13 players on each team, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink enough ships to win.
Fleet: One galleon and two hoys vs one galleon and two hoys, deplete enemy reinforcements or sink enough ships to win.
PROs
- Completely debugged in closed alpha
- Most stable early access release I've seen so far
- Fun community
- Skill based, no level advantages, only cosmetics
- Game being updated regularly
- Developers are actively responding to feedback from the community
- Hilarious moments (example: see H2ODelirious on Youtube, Venalis_21 on Twitch)
CONs
- Not fun without headset
- People might rage on the losing team
- Not many ship models, these will be added in the future
- No progression, only cosmetics have to be unlocked.

TL;DR: 6/10. Great game for XCOM fans, lots of technical problems and bugs. Mods save this game.
This is a great game, I absolutely love XCOM games. It is interesting to play, it has lots of gameplay mechanics and lots of replayability, it has some notion of story that is interesting to follow the first playthrough (though this game is absolutely not about story). The WotC DLC added a lot to the game so it feels fresh and entertaining. There are plenty of reviews out there, so everyone knows what XCOM is.
My gripe with this game is simple: LOTS of bugs and poor performance. I initially bought this game on its launch and it wasn't pretty then. The performance was awful, the frame rate was all over the place and up to second long stuttering was happening all the time. The load times were way too long for my system. The game was buggy, the most innocent bugs being visual and physics (e.g. unnatural behavior of bodies and objects after death or explosions). Missing or inappropriate animations (guns shooting sideways or through walls, grenades exploding immediately after the shot because the game doesn't know how it's supposed to fly to the target, windows breaking before the soldier hits it before shooting - the list is endless). The most annoying bugs were affecting the gameplay, like missing or incorrect indication of when your unit reveals the squad. But the game was interesting and new and I was willing to give it some slack for teething problems. I finished it as it was and forgot about it.
Fast forward 1.5 years, WotC DLC comes out with lots of new stuff. I install the game and what do I see? Nothing changed. Same performance, same visibly streaming textures. You'll have to fiddle a lot with graphics settings in order to reduce the insane memory consumption (16GiB RAM is *not* enough for this game on its max!) and make frame rate more stable and acceptable. Load times got a lot shorter, but most of the time you're staring at the black screen instead of the mission brief - not a welcome change, IMHO. The game occasionally crashes, especially with some mods. And you'll want to mod this game because mods are the way to fix gameplay bugs and make the experience a little less miserable. I mean game mechanic bugs here, like ammo types not working for Face Off. The physics, animation and visual bugs are still there as well, if not more, and unfortunately not fixed by mods. Alien turns have a chance to hang or get stuck in the slow motion. Firaxis, what were you doing those 1.5 years?
Initially, I downvoted the game because its technical execution is awful. It's a great game, but the bugs ruined it for me. Then I tried modding it and tried different graphics settings and it became more playable. So if you're into modding and don't mind tweaking game settings for it to run relatively smooth then this is a great game with a lot of fun. Just don't expect it to be a butter experience and assume the game will cheat you more than once because of bugs.

Just finished the primary game and had a blast with this turn-based, sci-fi mission game. Didn't play the original, but premise is you're rebels against an invasive alien presence on earth. You recruit soldiers who gain experience as they go on missions (or die), and between missions you act against the clock to keep the bad guys in check while you obtain supplies and intel to create new armor and weapons.
Pros:
- Combat is a blast, though with a high learning curve if you haven't played this type of game before. There isn't really a solid tutorial, so I learned the hard way to use cover, not charge ahead, and once I got more gear, bring items for all occasions (e.g. armor shredding)
- Large variety of soldiers, which leads to great strategy and synchronization
- Appearance customization on everything
- Tons of in-between mission action to upgrade your base, contact the resistance, so not all combat
Cons:
- Slow loading times between missions. I have a decent processor, but it took a minute or two to load a mission, and around 3 or so to end a mission. Not a clue why, though I could alt-tab out and read the news while waiting.
- High learning curve if new. The first mission can be extremely rough, and you can expect a good chance at a casualty
- Don't get too attached to your soldiers. One of your favorites is going to die at some point, whether a fluke crit or just a bad spot to hunker down. You'll get upset that you spent so long customizing him/her.  Then again, if you're that upset, the game does have a load/save feature and autosaves during combats...
- The missions can get repetitive over a long period of play,  primarly for players who might seek perfection (getting all research, making all items) instead of pursuing the main story line. Given how rough the finale is, you'll want that research and gear.
I think it was the DLC that came with my purchase, but there were missions in which a random enhanced "boss" would show up, wreck my day, and retreat to harass me another day. You'd have to wear the boss down over a series of missions, but the rewards of researching some unique gear were worth it (in retrospect). Since each boss gets 1 action EVERY TIME you take an action, they can be a severe hardship. Just FYI. But once you kill them...satisfying.
Also, FYI upgraded psionic characters are monsters on the field. They don't get XP on missions as far as I can tell and can only be upgraded at the base. But, they have amazing abilities, above and beyond your gear.
All in all, this game rocks and had a blast.

Half-Life put first person shooters in the limelight. Sure, this game is by no means the first of its kind. There were plenty of FPS games before, and there will be plenty that come after. But few will reach to the standards of quality set by this game. This game came out in 1998, and it just goes to show how prophetic this game is that it still holds up a decade plus later. Few games could even dream of being relevant a few years later, with how fast things are moving now.

Any run of the mill FPS game can rattle off the industry standard arsenal; the bad guys, the bombs, the grenade throwing shotgun blasting yehaw games that we've all played a thousand times by this point. It takes serious effort to innovate. Do anything new and exciting. By this point, we've seen so much of the same. You know what would really be super? To look at a game made in a time when these rules were still being written. You didn't need fancy particle effects, slowdown bullet time, or any of the gratuitous garbage you would see in any dime a dozen unity project.

Half-Life is a simple game about escaping Black Mesa. That's it. You play as a dude with a crowbar and a suit of armor. It's just so hard to express how engrossing this game is, especially after a few hours of gameplay. Its easy to forget that you're essentially walking down hallways, jumping across rooms with one entrance and one exit, and fighting the same enemies. Its just, the game executes everything to well that none of it's limitations matter. Barney is every security guard? Doesn't matter. Don't know where to go? Doesn't matter. The graphics aren't that impressive anymore? Doesn't matter. You can honestly forgive a lot solely on how amazingly smooth the gameplay is. It's rock solid except for the spare few times I got stuck in a wall or crashed the game. For a game this large, that's an achievement.

This game is nowhere near perfect. Not even close. I think an argument can be made that the silent protagonist trite can be traced all the way back to the grand daddy himself. I think my only other major complaint is that the game starts to drag it's feet in maybe the last hour of gameplay. Right up to the final boss. The muddy textures don't do the game a lot of favors when they're stretched and repeated. Nor does the level design at that point. It's a bit of slow down in what otherwise is an amazing experience.

This is a classic. I'm glad to have played it. Not only that, but I recommend anyone who is mildly interested in FPS games to try it out. It's the great grand dad of them all. It just does so much perfectly.

XCOM 2's predecessor XCOM: Enemy Unknown was a fine enough game, though even with its expansion (Enemy Within) and mods such as The Long War, I often felt myself growing bored towards the latter half of the campaign. Snipers were too overpowered with the jet pack suit and high ground perks, the overarching strategy layer was tedious to manage for the majority of the game and non-existent once you got enough satellites up, and the UFO combat instances were pretty bare-bones and not very much fun. I often found myself getting into the game a bit before growing bored and putting it down. I've only ever finished it once despite my nearly 100-hour playtime on Steam, which does not include another 50-60 hours of playing time on the Xbox 360.
Most of this has been solved by XCOM 2's sheer added depth. The overarching strategy layer has been completely revamped from Enemy Unknown and now gives me an extreme sense of "just one more round" that I've gotten from some other games such as Firaxis' own Civilization series. XCOM 2 is incredibly addictive and weaves into tactical combat missions way more intuitively than the strategy layer in the first game ever did. UFO combat with your own fighters has been completely removed, replaced by UFOs that hunt your big airship and involve a specific mission type that I won't spoil because it's amazingly fun and legitimately surprised me when it first happened.
But more than anything, XCOM 2 features something I didn't realize was lacking in the first game until I played the second: A far more effective mise en scène and an immersive quality that the first game lacked. The first XCOM feels like a game. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but XCOM 2 really puts you into the cast's predicament in a way the first game does not. There's something about the maps and the added character depth that I think adds this feel, but I can't put my finger on it. Perhaps it's the way the maps sometimes will feature the overgrown ruins of gas stations, towns, abandoned family homes, and ruined cities, or how engineers and scientists now have names and all of the soldiers have written backstories. It really provides the feel of a grassroots guerrilla effort in a conquered world, which was a much more interesting premise to me than the first game's invasion defense. The story is also more interesting, with a few more unique twists than I would have expected.
Storytelling, though, is obviously not this game's forte. The strategy layer is much, much improved from the first game, and though the tactical combat and RPG management system of both the Avenger (your aforementioned giant airship) and your troops and equipment is mostly unchanged save for a
of added depth. Weapon mods have been introduced and there is now a new, semi-random way of developing the most powerful mods and utility items for your troops, which helps to add to the addictiveness of the strategy layer since you're constantly looking things to do in order to give your engineers time to develop the next shiny new toy for your troops to use. Armor types are more balanced and include flavor from the mechanized units introduced in Enemy Within. Psi Operatives have been completed retooled with their own twist that I think works incredibly well, certainly much better than the first game. The entirety of squad management has been retooled and streamlined.
The strategy layer and the tactical combat feature an added emphasis on creating tension, and while this works well and feels natural for the strategy layer, it sometimes comes off as forced with clumsily inserted mission timers in the tactical missions themselves. I don't mind the occasional timer, but I feel it could have been better implemented than just "blow up this common-looking piece of alien machinery before the timer ends" missions. The absurdly common mission timers served to keep me from buying the game for nearly a full year-and-a-half after its release before I finally found it on sale for ~$20, and shortly after some vanilla gameplay I ended up downloading a mod that removed them entirely. I would have greatly preferred having mission timers for much fewer encounters, perhaps only for one or two specific mission types. It feels like a crutch, like somebody at the top decided the tactical missions needed added urgency in order to create tension, and the people designing the missions either couldn't think of a good enough game mode to do this, or didn't have the time to do it.
The game looks just like an improved version of the initial XCOM, with some really nice lighting and particle effects. Unfortunately it also runs surprisingly poorly. I'm playing a nearly 2-year old game on a GTX 1080, and I'm experiencing regular dips down to around 30 fps when I'm zoomed out, or there's a lot of fog on the screen. That's pretty inexcusable for a turn-based tactical game like XCOM, and it's really disappointing that the team couldn't have optimized it better. It doesn't affect gameplay (which at this point is far less buggy than the original XCOM; I haven't seen even half the glitches in one full XCOM 2 campaign as I did in even half of a campaign of Enemy Unknown), but is quite an eyesore.
Another complaint I have is regarding the game's soundtrack. Michael McCann (of Deus Ex Human Revolution fame) did the first game's score, and it was fantastic.
, and that feel is sorely missed in XCOM 2. The score here is utterly forgettable; the same cheesy, uplifting Hollywood tunes seem to play whenever you enter combat. It takes away the feeling that this is guerilla warfare against a technologically superior enemy that is committing various atrocities against your species, that you are hopeless outgunned and scratching and clawing at an enemy that has its boot on your throat. Instead it makes the game feel like a triumphant, heroic Hollywood action film; that you're destined to win in glorious combat. It clashes directly with the games maps, which feature ruined and decrepit homes and the absolute destruction of the human way of life, replaced with a polished cities that just seem off. It fails to impart the sense of an epic struggle, in which many of your own troops will die in the missions that you will not always succeed in. After about 15 hours I simply muted the music in the settings and resigned myself to getting by on just the ambient sound design of the tactical levels and the Avenger instead, which is really quite good compared to the stale, monotonously average soundtrack. At its best this soundtrack is a poor imitation of McCann's previous work, at its worst it's an overly loud cacophony, egregiously clashing with the tone the rest of the game tries to impart. I should note that the music is not
, it's actually quite good, and composer Tim Wynn is obviously a talented man. I just feel that not only did it not fit the game, it actively dampened my experience. Perhaps this is due to the direction given to Wynn and not the man himself.
These criticisms are really not a big deal, though. XCOM 2 does not strive to be an artistic game, and so it probably should not be judged as one. It did, however, succeeded in grabbing me in a way that I rarely felt from XCOM: Enemy Unknown and that only the best of video games seems to do. It had me fiending for just one more scan, one more mission, one more piece of tech researched. It had me playing until midnight on a work night, skipping my runs and workouts to play for just a few more hours. And it held me throughout without fizzling out and becoming tedious. It's a great game and there is a serious dearth of good tactical RPGs on the market these days. Jake Solomon and Firaxis have succeeded in making a game that you can play forever a la Civilization, and I can't wait to check out the War of the Chosen.

As current law enforcement I can say that this game is decently close.. But still has room to expand.
Positives:
Decent Roleplay
Easy controls/Xbox 360 controller compatibility
Customizeable vehicles
Interesting scenarios, from traffic stops to drug busts
Large map with varrying terrain/environments
Negatives:
Graphics are a little behind the times, and some animations become flawed. The former is tolerable, but the latter could use minor work.
Load points are.. Obvious, a bit to obvious. You can see their green glow from far across the cell. Other than visually unappealing, they function well.
Perpetrators tend to have three modes, shoot, run, or surrender. When they shoot, it's tolerable, and requires some fast thinking. When they run, there is an issue.. You character can't run as fast as the AI, so being away from your vehicle on foot chases always fail unless you can get them to surrender quickly. When they surrender, there are some arrest issues. Such as when you go code 3 because someone blows through a blockade, pointing a tazer at them costs points. Other times they work fine.
Cars/people are unvaried. There are a couple several models for both, different clothings, skin colors, car colors, and issues with the cars. However, increased detail, in-depth conversations, random generated rap sheets and more models and even clothing would make the depth and roleplay value tenfold.
Physics is... Simple. In Enforcer. Gravity seems to be low. The impact of wrecks causes more of an ice-skating situation. And punching the breaks at high speed causes some interesting/unrealistic sliding. Also, don't worry about running over civilians, they will levitate over your vehicle. And sometimes even run over the top.
Vehicle specs/damage could be refined heavily. I have drove a P-71 Highway Inteceptor for a few years. The top speed is not 70mph, it is more in line of 140mph (With the govenor, it's more like 120). All vehicles need the physics refined, and the specs adjusted. The damage to the vehicles could be more specific. Such as flat-tires, optional upgrades for tires, bumpers, lights, ect..
No fires. Ever. Which is disappointing. Happening upon a field fire would be nice. At least to report.
You and the dispatcher are the only directly interactable public service. Other police vehicles/paramedics/tows and ect would be nice. Being able to call backup, or to see another officer pulling over speeders would be cool.
Certian situations are cause for arresting someone. There are occassional bugs where someone shooting you will get you punished if you fire at, or arrest them.
More/better houses could be added, upgrades and all that.
More weapons/outfits/character customization would be nice. Actual vendors/shops and inventory would be cool.
Instead of taking perps directly to the 200sqft police station/jail you should take them to a penetentary.
Traffic lights and laws for AI needs repaired/overhauled.
... I can't think of any more things right now, but I am sure to renew and revise this opinion as the game developes. I would very much like to hear from the developers about my views/opinions.
All in all.. This game is well worth the price. It is good. It has potental. If you like law enforcement rp, buy it. :)

Before I start, let me preface this point: this is my second Tales games that I have played (the other one being Zestiria).
Pro/Cons come before my overall thoughts of the game.
Pro:
- Amazing story that employs dark themes
- Unique party members that are very well developed
- Great OST
- Combat is very fluid and fast
- Skits are plentiful and very funny
- Named NPC's add a lot of flavor to the game
- PC port is solid
- Dual Audio (I wholeheartedly recommend the JP audio)
Cons:
- AI bugs that can be fixed via patching
- Some dungeons + zones can be very lenghty which can lead to some annoyances
- Very little variety of costumes compared to Zestiria
- Every good costume is DLC that is quite pricey
Now for my thoughts: this is one of the best JRPG that I have ever played in a while.
From the great story to the banter between the party members and NPC's you encounter to the funny skits and addictive combat system.
These all come together to form one of those JRPG experiences that you should NOT SKIP. If you have been "burned" by Zestiria and have lost faith in the "Tales of" franchise I wish you to reconsider, because this will be the game that will show you how well can a game improve over it's predecessor.
If you've played/finished Zestiria you will appreciate all the references.
If I were to rate this I would give it a 9/10 and it was an experience that I will not forget.
Also, I would like to commend Namco Bandai for learning from their mistakes and give us such a good PC port that includes Dual Audio and releasing it in day and date with the PS4 version. I wish other publishers, especially japanese ones would follow suit.
In conclusion, SHOULD YOU BUY Tales of Berseria? If you enjoy JRPG's then the answer is a most definite YES!

You play as Velvet Crowe, a 19 year old woman who turned into a demon (Therion) where her main mission in life is to kill her brother-in-law Artorius who has sacrificed her brother (Laphicet) during the events of the so called Advent (ritual). At the start of the game you see a younger version of Velvet and Laphicet being saved by their brother-in-law as they try to survive the Scarlet Night. A disease where other demons started appearing and taking other people's lives. Fast forward a few years, you see the protagonist and her brother all happy dandy until the anniversary of the Scarlet Night returns. This is where the SHTF and is the main objective of the game (to seek vengeance for the death of her brother)
Pros:
+ Better battle system than Zestiria
+ Plot is decent (the darkest story in the Tales series)
+ Equipment management is good (enhancing equipment to boost stats)
+ Soundtrack is good (Not YS soundtrack good, but decent)
+ Lots of graphics settings to adjust (supports 4K - upscaling) > 60 FPS @ 1080P Ultra/MAX settings
Cons:
- DRM (Denuvo) > this really depends on your opinion on DRM (likely to be removed months down the line)
- In game combat can feel like a grind sometimes (to be expected when playing a JRPG)
- Graphics are a bit dated (PS3 graphics)
Honestly, I would only pick this up if the game goes on sale. $64.99 CAD or your currency equivalent is a bit steep for a JRPG game. For 1/2 the cost you can buy Atelier Sophie for more or less the same amount of play time.

Expect some cheese and maybe a little cringe if you aren't into anime, and some even if you are.This installment lets you play as the villians/anti-heroes of the story, which is supposed to bring a more dark tone to the game. There have been moments where the supposed "good" guys look like complete villians.
I really can't say much about the characters so far. I enjoy the main cast and their reactions with each other, but so far, I only really know about Velvet's, Rokuro's, and a bit of Eizen's backstory and motivations. It doesn't go into much detail from what I have seen so far too, so if you are comming off older Tales games, you might find the character progression kind of slow/dull in comparison.
The combat, however, is probably the most fun I have had in a Tales game to date. The attacking is very smooth, chaining up combos feels powerful, and the different burst/soul moves for each character give you a chance to play using different strategies. I have played all of the main cast so far, but I feel like I am attached to Velvet since she has such a powerful moveset.
There have been quite a few reported bugs/problems with the steam version which you can read all about in the community forms, specifically here:
All in all, I feel like this installment of the Tales series is defiently worth picking up. The combat is enjoyable, the story as of my 24 hours of playing is pretty good, and the characters are interesting. If you are willing to deal with some of the bugs and problems known so far, I would say pick it up.

Lets take a look at hatfall. I will review the game on a pro/ con style and ending it with my own conclusion about the game.
Pro:
The game is simple. The premise of the game is just to move left and right to catch one falling hat per level while avoiding falling cars, stop signs, ect. It gets trickier the later levels since the other AI can closely resemble Yatzhee making it an obstical to figure out which is the actual player.
The jokes. The game is full of funny moments from mini games, failure sound effects, and the level start up. They are bare bones and you will see some multiple times but it doesnt subtract from the joy of seeing them.
The buyable egos. Buying these egos help make the game easier by making it easier to spot the character in the vast ammount of people in the level. Dont worry you dont need to spend actual cash to make the game easier, you just need to collect hats. They are the currency in the game.
The unlockable items. For the most part the unlockable items are gained from gift drops given after a specific number of hats were caught. Some items are pretty useless like the glasses making the game a shade of pink or the beard displaying censored curse words. Other items active mini games which adds more enjoyment in the game as well helps score some easy hats.
Con:
Repetitive. The game is very samey but that isnt bad if you are just playing to just get through the game's somewhat existing story. If your going for all the achievements it is a slug fest of grinding away at hats. A few achievements are such a pain to get and unlocking the last few egos are a nightmare.
Conclusion:
Its a fun game for the fans of zero punctuation. It is very samey similar to games like bejewled. The idea of what makes the game good is how simple it is. It isnt hard to play it or learn to play it. The jokes that are in the game are pretty good and provided a few laughs here and there. The mini games were a blast to do. The only issue is how grindy the game gets and through that it kills the fun because of doing the same things over and over. I can still reccomend the game, it isnt great but it is a nice fun token and a blast to support yatzhee.

+ Developing your own engine & having the option to license it to other developers
+ Having the option to release games through publishers or publish your own games
+ Being able to publish games from other studios
+ MMO's and special "add-on's" for MMO's (you even have to have a server room)
+ Special facilities for graphics, audio and quality control departments
+ Full control on what is focused on during development via sliders
I could go on. I found the game surprisingly deep and I'm having a lot of fun. I recommend this to anyone that has enjoyed other similiar titles.

Out of the many games I owned and played on the Steam platform for a year now and four months away until reaching two years now, The Walking Dead has been one of my favorite games to play on this platform. The game ranks up their with the other great games such as Team Fortress 2 and Borderlands. I may have cracked only above ten hours on the game now but its been a blast playing through the game. The choices, the characters and even the gameplay has kept me playing through the game and I could only say is....
Welcome to my review on The Walking Dead
*Background*

The game is based off on the television and comic books of the same name, The Walking Dead. Though, the game may exist in the same universe as its other counter parts, the game follows another set of characters surviving in the disaster that is the game's universe. Our main character is Lee, a convicted fella going to jail after murdering a senater for reasons unknown until playing the game. He takes care of a young girl he found while finding help, Clementine. The game revolves around the decisions you made in episodic format and you can only trust who you think are you're friends. With the decisions, you have to live with it and having a girl around you to protect, thats gonna be a hard choice. But you can always expect this kind of gameplay with the creators of the game, Talltele Games, with how detailed they are with their dialouge. TallTele Games made a great effort and making me want to buy the second or even third game when I'm done with finishing the game.
*Gameplay*
The gameplay is all about the dialouge and the choices you made during the storyline that could change how the game plays for your playthrough. Their would be a lot of dialogue during the entire story and talking to your other fellow survivors is the key to who woud lives, dies or be an ally to you during the last episode. The dialogue is very important to how it plays and even the littiliest of choices has a big impact on the story, like if you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off someone by your opinions and then later on they're still be mad about what you said. The biggest of decisions are always told to you at the end of the episode and you can see what percentage of people sided with you on your decisions. The biggest decisions tells you what happens and how your characters can adapt to your decisions, TellTale Games did a great job on the dialogue and how it effects your playthrough. The other gameplay is point-and-click, its how you do certain actions and can react to fast pace actions when it occurs. Both of these gameplays help bring this game to life and it makes me feel like I have a big part into the sayings of what happens to the characters. They are the big engines that keep this game going and I'm a proud passenger of that engine.
*Story*
Our main character is Lee, an African man being brought in to jail after murding a senator for reasons explain in the game. After some nice chat with a police officer, they get hit by a Walker and crazing down at the side of the freeway. Lee wakes up hours later and find himself in the car as the officer's body lay motionless on the ground. Finding a way out and killing the officer's animated corpse later, Lee try to find help in a house he happens to be at their backyard after jumping the fence like a criminal. He looks around the insides of the house while hearing the phone machine goes, Lee founds a Walkie-Talkie and becomes the guardian of a little child name Clementine, after killing her dead babysitter. Now, after that we are given our first big choice of the game, but thats how far I can tell the story in text form since their are numerous branching storylines with each decisions and finding out everything is a nightmare, also its not my job to tell the story if it keeps on changing with every little choice, so thats how the story is at the beginning at leasts.
*Final Thoughts*
The game was a blast to play through though there are some things that bug me the hell out of it. First, the achievements during the entire game are very easy to gain except for one which is a bit stupid to get but then I remember I play Team Fortress 2 so thats thrown out the window. The achievements are just completing a chapter in the episode or completing the episode fully. Second, some of the choices don't really have a big of a impact as it should while a few I hate because it totally forgets about my previous deeds that I made with the characters like Kenny. The finally, the game is too easy to beat as most of the action scenes are just smashing one button and then the other or shooting people. However, those are small details that I can forgive as I really enjoy the game even though its a bit short since I'm on the last episode even though I have ten hours on it already.
Overall, I strongely recommend this game to anyone who are interested with the storyline, dialogue, characters and the gameplay overall. If I was a game critic, then I would really push you to try the game, and with the gameplay its easy to pick up. The Walking Dead gets a five out of five (5/5).

What makes Mad Games Tycoon better than other game dev tycoons?
In the little bit that I've played of Mad Games Tycoon, I am already really enjoying it!  It has everything that other game dev tycoons offer and even more than that.
First of all, CUSTOMIZATION.  Mad Games Tycoon gives you customization opportunities out the wazoo.  It really opens up the door for extremely close and personal gameplay, so that no two players' games look the same.  Where other games have offered its players the ability to name each game, what kind of game it is, who you hire, etc., Mad Games Tycoon goes much deeper than that.  In MGT, I am given the privilege of customizing my headquarters just the way I want it, down to the foliage scattered around in my offices and even vending machines in my staff room. Customization options when making games are also pretty hefty as I am able to customize every game down to even choosing a publisher. The customization options in MGT really make me feel like I'm playing MY game and not a game that everyone else is playing.
Second, REWARDS.  MGT so far has proved to be an extremely rewarding experience.  As I progress further into the game, new opportunities unlock for me (and I don't just mean new consoles and/or game genres).  The more I do in the game, the more I'm rewarded with things like new office spaces, new items, and new publishing opportunities.  The reward system of MGT takes place on a greater scale than any other game dev tycoon I've played.
Lastly, THERE'S ALWAYS SOMETHING TO DO. A problem I've run into with other game dev tycoons is running out of things to do once I start development on a new game.  I would always end up hitting the fast forward button to finish the game as quick as I could.  But in MGT, there's always something to do whether it's customizing your offices, hiring new people, buying licenses or whatever you want really.  The only downside of this is that as far as I can tell, when you're doing most other things while the game is being developed, I'm pretty sure that development pauses.  But I could be wrong.
So far, what I've played of MGT has proved to be an immensely satisfying experience.  I wasn't sure about it at first, but the game proved me wrong.  I would suggest Mad Games Tycoon to anyone interested in this genre of game.

The thing with Starbound isn't that it's necessarily a "bad" game. The thing with Starbound is that the devs aren't focusing their attentions on it as much as they should, at least, not anymore. It's been in Early Access for over two years now, and updates tend to be few and far between. Updates tend to be cosmetic ones mostly, just new random blocks, nothing really eye-catching.
Starbound seems to have lost a lot of its initial life. Cookie-cutter dungeons and towns, lack of real interaction with NPCs (you can barely do ANYTHING with them) and an ultra-linear progression system (minus the three endgame crafting stations) just make it seem kind of...  bland. I got to the "new" endgame content in about 4-6 hours of play. For a game that's supposed to be something like Terraria, but with more depth, that's pretty sad. It looks great, but it's like a model. It looks good and it's not lacking much at all in the visuals department, but there's no real depth. It's very shallow.
Starbound had a lot of life at first, and it looked promising. But then the devs began to really slow down with updates and news, and the updates we did get were mostly just tuning and some additions that nobody really wants. Admittedly, the overhaul to the fuel system was a good idea, but other than that...?
I don't play it anymore. I got my money's worth from it, but it's no fun now. Hell, even Destiny is better in my books, just because the replay value is still there, and you can't get everything good in like two hours. At least in Destiny, you (normally) have to work to get your endgame stuff.

Serena is a nice story-driven point-and-click adventure game which you can pick up for free. The game has great atmosphere that changes subtly to put you in the mood of the narrative. The game does have a rather creepy ambiance but no real jump-scares, so you don't have to worry about being on edge.
Some people dislike the game because they feel it is too short or doesn't have enough hinting to the ending, but from what I've seen they aren't playing it to its full potential. This game is best enjoyed by looking for hints to the back story, instead of just looking for the story progression "Triggers." You should keep in mind that the objective isn't to beat it as fast as possible, but rather to get engrossed in the story telling; you wouldn't skip a few chapters of a book to "Finish" it faster would you? In the worst case scenario you haven't lost any money anyways, so I say give it a try.

This is probably my favorite game.  Despite it being about 2 years old at this point, it is still my go-to game and one I come back to time and time again.  Fallout 4 is a post-apocalyptic open world game that is completely addictive.  What I love about it is that it's a non-linear game that you can play so many different ways...  You could literally just explore and loot, complete quests, pick fights or sneak around them, build settlements and suits, collect and craft things, turn people into allies and enemies and so much more.  It makes the gameplay diverse enough that you don't get bored playing.  The aesthetic is this unique blend of futuristic and 1950s, which becomes it's own flavor of familiar. Alarameth TD is a simple tower defence game where you protect your fort against enemies by building towers on pre-defined and free spots. The battle arsenal contains few upgradable towers and on some maps a maze that you can define yourself.
Sadly this game does not offer a story at all, like some other tower defence games manage to do, instead it just throws you into the level with some minor tutorial on how to place and upgrade towers. The gameplay overall is absolutely boring since each level is almost the same - hordes of enemies walking down a pre-defined path that in some cases you can alter by building a maze on the way. It takes quite a while until you unlock all the towers and their functions and that makes the game feel rather slow.
If you played any TD before, you will most likely build on the right spots from the first try even on hard difficulty. The worst part about the challenge in this game is that sometimes one single tower of a single type at special time decides if you finish the level without leaks. On the first level for example you build Arrow-Arrow-Cannon-Arrow. If you build for example 3 Arrows, you will leak. If you build two cannons - you will leak. That makes the game feel absolutely static and without multiple alternative solutions like it is mostly in good TD games where you can use different strategies for building your defence levels.
The graphics in this game are simple and sadly look absolute lifeless. Its like chess pieces moving on a board - nor the enemies nor the environment have any special details or graphical immersion effects.
As stated before, the progress is simply based upon waiting for enemies to run into your towers and if you leak, you simply restart and build another tower in the same order.
Both the sound and the music are absolutely boring. The narrator/advisor voice starts to get on your nerves after few minutes aswell.
Alarameth TD is a boring grindy tower defence game, without any real strength but quite some weaknesses. There are tons of tower defence games that offer you a story, better sounds and immersion, far better progress system than simply retrying same level with same order and just witching towers one by one until you figured perfect combination for finishing without leaking.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.
~ForestWolf

Alarameth is in some ways a typical tower defense game.  You're given squares where you can build towers (and sometimes they're in the path of the enemies, so you can build mazes for them to traverse), you earn points when you kill things, which allows you to build or upgrade towers, and you have to prevent enemies from reaching a specific location.  There aren't any hero units or skills, so you have to rely on your towers for everything.
Where Alarameth is different is that you have to face hordes of enemies -- thousands per level once you get past the introductory areas -- but your towers aren't very effective against them, so you have to build dozens of towers and wear enemies down as they travel along their route.  You can't have just one "kill zone" and take care of everything there.  You have to spread your damage out over the entire level.
The bad news is that because of the mechanics, the game sort of a boring slog.  You have to play the difficult levels multiple times to figure out the right strategy, and even then if something goes slightly wrong, there isn't really anything you can do about it other than start over.  I quickly gave up on trying to get a perfect score for each level; just completing the levels was tedious enough, especially since the game likes to crash at the end of long levels.
The good news is that there are some fully-voiced actors for each level, and they give you the reasons why you're there, and they also give some hints.  The dialogue is amusing and well-presented, but it starts to wear out its welcome after a while when you get stuck on a level and hear the same conversations over and over again.
I finally gave up on Alarameth after failing the 7th level for the fifth time (twice because of crashes).  Alarameth is different, and it's inexpensive, but I didn't like it much.
Edit: After putting Alarameth on the back burner for about a week, I went back and played it some more.  I finished level 7 on my first try, and then I worked my way through the remainder of the campaign (levels 8-15).  The remaining levels weren't as irritating as levels 5 and 7, and I only experienced one more crash.  Alarameth still isn't one of my favorite TD games, and so I'm still not recommending it, but it at least moved up more towards "meh" rather than "bad."

I stated playing through Alarameth TD and already by the second level I wasn't sure I wanted to finish it. Part of the reason was I expected that it would not be so difficult to not let any monsters through on those levels. It was. The main developer himself even wrote that it would be challenging. I even stopped playing for awhile and moved on to other games. But in the end, I played through the whole game on the casual difficulty (which was still sometimes difficult) and am glad I did. Having just finished it I will just make a few remarks while they are fresh in my head.
Random positives as they popped into my head: The voice acting at first seemed a bit obnoxious - and it would be if you had to repeat the same level over and over again - but some of the dialogue is amusing and it provides a nice addition to a casual play through. Some of the later level designs are clever and fun to play, especially the Gnome Lab.
Less random negatives that made the game less enjoyable: The game sometimes suffers from the "Last Wave" problem, where you can be playing perfectly until all of a sudden a large number of a certain monster type appears for the final round and breaks through your defenses. Occasionally there are also moments where you can't seem to build new towers fast enough to weave the monsters before they will escape and reach your base so you have to start over or accept that you will not get a perfect on the level. Were it simply a matter of strategy it would be one thing, but I found that the first 1 - 3 waves were consistently usually the hardest unless the level had one of those killer last waves I mentioned. Some of the levels also seem way too long, even the first level. Later levels will sometimes have only 14 waves, but there is an early one (first or second, I forget) that has 25 waves. For whatever reason, the developer decided not to build up to a challenging finale but ordered the levels and their difficulty somewhat randomly.
There is nothing too unique about Alarameth TD aside from the voice acting and ultimate tower on the final level, but so long as you don't care about getting all the achievements, it is a decent TD game in small doses. I wish I could give this a neutral review, but as I cannot, I lean slightly positive though having beaten it I don't foresee returning to it.

I feel like people don't give this game enough time before reviewing it. That part where you put hats on (you know, the main part of the game) is just that: *part* of the game. In itself, it's simple in concept, yet challenging and silly. You run around, trying to catch a hat falling from the sky onto your head. Except there's more than one person on the screen and they all look identical to begin with. And sometimes it's not just a hat that falls from the sky, it's a refrigerator that will kill you upon impact. Or a stop sign that will kill you upon impact. Or both. Don't forget, if you get far enough, you'll catch a wizard's hat instead, causing him to curse you with a negative effect you have to deal with on the next stage. If you win that stage, you get a bonus, be it double hats or an extra life. Eventually, you can buy a gift from the gift shop. THIS reveals the true nature of this game; as you collect gifts, you play a different minigame to acquire a buttload of hats. Get enough hats, then something strange happens (I won't spoil it for you), and you must seek answers from within the minigames. Eventually you end up taking out a final boss and cueing the end credits. If you didn't realize that this game had a final boss, then it is my opinion that you had no right to review. It doesn't take long to get from start to finish; you can do it in a couple of hours. Once you realize what's really going on, the game has a very meta-game feeling to it where the hat-collecting is a small part of the whole, even though that's literally 90% of the gameplay. That's why I nominate it for the "Game Within a Game" Award for the 2016 Steam Awards.

Ittle Dew is a single-player game which at first glance is very similar to the old NES and SNES Zelda games. That is accurate, but there is a lot more to it.
If you play for even a small amount of time, you will notice that Ittle Dew has a great irreverent style of humor which is enhanced by the lovable characters, and the mix of puzzle and combat gameplay suits it perfectly. There is very little fluff - by which I mean you will use the same puzzle elements over again, but in increasingly clever and novel ways. It is clear that the developers (Ludosity) took great care in crafting their game and distilling it down to a small, but densely packed experience that conveys constant quality.
There are five boss fights in the game, of which three, including the final boss, are required to beat the main story. A fourth is required to gain all of the items. Each of the three dungeon bosses have specific mechanics which require you to use your new dungeon item as you have learned in the preceding area, creating a diverse experience that never gets tedious. There is also a fifth (tough) boss that is completely optional.
Aside from the main story, there is an optional 'Master Cave' with twelve puzzles. They begin slightly more difficult than what you have done to beat the main story, but the difficulty ramps up quickly and some will leave you thinking for a long time before you can beat them. I was amazed at how clever some of the solutions were.
__
The game also has a sequel, Ittle Dew 2. It's bigger and more combat-oriented, but it has a lot of what made this one great! I recommend both games.

---- Preface
This game is pretty darn good and it's FINALLY out of Early Access! I bought this game a while back in late 2015 right after looking over the shoulder of my brother who was watching a lets player playing it. I just had to have it because it looked so darn good... and it WAS.
So why is this game so good? Months before this I had bought Game Dev Tycoon and thought it was the most addictive game to ever be released on steam. I played that game for long hours and long nights and would be quite fulfilled, but something was missing.
One might jump to comparing this game to Game Dev Tycoon, however while the game is about making games and becoming a successful game developement or console developement company Mad Games Tycoon takes Game Dev Tycoon's preface to a whole new level in terms of gameplay and offers a much more refined experience in my oppinion.
---- Game Dev Tycoon vs. Mad Games Tycoon
Game Dev Tycoon was a brilliant game back when it was released and to this day it provides a fun experience but Mad Games Tycoon gives MUCH more freedom to choose what you want to do with your company. Game Dev Tycoon forces you to follow one path. The only thing you can hope to do in Game Dev Tycoon is to make good games and produce consoles so you feel extremely limited whereas Mad Games Tycoon lets you make almost any type of gaming company that you want. You can be a developer, engineer, publisher, console maker, or my personal favorite: PUBLISHER'S ♥♥♥♥♥! Yup! You can be Bungie, Infinity Ward, Dice, and Treyarch in this game! Nothing like being Activ-Vision's or Electronic Artist's ♥♥♥♥♥ ammaright? Jokes aside, this game gives you many more options than Game Dev Tycoon for what kind of company you want to be. You can also customize your building and choose what kind of offices there would be and how big they would be and where they were. Bottom line, this game is SOOOOO much more customizable and less stream-lined than Game Dev Tycoon. Whether or not that is a good thing is up to you but I LOVE this game's customizability.
---- Pros
- Balanced and Rewarding Gameplay
- Not Terrible Graphics
- Runs Well and Doesn't Crash (as far as I have played)
- It's Just Dern Fun
---- Cons
- Game Gets Boring at the End
- Graphics Not Amazing, But for a Theme
- Doesn't Really Seem to End, Just Goes On
---- Last Thoughts
Mad Games Tycoon is a pretty darn good game but it is not life changing. It's a lot like Game Dev Tycoon with a heck of a lot more to do and a lot more freedom. If steam had a /10 rating system I would rate it at 7.8/10 -Too Many Rooms

While there isn't much content as of yet, the game in its current form is worth a buy for any dinosaur or animal enthusiast. As of writing this review, you're able to take control of a Dakotaraptor from infancy to adulthood in the dangerous, prehistoric Hell Creek. You can explore the terrain, though there isn't much variation, and encounter other animals (including the famous Tyrannosaurus rex) through the eyes of your raptor. The game itself isn't very optimized, but, as it is Early Access, I'm optimistic in that regard. The animal design in the game is famous for having the most paleontological accuracy of any game out there, and it really shows. The attention to detail in each creature provides for a very immersive experience, as the dinosaurs feel right at home in the environment. Definitely purchase this game if you'd like to support the devs, and be sure to keep an eye on it even if you don't want to buy it in its current state.

It's still a pre-alpha, there isn't an absolutely huge amount to do other than survive but what's there is an exciting indication of the future.
To explain the current gameplay;
Basically you begin life as a Dakotaraptor hatchling, it's quickly explained that Dakotaraptors are terrible parents (and one will usually eat one of your siblings just...to prove that point) and you're then off to fend for yourself. You'll start life scavenging and hunting small lizards before you progress in a vaguely Isle-esque system in that the longer you survive the more exp you accrue until the point you can develop into the next maturity stage. Other than yourself (only Dakota playable for now) you'll find Triceratops, T.Rex, Pachycephalosaurus and a handful of other ambient creatures such as particularly brutal little crocodiles.
You wander the world, meet other dinosaurs, run away from other dinosaurs, and try to survive. It feels like a living and breathing ecosystem wherein there's other stuff always going on even if you're not involved. It's definitely a little buggy and janky, the night-time looks absolutely bizarre with weird colours and effects everywhere, and swimming is a crapshoot as to whether you'll make it or begin incessantly vibrating... but it's a pre-alpha, you go into this looking for the beginnings of a game that could be something special, and I think that's what Saurian is.
And to finish off I'm just going to go ahead and plug my own gameplay of it under the guise of showing you guys what the game is like but really just whoring myself out for views.
Much love.

The thing with Starbound isn't that it's necessarily a "bad" game. The thing with Starbound is that the devs aren't focusing their attentions on it as much as they should, at least, not anymore. It's been in Early Access for over two years now, and updates tend to be few and far between. Updates tend to be cosmetic ones mostly, just new random blocks, nothing really eye-catching.
Starbound seems to have lost a lot of its initial life. Cookie-cutter dungeons and towns, lack of real interaction with NPCs (you can barely do ANYTHING with them) and an ultra-linear progression system (minus the three endgame crafting stations) just make it seem kind of...  bland. I got to the "new" endgame content in about 4-6 hours of play. For a game that's supposed to be something like Terraria, but with more depth, that's pretty sad. It looks great, but it's like a model. It looks good and it's not lacking much at all in the visuals department, but there's no real depth. It's very shallow.
Starbound had a lot of life at first, and it looked promising. But then the devs began to really slow down with updates and news, and the updates we did get were mostly just tuning and some additions that nobody really wants. Admittedly, the overhaul to the fuel system was a good idea, but other than that...?
I don't play it anymore. I got my money's worth from it, but it's no fun now. Hell, even Destiny is better in my books, just because the replay value is still there, and you can't get everything good in like two hours. At least in Destiny, you (normally) have to work to get your endgame stuff.

A buggy waste of space on my hard drive.
I wouldn't play this game for free in my browser; hopefully steam will give me a refund.
Until then, know that it's just about standing under little black shadows to catch a hat.
It's supposed to be "tricky" by flipping the screen or sticking other characters in, but the game sticks in a bunch of characters that are EXACTLY IDENTICAL TO YOU IN EVERY WAY. They even go so far as to move the same direction as you when you hit the controls.
So I've got two guys with tilted faces, one imp, and three identical guys overlapping each other. Which one of the three identical guys is me? I press right really quick, two step right and one steps left. Everyone else runs randomly around at random intervals.
Telling the "pillocks" and imps from myself isn't too hard, but it's near-impossible to tell which character is you. You have ~4 seconds to figure out which guy is you *and* get him over to the falling hat, while simultaneously discerning which shadows are hats and which are murderous objects. Again, these objects can be just slightly faster *or* slower than hats, giving you very little means of discerning them from one another.
The end result is a game that tasks you with catching 1500 hats, while making the whole thing practically unplayable past the first few "tutorial" hats. Every so often, you'll trigger a little event, but nothing worth grinding away for.
Even as someone who watched ZP from the beginning, I don't feel this game is worth my time or my money. I don't find it particularly funny, and the gameplay is so godawful I'm surprised Yahtzee agreed to put his name on it and allow it to be sold.

It's definitely a "never the same game twice" kind of game, even when loading from a save file and playing from that point on - depending on speed and difficulty settings, combined with random events, I've had all kinds of experiences, from the company that skyrockets to become an empire in a handful of years, to a small company just barely managing to make ends meet after thirty years in the business due to some overly ambitious decisions.
You can basically grow into whatever kind of company you want. Sure, you could make top of the line games that come in a box filled with extras like a t-shirt, and pamper them with updates and expansions to keep it selling for a long time. You could also just focus on cranking out a ton of solid but unremarkable games and ride sheer volume. You can nurture franchises, or even publish other companies games for them.
You can even churn out buggy movie tie-ins for consoles if you so please - and can manage to make it profitable.
What's more, there's plenty of starting options too - starting decade, an option to leapfrog to an office (rather than starting in your garage), randomization options, speed, difficulty - there's plenty to explore that will have an impact on your game.
It's an excellent tycoon game and I'm glad to continue developing the Sexy Puzzle Moms series of puzzle games, aimed at adults with the theme of fashion and eroticism.
