is a game which made me realize that the Zelda-like genre of games is inherently awful and that people who like them probably only like them out of nostalgia. It claims to "boil down the classic adventure formula until there is only fun left" but I've realized no amount of boiling will get rid of the BS that goes straight to the very bones of this game and games in similar veins. I understand that there is a level of subjectivity involved, that maybe this genre is just not "for me," but this is my review based on my experience of the game, most of which is negative.
Mechanically, nearly everything about this game is bad. It does not modernize or simplify ("boil down" to use the devs' words) any of the frustrations of old school Zelda, it literally rips the most infuriating aspects of those games out and reskins them. It manages to even add some of its own terrible ideas to the pile of garbage. I don't usually do this but I listed them down.
1) Your weapon attack has no arc at all. You literally cannot damage something that is right next to you but diagonal despite  the sword having a visual arc and enemies being able to knock into you and kill you like every game. This isn't Final Fantasy Tactics, I don't understand what the problem is.
2) The hearts mechanic. It's so pointless to make your HP into collectibles, I don't understand why you would even bother when there's nothing to gain from killing enemies that aren't linked to puzzles. You're more likely to lose hearts than gain them given how your attacks are bound to the four cardinal directions whilst enemies fill the rooms and spam them with projectiles and fast moving bodies. Then when you die, you just gain back all your hearts anyway. And this is a game that encourages speed running. It literally does this just to emulate Zelda, there's absolutely no mechanical reason for the game to have this archaic system.
3) Respawning enemies. Again, just run past everything because even if you kill anything it only serves as a removal of a distraction anyway.
4) Respawning enemies in puzzle rooms.
5) Undefeatable instant kill enemies. Yup, they stole Wallmasters. The most garbage enemy in all of the Zelda franchise and you decided to emulate that.
6) UNDEFEATABLE INSTANT KILL ENEMIES IN PUZZLE ROOMS. Just go to hell and stay there, please.
7) Puzzle bosses that have to be hit more than once. It's a puzzle right? The same puzzle three times over doesn't make it more difficult, it just makes it tedious.
8) Dexterity tests. This is where I finally drew the line. I was having trouble with a puzzle in the Master Cave and finally gave in and looked up the solution and as it turned out the solution involved pushing a dozen buttons in the correct order in a very small window of time, which the game asks you for nowhere else. Someone asked about the same puzzle on the front page of the forums at the time of this review, and the devs literally reply "Sorry not sorry." Are you kidding me.
I'll give them props on two fronts: they don't make any of the collectibles missable despite having branching dungeon designs, and the worst parts of the game are optional. In fact, a lot of the game seems to be optional. Kind of makes me think they were aware that people would want to skip playing most of it.
I'm being mean. This is probably a really good game for the genre, definitely compared to most of Steam. I also genuinely love the art style. But as I said at the start, I realized that this genre as a whole is just bad, the aspects of it that are considered its trademarks add nothing but artificial difficulties to a game which doesn't have a strong core of anything. If it's about the puzzles, why have all the enemies distracting you from them? If it's about beating things up or performing pro gamer moves, why are the mechanics all so wanky? It can't be about story, there's no story barring some snarky jabs at its predecessors.
Games of this breed of "action-adventure", a kind of mix and match of everything, belong to another time period. Having a modern version just highlights how badly the ideas have aged with time and how the genre doesn't hold up without quality of living adjustments that other games have evolved over time. So the thing that I gained the most out of playing this game is an acute awareness that I don't actually like games like this.

Now that the game has been released, I guess it's time to give it some attention. According to Steam Spy, this game has sold ~50,000 copies while Game Dev Tycoon (GDT) has over 1mio owners here on Steam alone. In my opinion, this doesn't reflect the games' general quality at all. It's not a perfect game, but a good tycoon sim and a lot better than its direct competitor GDT. I will try to argue what makes this game good on its own, but I guess some comparisons to GDT have to be brought up. But first, for the lazy ones:
: It's a good game. Do you like games like Game Dev Tycoon or older tycoon games like Theme Hospital? Buy it. It puts together the room and staff managment from Theme Hospital with the game dev elements from GDT. Is it perfect? No, it has some problems that might annoy you.
After choosing some attributes of your company founder, in which country your studio is located in (which will have impact on your sales) and the game's difficulty, you'll start as a small dev in the early 80's. In the beginning, you'll try to survive by making small (and probably mediocre) games and doing minor additional missions to earn some money. As the time passes your possibilities and obligations grow. You have to research new technologies, build different facilities to ensure the quality of said technolgies in your games, hire staff specialised on those techs (or hire uneducated ones and put them into your training facilities), fix bugs, release updates to keep the game interesting, create marketing campaigns, analyze your games etc. You'll also have to switch your studio's location: In the beginning you develop your games in a garage. But you want to end up being a big publisher with over a hundred staffmembers working for him. So the garage might not be the perfect place for long.
This game offers you a lot of different means to make some money. Besides the obious "develop a game and give it to some publisher to release it" these are some of your options: you can start developing a console, you can become a publisher yourself that releases not only his own games but also other studios' games. If you do so you have to manage the content of your boxed games (will it come with a coloured manual and a free T-Shirt or will it be a bland box with nothing but the game's CD in it?). You even can become the next Electronic Arts and buy other developers, harvest their success and after you have ran down the company sell it again.
This is what sets the game apart from GDT, imo: the possibilities. You can focus on becoming one thing or do a lot of stuff at once. This raises the replayability of the game greatly. Another difference is the game's size: in GDT your highest amount of developers is around 6 or 7 guys. Well, in Mad Games Tycoon you might end up with over 100 people. You can have one team that does nothing but developing updates and expansions for your latest World of Warcraft clone. A different team does nothing but market your games and consoles. Working at multiple games at once? Not a problem at all. Fire all your dudes and do nothing but earn money with the games coming from other developers? Sure.
But the game has some problems. When you play it for the first time you can't know what it takes to develop a good game. Sliders decide, how much focus your developers lay upon a certain aspect of the game. How do you find out the perfect placement of a slider? Trial and error. You can analyze your games later to check if your slider placement was correct, but it will take a while. As soon as you know the perfect 'slider position' you'll produce one great game after another. This also was a big problem of GDT and while the devs in this game made it a tad more elegant, the same problem remains. A different problem of the game is its way of building: Sure you can design a nice office that looks nice. But it will be more efficient to put as many desk as possible into small rooms. Your staff won't mind as long as you give them what they want as soon as they complain. I also have some problems with the game's visuals. It looks like a tycoon game from the 90's (while obviously having nicer textures etc.). You might find that charming or disturbing - that depends on your taste.
But in the end, this is a game worth its 15 bucks (or your regional equivalent). It's a great and fun indie tycoon game and worth a shot. Like in so many tycoon games you'll get your money's worth, if you like this genre.

I've been enjoying the game so far, much more than Zesteria which had some problems that kept me from enjoying it enough to beat it. I mention this only because I was worried the same trends would carry into this and thankfully that's not the case.
Berseria is better looking, better mechancially and better written. The characters are better and the levels wind up being better looking because of the flaws of Zesteria's battle system that required all field maps to be gigantic to be able to have combat in. Berseria has combat in it's own 'world' like other rpgs and keeps the battle arenas simple and not annoying and the fields to look more normal and less like a MMO where everything is overly open and empty.
With Zesteria I couldn't get on with the main character, much different with Berseria.
Enough about comparing, on it's own merrits the game so far is turning out great. Nice music, the visuals are nice enough, combat is fast and keeps things interesting. You get both english and japanese and thankfully the intro has lyrics.
The visuals, some will probably complain. It looks like an enhanced last gen game at points, some bits are rough around the edges but overall because it's stylized it looks nice overall..
The game has a variety of settings to change, apparently goes up to 4k even. At 1080p I have everything maxed out and thankfully they listened and the game runs at 60fps making things more fluid.
My specs:
i7 4770k
8gb ram
GTX970
Windows 10
The voices sound nice but I've also been playing only in japanese, will have to give the English voices a-go at some point I guess. I'm just happy Bandai Namco decided to let the west have the intro ith lyrics. The intros without lyrics are just ...lacking. Thankfully that isn't the case with Berseria, it's got lyrics and is lovely.
Gameplay, it's a jrpg with active action battles, as I said they're fast and have mechanics you'll have to grasp to get the most out of but if you're not interested in diving too hard into that, there's a variety of difficutly options. I'm not super far into the game (2.5 hours in at time of writing) so they haven't given me all the tutorials I'm sure will come along but so far it feels like the PS3 exclusive Xillia.
The combat is fast and keeps things moving and seems pretty deep.
The story is only getting started, while it's started a bit cliche it has a lot of emotion and effort put into it so far and I'm really getting into it. Velvet has a strong motive and the events are really quite crazy. It's darker than other tales games with the exception of the incredibly lacking sequel to Xillia (Xillia 1 being great) which really doesn't make or break a game, but it's worth noting I guess if you want a more cheery game.
I'm really enjoying this game so far, I'd go so far to say I love it minus one or two silly characters you run into. But so far it's great!
I've seen some complain about the Adventure Item DLC, it's comically overpriced. But, if you buy that, that is on you. It offers what amounts to a bunch of cheats. Yes stupid to charge for them but you don't need them and it adds no depth to the game or new content, if anything it ruins the game. Safely ignored and if you think it's dumb don't support it, I didn't either.
I'll be sure to update this, but so far it's been great.

I've had an amazing time playing this  game so far dropping 30 hours within about 4 days. IT is incredible that this game is only in ALPHA! Most big early access games don't come out this well put together and the devs are highly active.
The game is played in first person while maning a ship. The game requires cooridination between the captain which is steering the ship and the crew which is reloading guns (with diffrent shot if needed), repairing holes or sails, pumping out water and putting out fires. One person cannot be a hero in this game. To succeed you need to have a well coordinated crew to support the captian and a smart captain to support the crew - BOTH are needed.
This game also allows you to have a good old fashioned musket, blunderbuss, pistol and sword fights. When boarding or sailing along ship side the tension is felt as one musket shot is your death. (Respawns are present)
I only see this game getting better with time with HUGE potential for esports.

Its hard to give this game a Thumbs down when its one of my favorite games of all time.
Or well, it WAS one of my favorite games. I've put about 500hrs+ into RotMG. It was always a fantastic game with a community based on helping each other out. If you just died and lost everything, there was always someone to throw you a few high tiered items to get you back in the game, and in return if you find something you can't use, give it to someone needy. To an extent this is still true, but now it can take hours to have someone help out, more times than not, someone that offers help, is really teleporting you into the middle of godlands *Giant boss monsters* to watch your grave fall from the sky.
It wasn't the community itself that did this, but the developers. Kabam took over RotMG, and with there tentacles they squeezed the game for every last drop. They ignored hackers, they ignored scammers, they ignored DUPEING! There $$$ grabbing tactics and complete disregard for community security eventually ruined the community. Besides that, Kabam would truely spit in the faces of the community who offered advise, reported hackers, reported bugs, ect ect.  Basically all of the greats in the community abondoned the game. And it was left with children with there moms credit cards begging and yelling at each other. Dragging people into godlands to watch them die.
The game is also littered with Buyer-Bots. Hackers who've farmed Godlands for pots *the community agreed currency* and trades them over-pricedly for higher valued pots which are all sold online for $$$ to the same childrenz. This also causes players to no longer help each other out, but instead try to over-price each other in exchange for pots to sell to bots, or websites for $$$.
At one time there was even a problem with peoples entire accounts becoming deleted from bugs after dieing. I had this happen to me, and was told by a Kablam Dev "That sucks, buy some tokens and start over then."
That was the only reply i ever got. That sucks, Give us $$$, and start from scratch.
---
Its not quite as bad as it once was, and
keeps bartering alive to some extent. It can still be fun to play in small doses, but don't be fooled into throwing $$$ away. Kablam doesn't deserve it, and its only gonna last until you die anyway! :P

I picked up XCOM 2 after War of the Chosen came out, having been scared away by some of its early negative reviews.
I don't know if a combination of DLC or patches have since fixed earlier issues, or if they were just overblown to begin with, but XCOM 2 is fantastic, maybe the best one yet, partixcularly with the Chosen expansion.
The pace of the game is hectic, you always feel like you're just on the edge of being snuffed out. But there's a satisfying progression to the difficulty, both in terms of how much stronger your soldiers get, and interesting new challenges the aliens throw at you.
I also found myself much more attached to the story and characters this time around. Not that they were bad in earlier games, but far less defined. There's still emergent narrative, but there's also real narrative too, and it adds a lot to the experience. Although it might make replayability slightly irritating and predictable.
All the negatives I've heard people mention, particularly BS difficulty and the infamous "timers," I feel either didn't detract from the experience, or actually were good additions to the game. Timers disincentivize the classic problem in strategy games like this, turtling, and while I did occasionally save scum when I lost my best solider to a random crit from behind full cover, I rarely felt liket he game was being unfair to me. RNG is inherently that way, for better or worse (worse IMO but, that's how these games have always been designed).
Put shortly, it's great, I loved it. If you're a fan of XCOM, going all the way back to the DOS original, you most likely will too. If you're new to the series, I'd recommend starting with the first one and its DLC, but this one is just as good, and only vaguely needs you to have played the first.

This game is probably the most absurd and ridiculous games I have ever played. One moment you're collecting hats, the next playing an anime dating simulator, and the next embezzling funds from your real estate company. Great for fans of Yahtzee's Zero Punctuation series, and people who just want to play a game and think "what in the actual crap is going on".

You know how everyone talks about how Morgan Freeman says things, making mere noises coming from the mouth into awe inspiring pieces of art? Yes, now imagine a game like that.
Bastion is a game that not only has great hack-and-slash action, but a "Stranger" that narrates everything you do as you do it, commenting on you specific weapon loadout, combat status, and even the various knickknacks you find along your journey. This alone makes the game a great experience, but Bastion goes further than that and provides even more.
Set where most of the world has been destroyed by the "Calamity," you play as kid simply known as, well, "The Kid" as he explores the shattered and deserted world around him. Soon enough, you will find the Bastion itself, a floating piece of land that is fueled by the "Cores" of the land that once was, gaining more buildings to aid you on your journey as you go along.
From the Bastion, you can fly to any unexplored area within range, which, unfortunately, is only one or two at a time (excluding any special challenge maps you find.) While only a few areas felt particularly special to me, the narrator provides backstory to each of these areas as you progress, making it a worthwhile trek to the areas' Cores.
The combat is fluid and satisfying, with a myriad of weapons, skills, and passive abilities backing you up. Enemies can be tricked into striking each other, and even lured into being pushed off cliffs. For the most part, combat isn't particularly challenging, but it can be modified using "Idols" that make the game more challenging in specific ways (increased enemy speed, enemies dropping active bombs on defeat, etc.), with extra money and exp given with more Idols active. This makes the game only as challenging as the player wants it to be, which was an interesting and very welcomed change from most games that can either be one extreme difficulty or the other.
One of my favorite parts of the game was near the end, where Bastion decides to change things completely from the rest of itself and give me multiple choices that really had my mind torn. Though, unfortunately, for the sake of not spoiling anything, I won't go into further detail.
To top it all off, Bastion has a lovely artstyle and a spectacular soundtrack (which you can buy on its Steam page or at Bandcamp.
All in all, I say that Bastion provides a great experience that I appreciated feeling. At only $15 on Steam ($2.50 if you catch it on sale, I believe), it's definitely worth a buy.

I adore this game! Usually when I play a game it takes a good five or ten minutes to grasp my attention but this game... this game was different. From the very beginning and all throughout the game, you are treated to a wonderfully performed narration that reminded me of all the good that's come out of the merging of the wild west and steampunk. Firefly immediately sprung to mind whilst I listen and soaked up the story. Meanwhile my eyes were being treated to some of the best graphics I had the pleasure of wandering around in... and destroying.
The gameplay is rather simple to begin with. You get given a heavy thing, hit the moving thing with the heavy thing! But when you discover all of the weapons and all of the possibilities for tactics and planned strategies through levels, it becomes so much more. And you can upgrade your weapons with trinkets you find throughout the levels! Each level takes the form of two different criteria and it's up to you to decide which best suits your playing style because later on they stack and you can only pick one side to stack at a time. I experimented the first time but then went back and am playing through the game again just messing around with different combinations. And trust me, the first time through you'll miss something. And that's great, missing something. Because it means you can play the game again and it won't already be finished.
The music is great, the gameplay is so free and fun to mess around with, the narration is superb, the atmosphere and story are really excellent and I really can't say any more about the game than that. I've intentionally missed out a lot of what the game has to offer because the surprise of finding out for myself was too awesome to spoil. I award this game enormously and rank it alongside 'Dust: An Elysian Tail' as my favourite playing experiences of recent memory.

I don't often review Early Access titles, but I also don't tend to buy them either.  This is a very worthy exception.  As a game dev myself, I've definitely played Game Dev Tycoon and had my fun with it but found the lack of depth quite lacking.  I wanted more control over my environment even if it might not resemble a real game studio.  Mad Games Tycoon brings that to the table - this is the first one I've played that felt more like I was crafting an actual studio and reacting to the market place with all its ups and downs.
For an Early Access release at this price point, I'm surprised at how much is already in the game.  At this point you have a functioning sandbox with a compelling upgrade tree and system to work out for progressing your company.  Customizing the office to do what I want is already there, letting me prioritize how I want - including making multiple projects happen at once as my studio expands.  You can decide pretty early on how you want your studio to function, as a studio that primarily specializes in its own projects and later on you can even build your own production warehouse and start printing and publishing for others.  You can be a handheld developer or a AAA MMO powerhouse.  The sheer amount of options you can build up to as the projects grow in complexity is mind-boggling even at this early stage.
Right now the biggest con is that you hit a point where about late game you start to run out of research options.  There's no campaign or score, its just the sandbox, so you will hit a point where all you can do is just make millions.  It takes quite a while to hit that part, and the office space upgrades in particular are expensive enough to give you goals to work towards, but there isn't as much competition as I'd like.
The other big con is that the tutorial is VERY short and a lot of features are not well explained when they come into play, leaving you guessing how they work.  For example, random events don't provide a lot of data on such things as how long they last - a big deal when you're camping on a game to release it to market AFTER a market crash!  A lot of the data the game tracks isn't useful either, or broken up over several screens when it should be in just one.  I was particularly annoyed that I couldn't just pull up an easy stat screen on a finished project that included release date, sales, financial data, and scores.  The guesswork in the development process could also use some fine tuning - right now, after you ship one game in a genre, the next one you ship in that genre will display arrows providing hints as to which direction you need to devote resources... but nothing more concrete.  It would be better if after shipping a LOT of games in a genre, the UI became more precise to let you know exactly what the sweet spot for resource distribution is.  Right now there's also no data given when you assign priorities to development, leaving you guessing even when you've succeeded as to why you did well.
I bring these issues up because updates are rather frequent at the time, and address things like this.  I'll be keeping an eye on this game to see how it keeps shaping up.

I love police games and have played many variations over the years. I was looking forward to purchasing this game and trying it out. Unfortunately, it's fallen not short, but extremely far from my expectations.
This game at best feels half done. From the graphics, the game play, and especially the driving almost nothing exactly feels right. The one thing they did try is attempting to give the player more options in how to catch those who break the law. Even this they did with a great shake.
Enforcer : Police Crime Action resembles GTA in it's works. You are a police officer who can switch on and off duty by changing clothes inside your house. The house and your clothing can be customized/purchased and a car can be purchased for your own personal use. When you start out without a car, you'll be getting around by cab fare. There are three main bars you need to worry about : stress, hunger, and energy. Stress can be relieved by sleeping or hanging out with relatives, while the other two are quite obvious in how to replenish. What the game sort of did right was the simplicity in choosing what to ask a suspect. For example, imagine me standing on the side of the road and I see a car. I press C to tell the car to pull over then interact with the person inside by pressing the right mouse button. Upon pressing this, I'm given a few options to choose, from asking the person to step out of the car to using a breathalyzer. The animations are basic and none vary from person to person. Some drivers will be intoxicated or some sort of reason will pop up for you to apprehend them.
Although it be it the case, I will give the game kudos for adding decoration to the command menu. When setting up a road block, you are able to walk up to your car and pull out some cones. You can also set up a radar to catch speeders but your involvement in that is literally minimal. You set up the radar and that's as far as you go. You will be waiting until you've reached the goal amount or until you get interrupted by a call on the radio. The game is sort of stale for this reason and other users have mentioned this as well. When a call does come up, a little adrenaline rush comes up and so does excitement... only for so long. Upon arriving on the scene of the crime, you will not catch the perpetrators in the act. Rather, they will be somewhere in the area and it's up to you to ask people for suspicious activity. Approach a perpetrator without a gun cocked and you may be kissing the pavement reminding yourself for the next time to run around like an idiot everywhere with his gun drawn. The game tries to act like a cop game, but I don't know of a single cop willing to run around with their gun in their hand pointing them at everyone and telling everyone hands up. This is the other thing, the objectives for the day such as issuing tickets are fun (to an extent) but when you get a call and usually the outcome involves you firing at the suspect and calling an ambulance, there isn't much to brag about. In the game SWAT 4, suspects were unsure whether they wanted to surrender or not which put the player in a real hot seat and gave them a feeling what it was like to be an officer. Here, the scenario always ends up with a call to the paramedic.
It is cool that they give you all sorts of options such as being able to call for a police pickup-up of a suspect or being able to tow a car, but even then options feel quite limited. You are able to stop and frisk anyone you see in the street, but again, it's very limited in how everything goes down. People will 99% of the time shoot at you when you answer to a call on the radio. When stopping people on the street, they will give up right away. If they drop anything while they put their hands up, you are able to collect the evidence. Doing jobs properly will result in acquiring more XP and $$. I should mention that cars do get out of the way when your sirens and lights are on. As an added bonus, you can use your turn signals and even put your hazard lights on.

What can I say? I liked it. I'm trying to figure out how to describe the game. In terms of gameplay, it's a "point-and-click adventure" but there really isn't much adventure and there are really no puzzles to solve. In terms of concept, it's a "horror walking simulator" though there isn't much walking and the horror is all psychological; there are no jump scares, though the game is atmospheric and it tricked me into bracing myself for jump scares that never materialized. This game is like a one act play or a one-man show in which the story (non-linear, ambiguous, and open to interpretation) takes place in only one setting and is gradually revealed though the protagonist's inner dialogue and flashback memories. The voice acting is good enough to evoke some emotions and instill a sense of dread as story builds to a very creepy climax. Sound effects and music are used very sparingly, but to good effect. This game is free, takes a little over an hour to play, and has a chilling story.

On a hunch, I put my dual Radeon HD 6950s in CrossFire mode and then the game worked for me with no problems. If I had not thought to try this, I would have missed out on a really cool and creepy experience.

The Facts~
Game rating based on the ESRB: E (Everyone)
Single-Player
Platforms: Microsoft Windows, Mac OS C, XBox 360, iOS, GoogleChrome, Linux, OnLive.
Developer: Supergiant Games.
Genre: Action Role-playing.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Plot-
A great calamity has struck the world, and you, a lone kid has to find out why and how to fix it. You travel through the world searching for various items to restore the Bastion and to find what survivors that you can. Challenging foes and exploring what is left of the world until you finally find what you can to prevail.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Character Design-
Playing through you will find that at the start, you didn't know anything about the characters, as few as there are. Through the gameplay you will find out more and more, who they were before the story began, and how it was changing them. It doesn't stop there either. Characters that have no place in the game yet were every bit as significant in the past come into play and you get to know a little about them and how they fit into the world that once was.
Through the telling of the characters you will begin to feel a bit attached and even befriend the narrator through all the story.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Music & Artwork-
This is where the game hits a home run in full, with music playing constantly in the background of gameplay it adds for a wonderful aura to the game, you are never left to feel alone and it is always a mellow tempo until a fight ensues, and then it picks up pace a tad. The sounds the emit from battle are flawless and the narration is one of my favorite details.
The artwork is suburb, the coloration style and way the world literally builds itself before your very eyes is uncanny. It truly makes you feel more in tune with exploring.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Gameplay-
The controls are actually incredibly smooth for an indie game, I was very impressed. There is not much to be said other than that.
Customization was a large feature in building the bastion and even in picking what weapons and special ability you wanted to have by your side in the heat of a battle.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion-
All in all, after getting this game, I learned never to judge a game before I play it again. This was a fantastic game and I am proud to own it. With all this said I proudly give Bastion a 10/10 with a 8.5/10 replay value.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This may look like a Zelda clone (and it is), but it is so much more than that. Sure, you have the usual mechanics of hacking and slashing monsters of increasing difficulty, you have powerups that let you solve harder puzzles, you have dungeons with bosses that are defeated by your most recent powerup, you have even the same kind of 2-D world, even down to the platforms and bridges. You've even got the same sliding of boxes to unlock doors and using bombs to unlock hidden passageways. But does Link get to MAKE his own boxes? Does he get to warp around within a single room of a dungeon? No, but Ittle Dew does (I think that's her name. Otherwise the title makes absolutely no sense and is completely arbitrary).
The main difference between this and Zelda is that there is much more block moving, as this is the main mechanic. You have four main powerups (fiery sword to light things on fire and break ice, portal blocks that act as weights, portal wand that targets things and sends them through where your portals are, and an ice wand that freezes blocks for easy pushing and douses flames.) The puzzles are based on combining all of these weapons to traverse a very Zelda-like dungeon. The difficulty increases as they put you in rooms that are supposed to be solvable but without explaining additional things that you can do with the powerups. (e.g. if you shoot ice on a wall, it makes it reflective, which means you can zap yourself with the portal gun. Took me a loooooong time to figure that out, and it was by accident.)
Ittle Dew also has some good meta-humor. It knows it's a Zelda clone, and has fun with it by poking at the various tropes along the way. For example, enemies drop hearts, which replenish your health, but they're actually fleshy hearts that flop to the ground with a sickening squelch, and the character actually eats them like an apple. There's a sidekick animal that is called Tippsie that always looks drunk on whine (though, you can see it's actually health potions).
It's not very long, so don't expect Zelda length playtime. Mine was a few hours, mostly because I spent a long time experimenting in just a few dungeons that were giving me trouble for dozens of minutes, whereas the average dungeon took about 2 minutes. The final boss is also a doozy, but mostly because there are 7 stages and it's not clear what you have to do. Fortunately, there are checkpoints after every stage for the boss, and in normal levels, you just go back to the nearest door (not the entrance to the dungeon, as in Zelda, a plus for Ittle Dew!)
Overall, I enjoyed it. Probably won't play it again, although there are "Professional shortcuts" scattered all around for repeat players who already know some of the advanced move combinations and want to speedrun through. I think for under $5 it's worth it. I got it in a Humble Bundle with, like, six other games, so I definitely got my money's worth in that case. Buy it on sale, especially if you like puzzle games or Zelda.

Well it's finally here. I am writing my first review and it makes me feel like I'm about to throw up. Not because of this group but because of the person that introduced me to it. They were one of my best friends but I did something to hut them and we are no longer friends and it makes me feel sick inside thinking about them. I screwed up and I feel so bad just thinking about all the things I did wrong. This person and I will never be friends again (no matter how much I want to and keep saying sorry) but some wounds never heal and thats something I've had to live with for these past couple weeks. Anyway this review is dedicated to them even if they don't take the time to read it .
Intrusion 2 is a classic style run and gun platformer thingy. It harkons (I don't know if I spelled that right) back to the days where arcades where king and games like this were popular. It is in the vein of Contra and Super Metroid in the style of its gameplay. It is based on the original game Intrusion (which is a free to play flash game on the internet) that I have fond memories of. Back in my younger days (even though I am not that old) I used to play alot of flash games and this one stood out because it was extremely difficult for me at the time. My brothers would always challenge me to beat the first level (which I still haven't done yet but with my gaming skill now I probably could) and I would always fail. The character who we called red scarf man (for obvious reasons) always taunted me with his cool guns and supposed skill except when controlled by me which then he would become a running target that screamed "KILL MEEEEE!!!!"
Now back on track. This game is AMAZING! it is $10 for 9 levels. It has a graphics style which to me seems like psuedo 3D and a physics engine. You start out parachuting into a snowy location and you can guess the rest (anyone but you, you kill). The game is infested with charm. Like most games now it has a silent protagonist (Red Scarf Man) which I would like to believe is like a super secret Russian agent (the game is Russian if you didn't know). I don't know the bad guys name but who cares they're bad guys you don't need to know their name all you have to do is shoot them. After progressing for a while you start to see the effects of the physics engine really shine. You can crush people with large rocks, land on them from great heights and hurt them push them off cliffs etc. You also get to ride wolves; YOU GET TO RIDE A FREAKIN GIANT WOLF WHILE RAINING BULLET HELL UPON BADDIES, HOW COOL IS THAT!! I have found a semi cool trick where you can manipulate the physics to get the wolf to run straight up a wall, but after that you get to the first boss fight which is a giant ship thing where *spoiler alert* you have to shoot its engines and cockpit (haha sex joke) until it blows up. Of course you have a giant array of kickass weapons to back you up like a railgun.
The next area (if I remember correctly) is a sort of skiing thing where you have to fight robot dragons that rain from the sky and bury in the snow. This part I had some trouble on because they would pop out of the snow at you (I wasn't paying much attention). Then after you dismember them you get to the water world part thingy. Here (if you want an achievement) can push people into the water where the mutant pirannas (something I'm also wondering if I spelled right) will promptly devour them. Seeing as how this saves you bullets I would reccomend it. Then after you gone through an enemy base you meet this giant gun weilding robot lady who proceeds to shoot at you. She goes through several stages of the fight including a disco ball laser rainbow reflection thing. After she is defeated you take her very overpowered gun and proceed to fire the rest of the laser so it burns a hole through a mountain to escape.
After this you escape and you find mechs. The first of your choices is a sword mech, but as you go on you can get a machine gun mech with a rocket launcher and you go through the levelt\ feeling overpowered until you fight the weird cat robot thingies. It is not very difficult to beat them but your mech does have a limited amount of health so keep that in mind. But you should be fine.
After this in my opinion the levels become slightly repetitive just a little until you reach the final area. I wont explain the end or the final boss cause It's something you have to experiene for yourself. But now its time for my final thoughts.
In conclusion I really loved this game. It does warrant a secong playthrough if your an acheivement hunter but i'm not. I've logged 37 hours into this game just replaying my favorite stages and trying to find all of the secrets. It is very strange to find an indie Russian game especially one that is this good. This game is a great throwback to those of you who enjoyed the old arcade style games. Even though I wasnt alive to experience the Golden Age of Arcades I can still appreciate this game. From a great price to engaging gameplay, guns, physics, and crap tons more I think this is a must buy to those of you who like a fast paced game with fun gameplay and great physics.
It has great gameplay, a good price, a kickass soundtrack, and a nice length but it could use some better option configuration and multiplayer because this game would greatly benefit from it.
In conclusion I give it a: 9/10

So far the best tales game I've played,
No other party has captured the essence of what it means to be a rogue.  This isn't the story about people trying to save the world, its a story about people who were rejected by the world that they live in.  The change is refreshing and entertaining as hell.
These are not nice people.  The party does some pretty controversial things, but there is also an understanding that comes with the way their story is presented.  It's nice to see that the story isn't driven by some greater good, but by personal vendettas and goals.
It's nice to see the character flaws presented so well and critical decision being driven by impulsive emotions instead of a hero's unflawed moral compass.
The story is definitely the best draw.  The combat is also incredibly fun, with each character playing well into their personality types.  This is especially true for Velvet, who plays like a screaming freight train that just rolls over everything with rage.
Dungeons and exploration is meh, but I didn't see it as too much of an issue.  The games engaging story and fun combat more than makes up for it.  I run this at full screen maxed out, no issues.  AI bug is there, but I'm sure this will be fixed and really you don't need strong AI if you combo right.  The difficulty is adjustable and I never found it too hard to bar me from the current story.
To be honest, I am enjoying this far more than FF15.  The animation scenes are also incredibly well done.  Also despite what people say, I find the english VAs to be fine.
Definitely fully recommend.

GTA4 in Hong Kong, only without the distraught writing, without the terribad driving, no phone spam from your buddies, and an actual, fun melee combat system.  Actually, don't compare GTA to Sleeping Dogs.  GTA4 sucked.  Sleeping Dogs doesn't.

What I like:
- Interesting cast. Every single one has a solid backstory, and ones that didn't have enough personality for me to enjoy looking at.
- Smoothest and most interesting battle yet. It's simple, but satisfying and demands just enough strategy to keep you from mindlessly mash your face buttons.
- Graphics. I find some people are saying this game's graphic sucks, but I actually like it's art style and I think it's detailed enough to accompany your journey.
- Story. Complemented nicely by the cast's background.
- Equipment system. Some say it's complicated, but after Zestiria's chaotic mess, I find this simpler and actually more believable than previous entries.
- Additional mechanics like Expedition are quick and clean, albeit a bit randomized. But I find it much more tolerable than Xillia 2's Cat Hunt or something.
What I don't like, and for good reason:
- The game as of the time I wrote this review is no longer playable. It simply crashes on startup. I've tried every fix (Kaldaien's, unplugging physical controller during DLC check) and while it works 50% of the time, 50% of the time I get to not play at all unless I restart my computer. This might change later, but for now, beware.
- AI. There is a workaround, but honestly stuff like this should not need a workaround in the first place.
- Vast world, slow movement. Based on the demo, there should be a game mechanic that helps me traverse faster later on.
Summarized:
I've preordered this and, despite some claiming that they've returned the game simply because of the bug, I wouldn't. I enjoyed it when it was playable, and am sure that devs will fix this in time. Still, to be fair, if you don't own this game and are planning to buy it, I advise you to wait until the bug squashing are done.

One of the best management simulations on steam right now IMO. If you've ever played Game Dev Tycoon but wanted more depth, you can stop reading and buy this. If you haven't, Mad Games Tycoon is a management simulation about starting a game development studio.
You decide what genre(s), topic(s), target audience, game engine etc etc, the game is going to have/use. You oversee the development deciding whether to go more heavily into one catergory (like gameplay) over another. But you don't have to actually make games, I mean at the start yeah but not after you get established. You can make an awesome engine and sell it and make a good bit off of it. Or you can just publish games and try to turn a profit. Many different avenues can be taken to make a fortune.
Pros:
- Deep gameplay, with many options
- Graphics are pleasing. Not amazing, but they work and add to the charm
- I like the music.
- Addictive
- Adjustable pace.
- A few different starting points (1980, 1990, 2000, 2010 IIRC. Only looked at it once)
- You can set trends and be a hipster
- You need to attend to people's needs. No being a slave driver.
- With the sheer amount of topics (something like 300 i think), you can get some hilarious games made that'll sell well. Imagine that's a big plus for streamers/Youtuber people.
Cons(minor):
- The UI can be frustrating/clunky. (have to click like 3-4 Xs to leave a build menu)
- The amount of sounds from completing research/parts of games etc can become constant in a big office. (thank big gunz upstairs for volume control)
- Have to rebuild the entire office after each move. Understandable from a realism perspective, just sometimes can be an annoyance if you don't want to do that for 50+ people.
- Have to be smart. If you have a dumb-dumb moment and move into a bigger building just because you have the cash to buy it, well read the point above again. You'll have to take out a loan, possibly at 200% the normal interest rate. In other words, a small tooltip there would be handy.
- No way of grouping people into "teams" that i've seen. After a move, or a big class session, it's a pain to sift through your people to find the ones you had developing, researching, doing the graphics etc. Would be amazing if that little nuisance was plucked in the butt.
- Addictive.
- Nothing to really indicate when a new console is coming/when it's going to be taken off the market. No/not much historical news either. I'm in '94 right now, and haven't seen one yet.
Overall, the game is very good as it is. The cons are just minor frustrations that will probably be dealt with before full release (or it's my own ignorance/dumb-dumb moments that made the cons). This is defintely worthy of a pick up if you're into management style games. If you're looking to start playing management games, this ain't a bad place to start.

Well, I'm pleased to say I was wrong. I had a negative review of Starbound, being in Early Access hell and never being stable enough to play being my major complaints.

That being said, the childlike glee of exploring different colonies, working with (and against) NPCs, spelunking into a poisonous caverns, hunting abominations for food, building a homestead, shooting off into the depths of space, raiding settlements, farming, taking care of your pet, discovering your own story and simply surviving in the universe of Starbound brings me back every time. An incredibly ambitious title that seems to have achieved its potential before it has been released.
As a final note, players should always remember the broken promises of this dev team. Simply because they have created a spectacle over time does not mean that they did not rescind on promises and have a terrible update schedule. Here's to hoping the bugs and slowdowns are worked out and that the game releases in the forseable future.

Roguelikes are meant to be hard, and even unfair sometimes, but when a game only throws nonsense at you for no reason, I can't recommend it. Yes, even Nethack has nonsense things sometimes too, but at least they're funny. How about missing a hit eight times in a row and constantly breaking your equipment with almost no means to repair it? This is Dragon's Dungeon in a nutshell.
This game doesn't do anything to change its mobile roots - you can't use keyboard for movement and attacks (only for hotkeys, and they're not rebindable), and despite being a paid app on smartphones, it feels like it was designed to screw you over to sell microtransactions to make you win the game, with the exception that you can't buy anything to help you even if you wanted.
I haven't played too much, but this is just because every session rapidly become a chore. This is the kind of game where you basically only attack and drink potions, with no strategy. It's so automatic that when you die for being inattentive, thanks to the boredom of the gameplay, the game even mocks about the whole situation, saying "it's too late to drink your potions". In another words,  Dragon's Dungeon is a game of constant attacks (if you get lucky to hit the enemy) and heals, and if the procedural generation doesn't generate potions enough, you're screwed.
It isn't a matter of "git gud".
, made by a player with more than 100 hours on the game saying it's unwinnable. Also, just a few weeks after the game was released on Steam, the developer doesn't reply to anyone. He posted that
, but honestly, what's the point if he doesn't listen to the community?
All in all, if you're searching for a good roguelike (a true roguelike) on Steam, there's a lot of great games, such as WazHack, Dungeons of Dredmor, Tales of Maj'Eyal, The Curse of Yendor, Ananias Roguelike, Golden Krone Hotel, ADOM, Sword of the Stars: The Pit, etc. This just isn't a good one.

Dragon's Dungeon: Awakening is a roguelike dungeon crawler harking back to the very first origins of the genre - ASCII dungeons such as Rogue itself, Angband and derivatives. It has 25 levels across 5 different areas, as well as 5 quests for each area. The store page boasts 600 items and 150 monsters, which I haven't personally counted, but sounds reasonable enough. There are 7 classes, each with a different skillset and a skill tree that upgrades as you level - although it can be a lot of work to unlock it. There is a town, with crafting and a way to boost your character with gems - permanent upgrades that make this a roguelike rather than a true rogue. In this sense, like many roguelikes, you're meant to die sometimes - start again and get stronger.
It falls a bit flat as although there may be many monsters and items and levels, everything feels very much the same once you enter an area. Even fighting a boss doesn't feel significantly different to me. The first true boss I encounter simply summoned more of the monsters I've already been fighting until he ran out of mana, then I hit him in the face until he died.  Each area does have a different feel to it, but with 25 levels to each, it starts feeling like a grind very early on. Mana classes are very weak and will struggle, having to upgrade at town quite a lot. I had the most success with my warrior, who managed to get to level 15 of the first area before I ran out of health potions.
The gems you get for upgrading are quite limited and you can spend them on items, potions, skill points, in unlocking new classes or unlocking a new area. Spend them very wisely - I recommend maxing out your skill points first, as this will unlock new skills and passive bonuses. If you don't do this, it can be quite hard to reach new skills, leaving you with one ability for a long time. You never automatically get a skill; you need to follow the progression on the upgrade tree to unlock the question marks.
The first time you complete a level you'll want to kill absolutely everything for experience before going down a level, or you will quickly find yourself at risk of death. For weaker characters - such as the mage who is incredibly fragile - you're going to have to skirt around creatures and try to get the chests and upgrades without fighting too much until you're a bit stronger. Classes definitely do not feel balanced, and it's a shame that the most boring character, Mr Hit 'em In The Face Until They're Dead Warrrior is by far the easiest and strongest to play. I really love squishy long-range characters but without the right mana balance it just feels frustrating as getting punched in the face is pretty much K.O.
Although I enjoy this sort of gameplay and I like the amount of content in the game, it just didn't really have a visceral feeling of fun or any compelling reason to play longer than 15-30 minutes at a time. I admire the concept, but something didn't quite click for me. I have gone back to it quite a few times to get a full idea of the gameplay and it's definitely more fun in small game sessions.
Dragon's Dungeon is available on iOS, Android and Windows Phone for $1.99. This is an updated version - hence the "Awakening" name - with more creatures, items and an updated UI, but at the same time, retains the core gameplay. It is hard to understand a pricetag of £6.99 just to play it on Steam over mobile, especially on a title that is entirely suited to mobile play - simple clicks (swipes) and bitesize chunks of gameplay. I would definitely recommend it at $2.
Whilst I have enjoyed the game, I do think it's going to struggle at this price point and wouldn't be surprised to see it heavily discounted in sales or bundled.

As a long time fan of terraria, this is a game I was hugely excited about when I first heard of it. I finally got gifted it a couple of weeks ago (Thanks Feyth), and I went in with an open mind, knowing little about the game itself and looking forward to a few hours of getting used to the gameplay, before maybe jumping into multiplayer and then shelfing it. How wrong I was.
I won't lie, the first hour or so was tedious. Mining early on is slow, and getting to grips with the slightly awkward controls made me consider giving up. But I wanted to fly a spaceship at least once before I put down the game, and so I powered on, eventually repairing my spaceship and opening the doors to the Starbound universe. As soon as I had escaped the tutorial world, I became hooked. A giant space monolith with a portal to an ancient cavern filled with propecies and hints at a complex overarching plot? A frontier town with questing, minigames and NPC's with stories to tell and florans to hate? I was amazed. Finally, a sandbox game that felt ALIVE. For the first few hours, every planet I visited made me feel as if I was right there. Every new NPC had a story to tell, every dungeon had a hidden secret. Some aspects felt a little odd, and unfinished, but hey, this is early access! I was thoroughly enjoying being a part of the fantastic and beautiful universe that Chucklefish have created.
And then suddenly, to my horror, I realised I was done. I had finished all the quests. Upgraded my ship as much as I could. Discovered every kind of generated dungeon. I was mortified. I was so ready for more. More upgrades to unlock, new bosses to fight. What happened? Did they just forget to put in the rest of the story? Have two years of development led to just this? I couldn't believe that for such an expansive game, all the challenges were finished within a day or so. I was so utterly dissapointed that I just closed the game and watched ghostbusters while crying into cups of tea.
And then came the revelation. I was wandering through my ship, and noticed along my travels I had picked up a fridge. "Hmm, WinterBear. Maybe I could set up a little kitchen, see what recipes I can cook up?". Then I stopped at an asteroid field. "Hey WinterBear, you could totally build a sweet space station here!". Then I discovered wiring. "WinterBear WE NEED COMPLETE DOOR CONTROL FROM THE BRIDGE OF THE SHIP". For I had been mislead. Wrong all along. For starbound is not a survival adventure rpg as the first few hours of gameplay had indicated. It is not an epic space opera with horrifying aliens, and dashing heroes, as the lore would have you think. Oh no. It is a SANDBOX. I suddenly realised, that while the story was over, my adventures had just begun. All the useless junk I had picked up along my way suddenly became valuable building tools to create my own stories. The game became fun again, as I made my own projects to keep me entertained. I built smuggling outposts in harsh desert storms, sailed lava lakes for lost treasure, and furnished my spaceship with only the highest quality decor.
Because the truth is, while clearly the developers are working on bringing the story and the characters to life, that part of the game is just not ready yet. But the sandbox side most certainly is, and there are hundreds of truly beautiful items to find, and build with. I have every hope that starbounds storyline will be just as epic as I hoped it would be, but even if it is not, I would be lying if I said I had not enjoyed this game. It has some of the greatest potential I have ever seen in a video game, and I literally cannot wait for more.
So yeah, don't go in expecting Knights of the Old Republic 2D. Because thats not what the game is about. And don't go in expecting a hardcore survival experience either, because you will be disappointed. But if you approach this game as what it is, a sandbox with a nice flair of adventure, you will thoroughly enjoy it.
Oh and my cooking hobby? Well, I'm opening a chain restaurant across the cosmos, coming to a planet near you.

I have to write a review for the particular game, because it deserves attention, and I believe it is a very polished and
cleverly designed little game. Furthermore, besides its obvious flaws which derive from its mobile roots, it stands bold
and brave within a universe of similar games (dungeonmans, dungeons of dredmore, quest of dungeons etc.) only to
make a difference with its wealth of material and choices. Although until now I believe I have scratched just the surface
of the game's levels and characters, I see the amount of work that has been done in every little detail.
It plays and feels like most turnbased roguelikes you have already played, and if you are used to similar game systems
the game will make you feel like home. When you begin you are at an overworld map with a town and some places to explore. The town allows you to unlock new characters, buy various upgrades and learn parts of the game's lore. The places to explore are 6 variants which are always the same on the map but with random dungeons when you enter. Each level ends fast, but the enemies progress in almost similarly as you
making the game quite tough in my opinion. It has plenty of loot, plus various random mechanisms which you find spread
in the dungeon that allow you to do some generic crafting. You also find shops specialized either in potions or in armor/repairs. Every 5 dungeons you meet a tiny boss followed by many minions, something that adds to the chalenge.
Gameplaywise it offers many ways of advancing and exploring, and if we add the unlockable characters we look at a serious amount of game time. Depending on the choice of character it can get kinda repetitive but  I suppose it is a constant of the genre.
In order to concllude the game is totally recomended especially for fans of the roguelike/tactical rpg genre. I was a bit hesitant when I first saw it at the store, but it worths every penny. You will definetely get many hours of gameplay out of it.

Okay.
The game, it's good, i'm not going to lie to you, it's good in some ways. Yet everyone has their own perspective and preference for games, and as you can see by the, uh, "Overwhelmingly Negative" percentage of reviews, a lot of people do not at all like the game. I like it. But there's just, some things that I couldn't get the feel of. These are issues that all games are going to face in their lifetime, some suffering more than others.
So let's get in with the thick and thin of it (TL;DR at the bottom):
I'm a gamer, as 90% of the steam community is made up of gamers. While there are gamers, there are of course, games, and they come in various different types, shapes, sizes, so much more. It's possible to list them all in one sitting, but I'm pretty much too lazy to do so.
Anyway, gamers, along with their games, tend to select what games give them interest. Let's put Fallout 4 for an example (after all, it's the game i'm putting a review on). Fallout 4 is a post-apocalyptic RPG (Role-Playing-Game) where you play as either a male or female that has served in the American US military and is selected for eligibility for entry into a Vault (nuclear bomb shelter designed to last several lifetimes). Being that this is an RPG game, it would definitely appeal to gamers who like to Roleplay.
Here's where an issue comes in: RPG's tend to have characters who are essentially blank slates, opening up to several different possibilities one could piece onto a character, such as a gamer could go: "This guy was like, a medic in the prewar times," or "Garret was a mechanic trying to survive a wasteland," or "Trish was a raider who was banished from her tribe and seeks revenge." That is essentially what Roleplay is. Unfortunately with Fallout 4 (I will call it FO4 from now on), the character's experiences has been predetermined, as mentioned before. I personally was completely fine with this arrangement of character origins, not exactly how I wanted it to be, but hey, I still liked it.
However, most "RPG Gamers" want their RPG's in their conventional arrangement, as that is the way it's clearly supposed to be. FO4 does not achieve the RPG norm, unfortunately, and continues to recieve bad reviews strictly because of this issue. I, for one, oppose this, but let's get back to that later.
Now onto other matters, gamers, obviously, are attracted to video games. Video games come from a big screen attached to a box with a couple of fancy boards and wires inside of it, to put it lightly. Chances are good you're reading this from such a screen right now. Every computer is different, and each have a capacity and limit to their computing capabilities. Every video game has a set of requirements for a computer to be able to run properly, and FO4 is no exception. FO4 is a huge, really huge game that can take a toll on, as most would call it; "potato computers", and requires a decently functional PC to run.
When I first started FO4, it was absolute hell to even try and get through the first area of the game (!Spoilers!)
because everything was so laggy and it was hard to even shoot the radroaches that were attacking me (Thank God for V.A.T.S.), so I figured it was time to mess with some settings.
Here's where another issue arises, game preformance. Gamers and non-gamers alike don't want to play a video game that they can't play, after all, what is a game if you can't play it? Could it even be called a game? Some gamers have superpowerful computers that can withstand a hurricane of preformance. Some aren't so blessed, with computers who can barely run Internet Explorer. I didn't mind to spend some time to change some settings around so my aim with my gun wouldn't teleport from one place to another in increments of one second (The darn Godrays, even on low they'd kill me more efficiently than a Deathclaw...). Most gamers don't like to spend time fixing their game to run on their computers, I might say i'm the only one who doesn't mind at all.
FO4's issue with preformance is a kind of major issue, as compared to the minor issues (Major being spread across multiple aspects of a game, that can be experienced by other games as well, Minor being focused on a single aspect, such as RPG elements in a game, as stated before.). Yet, it is mostly an issue where it's the gamer's fault for this happening in their game. As mentioned before, some gamers all have different devices with different limits. Some may not be able to run FO4 so well as others. If a gamer has a crappy computer that doesn't run games well, it's on him/her that he/she doesn't want to spend time to make the game be able to run on their potatoes, that is, if the game itself requires a higher level of computing. If a gamer has a really good computer that's able to process tons of data, and somehow the game is still running badly, it's on the game, if the game requires a level of computing beyond seriously advanced levels.
FO4 requires a high-preformance PC (or console, whatever your platform, which raises a whole slew of other issues regarding the game, but this is for PC, so I shouldn't get too complicated, as it already is.) that can run advanced graphics and is capable of taking a lot of data in at once. So, in short, those who have good PC's are likely to have clean, smooth animations without the hassle of lag, and vice versa.
This review has honestly gone too long, and i've ran out of brain power at this point, so I don't want to keep you reading a  book (though it is helpful to), but I hope you get the gist of what i'm saying.
TL;DR: Every gamer is different, each with their own preferences. Fallout 4 has many different issues that every game could face in their lifetime, and has an appeal to a specific type of gamer, the RPG type.
I recommend this game to those who prefer RPG's, and not to those who don't. Everyone is different, anyway.

Ittle Dew is not only a clever name, but a very clever game. It takes Zelda's block pushing, torch lighting, and enemy managing puzzles to a point where they actually take some thought. The main game can take as long or little as you want; it took me about six hours to explore the entire castle and collect most of the cards, but the game can be completed in under 15 minutes (thank you, achievements, for pointing that out).
Furthermore, you technically only need two of the game's three items to complete the game, a feat accomplished by clever level design, multiple routes, and puzzles with multiple solutions. Each item is functionally very different from the others, so puzzles that are easy when you have the teleport wand may be really challenging without it.
There are also two levels in the world that only exist to offer more challenging puzzles to those that want them. I found them to be really enjoyable, but I'm happy that they are optional.
The game's art is simple yet clear, and it gives the game's characters plenty of personality. The dialogue is witty and occasionally pokes fun at game tropes, though I wish there was an option to disable the dialogue for future playthroughs.

Generally good zombie survival title, but not a great one.
The game takes place in a usual way. You play as someone waking up with a head injury during a zombie apocalypse and must join with others to survive. You're delegated a list of camp opportunities, tasks, and missions to run while the calendar ticks down. You meet new survivors, craft gear, etc. You basically know how the flow of this game already works.
Story and characters are decent. More than nothing, but nothing too incredible usually, although the game has the potential to play out differently based on who you recruit and what you elect to do as the clock ticks down. As such, there's some replyabability. Graphics are okay, not great. A lot of colors are washed out, but characters have recognizable features and come off as realistic. Animations take place during combat and these look a little better than not. Speaking of combat, it's a mixed. I love that it's turn based, but it's also very sloggish... both zombies and players have very high hp and low offense for a while, broken up mainly by tougher npc Mad Max type human enemies with guns. You run out of resources very fast and are forced to contend with making dull weak melee attacks for a bit too long. I found myself dozing off occasionally during long runs in combat, unfortunately.
One particular issue I have with Dead Age is the menus. They're very clunky. You'll figure them out eventually, but they don't flow well at all, and there's a ton of 'do this, to get to that, to arrange this...' design to it. It's kind of a mess.
The music is decent at first, but gets very monotonous. Bring your own and mute the ingame track. Sound effects are also a bit repetitious. The lack of variety in the audio is a bit disappointing.
This is a decent game, perhaps slightly above average, but it's not by any means incredible. A lot of "you've seen this before" comes up in it... perhaps akin to a poor man's The Walking Dead. There's a decent playing experience to be had, but the game has made some tiresome design choices I felt only slowed things down more than I would have liked. It's not very visceral and the pacing is just enough to keep you wanting to see more, but not enough to generate a lot of excitement. All in all, decent and nothing further. Definitely worth getting on a modest sale, at least.

TL;DR: Wish Guns of Icarus lived up to its potential? Love pirates? Have a few friends willing to drop $20 on this? Buy it. Stop sitting on the fence. Just try not to take the game too seriously.
---------------------------
Let me preface this by saying that you'll want friends to play with. If you don't have a group of friends willing to drop $20 on this game, then you best hold off. That being said, it's certainly worth the money.
Blackwake is everything I was hoping it would be. I was very skeptical due to it being early access, but the developers' constant communcation and frequent updates helped me to get over that fear. I've been a sucker for early access "bait-n-switch," and I was very cautious... But my love for pirate games pushed me over the edge to get this (that, and Hat Films' livestream).
Blackwake has a fantastic balance of intense and comedic moments. Cooperatively sailing a vessel is addicting, every match bringing about its own unique moments. One second you'll be loading up a cannon, and the next you'll find yourself treading water as the hull of your ship was breached right where you were standing.
However, your enjoyment of the game will largely depend on the crew you're with (which is why playing with friends may be the best choice). Try to find some people who don't take the game TOO seriously, while still looking to succeed. Those will often be the best crews. Take this game with a grain of salt: it's not meant to be a hardcore, boat simulator. The game constantly reminds you of its goofy undertones every time someone next to you gets eviscerated into a pile of chunky bits by a stray cannonball.
If you're on the fence, and love games like Guns of Icarus (and were disappointed by Guns of Icarus' arguably squandered potential), then you'll love this game. Just be sure to have a good group to play with, and don't be a salty sea-biscuit who takes everything too seriously.

Starbound is a seminal example of a game with a good idea and a lot of hype, but with a disjointed, failed execution that results in a weak overall experience.
At alpha release, the game was promising, with a fun though limited game loop. Similar to Terraria, the player collects ore to build new armor and advance to more difficult terrain. The universe provided a lot of different options and experiences, and had a vast array of items to collect to enhance your home and ship.
As development continued, changes to combat made fights with monters more lethal but did not increase the variety of encounters. Even though monsters are procedurally generated, their attacks and combat maneuvers are well stereotyped. Further, a lack of difficulty options may prevent players who are primarily interested in exploring and building from experiencing the universe.
The most dissappointing change was the introduction of the quest system. While questing could have been utilized to create interesting adventures, the previously mentioned changes to combat make some missions frustrating. Many missions are simple "fetch quests" and don't contribute meaningully to player experience. Furthermore, the quest systems have resulted in a linearized and gated progression that forces players to complete missions to expand their starship and explore new worlds.
Ultimately, the game may appeal to people who are very interested in the combat system and are willing follow the railroaded questing path. For players who are looking for an exploration game, be aware that you will have to progress through the quest chain to unlock all the worlds and be free to explore the universe at your lesiure.

I highly recommend this game to just about anyone who's looking for something unique. I truly believe this game is why video games can be considered a form of art, it is that good.
And if the game isn't an art, what's in the game definitely is in both literature, and design.
The game is a Hack and slash style RPG, with numerous weapons you unlock as you progress through the game, starting you with a hammer. Every weapon is distinctly different with the way it handles, and how you upgrade them.
The upgrading system for the weapons is great as well, allowing you to give them different advantages over your foes. Some weapons can ignore armor through upgrades. Some allow you to hold more ammo, or dish out multiple projectiles.
To increase variety in gameplay there is also a distillery, and a Shrine. The distillery can change the kid's properties and/or stats accordingly to help fit into how you like to play, and the shrine can make the game more difficult for more rewards by changing the enemies' properties, like making them move quicker, or have regenerating health, etc.
The varying gameplay with the weapons, distillery, and shrine give it a fantastic way to play the game the way YOU want. Plus it has a new game plus mode, and a score attack mode once you beat the game, if you ever feel the need to try things you didn't have the chance to, or try to dominate leaderboards.
As for the story you dive head first into an apocalyptic like situation in a fantasy world, Caelondia, admist something frequently called "The Calamity" narrated by a character named Rucks. Rucks tells the story of the nameless "kid" you play as, and gives context and background to the world you play in, while you're playing in.
In other words, the story unfolds as you are actually playing through a game. No cutscene breaks, no elongated needless lore explanation as with some other RPGs, just Rucks, and you/"The kid".
That being said, the story of the whole thing is way too good to actually say anything more about.
Lastly, presentation. This game looks, sounds, even feels incredible. At the beginning, the world around you is crumbling apart, and it seems everyone has turned into pillars of solid ash, and the music sets in, giving the whole world breath to it. On that note, the music is fantastic, and can really move you just by listening to it. That, coupled with the beautiful artwork that feels so immersive almost puts you right into the game, giving the definition of presentation it's purpose: to pull you in, even before you start.
tl;dr this hack and slash rpg is a brilliant piece of art with varying game choices, an incredible tale to tell, and some of the best presentation I've seen in a game ever.
I truly think this game is deserving of a 10/10, and think that people who have even considered looking this game up should not hesitate to purchase.

I'm a fan of puzzle-platforming games and CamObs was recommended to me in a said genre bundle pack. Bought it and started playing it. I have mixed feelings about this game, because while it feels kind of a puzzle to figure out how to navigate through the level, it is more of just a platforming game. The game itself isn't that much of a puzzle as you just navigate the character around. If you are inclined to collect the story bits via the polaroids, then it might be slightly more of a puzzle to reach said story bits as some levels have them tucked away at niches that you might miss or don't know how to reach. Looking at the guides, it looks some a few are really hard to get and one that no one knows how to reach at this point.
To which, this leads to the game mechanic. It is interesting as you take images to extend your platform so you may reach farther than what the game is orginally designed. This is the entire basis of the game and while it is a bit dull, it is amusing to fiddle around and play with it during the game. This part of the game mechanic is to be applaud, but the camera pan mechanic to look further isn't as amazing. I'm using the steam controller and when I scroll to look ahead, it just scrolls back almost immediately. Maybe I need to configure the controller a bit more, but the scrolling ahead doesn't appear to be of much use except for to find out if jumping to that ledge yields a path or not. Then again, you can always just try jumping up there to see if there is anything without panning the camera that way. Probably, there will be a game level where mechanically, you need to simultaneously pan the camera and snap an image to extend your platform to reach the end of the level. (oh boy).
Overall, the game can be fun if you enjoy platforming and learning about the storyline bit-by-bit. I would have liked more instructions on how to play the game before the game begins. That and clearer understanding of how the camera flash works instead of just trial and error to get a feel for it to understand it. Still, I'll play it in the long-term until I get bored of it.. 6/10.

The game revolves around a female protagonist with a special camera/ability to take "afterimages", cloning her surroundings (platform blocks) and move them for a short time to help reach other platforms. I find it frustrating at times trying to reach them, so I know it's good for people who like challenges. . :)

All that really bugged me was how stale that was, but to be fair it is an indie game so... Meh. Levels were thought out well, but its a 2D game so I figure it wasn't that hard. This game honestly might get buryed considering how it is 2017 and most people are looking for bigger and better things, like graphically and with a vast, deep story. Which is a real bummer for a game like this. Considering it just wants a chance, just one. Well, that is why we reviewer
people are here. We can be here to say "Hey, for a cheap game this wasn't half bad" and it's not. Pick it up and try it. Cheap and simple, but hey... It's not half bad. Also! Almost forgot to say it has a level editor and achievements!
