I give this game a very cautious recommendation.
I picked it up because I'm a huge Zelda fan, and it was on sale at the time. The gameplay is similar to a 2D Zelda in many regards in that you explore, fight, and solve puzzles using your trusty stick/sword and items that you gain throughout your adventure. So yes, there are a lot of familiar elements here if you like these kinds of games.
That said, it doesn't PLAY like a Zelda game. That's not necessarily a bad thing depending on why you enjoy these games in the first place. Whereas Zelda has very tight, simple combat and excellent monster design, it becomes apparent soon after starting this game that combat is not the main focus. Ittle's stick has a short range and some enemies do not suffer knockback when hit. There are also not many enemies with unique weaknesses. Most of them are a simple hack n' slash affair.
Where this game truly shines is in the puzzle department. I would even say that this game is more of a puzzle game than a 2D adventure game, because the world is compact and filled to the brim with puzzles. Many of them are actually challenging! I literally spent hours in the Master Cave, an optional dungeon filled with the toughest puzzles that this game has to offer, because the puzzles were so difficult and I was determined to solve them without a guide. Though I felt like ripping my hair out at the time, solving these complex puzzles was a rewarding experience in and of itself, unlike in Zelda dungeons where it sometimes feels like puzzles are just there to pad the game out.
This is a short game, and there are only three items (besides the default stick) that you can obtain. The twist is that these items work together to help you solve puzzles and traverse the main dungeon. For instance, you can combine the portal wand and the ice rod to create an ice block that warps you to the other side of the room. This part of the game was handled ingeniously. There are so many things you can do with these three items and the objects in your environment. There are also multiple ways that you can beat the game, and you don't even need all of the items to do it. Pretty cool!
As mentioned, this game is short. If you skipped the Master Cave, it would likely take you about 3-5 hours on your first attempt. The replay value comes from finding out different ways to beat the game using different combinations of items. The game is also uniformly hilarious and aware of its genre. Even the credit sequence is funny.
TL;DR - This is more of a puzzle game than a 2D adventure game. If you like puzzles, you will probably like it.

Camera Obscura is a simple and self-explanatory platformer. When the game starts off, it doesn't look all that promising and "innovative and exciting" as the description on the store page suggests. You are supposed to jump over obstacles and reach the door to pass the level. So,  It is as simple as it sounds. But later on in the game, it gives you the ability to manipulate the enviroment by creating an after-image of the obstacles with the push of a button, allowing you to use them as a boost for a short amount of time. There aren't many other elements (which makes the game kind of dull in my opinion) and that's mostly everything about the gameplay.
If you are enjoying, there is workshop support for more. Thus, taking its price into account, it offers great value in terms of replayability and lenght. There is also controller support if you have one.
However, the only thing annoyed me was that, even though the graphics are old-fashionably cute, the game does not run on 16:9 ratio. (At least I couldn't make it run)
All in all, it's worth it if you are platformer enthusiast. If not, you might find it a little bit dull. But for the price tag, you can't go too wrong with it.

This game is dumb. I literally have a wide open shot 2 squares away and because he's standing near a big rock he gets high cover bonus which made it a 50% chance to hit. I died. The rock wasn't even protecting him. I have clear line of sight, 2 squares away. Where is the flanking bonus?? So many times I've run straight up to them and rushed them and it only gave me a 80 percent chance, then they miss. That just doesn't feel right to me. If I rush directly next to him I should at least get a 90% percent chance to hit without having to upgrade my troops. The chance to hit numbers feel off and punishing. I prefer games like these to incentivise flanking more instead of having unrealist shot chances when hiding behind cover and when I actually do flank, give me the freaking bonus.
This one time I was behind full cover and the animation of the bullets went through these crates to kill me. What, is the game revolving around the idea that your guys are peaking their heads out of cover and then it clips them? Full cover should give you almost full protection against shots being around 10-15% chance to hit. In this game that's not the case, it's normally a 33% percent chance to hit which is too high imo. Half cover should give you a decent chance to hit at 60% and flanking should be 85% or more, give or take depending on the range.
I've played other turn based games like this and the numbers actually felt right and rewarded flanking, grenades and ambush tactics. Where if you're behind full cover 95% of the time you are safe, which leads to having your front liners go around to flank, while your sniper sets up an ambush. They try to pull this off in this game but made it too unrealistic by adding the chance to hit behind cover too high and the chance to hit when flanked too low. This game you just pray to RNJesus and even if your tactics are really good, you get punished by unrealistic chance percentages

There is also some gunplay which while feeling pretty good, does not work well on mouse and keyboard due to the way the controls are done. You have to hold the shift key in order to zoom in and that just feels terrible. The right mouse button is already taken up by interact and counter so this leaves the shift key or you need to work something else out. Since there is also a lot of driving in this game, I would recommend you just use an Xbox 360 controller to play this game. The graphics and sound in this game are really nice. The game does not support XP due to use of DX11 features and the game looks really nice with them enabled. The game will last about 8+ hours for the main story but 100% completion will take a lot longer. I break a rule in writing this review for the game. It is still in beta, or early access, or whatever we're calling it. But, in so doing - I rate this game at its current state, with no hope of it finishing early access, as such is only fair. It appears to have been in Early Access for quite awhile.
I break this rule because it's worth it. This game. It's pretty nice, definitely worth the pre-release price I've paid.
Starbound is a breath of fresh air in the 2D sandbox genre, of which there aren't many successful titles. Terraria is perhaps one, but not one I'm particularly satisfied with. Terraria feels undeveloped, wanting, and repetitive. Starbound shares some qualities, but branches out in a unique way that is invigorating for those of us who might enjoy it.
Starbound is not a pure sandbox, where you are left to your devices in a single worldspace. Starbound possesses a basic narrative, that you can pursue at your directive, with some sparse side quests for enjoyment. You travel to other worlds, where - gasp - there are other people! NPCs can occur, some of which may not kill you on sight. Some you can trade with, others are atmospheric. Biomes have variety, monsters have variety. I'm not sure how many max tier playthroughs it'll last you until your bored, but I think for someone who's serious about the genre - it should last you at least 60-80 hours worth, as I'm not serious about it and that's what I'm clocking at.
So, $15 for 60-80 hours of gameplay? Seems fair. That's not even including multiplayer.
Equipment is also a new take in the right direction. You have TWO HANDS. What does this mean? Well, I feel this game actually takes an account for different playstyles. You can use two one-handed objects at once, making dual-wielding items, keeping a weapon and a utility object handy, two-handed weapons, two-handed tools, and all sorts of situations possible. There are also body upgrades, a basic armor system with cosmetic slots, a dye and sign creation system, upgradable ships, one and two handed guns, and many different biomes. You also have a pet, that you can play with, which my lady found very amusing.
You also have your computer, which can handle tech upgrades and something called 3D printing. Essentially, any non-crafting based item can be deconstructed, then recreated using money. This is good for builds, as most of the 3D printing produces furniture. You can also find a guitar, where you can play music, and download mods to give you even more to play with. There is a hub that is unlocked that you get easy access to, and where your 'main quest' sequence is generated. I haven't finished it yet, but it keeps some appeal by tempting you with a mysterious gate in an ancient ruin out in space. The main quests are in isolated areas where you can't build, but you get a challenging combat, with a distinguished boss that may or may not have a gimick used to kill it. Very reminiscent of old Zelda or SNES titles. There are also SO MANY DIFFERENT WORLDS in a single save, that it's unreal.
Gameplay is solid. I've only ever crashed in its earliest versions, attempting to run different modes for testing purposes. Standard modes run rather well. One patch I had to use OpenGL, but - that lasted a week I think. The community and the creators are determined; I was worried at the start, feeling they weren't cranking out content. Though, they've proven those concerns wrong, developing core mechanics and pushing the game to a more polished state.
Some issues? Hitboxes aren't perfect. Some creatures have their heads slightly out of hitbox because they're elongated, and you can't wammy them. Creatures don't have critical hit regions, but I think players do - so there's that for PvP. I haven't tested multiplayer extensively, but I know it works. Descending down through platforms can get tricky since you can't drop through them, and you jump so high. I created a character for my girlfriend, and apparently, I share the same universe as her, as the homeworld her different race, new character has was my homeworld - complete with my base and chests. She has different bookmarks though, so I set her up with an unused planet in the system that she could farm and start off in. Tiers might get repetitive later on, but - playing this game casually solo has still been keeping me interested, at the very least having finished the Titanium tier. The most serious drawback? They update this game very slowly. But, the updates bring solid content, they produce other titles, and they're a new company. Maybe they'll learn from it, maybe not.
To compliment all of this, the modding community looks like it'll really take off. The developers are really supporting them, and giving them spotlight. I anticipate with the modding community the game has, it'll be great to see in the future if the game finishes early access - or stops updating. Also, whoever the audio artist is, he's a godsend. The game's music is fantastic, and the art - yes pixel-art is art - is pretty impressive. Very clean, with good animation and articulation. Solid character customization too with aesthetic things to find and wear in your cosmetic slots!
My personal feelings on the game?
For $15 USD: 7/10, pretty impressive, and I write this with no plans for improvement. Great additon to the visually basic, but functionally deep Sandbox / RPG genre.

This game is one of the finest interactive examples of what it means to be truly Awesome, with a capital A.
A labour of love created with unparalelled attention-to-detail in a platformer, partnered with well-tuned physics that make every fight unique, no matter how many times repeated.
Wild 80s science-fiction, heavy on the action, low on the subtlety. Ride direwolves while firing double-barrelled machineguns at giant leaping robotic quadrupeds with bladed whips forty feet long for tails. To exactly the kind of music you'd imagine partnering with that image. A bizarre fusion of intense physics-based action platforming, the adult form of the clunky, old-fashioned Contra or Metal Slug games, and high-challenge Japanese bullet hell boss battles, without ever being anything less than exciting.
A short but intensely satisfying experience even I can replay. I have trouble with *finishing* most games before I grow bored. This one has the freshness of a randomised experience, despite the hand-crafted levels, courtesy of the rich variety a physics-enabled world provides. Rely upon it to continually surprise you with a higher level of intensity, all the way to the end.
I've honestly never played a better shooter-platformer - Aleksey Abramenko is the new king of the genre.

Game plays quite nice once I got a few days into it. Though neither graphics nor animations are all that pretty to look at, the combat is interesting enough, with good variety of opponents, provided most of them are zombies. Combined with the scarcity of resources required it is quite engaging.
The story so far flows along nicely, it's a zombie game, so I don't expect them to reinvent the wheel, but so far what I've seen ties nicely into the gameplay.
Points of criticism for me would be the little amount of interaction I've had with my fellow survivors so far, I'm at day 12 so far, so that might change but apart from getting them into my group I haven't really talked to them.
The combat does get tedious after a while and starts being monotone, as do the random events during patrols as you manage to achieve higher areas you'll often see the same more than once during one outing.
I'd also believe that a more comic-like style for the combat graphics would have benefitted the game more. What's there doesn't really hurt, but it's far from memorable.
The facebook button in a corner of the main menu was something I personally disliked as well, though it's a fairly minor point.
I'd also like to express my thanks for the quick help I got with my problems getting the game to progress though the prologue, though I ultimately didn't take it. Still nice, not to be ignored.
All in all, I definitely like what the game has presented so far, though it took me a bit to get to this point. I got it on sale and it's money well spent. There's quite a bit to be improved upon, but for their next project  I'd give the devs the benefit of the doubt.

I honestly cannot recommend this game in its current state.
While Fallout 4 may hit the mark with its stellar gunplay and stunning (but GPU intensive) visuals, it falls flat on nearly every staple RPG element that its predecessors had before it.
-Player choice in the game is watered down to selecting some dialogue options that may give you some extra exposition and world building but (almost) never effects the outcome of a situation. With most dialogue choices being, (a): passive/clueless response, (b): aggresive/vengeful response, (c): sarcastic/jerkass response, or (d): please spew exposition at me response. The game may also on extremely rare and far too infrequent occasion, throw a Charisma check at you, but those don't matter either as you can completely just savescum your way through those with the Quicksave/Quickload keys.
-Player morality has also been extremely stripped down to bare minimum, as was the case with ESV:Skyrim, where you are forced to play the good guy, and the only bad choices you can make, is murdering NPCs for absolutely no justifiable reason. Which doubly has absolutely no benefit whatsoever for you when most NPCs you'll meet are shopkeepers, and I can't think of any reason why you'd consider murdering your main source of income/items. With the release of the Nuka World DLC you can become a raider and take over settlements as the 'bad guy', at the cost of screwing everything else over. Once again the cost doesn't justify the means.
-The Main Quest and side quests has you on virtual rails as you travel from point A to point B, with a extremely overpowering emphasis on "Shoot first, never ask questions." You'll be killing things non-stop, despite most real humans having actual motives, families to care for, or just looking out for themselves. There are almost never any situations where there is a moral grey area, where upon you'll be forced to choose between the lesser of two evils, or even a situation that has lasting implications or effects beyond the immeadiate "hey good work here's some caps".
- Fallout 4, unlike its predecessors also lacks virtually any sort of mature or dark themes, with storytelling that is in my opinion, fit for a game rated T, or on the level of Call of Duty games. Swearing is about as far as the game gets for "mature storytelling", and the game will at times, very immaturely toss up the F word in dialogue, often for the purely comedic "Ahahaha, he said f***." treating us like kids in middle school.
- The game has a overall feel of watered down simplicity to it. Long gone are the immersive perk systems, or riveting storytelling that games like Fallout 1, 2 or New Vegas had. If you want a great game that treats you like an adult, has a gripping story and excelling world building, go pick up Witcher 3. If you want the classic Fallout feel, go pick up New Vegas, or even 1/2.
As many have said before me, "This isn't a Fallout Game." It's a Fallout theme open world shooter.

I highly recommend this game to just about anyone who's looking for something unique. I truly believe this game is why video games can be considered a form of art, it is that good.
And if the game isn't an art, what's in the game definitely is in both literature, and design.
The game is a Hack and slash style RPG, with numerous weapons you unlock as you progress through the game, starting you with a hammer. Every weapon is distinctly different with the way it handles, and how you upgrade them.
The upgrading system for the weapons is great as well, allowing you to give them different advantages over your foes. Some weapons can ignore armor through upgrades. Some allow you to hold more ammo, or dish out multiple projectiles.
To increase variety in gameplay there is also a distillery, and a Shrine. The distillery can change the kid's properties and/or stats accordingly to help fit into how you like to play, and the shrine can make the game more difficult for more rewards by changing the enemies' properties, like making them move quicker, or have regenerating health, etc.
The varying gameplay with the weapons, distillery, and shrine give it a fantastic way to play the game the way YOU want. Plus it has a new game plus mode, and a score attack mode once you beat the game, if you ever feel the need to try things you didn't have the chance to, or try to dominate leaderboards.
As for the story you dive head first into an apocalyptic like situation in a fantasy world, Caelondia, admist something frequently called "The Calamity" narrated by a character named Rucks. Rucks tells the story of the nameless "kid" you play as, and gives context and background to the world you play in, while you're playing in.
In other words, the story unfolds as you are actually playing through a game. No cutscene breaks, no elongated needless lore explanation as with some other RPGs, just Rucks, and you/"The kid".
That being said, the story of the whole thing is way too good to actually say anything more about.
Lastly, presentation. This game looks, sounds, even feels incredible. At the beginning, the world around you is crumbling apart, and it seems everyone has turned into pillars of solid ash, and the music sets in, giving the whole world breath to it. On that note, the music is fantastic, and can really move you just by listening to it. That, coupled with the beautiful artwork that feels so immersive almost puts you right into the game, giving the definition of presentation it's purpose: to pull you in, even before you start.
tl;dr this hack and slash rpg is a brilliant piece of art with varying game choices, an incredible tale to tell, and some of the best presentation I've seen in a game ever.

A mix of RPG and pinball. Your party members / party balls smash through obstacles and enemies, navigating encounters and using their special abilities to interact with unique levels / tables.
The integration of RPG mechanics and pinball. Your party "tanks" are really good at smashing around the table, but they're also large in size, which means it's physically harder to lose them - an approximation of having a lot of HP. Your rogue or alchemist can do a lot of damage if you can aim them well, but they're also very easy to lose.
You can probably ignore all the special RPG abilities if you're a pinball wizard - and conversely, if you never seriously played a game of pinball, like me, the RPG mechanics can save you.
The story itself is pretty good, and all the party members you recruit have simple yet memorable personalities that are reflected in the gameplay.
The game is fairly short. 4 chapters, each with 5-8 maps, which change slightly between the main story missions and replays for loot and xp, and another chapter that you can't repeat. If you repeat every chapter once, you'll end up with 5-7 hours of gameplay.
The voice-acting is also... not great.

It’s a well-known fact that you can apply RPG elements to nearly any kind of game, but there yet remains a few genres that this cross-pollination has not touched. You can cross pinball games off that list thanks to Rollers of the Realm, a medieval romp through forests and castles as adventuring classes of balls. It’s not a tongue-in-cheek treatment either, for the pinballing exclusively covers the mechanics of gameplay while the story traces the characters those balls represent. I never would have thought to approach RPG pinball from this angle, but I also wouldn’t have expected it to be this fun.
The story opens with a young thief and her dog in the midst of trouble, as thieves are wont to do. Her struggle leads her to cross paths with a drunken knight, a timid healer, and many more colorful characters as they uncover a plot that spans the entire realm. Getting to the bottom of it will require enlisting the aid of druids, exploring ancient tombs, breaking into secured keeps, and more. Only clever use of her allies’ skills will allow the thief to break through the bandits and barriers in her way and maybe, just maybe, get some peace and quiet for her and her dog.
Levels are heavily informed by the plot as you progress, placing you in forest clearings, market squares, dismal dungeons, and other common fantasy locales. The difference here is that they’re laid out like simple pinball tables, and you heroes are balls. Launching your chosen ally onto the field, you must use the often numerous flippers to get them into the parts of the map needed to progress, bumping off enemies and gathering gold and treasure along the way. Goals can be anything from defeating a jailer to nailing trickshot off a table and out a tower window, but all of them require fine control over your rolling heroes.
Holding a ball in the launcher or on your flippers lets you switch freely between the classes at your disposal. Each has stats and skills to be aware of, like the thief being smaller and doing more damage from behind, or the knight being larger and resistant to being knocked around. They have special abilities as well, everything from calling in additional balls to blocking gutters to reviving lost heroes. When there are no enemies around you can flip balls around willy-nilly without losing them but when foes turn up, gutterballs are lost unless revived by the priest ball. Enemies attack by striking your flippers, cleverly chipping away at them until they’re too short to be of any use.
The mechanics of the game are extremely well thought-out and do a convincing job of imitating a classic tale of adventure. You’ll get plenty of voiced interludes from your character which feature some snappy, entertaining exchanges. Additionally, that gold you collect is used to purchase item upgrades which improve the stats of your heroes or grant them new abilities. It’s the total RPG package, marked only by a few missteps. Some levels aren’t designed as well as others and can require frustratingly precise shots or transfers to complete. One forest level took me ages to beat because the path through it was needlessly obtuse. There’s also not a huge amount of levels, especially considering how quickly you can burn through them once you get the hang of the game.
The soft, pastoral tones and simple shapes are perfect for a game so steeped in classic charms, though some parts like the character portraits are not up to the same quality. Don’t expect anything spectacular from the sound design, but it does what it’s there to do. You’ll get a few good hours of adventure out of this one, more if you give the optional arena mode a shot or go back to dig up hidden treasures in each of the levels. Rollers of the Realm does a fine job of executing its premise and making it a rollicking good time, it’s just not terribly ambitious about any of it. Put this one down for when you need a chill adventure, and you won’t be disappointed.

There are certain qualities that make a game good.  Good controls, or combat system.  Maybe a fun unlock/leveling system, or a great storyline that sucks you in.  While I can't say Ittle Dew is exemplary by any means (specifically, the ones previously listed) it excels well in understanding its unique charm.  The flaws, in this sense, actually improve the game (subjectively, of course) since the whole game is just filled with character.
The Zelda-esque gameplay has been done a hundred times, so you should know the exact gameplay you're getting into--As a side note, it is pretty unique in that its short, but certain items (which all help solve the game's puzzles) can be collected in different orders on your playthroughs, though I admit I've only played through the main game once.
My favorite part of this game though was the dialogues--Its very rare in a game do I get excited to drop the controller and see some back  and forths, complete with animated character portraits, that, once again, are filled to the brim with developer charm.
The world is colorful and the characters in it are what I'd consider the game's top aspect. With that said, the $10 price might be high, but at $5 or less you shouldn't pass up on playing this game at least once.

Berseria does a better job of highlighting Sorey's heroism and virtues than Zestiria did, and he doesn't even appear in the game.
Berseria is (at the time of writing) the single darkest and mature entry in the series, competing with maybe only Xillia 2.

...
Slightly more meta commentary:
I know some people aren't going to like it when I say this (because they hated Zestiria), but this game IS a prequel for it, so I suggest you play Zestiria first, then alternate between the two. I'm a big fan of the Tales series for roughly a decade or so now. Played every game in the series except for Destiny. Following the train wreck of Xillia 2 and Zesteria, I was pretty much ready to give up. I decided to give Berseria a try thanks to many positive feedback from the community. So much to say about this.
First graphics is gorgeous. Berseria retains the anime styled character design but this time, the landscape looks amazing.
The only downside is that the environment looks so pretty, I didn't notice the monsters at times.
Music, you get the usual Tales styled music, nothing sounds bad, but most songs aren't memorable.
Gameplay, it's good to see that there's FINALLY free camera control during exploration. Or it's just been that long since I cared about the franchise. Exploration is fairly on par with Xillia IMO.
Combat. IT'S FUN AGAIN!!! Thank you Bandai Namco for not making combat a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Looks like initiating combat right on the map is out the door. Which means all the potential terrible camera angles go out with it.
This time all your attacks are Artes and you can map them to the four face buttons. You have the A-Arte tree of Graces F but the tree is fully customizable. Free move is the primary form of movement this time and it's a welcomed change.
Long story short, if you like the Tales series, this will be a fun new entry to the series. If you hate anime and action based combat, then move along. For me, this rekindled my interest in the franchise. (Bandai Namco NA, please stock more Collector's edition next time)

1. Gameplay:
Gameplay is fast and fun, and can be played with a controller or mouse and keyboard. The shooting mechanic is easy to understand and the guns to choose from are quite nice. Movement in the game is quite easy as well, but can be a bit strange at times (getting stuck under things and having to slowly move stuff to advance). 2. Graphics:
First sentance up top; IT FEELS LIKE A FLASH GAME. Graphics are not great, but with games today, graphics usually don't matter. One thing to point out though; sometimes the character models limbs can move in weird ways. Only thing I found weird about it. I love the style the graphics give off, regardless if they are made with Flash.                  4/5
3. Difficulty:
Now I am not the best at side-scrollers, and I am not the best at contra, but dang, this game gets hard fast. First big boss lasts quite a long time but is easy to figure out, but the next boss could send you for a loop due to the controls and your lack of ammunition if you are running low. Inbetween boss fights however, the stages are challenging, but not brutal, besides some mini bosses.                                   4/5
4. Sound:
WOW! Awesome music. It gets your addrenaline pumping and gets you ready to fight whatever is ahead. Although it is nice, there seems to be a few tracks that loop a bit too much. Love the music, but not the same song over and over again. Still gets a perfect score due to how BADASS AND AWESOME THE MUSIC IS.                                  5/5
OVERALL:
I got this game for free in a contest, but, if I had played the demo of this, I would have definitely bought it. Awesome and fun game to take your stress out on.

As a long time fan of terraria, this is a game I was hugely excited about when I first heard of it. I finally got gifted it a couple of weeks ago (Thanks Feyth), and I went in with an open mind, knowing little about the game itself and looking forward to a few hours of getting used to the gameplay, before maybe jumping into multiplayer and then shelfing it. How wrong I was.
I won't lie, the first hour or so was tedious. Mining early on is slow, and getting to grips with the slightly awkward controls made me consider giving up. But I wanted to fly a spaceship at least once before I put down the game, and so I powered on, eventually repairing my spaceship and opening the doors to the Starbound universe. As soon as I had escaped the tutorial world, I became hooked. A giant space monolith with a portal to an ancient cavern filled with propecies and hints at a complex overarching plot? A frontier town with questing, minigames and NPC's with stories to tell and florans to hate? I was amazed. Finally, a sandbox game that felt ALIVE. For the first few hours, every planet I visited made me feel as if I was right there. Every new NPC had a story to tell, every dungeon had a hidden secret. Some aspects felt a little odd, and unfinished, but hey, this is early access! I was thoroughly enjoying being a part of the fantastic and beautiful universe that Chucklefish have created.
And then suddenly, to my horror, I realised I was done. I had finished all the quests. Upgraded my ship as much as I could. Discovered every kind of generated dungeon. I was mortified. I was so ready for more. More upgrades to unlock, new bosses to fight. What happened? Did they just forget to put in the rest of the story? Have two years of development led to just this? I couldn't believe that for such an expansive game, all the challenges were finished within a day or so. I was so utterly dissapointed that I just closed the game and watched ghostbusters while crying into cups of tea.
And then came the revelation. I was wandering through my ship, and noticed along my travels I had picked up a fridge. "Hmm, WinterBear. Maybe I could set up a little kitchen, see what recipes I can cook up?". Then I stopped at an asteroid field. "Hey WinterBear, you could totally build a sweet space station here!". Then I discovered wiring. "WinterBear WE NEED COMPLETE DOOR CONTROL FROM THE BRIDGE OF THE SHIP". For I had been mislead. Wrong all along. For starbound is not a survival adventure rpg as the first few hours of gameplay had indicated. It is not an epic space opera with horrifying aliens, and dashing heroes, as the lore would have you think. Oh no. It is a SANDBOX. I suddenly realised, that while the story was over, my adventures had just begun. All the useless junk I had picked up along my way suddenly became valuable building tools to create my own stories. The game became fun again, as I made my own projects to keep me entertained. I built smuggling outposts in harsh desert storms, sailed lava lakes for lost treasure, and furnished my spaceship with only the highest quality decor.
Because the truth is, while clearly the developers are working on bringing the story and the characters to life, that part of the game is just not ready yet. But the sandbox side most certainly is, and there are hundreds of truly beautiful items to find, and build with. I have every hope that starbounds storyline will be just as epic as I hoped it would be, but even if it is not, I would be lying if I said I had not enjoyed this game. It has some of the greatest potential I have ever seen in a video game, and I literally cannot wait for more.
So yeah, don't go in expecting Knights of the Old Republic 2D. Because thats not what the game is about. And don't go in expecting a hardcore survival experience either, because you will be disappointed. But if you approach this game as what it is, a sandbox with a nice flair of adventure, you will thoroughly enjoy it.
Oh and my cooking hobby? Well, I'm opening a chain restaurant across the cosmos, coming to a planet near you.

I wanted to like this game. It is a novel mashup of RPG and pinball, but there are a number of issues that make the game hard to suggest to others.
The controls have a pretty noticable lag between when buttons are pressed and when the flippers activate. This isn't the end of the world because the user can anticipate the ball movement and press the button before when they actually want the flipper to activate. This becomes much harder to do though when you're trying to deal with stuff that's only inches away from your flippers. When enemies are near, it's near impossible to react fast enough to not gutter the smaller balls. The real issue comes with switching between the different characters and the character's different abilities. The spacebar is used to launch balls, revive fallen characters, and use their special abilities. This is a lot for one button to do, and I've lost quite a lot of mana, the currency used for reviving characters and using special abilities, because of it.
The level designs are god awful. There are a number of times where lauching a ball at start causes it to go right through my flippers and kill the character. A lot of the time there's a special character that's needed for one task or another that causes the levels to be exceedingly tedious as it's almost never the ball that would actually be helpful for the given situation. I found myself switching back and forth quite a bit to mop up, fix my flippers, and then finally use the ball they wanted me to use in order to progress the level.
I have never yelled at my computer in anger because of a videogame before I played this game. This game has some portions that seem easy, but level design and poor controls make it rage inducing. Save yourself the trouble, don't get this game.

Excellent story
Serena is a 3D first person point and click game adventure game developed through the colaboration of sevral video game companies. You play as an old man who has lost his memory and trying to find where his wife Serena is.
The story is superb. Plot is told through the voices of the protagonist as well as his wife. Narrative to well paced to still wide range of emotions including happiness, sadness, regret, fear and anger. There are many plot twists in the game which will leave you guessing what's going on. The ending as well as the overall experience will leave you reflecting on your experience as well as the dark story which has been unravelled...
Graphics are good. The dark colour on objects instills a dark and uneasy atmosphere. Objects are well detailed, but nothing spectacular.
Gameplay is reminiscent of others in it's genre. You interact with objects by clicking with the left mouse button. There are no keyeboard controls, except for the 'escape' button which closes the game (be careful of this) as well as the 'space bar' which highlights objects to interact with. Movement is also controlled by indicating in a direction with your mouse and left clicking. There is no save system in the game, so you have to complete it in one playthrough. Progression is made from interacting with the objects in the cabin which will cause the main character to reflect on his past and shine light on the where about of his wife as well as his current predicament. You will have to interact with the same items more than once to getter a better understanding of the story and move the game forward.
Audio is top notch. The player character (who is also the narrator) voice acting is authentic and relatable. The female voice actor is good as well. Interaction sounds with objects are clear and realistic.
With an excellent story as well as being absolutely free, there is no reason not to pick up this masterpiece whether your fan of point and click games or curious to try it out.

Fun Zelda-esque Puzzle Adventure Game
This is NOT an RPG. It's a cute adventure game focused strictly on solving puzzles. You solve one, open the door, move to the next room and so on. The only few rpg elements include things like health upgrades and cash to buy items (3 items that open up more puzzle mechanics).
PROS
- Lovely art style and animation, very fitting.
- The writing is really fun. Expect lots of snarky comments and quirky dialogues.
- The base game is challenging enough for casual playthroughs. There's an optional "dungeon" full of super hard puzzles for the aditional challenge
- 60fps goodness, runs so smooth
CONS
- All the puzzles in game revolve around box pushing mechanics. Provides a good challenge but could get boring after a while.
- Lack of exploration
- I wish the characters had more story or progression, loved all of them.
- Not much replayability unless you want the achievements, most of which are rerunning the game with some sort of handicap.
- The game is short (my first blind playthrough was 2:30 hours, got all collectables and completed the extra hard dungeon too)
SUM
If you like puzzlers and don't mind lots of box pushing, you'll love it. The humour is great and the game is very pretty to look at. The puzzles can get extremely difficult (even convoluted) and provide a great challenge. If you're into speedrunning the game's got that too.

I read some of the negative reviews.
Someone says this game is just pixel hunting. Yes, I sometimes missed small objects. But I was also playing with a touchpad which makes moving the cursor (and therefore searching) quite difficult. Call of Cthulhu: Prisoner of Ice is and old-school point-and-click adventure game starring Ryan, a young soldier who must solve the mystery surrounding strange creatures discovered near the arctic. As you would expect from the title, the story is based on works by HP Lovecraft and you will hear your fair share of ‘f’tangs’ and ‘kaa naamas’.
Surprisingly, this game hasn’t aged too badly as far as games in its genre go, but there are a few gripes to be had. Prisoner of Ice breaks one of the most important rules of making a good point and click adventure: never ever force the player into a pixel hunt. If you want to be successful at this game, you will need to take some time to scan each screen with your cursor. The game also has some issues with the soundtrack freaking out in dosbox. The fastest way to resolve this is to turn the music off in the menu, wait for the music to cut off (it doesn’t happen immediately), and then turn it back on.
Once you have those two issues tamed, the game is somewhat enjoyable save for one or two puzzles where you might have to go grab a UHS (par for the course for older PnC games IMO). That being said, Prisoner of Ice is not bad for what it is and I find myself more on the thumbs up side for this particular title.

What a mess! After playing Shadow of the Comet (I loved it! Read my review!
, I was looking forward to playing this. After ten minutes, my hopes were diminished, and after an hour, my hopes were dashed and by the end, I was a very very confused gamer.
Prisoner of Ice went backwards in terms of so many things. Trying to blend 3dish/claymation looking characters in 2-D settings just doesn't work. The story is an absolute mess, trying to loosely branch off of The Mountains of Madness, and serve as a kind of continuation of Shadow of the Comet.....within 3-4 hours (Steam says 6 hours, but I had long periods of being AFK). It's so short, there is no time to care about really any of the characters, and those we do know from Shadow of the Comet, it feels like they threw them in so we could kinda care about somebody! Maybe if they had made this game longer, they could have developed the story a lot better, but they didn't and we are now stuck with this. I honestly couldn't even really explain to you the plot. I had to go to Wikipedia just to find out what in the world I just played. For those who know my reviews and what I play, that should definitely tell you something. Pixel hunting is back!...and man is it annoying. Shadow of the Comet threw pixel hunting out the window, and the graphics were all pixelated. Now in this mixed mess of a game, good luck finding the key you need in a timed puzzle. Oh yes, this game is full of timed puzzles. The gaming community consists of a lot of people with a lot of different tastes in games. One thing that most gamers have in common however is that almost everyone knows what Half-Life is and most people have also at some point or another played a game that is, or originated as a mod to Half-Life. This is something that makes this game so special; there are very few games and game series that can compare to this one in fame.
Well, Half-Life is a First Person Shooter game that was introduced to the world in 1998. The game was made by a newly founded company called Valve. The game is about a man named Dr. Gordon Freeman who works at a research facility called Black Mesa. The game is divided into 18 chapters that vary in length and creativity. Some chapters are around 15 minutes and some are almost an hour long. The game is based on the Goldsource engine which actually looks kind of decent to this day and behaves much like the later source engine.
In the beginning of the game you go to work to do an experiment. This experiment, however, goes horribly wrong and accidentaly opens a portal to an alien dimension called Xen. This grants the aliens access to our dimension which soon leads to the aliens trying to take over our world. Your job as Dr. Gordon Freeman is to escape the underground facility and try to stop this chaos. On your way you will have to fight enviromental hazards, aliens from Xen, soldiers ordered to cover up the accident and more.
Yes, absolutely. This game may be 18 years old but it's still very up to date. It has okay graphics, and thankfully it's easy to see if you can interract with an object or not. It also has a great feel to it's gameplay, and you can improve your playthroughs a lot and try learning some tricks to make it enjoyable a lot longer. If you would however feel like this game is a little too old for your taste I would absolutely recommend the game Black Mesa to you. It is a remake/reimagination of the original Half-Life that changes the worse parts of the game e.g the chapter "On a Rail", and it also makes the areas a lot bigger as it does not have the same hardware limitations. This means that some areas (e.g outside of a lab) is about 5 times larger and that adds for some interesting encounters.
To end this I just want to say that this is a truly amazing game. If you pass on this game you will have missed something very spectacular.

Recommended?  Easily!
The game is loosely based on the Cthulhu mythos in the world of H.P. Lovecraft, though readers familiar with that universe will know that even in most Cthulhu stories the octopus god doesn't show up much.  But, still, this game has some twists and turns the way you might expect from a Lovecraft story.
Journey back to 20 years ago in computer-game development, the days when MSDOS still ruled and many people were trying out Windows 95 for the first time.  Sure, the graphics are dated -- but at the same time they're kinda cool!  Isn't that why all of these retro-style games are in vogue now?
Like many games from the time, I can't say much about the music or the voices other than I found it helpful just to turn them off.  Luckily, this was one of the games at the time that allowed you to have subtitles along with spoken word.
However, also like many games of the time -- this game actually has a well-written plot and is accompanied with some detailed storytelling.  In other words, this game is from a time when graphics and sound weren't that good and so developers had to actually design a COMPLETE game in order to it to be considered good.
Of course, one of the drawbacks is the point-and-click interface.  And, yes, this game reminded me of why I found these types of games so frustrating as sometimes you engage in the battle for pixel spotting. Tales of Berseria is fantastic, simply put.
I enjoyed Tales of Zestiria, despite some plot shortcomings toward the end and a battle system that in contrast, is a tad underwhelming, I still enjoyed that game, but was always left feeling... a bit let down.
Tales of Berseria, not only stands up for itself, more than enough. But also stands up for Zestiria, protecting it's elder brother.
-Combat-
The combat system, whilst a little different from most games in the series, is a refressing take, the Liberation LMBS is fantastic. Taking souls from your enemies and gathering your own to increase combos and power is actually really fun, and creates a fantastic challange, the combat system ends up being really enjoyable, despite the fact you can cheat the ABXY controls by putting four elements on each one and just mashing them, the game almost punishes you for that tactic in a multitude of ways, and actually endorses using the buttons more strategically. Whilst I do still miss overlimit, busting out Velvet's arm honestly me feel good, oblierating enemeis with combos, and finishing it with some Lethal Pain.
-The story-
I enjoyed every second, every emotional scene, every laugh, every smile, every tear. The story's focus is fantastic and putting so much effort into it, the english voice cast is good as well. I don't want to put too much here for spoilers, but the story, in my humble opinion. Is fantastic. What I can say is the characters are great, whilst at the beginning certain' characters may feel out of place, by the end of the game, you completely understand why everyone's here, and what everyone's doing, and if you've played Zestiria, you're in for a treat. Characters, story and all.
-Dungeon and map design-
Not overly exciting, but there were some cool areas I liked, honestly the dungeons and field stuff is still the least exciting bit, though the adding in of characters speaking in recent titles helps with the lul. I never found my self enjoying the dungeons though, so I ended up jumping right back into combat at the first chance. But there we go.
-Overall-
If you're a fan of the series, Berseria might feel a tad too foreign for what the series is good for at first glance. But upon closer inspection, this is a Tales game heart and soul. It was about midway through the first ark where it hit me that "Yeah, this is Tales, this is what it feels like" a feeling I sadly never got with Zestiria. If you're not a fan of the series, I highly recommend it and if you are, it's fantastic.
Enjoy the rest of your day and steer your own rudder ;)

I break a rule in writing this review for the game. It is still in beta, or early access, or whatever we're calling it. But, in so doing - I rate this game at its current state, with no hope of it finishing early access, as such is only fair. It appears to have been in Early Access for quite awhile.
I break this rule because it's worth it. This game. It's pretty nice, definitely worth the pre-release price I've paid.
Starbound is a breath of fresh air in the 2D sandbox genre, of which there aren't many successful titles. Terraria is perhaps one, but not one I'm particularly satisfied with. Terraria feels undeveloped, wanting, and repetitive. Starbound shares some qualities, but branches out in a unique way that is invigorating for those of us who might enjoy it.
Starbound is not a pure sandbox, where you are left to your devices in a single worldspace. Starbound possesses a basic narrative, that you can pursue at your directive, with some sparse side quests for enjoyment. You travel to other worlds, where - gasp - there are other people! NPCs can occur, some of which may not kill you on sight. Some you can trade with, others are atmospheric. Biomes have variety, monsters have variety. I'm not sure how many max tier playthroughs it'll last you until your bored, but I think for someone who's serious about the genre - it should last you at least 60-80 hours worth, as I'm not serious about it and that's what I'm clocking at.
So, $15 for 60-80 hours of gameplay? Seems fair. That's not even including multiplayer.
Equipment is also a new take in the right direction. You have TWO HANDS. What does this mean? Well, I feel this game actually takes an account for different playstyles. You can use two one-handed objects at once, making dual-wielding items, keeping a weapon and a utility object handy, two-handed weapons, two-handed tools, and all sorts of situations possible. There are also body upgrades, a basic armor system with cosmetic slots, a dye and sign creation system, upgradable ships, one and two handed guns, and many different biomes. You also have a pet, that you can play with, which my lady found very amusing.
You also have your computer, which can handle tech upgrades and something called 3D printing. Essentially, any non-crafting based item can be deconstructed, then recreated using money. This is good for builds, as most of the 3D printing produces furniture. You can also find a guitar, where you can play music, and download mods to give you even more to play with. There is a hub that is unlocked that you get easy access to, and where your 'main quest' sequence is generated. I haven't finished it yet, but it keeps some appeal by tempting you with a mysterious gate in an ancient ruin out in space. The main quests are in isolated areas where you can't build, but you get a challenging combat, with a distinguished boss that may or may not have a gimick used to kill it. Very reminiscent of old Zelda or SNES titles. There are also SO MANY DIFFERENT WORLDS in a single save, that it's unreal.
Gameplay is solid. I've only ever crashed in its earliest versions, attempting to run different modes for testing purposes. Standard modes run rather well. One patch I had to use OpenGL, but - that lasted a week I think. The community and the creators are determined; I was worried at the start, feeling they weren't cranking out content. Though, they've proven those concerns wrong, developing core mechanics and pushing the game to a more polished state.
Some issues? Hitboxes aren't perfect. Some creatures have their heads slightly out of hitbox because they're elongated, and you can't wammy them. Creatures don't have critical hit regions, but I think players do - so there's that for PvP. I haven't tested multiplayer extensively, but I know it works. Descending down through platforms can get tricky since you can't drop through them, and you jump so high. I created a character for my girlfriend, and apparently, I share the same universe as her, as the homeworld her different race, new character has was my homeworld - complete with my base and chests. She has different bookmarks though, so I set her up with an unused planet in the system that she could farm and start off in. Tiers might get repetitive later on, but - playing this game casually solo has still been keeping me interested, at the very least having finished the Titanium tier. The most serious drawback? They update this game very slowly. But, the updates bring solid content, they produce other titles, and they're a new company. Maybe they'll learn from it, maybe not.
To compliment all of this, the modding community looks like it'll really take off. The developers are really supporting them, and giving them spotlight. I anticipate with the modding community the game has, it'll be great to see in the future if the game finishes early access - or stops updating. Also, whoever the audio artist is, he's a godsend. The game's music is fantastic, and the art - yes pixel-art is art - is pretty impressive. Very clean, with good animation and articulation. Solid character customization too with aesthetic things to find and wear in your cosmetic slots!
My personal feelings on the game?
For $15 USD: 7/10, pretty impressive, and I write this with no plans for improvement. Great additon to the visually basic, but functionally deep Sandbox / RPG genre.

So it's pinball, where each ball is a character with stats and special abilities. Multiballs are sidekick characters and the tables are locations in a fantasy realm that provides the backdrop to your quest. It's all a rather neat implementation of an RPG lite game ensuring a few hours of pinball / levelling up fun.
Each character does their part, some characters are best for destroying scenery, others for melee combat, others to gain resources, others to wipe the floor clear of vermin, etc, etc. The locations provide battle arenas, puzzle areas, bonus collecting areas and of course a shop, so there's a smattering of variety to shake things up a little.
But.. Rollers of the Realm is begging for a sequal that takes the core concept and make it a bigger, better game.  Most of the locations are small, feeling quite clostraphobic at times. It would benefit from larger tables thrown into the mix where you can spend more time bashing your characters around its nooks and crannies.
The end of a table can come abruptly, it would be nice to keep things active and maybe offer a way of gaining a bonus before moving on. Sometimes you see a semi cutscene appear on screen while your balls drop without coughing. You're not dead, it just feels odd.
The battle system is ok, but it would be nice to use more pinball traits to offer things like special attacks, critical hits, instant kills, etc. This would provide more incentive to revisit tables and spend more time with them in arena modes.
That aside, its a fun thumbs up from me, albeit a short one..

Bastion is an amazing game, with entertaining gameplay, a unique and beautiful artstyle, and most importantly an intricate, thorough, and moving story. The gameplay and combat is fairly straightforward, but the combinations of two weapons and a single skill can allow for many styles of play, and the lack of straight upgrades adds to this dynamic as well. Additionally, the system of leveling up was unique and further added to the styles of play, and the difficulty of the game scales well, with additional options to offer a greater challenge. Regardless of the engaging gameplay, Bastion excelled in its storytelling. Told through amazing narration, you experience the story of the world of the Bastion. The environment is defined by the artstyle and the soundtrack (which is definitely worth a listen). What stood out most to me concerning the story, however, was its ability to invoke an emotional response from me. As someone who usually plays games for just their gameplay, the whole story (and particularly the conclusion) I was surprised at how much I actually cared about the kid and the characters he meets.
Overall, Bastion is definitely worth a purchase. Decent gameplay in an amazing environment with an engaging story made for a great game.

Short, simple pinball game with light RPG mechanics. The campaign is relatively short (which on its own is fine; it's the right length for this game) and despite a great amount of variety in level design, it's all still pinball, y'know? There are more fun strats to be tried out and experimented with and refined than there are levels to try them out on.
(There is a challenge mode and most of the levels can be replayed with different starting layouts, so if you absolutely love pinball sims, there's plenty for you to do. I spent a little while grinding for upgrade money, and the levels were still fun to replay.)
So, y'know, it's not reinventing the genre or anything, but it's a fun, short game that a lot of love went into. The campaign has more heart than you might be expecting, which was very gooey and pleasant.

Light RPG elements thrown in with light pinball elements makes for a very entertaining and ballsy game! The storyline is rather generic fantasy but I enjoyed the rogue-angle and there's a bit of a plot twist towards the end. I aso liked the inclusivity of the many types of balls: brown balls, bald balls, white balls. I felt like there were many balls I could play with.
The sound, music and voice-acting in this game is well done! All the balls are voiced.
As you progress through the levels you acquire more gold to buy upgrades with. These upgrades make it easier to control the balls, make them do more damage  or otherwise add to or upgrade their special abilities. You will unlock more balls as you go and each ball has unique capabilities such as squirting out more balls or shooting something out of the ball. Each ball also represents one life of the battlefield and although you can revive balls when they go down through fillinhup your mana supply by smacking your balls into objects, losing all your balls means losing any progress you may have made that round.
At some point I was rather overwhelmed by the sheer amount of balls I was told to play with and it's somewhat difficult finding a purpose for each and every one of them. I found myself playing with only a certain set of my balls in particular halfway through the game and altough the game has some challenging maps, once you've acquired the more useful upgrades the game becomes rather easy. You can revisit maps later on for more gold but that tends to make the game even more easy as you can milk your balls for gold on these maps endlessly.
I consider myself to have become rather good at playing with balls so here are a few tips for when you're playing with your balls:
1. Bind flipper left to CTRL and flipper right to ALT. Bind move ball left to left arrow and move ball right to right arrow. Made the game a whole lot more comfortable for me than the standard keys. They were horrible.
2. I found using most special abilities a waste of mana and gold. I went mostly for passive stats to increase damage and that paid off.
After all is said and done, I really enjoyed playing with all the different balls and I hope you do too.

Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I have somehow not written a review for Ittle Dew yet.
To call Ittle Dew a Zeldalike is to do it a disservice. While the inspiration is clear, Ittle Dew focuses almost completely on the puzzle aspects, and completely outdoes Zelda in this regard. In the game, there are only three items. One item burns things, one item freezes things, and one item moves things. All of these items interact with each other, and create interesting puzzles as a result. The game is beatable with all three items, or with any two. The items can be acquired in any order. This actually dramatically changes the way you'll progress through the game, as well as the puzzles you will encounter. There is also a sort of modular difficulty, in that many puzzles are solvable with only one or two of the items, but are difficult. If you come back more fully equipped, it usually makes the puzzles much easier.
That's all I have to say mechanically, which I think is the primary draw of the game. However, it also oozes charm. It uses a Home Movies-esque Squigglevision style animation which lets you immediately understand what is interactable on the screen. It has a lot of cute dialogue. The characters are one-note, but they do what they need to, and have some pretty funny jokes involved with them.
I think this is easily in my top 10 games. Everyone who has an appreciation for tight design should play it.

This game is awesome! I haven't been addicted to a game like this in a while. I played GameDev Tycoon when it came out and loved that one as well. Always hoped for a sequel to it. Well, Mad Games Tycoon is the sequel I've been waiting for! Tons of topics to use with lots of genres that you can mix, match, and blend together. The scoring of games seems to take more into account than just how much higher your score was from the last game you developed. As such I've been able to make some smaller B+ and A games that my company can release while I develop the next big AA and AAA games. The smaller games still sell well enough to keep the cashflow coming in. With several different buildings available for purchase and lots of objects to fill them with, it's easy to customize the layout to your liking. The bigger buildings give you more than enough room to make a massive gaming empire.
So far I personally haven't run into any bugs. However, I would like to see more miscellaneous objects with higher ratings to decorate the office with. Also, the option to have multiple doors on a room would make designing the layout of the floor easier. Some more tooltip popups on some of the other menus would also be helpful. A brief explaination of buying and selling shares of other companies would be nice as well. Other than those things there isn't anything else I can think of at the moment that could be improved.
All-in-all, this is definitely one of the more complete and polished early access games I have played. One of the better purchases I've made. The devs seem to be pretty active as well. I would totally recommend giving this game a look if you're into tycoon type games.

I went into Sleeping Dogs expecting to shoot people in the face and slam some dude's heads in doors. I wasn't expecting it to wow me and give me hope for the future of storytelling in-games, but it did.
I'll start with the story and the characters:
Sleeping Dogs has one of the best stories in open-world games, maybe the best one, provided you have a little bit of cognitive dissonance. You play a cop turned double agent, working to infilitrate a brutal and vicious triad to take it down from the inside. The characters are well-written, nuanced, and human; there's no complaints there. You feel for a few of them, you understand almost all of them, and you genuinely like a handful.
The storyline itself is full of twists, tragedy, some laughs, and overall is told well through real-time cutscenes (real-time being interesting because it means your crazy outfits will show up in the scenes). It takes you from mission to mission, with downtime in between to do side missions, etc.
But you'll have to suspend your disbelief because on some of the missions, you have to escape the cops. And to do that, it's easiest to shoot out the tires of cop cars... which generally blows the car up and kills its occupants. So you're a cop trying to stop senseless and violent murder who has to violently murder cops in order to stop senseless and violent murder (sometimes of cops). These issues don't generally detract from the story, but it did make me a lot more likely to try to avoid running over people or shooting innocents, as I felt like Wei Shen wouldn't.
Story: 9/10
Mission variety: 10/10
Side missions: 9/10
There are 3 main systems to Sleeping Dogs: The driving, the gunplay, and the melee. The driving itself feels nice and is generally easy to control, and the Vehicle Melee and Action Hijack systems are well-utilized and hell of a lot of fun, if unrealistic (and they're both borrowed from The Wheelman). However, at least on KB/M, taking sharp turns can be difficult, and it doesn't take me long before I scrape some of my paint on the walls. Could use some tuning, but I like it.
Driving: 8/10
The gunplay is excellent if you go into it with the mindset that this game isn't a shooter. Guns are not perfectly accurate, adding a bit of realism. Ammo and guns are limited, so when you get a gun, you feel powerful as hell and you wreak some serious havoc. The gunplay ties into melee and parkour fluidly and slow-motion kicks in for certain actions.
Gunplay: 10/10
The melee combat mimics the Batman games' combat, but much more brutal. You'll do most of the combat hand-to-hand, picking up melee weapons scarcely, and it's not only fun to play, it's fun to watch, breaking people's arms, snapping their legs, and throwing them over your shoulder. There are also environmental attacks, where you'll slam someone's head in a fridge or mash their face into a table saw. There are some slight control issues (Still using KB/M) such as accidentally hitting the wrong character in a multi-enemy fight, but nothing too glaring.
Melee: 9/10
On top of all of that, there's a four-way upgrade system that adds light RPG elements:
Do missions while hurting rival triads and blowing stuff up, you get Triad XP, do them without killing innocents or causing property damage to get Cop XP, do missions and side missions to get Face XP, and find statues for a kung fu master to get Melee Upgrades. A nice system to help pacing.
RPG elements: 10/10
Overall, so far, Sleeping Dogs is easily my Game of The Year 2012 and a game I think everyone should play. It's got a ton of content, some nice but nonessential DLC  (six more months of content DLC as of this writing), and a good story that ties the whole package together. There's even some leaderboards-style community options thrown in to try and beat your friends' scores.
A 10/10 isn't perfection, and neither is this game, but it's the score I'm giving this masterpiece of gaming.
10/10 Bullets, Blades, and Betrayals

This game is a breath of fresh air.
Coming from Zestiria I was disappointd to see the latest installation of the Tales series to be so lackluster, boring, and tedius. I was hesitant to give this game a try, but I'm glad I did.
From the get-go the story is vastly superior, the characters are interesting and I'm actually inspired to find out more about them.
The combat system has gone back to a better place, and the new mechancis introduced are alot easier to work with than in Zestiria. The camera also DOESN'T FIGHT YOU like it did in Zestiria! The camera certain got an AI upgrade to say the least. All in all it feels smoother and easier to manage.
NO MORE SKILL BOARD!
Jesus that thing was a nightmare. No longer will you have to get 40 peices of gear just to find the RIGHT one with a skill to transfer over to another piece of gear, just to replace that gear later on. Now, you break down unused gear into materials which can be used to flat out upgrade other materials, increasing their base stats and unlocking extra skills. When it comes time to swap to new gear, break down the old upgraded gear for rare materials and use those materials to upgrade your new gear! You also get to KEEP one skill from mastered gear permanently on your character, so each new gear mastered adds permanent benefits.
There are some re-used assets from Zestiria, and not just items. Character models, animations, enemies, you'll find yourself thinking "wait, I've seen that guy before" or "Why is this dude using Lilah's moveset?" and "Hey! He's using that cosmetic weapon!" but it's not a bad thing, it's just something you'll notice.
All in all I believe this is a step up in every direction from Zestiria, and I'm looking forward to playing it more.

I break a rule in writing this review for the game. It is still in beta, or early access, or whatever we're calling it. But, in so doing - I rate this game at its current state, with no hope of it finishing early access, as such is only fair. It appears to have been in Early Access for quite awhile.
I break this rule because it's worth it. This game. It's pretty nice, definitely worth the pre-release price I've paid.
Starbound is a breath of fresh air in the 2D sandbox genre, of which there aren't many successful titles. Terraria is perhaps one, but not one I'm particularly satisfied with. Terraria feels undeveloped, wanting, and repetitive. Starbound shares some qualities, but branches out in a unique way that is invigorating for those of us who might enjoy it.
Starbound is not a pure sandbox, where you are left to your devices in a single worldspace. Starbound possesses a basic narrative, that you can pursue at your directive, with some sparse side quests for enjoyment. You travel to other worlds, where - gasp - there are other people! NPCs can occur, some of which may not kill you on sight. Some you can trade with, others are atmospheric. Biomes have variety, monsters have variety. I'm not sure how many max tier playthroughs it'll last you until your bored, but I think for someone who's serious about the genre - it should last you at least 60-80 hours worth, as I'm not serious about it and that's what I'm clocking at.
So, $15 for 60-80 hours of gameplay? Seems fair. That's not even including multiplayer.
Equipment is also a new take in the right direction. You have TWO HANDS. What does this mean? Well, I feel this game actually takes an account for different playstyles. You can use two one-handed objects at once, making dual-wielding items, keeping a weapon and a utility object handy, two-handed weapons, two-handed tools, and all sorts of situations possible. There are also body upgrades, a basic armor system with cosmetic slots, a dye and sign creation system, upgradable ships, one and two handed guns, and many different biomes. You also have a pet, that you can play with, which my lady found very amusing.
You also have your computer, which can handle tech upgrades and something called 3D printing. Essentially, any non-crafting based item can be deconstructed, then recreated using money. This is good for builds, as most of the 3D printing produces furniture. You can also find a guitar, where you can play music, and download mods to give you even more to play with. There is a hub that is unlocked that you get easy access to, and where your 'main quest' sequence is generated. I haven't finished it yet, but it keeps some appeal by tempting you with a mysterious gate in an ancient ruin out in space. The main quests are in isolated areas where you can't build, but you get a challenging combat, with a distinguished boss that may or may not have a gimick used to kill it. Very reminiscent of old Zelda or SNES titles. There are also SO MANY DIFFERENT WORLDS in a single save, that it's unreal.
Gameplay is solid. I've only ever crashed in its earliest versions, attempting to run different modes for testing purposes. Standard modes run rather well. One patch I had to use OpenGL, but - that lasted a week I think. The community and the creators are determined; I was worried at the start, feeling they weren't cranking out content. Though, they've proven those concerns wrong, developing core mechanics and pushing the game to a more polished state.
Some issues? Hitboxes aren't perfect. Some creatures have their heads slightly out of hitbox because they're elongated, and you can't wammy them. Creatures don't have critical hit regions, but I think players do - so there's that for PvP. I haven't tested multiplayer extensively, but I know it works. Descending down through platforms can get tricky since you can't drop through them, and you jump so high. I created a character for my girlfriend, and apparently, I share the same universe as her, as the homeworld her different race, new character has was my homeworld - complete with my base and chests. She has different bookmarks though, so I set her up with an unused planet in the system that she could farm and start off in. Tiers might get repetitive later on, but - playing this game casually solo has still been keeping me interested, at the very least having finished the Titanium tier. The most serious drawback? They update this game very slowly. But, the updates bring solid content, they produce other titles, and they're a new company. Maybe they'll learn from it, maybe not.
To compliment all of this, the modding community looks like it'll really take off. The developers are really supporting them, and giving them spotlight. I anticipate with the modding community the game has, it'll be great to see in the future if the game finishes early access - or stops updating. Also, whoever the audio artist is, he's a godsend. The game's music is fantastic, and the art - yes pixel-art is art - is pretty impressive. Very clean, with good animation and articulation. Solid character customization too with aesthetic things to find and wear in your cosmetic slots!
My personal feelings on the game?
For $15 USD: 7/10, pretty impressive, and I write this with no plans for improvement. Great additon to the visually basic, but functionally deep Sandbox / RPG genre.

Bastion is an amazing game, with entertaining gameplay, a unique and beautiful artstyle, and most importantly an intricate, thorough, and moving story. The gameplay and combat is fairly straightforward, but the combinations of two weapons and a single skill can allow for many styles of play, and the lack of straight upgrades adds to this dynamic as well. Additionally, the system of leveling up was unique and further added to the styles of play, and the difficulty of the game scales well, with additional options to offer a greater challenge. Regardless of the engaging gameplay, Bastion excelled in its storytelling. Told through amazing narration, you experience the story of the world of the Bastion. The environment is defined by the artstyle and the soundtrack (which is definitely worth a listen). What stood out most to me concerning the story, however, was its ability to invoke an emotional response from me. As someone who usually plays games for just their gameplay, the whole story (and particularly the conclusion) I was surprised at how much I actually cared about the kid and the characters he meets.
Overall, Bastion is definitely worth a purchase. Decent gameplay in an amazing environment with an engaging story made for a great game.

Lots of fun, addicting gameplay. GUI takes a little bit of time to get used to. Interesting plot, good replay value with medals. Graphics are good, music is well done. Not a lot of variation with soundtracks, but the ones they have, like the boss theme, are well done and convey the mood.
The allied characters have brains (no pun intended) which is nice for those of us all too familiar with the zombie survival horror theme (with characters being typically very dumb and easy fodder for the screen). Better to have a few that the player can relate to than a mob of individuals no one cares about.
Base building is a non-issue (into day 12 of the game). Survivors can be assigned to job, like many other games, but because the number of items one can craft in relation to other activities is strategically limited, I would advise players to really think about their objectives with a primary team in leaving the base. The single most useful skill is likely the melee option, and it pays early to invest in it. If you're not going out on a certain day, make sure everyone has something to do. The job skills can come in handy, and it pays to have a few specialists working in the camp.
I would like to see a little more variability in the weaponry. There's a few very minor spelling errors but nothing that would detract from the game or the meaning of the text. Considering that the gaming and dev community are both filled with polyglots working through multiple languages, I mean no disrespect.
It would be interesting to have fights and parties with more characters on each side (excusing the computer-controlled random NPCs the player sometimes finds).
The combat style (FF7-like) is a throwback to the classic RPG style. It also reminds me of the seamlessly well-conducted combat sequences of South Park: The Stick of Truth.
Engrossing, to say the least. I was pleased with my purchase. I will await future games from this publisher. Well done dev team.
