This is the best Game Dev game I've ever played, and it's not even done yet. It's got a ton of features, and the devs update it just about every week, and they're big updates, so just when I think it couldn't get better, it does.
There's so many possible playstyles that it never gets old. You can do solo-dev runs, ZUN style, or you can become the evil mega-corp that buys up all the studios, EA style. You can make your own consoles from the get-go if you want, or you can never touch Consoles at all. You can be a publisher who doesn't even develop the games, instead funding other devs and then producing their games for them in your factories. You can even be a company that does nothing but make and sell Engines. That's not even everything you can do!
But it's best not to take it too seriously. The animations in this game are VERY goofy, and much of the random dialog can be extremely corny (you can turn it off though). The English localization is also somewhat weak, and you'll spot some Engrish here and there. Thankfully, you can optionally turn off just about everything in the game, so if you find something annoying, you're not stuck with it.
Unlike with Game Dev Tycoon, there's no "story" to speak of. As of this writing, there's no newspapers that pop up and talk about you or your company if you do something amazing, there's no fan letters (that you can read), it mostly just leaves you to your own devices and then gives you a pop-up saying "your fans are pleased with this game" or somesuch. I personally find this somewhat disappointing, since you felt like you were being acknowledged by _a person_ for your good work in Game Dev Tycoon, even if it wasn't real. Here, you get a good-scoring game and your numbers go up. The "human" element is lacking. The game tells you THAT fans are happy, but you never get to see a hypothetical person go "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ this guy is doing all this in a garage!?" the way Game Dev Tycoon does.
That said, while I think Game Dev Tycoon is better narratively, Mad Games Tycoon squashes ALL the competition flat when it comes to features, game feel, and overall fun. I can't even bring myself to play Game Dev Tycoon anymore because it's missing so many features that Mad Games Tycoon has and lets you use from the get-go (if you want). And it's not even finished yet! That, more than anything, is why I have to recommend this game. Even in its current state, it's fun as hell.

You can probably see how bad that can get, and just how fast it can get there. But the problem is you can't plan for it. You don't know what will happen.
Contrast this with Enemy Within(or Enemy Unknown), and you can immediately see a very similar system in the panic level of different nations(which also goes into how bringing down their panic level actually rewards you, but that's a whole different thought).
But you know what will happen if you take an abduction mission and ignore a different continent. You know you either do or do not have enough time and resources before the next council meeting to manage the panic.
The random chance enhances the system that's in place by not knowing which continents will be hit next. But what you don't have is randomly increasing panic levels, screwing you over before you even have a chance to respond.
...So why? What possessed them to put that into this game? If I want to make my story about how humanity almost got beat at the beginning, but by the end of the war all human soldiers were mechanized, enhanced, psionic superheros(and if I'm willing to put in the time), why take that away from me? But instead in Xcom 2, you can lose so fast for the smallest of mistakes.
Again, you can be a lost cause just for starting the game. This is not 'hard'. This is stupid.
But let's talk about the two systems I just mentioned. So you start a mission cloaked(awesome). So you can take your time and set up the perfect strategic ambush, right?
Nope, there's a timer. And by the way, once you lose the cloak it's gone for the rest of the mission.The two systems are at odds with each other.
On top of that, for however much time was put into this random chance overarching-instant-lose timer system, they probably could have come up with some sweet way of regaining your cloak from the beginning. It could be such an awesome system! A blend of Invisible Inc and Xcom! You could spend the mission sneaking up behind aliens like ninjas, getting caught and disappearing again! Distractions! Line of sight! Sneaky powers! WHO KNOWS WHAT COULD HAVE BEEN?!
...but that didn't happen. Instead, they give you a timer and a crazy amount of overpowered enemies right from the beginning. Which again, the enemy difficulty wouldn't be such a big deal if there wasn't a system in direct odds with the strategy! So now, your soldiers will die...but is it really your fault?
Which goes into another point, that game just feels...hollow. With so much random chance, why bother? If I lose, I really didn't lose, the game just decided I lost because that's the dice it rolled. If I win, it's the same.
The result is I not only don't feel like my decisions matter, but I don't feel very attached to my soldiers, because they could die a hollow death any second by getting screwed over from the hit chance.
It feels more like I'm just watching something happen to these people I designed, rather than commanding them in battle, trying to get everyone home alive. 'Oh look, the engine decided some of my guys died. Welp...that kinda sucks'.
And yes, Enemy Within has hit chances.But there are only so many 95% melee strikes my soldiers can miss(and then immediately die after) before I say: "I don't know what changed in the engine, but this is not the same."
So you might be thinking, "but if they take out the random chance, this game would be boring! It would be way too easy!" and I agree! But I would say that's because they(again) chose to use random chance in the first place to make their turn-based system hard. I wouldn't say it shows random chance is required to make a game hard.
All this could definitely sound like I'm just hating on the developers themselves, but I don't mean to. I would never have taken the time to write this(and now edit it extensively), except that this game is being hailed as one of
turn-based games, possibly ever.
And they deserve it! This game is fantastic in so many ways!
...but that only makes it more of a disappointment that it seems they had a good direction they wanted to take, and then just didn't.
So if this is the future of turn-based, I'm throwing my opinion on the pile because I don't want more strategy games like this. I don't think this is strategy. I also(personally) don't think this is 'hard'. Random chance isn't hard. It's random. ...that's it.
I would love to see a melding of Invisible Inc and this game. I think that would be the pinnacle of turn-based strategy games.
But as far as this game goes, give me a challenge. But give it to *me. Not roll some dice and tell me that I got outplayed, let me actually play.
Take it a new direction! Some new systems will probably suck! And that's ok! It will be forward motion.
But please stop not only relying on in the first place, but incorporating more random chance into strategy games.
Because ultimately that's not a strategy game.
That's a Random Numbers Game.

Bastion has become one of my favorites games here on Steam (not that I have played THAT many games here, I admit).
I won't go into how the game plays, the looks and sounds because everyone has said something about it already.
Instead, I'll comment on what made the game great for ME and why it is NOT for everyone's taste.
See, while I'm far from being OLD (I'm on my 30's), nowadays I don't have the patience nor will to sit in front of the PC/TV and play for loooooong hours straight. I have done that a lot when I was younger (have been playing videogames since Atari, mind you) This is why I don't enjoy most of current games, so full of things to learn, to do, all for the sake of 'replay value'. Most of the time I want to play for few minutes, do something else and come back to play again later. So I want a game that's easy to pick up and play, well done and polished. Having some gameplay depth and replay value is a bonus. And Bastion offers all that.
The gameplay isn't anything new, for sure. Basically hack and slash. But it's a nicely executed hack and slash! Controls work just fine, you have a nice selection of weapons, all unique, with strenghts and weaknesses. You can somewhat 'customize' them with their upgrades and always have two weapons at once, so you can try inumerous different 'combos' until you find what suits best for you or, perhaps, just for the sake of personal challenge.
Usually I don't like plataform games that have blocking ability, they usually are useless but in Bastion blocking does work pretty well and rewards you for doing so (you can actually kill enemies by parrying their attacks when timed precisely).
Overall it's an easy and accessible game. It CAN be made more difficult by adding the gods (once you get them). But then, it's not necessary.
Another thing that I liked it is that each scenario is short. So you can just play for 10~15 minutes, save, and then play some more again later. You don't HAVE to sit for long hours in front of the computer if you don't want to (but it's a fairly short game. Perhaps within 3h you'd be able to finnish in one go), so it makes a great casual game as well!
The biggest flaw, which may upset a lot of (hardcore) players is that the game is just TOO linear. You go from one place (town?) to another, in a linear fashion. You can't even revisit the places you have already beaten (unless you're playing that Score Attack Mode, which is unlocked after you've beaten the game for the first time)! So, make sure to explore every-single-part of the map, because there ARE missables!
So, overall I really recommend this game. But I understand it's not for everyone, specially if someone is expecting a REAL challenge or anything new.
The game is neither hard (again: it CAN be, but it's not necessary) nor terribly original, but it's as good as it gets in its basics and premises.

I got this game because the trailers reminded me quite a bit of Zelda 3.  That impression proved to be largely inaccurate.  They share some superficial similarity... a tope-down perspective, a sandy haired protatgonist clad in green, some hack and slash gameplay, bombs, wands, and puzzle solving...  But Ittle Dew is much more oriented toward the puzzle solving.  The controls are quite firm-feeling, and are not well-suited to extensive swordplay, but the level design doesn't push a lot of hack'n'slash action.  Most rooms have puzzles to be solved, and the game is mostly non-linear.  In fact, it offers built in challenge modes by purchasingonly 2 of the 3 items offered for the completion of the game's puzzles, with semi-secret alternate routes to accommodate those that choose the handicap.  It also has some extra challenge rooms at the end of the game, after all the items are unlocked.  Some of these border on unfair by featuring puzzles that exploit mechanics that were never seen in the main game in ways that aren't intuitively very clear.  The main quest, by comparison, is almost too straight forward and kid-friendly in its puzzle design.  Approach it with tempered expectations and it's fun game on its own, worth spending a few hours on.

Ittle Dew is a fun, clever, and amusing gem.
The gameplay is top-down adventure stuff, the kind Zelda players will be at home with. The game is mostly puzzle based though also containes a lot of enemies to fight. But it's definitely the puzzles you'll be concerned with, since they get HARD. A few of the required puzzles are very brainbending, though for the most part quite passable.
The optional puzzles are a different story. In addition to puzzles in out-of-the-way caves for collectable rewards (Either superfluous cards or helpful bits of paper) there are "professional shortcuts" which allow you to bypass most of the game if you're smart and skilled enough to use them. You probably won't be, by the by. Shortcuts aside though, the game works quite well mechanically, and the three tools you get to solve puzzles with open up a lot of variety and give way to clever puzzles. Some puzzles were so clever I never figured them out, and I probably never will. And that's okay.

Gridberd is a first person horror game that lasts roughly about an hour and half. We explore the abandoned Johnson Mansion and figure out the reason for the recent mysterious deaths surrounding the old building.
Let me start off by saying, I will not be mincing my words here.
Let’s start with the story. I will try not to put any spoilers. So the gist is there’s a vengeful ghost, Kary. Filled with rage, he locks up the player character, Sam Rogers, with the intent of killing him. However, before Kary can kill him, the spirit forces Sam to witness some of Kary’s dreaded past and later on, we learn a terrible sin Sam had commited, which plays a part in why Kary’s spirit hasn’t move on.  So instead of killing him quickly, Kary toys with Sam, taunting him with several corpses strewn around in the mansion. Oddly enough, these lifeless bodies bear a striking resemblance to Sam. Spoiler:
Kary allows Sam to explore the old mansion that once belonged to the specter, giving him a chance to investigate the recent tragic events and search for the truth. Kary narrates the story, with notes and the radio broadcasting the news supplementing the narrative. The storyline is compelling enough but then towards the end, it left a bad taste in my mouth. I just feel as though it is rushed. That’s all.  As a side note, Kary’s voice actor is just trying too hard to sound ominous. It fails and he probably needed tons of throat lozenges after the recording. The other voices are fine actually.
Now let’s move over to the “scare factor” of the game. How much did it scare me? On a scale of 1-10 (1 being, “me looking for something to scare me but couldn’t find it, no matter how hard I tried” and 10 being, “I♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants, I should’ve worn a diaper”), Gridberd was a 2. The only time I genuinely felt dread was when I saw a couple of spiders and I don’t think those little guys were the main threat. There are jumpscares but they aren't startling. There aren’t too many ambient sounds (it was mostly silent throughout the game) and the music feels out of place sometimes. It’s too epic sounding. Like you’re going on an adventure and it had no place in the setting of the story, in my opinion.
In the features of Gridberd, it’s written that there are “riddles and puzzles, as well as hidden paths that can reward you in the most diverse ways.” I played through the game twice (I had to play offline because my internet cut off so my playtime is more that what is shown) and found no riddles and barely any puzzles. I also scoured the Johnson mansion for any diverse pathways but I couldn’t find them. Maybe, I’m just blind. May I also add that the walking speed of Sam is atrocious. It’s so bloody slow! I don’t know if it’s like that to build tension but at the times where you have to backtrack, goddamit, my patience meter went off the charts. It made exploring tedious since sprinting isn't available. There is a silver lining to the sluggish walking speed. It made the boss battle hilariously entertaining…that’s all I’m saying.
The graphics is decent. It’s on the CryEngine. I have no problem with it, in terms of framerate drops, but I’m reading that some people are struggling to maintain their fps. In addition to that, the game is littered with terrible texture glitches, bugs and strange character models. The subtitles are way too fast, with multiple spelling errors and sometimes the characters talk on top of one another. The voice actors have an accent and their English for the most part, is understandable but the subtitles help when they’re pronouncing a word that might sound different than what I’m used to. These might seem minor, but it’s distracting, for me at least. Bugs can be fixed with patches and I’m not expecting a perfect game but I’m simply calling it how I see it.
Lastly, with the length of the game (1.5 or less) and its price, coupled with the various problems mentioned previously, I cannot recommend Gridberd just yet. I want to because I can tell the developers worked hard on it. I enjoyed the story but most people probably would not play a game mostly for the story.
That’s my input of Gridberd. Thanks for reading :)
TL;DR
Pros:
- Compelling story
- Decent graphics
Cons:
- Buggy, glitchy gameplay
- Short game (<1.5 hours of gametime)
- Not as scary as I would like
- Walking simulator (slow walking speed)
- Optimization problems (people are reporting of low framerates)
- Sound problems.
- Price tag might not be agreeable to some

The only complaint I have is that the game can be awfully laggy at times, even though it seems like such a small little game. Maybe with all the people logging in... I don't know. Finally, fun. And this game has a lot of it. You have to learn to interact and be nice to people so that suspicions don't rise. And if you die it is extremely frustrating. But, no matter what, nothing can take away that awesome feeling when you win a round. 10/10

Stop for a minute and read this if you're debating whether or not to buy this game.Before I dive into the game, a little back story may be necessary. TL;DR at the end.
/////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
Telltale was struggling for a while. The last project they made was Jurrasic Park. It was an ok at best sort of game. Sales were not so kind to them. This put the company at the brink of bankruptcy. The Walking Dead was there last shot, so to speak. I remember that the first episode of the game was free to download. I did not know what to expect at the time when I started episode one. With no investment on my part, I started my journey. To say the least, it was well worth it. You play as Lee. A man from Macon, who is on his way to jail. Something happens along the way, and next thing you know the dead are walking. This starts your journey to find a safe place to live with a group of survivors. As Lee, you must make tough decisions that will change the way surviors interact with you. Some may consider you a great friend, while others would love to watch you die. These decisions range from simple to almost impossible. As the tensions rise in the group, so do the consequences of your actions. This all builds up to the season finale, which made me cry. I was raised to be a man that held his emotions in. Even when I lost close family and loved ones, I never cried. Not once. This game; however, it made cry. At the time, I was only sixteen. Now that I have played it again, knowing the outcome, I shed another tear. This game does play on your heartstrings. No doubt about that. That makes it a must buy in my book, no matter the cost. I will list the pros and cons of the game as followed.
Here are the Pros:
1.) An amazing story with great characters and a great protagainist.
2.) Simple controls.
3.) The game looks very similar to the comic book its based on (it's its own story, but takes place in TWD universe).
4.) Decisions actually matter.
5.) The choices you are given are not some simple black and white decision. There are always consequences.
Here are the Cons:
1.) The framerate can drop at random times. It was worse on console in my opinion. I only had about three framerate drops in my playthrough.
2.) Sometimes the controls can crap out on you. It may not recognize a mouse click, which ends up getting you killed.
3.) One decision in the game can a certain character hate you for the longest time, even if you supported them early on.
4.) It can get real slow at times, and even a little confusing with the puzzles.

The game starts you off in the early days of computer gaming as a developer. Mad Games Tycoon takes a more realistic approach than some others in the genre as you hire far more employees, can upgrade to huge buildings and have far more options for your gaming empire. Here you can produce your own consoles, publish your own (and others) games, acquire other developers and eventually make massively multiplayer games that require a server room. Along the way you need to research features, console parts and an almost endless assortment of other things to keep on the cutting edge of gaming.
The heart of the game is making games. This entails making game engines, which you can sell, choosing genres and sub-genres, optimizing settings for that genre, choosing a desired audience from kids to senior citizens and eventually having graphics, sounds and animation departments added features. Oh and you'll need a group of playtesters to stamp out bugs.
At points it can all feel a bit overwhelming, but it is a vast amount of managerial fun if you like management times games and can handle some micro-management along the way. The game has constantly improved along the way as the developer is responsive to the community and updates frequently.
I've played a significant number of games that are similiar and most are fairly good, but so far MGT is my favorite and it seems like everytime I figure I've played enough for a good long time, out comes an update with a new feature that I want to try. This is the good side of the sometimes problematic Ealry Access format and I commend the developer.

To me, a gaming masterpeice is a game which can entertain any sort of gamer. Bastion could be titled a gaming masterpeice, much like Dust: An Elysian Tail. It's gameplay core and mechanics are solid, and is good enough to keep you nice and entertained for a couple hours in one session, and the gold narration and storytelling is only there to refine and back it up. These two combined can result to some pretty damn nice immersion, which is a thing some games fail at doing, and some succeed at. Bastion succeeded and went over the charts.

'Rollers of the Realm' is a game that combines pinball and RPG (role-playing game). And it does so quite successfully.
The pinball aspect of the game is classic: you push buttons (on your keyboard or on a controller) to move flippers in order to control the ball and prevent it from dropping down the drain.
The RPG aspect of the game consists of the following elements:
The campaign consists of about 35 maps to complete. After finishing a map, you can revisit it to gather more XP and gold. While playing through the campaign, you'll unlock 'arena maps'. These maps are optional but the experience and (a portion of) the gold you earn carry over to the party's campaign, so they are a good way to grind a bit of both if you're having trouble with the campaign.
The graphics are isometric and look colourful and vibrant. The music fits the game splendidly and it's reminiscent of some typical tactical RPGs, which 'Rollers of the Realm' basically is, too. The dialogue is completely voiced. I would call the level of voice acting mediocre: not overly impressive but not particularly annoying either.
One thing that's missing is the option to disable controller vibration. Not only for people who want to play using a controller but don't like the vibration, but even when you use the keyboard and mouse, the controller will vibrate. If you don't want that to happen, the only solution is to unplug the controller.

'Rollers of the Realm' has 10 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 5 just for running the game. There are 32 Steam Achievements to be triggered. About half of them are quite challenging, actually, especially some of the 'arena' achievements. This game is certainly
'an easy 100% achievements'.

You go through a simple RPG story while you play pinball. I used an X360 controller (because it makes sense for me to use LT/RT for the left and right flippers) although it does allow for keyboard controls. You control the flippers and have limited control over the ball (you can make the ball go slightly left or right).
You have a selection of pinball characters to use. The more characters you unlock, the more balls (lives) you have. If you lose a ball (you let a ball get past your flippers or down another hole) you can revive it by gathering enough mana. Each character has a different set of passive abilities/attributes and (usually one) active ability that uses mana. You can switch characters during the level as long as you currently have the ball trapped on the flipper.
Levels are often (but not always) a mix of defeating enemies and getting the ball to target locations. Ranged enemies damage your flippers so you usually want to defeat them quickly. Melee usually just serve as blockers and can either block or hit the ball back at you if you attack from the front.
As you hit things you gain XP and gold which are used to upgrade your characters. XP limits what is available to buy and gold is used to buy them. Upgrades allow you to have more passive/active abilities, hit harder, and control your ball better.
Worth a try if you like pinball and like idea of a simple RPG layered over it.

Ittle Dew is a game of adventure and independent puzzle.
You control Ittle Dew, a young girl without shoes, who end up on an island full of monsters. Tippsie, her loyal sidekick, will give her some hints during the adventure. The only human being of the island, who is also to the manager of the local store, proposes her an exchange: a raft to leave the island, in exchange for an artefact hidden in the castle of the island.
A real adventure for the young Ittle Dew starts: resolution of riddles to move forward in the rooms of the castle; harvest of weapons and objects which will help her in the task; fight against monsters and boss until reach her goal.
The whole is made in a funny style, both in drawing and in dialogues. Monsters are completely stupid, and there is a lot of jokes about RPG: the hero who eats literally hearts to regenerate HP, the HP bar made of hearts drawn on papers and maintained between them with adhesive tape, jokes about useless items or achievements... We also collect cards of the bestiary of the game, which describe every character and their tastes in a parodic way. So we learn that some monsters like french fries, that other one is dizzy while it is a flying monster, etc...
The graphic style is original, with a real identity, childish and very colored style. Sounds and music are also very nice. On the other hand, it is a short game, between 3 and 4 hours to fully finish it, that is to say by ending the game, the secondary donjons and by collecting all the objects. Everything depends on your speed to understand and to solve the riddles. However, speedrunners and achievement hunters will be satisfied. Indeed, to get all the achievements, you will need to finish the game several times, and one in particular in less than 15 minutes!

I don't normally review games on here and when I do review a game in general, I like to have at least completed it first. But, I am not for this game.
I am a lover of JRPG's and like that more JRPG's are getting PC releases (even if some of them need optimising). Previously I've played Tales of Phantasia, Tales of Symphonia and Tales of Zesteria. But have not completed any of them, not to say I consider them bad games, because I've enjoyed them, but not necessarily hooked me long enough to play them heavily.
Tales of Berseria is different for me.
A few points:
Instead of being the chosen heroes to save the world from a seemingly unstoppable evil, as is common in JRPG themes, where you have characters who have their quirks and conflicts, maybe people who are yet to understand their potential, but are ultimately the hero types. I am not forgetting that there are anti-heroes in JRPG's too, but looking at type of JRPG Tales of Berseria is, I have come to the expectation of playing the heroic types.
But I feel in Berseria, you're not the playing the heros, or even anti-heros. I would say that you are the villain, whether you remain the villain in the end has yet to be seen (and if I did know, I wouldn't spoil it). The heros of the world are the Exorcists who protect the people from demonic hordes and have helped cleanse the land. Whilst they are a controlling force, the people see the nature of the Exorcists to be necessary and even as a ruling power, they are still considered heros. You on the other hand are playing the 'edge-lord', the character whose only goal is vengeance, using the power of the daemons (who're causing a blight on the world) as your weapon. Velvet will stop at nothing to get there, even if it means cutting down all those who stand in her way. She can be pretty merciless and the people she brings with her aren't the heroic types either (criminals, if anything), each with their own motives. So it sets a darker tone. And the fact I've referred to the MC as an edgelord may put some off, but she has depth, she has a backstory where you might cut her some slack and think, "fairdoes" and she gets character development. At times she fulfills the edgelord stereotype "I don't care", "whatever", like a moody emo kid in some ways, but I feel that is pacified in that the game is well written and doesn't happen enough to be a problem. It has dark themes, yet keeps the vibrant colours of a Tales game, which doesn't hurt the atmosphere when it is needed for those darker moments. So it very much still plays like a Tales game, but looks at things from a different perspective. And I feel the characters may end up finding themselves in a complicated moral dilemma, due the game's running theme, "emotion versus reason". Because "good" and "evil" should not be so black and white.
Though, and perhaps to be expected from these sorts of games, I don't understand why Velvet's practically naked, I didn't think it felt to be "her" but as soon as I unlock a costume that is, I'll be using it. At least there is that option. But fan service is there if it is your thing. I am one of those who likes characters to be dressed for what I think suits them as a character, so skimpy is fine, if I think it's what the character would wear. But I won't deny, it is a fan service in this game, but at least they make some fun of the fact she is not wearing much at all (aren't you a bit cold?).
The story elements feel well paced out too, without feeling like you're having to grind between content and the gameplay is fun and exciting enough for me to not get too used to running away from enemies because I want to progress. And the amount of encounters I feel is appropriate. Not feeling like you're being bombarded with hordes or on the other end of the scale, not feeling like you're skipping down a hallway.
The combat system is very fluid, and heavily customisable, you can manage your own combos for how you want to balance the battle out and you have a good system for managing AI of your party members. Given some enemies are weak to certain elements, I have my different combo sets to match different elements and break them up with physical attacks in between. It works quite nicely for me and I've tweaked it to my playstyle. It is also fun and varied and different enemy types prefer to killed in different ways, whilst there is a butting mashing element, there is still thought in what you're doing. A balance between action and strategy, which is what you would come to expect in a Tales game. But, I am getting a similar enjoyment in the battle to what I got when I played Star Ocean 4 (I didn't play the new one, so cannot compare), though I am not saying that it is the same as, but I rate SO4's system highly for how it balanced action and strategy and how it created a diverse and enjoyable combat experience for me that didn't get old. It can be easy for a battle system, whilst well made, to end up bland.
There's also a decent upgrade system for weapons and gear, you can buy your gear, break down old gear or duplicates of gear and end up creating enhancements. Which is nice for when you do end up with gear you don't need, instead of vendering it, you can make use of it.
The graphics. I almost snubbed the graphics, on the basis this is a £39.99 game, almost (so put your pitchforks away), I don't think good quality graphics are required for a great game, but at that price, you might expect something that feels like it has a higher production value. I know some will say it is shallow, but I bring it up as there are some that may be put off from paying that much for something they might otherwise pay £15 to 25 for. But I value a game on enjoyment and how many hours I get out of it. The art style is beautiful and the graphics are still great and environments and characters are all well designed, but to a lower polygon count, lower texture resolution and fewer shaders than one might expect out of a new game. But, as graphics improve, it can mean developers are spending more time trying to make the game look gorgeous and less time on gameplay elements and story. Given they have a time frame and budget, I personally prefer, particularly in a game like this, for them to focus on gameplay and story, which I felt they've done.
The other point to note, partially related to graphics, is how it fares as a PC port. It works very smoothly at 60fps, I've not encountered bugs and no slow downs and it feels optimised for PC users. With the option for Fullscreen Windowed is nice, as I am a heavy alt-tabber. The option for Ultra-wide resolutions support would have been nice, but something I have come to accept with some games, that my monitor will get black bars. Another note to ultrawide gamers, running this at an ultrawide resoluton keeps the black bars, but will mess up the UI when it comes to story panels, so better to run it at 16:9 (as you'll be viewing it as 16:9 anyway).
Overall. I am enjoying it much more than I thought I would. The combat and story being the strongest selling points for me. It hooked me quite quickly. More than I expected it to. I would recommend it to others. I would recommend it over other Tales games on the Steam store. And fortunately, there's a demo to try it out, to see if it is the sort of thing you might enjoy.

With sharp graphics and sound, Gridberd builds a thick, dark atmosphere. The story is ok, and the developers obviously cared and worked hard, but bugs and design choices blow it. It's like someone set me a beautiful dinner table - with candles and music - and then served me poop.

If you see a journal page in the environment, a visible key-prompt appears ( [F] ) which lets you pick it up and read it. But often, standing in front of the page and looking at it doesn't elicit a prompt. I repeatedly had to scurry about the floor randomly, waggling my head, until a visible key prompt appeared - often at the corner of the screen. But occasionally, it was wasted time because the page turned out to be non-interactive. And once (in the dining room) I was able to read a page by pressing the interact key after completely failing to find any visible prompt.
Gridberd is a few months and some tough feedback away from being a solid, very scary game. But once you serve me poop, I'll be eating out, thank you :)

There are three things I would like to note upfront, in order to help users quickly discern if this story is right for them:
As a writer, I am always looking for games with deep, rich story. This review will be a basic breakdown of what this story does so brilliantly... and why I think you should play it. This will be, mostly, spoiler-free.
The game
somehow ended up in a recommended game section to me, and as my name is Serena, I was immediately intrigued. My boyfriend and I both downloaded it as soon as we saw it was free, and I played the story with my sister. I could tell that nothing about this game would be light-hearted, and it lived up to its projected potential.
The option to make it impossible to exit the game without starting over was a very intelligent, thought-out one on the part of the programmers, and I applaud them. This is a story that was meant to be sat down and finished. Doing it in parts disrupts the mood that this game works laboriously hard to do but pulls off so effortlessly.
I'm going to attempt to say what other reviews haven't: so, yes, it takes place in a cabin in the woods, and yes, we have a narrator, and yes, we find out things about both the nameless narrator and Serena through interacting with the objects, and yes, the narrator doesn't remember himself, but it's
than all of that.
The tools that this game uses to frighten you is foreboding and psychologically abusive, and it's done so well that, at times, you literally lose yourself in favor of the story you're in.
There are three stages this game goes through, and each of them are compound: depression and sentimentality, anger and hatred, and guilt and horror. The guilt cycle lapses back into the depression and anger, and
, this game does it well. The anger cycle is one of those jolting, shivering catalysts that throws you completely out of the quasi-comfort zone you'd found in the midst of the story. You're sympathizing, at first, with the main character so vividly that you legitimately forget you're not him.
And that's one of the harshly haunting things this game does to you. As you pick up things that are ghosts of his past, you begin to feel sentimental yourself. You begin to identify as a narrator who, literally,
.
The foreboding in this game is continuous and everywhere. I'd point out examples if I wasn't scared of spoiling others, because this is one of those games that simply cannot be spoiled. This is one of those games that you don't truly understand until the foreboding of previous sinks in. Days after you've finished the game, you'll be doing the dishes, and suddenly one of the lines from the game will come at you, and you'll be standing there in shock of what the writers have done to you, and how they pulled off things, and you're running around, wondering, "Did anyone else notice that, too?"
This is one of those games that after you finish, you send it to your friends and family to play just because you need people to talk to about it. You need to spit-ball ideas, you need to see their reactions. You need to see if they see what you do.
Open-ended psychological horror is quite literally one of my favorite things. I've written two books with that theme. And that is
. The ending was satisfying in a way that you can come to hundreds of your own conclusions, but what you're given is so complete that at the same time, you really don't feel like you need more.
The writers, simply, are something of geniuses, and that is exactly what we needed for a game heavily relying so heavily on story. So little story is given, but when you're done, you feel as if you've finished a trilogy.
is something between a game, a story, and a piece of art. Though others may disagree, I don't know why it can't be considered all three.
There were a few complaints I have, however, but they are very pale in comparison to the dark, heart-racing aesthetic that
exists in. The silence is scary. The clock is scary. The music is scary. Nothing jumps out at you, blood doesn't drip from the walls, nothing lunges at you. But this is one of the scariest games I have ever completed.
Why?
Because you are powerless. More than so
, as you can never even exit the house you're in. You can't escape the kind of horror that's around you. It's there, and you can't forget or ignore it for even a moment. You can't run away, you can't hide, you can't find a way out. From the start of the game, there's something that tells you there is no escaping
. Beating the game will not guarantee your survival, or the saving of your soul, and this game grasps at the theme that you're completely trapped expertly. The windows are old and covered, which truly make you feel like there isn't even an outside to go to. The house is small and confining, and somehow, even with everything there is to look at, it feels like you're only looking at half a life.
Complaints
I have one more complaint, but it's story-related, and I'd rather not spoil, so I shall keep it to myself.
Overall: great game if you're looking for something to impact you and surprise you, enjoyable enough for a second play through.

I wish I have more time to play this game before I wrote this review.
Anyway, do I recommend this game? Absolutely yes. See detials in the following list:
1. It is a legit PC port, you can definitely see the efforts developers put into.
2. Interesting combat system. + Allow you to build your own combo for all characters.
3. Great character designs. They are all unique and everyone provides a very different combat experiences.
4. Great story and animation.
5. Requires no prior knoweldge of its predecessor.
Here are things that the developers are doing okay:
1. Character building. There are some depth to it and not a whole lot.
2. Character models. I know they are all very good looking, and I know it is a JRPG, but if there is only a certain number of characters and they are staying that way for the entire game, put in a little more time to make them extraordinary is essential to the game experience. Make Velvet's hair more realistic, I want to see every hair moves through the wind. Give her more poses, make her vivid!
3. Monster design.
And here are the things that I think it is either bad or straight out missing:
1. What is this god damn navigation system? Huh? The navigation in this game is so bad that you might as well not even bother to look at it. I've spend (to be consider as) a lot of time (for a JRPG) to look for a NPC or wherever the quest is telling me to go; and it doesn't happen just once, twice, it happen all the time. I find myself taking educated guess of where should I go the entire game, and the time spend on this for a RPG is punishing.
2. Where is fast travel? Okay for the 14.2 hours I spend on this game there is so far a total of 1 fast travel, and it is basically place at the end of a dungeon like place and that stuff will only take you out of the dungeon. Alright I get it is not an open world type of game, but it is boring as hell to walk from A to B and then from B to A. Make it more enjoyable.
3. What is this $9.99 DLC to unlock unique costumes thing? $9.99 for a costume set? You have basically zero option of your characters' outfit, the majority of them are no way near the level of original outfits. After looking at the same outfits for more than 10 hours makes me want to buy a new set of costume. Yes, there are ways to get them in the game but they all suck (expect for the waiter dress of Laphicet, how cute).
The give away is, Tales of Berseria is an excellent JRPG, although not perfect but it does provides an great gaming experiences. I might be a bit harsh on the developers but it is because I love this game very very much and want the game to be better just like any of you.

This game is amazing.  I didn't know what I was getting into when I purchased it based on a co-worker's opinion - but I'm so glad I dove in.  Its turn based combat - and its pulled off great, and your soldiers are fully customizable.  I spent 2 days creating a huge pool of personalized, named soldiers before I even started playing.  The story line only adds to the immersion and I really enjoyed it.  The writing is creative and engaging and I quickly became addicted.
Basically, its the love child of a first person shooter and a really good turn-based RPG.  The turn based fighting is not boring - there are dramatic zoom ins and bad-a$$ action scenes like we see in the new Fallout games - with boat loads of options of who to attack, your percentage chance of hitting them at said angle and elevation, how to attack them (Pistol, rifle, grenade, special skill, heavy weapon), or perhaps you want to use the soldier's turn to move or duck and cover (to reduce chance of enemy hitting them), etc.
There are tons of weapons, weapon modifications, armor, ammo types, experimental suits and blades and guns, and LOADS of gear and ammo to discover and unlock through completing objectives and having your science dept perform autopsies on downed enemies.  Each class of soldier you have (Sniper, Ranger, Grenadier, Psy Op and Specialist) has a skill tree so you can fine tune them for specific things.  And one of the best things of all.... Your soldiers are completely customizable.  At the start of every mission your named, customized soldiers drop down that rope in the latest gear you've dug up for them, looking hot and ready to dominate.  LOVE this game.
I see a lot of criticism that the game has timers on battles.  I really don't find this is an issue.  By "timed" it means that you must destroy or recover an object or person in X amount of moves.  Firstly - not every battle has this timer - in fact very few do.  Secondly, its not at all impossible to complete the mission in the amount of turns allowed.  If you are dropping into enemy infested territory and need to extract someone before a bomb goes off, of course there is a turn timer.  But its not an unrealistic turn timer - and I've only encountered turn timers in about 15% of the missions I've come across.  Seriously if you want a nice, customizable, engaging, well written story with LOTS to discover and endless options for gearing and skilling your soldiers, try this game.  Its been a long time since a game challenged me to think.

I can't recommend it to anyone but small children.
Graphics are good, the backyard setting is cool, and the physics are ok. That's where the good stuff end.
The gameplay is just meh. The money/shop/unlocks just doesn't work. And the game is waaaay too easy: I've beaten most tracks on insane (highest difficulty) with the first car (the only one I've got, it's pointless to save a loooot of money to get another). It's both too easy and the sense of progression was
not really thought out. In fact there isn't any. Unlocking tracks is also a silly chore as you don't get enough money to unlock the next even when you win a race, forcing you to race it again even if you didn't like it or if it was way too easy (it always is).
The races are fun here and there, with a little bit of chaos at the very start. Why do we
start last by the way? No clue but it has to be because the start is the only fun you'll have. After 30 seconds it gets boring as you'll be up front and nothing goes on. Sure there are mines and missiles but they don't even slow you down. In fact hitting mines can be good as it gives you money for air time (?) while not slowing you down.
Usually during races I find myself trying to get turbos instead of mines or missiles, not to actually pass anyone but just so that the races end sooner because I'm just too bored while "racing".
There's a "car reset" for when you get stuck (?) but you never get stuck. You never end upside down or anything. But the computer resets its cars all the time, which contributes for the game being sooo easy to beat.
On the technical side there are some things that are just lazy. The key binding options are on the launcher. Then I can't unbind a joystick. To make it worse, I have some 5 joysticks (wheel, pedals, shifter, gamepad, button box...) connected to the PC but the game only recognizes 1. That means that "button 3" in any of the controllers will have that effect, or at least seems like it. I didn't test a lot because I just preferred to play with the keyboard instead.
Even small details started to bother me just for corners being cut in the programming, like my ears getting blasted by loud sound for a quick moment when the game is launched before the in-game audio volume settings "kick in".
A shame really, I like the genre and I like the idea but this title just falls short of delivering an entertaining experience.
I'd recommend Death Rally instead. It's top down view but it sure delivers in terms of fun and enjoyment what this one fails to.

-Foreword
I expected this game to be total crap, but actually, its pretty good.
-Graphics
The graphics were obviously not the best, but i really loved them! I'm a huge fan of this type of graphics.
You are able to change Wheels, paint and Antenna color of your car (Which costs coins, not p2w)
-Gameplay
The game features 16 Circuit Maps, 8 Sprint Maps and Coin Racing (which i didnt try).
It shows the laps left, also on Sprint Maps sadly. It shows "1/1 Lap" instead of "20km left" or something.
There are really many cars availiable (~30 i guess) which as much as i've noticed dont give any advantage (except for better "rolling" maybe, im not sure about that though). In the Pimp Shop you can configure their Wheels, Paint and Antenna which costs Coins.
There are two different currencies: Dollars and Coins. You can get coins by converting 250k$ into 5 Coins.
You get ~50-100k$ per race, a Car costs ~20 Coins, do the maths...
Tracks also cost dollars, so dont waste all your money on cars.
Also, there are 4 different difficulties, Easy, Medium, Hard and Insane.
I jumped from Easy to Insane and noticed no difference. The game is pretty easy, if i want i can be 1st in every single race. The Bots are just too bad.
Oh, you've also got Mines and Missles :3
-Sounds
The Audio was insanely loud when starting it (Its just my fault i guess, should finally lower windows volume >.<)
Other than that, the sounds were pretty good.
I only heared one song, muted the music then though because i had my own music running. Its not too bad.
-Controls
The controls are basically W,A,S,D to accelerate, brake and turn your vehicle, space to shoot missles and C to throw mines.
-Quality
The quality was a lot higher than expected.
The Sprint mode only shows Laps (1/1 Laps) instead of KM left or something.
You are able to set the resolution in the Launcher which is insanely great!
The Escape button doesnt work always.
The Bots are really bad.
Well, thats it, its a really fun game for a while, had fun for 50 Minutes and will definetly have fun for 5-10 more hours in the future!
-Overall Experience
The Game really is great! There are some little bugs which dont really matter, the only bad thing is bots being insanely bad even on the "Insane" difficulty, but thats it. Other than that its a great RC Racing Game ^^

Without mods, Fallout 4 is an okay game. Long and wide, but lacks depth. It's too easy in some places, and has weird spikes in difficulty in very strange places. The game likes to have the player depend on VATS a little too much, and the crafting system has potential, but the implementation leaves a small bit to be desired. The resources are pretty decently spread out though - the rare ones are definitely rare, and the common ones are everywhere. Definitely a real pain to gather things with a small inventory. Mods help a lot.
However, like pretty much any Bethesda RPG, there's boatloads of mods. Nexus Mods is a great place to find dozens of them. They can add content, improve balance, and all sorts of stuff. With mods in mind, Fallout 4 becomes a very fun game. If your computer isn't strong enough to handle all the extra load, don't get this game unless it's on sale.
Also keep in mind many mods require all the DLC now, so the base game isn't very worth it.

In conclusion I highly recommend completing Bastion if not for the awesome art style and music, then for the story.

I am recommending this game because it really tries to do something interesting as an pinball/RPG hybrid.
An experiment in pinball that swings for the fences but doesn't quite hit a home run.  Each of your party members is a ball with different properties such as size, damage, maneuverability, and healing which can be augmented by earned items.  The physics of the boards feel like an old wooden version of pinball, which can take getting used to, especially when your ball gets hit in a way that tosses it over the board's obstacles.
Each party member (all very well-voiced!) has a special ability which can be triggered when enough mana is collected from the boards.  Boards often take less than five minutes to beat and range from the interesting to the absurdly simple, with the player having to get their ball into a specific area or defeat a specific enemy to pass.  I think I would have enjoyed a board or two that could be played endlessly like classic pinball after the main quests were beaten.  Story mode will take about 5 hours to complete on a straight plathrough but there is little reason to return to the game afterwards.
I love some of the puzzle aspects that shine through the duller filler boards, especially those which encourage (but don't require) the player to switch between different characters to finish a board more easily.  Unfortunately, these are more uncommon than not, but it illustrates the potential of the concept.

I have to say after a few hours of playing this game it's pretty good.  If you like zombies, turn-based rpg games, and roguelikes, this is definitely a game I'd recommend trying.  From a game design perspective, I have a few complaints, but I'll try to sum it up as concisely as possible.

Pros:
Challenging gameplay: definitely unforgiving, but because your progress in previous playthroughs allows you to build yourself up in future runs, it's not enough to turn you away.
Choices: I haven't made that much progress with it, but from the way it looks there seem to be several survivors the protagonist can "romance".  Although the missions to do so are brutally difficult, the rewards are pretty good
Art: The artistic style and music aren't bad at all; after hours of play the music still feels pretty fitting.  Definitely surprisingly good for an Indie game, though it does have that feel that makes it reminiscent of old school flash games, it definitely feels like there's enough content, though I also got it on sale.
Cons:
Resource Management:  You'll find yourself scrambling to sustain numerous resources which is to be expected in a zombie survival game but in particular, My biggest gripe is that in order to have extra party members do a "Job" for the day, most jobs cost you rations AND tools, which I feel is too much, given that tools are extremely hard to come by.  Rations are a sustainable resource so from a game design perspective, it's balanced and fair to expect a player to manage and sustain that resource, but tools are a random and rare drop from events or from battles in one of the hardest areas of the game, which is suicide to farm unless you're already level 6+ by which point you're already out of tools usually.
This could easily be remedied by adding a "Job" that allows a designated survivor to craft tools for the day, which would cost materials and would be fair.  Just an idea.
Steep Learning Curve:  If you have experience with survival games of this nature, you won't have as hard of a time with this one, but I could definitely see new players struggling.  There's a lot of information crammed in a very short span of time and during my first 3 runs, I received quests for survivors that I couldn't complete, partly because I was still learning the game's mechanics and partly because my characters weren't a high enough level to even attempt them.
Glitchy UI:  this gripe is pretty specific and probably an easy fix, so if it's addressed later ignore this, but there are weapon/armor upgrade items that must be click/dragged onto the gear of your choice to upgrade, however upon doing so, it can bug out the item menu so that item icons overlap making it impossible to click on other items under it.  I though switching tabs or going on an adventure might fix it but it's remained consistent.  It also does this is you drag any other items in your inventory for any reason so be very careful with that.
All in all, a pretty good game for what I paid, and as far as indie games, I would definitely recommend it.  at this time, I'd give it an 8.5/10

This is the first game of the Tales series that I've ever played, and which I also preordered about a month before its release date with high expectations. Being a person with somewhat preference for JRPGs, at the time of writing this I have about 22 hours of play time logged into Tales of Berseria within two nights of purchasing and I've enjoyed every second of it.
Firstly, the real question anybody comes to this section is, at a steep price of $50USD, is the game worth buying? (or $90NZD, but you can get it for a lot cheaper buying a steam key on another site that doesn't follow NZ pricing. Personally I bought a key for about $45-50NZD)
At first glance, the graphics look clean, which should be expected since it's a fairly recent game.
Considering the game supposedly has 50 hours of gameplay, you are paying effectively $1USD/hour which is a very nice ratio compared to other JRPGs such as Neptunia's series. However the amount of gameplay you get compared to the price shouldn't be the only deciding factor as to whether the game is worth it or not; a game with large quantity of gameplay is worthless if the gameplay isn't high quality.
Let's talk about the combat system.
I may be a bit bias here, but I'm just bored of turn based, spell spamming, huge AoE mob clearing combat systems. That♥♥♥♥♥♥just isn't fun and after a few mob encounters in those types of games, combat just becomes a nuisance and rather than any actual skill involved you're just using the same spell over and over again.
Being the first game I've played in the series, the combat feels very engaging.
Your party consists of four characters with two others being subs, and during the story you get characters pretty early on in the game. You control only one character during battle engages, and the other three characters will be controlled by AI; you  can change their aggressiveness and behaviour with the game settings i.e. the mage AI may cast more offensive spells or sit back and cast more heals. During combat you can switch your controlled character, so for situations where Velvet is ineffective, you could switch your control to Magilou.
The difficulty feels just right as a new player. I cranked up the difficulty to the highest I could, which is intense I believe. I'll admit, I did (and still do) get my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me from "Dangerous Encounters" and dire mobs and even some main story encounters, but the combat feels so rewarding when you learn how to effectively use status ailments, blocking and quick step timings, as well as using effective artes (basically skill names).
Let's talk about the story and characters now.
Before I start, I don't like to go into too much about the setting of the game, because when I read reviews myself, I'm only looking into the gameplay itself and not for a blurb.
About the story, it's pretty generic. Basically another MC with a revenge plot. However I find that the characters themselves make the plot very enjoyable. Since you get the characters pretty early in the game, the plot isn't entirely revolved around the MC and so the story sort of branches out and alligns for each character.
tl;dr
$50USD price tag, 50 hours game play on first play
+ beautiful graphics
+ engaging combat system
+ very likeable characters
- somewhat generic story

Good job Bamco. Now give us more DLC costumes. (Edit: We got em!)
EDIT at 18 HOURS in:
Okay, I've had some decent time with this game now and feel more comfortable talking about the actual game.
I have to say while Berseria is a huge improvement from Zestiria, it still kind of pales in comparison to older games in the series and I've noticed this has been a trend starting around Xillia I think.
The combat system is good, Velvet's Break Soul is way too strong in my opinion (it's actually pretty game-breaking, for the uninformed for a small cost Velvet basically can't die when this mechanic is active and she can't be staggered/stunned either) while other characters' Break Souls either seem too weak in comparison or are just not as useful. There's some definite issues with game balance and it's very clear that Bamco put most of their efforts into Velvet as the main playable character even though there are plenty of other characters that interest me.
Aside from balance issues, the combat system is still great, no real complaints. I do advise to play on at least Moderate/Hard though, or you'll just breeze through things (unless that's what you desire).
The main issue I have with  Berseria (and subsequently, Xillia, Xillia 2, Zestiria) is the actual WORLD. While the game is very pretty and the environments are wonderfully crafted, it's so... vast and EMPTY. I had this issue especially with Xillia where I spent a good chunk of the game just running across land and battling monsters and checking every possible search point just in case I miss out on some item/drop.
Though overworld monotony is common in JRPGs, it feels accentuated in the more recent Tales games, including Berseria. Symphonia and Abyss did not feel as stale as Berseria does outside of combat.
I believe one of the main reasons for this is also the dungeon design - I think it's lazy. I may only be 18 hours in but so far I haven't encountered a single dungeon that was actually interesting. The game just requires you to go from point A to point B, kill monsters along the way, kill a boss, proceed. The older Tales games' dungeons were chock full of little puzzles and obstacles that you actually had to at least think for a minute to solve.
A prime example is a dungeon in Berseria where you're underground in the sewers and you can flip a switch to adjust the water levels. In other (good) games, a switch like that would both lower the water levels in one area and raise it in another (thinking of early game Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess) and so you'd have to sort of think about things as you do them, and find the right pattern of triggering water level changes to proceed to the next part of the dungeon.
However, in Berseria you simply just flip the switch, proceed, flip another switch, proceed. Brainless. There's no point in having mechanics like this if they don't actually add any depth to the gameplay.
Even in Symphonia which I played 10 years ago I can still vaguely remember crunching my mind over the puzzles that the dungeons would have you solve in order to proceed.
While I'm still enjoying the game in terms of the story, the characters and their interaction, the combat system and the DLC content (sucker for costumes), I can definitely say that for a majority of the game you will be just running along long pathways consisting of nothing but a few enemies that seem long for the sake of being long.
There's even a particular area of the game that's needlessly large and annoying to navigate as you spend so much time just covering ground instead of actually engaging in any meaningful gameplay. I'm sure there will be many more areas like this as I play through the game.
But that being said, that's my MAIN COMPLAINT with the game, but there are definitely more joys I have with this game than I have complaints.
The characters are decently interesting and unlike Zestiria's cast I have a genuine interest in some of the characters in Berseria. Magilou in particular is a very interesting character and I'm interested in seeing how her personality (hopefully) develops and unfolds.
Velvet, the protagonist, is a bit of a stereotypical angst-ridden character who's sole purpose in everything is revenge. It's badass at first but then kind of gets old after a certain point, I have to admit. It's noble of her to go to such lengths to fulfill her revenge but I really do hope that there's more to her character than just anger and hate as the game progresses. She has a soft side like most of these kinds of characters do, but that's not what I'm referring to when I mean I hope she develops more - I mean I hope there's more depth to the character.
The other characters in the cast are also not bad, and none of them are insufferable which is always a plus.
The story is nothing ground-breaking but Tales games are never really remembered for their stories anyway. Long story short, the plot is looking like one of those "Good guys are actually corrupt and manipulating the masses, group of rebels work to stop them despite the odds" kind of  plots, though at the point of the game I'm at there's still plenty of room for more development and depth.
The music is great in the game, and I especially enjoy the opening song. Tales OST have always had a special place in my heart.
OVERALL, I'm enjoying this game a lot so far. I definitely recommend people to give it a try. Even though the game may feel bland at some (or many) points, I think it's worth it to give a Tales game a shot at the long haul. End-game content is usually pretty good in Tales games, as well as replayability. There's also some mini-games that I've found so far that are pretty damn fun as well.  I'm looking forward to the rest of this game.
TL;DR - Despite some major flaws with the game, Tales of Berseria is still a solid JRPG with an engaging combat system and many other redeeming factors that make it worthwhile to invest your time in.
P.S - If you can, do yourself a favour and try to get your hands on Tales of the Abyss, Tales of Symphonia, Tales of Destiny R or even Tales of Phantasia (PS1 of PSP version, don't touch the GBA version). Those are some really great games that set the standards of Tales games for me.
Tales of Graces and Tales of Vesperia are also pretty good according to many fans. Graces for the battle system and Vesperia as an overall title. Check 'em out. Thank me later.

Half Life, bir gizli araştırma üssünde meydana gelen bir kaza sonucu ortaya çıkanları anlatan, bunları kahramanı Gordon Freeman’ın gözünden anlatan 1998 yapımı bir FPS oyunudur. Kısaca bahsetmek gerekirse, spoiler vermemeye çalışarak, araştırma üssüne bir taş benzeri bir madde ulaşmıştır, maddenin uzaydan geldiği varsayılmaktadır ve M.I.T’den mezun olan Gordon Freeman’ın ekibi olan olağandışı maddeler ekibine üzerinde deney yapılması adına verilmiştir. Ardından yapılan deneyde bir aksaklık olur ve macera başlar. Bundan sonrasını anlatacağım merak edenler için. Altta bir link verip oraya yazmayı planlıyorum. Oyunun altında oldukça ve oldukça sağlam bir hikaye var.
Biraz da oyunun tarihinden bahsedelim. Valve’in çıkış oyunudur Half-Life. Gabe Newell ve bir kaç arkadaşı eski Microsoft çalışanıdır. Windows 95 ve 98’de çok büyük katkıları olduğu söylenir Gabe’in. Microsoft ekibinden daha önce ayrılan bir ekip id software’i kurmuştur. Çıkarttıkları oyunlar ile iyi bir başarıya imza atmıştır. Bunu gören Gabe, id Software’dan olan arkadaşları ile iletişime geçer ve Microsoft’dan ayrılır. Ardından Quake’in oyun motorunu düzenleyerek ilk Half Life’ı yaparlar. GoldSrc adlı oyun motoru ile Half Life sunulur. Half Life FPS tarihindeki ilk hikayeli oyun olma tahtına da sahiptir. Ondan önceki oyunlar sadece vur ve ilerle mantığında idi. Valve, Half Life ile yepyeni bir FPS devri başlatmış ve çok çok büyük bir başarıya imza atmıştır. Ardından kendi source motorları ile tekrar ele almışlardır.(1.6 sürümü source ile yapılmıştır.)
Oyunun havası oldukça kasvetli. Her an her yerden saldırabilecek düşmanlar, her tarafta onun dışındaki cesetler, çok az canlı insan, havalandırmalarda geçen yollar,kısıtlı cephane.. Oyun atmosfer olarak size o an oradaki insanın psikolojisi nasıl olursa aynen onu yaşatmakta. Karakter Gordon Freeman ise soğukkanlı ve kolayca bağ kurulabilecek bir karakter. Kısacası oyunu oynamaya başladığınızda kendinizi oyunun içerisinde hissedeceksiniz.
Single Player’dan sonra efsanevi multiplayer’ına geçersek, Multiplayer’ı da Single Player’ı kadar efsanedir. Oynanabilirliğin çok yüksek olması ve kısa sürede adapte olabilmek oyunu daha da çok oynanabilir yapmıştır. Hala daha oynayanı vardır.Çünkü onun deneyimini ne battlefield’dan ne call of duty’den yada başka bir fps’den alabilirsiniz. Bambaşkadır.
Oyun kısmından çıkarsak, Valve geliştirdiği bu motorun üzerine bir çok oyun daha oluşturmuştur. Şüphesiz bunların en meşhuru Counter Strike’dır. Ardından Ricochet, Team Fortress, Deathmatch Classic gibi oyunlarını da eklemiştir. Bir kaçını yeni versiyonları ile günümüzde görmekteyiz.
Half Life’ın başarısının hemen ardından Valve, Orada olanları farklı gözlerden anlatan Half Life Opposing Force, Half Life Blue Shift, Half Life Decay oyunlarını da çıkartmıştır.
Daha önce oynamadım, oynamak istiyorum diyenlere şiddetle tavsiyemdir. Daha iyisini bulmanız pek mümkün değil.

Now, i know alot of people are rather negative towards realm nowadays, but hear me out. If you arent familliar with this game, its a top-down bullethell mmo shooter with mostly fantasy aspects, and a pixel art finish. If these things dont interest you, i still recomend the game, as its free to play and you may be suprised at how fun it is. If not, feel free to sue me. Hard.(JustKiddingPleaseDontSueMe).
Anyways, so you start up the game and first you have to select a class. (actually the first thing you SHOULD do is choose your server and set up keybindings but i digress).you start out with a plain old wizard; easy to use and a viable choice for the noobs, the average player, and the hardcore alike. his particular ability is an AoE spell that can do massive damage at the cost of mana. getting to level 5 with the wizard will unlock the priest, who heals himself and those around him, at the cost of mana. the pattern continues and you unlock more classes by leveling up more classes, however, unless you spend realm gold (purchased with real life money) on a character slot, you can only have one character at a time. did i mention there's permadeath?
fear not, you are given one vault chest to hold items in which are always there, even if you die. you can get more vault chests by using realm gold, however i dont recomend it.
After you've gotten your class, and gotten a unique name by clicking on the gold armor statue in the nexus, you can start playing the game itself (i know, all that stuff to do beforehand, and you get a whole GAME afterwards? Score!) you start out by going into the main room and finding a server to go into. they have names such as "beholder" or "medusa" and they look like little caves. after entering you should find yourself on a beach. this is where your adventure properly begins. kill enemies to get exp and loot, and do quests to get better exp and drops. just keep doing quests, fight harder stuff, and maybe find someone to team with you along the way. have fun!
overall, i highly recomend this game, despite the fact that it can be infuriating at times, and ocassionally just wont stop asking for money, but i think it deserves 4.5/5 stars.

I've put 20 hours into this game and I'll probably put many more. I've played several Game Dev sims and this is the only one besides Game Dev Tycoon that I have thought was worth the money. I loved Game Dev Tycoon and have spent quite a bit of time on it, I was even part of the group that bought it back before it was on steam and was still in development. I have crafted numerous companies in that game but was always at the end left wanting a little more. Mad Games Tycoon gave me that. There is a lot more to being successful in this game and once I got the point my company was making real money and was in a medium sized building I found myself constantly engaged. Between marketing, development, research, employee training, meeting employee desires, hitting trends, contract work, rearranging, etc I stayed on the move constantly. The career felt so much longer than GDT's (which if you can't tell is the standard for me) and I even wanted to keep playing after the consoles stopped rolling in from other companies, which is usually when I would restart in GDT. It took quite a few hours to get to that point too because you can choose several options when choosing difficulty regarding how quickly time passes. Of course in game there are the standard Sims style speed buttons but you can choose how quickly beyond that days pass. After 20 hours I have a company worth 16 billion dollars with several successful consoles, MMO's and AAA titles to my name as well as a 97% positive reputation in the industry. Even after all that I still want to keep playing, maybe even restart now that I know what I am doing and see how fast I can get back to that point. I loved this game so much I actually took the time to write this, my first written steam review. That should say something.

I wouldn't recommend this game at full price. However, if you're getting a bundle of 7-8 games for $2.00? If you're interested at all in racing, I'd say this is worth a solid 1-2 hours of mildly amusing gameplay. It's definitely a good bundle toy.

Rollers of the Realm is an interesting cross between pinball and an action RPG.  There is a story line which progresses you through a sequence of maps.  As you proceed you gain gold, experience and new companions.
In the pinball segment each character is represented by a different pinball.  The balls all have different statistics, some are small and agile while others are large and do lots of damage. You often need to fight enemies, smash through obstacles and navigate through different "layers" of the pinball table.
Overall, Rollers of the Realm is an interesting exercise and is short enough not to get stale.  If you want more game time there is an arena section with different challenges for a number of the tables.
In between areas you can visit the port to hire more characters or buy equipment to make your balls better. You can reply tables for more experience and gold.

PROS:
+Can be entertaining in small bursts.
+Sandbox
+The game does have potential (maybe not anymore, but it did).
+It has an aspect of realism to it.
+The updates are free (as they should be), and the developer stated he didn't want DLCs.
+Developers respond to you if you ask a question or comment on something.
+Pretty cool customization of your police unit. You can also purchase things like a new flatscreen or a couch for your house with your hard earned cash, which is sweet.
CONS:
-Bugs/Glitches (apparently not enough to be game breaking as the game is completed--spoken by developer)
-Stiff movement system for driving and on-foot. Frustrating controls.
-Poor animations.
-GTA 3 graphics.
-Not enough content to warrant a $20 price tag. It needs more missions/guns/cars/skins/buildings/everything.
I really wish this game had more fans and a workshop, because that would change things. More content, better graphics/animations, more skins/customization, would add to the longevity of the game. At the state that this game is in, I cannot recommend this title.
Verdict: 5/10

Short review:
4/10
Completed main game in ~75 minutes
+ Car models are well designed
+ The system of unlocking vehicles and maps is a nice idea
+ No game breaking glitches and it works fairly well.
+ Graphics are decent (but a little inconsistent)
- Very little character is added to the game and it doesn't seem like there's anything unique to seperate it from other racing games.
- The environments aren't very detailed and are quite basic. It doesn't seem like enough creativity was put into designing the environments because it doesn't seem like there's anything at all interesting about it. Each circuit is a small section of one map (a neighbourhood) but there's not really anything interesting about the map.
-The circuits aren't layed out very well as it doesn't give you a good sense of direction and i found myself getting disorientated, especially in the maps where the track loops in on itself because it isn't seperated well enough and the arrows don't always point to the right direction.
- Music is completely generic and not engaging. Every track is generic rock, which isn't bad but it's very boring and repetitive. Sound effects are a little better, but not much.
-Gameplay feels like a grind if you want to unlock vehicles as it takes a very long time to unlock them. I had finished the game and didn't even get close to unlocking any new cars. It seems pointless to have to unlock the circuits if you just get enough money from doing each race to unlock the next race anyway.
-From what I can tell, the other vehicles have nothing different about them anyway, so they don't actually control any differently from the regular car.
- UI is basic (but functional)
- Only 3 powerups, which are mostly pointless. The mine is OK, but the homing missile seems to not work very well and sometimes randomly picks a target rather than going in a direction that makes sense and the boost is annoying since it makes it difficult to control, and most of the circuits aren't big enough for the boost to be particularly useful anyway.
- 3 modes which aren't very interesting and no multiplayer mode.
It's not a bad game, but it's just not very interesting and honestly there's a lot of other games on steam which are better, and it feels like it would be a decent free to play game, but not a game that you should spend money on. For a game that was made in 2015, unfortunately it feels similar to the freeware games made in 2005.
That said, it's not the worst game on steam by far, it's not not really

After an extended period of playing this game, you will see it's shortcomings and eventually get bored, although that is the way it goes with most games. I'd say you can easily get at least 300 hours into Starbound before you start to get bored. After some time though, it gets repetitive and there's not much of it an update can fix. Just remember that 300 hours for a game at this price is a steal, and if you enjoy these kinds of games you will definitely not regret it.
The game has a progression system where you go from easy planets to progressively harder planets when you advance to higher levels, meaning better armor, weapons and abilities. This system does work, although it has it's downsides in a creative game like this. The fact that to progress the game you have to go from planet to planet means that you constantly feel like you have to abandon your previous buildings and creations, which discourages creativity.
Something they implemented to fix this was portals. You can place a portal anywhere and then you can teleport there anytime you want through your ship. The problem here is it makes the world feel incredibly small when it once felt endless and exciting. Just teleporting from one solar system to another instantly without anything indicating the length between them is not a good way to fix this issue in my opinion.

Terraria had a randomly generated world which was big, but not infinitely big. Honestly if anything this game proves a flaw with the procedurally generated structure games. That sure, you'll get a large number of places, but it will generate samey structures, samey biomes, and samey enemies. Sadly this game does have a crazy amount of potential, it could literally be a terraria killer but it won't at this stage and I don't see it being one any time later.
The best thing they could have done with starbound is limit it to around 4-6 Fixed planets to explore, that way the devs can put there love of their game in each planet rather than having it just generate itself which makes the game feel souless.
