UPDATE: Still extremely happy with this game after beating it and working at a bunch of side stuff. It only gets better as the story continues, with some surprisingly heartfelt story scenes further bolstering my thoughts on the high quality of the characters and story in this entry into Tales' series. 65 hours and nothing has changed about what I wrote below after 15, stellar JRPG and beautiful return to glory for the series after quite awhile. And the combat pretty much still hasn't gotten old--chaining artes and managing break souls always feels great!
______________________________________________________________
Quality as ♥♥♥♥ JRPG, really enjoying so far. Interesting characters, pretty focused/enjoyable plot, game starts strong and grabs you pretty quickly, the game isn't an ultra slow starter like Zestiria. Combat is extremely fluid and refined, nothing totally new for Tales of but it flows insanely well this time. Break soul feature makes combat feel really impactful and fun when you chain big combos. Some of the underlying combat mechanics are a bit different this time (no TP, way that you chain combos is a bit diff, only use 4 face buttons on controller and no directionals etc), but it's still Tales. There's an equipment customization system (upgrading via mats and breaking down old equipment for mats etc) that is very simple but a good addition. The game is fairly easy on the hardest initially available difficulty (hard) so far imo, but I'm also only like 15 hrs in as of this writing, so take that as you will. There are also 2 harder unlockable difficulty modes I believe.
Environments are a little dull and repetitive but they get the job done, by no means something that really stands out as a sore point, just could be better. The game has some cool side stuff without feeling overbearing, there's a "rare creature hunt" system as in any good ole RPG, the way that Tales series "Katz society" plays into this game is a bit new, you find Katz in chests that you unlock with a platformer-like collectible item that is everywhere in the environments, and you pick up by moving into. Stuff like that.
Some good tunes in the soundtrack, nothing super memorable that I've come across yet though. Game obviously isn't visually super-impressive but has a nice art style and is fairly easy on the eyes. It looks fine. Port is flawless, game runs at 60 fps constantly on high settings (GTX 770 / Haswell i5), 0 hitches or crashes, haven't come across a single audio bug or anything else that might come with a bad port. Play with controller, this type of game works way better with them.

Really focused and polished entry into the series even if it doesn't break much new ground. Highly recommend for both Tales of fans and anyone that just wants a good JRPG. This is a good place to try this series if you're interested but haven't played one before. Plz bring more of the old entries to PC Bandai Namco, and plz continue to port the new ones so that I have more reasons to hold off buying a PS4 for now, will keep buying this series as you put them out. Thx!

TL;DR: The new gold standard in TBS gaming. Seriously. The only downside worth mentioning is lackluster performance.
GOOD:
- The sense of accomplishment when you successfully complete a mission. This is hugely important and this game delivers.
- The graphics are really nice. I thought they were good in Enemy Unknown, but this game is a joy to look at.
- Replayability. Increase the difficulty, go Ironman, do it again. Sure, every game is "replayable", but the maps are semi-random, meaning you'll have the same "mission" the second time around, except on an entirely different map, which makes it a new experience. Plus, you can level up your soldiers differently, try different strategic or squad composition tactics. It's almost endless.
- Moddability. There are already some must-have mods, like "don't waste my time" which shaves off a second here, 3 seconds there on the awkward and completely wasteful delays the game introduces for no reason at all. And then there are awesome mods like "The Long War 2" which does basically the same thing as "The Long War" did for Enemy Unknown, and so on.
BAD: there isn't anything downright bad about this game, but there are some "meh" items...
- Sound: While the overall dialog and combat sounds are downright fine, the soldiers' voices are a bit "meh" in that you can either choose to have soldiers' voice match their country of origin, but only SOME countries of origin. If your soldier is Polish, don't expect him to speak Polish. If he's Mexican, he'll speak Spanish with a SPANISH accent, which is downright annoying if you know the language. IMO this has been a mistake. The soldiers' speech should match your game language (how do they communicate if they have no language in common?) but with an ACCENT from their country of origin. Now of course there would be mods for this, except it would take a fairly extensive community effort.
- Pacing: the game includes some strange pauses, the most annoying one being the roughly 10-15 seconds staring at the monitor on your drone AFTER it's done hacking into something. We got in or we didn't. We saw it happening. It's over. Get on with it dammit! Of course as mentioned earlier there are mods for this, sadly it appears not every delay is moddable, and most of this insanely long and useless pause in the action is not.
- Cursor sensitivity: sometimes you aim at a tile to move to or to shoot at, and in clicking, if your mouse were to move by even a single pixel, the tile next to it will be selected. Introducing a dead zone between the tiles, even a very thin one, would prevent this. Also, sometimes you think you are sending a soldier to the roof in the foreground, but nope, he's actually going in the middle of the street in the background. It should be more obvious where he's headed. You do get used to it, but it should be obvious enough that you don't need to.
- Performance : This is the single most negative aspect of this game. Load times are crazy long, and the game chugs on a fairly good rig (i7 @ 4.4ghz, 24gb RAM, 2xGTX 970 in SLI, game loaded on an SSHD). I could put it on an SSD but the game is humongous. I suspect there is zero compression in the game files.
FINAL SCORE TALLY:

INTRUSION 2 is a 2D run n' gun action platformer along the lines of Metal Slug or more vaguely Contra. This is one badass, fun game, with epic, memorable bosses and creative elements like some pretty basic physics and destruction. You can destroy log bridges to send everyone falling to their doom, blow up the supports of watchtowers. Crush enemies under boulders you push over. Physics like that, which add to the fun. The enemies can take a beating and the weapons feel good, but even if there is a variety of weapons, not many feel different from one another. The levels seem like a marathon. They are so long you might find yourself wondering when they end. This is probably good.
Earlier I mentioned epic bosses. I don't use that term lightly. It makes me feel weird, but let me tell you about the first boss, a helicopter or hovercraft with arms with multiple phases. If its not shooting at you, its dropping soldiers out. If its not trying to hand pound you into the ground, its literally crawling after you. Its insane and awesome. It is very memorable and covers a lot of ground.
To keep things fresh, you can pilot mech suits... if not grab the gun off of a destroyed mech and use it on your enemies. Oh and if that's too normal for you, in the first level, you can ride a giant Arctic wolf. Its pretty nice.
The game is challenging, you do have a health bar, and ammo depletes, and you can die more from the controls than you do anything else, BUT the game is very forgiving, with plenty of checkpoints.
The controls take a bit of getting use to. You have your standard jump, duck and weapon switch keys, but then to aim you use your mouse. This allows for more precise aim, but I'm more used to the Contra controls of having 8 direction shooting instead of precision. If you're used to Teraria, you'll be used to this. There is floaty jumping that can take some getting used to and the physics seem really light and springy. The boxes will bounce around if lightly nudged. Some of the animation is springy like old cartoon characters. That is probably Flash animation for you.
It took a while to get over it, but when I did, I found this game to be really fun to play. There are crazy Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥moments, and moments where the physics can have some unique experiences for a 2D run n gun game, such as seeing a mech jump onto a floating box. The box bounced the mech up and kinda floated away just enough for a giant fish to eat the mech. That wasn't supposed to happen, but it did, and it was cool.
Well worth $10.

The combat very similar to Zesteria and feels right at home if you played that.  Graphics has not improved at all from Zesteria but both games were made during last generation of consoles in mind, so dont' expect much in the graphic department.  The game outdoors and towns look very vibrant and sharp. However, dungeon are very grey and uninspiring.
Storywise, I like it a lot more and prefer the darker tone the protagonist exult.  Its a bit more engaging and this time around your not going up against some form of demonic ultimate baddy about to take over the universe but more like human villian with magic.  I prefer that type of villian better.  All the cast are introduced faily early, I would stay within 5 hours of game time.  Things get rolling very quick , roughly within the first hour.  The English voices are very good just like Zesteria.  I believe the main protaganist is voiced by the person that did lighting in FFXIII, if I'm not mistaken from the voice.
When it comes to music, tale games doesn't have many catchy or memorable tunes when I compare to FF or other series.

Overall i'm having fun with the game and this time around I can tell Namco put more effort into the port.  Looking forward to their next generation tale game.

30 hours in, early access review.
Thumbs down because it's in Early Access, it needs a lot of balancing, and some of the current implementation seems baked in that I don't like. However...
The game gives good process, in a Civilization-like manner. You have a couple desks, you release a game, make money, buy more desks, add more rooms, sell more copies, buy a bigger place etc etc etc. This part is very addictive since there really is a ton of stuff (9 different desks, 20-some different rooms, 100+ game subjects etc) to build and set up. However...
Balance: Easy is a walk in the park, while Normal suddenly becomes practically impossible to make money, unless you just concentrate on making game engines and doing contract work. I can't imagine this being what the develoers had in mind. You can release a game that gets good reviews, and release a game with the same staff and setup 6 months later and get Worst Game Of The Year award.
Design decisions: You start in a garage with not much space, but enough for a small dev space, research center, toilet, and perhaps a marketing office. All this needs to be outfitted a la The Sims. Desks over there, plants over here, lighting, heating, ceiling fans, first aid kid, and on and on. Quite fun in fact. But then you make enough money to move to a bigger place. The game sells all your stuff and plops you down in an empty room where you have to do the whole thing over again. This is less fun. And there are TWELVE different building sizes, and each time you have to put the rooms, desks, plants, lights... This appears baked into the design. It would be so much better to add onto existing space, so you could have fun designing the more exotic rooms you didn't have access to before, because you didn't have the space.
There are other balance issues, like getting access to console research when you barely have enough money to buy toilet paper, the bank's suicidal-like willingness to continue to loan you ever increasing amounts of money, despite never having made a successful game (Normal difficulty), but this is EA, so we'll see.

Sizlere hepimizin en azından adını bildiği efsane bir oyunun incelemesini yapacağım.
Bir dönemin internet cafelerini zengin etmiş, öğrencilerini sınıfta bırakmıştır bu oyun. Ailelerine çocuklarını fellik fellik aratmıştır. Şakası bir yana ciddi anlamda başlayalım.
Half Life, bir gizli araştırma üssünde meydana gelen bir kaza sonucu ortaya çıkanları anlatan, bunları kahramanı Gordon Freeman’ın gözünden anlatan 1998 yapımı bir FPS oyunudur. Kısaca bahsetmek gerekirse, spoiler vermemeye çalışarak, araştırma üssüne bir taş benzeri bir madde ulaşmıştır, maddenin uzaydan geldiği varsayılmaktadır ve M.I.T’den mezun olan Gordon Freeman’ın ekibi olan olağandışı maddeler ekibine üzerinde deney yapılması adına verilmiştir. Ardından yapılan deneyde bir aksaklık olur ve macera başlar. Bundan sonrasını anlatacağım merak edenler için. Altta bir link verip oraya yazmayı planlıyorum. Oyunun altında oldukça ve oldukça sağlam bir hikaye var.
Biraz da oyunun tarihinden bahsedelim. Valve’in çıkış oyunudur Half-Life. Gabe Newell ve bir kaç arkadaşı eski Microsoft çalışanıdır. Windows 95 ve 98’de çok büyük katkıları olduğu söylenir Gabe’in. Microsoft ekibinden daha önce ayrılan bir ekip id software’i kurmuştur. Çıkarttıkları oyunlar ile iyi bir başarıya imza atmıştır. Bunu gören Gabe, id Software’dan olan arkadaşları ile iletişime geçer ve Microsoft’dan ayrılır. Ardından Quake’in oyun motorunu düzenleyerek ilk Half Life’ı yaparlar. GoldSrc adlı oyun motoru ile Half Life sunulur. Half Life FPS tarihindeki ilk hikayeli oyun olma tahtına da sahiptir. Ondan önceki oyunlar sadece vur ve ilerle mantığında idi. Valve, Half Life ile yepyeni bir FPS devri başlatmış ve çok çok büyük bir başarıya imza atmıştır. Ardından kendi source motorları ile tekrar ele almışlardır.(1.6 sürümü source ile yapılmıştır.)
Oyunun havası oldukça kasvetli. Her an her yerden saldırabilecek düşmanlar, her tarafta onun dışındaki cesetler, çok az canlı insan, havalandırmalarda geçen yollar,kısıtlı cephane.. Oyun atmosfer olarak size o an oradaki insanın psikolojisi nasıl olursa aynen onu yaşatmakta. Karakter Gordon Freeman ise soğukkanlı ve kolayca bağ kurulabilecek bir karakter. Kısacası oyunu oynamaya başladığınızda kendinizi oyunun içerisinde hissedeceksiniz.
Single Player’dan sonra efsanevi multiplayer’ına geçersek, Multiplayer’ı da Single Player’ı kadar efsanedir. Oynanabilirliğin çok yüksek olması ve kısa sürede adapte olabilmek oyunu daha da çok oynanabilir yapmıştır. Hala daha oynayanı vardır.Çünkü onun deneyimini ne battlefield’dan ne call of duty’den yada başka bir fps’den alabilirsiniz. Bambaşkadır.
Oyun kısmından çıkarsak, Valve geliştirdiği bu motorun üzerine bir çok oyun daha oluşturmuştur. Şüphesiz bunların en meşhuru Counter Strike’dır. Ardından Ricochet, Team Fortress, Deathmatch Classic gibi oyunlarını da eklemiştir. Bir kaçını yeni versiyonları ile günümüzde görmekteyiz.
Half Life’ın başarısının hemen ardından Valve, Orada olanları farklı gözlerden anlatan Half Life Opposing Force, Half Life Blue Shift, Half Life Decay oyunlarını da çıkartmıştır.
Daha önce oynamadım, oynamak istiyorum diyenlere şiddetle tavsiyemdir. Daha iyisini bulmanız pek mümkün değil.

Realm of the Mad God may not be a game for everyone, but in my opinion, it isn't how people say it is. Back a couple of years ago, Realm of the Mad God was owned by a company called WildShadow. Everybody was fine with WildShadow and the game was going well. But at one point a company called Kabam offered to buy the rights for the game from WildShadow and WildShadow accepted it. Everybody now thinks that Realm of the Mad God got worse. Indeed it get worse in some ways but it is still a great game.
I've started playing Realm of The Mad God a couple years ago (my main account is on Kongregate) and Kabam has changed the game in bad ways but also in good ways. Kabam did two main things that the community hates.
1. They made UT items (most UTs are really overpowered top) untradable and soulbound.
2. They want money and like to shoved buyable items in your face like a clown and a pie.
Now I personally hate that UT items are soulbound because it ruined the trading aspect of the game. But I guess Kabam intended them to be harder to obtain so then everybody wouldn't have a bunch of great items they could profit off of trading.
Kabam does care about their money and want people to buy their special item packs and mystery boxes, but plenty of free-to-play games do the exact same. For example Trove has a whole store page in game with all their special costumes and mounts and stuff. People don't complain because the game isn't pay-to-win even with the micro(not always so micro)transactions. Realm of the God isn't pay-to-win and it has microtransactions. So why do people care so much?
Anyways, Kabam has been doing a good job on the game updates. Many cool dungeons have been added into the game and new special sets. Pets were also a great feature. I don't know why there is so much hate on Kabam, but an opinion just an opinion.
Another thing people don't like about Realm of the Mad God is the community and spam bots. Kabam recently had an update to help silence spam bots by having chat restrictions by star. The community however people still don't like. Everybody says the community is a bunch of money paying 10 year olds. I find this false because one; how would you know if there is no ingame voice chat and two; I have barely noticed any changes in the community!
Overall Realm of the Mad God is a great game. Before and after Kabam bought the rights to it. Maybe this game would have been better if Kabam never bought it, I don't know. Realm of the Mad God still has the familiar feel to it that will always stay the same. If not, then I quit. So far I think Kabam has done a good job despite the bad changes they made.

What is RC Mini Racers?
Genre: Racing game
Setting: RC car racing in a suburban nieghborhood
Difficulty: 3/10 --> basically easy
Length: 2 hours for a single playthrough, up to 6 for completing every track in every difficulty
Mode: singleplayer campaign
The positive aspects:
- RC racing cars resembling real cars in a funny way
- runs perfectly and smoothly, constantly high framerate
- basically no loading times
The negative aspects:
- no car tuning (=cars' stats are all the same), only cosmetical changes which cost a fortune
- only a few circuits, always in the same nighborhood, only marked out differently
- repititive gameplay, lack of content
- two totally imbalanced currencies. In order to unlock all tracks and cars grinding is inevitable
- only three power-ups (rocket, mine, turbo boost)
Result (and summary for those who have no time reading):
RC Mini Racers is good for an hour or two, after that the lack of car stats and/or tuning and also tracks makes the game boring. Not recommended - there are better games out there.

A neat little Unity racing game that I feel doesn't quite have enough content to support its $4.99 price tag.
The game itself is completely functional and plays well, however the issue I had is that I just wasn't satisfied with the amount of content for the price I had paid. Yes, I know. Five bucks really isn't that much money, but considering all the other 'neat little Unity racing games' on Steam within the same price range, RC Mini Racers is pretty disappointing by comparison.
There is quite a number of levels, however they all take place within the same map, utilizing the same assets, which eventually (and relatively quickly) become visually fatiguing. This could have been excusable if the surprisingly large and diverse lineup of vehicles had more varied handling. There's not much point to saving your coins to unlock a flashy new car when it doesn't handle that much differently than the bulky pickup truck you're initially given at the start of the game.
Unfortunately, these two major flaws really affected my incentive to play the game, and after an hour and a half of game play time, I felt like I'd already seen all the game had to offer. In summary, the game is functionally good, but definitely lacking in content. In my opinion, $0.99c would be a much more palatable price!

Simple, short, fun.
It's not the "game changer" that Puzzle Quest 1 was, but Rollers of the Realm is a fun pinball game that benefits from dabbling with RPG elements. You have a party of pinballs that handle differently and have different abilities. There's some interesting mechanics in there, like archers who will break your flippers and make it harder to play, and the Healer, who can repair them by gaining mana.
The rest of the RPG elements are pretty meh. You can buy items, but most are just stat boosts that you won't notice. Story is pretty boilerplate, I don't even think most of the characters even have names, just their class descriptions. But it is fun. If you find it on sale and don't go in expecting Witcher 3 meets Midway's Addams Family Pinball, you'll enjoy it.

Opening with you sitting at a decrepit wooden table in a dreary and minimalistic cabin, not much is to be expect in terms of overall gaming experience. But it is in that simplicity that lies the beauty of this game, your heart pounding thrill is etched in the games minimalism. Being confined to a small cabin secluded from civilization you are tasked with remembering the identity of your dearly beloved wife who has fled from your memory. By looking at and examining objects in the cabin you once lived in and loved in together you unravel the mystery as to the whereabouts of your love. With twists and turns at every memory you slowly begin to piece together the location of your beloved
The game keeps you on the edge of your seat in a suspensionful anexity as the dark secrets of your life unfold. The game is able to provide an atmosphere of forboding with simple story progression, not relying on cheap jump scares or monsters in the closet for kicks. With twists and turns at every memory you slowly begin to piece together the location of your beloved. With a stimulating and intriguing story "Serena" is a must for all gamers.

Camera Obscura (“Dark Chamber” in Latin) is a 2D platformer that pays homage to old school 2D platformers but also tries to innovate with a pretty interesting gameplay mechanic. The game’s story revolves around the quest of photographer to climb the ruins of a tower. And the innovation comes in the manipulation of the levels themselves in a similar manner to Fez. But the afterimage effect is more than just a gimmick and it works very well with the storyline. It is not an easy game and you will be restarting levels often enough. The soundtrack is surprisingly good for a platformer and the introduction of Achievements and Trading Cards make Camera Obscura, a nice addition to any collection.
+ Clever gameplay mechanics.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.

I'm cautiously giving this a recommend vs. a not recommend solely because it's cheap and an interesting gameplay gimmick. Mostly I want to get some caveats out there for the penny-pinchers of you who might read this, though I don't think are enough negatives to outweigh the positives (yet).
The game runs SOMETIMES. I've had to delete the local content after trying to download custom levels, because even when I uninstalled, reinstalled, and restarted, it fails to recognize any custom levels even when the game loads. Mostly I get a message that the game is running... then it synchs, then it's as though I didn't load the game at all. Luckily, all progress is (or can be) saved to cloud storage.
When the game DOES work, it's rough, but for the most part an interesting challenge; besides the basic "get to the exit" goal, there are speed and "fewest number of flashes" medals awarded per level, plus bonus mementos to find.
The biggest problem is the flashes, though. I normally get motion-sick when playing 3-D games, so it surprised me that I started to feel nauseated after playing a basic 2-D platformer for about an hour. I can only figure it's from using the camera flash so often, so if that kind of thing bothers you, try to go easy on it.

I have noticed that all of the problems have been corrected and I give a big thanks to the people who worked hard to get the errors fixed! Tales of Berseria has definatly become one of my favorite games in the series and now there is only one thing I would ask Bandi Namco to do which is to bring the other Tales games to steam I would especially like to see some updated versions of the older games if at all possible.

TL;DR: The new gold standard in TBS gaming. Seriously. The only downside worth mentioning is lackluster performance.
GOOD:
- The sense of accomplishment when you successfully complete a mission. This is hugely important and this game delivers.
- The graphics are really nice. I thought they were good in Enemy Unknown, but this game is a joy to look at.
- Replayability. Increase the difficulty, go Ironman, do it again. Sure, every game is "replayable", but the maps are semi-random, meaning you'll have the same "mission" the second time around, except on an entirely different map, which makes it a new experience. Plus, you can level up your soldiers differently, try different strategic or squad composition tactics. It's almost endless.
- Moddability. There are already some must-have mods, like "don't waste my time" which shaves off a second here, 3 seconds there on the awkward and completely wasteful delays the game introduces for no reason at all. And then there are awesome mods like "The Long War 2" which does basically the same thing as "The Long War" did for Enemy Unknown, and so on.
BAD: there isn't anything downright bad about this game, but there are some "meh" items...
- Sound: While the overall dialog and combat sounds are downright fine, the soldiers' voices are a bit "meh" in that you can either choose to have soldiers' voice match their country of origin, but only SOME countries of origin. If your soldier is Polish, don't expect him to speak Polish. If he's Mexican, he'll speak Spanish with a SPANISH accent, which is downright annoying if you know the language. IMO this has been a mistake. The soldiers' speech should match your game language (how do they communicate if they have no language in common?) but with an ACCENT from their country of origin. Now of course there would be mods for this, except it would take a fairly extensive community effort.
- Pacing: the game includes some strange pauses, the most annoying one being the roughly 10-15 seconds staring at the monitor on your drone AFTER it's done hacking into something. We got in or we didn't. We saw it happening. It's over. Get on with it dammit! Of course as mentioned earlier there are mods for this, sadly it appears not every delay is moddable, and most of this insanely long and useless pause in the action is not.
- Cursor sensitivity: sometimes you aim at a tile to move to or to shoot at, and in clicking, if your mouse were to move by even a single pixel, the tile next to it will be selected. Introducing a dead zone between the tiles, even a very thin one, would prevent this. Also, sometimes you think you are sending a soldier to the roof in the foreground, but nope, he's actually going in the middle of the street in the background. It should be more obvious where he's headed. You do get used to it, but it should be obvious enough that you don't need to.
- Performance : This is the single most negative aspect of this game. Load times are crazy long, and the game chugs on a fairly good rig (i7 @ 4.4ghz, 24gb RAM, 2xGTX 970 in SLI, game loaded on an SSHD). I could put it on an SSD but the game is humongous. I suspect there is zero compression in the game files.
FINAL SCORE TALLY:
-1 point for performance and loading times
-0.5 point for the aforementioned pacing issues
So this is an 8.5/10 from me, and I am really picky. Others would give it a 12/10, but I like my reviews brutally honest. And honestly brutal. So while I hesitate saying that this game is worth its full price - what game is worth this much money, really? I think even at 20% off you are not going to regret your purchase.

Realm of the Mad God may not be a game for everyone, but in my opinion, it isn't how people say it is. Back a couple of years ago, Realm of the Mad God was owned by a company called WildShadow. Everybody was fine with WildShadow and the game was going well. But at one point a company called Kabam offered to buy the rights for the game from WildShadow and WildShadow accepted it. Everybody now thinks that Realm of the Mad God got worse. Indeed it get worse in some ways but it is still a great game.
I've started playing Realm of The Mad God a couple years ago (my main account is on Kongregate) and Kabam has changed the game in bad ways but also in good ways. Kabam did two main things that the community hates.
1. They made UT items (most UTs are really overpowered top) untradable and soulbound.
2. They want money and like to shoved buyable items in your face like a clown and a pie.
Now I personally hate that UT items are soulbound because it ruined the trading aspect of the game. But I guess Kabam intended them to be harder to obtain so then everybody wouldn't have a bunch of great items they could profit off of trading.
Kabam does care about their money and want people to buy their special item packs and mystery boxes, but plenty of free-to-play games do the exact same. For example Trove has a whole store page in game with all their special costumes and mounts and stuff. People don't complain because the game isn't pay-to-win even with the micro(not always so micro)transactions. Realm of the God isn't pay-to-win and it has microtransactions. So why do people care so much?
Anyways, Kabam has been doing a good job on the game updates. Many cool dungeons have been added into the game and new special sets. Pets were also a great feature. I don't know why there is so much hate on Kabam, but an opinion just an opinion.
Another thing people don't like about Realm of the Mad God is the community and spam bots. Kabam recently had an update to help silence spam bots by having chat restrictions by star. The community however people still don't like. Everybody says the community is a bunch of money paying 10 year olds. I find this false because one; how would you know if there is no ingame voice chat and two; I have barely noticed any changes in the community!
Overall Realm of the Mad God is a great game. Before and after Kabam bought the rights to it. Maybe this game would have been better if Kabam never bought it, I don't know. Realm of the Mad God still has the familiar feel to it that will always stay the same. If not, then I quit. So far I think Kabam has done a good job despite the bad changes they made.

RC Mini racers reminds me much of Revolt, but without the imagination.
The game involves racing toy RC cars around various tracks in either of 3 modes, Circuit Race, Sprint and Coin Race. Circuit is exactly that, Srint is A to B and Coin Race has you searching the map for randomly sporning coins. At the end od each race you win money that can be used to unlock other tracks or can be saved up to by coins.
Coins are used to unlock other RC Cars or mod them by changing the colour or wheels or the arial. Getting coins can be either fun or a grind depending on your point of view as it takes quite a while to aquire them.
The graphics are basic but suitable for this budget racer. The only fault I noticed was occasionally the wheels clipping through the floor. One other perculiarity I noticed is that the wheels are not actually attached to the vehicle. While this in no way spoils the game, it just look strange when the cars flip over.
Control is by either keyboard or game pad. Controls are not changable so your stuck with what is. I use the gamepad and steering, accerate and brake are all on the left thumbstick. Dual thumbsticks would have been much better, or at least the option of.
The gamepad only controls the cars though, not the menu. So mouse clicking is also a must.
The cars themselves sound and handle like toy electric rc cars from the local toyshop. So don't expect any Pro racing here. Weapons are also included, Missles, mines and a speed boost.
This game is a fun single player ( no multiplayer ) rc racer with weapons. Its a budget game but does what it does pretty well. As long as you don't expect to much from it its worth the asking price.

TL;DR Fallout 4 is a great shooter, but an awful Fallout game.
Fallout 4 is the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of the 3d Fallout games so far.  Fallout 3 was experimental, and worked pretty well despite being a little empty.  Fallout New Vegas improved on every aspect in 3, and forged itself a completely new identity as a true RPG.  Fallout 4...didnt do either of these.
Pros : Fallout 4 was fun, I'll admit.  I've sunk 500+ hours in the game, so I think I have some precedent to my opinion.  As a shooter it shines, and I'd daresay if this wasn't a "Fallout" game, people would be much more receptive to it.
Cons : As an RPG, it flops.  The skill system is difficult to keep track of, and the menu for it just feels bulky.  The dialogue is limited as hell, and the story itself just isn't engaging.  In my 500+ hours, I've never even entered the second act of the game.  It's also worth noting that a lot of the content for the building aspect of the game - one of it's big selling points - are locked behind DLC.
Truly, if you can pick Fallout 4 up for $20 do it, I don't think you'd regret it.  However don't go into this expecting New Vegas depth or the memorability of 3.

I must say I quite enjoyed the time spent with this game, working through the paradigms unusual or straight-up unheard of in the classic game of pinball. It is much like a careless stroll through the dungeons in an RPG games, but the party members are balls that confront quite human-looking enemies. They can die, be healed, use special abilities and even summon pets, all to prevent the enemy force from destroying your paddles so hard that you can no longer operate the table properly - which usually results in your balls meeting their end nearly instantly after being released.
If you thought that is abstract, wait for me to tell you that the balls swing actual weapons and one of them shoots a bow... on top of your starting one being able to pickpocket NPCs on the stage. Why would she do that? To buy equipment that strenghtens your spherical party, of course! For all the things that should be obvious, I found myself scratching my head quite often, wondering how did it happen that people didn't make a game like this earlier (at least to my knowledge).
The gameplay is as self explanatory as a modified pinball can get, and for the most part quite pleasant - the urgency of hitting specific objects is multiplied quite dramatically when they are capable of killing your paddles off, and  clearing all adversaries is the objective of majority of the levels. Not all, however - there is a fair bit of maze-like adventures that ask you to figure out how to juggle your balls well enough to traverse to the point marked as an exit, all while seeing treasures hidden in the corners and trying to get to them as well, for the sake of easier time in later, combat-focused stages. I would like to add here, that great many of 'combat stages' actually has additional quirks to them, so it is nowhere near as dull as one would expect from the very generalized name I assigned them.
While I would like to say that the tables were consistently good across the entire game, that isn't the case, sadly. As the story progresses, the player is thrown into increasingly more crowded
smaller stages, where a single mistake can make them lose the ball in nearly an instant, while the onslaught that whittles away paddles' healthbars continues. This is really problematic because there is only one ball good at healing, and losing it places you in a serious trouble. While there is a secondary method of healing, it uses the same precious mana that is required for reviving the balls. I am aware that this is largely the issue with the balance of the game, but when combined with merciless table design, it turns the last few levels into a complete nigthmare for anybody not crazily skilled at pinballs (like me).
There is a story to the game, and presented quite nicely - while I can't say the plot was particularly memorable (nor was the music) it kept the warm, familiar vibe of a fairytale, with well-chose voice actors for the entirety of the cast. No line felt like it was forced, as cheesy as it might've been. Really good job there, especially the Girl and the Knight.
After the campaign is concluded, you are free to explore the arenas which prove additional challenges, usually about clearing already discovered maps off enemies, with their own sets of additional objectives. It is a simple device for a replayable experience. Doesn't hurt, but wasn't all that interesting for me.
Overall: worth a play, will take at least a few hours of your time. If you want a high count of hours per-Euro, consider waiting for a sale. The 8h I have on the counter include replaying the final levels a fair amount of times.

Rollers of the Realm is a delightful little game that combines pinball machines with an RPG: the balls represent your characters, each with their own set of abilities and strenghts. Learning when to switch between characters is the key element to success in this game, not just pinball wizardy on it's own.
It's not a very long game, but after the campaign there are a number of arenas where you either compete against the clock, or try to score as high as you can until your lives run out. These offer a different kind of challenge to the main game.
The boss battles especially are very clever, and while it does feel and handle like a pinball simulator, the tables are clearly fantasy rpg maps, and the bosses require some careful strokes, sometimes with the right character, to be taken down.
Fun game for anyone who enjoys pinball, and the story isn't half bad either.

Bastion is beautiful in every way.  It feels more like a work of art then anything else Iv'e played before.
The gameplay is pretty simple and straight forward, venture into different areas to find shards that will help repair "The Bastion."  While doing this you destroy varying types of enemies with weapons you find along the way, wether it be a giant hammer, a katana, a rifle, or the many other weapons that you find.  Every shard that you find allows you to upgrade the bastion in some way that unlocks other aspects of the game.
Sounds pretty straightforward but what makes Bastion great is it's approach to this style of gameplay.  The beautiful hand painted environments spring up around you as you venture through the lands, while a narrator reacts to your every move.  Supplement this with a wonderful bluesy-folk soundtrack, and you have a game that is really appealing to your emotions.
I would recommend that anyone pick this game up given the chance.

A part of me really doesn't want to recommend it, but that's just the rage talking.
A short, sweet, puzzle adventure game with great art direction and humor. The main storyline puzzles are fairly simple to figure out, while the side-mission 'trading card' puzzles will probably require you actually sit there and think a bit. Then there's the Master Cave that will likely require most people to devote a rather hefty amount of time to get through those 12 puzzles, as they tend to push the limitations of your items as far as possible.
But where the puzzles shine, the combat falls completely flat. Your attacks lack any sort of knock back so unless you are backpedaling they will simply walk over you, which is exacerbated by the fact that your sword lacks any reach or arc to its swing, meaning that you will likely be trading hearts with your foes until you perfect the distance. But this isn't a huge flaw as enemies aren't a huge threat and even boss fights are usually more based around item gimmicks than fighting. Usually...
The one, ONE, huge glaring flaw in the game is that the Master Cave I mentioned before, the optional end game with the 12 most difficult, mindbreaking, walkthrough inducing, puzzles in the game... ends in a boss that is nothing more than a button mashing lesson in rage and futility. Your items do nothing. The skills and techniques you've worked on through 4+ hours of gameplay are useless. You are stuck using only the shoddy sword combat mechanics, and praying to every deity under the sun that it will bug out and stop attacking so you can kill it sometime this millenia. A massive black spot on an otherwise great puzzle game. I solved every puzzle, collected every card, but due to stupidly dodgy combat mechanics, a lack of luck, and a lack of perfect precision manual dexterity on my part, I couldn't beat it after a full hour of trying. I've no desire to ever try again, and likely will never play this game again because of that stupid boss. Why devs why... why would you do that...

I want to start out by saying that if you're a huge fan of the Tales series, you might still love this game. The characters are surprisingly well written, the story is much more complex and interesting than any of the Tales games I've played since Abyss, Destiny, and Vesperia, which are my three personal favorites. The game has a lot of funny interactions and the comic relief characters are archetypes, but still provide some fun. When I started this game I fully expected to really enjoy it based on my past experiences where I got through the boring stories because of the amazing Tales combat system that we've all grown to love.
Unfortunately it's the exact opposite in Tales of Berseria. I loaded up the game and started on the hardest mode available and at first I was loving the combat. The new combo system is fantastic and being able to use unique chains to find weaknesses is a huge reason why the Tales series holds a special place in my heart. Unfortunately you are eventually given a special attack ability binded to your RT button (on Xbox1 controller) that makes your playable character use a unique skill or combo. Most of the character's special abilities make sense, are situational, and interesting to use. Some of them have unique drawbacks and have to be used in specific situations, which make them very fun to use. Unfortunately Velvet was given a skill that dwarfs all the others.
Velvet's special ability gives her a power boost that either starts a new combo or extends the combo you had going before you activated the special ability. It's the strongest ability in the game, it's AOE, it has no drawbacks other than using the resource that all special attacks use, it chain CC's all enemies, and usually you will do enough damage with it to kill an enemy and gain back the recource you used to start the combo. It's absolutely gamebreaking and makes every normal battle quick and easy.
Unforunately the game is balanced around this broken mechanic being in the game so most enemies are meat shields who constantly guard and take shots like 50 cent unless you're using Velvet to one shot kill them in a combo from hell. Velvet can single handedly win normal fights in 10 seconds, and solo bosses by waiting until you have max "souls" and then chain comboing until the boss is dead. It completely ruins the fun of the entire game as the game is tedious and annoying if you're not using Velvet, but easy and insanely boring if you do.
It's unfortunate that this is the case because the game is otherwise very interesting, but I mostly play Tales for the amazing combat system and by butchering the difficulty and putting a combat breaking skill in the game it has completely ruined the game for me. I don't understand why the last two Tales games have included this type of mechanic and it will make me vary wary of purchasing any future Tales games.
UPDATE: I've played a quite a bit more and the game is only getting more reliant on spamming Velvet's special. I'm still playing on the hardest mode and they introduced "Code Red" fights where you fight a special boss that is a beefed up version of normal enemies. These fights would be an extreme challenge and would be fun. I've tried beating a few of these bosses without Velvet and have consistently failed time and time again, but I'm going to keep trying. Unfortunately I've loaded up a save and tried the fight with Velvet and spammed her special and was able to beat the boss without taking damage.
There are separate fights where you provoke two separate enemies on the map to attack you at once and it starts a more difficult version of regular fights with hoards of higher level versions of the regular enemies. Every single one of these can be beaten in about ~1 minute by spamming Velvet special. If you don't spam the Velvet special it is a frustrating experience where your characters die in one combo. This is another horrible experience where the game was balanced around Velvet being able to AOE slaughter the entire enemy hoard without any skill or ability at all. Here's a prime example of one of these fights.
Final Update:
I've gotten as far as I can stand with the combat system. I'm playing on insane mode now and I've killed every single Code Red enemy and boss to this point, minus one, by spamming Velvet's special move. It's gamebreaking, it's stronger than every other character combined, and still has no downsides or special nuances. Velvet is the only character you need to use and you only need to know how to parry, click R2, and mash an attack button to win every single fight in the game. The Tales crew obviously spent a lot of care balancing the other characters in the game, but when it came to Velvet they decided she should have no weaknesses and give her the ability to solo kill every single enemy and boss in the game and then balanced the game around her being that strong so if you don't use her it's just a pain.
Again, if you like Tales games or button mashers you might still enjoy Tales, but I would definitely recommend waiting until the game goes on sale.

This game could have been good with better/more development. There's a twist at the very end (after the initial, unbearably obvious "twist" that you can see coming just by reading the game's description.) but it's so abrupt it just feels random. It feels as if the developers did a quick play through after finishing the game and realized it was terrible, so they just tacked an additional ending and hoped no one would notice.
Character development was really just boring, You play a stereotypical pretentious writer, the type of person that would fill a bookshelf with books that "are just life-altering" in order to look smart, but has never actually read any of them. He's hung up on a blonde chick who wears perfume and combs her hair. The voice acting for both of them is robotic at best, and only highlights how bland the characters are.
As irritating as the primary mechanic is (clicking on everything over and over until the protagonist realizes something, clicking on the same things over again, doing it again, doing it again, doing it again, doing it again,....), I can see it actually being workable if it was just done better. However, none of the things that could have salvaged it, such as interesting story/characters/dialogue, are present in any way.
I really, really wanted to like this game, I really wanted to shrug my shoulders at it's short-comings and say "it's just artsy", but it's not. It's not "A (twisted) love letter to the adventure game community", there's no "Extremely depressive mood, and a bit of fear here and there", and there definitely isn't "A haunting story that will challenge your intellect (and temerity)" or "Amazing voice acting". It isn't any of that.
It's just bad.
NOTE: I literally spent more time writing this review than playing the game. in the 1.3 hours I played the game I beat it twice, despite being unnecessarily thorough.

At first glance, Bastion may seem like a delightful game based on the vibrant colours and the beautiful art used for this game, but it is far beyond that. Despite its colourful persona, Bastion takes place in a gray world where Caelondia once stood tall an proud before being brought to its knees by the Calamity and all that is left is melancholy, loneliness and nostalgia. Followed with deep narrative and good bluish music, the story delivers and all the scenes are expressed well, especially the somber moments. And to verify that this is a game, the gameplay is well with its varities of weapons and upgrades to choose from in order to approach the game and the enemies. My only problem with the game is how when the player uses ranged weapons, you have to aim under the enemy just to hit it. Other than this problem, Bastion is still heavily recommended for players looking for good story and fun.

This is such a great game.  Yahtzee's YouTube series "Zero Punctuation" has always been super entertaining but now he has brought us an equally-random experience that is now only interactive but endlessly unique every time around.  If you are a fan of his show, you will enjoy this game, definitely!
You get gifts for collecting enough hats, and most of the hats offer a unique twist on the gameplay.  Some were more pointless than others but the whole game experience is affected in at least some way by each present.
The gameplay is quite simple.  There is a hat falling and you have to stand under it.  With each hat you get, it gets harder and harder, with multiple objects falling at once (and you have to guess which is the hat and which is something less enjoyable like an anvil) and you advance if you guess correctly.  It can get very difficult when there are clones of yourself and you have to figure out which person you are controlling -- all in a matter of a few seconds.  If you are really bad, you will still gain presents as it retains however many points achieved.  High score is also tracked, but I love it how you will still get hats towards the ultimate prize even if you can only last through the first few stages.  I'm not entirely sure what the gift is if you get 1500 hats.  I guess I'll have to keep playing to find out!
Overall, a great game, worth a buy.  It's not much more than that -- a minigames and funny commentary -- so if you are expecting something more than that maybe wait for a sale.  But for Zero Punctuation fans, it's a buy.

Rollers of the Realm is the most unique game I've played in years. The concept is what originally caught my attention. A combination of pinball and RPG elements, how is that going to work? Well, it probably shouldn't, but in this case it does.
The quirky pinball characters are unique and even funny. There's great replayability here, too, as you'll need to decide which character, or ball, is best suited to a task, considering width, height, weight, and special abilities, like healing, increased damage, or special attacks.The graphics are beautiful, and the controls are responsive. There is a challenge to some of these areas and puzzles, too, so experienced pinball players and puzzle enthusiasts should find plenty to appreciate here.
It's evident that a lot of time and attention went into the detail for the characters, environment, clothing, speech, and story. The outcome is a very consistent experience that's easy to get into and enjoyable. Gamers of all ages should consider giving ROTR a try.
One thing that I want to point out is that there is an interruption in flow as new goals are met or characters are introduced for the first time, and that can seem awkward at first. However, that interruption is part of the story and RPG aspect of the game, so it's definitely necessary, and it's easy to get used to. Afterward, the pinball gameplay is uninterrupted, and players can revisit areas to obtain loot or treasure they might have missed, without repeating the story. This is certainly not a negative, but it is something I noticed that others are very likely to experience. It was awkward for me at first, and I wondered if I was going to be able to enjoy the pinballing aspect of the game. I hung with it, though, and soon that wasn't even a consideration.
I'm fascinated by this game, and I applaud the developers for taking such a bold risk by pairing these gaming elements into one cohesive experience. I intend to play this game again, and I hope to see more.

Man, this one was certainly a pleasant surpise. I expected something at least decent but what I got was a great and clever puzzle game with high replayability and amusing dialogue/parody.
The core puzzle gameplay is based around sliding block puzzles, yes, but with interesting mechanics I've not seen done before, especially not all together in the way this game does. Every puzzle feels unique and fresh, and they range from the simple to the mind-numbingly difficult (though I admit that I looked up solutions to a few in the master cave... the harder ones there are also kind of the weakest, lots of secret mechanic stuff you need to know :s )
On top of that, there are four different ways to complete the game. You can get all three items or any combination of the two, and the paths you can take through the castle are quite different for each 2-combination. I quite enjoyed working out the different ways to make it through to the end, it kept replays fresh and interesting. The achievement set is also pretty great; a few bonus dungeons, 100% collection, and an added challenge to one of the routes for beating the game without harming a few specific enemy types (only possible via one of the four routes, sadly, and there's a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥move possible right after the final boss if you don't set up the castle properly... but ehh!)
The writing is also amusing, toying with lots of RPG tropes (especially Zelda tropes, which is this game's closest comparison to begin with) but not going overboard. It's very self-aware but clearly the devs loved the kinds of games they're mocking.
The one weakness of the game is the combat, which is very bare-bones and kind of picky; weapon seems to be a bit shorter than it appears on your character, most notably. It's not a big enough flaw to really detract from the overall experience, though.
The main game will probably only run you 3-4 hours by itself, including all the extras, but replaying is worth it even if you're not achievement hunting since it does change the game quite a good bit. I think the price is fair, although I did admittedly get this game via Humble. But in the end I'm quite pleased with this silly little game, it's quite a good time.

Date: 2/7/16
Review Number: 11
Game: Rollers of the Realm
From (Creator Publisher): Phantom Compass
Played On: Laptop
Steam Price as of Review: $1.99 till 2/12
Total Time played: 30 minutes
Review:
Today’s randomized little misfit is the game Rollers of the Realm by Phantom Compass.  Now, given the title, brief half glimpses of screenshots and the icon (which is usually all I get with these games, by the way) I had assumed I would play an hour in a typical indie RPG game of some sort.  I was somewhat taken aback by the fact that this game is, indeed, and RPG, but instead of the typical RPG format, it is a digital pinball game.
Now let me give you a few facts first.  One: I am actually rather fond of pinball.  One of my side projects is a decent sized digital pinball machine, flipper buttons and plunger and all, which has gone through at least two full wood revisions.  Two: I am actually rather fond of most RPGs.  I am actually planning to buy a next gen console solely for being able to play Kingdom Hearts 3 (no shame) and if you look at my play history, the amount of time I have spent playing Tales of Maj’Eyal far outstrip most of the other games in my collection.
These things being said, I am rather disappointed to admit that I find this game to be, well just kind of blah.  The pinball physics are interesting at times, but mostly are reminiscent of the tiny half size table top pinball machines you see in little kids rooms.  The RPG elements add a bit of a twist, but really just serve to try and keep your attention by choosing a different ball at different times, whereas for the most part you can get away with completely avoiding using any of the rpg elements if you have a decent enough skill with the flippers.  In the end, neither side of the game are attractive enough to me to be worth putting a lot of time into.  I will admit that it at least kept my interest long enough that I didn’t feel I had to slog through the minimum 30 minutes, but beyond that, I just can’t recommend this.
Game’s Fate: I like pinball, but nope.  gone.  Its nice, but not worth the HD space right now
Buy/No Buy: If you like pinball, especially digital pinball, maybe.  especially while its on sale, but at the 10 bucks it usually goes for?  nah.
Personal note:  also, apologies for my shame.  Not even two weeks in and I missed a review day.  Though admittedly I missed it to go see Metallica in concert, so not too upset about it.

At the time of this review, I have clocked over 400 hours in Starbound. I write this as a person who not only plays Minecraft and Terraria, but as a person who loves open world games and hates when a game gets stale.

The development team also maintains a blog about what all they are working on, and when things become implemented in the Stable version. I love checking the blog because I know the team is constantly making new dungeons, improving NPC interactions, adding new biomes, items, or some other crazy crap. In the time that I've owned Starbound, there have been multitudes of changes, and frankly, they have ALL been for the better.
If you haven't tried it, I suggest you do. For the amount of work that is going on with Starbound, $14.99 as a regular price isn't bad. Looking at Minecraft which is $25, I'd give the Starbound team my money all over again.

Alright, as promised. . . a review on Silent Dreams Dead Age (V1.3):
Casual mode brought the fun back (at least for me) - because in all honesty, I'm a casual gamer (so are a lot of other people, whether they admit it or not, if you don't spend an a LOT of time strategizing on how to get the best experience out of all of your games then you're a casual gamer).
Casual mode tones down some of the intensity of grinding in combat, which surprised me, because the only things that seemed to change were the sizes of mobs, enemy health, and enemy damage output (which seemed like it had only been tweaked slightly) - but even though there were no huge changes to combat that I could distinguish, Silent Dreams somehow worked magic on their combat system in casual mode.
The combat is smoother, quicker, less of a grind (I say less because as you get further along in the game it ramps up difficulty, which it always has and (hopefully) always will do), and is actually really enjoyable.
Pros -
A game with interesting dialogue and stories behind each character
Choices that have lasting effects
Rogue-like permadeath for EVERY character
Crafting
Resource/Character Management
Devs who care about making sure their games are fantastic and their fanbase is happy
Cons -
Combat provides little XP
Missions/Story are all very linear (it would be nice to see that some missions instead of instantly killing someone if you fail, there's a 50/50 chance the story ACTUALLY changes a bit either giving you a chance to fix the problem, or forcing you to minimize the damage)
Autosave only allows you to save after a day is finished (I can understand why this might be necessary for hardcore mode, but casual mode could really use a manual save option)
I hope that Silent Dreams continues to treat their games and fanbase with respect and care, because it's just rare these days to find devs who continue to listen to their fans and make sure their products are high quality.
Previous Review from Nov 18 (Dead Age V1.2):
This game was fun, then patch 1.2 came along and made a reasonably difficult game into a deathtrap where completing even a single mission is a grueling and agonizing grind (even on easy mode with a whole occupation fully upgraded)!
If you're going to add "normal" enemies that can't be stunned AND can't be KO'd, at least make that a feature of Hardcore mode, so casual gamers actually have a chance to complete this game on easy mode (or at least one runthrough of it).
Making "normal" enemies tougher just made this game an even bigger grind than it already was - the game was already incredibly difficult (yet reasonable enough to actually make progress) before 1.2 came out, how do you expect anybody to actually finish missions now?! Let alone actually survive for longer than a week (if that)!
And don't even get me started on the daily autosave function, in 1.1 you could actually make progress, it just took anywhere from 15min - 1hr or so to complete a day.
So in that time if your power goes out, you have to leave, or forget about the autosave only waiting until the game decides you can have a break - you lose ALL of the progress you've made.
(Honestly the autosave was the only thing I didn't like about the game before 1.2, but now it's unplayable because the devs kind of forced (Pokemon style) "tactics" into the game when the mechanics already worked.
If Silent Dreams changes Dead Age's mechanics back to the way they worked in the last patch (at least for easy mode), and make a manual save optional, then I'll give Dead Age a better review - and I might even consider trying out one of their other games.

Sleeping Dogs is a welcomed addition to the list of games that I deem masters of their genre. Much like the sandbox games before it, Sleeping Dogs offers a lively world decorated with numerous quests from racing to chasing criminals, all tied together by a coherent plot. However, simply mastering these core concepts don't necessarily translate to a great game.
If there are two things unique about this title, it'd be its combat and narrative. Unlike the gunplay which many may be accustomed to from GTA or Saint's Row, Sleeping Dogs emphasizes melee combat consisting of counters, grapples, and light/heavy attacks.
The plot is intricate and engaging, even often times successful in instilling the sense of paranoia that pervades our hero's mind. Unfortunately, the story distances itself too much from the audience. When the protagonist must balance life as a cop and criminal, the final alliance should be an open choice. Alas, it is not.
Square Enix should've taken more risks.
Grade: B

Camera Obscura is a platformer with an interesting mechanic, but some glaring issues when you're going for 100% completion. If you're not, it's an ok game, but you'll need some patience anyway. It has alot of unfair and unnecessarily annoying sections, that have not much to do with difficulty and platforming skills but are just plain bad level design.
- horrible collision detection with enemies. The hitbox is a box with always the same size, even though some animation frames make enemies very small, filling only a tiny spot in that box (slime's fall animation, for example, for those how already know the game)
- the menu has some unskippable slow fades and transitions. That gets annoying when you go through there alot. Selecting a level is especially tedious, you have to wait through multiple transitions when selecting a level.
- ugly graphics. There are alot of games out there that prove that 2D pixel graphics can look great. This game is the opposite.
- no restart level button, you have to go through the menu to restart the level, which you will do ALOT.
- no on screen timer. When you try to beat specific level times for medals and achievements, you have no idea how you are doing, until you see the end screen.
- when you start a level (coming from the previous level or the level select menu), there is a fade-in time during which you can't see anything, but the level timer has started anyway. For beating the times, you regularly will want to immediately restart the stage to start without the fade-in.
- the story is presented in text snippets. Yes, simple text, nothing else. Not even an interesting or eye-pleasing font.
- several levels have long boring sections where you are just walking or even just waiting for a moving platform, for example. And you will have to repeat those sections alot, because afterwards there is no checkpoint and some difficult section follows. You'll die alot, and you'll wait through the boring section again and again in each retry.

I came into this game thinking I would be disappointed (because Zestiria was less than stellar for me). However, my experience of this game for the first few minutes proved me wrong, and the rest 10 hours did nothing to prove me right either. It was just so damn good. While Velvet won't replace Yuri Lowell in my heart, she's a step up from the likes of Sorey, Jude Mathis/ Milla Maxwell, and those from... graces *shivers*. I mean, where to start?
I suppose let's go with what separates Tales from other RPGs; their amazing skits. That's here! Still funny, and more animated than it has ever been! Every single one of them is interesting, fleshing out the characters and their relationship with each member in the party. They happen, not too far apart from each other, but they don't drown the game. Not only do you need to sleep in an inn to randomly activating one, you may do so by wearing a different costume, picking something up, or even just cooking! Because of these skits you always want to explore because going in somewhere simple like a corner of a dungeon might trigger one of them!
Next I suppose would be the characters. Velvet and her party mates are refreshing compared to the 'power of friendship rangers' that came before. Due to her unpleasant past, which you get to play too, she's willing to do unscrupulous things to get her way. The characters she meet in her path of vengeance feel essential to her growth, and interesting themselves. They're a band of misfits, condemned criminals consisting of demons, a witch, a pirate and a traitor. Because of that, unlike other games where you're either a prince, or basically a hero, not everyone is routing for you. In fact, because of Velvet's motives she's going against the world as succeeding with her goal means destroying the false peace the populace believe they're experiencing. Each character has a goal of their own, and a path to redemption unlike some who are just... err.... there.
Next, gameplay. This is an amazing pc port. Playing on the keyboard (not even using my mouse) feels so natural. Battle is fast paced, combos are easy to do but hard to master (exactly how I like it), and the artes are sights to behold. Never have I done Mystic Artes this much and not get tired of them! Better yet, dual mystic artes make a return and that's always a plus! Navigating the worldmap is easy too, as well as in the dungeons. Fighting enemies is still an option as you can out maneuver them or just plain escape in battle (tho some enemies are really fast in running in the world map and trying to outrun them results into a 'risky encounter'.
As for the plot, well I'll be honest, it's not that special. We've seen this before, it's a story of revenge and redemption, but I feel that ToBerseria told it in a special way. Sure there are cliches (at this point it's almost already a given a game would have them anyway) but I never really felt like the game was boring me with them because at the end of the day I still couldn't stop playing it!
I heard from other people that there are problems with the AI. I.... don't really see that. I mean, all I needed to do was go to 'strategy and tactics' and fix it, modify the different options to how I want each of my member to perform. Doing so, each of my party members did their job well! When I set my healer to 'defensive' i didn't worry about my health dropping to below fifty percent, furthermore they cured me of ailments as I needed. The characters I set to offense would properly beat down on my enemies as they're asked. Currently I'm at level 50 and I still have no complain about my companions' AIs.
The next problem I hear people have is that the map is small. If you're new to the tales games then I understand where you're coming from. However a veteran of the franchise would know that complaining about map size in a tales game is like complaining about the lack of happy and healthy civilians in a zombie game, it's just not about that. If you want to explore a large map, you have GTA, skyrim, Red Dead etc. This game certainly won't satisfy that itch.
Overall i think the game is great. I would recommend it. It's not for everyone, certainly, but old fans of tales and JRPG in general would find some fun in this. It's no abyss or vesperia but it's better for me compared to Zestiria, and Xillia; and certainly a lot better than Graces.

Hatfall is a great game. Combining both challenging and fun gameplay, Hatfall is sure to leave you on your toes.
To explain on this a bit, let's talk about the gameplay. You play as Yahtzee (famous from Zero Punctuation) who has lost his hat. Whilst this may not sound like something interesting, believe me it's quite fun. It combines a mechanic found often in mobile games, namely short and quick reaction gameplay. Your task is to get Yahtzee his nice looking hat back. Every 25 hats you get to choose between "gifts" indicated by the progress bar on the sections below the level. Said gifts, when unlocked, frequently permit a minigame to be unlocked: e.g. Unlocking Hatsassin's Creed causes you to be dropped of in a clear parody of a dating sim.
The game itself doesn't prefer to play nice on you. Instead it favors to downright insult the player. In-between level sections and a second before the level begins, you get a pop-up message. These message always involve doing something with a hat. If you succeed, you are greeted with another popup message, which always involves boosting Yahtzee's massive ego or make more fun about hats. But those things are insulting to the player who doesn't know what Zero Punctuation is: A webshow about reviewing Video Games on their negative points. Of course the game was going to be insulting.
Although I don't know what the 1500 hat collective does yet, it will probably involve Yahtzee laughing at me for wasting my time on this great addictive game.

so like there's like a game series called "The Legend of Zelda" that you might have heard of and this game is basically a parody of that, and it's also actually really good
After crashing their makeshift raft into an island (like a certain other game), hotblooded adventuress Ittle Dew and her potion-chugging sidekick Tippsie set out to rob the island's castle of an artifact, which they need to give to the local shopkeeper so that he'll carve them another raft to leave the island with. It's an entirely lighthearted affair filled with charming characters, whimsical creatures, and colorful sights to behold, and the writing, while a bit too self-aware at times, does a good job at poking fun at the conventions of a typical top-down adventure.
Gameplay, as should be clear by now, is like a condensed 2D Zelda. There's a small overworld to explore with caves to spelunk, three main dungeons, two bonus dungeons, and the island's castle, a sprawling, two-story locale which Ittle can only conquer in multiple trips, somewhat like the Tower of Spirits in Spirit Tracks. A variety of enemies roam the island, though it's usually not necessary to kill them because they can only drop hearts, and there are boss battles at the end of each dungeon, including one of the best bonus bosses ever conceived. Treasure comes in the form of Paper Scraps (Heart Pieces), Collectible Cards, and Lunch Money, which Ittle can use at the shop to buy the game's three weapons.
What is particularly interesting about the game is how it offers a lot of choices. The main dungeons can be completed in any order, and they as well as the castle have multiple paths to take through them, the shorter ones — "Professional Shortcuts" — being tougher to traverse. Astoundingly, the adventure can be finished with either all weapons or any combination of two of them, meaning there are four different ways to beat the game; the game even records players' best times for each combination!
Of course, a Zelda parody wouldn't be complete without puzzles. There are TONS of puzzles in this game, involving familiar concepts like block pushing, switches, mirrors and the like. The mandatory ones generally don't require too much thought, but the aforementioned Professional Shortcuts as well as the overworld caves contain puzzles that tended to take me a good five minutes to solve. One of the bonus dungeons, the Master Cave, is made of twelve incredibly difficult puzzles that really stretched the limits on how Ittle's weapons could interact with each other and the environment; some of them were so devious that I resorted to a guide and I was truly flabbergasted by their solutions. Suffice to say, the puzzles were the highlight of the game for me.
The only iffy part about the gameplay is the combat, specifically Ittle's basic attack. In most 2D Zelda titles, Link swings his sword in a wide arc, but Ittle only swings in a short line directly in front of her. There were several occasions where I would attack only to miss due to the small hitbox, which usually resulted in me taking damage. Thankfully, enemies aren't that tough to take down regardless, and dying only sends Ittle back to the start of the room.
If you haven't watched the trailer for the game on its store page yet, you should do so now because the graphical style of the game is delightful. In addition to being bright and vibrant, the game uses squiggly outlines for characters and moving objects; it reminds me a lot of Ed, Edd n Eddy, which is basically my favorite cartoon to this day. The music, while not as notable, is still pretty good and relaxing.
Overall, Ittle Dew provides a surprising amount of pure fun for its scale and price. I clocked in around six hours my first playthrough and I'm already considering going through the game again with one of the two-weapon routes. Highly recommended.
