Ittle Dew is a little game that stands somewhere between Zelda and Sokoban, with a very humorous tone, and featuring friendly game design, with aspects that can be appreciated by pretty much everyone.
From casual playthroughs, so rock-hard puzzles and 15 minutes speedruns... it's got it all! It's weird, but it's very nice to see how almost every aspect of this game seems to just fit it and provide a great experience, despite its apparent simplicity!
Undoubtedly, one of its strongest aspects, especially at first. The cartoon-y
is very well done, with a pleasant color scheme, very clean, with added lighting effects modernising its look, somewhat. The highlight here for me, though, is the character design. Everyone looks unique, is a clumsy and silly way, and with their own backstory to support them. It's pretty good!
Another detail I liked is how every line moves slightly, making everything seem more alive.
The
and
didn't standout out too much for me, but fit nicely with the rest of the presentation, and it wasn't bad by any means! Just didn't seem to carry the experience, for me.
I also found the
to be funny at times, and it just gave the game a very light-hearted and self-aware tone the whole way through. Ranging from the dialogues with your health-potion drunk companion, to the enemies' entrances and the mocking signposts spread around, everything had something to make fun of.
Very much like a Zelda game, actually. You have an island to explore, and go through several dungeons to beat it. There is also some exploration done outside the main and tutorial dungeons.
Near the beginning of the game, you'll find a shop. The shopkeeper tells you he can give you a raft to escape the island, if you get him the artifact in the castle. And off you go. He also has 3 items to sell. You'll find the gold for it in the castle. The game's puzzles revolve around these 3 items: you'll have to combine their abilities in very varied ways to solve the puzzles.
The castle has many shortcuts, that you can take by solving much harder puzzles. If you're stuck, you may as well try another way, or go buy another item. There are many different ways of making progress, too!
The castle puzzles are pretty straighforward, though, so anyone can safely play it without fearing getting frustrated.
Outside the castle, though, there are other smaller dungeon, with harder puzzles. These usually contain Cards with the game's characters. These are merely collectibles, but they're pretty charming too. The puzzles there can also hint at some mechanics you may have not learned throw the tutorial puzzles.
As a segue, when you have enough gold, you can take one of several portals spread around the castle to fast travel. When you buy an item, you'll be catapulted into another part of the island. These are the tutorial areas. Your items are all stored near the shop, and you'll have to beat the dungeon only with your newfound item. With this, you'll learn how the item works well enough, and do that through play! I think it's a nice way of doing it.
These dungeons also contain several paths and shortcuts. One important thing is that you'll never be able to leave the cave while missing important items. When you leave the dungeon, it will be sealed, but you can rest assured that you haven't missed anything important. This is also told to you after your first dungeon, in a sign post.
: since there are multiple paths, it's very likely that you'll miss part of the map, and become worried after leaving the dungeon. Right when you're worrying about it, the signpost clarifies it for you.
There are many places like this in the game, making tutorialisation nicely paced.
I think that about covers it.
This game has both combat and puzzles, although the focus is mainly on the puzzles. There are also some Boss Fights, most of which are more puzzle-driven than combat, although both blend rather nicely, items being multi-purposed.
The combat is very straightforward. Your basic attack attacks the tile in front of you. There are also projectiles attacks. There are several different enemies, some that attack only in front of them, some have projectiles, etc. Different enemies require different approaches. Also, they'll respawn each time you enter the room, but it's never a problem as they're easy to avoid. Some puzzles also reset, but only when the initial conditions are necessary for you to solve another puzzle in the room (or perhaps to use a shortcut).
The only problem I've had with the combat, is how the movement is a bit
, and there's a
with some enemies. The enemies often drop hearts to replenish your health, and the game is overall not punishing in the least, so it's not too big of an issue.
That's mostly a good thing, but it sometimes holds the player's hand too much. For example, Boss fights have 3-5 phases, and there's usually a checkpoint between each. I've found that mostly unnecessary, taking the little challenge that they provided. I think boss fights should still be a threat!
On the other hand, each time you die, you'll simply reset the room, but never lose progress, or collectibles at all. That's a very welcome thing! It's always annoying to do 4-5 rooms again when you die, or lose progress over a simple miss-step.
The
are basically Sokoban, with a few twists. You have 3 items: a Flaming Sword, a Freezing Wand, and a Teleporting Wand.
The sword can set bombs on fire, to explode after a few seconds. The Freezing Wand can freeze enemies and blocks (making them very slippery when you push them, and also breakable), and can also freeze a wall, making it reflective.
The Teleporting Wand can create a Green block anywhere. If you hit bombs or enemies with the projectile, they'll teleport over to that block. This is basically all you need to know.
You combine these techniques with some more subtle quirks to the tiles and timing, and you can be faced with some evil difficult puzzles.
Difficulty.
Usually, to beat the game, you have some fairly easy puzzles. To collect the cards, it's a different matter (although mostly doable). There's a final dungeon with 12 puzzles however, that is really hard! At least for someone inexperienced in Sokoban. I often had to peek into a walkthrough, and was constantly surprised with a new way of combining my items.
The problem is that some of these puzzles required extremely precise timing, with the game's controls don't provide very well, in my opinion. Also, these puzzles constantly made you restart at every wrong move. A time rewinding mechanic would be welcome, even if just on this cave. I had to restart these puzzles many times, making it a bit too frustrating. It wasn't just a puzzle to solve, it was something that heavily relied on execution, which I'm not a fan of.
Then again, these were completely optional! And the game warned you that they were hard. If you complete it, you'll get some more cards, and also Development info, which is very cool!
H.Mention: The castle can be solved with ANY combination of 2 items. I'm very impressed with this! The castle is so nicely designed that you can beat it with any combination of the two items, and the game aknowledges that with achievements. Also for cards, speed, etc.
There are many ways of playing Ittle Dew, which is why I think it's a neatly designed game. Many ways that tie together brilliantly!
Full Recommendation. Also, check Card City Nights!

Like many Steamers, I have a forever growing list of games cultivated for my minor addiction for purchasing video games. So in the perpetual sea of Steam deals and "Humble Bundles" I am quick to ignore the freebies offered in my Steam library without a second glance.
The only reason I happened upon Serena was because I was flipping through my list looking for another game and noticed this indie adventure horror title. I dig horror especially when it's heavily reliant on the story. When I first ran Serena it reminded me of walking through the alleyways and rooms in Amnesia minus the scariness and evil things lurking around each corner. Created via the same game engine (Dagon) as the upcoming Asylum, Serena is a positive preview of what's to come this year when Asylum is released. As it's based in one cabin with minimal room to roam, it doesn't expect much from you and is a practically zero stress game. If you like watching horror films but dislike partaking in gory FPS games, you'll enjoy the ambiance in Serena. It has sinister context set in a mildly soothing atmosphere which is the best formula for an entertaining but laid back experience. You don't do anything but click random objects and read/listen to plenty of text. It's a fun change of pace for horror gamers and easy to sample for those less inclined towards the genre. Just sit back, and enjoy the story. It's like those interactive flash games back in the day that just gave you a wicked storybook with sounds and moving pictures and that was it.
What's more, the game has no control menu so once you start you should aim to finish as it hasn't got a save mode either. It doesn't require one as it isn't challenging to finish and relatively short to play. There are specific places you can click with your cursor to hear snippets of memories and clues to what has happened in that cabin which has a intense atmosphere of "something gravely wrong" from the get go.
After a few minutes wondering about, clicking all you can, in turn collecting an abundance of information on the couple introduced in Serena, you may get stuck. If you do you always have the option of pressing SPACE BAR to toggle hot spots. That way you can scan any object you haven't checked out and move on with the story.
Personally, after 20 minutes I looked up and read
play-through (no plot spoilers) on Steam's community hub and breezed to the end, finishing Serena in half an hour. It would have been even more entertaining had I saved myself from previously Googling the game and noticing a huge spoiler in the search results (basically the ending and what I'd find somewhere in the cabin). I suggest making sure you have an hour to spare just "wasting time" clicking stuff and seeing if you can get through the story on your own. If progression is slow, then use a simple run-through like the link above so you know which actions to take but nothing of what will occur.
Using a guide for my last ten minutes of Serena is a probable culprit but it wasn't a rewarding game and I could see why it's free (on PC). My review is a positive one only because it's free and quick, it is well made and finished the simple task it was meant to do which is tell a short horror story in the likeness of Edgar Allan Poe's literary creations.
The game itself has a bit of IRL drama behind it that wasn't too interesting to me as an outsider so I'll skip that and move onto the story. Serena is fantastically narrated by Josh Mandel which makes the repeated clicking, reading and listening more enjoyable. He plays Serena's husband, the character the gamer will play in first person. Your memory is foggy and you're extremely disorientated as you move around the dusty, abandoned log cabin you seem to reside at with your "better half". But she's nowhere to be seen so you look around the cabin, thinking back to distant moments that seem somehow distorted now. Your goal is to reach the end of the story by clicking certain objects in a somewhat set order and releasing a change in your perception, the truth of what happened to you and Serena and why.

TL;DR Fallout 4 is a great shooter, but an awful Fallout game.
Fallout 4 is the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of the 3d Fallout games so far.  Fallout 3 was experimental, and worked pretty well despite being a little empty.  Fallout New Vegas improved on every aspect in 3, and forged itself a completely new identity as a true RPG.  Fallout 4...didnt do either of these.
Pros : Fallout 4 was fun, I'll admit.  I've sunk 500+ hours in the game, so I think I have some precedent to my opinion.  As a shooter it shines, and I'd daresay if this wasn't a "Fallout" game, people would be much more receptive to it.
Cons : As an RPG, it flops.  The skill system is difficult to keep track of, and the menu for it just feels bulky.  The dialogue is limited as hell, and the story itself just isn't engaging.  In my 500+ hours, I've never even entered the second act of the game.  It's also worth noting that a lot of the content for the building aspect of the game - one of it's big selling points - are locked behind DLC.
Truly, if you can pick Fallout 4 up for $20 do it, I don't think you'd regret it.  However don't go into this expecting New Vegas depth or the memorability of 3.

I'd say it deserves, at the very least, a positive or very positive rating. If this was an indie with a lot of negative reviews, I'd have probably left a "Thumbs up" do want to provide a less-than-rosy review highlighting the flaws. Personally, I think this is more of a "casual puzzle" game than pinball, really.
I HIGHLY recommend skipping this one if you are playing with a mouse/keyboard. It works a crapload better with a controller.
The most glaring problem I see with Rollers of the Realm are the
Most pinball I'm used to have longer-than-wide designs *for a reason.* That vertical progression is a key element of pinball. Finally hitting that "secret" and seeing what it does is part of the pinball mystique - Rollers of the Realm is easy for even a novice. Many of the reviews mention the lack of replayability, this is why.
I'm guessing this is because 16:9 monitors are standard and they wanted full-screen capability. I'd have preferred a narrow, but tall design personally. Really, it just feels like you're playing on a really short table all of the time. The tables feel far more linear and less replayable than the typical "pinball sandbox" you're used to.
The second problem is that
You have a cleric class who can revive your party. All you have to do is get enough mana to do-so. I suppose you could create your own "no reviving challenge" to combat this mechanic.
You collect point and gold from bumping into things. If you hit an enemy enough time, you defeat them. There are a "obvious" puzzles to acquire a key which can be used to open treasure. What I don't like is that there are a TON of worthless bumpers that exist just to "get you down the next corridor." Basically, you have to follow a linear path to finish a level then have the option to end it or continue playing. I really wish you could toggle "free play" so the "DO YOU WANT TO CONTINUE" was disabled every time you accidentally triggered the end of a level.
There is story and different classes - that's about it. It's really more of a series of medieval themed table than an "RPG crossover." You also have "characters" or pinballs with different functions. For instance, enemies slowly wear down the health of your bumpers. Solution is to use a cleric to repair them. It does add an element of gameplay, but could have been do much more.

Ittle Dew is a 2D puzzle adventure game. Basically, it's like a 2D Legend of Zelda game with a heavy focus on the puzzles. You're washed up on a mysterious island and, as any good adventurer does, you start to adventure. It's pretty straightforward in terms of adventuring. You go from dungeon to dungeon as they become available to you, work on puzzles with the dungeons in order to complete them, and then receive items to help you progress further. Upon getting an item, you generally are sent to a new area without the other items, forcing you to get acquainted with the new item and its uses before being able to combine the uses of all your items. There are a few optional shortcuts and slightly hidden puzzles you can go after, which is nice for even more puzzle solving. It is also entire possible to complete the game without getting all of the items. You can beat it with a few combinations of a few items. These are reflected in the achivements, but... I'll be honest, I had enough trouble with the main game using everything. There's also some funny little dialogues going on in parts of the game which give it some life and keep things from getting too harsh on your brain. Almost like little rewards for continuing. And there are boss fights which will give some action to your problem solving skills. A nice blend for the game.
There are a few downsides though, as all games have. One is that the game is rather short. Most of the playtime here will be from getting stuck on tricky puzzles. There's not much adventuring, as most of the places you go to are rather straightforward and without missable secrets. Even the optional puzzles are pretty easy to find. So I guess there could've been more adventure for my taste. Also, the combat is a little rough. It just feels a bit stiff and non responsive. There's less focus on it, but still, a little more fluidity might have been nice. Not a big deal, though. You can adjust. There were some pretty interesting puzzles, some involving good timing, but the game doesn't do a great job of teaching you the timing based techniques used later in the game. Also, there's an awful lot of block puzzles, so... if you don't like those... stay away.
Overall, it's a pretty cool game. Is it worth the ten dollar price tag? Well, if you're a Zelda fan or a puzzle fan, yes. It's definitely worth checking out. For others? Possibly wait for a sale, or just give it a shot. It's a decent price for what you get. It has some neat sound and a fun art style. The music went well the the mood. It's definitely something anyone could enjoy, but recommended for only the Zelda fans or puzzle crowd, I'd say. If you're looking for more adventure, it may not be your cup of tea. And I must say that, even though it is a bit on the short side, it doesn't FEEL short. It feels like a full game, and that's where it counts. I'd give Ittle Dew 7/10. Good, solid game, but geared more towards the puzzle minded for sure.

When I first discovered this game, my first thought was that it reminded me of old pinball games like the 3D Ultra Pinball games. It's just lovely to see a creative pinball-based game after so long.
This one mixes in a little bit of RPG elements, but not an awful lot, and strictly nothing you have to pay too much attention to. It's all about making the ball go where it needs to go, and there's a story to go with it. The story is nice, if not terribly original, and the characters are charming. Around the pinball tables are different kinds of stationary targets that award "mana" to use with special powers, moving/attacking enemy targets that block paths and attack your flippers, piles of money, chests and corresponding keys. The tables are varied and often consist of several playfields. Oh, and you can swap between different balls (RPG characters) that are of various sizes and other properties, and special powers that ranges from reviving to setting enemies on fire or launch additional balls into play. You can also directly affect left/right movement of the ball to get into difficult spots.
The game is perhaps a bit short, with gameplay of about 4-5 hours or more (on casual difficulty) depending on your skill and how much time you want to spend on collecting money for upgrades. On the other hand, I've played shorter games that were a lot less satisfying. The game ran surprisingly well on the fairly low-end hardware I was using at the time, but in a couple of levels the performance was noticably worse than average. It's probably not an issue for newer/better hardware. The game supports Xbox 360 compatible gamepads out of the box, so I chose to go that route.
Not much to complain about. It was a game I enjoyed, and will warmly recommend, at least on sale. I just hope they add some additional DLC content or a sequel, because I'll likely buy it!

Enforcer: Police Crime Action has it's moments, but has had minimul effort put into it on certain topics of the game. When handling every day human emotions and requirements (e.g. stress, hunger, thirst) It adds to the realism within the game. When dealing with stress you can watch television, or perhaps go see a loved family member or friends, but quite frankly when visiting family or friends I noticed that you don't actually get to play the part in hanging out with them and instead it brings up a photo with the sentence underneath saying "You have visited a friend/family member" which is quite a let down.
The title being "Enforcer: Police Crime action" makes it obvious what the game is based on, but when performing traffic stops you have choices of what you can do to the driver you have pulled over. If you want to test a driver for alcohol consumption then you can, but if you decide not to check for alcohol use and it appears they actually had been drinking whilst driving you get "points deducted" from you, and all I could think to myself is "I don't recall Police Officers having magic powers telling themselves, after they had checked the driver what the driver had done wrong." And I also don't remember my local Police having "points" taken away from them, I mean they're treating it like it's a challenge when it is not.
Another thing that caught my attention was you can't actually begin your shift at the Police station, and instead you start it at your wardrobe which I thought was random. The thought of not having to go to your area of work placement, and taking orders from your boss/ Police Sergeant is another sign of poor effort, and I had the complete opposite image of the game before I bought it and when I was reading the description.
When I noticed that you could upgrade your home I started to slowly change my opinion to a positive state of mind about this game, until I noticed you cannot use them and is mainly there for show. When watching TV you don't actually get to observe anything. Another point which shows lack of effort is when your hunger level gets very low, to recieve food you don't go to the store and buy the food, you don't get the food delivered to you, you pay your fridge to give you the food which made me sigh deeply as I wanted this to be a simulator and not a life that takes it easy on your worn out legs relieving you from walking to the store.
As a conclusion I would not recommend this game to anyone. This is because what they say you can do in the description on the Steam page is not 100% accurate at all, and mainly consists of having text grief being thrown at you for when you don't check a drivers ID. Also for when you think you get to live a normal life in this game it is the complete opposite and you do not get to spend time with family or friends, you just get to see an image of them when you click "Hang out" with them on your mobile phone. Over all a 3/10, mainly because of the lack of effort that was put into this game. If more detail was added such as actually being able to spend time with people, and having to do what you do in reality then I could most likely bump it up to 6, maybe a 7.

For me the best parts are the art and the colourful roster of characters.  Everyone is unique and well-filled out, story-wise, and while the characters are limitted to portraits (which are beautifully illustrated!), the fantastic voice acting fills in any of the gaps you might see.

Dead Age is quite really a charming game set in a post apocalyptic world where the Dead have taken over the cities of the living, and reduced humanity to nothing more than a blip on the radar. If it sounds like the plot of many games, many movies, many television shows, that's because it is.
In a world chock full of zombie games, you have to create something special, something that sets itself apart from the rest. Indeed there have been a few, and you can add Dead Age to that list.
You play a guy who joins a camp of disorganized random individuals who each have skills that you may upgrade throughout your game play. Each day as dawn breaks, you are given new missions to complete, some timed, others at your leisure, but each with a purpose and reward. Sometimes you are rewarded with new items, other times new members of your camp.
There is a growing over-population issue within the game that demands a daily trudge through the woods for food, or on the highways for guns and ammo, and other various things of interest that outside of such an environment one would expect is an easy task, but the ever growing presence of the zombie horde makes even the small tasks, laborious.
What sets this game apart from a lot of games is that it features a few different genres of gaming stuffed into one, the survival aspect, but also the roleplay, and permadeath of characters should they die, including yourself. I'm not sure if this qualifies as roguelike, or roguelite as I have heard before but it does have some aspects of it.
The feeling I get when playing this game, is if one of those board games, or table-top games were somehow transformed into a video game, but maintained most of the elements that make it static as opposed to immersive.
Make no mistake much of this game is comparable to text-based adventures, if you swap out the text for pictures, and you swap the notes for on screen information. All of those things you might be doing by hand is there, but in a static way. And I can understand a person reading this thinking I did not like it, but apparently I do, because I have played it a lot. And that is really the defining quality that any game should have, whether you want to keep playing or not.
This game reminds me of mobile games. it has a lot of the management you see in some mobile games, however nothing is held back, what its in the game is there, even if its sometimes difficult to find on a given playthrough.
And you do want to play this game over and over, because each playthrough gives you opportunities to unlock portions of the game via in game achievements, you get these medals, which during a new playthrough you can use to upgrade your character.
There isn't anything special here, because its basically point and click, although there are points where clicking does nothing, even if on a previous screen in the same play a click allowed you to further the story along. It may be my only critique of the controls that I feel is a bothersome thing.
Again the clicking thing its bothersome, but it may be intentional as I have not seen it fixed over the last few patches.
A few complaints I might have is that there is no easy way to speed things along, it moves as fast as it moves and that is it. Even if this is my tenth playthrough, I know how things work, and I just want to move things along. That can be frustrating, as opposed to relaxing as I believe was intended.
I've played this game a lot, I've seen a lot, but each time I die, I play it again. And that tells me that for the few frustations I have with the game, I do really enjoy it overall, and thus I think it does deserve a positive review and score. Look the game isn't some Sixty Dollar AAA explosion, and if you go in thinking that's what you are getting you will be very angry at yourself. It's priced where it should be, and on the days it is part of a sale, its certainly a bargain worth grabbing.
It's fun, its addictive, and its a pleasure playing it, and that is why I recommend people give it a try.
I've thought about it, and if this game was asking for money it might get a lower score, but its a pretty good experience for the price, and enjoyable, thus I give it a score of 6.5 out of 10. It's not the Walking Dead, but it does stand on its own, and anyone playing it should be happy they did.

Personally, I feel like this is the best Tales game since Versperia - as an overall package. The story so far is much darker tone (kind of how I felt about Vesperia before this entry) and the characters are intriguing enough for you to legitimately care about them. Especially Velvet, which I'm sure will be a trend in most reviews that laud the game. I feel myself compelled to keep going to learn more about what's happening with each character, and see the stories unfold. Even when things get a tad cheesy - the primary focus of the story takes hold again. This was a feeling often absent in the previous entries between this and Veperia - with a clean cut happy tone. Some of the raw moments in the game, are a welcome change to the stories in the series.
Berseria makes the entire tale of Vesperia look flowery in comparison in just the opening bit - and tugs at in interesting ways - departing from the series usual delivery of emotional content.
If you like the Tales series, this is different in many ways. Battle starts off as simplistic, and can be managed with button mashing, but the elements of the battle system trickle in, and harder difficulties are unlocked as you achieve in game goals (which I won't divulge here). The Artes system is a bit different than you'll be used to, seeing as there are only artes and no standard attacks any longer. A demo play through can get you a feel of this - but the higher difficulty settings and special random encounters will definitely test your understanding of the battle system - and plenty of patience with more challenging enemies. This is the first time I can recall the difficulty settings in a Tales game being this adjustable/variable for gamers of different skill.
But all in all, I've picked up every main title in the series since SNES, and this is up there on the list. Perfect or the best? I don't think so - but fans of the series will definitely dig it. The story is the primary driver here, and you can tell much more effort went into this one that Zestria, or even Graces/Xillia1+2
Oh and I should mention, I can't believe this port works with minimal issues. PC was at long last, done sweet justice this time around, and with the multitude of graphics options/tweaks, this looks sweet on a good machine. Applause for that!
Note: I've had a single crash in my time playing (at random) so continue to save frequently and using "Surround" sound makes voiceover vanish. Otherwise, this is a clean port deserving of praise - even if simply being a massive improvement over Zestiria's launch.

NO SPOILERS HERE.
I hate to give a free, independent narrative a thumbs down, especially one that only takes an hour to complete.  So I won't.   This game has an interesting premise, bogged down by sloppy execution.
In short, the game unfolds inside an old cabin, with the main character's narration slowly revealing the plot while we examine different items inside.
The main problem is that I didn't care, which I attribute mostly to the writing.
The voice acting was atrocious.  Even if it had been good, I think it would've had more impact if it had been text-only.  But I had a lot of trouble identifying with the story while constantly being distracted by how poorly-read the majority of the lines were.
I spent a lot of time re-examining items that had exhausted their narrative use, which took me out of the already limited immersion.  This could've been avoided by adding a vague line or two from the narrator, indirectly suggesting what I should look at next.  It would've added a mild feeling of reward for unlocking the next bit of narration.  Sort of an "a-ha!" mechanic.  Instead, the exploration seemed rather arbitrary.
There were a couple musical prompts during my playthrough that temporarily elevated the experience significantly.  But the music was extremely rare.  I'm normally okay with a sparse musical score if its absence is used for effect, but I don't feel that this was the case.  It felt like a missed opportunity to inject some weight into the generally trite narration.
The story ends as quickly as it begins.  The reveal is interesting, and I didn't see it coming.  But I didn't really care.
Interesting premise, poor effort.  5/10.

Unless you are into zombie settings, know what to expect from a Telltale game and can turn a blind eye over use and re-used zombie tropes, then maybe this is a game for you. Otherwise I wouldn't recommend this at all.
I bought this game on sale and even then I regret getting it. As I mentionned above I got Tales from the Borderlands and absolutely loved it, but there's a number of reasons why TWD series simply doesn't hold up at all.
The game builds a world with a set of rules but goes on to break them every couple of minutes completely breaking the immersion they try and build up.
First of all can we stop having zombie games where no one knows what a zombie is? They've been part of pop culture for a few decades now and still every zombie game/movie no one has a clue what's going on.
Second, they emphasize you having to be quiet or you'll attract walkers yet so often your character or the others around you make a lot of noise. Shoot a zombie in the head? No better slam a car door on his head SEVERAL times because that's incredibly quiet. You just turned on a very loud train, let's keep chilling around I'm sure nothing will happen. The list goes on and on.
Third, every zombie makes a lot of noise on camera but when they aren't visible they're all stealthy ninjas and can teleport at will. This is one of the reasons I stopped watching the series on TV. It's just so lame and poor writing. I was hoping not to see this in the game, or AT MOST used in the beginning when people have no clue. Yet it still happens half way through the game. There's also plenty of times when you enter a space, you look around to see all doors blocked by crates, not to mention the room being EMPTY, then after a cut, SUDDENLY, out of frigging no where some walkers appear, and of course despite SEEING the room is empty and NOT heaing a peep they make tons of noise the second they enter the frame. This is just such poor botched writing.
Fourth, the overall lack of logic from characters. Some really over the top, unrealistic and strange reactions, lack of logic by leaving behind weapons, because obviously leaving behind the hammer or knife and only having your fists is going to help you.
Fifth, they keep telling you all your action have an impact and matter but they force you into situations no matter what by being unable to save certain character regardless of your decisions or being unable to have people NOT join your group. This is somewhat minor because there's a lot of work required to make all the different paths.
All in all, I'm incredibly dissapointed by the game, from poor writing and use of very weak zomebie tropes, I feel the game simply doesn't quite work in this setting, where there's supposed to be a constant threat from zombies yet you can take all of the time in the world to look at every single thing and talk to every single character, all the while your character walks at an excrutiatingly slow pace (further destroying the sense of urgency from attracting walkers). I think limiting the actions you can take would've slightly circumvented this (as it's mostly tied to the gameplay) i.e you can only look at a limited amount of things/talk to limited amount of people of your choice.
All in all, I'd give the game a 6/10

I've put a great deal of time into Enforcer at this point and the best way I can describe the game is a speed trap simulator. The first few days of a character are engaging and exciting. Hearing the radio chatter, responding to your first few calls, arresting a drunk driver. Unfortunately after that the game seems to fall pretty flat.
My biggest complaint so far is once you move past your first few shifts, the emergency calls seem to drop off to zero leaving you to complete the bland main daily mission (ticket X number of cars, Catch X number of speeders or drunks) Effectively turning the game into speed trap simulator 2014. Scanning the forums, this seems to be a major complaint stemming from the Steam release of the game. Many ideas have been proposed, like tinkering with the game data or quitting and reloading your game (this apparently gives you a call or two before it returns you to insane boredom). I don’t know about you but having to shut down every time I need a little excitement seems a little counter intuitive to me.
Don’t get me wrong, it is still exciting when a driver bails from their vehicle leaving you to give chase on foot, though you will soon find that all runners will return to a walk no more than 100 paces from where they started leaving you an easy target; and this brings me to another point of NPC pathfinding. Nothing ruins a good chase than your suspect suddenly getting stuck on a wall....or a car...or a street sign....
Finally I would like to address Super cop and his Jet Fueled police cruiser. Quite frankly, after having a load screen inform me that I could die in as few as two bullets; having a semi-truck plow into me only to be sent flying into the air as my officer stands stoically in his place seems a bit silly. Getting behind the wheel of your cruiser you’ll find yourself subject to some crazy driving physics too. There is very little engine noise from the vehicle giving you the feeling that you are more floating than driving. Oddly enough driving on the shoulder is more engaging as the noise of tires on gravel begins to create the illusion of automotive transportation.
In summary, given the current state of the game gives this the feel of an early access game being sold as a finished product. From the sound of it this is very much still "in development" with the dev's still looking for ideas to expand and grow the game which is commendable. Unfortunately this has left quite a bit to be desired in the base game mechanics.
If you are a hardcore simulation fan and need something new to eat up a few hours this may be for you, otherwise steer clear until a bit more work is put in, or it lands in your local bargain bin.

At first I thought this game wasn't worth my £7.49 I payed for it. However, the game wasn't as bad as I thought it was. The game does have some good points but I have noticed a few minor errors within the game that should be addressed. First of, there are some mistakes in spellings and grammar. For example in the "Contacts" menu, it says "4+h" when it should say +4h. Moreover, in a some places the developer has forgotten to add a "s" on the end of words.
Another issue is that the car picks up speed quite quickly making handeling difficult. Moreover, the speed on the roads need to be increased. On long back roads the speed should be 50 or 60 MPH and not 30 MPH. This gets annoying when the NPC drive really slowly and you are stuck behind them...
I am also having an isssue in the car customization and when I change to get on duty where the screen just freezes or I cannot move. I don't know if this is a problem on my side.
Right now I just pull over random cars and find many things wrong with them without me even knowing. For example a car looks fine but when my officer goes to speak to them there registration plates are illegal or their brake lights don't work or they are drunk , but from their driving they don't look drunk... The game needs to add more of a realistic feel when pulling over cars.
Overall, I would give the game 3.5/5 stars. As far as recomending the game to anyone, I am on a fence. This game still need a lot of work and I don't believe it is worth 15 quid. There are better games out there at around the same price. However, once all of the issues have been addressed then the game would be more fun and seem more realistic. It would be cool instead of making the car teleport to the station you could see the actual tow truck or prisoner transport show up and take them. The map also needs to be faced the right way as you do not know how many times I have taken a wrong turn due to the oreintation of the map.The game came out on the 24th October 2014. Right now it is the 9th April 2015. So I'm wondering what the developer has done as the game still feels as a Pre-release or Alpha version and not the full, final version of the game. The game can be fun but as days progess it feels like you are doing the same thing over and over again...
Once the car controls have been masterd and most other elements of the games have been ironed out this game can become big! The game is fun at the moment but when new features get added the game will be a lot more. Kudos to the develpors as this is their first shot at PC gaming. Hopefully I don't have to change my review. Also get the game whilst it is cheap (7.49 pounds) as I don't see anyone buying this for 15 quid! Thanks for reading.

I bought this game a while back based on my time with Terraria, and loving that game.  This game at first seems like a massive upgrade to that.  In the short term it is.. and maybe at one point it really wanted to be.  But as it stands, it has none of the heart that game has, when it comes right down to it.  Think about it like this:  JJ Abrahms makes a movie, because he loves those kinds of movies, and it may have all the same actors, better cgi, and a bigger budget - heII, he may even have the same screenwriters - but when it comes right down to it, it lacks the thing that the movies he loved all had: heart.  It's not too late.  Starbound, I have faith in you.  Please be the game so many of us want you to be.
EDIT: Starbound is out, and played for 40+ hours so far.  It's somehow less than it was before.  Weapons are MUCH MUCH better, there are some fun bosses, but overall, I'll leave the negative review only because they took so much time to get it just to a mediocre finish.  Worth 10 or so dollars and if you liked terraria you'll probably like this, but it's easy to see, after grinding and working hard toward something, just to have it be missing, or not fully fleshed out, why this game is not nearly the game it so deserves to be.
UPDATE:  The game is much much better now.  If you haven't played it, it's worth playing.  Mechs, space stations, space travel, the game is good.  Not great, but worth a buy if you're into these kinds of games.

No, my problems with the game are that it's not serious enough in tone, there's no characer customization, and I personally think the art is ugly/mediocre. I was under the impression that this would be a gritty, rough survival-rpg, and yet monsters have slapstick move names like "dishonorable discharge" when the zombie in question isn't even a soldier. The story makes an attempt at seriousness, but I can't care about the protagonist right off the bat just because I'm playing as him. Which brings me to my second problem; "Jack", I'll call him, is who you are off the bat. If there wasn't going to be any way to customize his appearance, why let the player rename him? Why not develop and build him as his own character? And you have to start off the game with him being referred to as a "student" as far as job title, but seriously, dude looks like a war vet. Which comes to my third problem; Jack is... well, generic at best. Character design is bland and unmemorable, for all characters encountered by the 20 minute mark. And maybe it's just me, and I know this is harsh, but these peoples' faces are...kinda wonky and uneven. The thick, black lines only seem to be on some characters' profile pictures and while it may be that the artist was perhaps going for a comic book look, the characters look flat and dull. I'd dare say that Darkest Dungeon wore it better.
Honestly, if even one of those elements were different, I'd be willing to forgive it, but as it stands, I wish I'd bought through steam instead of the humble store so I could request a refund. Perhaps I'll come back if it gets modding support so I can add in different 2d art.
tl;dr: if you're not bothered by its aesthetics and care more about gameplay than story, knock yourself out, but it's just not for me because I'm a snob.

I don't really do reviews, so I'll keep this short.
This game is good, really good. I think the reason I'm writing about this is because I wasn;t really expecting much from a pinball rpg, but the game is great. The voice acting is high quality and well delivered. The story starts a little slow, but is suprisingly engaging. The chracters are a bit generic fantasy fair, but develope through out the story and are well fleshed out.
The game mechanics are really solid. Probably the best non-tradition rpg I've ever played. At its core its ofcourse pinball, but the various properties of different chracters(balls) lend themselves to different roles. RPG Mechanics help to define the chracters strengths and differences, and ofcourse let you lean on the style of play you enjoy.
As for the mechanics themselves enemies serve as destroyable bumbers(essentially), different characters deal damage, and losing you ball will kill the character. But by amassing mana(points vaguely) you can revive characters or activate special abilities. Run out of characters and well you lose, Defeat all the enemies and or the boss and you win, or whatever other objetive a stage may have (collect x gold, break the statue). Ranged enemies and mages can damage your flippers, but your healers can restore them by collecting mana. The end result is a game that while starting off slowly and easing you in(early on you can't even die in certain sections), but ends up evoling into a hectic struggle to keep your characters alive and your flippers healthy. You learn when to switch your character for the different sections of the level and you probably end up replay the levels a few times.
The end of the day the game is on the lighter side, but has a good amount of depth and is throughly enjoyable.

The reason I bring up all the Tales games is because of how similar (yet different in combat) they all are.
If you have never played a Tales game before, it's a standard JRPG story/world for the most part, with an action based battle system that is tweaked in every entry. Instead of choosing your commands from a menu, you are actively fighting (say, combos as in a fighting game) your enemies. The rest is your standard fare - gold, new weapons, secret areas, new characters, betrayal, cooking!!!
This game has the best beginning of any Tales game I have ever played. The combat system is entertaining and active, and the camera actually works, unlike Zestiria. The heroine is powerful and dedicated so far, and I really like how ruthless she is compared to Sorey from ToZ.
No AI issues so far for me.
Amazing PC port as well! Graphics options, 60fps, controller support, everything you'd want.
I highly recommend picking up this game! It would be good for your first Tales game, or simply the next one in the line!

While I think the game can stand on its own merit for someone looking for 1-3 playthroughs of the vanilla game with all DLC included, that's basically where this game's experience ends.
Depending on how fast you clear instances, and how much you like to explore, entire faction questlines can be completed in a single sitting for someone with a day off and nothing to do. If you're looking to just speed through it, no dialogue and all.
I prefer to play stealth/guerrilla style combat when I play a game like this. As such I'm usually lightly if at all armored and sneak everywhere. Any way I can up my backpack capacity, I do. This makes my own playthroughs of a faction quest take days each just from all the hoarding, but in my action playthroughs, I've cleared entire DLC in a single day.
That said, I think Far Harbor has a lot more to it than an action playthrough would give it credit for. I went through a second time and found that it took me 3 days with sensible breaks to play through. The other DLC have similar stories, if you want something deeper, you gotta dig for it.
With all that said, you might be wondering why I don't recommend this game anymore.
The short answer, Creation Club breaks stuff in an already unstable game.
Essential mods often require the Fallout Script Extender, F4SE for short, to function. With every iteration or upload of a file into the Creation Club, the F4SE would need to be updated, therein breaking all my core mods installed.
Saves would be corrupted, or just crash to desktop. They may act funny, and some mod functionality could even be lost entirely if I'm not careful, even if I reinstalled everything properly later. This has a lot to do with scripts and save files.
And to speak to the "in an already unstable game" bit, the game is indeed stable enough to play, but you'll run into crashes where there would be no sensible reason one would happen. This is usually due to uncleaned files, which the team making xEdit so helpfully remedy with their program that cleans the vanilla add-ons and update file to dramatically reduce CTD chance. This is a must-have for any would-be modder, and mind you I don't think it needs F4SE but you're still heavily limited in the mods you can install when F4SE simply cannot be updated hourly, or possibly daily.
I don't know just how much work goes into these script extenders, but I can't imagine downloading and updating my script extender every single log-in.
Final note, the Creation Club installs the mod data before you even buy anything. Much like most add-ons in games like Borderlands 2 with their character packs, it installs the data but locks it until you've purchased the add-on for your own use. This could cause serious problems if the Creation Club only gets 25% of Nexusmods' FO4 database in Creation-Club-mods.
The vanilla game and DLC are worth a few playthroughs, and in terms of 1 dollar to 1 hour, I think most players would meet that 60 hour mark. If you're looking to mod the game, you may find that the majority of recommended mods out there are non-functioning thanks to this Creation Club. I loved the idea of CC, but I've had to uninstall FO4 because of its poor implementation.
The Creation Club is not an opt-in or opt-out service. If the Creation Club suddenly had an insurgence of fresh content that equalled 25% of Nexusmods' database for FO4, you would be required to install maybe terabytes of data just to play vanilla FO4 and its DLC.
There are safeties in place considering that it's mostly a human controlled process before it gets uploaded to the Creation Club, but even if it took 3 months for them to get that many mods which is far from unreasonable, you'd still be left with the same glaring flaw. A vanilla player would have to install more data than most xbox's can have at any one time.
I finished the game, but It's a story that I will be thinking about days after.

Gameplay:  8/10
The gameplay is fairly standard issue platforming fare but with the after image mechanic it finds it's own personality. The flash can make you have to think about how to get somewhere which I found gave this game a fun advantage over plain platforming.
Overall;  8/10
The value you get for you $2.00 is great. It's fun, it's different and well worth playing.

First off, I love this game. However, it does have flaws that need to be adressed.
1: Vehicle handling is awful. Doesn't even make sense at times.
2: Running criminals will stop and walk normally like nothing ever happened after 30 yards, instead of continuing to run or trying to hide.
3: Criminals with guns with will sometimes wait up to 8 seconds to start shooting you.
4: There are not enough things to spend your money on. You only get to buy 3 cars, and buying furniture for your house is nice, but not enough. It would be nice to be able to buy a new house, and place it wherever we want.
5: You can not recruit a partner, which is very unrealistic.
6: Gun play is not very good, considering there is no recoil at all. It would be nice if there was, and as we gain stress levels, the recoil becomes greater.
7: Criminal AI is awful, they stand in one spot when trying to shoot you, instead of trying to get behind cover.
8: We need more content, after you play the game for about 3 days, you have pretty much seen everything there is to the game. Give us more missions, more cars, more houses, more gun options, gun customization, a recoil system, partners, trucks, ect.
9: It would be nice to have an actual Story Mode. This would entice us to keep playing and staying interested in the game. It mentions that your grandparents dont have much time to live, maybe you could play on that a little bit?
10: MULTIPLAYER! The fun of this game would increse tenfold if we could play with a friend.
I'll say this again, I love this game and want to see it grow. However it is very unpolished and until the problems listed above are adressed, I couldn't reccomend this game to just anyone. But if you could look past the problems, you just may find your new favorite game.

The Walking Dead is an absolute masterpiece of a game and is near-perfect in every regard. Any fan of story games or The Walking Dead should buy this without hesitation.
- Compelling story and great writing.
- Memorable characters with complex and realistic relationships.
- Amazingly convincing voice acting.
- The choices keep you very immersed in the story and add a layer of personalization that a movie or TV show could never emulate.
- Well-paced with enough action to keep you attentive.
- Hard to put down. On my first Xbox playthrough I pretty much pulled an all-nighter without realizing it because I couldn't stop playing.
- I can't speak for the comics but this game is infinitely better than the show. I've become more emotionally attached to these characters in less than 15 hours of gameplay time than the characters of The Walking Dead show, which I've spent well over 70 hours watching throughout the years.
- Got it on sale for $7.00 CAD but it's well worth the normal price of $28.00 CAD.
- Performs well even on a slightly older PC.
- An experience any adventure/story game fan should not miss out on.
- Telltale Games are not known for their graphics, so that may be a con for some. I personally have no problem with it though and I think the games wouldn't be the same without this style.
- Clunky controls on mouse and keyboard. Plays great with a controller (I used an Xbox controller).
The Walking Dead is, in my opinion, the best Telltale game (Or at least is tied with The Wolf Among Us) and one of the best story-driven games ever created. More of an experience than a game, this is something absolutely nobody should miss out on. The Walking Dead sure as♥♥♥♥♥♥has my vote for the "I'm Not Crying, There's Something In My Eye" award.

A great concept, but sloppy execution. Think of True Crime New York City; you could give tickets, inspect cars, frisk people, etc. However, like True Crime NYC, this game is rather broken. The world feels empty, the NPCs are nearly identical aside from a few color differences in clothing, there is a lack of dialogue. In all aspects, the game can be done if you look past these things but it really needs a lot of work. The aimming is clunky, the driving is dodgy, the weather effects are ugly.
There is no denything that I still enjoyed the game. However, until the game is polished up, I will not be touching this game for a while. There are many ways the player can boost, or outright manipualte the way the game is meant to be played and quickly level up. Despite the bugs and exploits, you can have a fun time but the game can get really boring really fast, there's not much to do when off-duty.
In conclusion, if you can look past the bugs and exploits, you will most likely like this game if you enjoy police simulators. However, if you are like me and suffer from strong OCD, the glitches will really drive you insane. If and when this game is a little bit more playable, I will indeed consider rewriting my review. Great concept, fun at times, but it needs a lot of work.

If you have ever played GTA IV LCPDFR then you know the love of serious, realistic, police simulation games. In addition if you have played LCPDFR you know the struggle to get the mods you want to work, hell you had problems getting GTA IV to start, but you did what you had to, stayed up through the night to get everything working because you know how fun it is, and now you are looking at this game because its like LCPDFR except you don't have to worry about bugs, crashes, bad mods, no. Finally a game based around the idea of police simulation. Now the question is, is this game good? Is it what we all wanted? The answer, is yes. Amazingly this seems to be the first success of its kind and on my very first day of playing it I already had 5 hours, keep in mind this was not made by Rockstar, this was made by an indie developer so this is not GTA 6 Police, not even close. This game still has minor bugs, it still needs polishing, it is not finished. Currently the game is very enjoyable and playable, none of the minor drawbacks that I just mentioned damper the games "fun factor" at all. All I meant by saying that is do not expect GTA 6 Police, however what you will find is a game with good graphics, decent animations, a good selection of vehicles, and a good system of fighting crime. And I know that the one question you still want answered before you buy this game, so I will tell you, yes, you can
*Pull people over (Traffic stop). When you do this you have the option to check their plates and license, use a breathelizer, ask them to exit the vehicle, issue a ticket, and I believe a couple more. And yes, sometimes they do run and you must chase after them, but whatever the random situation is you have the choice of letting them go free, write a ticket, or if need be, arrest them and transport them to the station or call a police van. You also should tow their car however that is optional. Now for your characters abilites, you can fight with your fists, you have a pistol, you can direct traffic, you have a taser, and you have your radio to call a police transportation van, an ambulance, a tow truck, and help if your police car runs out of gas or has reached its maximum damage capacity. (Yes cars use gas I know its awesome!) And of course you do get random callouts. There is also a level system, I do not know off hand how many levels their are but I believe their is about 15 or 16. You start as a corpral and make your way all the way down to the final rank Chief of Police. Now depending on your rank you will get more dangerous callouts and get paid more at the end of your shift. Now I do not want to spoil the whole game but you do have shifts and off your shift you go to your house, you can go out with friends, own your own civilian car, eat, watch TV, shower, sleep, and many other things. Now this system of off duty is not the greatest, their is not much to do and it will probably be polished in the future. But I do think that it is good because in a game that is centered around police simulation it would be awkward to be on patrol 24 hours a day 7 days a week, so I do believe this is a good system that was put into play. So that is pretty much what you are getting, also do not forget the whole game is open world, no missions! Now if there was one thing that I could say was the biggest problem with the game currently it would probably the car physics, they are not unplayable but they are not Iracing physics. That is pretty much the end of my review and don't think you know everything now because I am happy to say there are many more features in the game still that you can do as a police officer! I do believe it is worth the money and my final rating on the game *CURRENTLY is a 8.7/10

I'm glad to have played this game, making dark RPG games titled No Pants Dragons, playful Shooters called On My Back, and outlandish Simulation games called Going Outside. This game is definitely at the forefront of Simulators for game making. Not that the "topic" is flooded at the moment, but I've played them all mostly.
Mad Games Tycoon gives lots of options and locations for building your company, not just office or studio, but eventually a game making conglomerate. It's lots of fun getting there too, buying or making game engines to power your games, hiring and firing employees and making them do thankless menial work like customer support, it gives you a good sense of being a di- i mean boss.
The games gets continuous updates since its release and continues to improve, and I hope it does because even though I've thouroughly enjoyed it it's falling a tad bit into a gameplay pitfall. It uses the same slider method of "making games" as other simulators. My problem with this is this is not a good method in my opinion, because it's easily solved by opening a guide and just notching as you see to get appropriate scores.

Rollers of the Realm is a pinball RPG.  Sorta...  Basically, instead of plain pinball tables to play, you've got these areas that look like a village courtyard with flippers and bumpers on the sides of it. You use Mana points to enable certain special abilities, and gain mana by bumping into various targets on the field. There are also people milling about as obstacles or enemies.  Depending on the story, bumping your ball into people may attack them or it may merely rob them of some gold.  In some cases, enemies sap you of mana points.
You start out with the lowly thief with a heart of gold and her trusty dog sidekick.  As you play through the story new characters are added and you have the option of hiring other characters (once every 4 levels). Each character has their own special ability, and you can use these abilities to add extra balls to the table, or prevent the ball from draining from the playfield (depending on character). There's also a store to buy new equipment which adds to your character's abilities.  Thankfully you can return to each level after completing the story part and attempt to farm some extra gold.
There's also two levels of difficulty...casual and challenge mode. I had originally thought that challenge mode would remove the ability to change the ball direction with the analog stick, but apparently this is not so.  I guess the enemies are just tougher and the traps may be easier to set off.
Traps?  Well, there's at least one level where after a certain number of times the ball hits it, the barrier will disappear leaving a way for the ball to exit the playfield (thus "killing" your character).  Thankfully, you can easily revive them later in the game, and if there's no immediate danger (enemies on the playfield) losing the ball doesn't kill your character off.  It also seems to revive characters between levels so it's not like it kills the character off for good or anything.
All in all though, the game is good fun and worthy of spending your time on.  If you're a big fan of a challenging pinball game, well, this is a bit too soft, but if you're a fan of pinball and you love a good story, then check it out.

Good:

Bad:
- Extreme lag in Fullscreen Mode no matter what settings you use

The game's a lot like Abuse in the sense that it's high action fun with ridiculous guns in a 2D environment. There's quite a bit of enemy variety and at times the game makes you feel like a true action hero (think Just Cause 2 combined with Metal Gear Solid, except in 2D). Sadly it's virtually unplayable in fullscreen mode due to the cursor lagging and warping all over the place and the characters going into slow mo' whenever the screen moves an inch. You can get around this by playing in windowed mode but you can't change the game resolution while doing this so you're stuck with a really small screen unless you change your desktop resolution to 640x480.
Another small gripe would be that the higher difficutly level is locked. Why make us play the game before we can play it on the settings we want. Although in retrospect the game was quite difficult as it is and you don't have to play the game through all the way on normal before unlocking the harder difficulty level so I suppose it's not too bad.
I'd say if you liked Abuse then you'll like this one assuming you don't mind working around the aforementioned issues concerning lag. I'd like to think that my computer can run a 2D game quite well without resorting to the steps I mentioned so the game is likely poorly optimized but still plays well enough considering it's been made by one man on his own.

Purchase with all the DLC. This is one of the most definitive strategy games of all time. Definitely a must-own.
The systems work with the story, the story works with the gameplay, and the gameplay gives you story. This is a masterpiece of design, where you are still given a goal but are completely free to choose, build and explore in a structured format. From the start you're put straight into the game, continuing from the first game (where it's canon that you failed), and within the first hour you already know and love both the primary characters and your created squad, and care about solving the problems and questions this world has to offer. Each quest you take directly influences your story and journey in a way no MMO has ever before, whether it's a slight gain to supplies that lets you upgrade a weapon or a facility mission that puts you down 3 ticks from the doomsday clock.
A lot of people complain about the chance, so here's the primary strategy: Never leave anything up to chance. Grenades do guaranteed damage, but also destroy cover - opening up a flanking/critical chance for every soldier within range. Shotguns and swords do guaranteed 100% hit chance early on, while grenadiers do guaranteed 3/4 damage/cover destruction twice. The primary strategy is to plan out your attack, and design the battlefield so that if any aliens are left standing after the turn is over, you'll be able to recover easily. This means taking the RPG statistic of clearing destructive small fry, or focusing fire on the only true damage dealer in the bunch and then letting your soldiers take small arms/will fire. Just like Poker, there's always chance, but there's always a way to play the odds in your favor.
If you are save scumming (reloading encounters to get the maximum possible result, or to re-calculate a roll/turn), limit yourself to two. Loss is just as big of a part of XCOM as is win. You WILL miss a 99%, and want to reset. Don't. Soldier on forward. Make a "Garrus Vakarian2" clone rookie. XCOM is at its best when you feel the weight of your decisions, whether you're just discovering a new mechanic (don't melee a "purifier" flame thrower) or miss a ciritical attack, or choose the wrong research. Winning makes you feel like a real commander, losing makes you feel like you are losing a game of monopoly - out of power, annoyed, bored, and angry. Not everything is up to chance - dust yourself off and get back in the game.
The new DLCs are incredible. I hate how they handle the classic bosses now, though. They're less frequent, and when they appear it's not that big of a deal compared to the contant attacks of the Chosen. They still have a tendency to appear at the worst times (the berserker appeared during the avenger defense mission, so many reloads). The immersive power the Photobooth brings, along with the alien propaganda flipping your missions, the new factions and characters, and the amount of power you can bring vs the powerless exploration and challenge you're forced against, it's well worth the price.
This is a challenging strategy game as much as it is a very personal RPG. If you like the challenge, love progress, love the tactical thinking that goes into reactive small-squad attacks as well as the long-game meta planning, buy this game. It will give you the time you spent back without feeling like a grind.
Good game. The boss fights are the best.

Despite being poorly made, this is still a fun pinball RPG... if you play on "casual" so that you don't have to constantly repair your flippers. An important tip: several characters have
abilities. Don't use them, and don't waste gold upgrading them! Unlike a normal pinball game where you only need to worry about keep one of the identical balls in play, secondary balls in Rollers are weak, the character still dies if its main ball falls into the drain (and it's often difficult to tell the balls apart in battle, especially with the Rogue's balls' dull colors), and secondary balls can't activate special board locations that advance the level. That last point leads to some almost buggy situations where, for example, on a very long board you can get a secondary ball up to the distant top of the board but the camera won't follow it. The only good part about multiballs is that the some of the Ranger's extra balls stick to enemies, so they're good for dealing with enemies that hang around right beside your flippers.
Oh, and the game makes it sound like Arena levels are good for grinding gold. They're not. You don't get to keep most of the gold that you earn on Arena levels, so just stick to grinding on old campaign levels.
The levels and enemies are so blocky and
that it looks like a port of an N64 game. I know that this is a low budget Canadian game, but there's just no excuse for a modern game being this hideous. (It even got $221,784 of funding from the Canadian government - where did my tax dollars go?!)
So instead of creating challenge with intricate, well-designed levels and creative enemies, what does Rollers do instead? Enemies wear down your flippers until they're nubs, that's what. I could understand if there was a rare special enemy who could briefly deactivate your flippers or even delay them, but shrinking your flippers is just a bad, frustrating game design crutch. Having reliable, full size flippers is the one thing that you should be able to count on in a pinball game.
I'm fine with hunting for a secret exit once in a while, but the game fails to tell you basic stuff like which button activates a flipper. (It's tough to remember in the heat of "battle", especially when the flipper points straight down!) On a level where you advance up to another screen, falling back down the drain should return you to the lower board, right? Nope. You just die.
Balls and character are often needlessly difficult to tell apart. Some of the balls have textures on them, so it should have been easy to visually distinguish them, but it's like they were deliberately made hard to tell apart. It was almost shocking when the game finally gave me a deep red ball.
Rollers is even terrible at giving you clear information in the item shop between levels - items have a wall of confusing statistics, and their flavor text isn't differentiated from the description of what they actually do. I guess the Canada Media Fund didn't give them enough money to afford
? When you get a new character, the game shows you a summary of his abilities, which you NEVER get to see again. The wording on upgrades is so unclear that I'm still not sure if the monk can heal flippers by default, with an upgrade, or not at all.
One girl's quest to find revenge... and her nearest hot topic!

In Camera Obscura you play a photographer scaling a decaying tower. Your camera has the strange ability to create after images of various platforms. These after images start off being able to slowly move based off your own movements but will eventually freeze up.
Once you learn to use the After Images this game becomes a lot easier and has a lot more variety in its puzzle solving.
Some of the puzzles are a little bit too frustrating. The game will sometimes task you with getting an enemy to a button to flip a door open, this enemy can easily be killed if you're not careful. These missions are some of the most frustrating missions ever.
The game is hard and sometimes unfair, however it is mostly enjoyable except for one thing, the level 8-2. This level is just awful, it's unclear what they want you to do and the flow is just horrible. The fact that every guide I found online was about ways to skip half of the level, should show you how hated it is. If you make it that far I suggest you learn how to skip it as well, it's not worth the effort doing it the way the designers wanted it done.
Thankfully the last level is fairly easy but has beautiful back grounds and a great musical score. It really does feel like the climax to your journey and is a great last level.
On the artistic side I found the back grounds to be pretty good. Some of them even are breath taking. While the sprite work is just average. The monsters don't seem to fit with the main characters art design, instead looking like your standard run of the mill monsters. It's a shame they couldn't come up with something more intresting than, slime, bat, bug. Though the ant eater is a bit different ( though they are Anteater games ).
However the true failure in this game, is the sprite animation. Slimes mysteriously grow butts, the main character jumps by just clapping her feet together. Your death animation is a silly double spin. The games animation is just a bit janky, nothing that upsets me, it just makes the game feel a bit cheap. ( Though the death animation IS hilarious ). However it does have artistic flourishes like having several idle animations that are pretty good, and even animating the scarf when she falls.
The story is given to you in bits and pieces, scattered across the levels in collectable polaroids. I collected them where I could and got above 75% of them, however I wish they didn't just use the polaroids. For example in Thomas was Alone, they had a voice over that gave you bits of the story and characterization. I would have liked something similar, maybe just text appearing as you played the level.
In the last level they have dialouge, but when you get to the end all you get is a samll image in the end credits.
All in all I think this game isn't the best game, but it has intresting mechanics and some fun levels with a story that is a bit charming. So for the price tag I say it's worth it to play, at least up till 8-2.
TLDR: It's 1.99 you get what you pay for. It's enjoyable for the most part but some levels will have you tearing out your hair.

This is an interesting game. It was done completely by 1 guy, which is impressive, the art style is interesting (if a little goofy at times), and the music can be pretty driving until you've heard them loop a dozen times.
The boss fights are pretty cool, except they are basically impossible the first time through. You will lose repeatedly until you figure out the bosses' patterns.This may be the generally accepted mechanic for games like this, but I've always found it frustrating.
The levels are very well-done, and are noticeably different each time. There are even little mini-levels where you're sliding down a snow-covered slope, which are a blast.
The controls are serviceable with a 360 controller, and I've heard they're good with keyboard+mouse too. Sometimes, though, they genuinely get in the way, and the way the wolf moves is inherently weird. It works, though.
The game is also rather short. I enjoyed it for the most part (other than dying 20+ times in the final boss alone. Frustrating to the max), but it's fun if you enjoy mindless side-scrolling shooters.
The game is at it's best when you are frantically trying to dodge one enemy's bullets while shooting another. It's at it's worst when you're trying to time precision jumps or dodge boss projectiles, and the controls get in the way.
If you use a 360 controller, I STRONGLY recommend you unbind the jump key from the analog stick, or you'll be jumping over and over and over and over and over when you never wanted to. I used LB instead, and left RB to cycle through weapons.

So, I'll be honest, after the great game that was "Game Dev Tycoon" (GDT) scratching an itch to be a game developer that I didn't know I had, I ended up talking and making mods with an associate of mine, and eventually ended up looking for games that came close to what we wanted to turn GDT into. The only thing that was 1) available, and 2) came anywhere close was a title called "Mad Games Tycoon" by Eggcode.
But it's not a title that appeals to just one type of simulation gamer, but multiple types. It aims not only at those aiming for perfection, but aiming for an experience that isn't easy.
True, you could take notes on things between games on where different sliders for game customization should be for different genres but to me that seems to lessen the experience a bit. This is a game where you start out in the early days of video game development. The first systems are a Personal Computer (PC) and an early Atari-type system. And it goes from there, with new consoles being released, competitors making their games and engines, liscensing your engines, and the reviewers being as critical as they ever were!
It comes in four difficulty levels and options to randomize the console popularities, and so many little intricacies that you can use to affect your scores on different titles that you can never be quite certain how things will turn out.
Oh, did I mention it's still early access? Yeah, it is. This game isn't even officially "launched" yet, and it's my benchmark for any title that wants to be a business simulator--yes, not just a game development simulation, but business simulators in general.
If you've not picked up Mad Games Tycoon, you should. Surely you can spare $15 for this gem of an early access title.

Sleeping Dogs is an excellent game, a strong contender to make my top 5 of 2012. It has a powerful story with exciting twists and interesting characters, supported by Hollywood quality voice acting and music, and gorgeous graphics. The three core gameplay elements, melee, shooting and driving, while individually not as outstanding as other games that focus on one element, are all good enough to enjoy here. Add in a wide range of side missions and you have a varied experience that is never dull and easily lasts over 15 hours. This is also a good PC port, with plenty of customisation options, the controls work well with keyboard and mouse and there are hardly any bugs. My only complaint is that the undercover setting is kind of wasted. The player never gets to make a meaningful moral choice like "can I avoid committing this crime without blowing my cover?". Every mission and plot point is fully scripted, and some players may find themselves disagreeing with Wei's choices.

This is certainly a novel concept, pinball mixed with an RPG. If I were to judge, I'd say it's heavier on pinball than RPG, since there's little customization to be done, just upgrading, and there's not much in the way of sidequests. The game is also pretty short, to its detriment - a maaaaybe 3 hour campaign and only a few arena challenges otherwise. I do think this is an enjoyable game though, as someone who isn't very good at pinball. The tables add more complexity as the game goes on and there are a few interesting fights at the end of the game, though the very last table of the game is a bit... ehh, difficulty spike-ish, to say the least. It's not too hard overall though. The plot is alright, not that special and on the short side of things, but alright. The voice acting is hit-or-miss, some of them sound alright and a lot more sound reeeally bad. Graphically it's fine and musically it's fine though nothing to write home about.
My interest in this stemmed almost exclusively from the interesting concept, and I think it's well executed, but I feel a longer runtime and a bit more variety would've made this a better game. The extra arena challenges don't appeal much to me - I tried a few and didn't feel like doing any more of them, they're okay, they give the game some replay value I guess. I'd say get this on sale but probably not at full-price unless you're a crazed pinball fan.
