I just finished the campaign so I figured I should write a few words about my impressions. I like pinball games a lot and I'm a huge fan of the RPG genre so when I had an opportunity to play a demo of this game at Momocon I was intrigued. When I saw it discounted during Steam's Summer Sale I bit.
I don't regret this purchase, and I don't think I would even at the current listed price of $9.99.  Rollers of the Realm is a fun combination of both pinball and RPG. The characters were enjoyable and the storylline was simple and not terribly original, but honestly better than what I expected from a pinball RPG.
The game play was usually enjoyable. I say usually, because the level design is pretty inconsistent and some levels are far less fun than others. There is an art to designing a good pinball table. One which the designers didn't study too hard because they hit upon the basics of a good table rarely enough that I suspect the better tables were more accidental than deliberate.  Only a few are actually awful, but the majority of tables are just kind of "Meh." They're mostly very simplistic and don't have much variety to them. Pinball machines tend to be hella elaborate.
Some characters are more fun than others as well, with half my roster comprised of characters that I never used unless all the cooler characters died.
Which brings me to my biggest complaint about the game. Because enemies damage your flippers pretty quickly later in the game, I was required to play the Healer far more than I would have liked to. While there's a few other characters that can heal the flippers, the Healer is really the only one that can do it well enough to be worthwhile.  This greatly reduced my ability to play the other characters and really frustrated me since the Healer doesn't even have any fun abilities to use while playing her. No multi-balls, no ranged attacks.
Minor annoyances were the game being fairly miserly with gold and a sequences of levels that without warning locks you out of grinding the previous levels for more gold and experience until you beat them (with a x3 annoyance multiplier when combined with the fact that when you lose a level you don't get to keep anything from them).
Ultimately, this is a fun and fairly unique game that could have been much, much better with some better design choices. It's worth playing in its own right, but I dearly hope either a sequel or knock off comes along and improves on the formula.

Pros:
+ Graphical Components are above average (even on "Fantastic" settings, there are still a number of visual oddities)
+ Story elements are solid, albeit somewhat predictable
+ Romance options are an interesting addition
+ Multiple potential endings, including fail-state endings
+ New Game Plus mode provides some incentive for replay
+ Requires a modest amount of strategy/planning to create an appropriate team build
+ Dat "traitor" moment tho
Cons:
- *Very* Repetitive Combat
- Character appearances are unchanging regardless of armor (aside from starting a new protagonist in New Game Plus)
- Missed opportunities for dialogue options for romance partners or even "favored allies" to make the grind more appealing
- No Base-Building/Expanding (Those wooden shacks are your life now and forever)
- Apart from Romance Partners and two other characters, All survivors you meet become bland and forgettable after their introduction scene/individual mission.
- No option for female protagonist/male romance options
- No true "Exploration", just wave after wave of enemies
All in all, I would definitely say the game is worth the money and is an interesting step towards a game style that I'd like to see more of in the future. It would've been nice to see Exploration mode be the actual exploring of environments rather than "ON TO THE NEXT STAGE" and "Maybe something different will happen that provides a % chance of a skill you may or may not have to grant you 1 extra line of dialogue that may or may not hurt or help you). Essentially, it's turned the "Random Encounter" aspect of the JRPG  genre into the primary focus of the game (or at the very least where you spend the vast majority of your time in the game) instead of building up relationships with characters through events. I would've expected the personality-void nameless "Sheriff" to have only been a tutorial character but boy was I wrong and not in the way I would've liked...

I'll start this off with a TL;DR: The game is worth every penny and much more. It is an amazing game. You owe it to yourself to play and you will regret it if you do not.
By far one of the best games I have ever played. Everything, and I mean everything, in this game just works so well together. The beautiful art is complemented by the wonderful character graphics. The soundtrack is amazing; it works so well with the graphics to add more depth and feeling to the story, and the narrator is simply amazing. He narrates almost every action that you make, making you want to actually run around the maps trying to get him to say something else.
The creators didn't try to stick every single idea they could come up with into the game, but instead sculpted a work of art that fits perfectly within its bounds and does only what it is supposed to do: entertain you for hours and nothing more. The game controls are simple and elegant on keyboard and mouse, but feel a bit different than normal on default controller bindings. The story is interesting and is only enhanced by the narrators voice. The game art is truly a work of art, and the soundtrack is amazing. All the elements of the game tie in perfectly to produce a well oiled machine that will not disappoint. The gameplay is pretty easy at the beginning but once you start adding idols to increase the difficulty even further things really get interesting. This is a game that you will always remember and will be an amazing experience to play because of how well every element of it complements the others. If nothing else the visuals and soundtrack of the game alone merit buying the game.

If you like the whole tycoon style of gaming, this isn't one to be overlooked!
Basic outline of the game:
The game has you start in your garage, you work for free (because you're that kind of guy!) and you possibly hire a few guys to help you out.  You research new graphical and sound techniques to keep up with the trends and work your way up in to a gaming powerhouse with your own motion capture studios and graphical studios, even being your own production company!
The similarities between this and other games of this genre such as Game Dev Tycoon and Game Dev Story are many, the mechanics are the same, the goals are the same and you research the same sort of technology, genres etc.  The difference comes in that it feels a bit more in depth, it isn't just 3 sliders to determine what goes in to the game, there are a few more sliders, but the same sort of thing! Of course it does look a bit prettier as well, less like a Windows 8 store game and more like a real game, so it has eye candy going in its favour too.
Being early access it still has room for improvement and I'm sure it will come. Is it worth £10.99? At the moment, probably not, I don't feel it has enough "pull" to keep me going for a long time, but £5.99 sure, I couild see that being a reasonable price in the current position (at time of review).

Ittle Dew is a compact, Zelda-like experience that's appropriate for kids and adults. It also comes packed with a sense of humor and plenty of optional puzzles should the main story not satisfy your thirst for solving. The game also encourages multiple runs and has achievements encouraging different styles of play.
You can expect to wield four different tools that interact with each other different and have special properties waiting to be used. One of my favorite moments in Ittle Dew was the time I discovered how to launch enemies into the heavens by accident. These tools also add variety to the combat with their different applications.
The combat seems okay for the most part. A certain few enemy types are not easily dispatched which can be annoying if you're stuck in a room with four of them. For some reason, there's some awkwardness when using the stick/sword for fighting. I tend to bump into enemies a lot before striking, but the game is forgiving with death (and failed puzzles) and only resets the room.
The art design is clean and cutesy. I do enjoy how the trees are very animated. The colors are well chosen. I have no complaints here.
Ittle Dew will provide quite a bit of entertainment depending on your skill level with its puzzles. You'll probably have a good time and if you're stuck, call on Tippsie or refer to a guide if even Tippsie can't help you. I highly recommend collecting the in-game card collectibles as you play. They're quite funny.

The generally accepted reason for why there aren’t more games like The Legend Of Zelda is that they’re just too hard to make. Ocarina Of Time is still widely accepted as the best game ever made, but that in itself implies that its creation was not a trivial task. There have been attempts to copy the formula, from early titles like Golden Axe Warrior through to Alundra, 3D Dot Game Heroes, and Ōkami, but not only are these efforts rare but they’ve generally been commercial failures.
That is likely to be the real reason for the lack of similar games, but such market realities are not something that indie developers generally worry about. Which is good because, despite a few caveats, Ittle Dew is one of the most enjoyable Zelda-a-likes we’ve played in years.
Despite what it may look like Ittle Dew is not a straight clone, but it does have perhaps the most legitimate excuse for copying another game: comedy. Ittle Dew isn’t just a love letter to the Zelda games it’s also a parody of them, and its spunky heroine Ittle and her Navi stand-in Tippsie (a wonderfully cynical magic fox) gently poke fun at the series’ specific peculiarities and those of gaming in general.
Tippsie in particular is hilarious, as she reacts with varying degrees of disgust to ordinary Zelda tropes, such as Ittle eating a heart to get more health to her quaffing potions when she’s not looking. Joking about smashing pots and what enemies do all day as they stand around in lonely dungeons may seem like obvious targets, but as we’ve often lamented games are strangely reticent to ever poke fun at their sillier traditions.
The jovial mood is enhanced further by the wonderful visuals, but despite the art style being very different from any official Zelda game overall Ittle Dew still ends up looking lawyer-worryingly similar. The game is scheduled for release on Wii U later in the year though so we assume that Nintendo gets the joke as well.
Ittle has a much more mercenary approach to her explorations than Link, happily stuffing her pockets with treasure as she goes about adventuring. Even the artefact she’s trying to obtain from a nearby castle is only to bribe a shopkeeper to build her a ship to get home. Although he does at least offer to sell her three items vital to her mission: a fire sword, an ice wand, and a portal-creating magic wand.
Unusually for a Zelda game these are the only three items in the whole game, which is certainly a bold choice. But despite all the puzzles being solved using only one or more of the items it’s disappointing that the meat of most of them still revolves around pushing blocks and hitting switches. In the traditional manner there are torches and bombs to be lit, pressure pads to stand on, and doors to unlock.
The puzzles might not be very imaginative but they are well designed and often have multiple solutions. You can even beat the entire game using any random combination of just two of the items. Some of the puzzles are very hard but the game isn’t interested in punishing you, only challenging you, and there’s a wide range of helpful hints given out by Tippsie.
The dungeon-like areas are very much the focus of the game and although there are overworld areas they’re smaller and less interactive than real Zelda games. The combat is also significantly less interesting, being barely any more nuanced than the original NES game and offering zero reward beyond extra health. The bosses are a mostly decent bunch though and also get some of the best lines.
Ittle Dew is rather short, at around three to four hours, although you’ll need much longer to collect everything and beat the optional Master Cave (the only truly difficult challenge in the whole thing). But for only a tenner you get a download that is not only fun but funny – a game that is amusingly self-aware but uses this as a means to enhance the experience and not just make excuses for it.

While the game is good if you're a fan of terraria, it suffers from a few problems.
1. The game was overhyped to hell and back. This was mostly because of features PLANNED, not on release.

4. As different the planets may seem, they rarely differ in any meaningful way aside from resource types.
5. Monsters are nice and all, but you can never tell if a monster is strong or weak based on how they look. How I mean that is a strong monster never "looks" strong, and a weak-looking monster can destroy you.
But hey, can't be 100% negative right?
The game has a pretty tight building system that kind of solved the problem that Terraria had which was the limited range and speed at which you could build. In Terraria the aesthetic of your buildings releied mostly on your skill and creativity as a builder, but in Starbound you can build much more freely and easily.

This game has pretty much perfected its genre. It has a depth that no other game development sims have. The skill floor is just low enough to be able to jump in with just a little help from the tutorial, while the skill ceiling is unimaginably high. There are many ways to increase the efficiency of game production, from assigning staff to certain departments, making sure you're fitting the current trend, and even having a reasonable office layout. The different kind of company you can be also beats out any of the game's competition. You don't even have to rely solely on games. You can produce state-of-the-art engines and license them, you can be a games publisher, and you can even be a console producer and just make a first party game every once in a while.
All in all, this game is thoroughly enjoyable and a definite must have for any fan of game dev sims. 9/10 in its current state.

TL;DR Fallout 4 is a great shooter, but an awful Fallout game.
Fallout 4 is the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of the 3d Fallout games so far.  Fallout 3 was experimental, and worked pretty well despite being a little empty.  Fallout New Vegas improved on every aspect in 3, and forged itself a completely new identity as a true RPG.  Fallout 4...didnt do either of these.
Pros : Fallout 4 was fun, I'll admit.  I've sunk 500+ hours in the game, so I think I have some precedent to my opinion.  As a shooter it shines, and I'd daresay if this wasn't a "Fallout" game, people would be much more receptive to it.
Cons : As an RPG, it flops.  The skill system is difficult to keep track of, and the menu for it just feels bulky.  The dialogue is limited as hell, and the story itself just isn't engaging.  In my 500+ hours, I've never even entered the second act of the game.  It's also worth noting that a lot of the content for the building aspect of the game - one of it's big selling points - are locked behind DLC.
Truly, if you can pick Fallout 4 up for $20 do it, I don't think you'd regret it.  However don't go into this expecting New Vegas depth or the memorability of 3.

The game is still in development, which means more is going to be added to it between now and when it's actually finished. That said, even if this were the finished product and there were no more updates to be had, I would STILL recommend this game.
The game is very similar to Terraria, a lot of the same people worked on both so that makes sense. There's a lot different, though. The most obvious aspect is that you're not bound to just one planet, and you get a ship that's enemy-free from the get-go. The other important differences are that you begin on a relatively harmless planet and progress the difficulty at your own pace, which makes this game far more relaxed than Terraria could ever be. Starbound also has quests and missions, so you have a pretty good idea of what to do- as opposed to being dropped in the middle of nowhere to figure it out on your own.
So far, there's still a lot of content that hasn't crossed over that I can tell- there's no way to keep from losing pixels when you die (at the very least), the crafting/cooking system seems much more limited and I haven't yet discovered traps either in natural settings or player created. I'm hoping that some of that is remedied in a future update, but even without it I still like the game as it is.
Players that struggle to gain headway in Terraria will find this a breath of fresh air. Players that really thrived in Terraria's harsh environment might feel under-challenged here, as the game really only barely lives up to Terraria's pre-hardmode complexity. However, Terraria didn't always have hardmode, so it's entirely likely that Starbound will increase in complexity over time as well. Keep this in mind when you make your purchase, because rating the game for what it is right now neglects these very likely possibilities for future versions.

This is to pinball as Puzzle Quest is to Bejeweled. If you like pinball then it's definitely worth a look.
As a weak to middling pinball player who still enjoys pinball games, the great thing about this game is that progressing through the levels actually provides a sense of achievement, instead of trying to beat your own score vainly trying to complete the minor objectives of a regular pinball table.
The RPG elements are well done - each ball/character has a specific use and it's nice to be able to build up the capabilities of the ones that fit my playing style.
The way that combat works on the tables is neat. Approaching enemies create a real sense of impending doom because they drastically increase the likelihood that you'll drain your ball, but you also need to worry about archers damaging your flippers, so you need to juggle your targets and characters.
The major downside of this game is the balance often feels a little off - trick shots don't feel like they're very tricky, or otherwise simple levels feel like they're nearly impossible.

Sleeping Dogs takes the fighting mechanics from Batman, the open-world sandbox of GTA, the slow-motion shooting of Max Payne, the in-motion vehicle-stealing abilities of Pursuit Force and the driving fun of some other game and blends them together to make one of the most enjoyable games I've played in years.
It's a story of a cop gone undercover to infiltrate a gang of Triads in Hong Kong. The graphics are outstanding, the story is solid, the voice acting top-notch, the character animations well above average and everything comes together to give you a AAA gaming experience like no other.
The game is relatively short (~20 hours) and the map is not as big as other similar games, but what this game has is "game-play density". Everything has been thought about long and hard and there is no unwanted fat in the game anywhere.
Sleeping Dogs breaks no new ground, but everything it borrows from is blended together with such skill that by the end you're left fully satisfied. Nine thumbs up.

I have to traverse map to map sections just to meet my quota! Oh. And some times are too generous. 25 Real time minutes is pretty much 2 shifts. But when your first shift ends, that progress is lost. Be alittle more less lenient on times..... And...Less illegally parked cars...More drugs and gang violance.
Progression. So far, I'm liking the rank tree and the standard 'Gain certain amount of EXP/Score' to rank up. Maybe unlock more uniforms/Vehicles/Housing and such as you level up. Hell. Driving. Okay. So far. This will be the main negative part for this. I took a car out, and I swear I was falling into a 'Back to the Future' Moment. Gently press the accelerate button...And...Atleast a second later. 99MPH..... I had to immediantly slam on the breaks to slow down. Heck. At one point I was going in reverse so fast I had to slam the handbreak on as accelerating did nothing! This requires quite abit of tweaking! And the car repair costs are manic, not just because its expensive, its more that its difficult to NOT hit anything. Cruise helps. But. Eh.
A.I. Uh. Its not great, but its not so bad either. Maybe some more character models for look. They're not so bad walking, they just horrific when driving. Stop one car, the one behind slams into it and slowly (And painfully) Tries to continue moving. Usually people stop as soon as they hit a car, (Or see a policeman giving a ticket to the person in front.) A bit of an intelligence tweak may be required on the drivers.
Customisation? Meh. Five off duty uniforms. Two on duty uniforms. Not great. Maybe add shopping here? Or a new flashy uniform when you rank up? Only one house. Little customisation. An expensive fridge does little to no better than your cheap stock one.
Overall Verdict? So far. So good. Alot of tweaks to be made. It does in its own way feel unique. Realistic. And none of that 'Good cop, Bad Cop' rubbish. (Though kicking in doors is quite a good one without caring for minor loss points.)
Improvements?
- A much stronger progression system. Maybe additional uniforms per promotion. Access to more equipment.
- The cars. The speed is an issue. If I go any faster, I might break the time barrier and see the game in the future.
- A.I. Yeah. Intelligence Tweak when driving.
- Either friendly Police A.I to assist you (Seriously, Can't be the only policeman in this valley right?) Or impliment a co-op feature (Though give that time, Co-Op and multiplayer is when the game is a good few builds away from completion)
Overall. Keep it up. And keep going!

Sort of like Cortex Command meets Soldat meets Metal Slug, a sidescrolling shooter with lots of physics. A good attempt at a great idea, but it got old fast for me. The physics routinely become a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥with somewhat arbitrary behavior and giant piles of detritus which bury things you want to reach and are hard to climb around on. The whole game feels floaty and the weapons are largely anemic little things with projectiles that waft gently through the air and barely offer any feedback on whatever they do manage to hit; sound design is pretty poor, including decent but way, way too short music loops. Level 1's boss is absolutely fantastic, but level 2's boss was annoying, and level 3's boss drove me to give up and uninstall the game. The most fun I had with it was piloting a mech equipped with a grappling arm and a big sword; they probably could have made a more solid game just out of that idea. It's alrightish overall I guess, if you're more patient than I am with 10-minutes-at-a-time boss fights, or many, many attempts at them when said boss just bumps you off a cliff to your immediate death. I'd have to give it something like a 6/10.

Regarding the Add-On "War of the Chosen (WotC)":
Just like before with X COM:Enemy Unkown & Enemy Within, the game itself stayed basicly the same.
However! instead of just getting Mecha-Upgrade for your soldiers and 1 new cutscene, the entire game has been modified and expanded by 3 new factions (soldier types) that can now be sent into battle.
- The Reaper (Sniper always cloaked; but with a chance to reveal himself when using an action)
- The Skirmish (Automated Handpistol who can fire twice a round for 1 action)
- The Templar (Psionic Warriors; with Warblades, like the Protoss in Starcraft or Elites in Halo)
The game now has the Resistance Ring, which allows you to set PERKS that effects your overall stats, decisions, incomines AND most of all COVERT ACTIONS; where you sent troops away for X days to gather information, unlock new "Quests"; bring you back supplies, upgrades, perm. Armor/Weapon+ stats; Instant research and plenty more.
You can now TRAIN your soldiers abilities in the Training Center, giving you the chance to learn all stats instead of choosing between one of two (or three) while earning these points in the field from specific actions (Kill a Nemesis, overcome a fear, Death from Above; Multiple Grenade kills...)
But most of all, the Chosen:
3 empored Warriors are set to hunt you and will frequently  visit you on your missions to make it tougher on you;
in order to stop them - you need to use above said Resistance Ring to track down their facilities and take em out for good.
Is it fun? Hell Yeah.
Is it XCom? FRAK yes
Overall enjoyable and recommandable? FRAK YES
The AddOn Takes XCom2 and makes it an entire new game, which in my opinion is worth the 30-40$ ;
because if you enjoyed X2 - you will enjoy WotC even more

Serena is probably the best indie horror game I have ever played in my life. This was such a great game with a lot of amazing things. What I liked about the game was; the graphics, the music, the voice acting, the erie suspense thrill feel, and the mystery surrounding around the characters girlfriend/ or wife, Serena.
What I didn't like about this game was these three things;
1. I didn't like the click and point movement. I'd rather prefer using w,a,s,d or the arrow keys to move the character(s). Though it was interesting to click and move, I'd rather have control of the character(s) that I'm playing as.
2. I didn't like that you couldn't explore the outside world to find some extra clues or events to the story. What I mean about not exploring the outside world is this; everytime I clicked on the front door of the house/ or cabin, the character would say, "I have to wait for Serena" or something among those lines. Yet though he said something about an outhouse near the house/ or cabin, also later in the game he says he sees some shadows, and later than that he says he sees the trees and sunlight.
And 3. The story was way too short. I like games the go way deep into stories, getting to know what happens to the characters, find some twists and turns, and move on to the next chapter/ or part of the story.
Overall, I would rate this game a 7 out of 10 stars, 6 thumbs up, and I highly recommend this game. It's a good suspense, thrill, and erie ride. Personal opinion: I would like to see some DLC (Downloadable Content) for this game. In some of the Downloadable Content, I would like to see the Serena, video game soundtrack, the digital artbook, trading cards, etc... and I probably would purchase them.

I wrote this originally in reply to a thread about "Why doesn't this game have more players?"  Here's my answer in the form of a brief review.  TL;dr at the bottom.
Master of Orion has the same problem that a taco product called "Big Mac II" has. In that it hoped to sell copies and maintain a playerbase using a particular brandname while doing fairly little to honor the substance of what its named after.
It's not that it's a buggy mess--though there are things that could be improved. It's not that the game is too short (I'm in a 500 turn game right now...I am still only 3/4 of the way through the tech tree and realistically, I couldn't have ended the game before now either...there's still content for me to explore even after that many turns in just one game).
The one thing the game is absolutely missing for me, and its a real shame, is that Real-Time battles are absent in multiplayer...you can still play a full multiplayer game and use the game's autoresolve function, but it really sucks the fun out of it for me, personally. So I play SP and just like any SP strategy game...once you figure out the AI's tricks, you can't really lose unless you are going to mod it or enable cheats for it or something.
Anyway, about purchasing the game:
If you are someone who has never played a Master of Orion game before, you are going to have a great time. Especially if you like or are interested in Stellaris and Sins of a Solar Empire. However, if you played Master of Orion (the original from the early days of computer gaming) or its actual sequel Master of Orion II, then you will probably hate this game. It's not turn-based like the originals, its combat, for better or worse is real-time and certain decisions about how to place your ships, for example, aren't as important as they used to be. The decisions you make in battle are really about which ship should fire at what enemy ship.
You still have enough influence to say, take a battle you were "supposed" to lose according to the little victory probability bar, and then through good management, win that battle. BUT it's not as significant as in previous Master of Orion titles. There are just some engagements you cannot win, and from what I remember about the originals that was rarely the case--you could win as an underdog, and even against the AI a technological advantage didn't guarantee victory. This made battles exciting, even against less developed AI empires. To a certain degree that's missing here in this title. Yes, you have influence over battles that you're commanding...no, you aren't going to defeat the Antarans with anything less than the end tier weapon and defense tech...there's just no way mathematically for your ships to do it.
Some people saw that as a major regression and not a real advantage of Real-Time battles and abandoned the title.
TL;DR:
So in summary: Good game if you come from it with a clean slate. It has AAA graphics and voice acting, and despite a few examples is bug free and performs well on a technical level. The real time battles suffer from the same issues as Total War: you have influence over the outcome if you command them BUT there are just some units you can create (or face off against) that WILL beat you no matter what because of their stats. Even so, it's definitely a good game for 2016/2017 and has no major drawbacks that aren't drawbacks in any of the other Turn-Based/Real Time hybrid strategy games.
That said, it's a bad Master of Orion game, much like a taco is a bad hamburger. If you are buying it for nostalgic purposes, you are going to be disappointed. There are probably other games that are better spiritual successors, ironically enough.

I had Bastion on my iPhone years ago, played it for 5 minutes, got frustrated with the touch controls, switched it off and never gave it another thought.
A couple of days ago I picked it up very cheap in the Steam holiday sale along with a couple of other games - with my main intention of building my Steam collection while it was so cheap to be honest. Once it had downloaded I decided to fire it up and give it a go. 8 hours later it was 7am and I couldn't believe it had taken me so long to play this game.
You play as "the kid" exploring a shattered world which literally pieces back together as you progress. The game itself is a top down action RPG and plays exactly how you would expect a good action RPG to play - melee combat with the kids trusty hammer, dodge rolls and sneaky shots in with my bow and arrow came almost as second nature to me and I felt at home with the combat system almost instantly. These aren't the only weapons for you to enjoy though, not by a long shot! You'll be prodding things with a spear, shooting dual pistols cowboy style, among a fair few others it even has you firing mortars to take down your enemies. The game introduces the weapons to you separately throughout the story which you are then free to use as you like - giving you ample opportunity to play however you want. I mixed it up quite a bit throughout my first play through and did not find a single weapon I don't like.
The story itself is rather short, but sweet. I think the it took me around 6 hours to complete the first time round. Finishing the story unlocks Newgame+ which allows you to start again at the level you finished at with all your weapons etc. I am currently working through this mode now, I started it straight after I finished my first play through - which is rare for me!
The game is a real gem, one that I almost missed out on! Thank you Steam sale!

A fun little puzzle game with nice artwork.  Don't let the screenshots or heavily inspired Link to the Past aesthetic fool you though, Ittle Dew is about 98% block puzzles and 2% other stuff.  Do not go into this expecting an action-rpg or some kind of dungeon romp with the occasional puzzle.  It's all puzzles and your enjoyment of them will make or break the game for you.
There are three items used in puzzles: fire sword, ice wand and portal blocks/teleportation.  This isn't anywhere as limiting as it may seem and the game's puzzle design is very tight and well-done.  Ittle Dew gets a lot of mileage with the different ways it incorporates using the tools together to solve puzzles.  I didn't realize until after I finished it that you can beat the game by only collecting two of the three items and with any combination of the two.   It adds a ton of replay value for future playthroughs.  The game also has "shortcut paths", basically hard puzzles that you can use to skip chunks of the game and beat it in less than twenty minutes if you know what to do.  Stuff like beating the game with different combos of items and the shortcut puzzles are cool mechanics/design decisions and I like to seeing them even if I don't necessary plan on ever using them myself.
The cartoony art is very nice and vivid.  The UI is simple and efficient.  You don't have to walk out of a room to reset a failed puzzle, you can just hit start and hit reset room to save yourself the needless back and forth you'd find in similar games.  The game lets you know how many items are in each area and most collectible item rooms will let you know if you have the correct item to solve the puzzle so you don't spend time beating your head against the wall trying to solve a puzzle you don't have the right item for.  There's just a lot of little things the game does to make playing it a non-aggravating experience.
In short, if you're down with games that heavily involve pushing blocks and solving puzzles, you'll probably have a solid time with Ittle Dew.  Just don't head into it expecting a Zelda-ish game.

Oops... after 1324 hours of Starbound, I forgot to write a review, Oh silly me. I'm too busy modding Starbound and building an awesome tower dungeon (which requires above mod) to click on the "Write a Review" hyperlink. Well I somehow wound up here, and I'm going to review it, so here goes:
I would have to say that Starbound is one of the most moddable games I've ever played. The features are rich, as we get exploration, dungeon crawls, treasure hunting, and fun silly stuff to boot. (As of this review, the colonization update has not been released on the Unstable/Stable development branches, so it will not be included, but I will post an update after it is released on Stable.) The in-game quests seem a bit mundane except for the mission quests, which is acceptable to me as a beta, as it does not spoil the unfinished content as much.
Multiplayer is fun when I can host a server and people wind up joining, otherwise I'm soloing in Single Player mode building who knows what crazy project I have planned, or on multiplayer mode multi-boxing a music band testing songs I've splintered out into seperate instruments, and showing them on YouTube or Steam Broadcast streams, which is also my second favorite feature of this game, believe it or not. In addition, there are plenty of large servers out there to join. (Many use Creeperhost to host them now, as it is its official server host)
Now stumbling to my favorite part. The customization! An novice-level dream for would-be level designers who has very limited programming experience, but a lot of ambition patience, and focus. There are so many block tiles, platform tiles, interactive objects, logic gates, etc. that will satisfy any level designer.
If you want to start modding the game, learning JSON (Javascript Object NotatioN, practically a way to modify, manage, and extend the game's data files) has a small learning curve, but it is very easy to learn compared to a programming language. I suggest you check out xSwatelitex's guides on the Starbound Forums if you would like to try your hand at it. It is well worth it and it expands your Starbound options to build the game the way you want to. It also features a limited Lua API for advanced modding many other aspects of the game, like AI behavior, objects, etc. Lua, since it is a actual programming language,  is more complex than learning/mastering JSON, but the rewards are well worth the effort, (I still haven't learned to use Lua myself yet, so I'm in the dark too.)
Either way you put it, this game has something to offer for nearly everyone. Casual and intermediate players can enjoy the game hunting, dungeon crawling, story quests and missions, building homes, towns, and other far out projects.
Advanced players can take advantage of its huge modding potential to make some great things.
I hope to see what some of you guys come up with!

First things first with this review, I do indeed RECOMMEND buying Fallout 4 only if it is on Sale. The reason as to why I am not recommending it is because of the recent Creation Club update is otherwise known as “Paid Mods”. I used to say “Just ignore it, it will not do us any harm whatsoever”, I was wrong about that. If you plan to mod Fallout 4 after playing the main game (Which I highly recommend) and eventually you will need to use F4SE (Fallout 4 Script Extender) so certain mods can be compatible. Now, the reason I was wrong about the whole “Ignore CC, and just use Nexus Mods” is because of the recent CC Update which added some more trash unnecessary mods it tampered with F4SE and at least half of the Fallout 4 community (I think) couldn’t play the game unless you downgraded it and we had to wait maybe two days until the good folks that made F4SE updated the script extender. So with all that out the way, let's get this review going!
To start things off, the storyline of this installment of Fallout 4 is very…. different and generic. In Fallout 3 (First Fallout game I started with), you were a Vault Dweller who escaped your Vault 101 in search of your father who is a scientist and you eventually come across BoS (Brotherhood of Steel); With Fallout New Vegas, you were just an ordinary Courier (Or so you thought) what was meant to send a very imperative package but also eventually get intercepted by a mobster who shoots you in the head but you amazingly survived and sought out revenge (I won’t disclose the rest of the information cause I want to focus on Fallout 4’s Storyline with this paragraph). Now in Fallout 4, you play as an ordinary human being enjoying the cliche “American Dream” in a beautiful modernized America until the Bombs drop and you are to flee to the Vault you registered your family in, Vault 111.
I will leave off the rest of the details of Fallout 4 since with all this given information, now you should already understand that Fallout 4 took a real massive turn away from the storyline of Fallout.
One thing I really want to touch upon is the graphics! It took a really huge step forward in a good way of course. This is really great for modders and people that plan to mod Fallout 4. Not only that but it’s something different that’s been actually wanted since Fallout New Vegas and seeing Bethesda do this was really eye-opening when it was shown at E3.
The combat is pretty alright, pretty alright as in it’s the same nothing much changed within it in my eyes after playing Fallout 3 and New Vegas. However, one of the most imperative features that were in the Fallout franchises which is the Karma system is no longer in Fallout 4 which is very disappointing. One neat thing they added is motion during VATS, I say this is neat because I felt like stopping the game and picking which body part to shoot while you’re not getting hit was a bit …much.
So once again, I do in fact recommend Fallout 4 however, buy it when it is on sale or if you see a really good price on G.2A and such. No one should suffer paying 30 bucks for a game in which you’re forced to update your game because of Paid Mods that you don't associate yourself in buying.
Disclaimer: I’m pretty new at reviewing games so if this review felt linear or boring or certain parts were unnecessary then please do let me know any feedback to improve my reviews in the future.

While commonly and quickly given the title "Terraria in Space," and yes it does appear to be that at surface level, Starbound is actually a fairly different game with some very different content and gameplay focuses. It also carries with it a good focus on combat, with many updates building and reworking the fighting mechanics to fit different styles and situations. My main gripe with the game is that it isn't updated as often as it should be (at least that was the case for a while), and when they do, hardly any of content added adds much to gameplay. While it may be nice to see new accessories and visual changes added as filler for smaller updates, it is a little more disheartening when they are practically all that makes up some major updates. Don't get me wrong, there are some kick♥♥♥♥♥things added to this game, it is just that there is a lot of filler that doesn't add much more than a few hours to gameplay.
Overall, I had really good fun with this game and would recommend it.

Intrusion 2 is a 2D platforming physics-based shooter with a whole lot of jank and even more heart. It's flashy (heh heh... it's made in Flash, also...), it's bold, and it's fun as hell. It's difficult. It's rewarding. Sometimes, it's downright frustrating. But it's an amazing game.
The pacing is top-notch, the game successfully funneling you through dozens upon dozens of enemies, mini-bosses, and tough as hell big bad boss baddies, while keeping you entertained with unique landscapes and new weapons. The level variety is good, with a couple missions having you restricted in various ways.
There's no real story to speak of, but that's alright: you don't need to know anything except you're a badass hero, you have an array of awesome guns, and you've got to kill all the things you see. The soundtrack, however, is top-notch; full of overdriven electric guitar and crazy riffs, you'll never stop jamming out as you unload thousands and thousands of bullets into enemies.
The whole package leads up to one of the best boss fights and one of the best levels I have ever had the fortune to play through, culminating in a long, difficult (but not unfair) boss fight against an enemy unlike anything you've faced yet.
Intrusion 2 isn't on many people's radars, and that's a shame. Do yourself a favor and pick this up as soon as you can if you want a roller coaster ride of adrenaline, shooting, and great music. The game can be a little janky in spots, but it more than makes up for it. It's not too long, it's not too short, and it never bores you.

The survival-RPG we have been waiting for...this game has so many different mechanics so I just list the games in the review and you can make your own assumption-easier on my sanity and hatemail and easier on you. Win Win.
First off, the graphics are amazing. Yes, yes I know...Jesus K, graphics mean crap all in a game, but in one at this price point with this content...the dev team did a fantastic job with the ambiance, character models and sound. Well done!
Now the game...you're the usual survivor in the usual town, after the usual zombie apocolypse decends on Earth and the usual case to find safety.
What's not usual?---It's all turn base...no real time so, for those who DO NOT like JRPG/turn base final fantasy/chronotrigger-esque game play then go away, this gem is not for your jewelry box.

For those who stayed....the team did one hell of a jb marrying the best aspects of 2 of the best games in their respective genres...Turn base strategy/RNG battle system a la the original final fantasy on the NES, and the RPG/survivor sim of state of decay.
The UI took me a few to get use to and understand what did what and why, but after about a solid 15 minutes and several re-starts due to deaths, I felt like an expert.
Speaking of death, how about some perma-death!! $%# yes baby!! None of that endless wandering and letting health regen, popping that phoenix down on a fallen party member...nope not here....you screw up, they die. This single mechanic is SO lacking in today's game cycle...Seriously folks. Any fire emblem fan knows EXCATLY what I'm talking about. Character attachment? Check. Favorites you try to coddle but make killing machines? Check. Throw mouse when said fav character gets killed because you were a little too brave doing that one extra battle versus going back to camp? CHECK BABY! Add to that the skill/job system building kinda sorta but not really from final fantasy 3 and then the camp-defending set up of state of decay. While it isn't always you battle whatever evil attacks your camp, it's more about assigning the guard job and the RNG will decide your fate...oh wheel of morality, turn, turn turn...
The story is obviously bland, but the script is entertaining and dragging at the same time...not the terrible "you were almost a JIll sandwich" kind of script, but not Skyrim either. This has a story I'm interested in seeing to the end, not bleeding out of my eyes reading it.
Since I'm not a spoiler kinda guy, you'll have to do your own research/homework/video watching to decide, but for the cost versus game play and every scenario/job/quest/survivor encounter is RNG controlled, it never feels like the same game when I die several times and obviously re start.
Give it a try....I'm usually pretty leary of titles like this but hot damn is it worth the admission price..
Now, if you'll excuse me...me and my besties have some zombie cheerleaders to roast with molotovs, and some crafting material to gather...

Descent: Road To Legend, is an absolute gem and shining example of the potential technology and board games can create together. With a team of up to 4 players you can play through either the short tutorial campaign, or the expansive Kindred Flame quest, which can be experienced over a session lasting days! with a convenient save feature and Exp/Item Tracker so you can pick up from where you left off anytime!
Each Quest in Descent is a challenging experience which will put your teamwork and strategy to the test with randomly generated enemies and encounters that can keep you on your feet the whole time around, your mettle will be tested but it is a rewarding experience after all the hard work!
However the games flaws can mainly be player induced, the lack of certain features can lead to some frustrating scenarios. If somehow you may have jumped the gun and mis clicked, the game does not have an undo system of any kind so you will be stuck with any mistakes you have made. so make sure you have somebody aware and not clumsy at the helm of the app!
Perphaps another minor flaw is that the entire game requires alot of reading, which can pause progress signifcantly and effect game flow, i feel like an option for a narrator would not go amiss! as the Quest Introductions demostrate some pretty decent voice acting! And one which makes me kind of wish the characters were speaking within the game for immersions sake! Though this is more a personal opinion then a game flaw.
Overall: If your a fan of Dungeon Delving, with a level of sadism where you love a challenge Descent is the game for you, though if you have a bad team this game may present alot of frustration for you. it can still be a fun time none the less.

A great (and free!) way to enjoy the Descent 2nd edition boardgame, whether solo or with up to 3 friends.
Word of warning, though: currently ignores all campaign quest guides content (So Heirs of Blood will be useless in this app).
The app turns the Descent: Journeys in the Dark (2nd edition) boardgame into a co-op game instead of the normal heroes vs overlord style of game, by making the players simulate the monsters' movements, following a list of priorities.
The campaigns are a lot of fun, with quite a bit of flavor/lore text for everything.
The game is turned into more of a dungeon delving game, by hiding pieces of the map behind locked doors (much like fog of war, if you will), instead of building all of the map at the start of the quest.
Currently, 2 campaigns are provided, both completely free, playable both with only the base game, as well as with any expansion you bought, be them boxed expansions, Hero and Monster Collections or Lieutenants. As noted before, the Heirs of Blood campaign, as well as the 3 Co-op adventures (Forgotten Souls, Nature's Ire and Dark Elements) are incompatible with RtL, but other than that any addition you have to the base game is very welcome.
There are Main Quests, as well as side quests in these 2 campaigns, with most of the maps (from what I've noticed) being built and played differently with each playthrough, and with even more of a pool of stuff to choose from for the app with each expansion you own, adding to the differences between playthroughs even further.
Another mode, the Delve, has just been announced. This will most likely not be a campaign like the 2 others already released, but not much info has been released about it, except that it will be available with in-app purchase (DLC, basically).
All in all, I very highly recommend this app, for a new (and pretty damn cool) way to enjoy the Descent: Journeys in the Dark 2nd edition boardgame.

Sleeping Dogs takes the fighting mechanics from Batman, the open-world sandbox of GTA, the slow-motion shooting of Max Payne, the in-motion vehicle-stealing abilities of Pursuit Force and the driving fun of some other game and blends them together to make one of the most enjoyable games I've played in years.
It's a story of a cop gone undercover to infiltrate a gang of Triads in Hong Kong. The graphics are outstanding, the story is solid, the voice acting top-notch, the character animations well above average and everything comes together to give you a AAA gaming experience like no other.
The game is relatively short (~20 hours) and the map is not as big as other similar games, but what this game has is "game-play density". Everything has been thought about long and hard and there is no unwanted fat in the game anywhere.
Sleeping Dogs breaks no new ground, but everything it borrows from is blended together with such skill that by the end you're left fully satisfied. Nine thumbs up.

A simple game with a simple idea and a fairly simple execution. As per required in the independent landscape, this particular "platformer with a twist" lets you create temporary platforms that move with you when you use your camera, hence the title. It's not a bad gimmick in the slightest, but one that I never felt was fully realized during my playthrough. While some of the level layouts were fairly interesting, the only times I ever found myself stuck was when I overthought a problem. Sometimes that can be effective, but there is a difference between intellegent misdirection and mediocre level design.
To be fair, there are a few sections that did have a couple of "aha!" moments, but even though the platforming was inoffensive most times, I can't emphasize enough the missed potential here. CO shines at its brightest when the levels themselves are puzzles, and its a shame to see that the majority of the game consists mostly of cheap filler. With more control over the afterimage effects, or maybe some sort of metroidvania skill ups for the camera to add new abilities within the fiction, I feel that while the game offered here is decent enough, there is little to engage the player all the way to the end. That is the real tragedy.
So why the Yes? Two simple reasons; for all my criticisms, this is still a damn fine game. While I'd be strained to compare it to Braid or games of that nature, CO still pulses with charm that echoes ambition I haven't seen a fairly long time on this storefront. The platforming is a little stiff, but for the cheap price I keep seeing it for, I think it's a great little gem to kill some time with. The second reason is a bit more pretentious of me; Camera Obscura screams of potential, and I would love to see where this concept and its creator go from here. We all have to start somewhere, and as Anteater's first game on Steam I can't help but appreciate an inspired idea, flawed as it may be. For less than a gumball from a gumball machine, I think this game is absolutely worth giving a look. The lovely ambient soundtrack is worth the admission price alone. Definitely worth grabbing when on sale.

You are gradually introduced to an exciting game mechanic that allows you to take snapshots of the platforms around you. I had Bastion on my iPhone years ago, played it for 5 minutes, got frustrated with the touch controls, switched it off and never gave it another thought.
A couple of days ago I picked it up very cheap in the Steam holiday sale along with a couple of other games - with my main intention of building my Steam collection while it was so cheap to be honest. Once it had downloaded I decided to fire it up and give it a go. 8 hours later it was 7am and I couldn't believe it had taken me so long to play this game.
You play as "the kid" exploring a shattered world which literally pieces back together as you progress. The game itself is a top down action RPG and plays exactly how you would expect a good action RPG to play - melee combat with the kids trusty hammer, dodge rolls and sneaky shots in with my bow and arrow came almost as second nature to me and I felt at home with the combat system almost instantly. These aren't the only weapons for you to enjoy though, not by a long shot! You'll be prodding things with a spear, shooting dual pistols cowboy style, among a fair few others it even has you firing mortars to take down your enemies. The game introduces the weapons to you separately throughout the story which you are then free to use as you like - giving you ample opportunity to play however you want. I mixed it up quite a bit throughout my first play through and did not find a single weapon I don't like.
The story itself is rather short, but sweet. I think the it took me around 6 hours to complete the first time round. Finishing the story unlocks Newgame+ which allows you to start again at the level you finished at with all your weapons etc. I am currently working through this mode now, I started it straight after I finished my first play through - which is rare for me!
The game is a real gem, one that I almost missed out on! Thank you Steam sale!

This is an unreasonably good game.  I do list a few nitpicks below, but they don't wreck the game.
First, the positive: This game is cleverly designed, adorable, and a lot of fun.  I enjoyed playing it, and I hope to see a sequel someday.  The puzzles were very well-presented, giving you opportunities to learn the tools before being thrown into a terrifying challenge.  You're always ready, but the puzzles always stretch you and I, for one, walked away feeling satisfied with my accomplishments.
There are only 3 tools, and yet... the ways they're used are magnificent.  You don't have a bag of gimmicky gadgets to fumble through; instead each puzzle uses one, two or three tools in really clever ways, and I often felt brilliant when I completed them.
The main game can be defeated when you have all three tools... but you don't need all three.  You can also beat the game with any combination of only two tools, which just warps my mind.  The puzzles felt so tight and so tough, and I was amazed to discover I could complete them with even less.  There's also various side dungeons where you can pick up more health, or collect optional cards.  The real reward is the feeling of victory and the wild ego boost that comes with completing them all by yourself, simply for fun.
For a really steep challenge, there's also an optional master dungeon that requires all three tools and some really clever thinking.  I strongly recommend it.
The characters and story are adorable and funny.  I liked them.  The animations are excellent, and I loved the look and feel of Ittle's world.  I also liked Ittle herself... she's charming, if devious.  Her little flying helper is also fun.  They do a good job of making fun of their genre, while adding a lot of their own character as well (which is more important than the parody, and done well).
A few minor niggles include:
-A bit of unclarity in hitboxes and figuring out whether an attack will hit.  It's not a huge deal, since combat is secondary to the puzzles and even this issue doesn't make the combat unfun at all.
-On a couple occasions, the master dungeon pulled some unwarranted tricks, like requiring incredibly fast movement (down to the millisecond) to be in position in time to act or stop a block, which felt like a deviation from the formula that makes the game good (clever puzzle solving, not brutal platforming skill)
But the major issue?
I was intensely offended by the optional side-boss fight.  Instead of having you employ all the great tricks you've learned just to reach him, he throws ALL of that away... he is instead just a standard run & stab boss battle, and a brutally unfair one at that (I eventually gave up).  Only your sword matters; you will not use the other tools at all (trying will get you killed repeatedly).  The best strategies I've read for beating him were simply to have lots of health and be fast.  It requires incredibly tight controls, which this game doesn't have, so a lot of it is luck and cheesing bugs and quirks in the AI and movement.  This was not a good climax to the otherwise brilliantly designed master dungeon; instead it was a malicious slap in the face, and god it hurt.
It still leaves me a bit grumpy, even after all these months.  >:(
But does this ruin the game?  NO!  It felt anti-climactic and I did feel betrayed and put upon by the developers, but the rest of the game is so good, that this just fades into background noise in comparison.
9/10.  This is a fantastic game.  Yes, I'm still intensely bitter about the optional boss (RAAAAGE!!!!), but that doesn't destroy the pure, unfiltered joy that is the rest of this game.  Everything in the main game and optional dungeons, save for that side boss, is excellent.  I still look back with extreme fondness!  I'm looking forward to playing the free Halloween update soon, which was a really cool thing for them to add.

Bastion represents a triumph of style over substance.  This should be a forgettable game.  The gameplay is nothing we haven't seen before, the controls are loose, and the story is about as forgettable as they come.  But the style, oh the style.  This is a beautiful game.  This is a game with an amazing soundtrack (thank you humble bundle for providing the soundtrack too).  This is a voice with a narrator to whom I would quite happily listen to as he read the phone book.  The game is boring, but I can't stop playing because I know there's more beauty waiting for me around the next turn.
With such beauty, it's a shame that the gameplay is so bad.  This game wants to be a completely run of the mill action rpg, but the controls are just too soft.  Targeting is an exercise in frustration, dodging is a waste of time, and blocking works some times.  The enemy variety is fairly limited, and they all do the same basic thing anyway.  The weapons are sort of nifty, however, and do provide a bit of variety in the gameplay.
I also want to note that I completely approve of the color scheme.  I've played too many games recently that seem to think that bright colors have no place among the pc gaming master race.  Bastion proves otherwise, even if it started out on a console.

The game is full of cleverly designed puzzles and a great hint system, with very few puzzles feeling like they were unnecessary. The game is a little short, but at this pricepoint it does achieve a respectable 3-4 hours on average the first time, but obviously in less time if you don't do the treasure puzzles. It also has a good amount of replay value. Loads of puzzles can be solved in several ways and there are plenty of shortcuts that require some serious thinking to get through. You can buy the 3 main items in whatever order you want (buying the Ice Wand - the most expensive item - first makes the game significantly harder), you can even reach and beat the last boss without all the items and there are even achievements for doing so; there are 4 separate last boss fights depending on which items you have.
Then there's also speed-running functionality built into the game. You can apparently finish the game in 15minutes somehow... I could barely do it under an hour when I tried (without memorizing all the puzzles tho).
And let's not forget the lovely graphics and funny dialogue. The "wobble" graphics are very unique, quite unlike anything I've ever seen. Kind of like a comic-book game in movement? That's probably the best way I can describe it.
The game does have one pretty poor part though: the combat. It's just clunky and kind of serves more as a way to add variation between puzzles. I can't say I've enjoyed the combat in any isometric 4-directional movement game though, so it might not be something everyone is bothered by. The boss fights are better than the other fights as they kind of involve puzzles in the fight.
It's a great puzzle game well worth playing. If you're even remotely interested in puzzle games I would recommend giving this one a try.

The game is still in development, which means more is going to be added to it between now and when it's actually finished. That said, even if this were the finished product and there were no more updates to be had, I would STILL recommend this game.
The game is very similar to Terraria, a lot of the same people worked on both so that makes sense. There's a lot different, though. The most obvious aspect is that you're not bound to just one planet, and you get a ship that's enemy-free from the get-go. The other important differences are that you begin on a relatively harmless planet and progress the difficulty at your own pace, which makes this game far more relaxed than Terraria could ever be. Starbound also has quests and missions, so you have a pretty good idea of what to do- as opposed to being dropped in the middle of nowhere to figure it out on your own.
So far, there's still a lot of content that hasn't crossed over that I can tell- there's no way to keep from losing pixels when you die (at the very least), the crafting/cooking system seems much more limited and I haven't yet discovered traps either in natural settings or player created. I'm hoping that some of that is remedied in a future update, but even without it I still like the game as it is.
Players that struggle to gain headway in Terraria will find this a breath of fresh air. Players that really thrived in Terraria's harsh environment might feel under-challenged here, as the game really only barely lives up to Terraria's pre-hardmode complexity. However, Terraria didn't always have hardmode, so it's entirely likely that Starbound will increase in complexity over time as well. Keep this in mind when you make your purchase, because rating the game for what it is right now neglects these very likely possibilities for future versions.

Oops... after 1324 hours of Starbound, I forgot to write a review, Oh silly me. I'm too busy modding Starbound and building an awesome tower dungeon (which requires above mod) to click on the "Write a Review" hyperlink. Well I somehow wound up here, and I'm going to review it, so here goes:
I would have to say that Starbound is one of the most moddable games I've ever played. The features are rich, as we get exploration, dungeon crawls, treasure hunting, and fun silly stuff to boot. (As of this review, the colonization update has not been released on the Unstable/Stable development branches, so it will not be included, but I will post an update after it is released on Stable.) The in-game quests seem a bit mundane except for the mission quests, which is acceptable to me as a beta, as it does not spoil the unfinished content as much.
Multiplayer is fun when I can host a server and people wind up joining, otherwise I'm soloing in Single Player mode building who knows what crazy project I have planned, or on multiplayer mode multi-boxing a music band testing songs I've splintered out into seperate instruments, and showing them on YouTube or Steam Broadcast streams, which is also my second favorite feature of this game, believe it or not. In addition, there are plenty of large servers out there to join. (Many use Creeperhost to host them now, as it is its official server host)
Now stumbling to my favorite part. The customization! An novice-level dream for would-be level designers who has very limited programming experience, but a lot of ambition patience, and focus. There are so many block tiles, platform tiles, interactive objects, logic gates, etc. that will satisfy any level designer.
If you want to start modding the game, learning JSON (Javascript Object NotatioN, practically a way to modify, manage, and extend the game's data files) has a small learning curve, but it is very easy to learn compared to a programming language. I suggest you check out xSwatelitex's guides on the Starbound Forums if you would like to try your hand at it. It is well worth it and it expands your Starbound options to build the game the way you want to. It also features a limited Lua API for advanced modding many other aspects of the game, like AI behavior, objects, etc. Lua, since it is a actual programming language,  is more complex than learning/mastering JSON, but the rewards are well worth the effort, (I still haven't learned to use Lua myself yet, so I'm in the dark too.)
Either way you put it, this game has something to offer for nearly everyone. Casual and intermediate players can enjoy the game hunting, dungeon crawling, story quests and missions, building homes, towns, and other far out projects.
Advanced players can take advantage of its huge modding potential to make some great things.
I hope to see what some of you guys come up with!

I got this game in a Humble Bundle along with several other games that I had been wanting to try out. Fact is, until I copied over the CD key I didn't realize it was even in the bundle to begin with. So when I say I didn't really expect much from this title, I really didn't expect anything out of it. In fact, I thought, "It might take my mind off of things for a few hours." One weekend and part of a Monday later, and I just finished this thing (would have been much sooner except my laptop lagged on a couple of levels, forcing me to redo them).
The game had me from the opening sequence. I felt for our poor little orphaned protagonist and I loved the knight. The story properly foreshadows the ending, while simultaneously creating a believable set of events that lead to it. I really never felt whiplashed because the characters leap into some complicated scheme that makes no sense in the wider context of the story (which happens all too often in video games). Everything occurs in a way that properly makes sense and is believable for the cast we're dealing with.
And while we're talking about the cast the one liners the characters spout off were both mildly funny and never grew old (and I don't think they would after hearing them a thousand more times). All of the elements of the game tell us something about these characters, their hopes, their dreams, and how they live: From the drunken knight to the fiery barmaid, which for me, is how it should be in gaming. I even grew teary eyed during a few dialogue sequences, which considering how this is more of a short story than a Final Fantasy esque novella, it was really quite impressive. I was quite attached to a fair number of the cast by the end. I should also mention that the cast was quite diverse and didn't feel at all cookie cutter, which is refreshing.
The game play feels like it is well balanced for the most part even though the campaign never really just completely devastated me. I did have moments where I used most of the main cast, though I did end up completely ignoring the last two characters and the majority of the hired hands (maybe due to the OPness of the Farm Hand). However, I think pushing the real limits of this game are reserved for the arena, where getting to the higher scores requires mastering the more 'squishy' characters and properly using the whole group. That being said the two easier characters in the game had to of been the Farm Hand and the Knight. If you want a more difficult game I suggest avoiding those two when possible. Though maybe do a few rounds in the arena with them, their one liners are pretty awesome.
The pin ball mechanics played well with the story, plot, and level design. It was actually sort of surprising. It was quasi-JRPGish, but not in a way that made you feel like you were going down a hallway (it honestly didn't occur to me until I started to write this review just how JRPGish this game really is).  Additionally, I felt fully engaged with what was going on combat wise which was partly due to great visuals, voice acting, writing, and 'action' despite the fact that the majority of targets were stationary. The last pinball game that I played did feel very 'abstracted' as to what was 'said' to be going on, so it honestly caught me a little off guard as to how well this game played.
That being said, there were issues. Primarily there isn't a lot of depth in leveling. All leveling does is unlock more bonuses and characters, so for those of us who like to power game by min-maxing characters or developing specific strategies (leveling wise), there isn't a lot there. I should also point out that while the story is very well written (4 out of 5 stars in my book) it is extremely short. I spent, I want to say about 12 hours finishing up the campaign, if that, which from where I'm sitting just makes this game all the more impressive. It might also behoove me to mention some of the characters are particularly well ignored. The Alchemist and Farm hand don't get a lot of dialogue in the main story (a few short lines north of zero). These are less big thorns in my britches and more me just being honest with people looking at this game. The devs have turned out a well polished ball of a game (hehe, I shouldn't do puns).
I really do hope to see more games released by these developers. Not only was this project an amazing game that seems to respect the intelligence of the audience, but it also does it's part to create a very equal caste from a diverse set of backgrounds. It doesn't force anything on us, but there's a part of me that feels that good writing that doesn't force people of other backgrounds into race/gender stereotypes, bad guy only roles, and/or quasi-inferiority to other, more (culturally) privileged main cast members is something that really needs to take the gaming scene by storm. Though that might just be me (I hope not). Either way, I want to see more games like this and more games from this developer.
To summarize:
Pros:
+Wonderful (but short) story that is fully fleshed out, both touching and mildly humorous.
+Amazing diverse cast of characters that you'll grow attached to: Almost every element of the game gives us a chance to explore the personalities of our party and fall in love with them
+Unique RPG battle system whose core is a pin ball game: Which is a lot more fun than it should be
+One liners that never seem to grow stale and help us explore the personality of characters
+Game play is well balanced for the most part
+Arena offers more extended play for those that wish it
Cons
-Extremely short story, which might be a problem for some
-Leveling and RPG mechanics are rather simple
-Some characters are especially ignored when it comes to writing
-Some characters are kind of OP (looking at you Farm Hand)
To Devs
-Keep on keeping on (AKA, moar!)

YOU NEED THE PHYSICAL BOARD GAME TO PLAY WITH THIS APP. If you don't already own the board game, don't bother.
And be aware that every mission has a hidden round timer that you can't see, until it announces that you will lose unless you complete the mission in two rounds.
More on that below.
This app takes the most unpleasant part of Descent, which is wrangling together other people to play, and makes that totally optional. Now instead of having to Overlord/DM, you have an automated Overlord who structures together the quest quite well, and adds in a new element to the game: actual surprise.
You don't know what's coming next! Normally in this game, all players know what is coming and when. Thanks to this app, you don't! Here's how the tutorial mission plays:
Game: "You encounter a pile of spawning zombies"
I destroy them.
Game: "Some giant wolves show up and bark at you."
What? Okay, I start murdering them.
Game: "The wolves flee this turn."
Wait what?
Game: "Now there are two cultists and a giant ettin who've shown up behind you to murder you. Kill that ettin to win."
Aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaah!
I really enjoy that.
Unfortunately, playing the game more, I've discovered that each mission has a hidden round timer that you can't see. The timer gets delayed when you perform mission objectives, kill monsters, open doors, etc, but it will keep ticking down on turns you don't. And if you take too long it will make an announcement that you have exactly 2 rounds to complete the mission, or you fail.
So all of the missions become stressful. Don't play this game if you want to relax or progress methodically.
You can run a campaign with as many heroes as you want to control. I'm starting with two, because of the recent rule changes for two heroes, and because I am playing this myself. So far, so good. If you want to have friends play with you, consider adding more heroes into your campaign.
The shop system is good. You aren't punished for spending on upgrades early, because you can sell items for full price later. The exp system is good, seems a bit generous in the tutorial campaign.
Standard rules apply, and the game tells you how to handle monster actions. It takes getting used to, especially depending on how familiar you are with the rules of the game. Goofs will happen, but you'll roll with it.
The campaign gives you time for side quests or special town actions between story quests, and
The content is dynamically generated based on the sets of the board game you own, which determine what effects and pieces and monsters you own.
Even though I only own the base game, and have trouble getting a group of people together to play it, now I'm seriously considering buying more sets to have more of this to enjoy in Road to Legend.
I somewhat recommend this, but the hidden timers on missions is a serious downside.

First off this is supposedly a full release game but when I start it up it says it's a developmental build, soooo... dunno bout the devs here. So, let me make one thing clear: This isn't a zombie game. No bite infections and no concern over drawing attention from gunfire are the big ones. This is essentially a 3D Epic Battle Fantasy, but with unimpressive UI and a huge lack of information during battles. And 90% of the game is battles with janky, unnatural animations and uninspired attacks and effects. The enemy zombies feel no different from enemy humans. No disabled limbs or killer headshots. Maybe I didn't play long enough, but it is definitely not a survival experience from what I saw. Every map looks the exact same whenever you're on it again, survivors always look the same no matter what you equip them with, and zombies are all identical based on what type they are (Cheerleaders, nurses, suits, pedestrians, etc). It's just uninspired and falls flat from being so incredibly boring after not even an hour. But for that reason, it's fairly safe to try it and refund it if you don't like it. I just personally find it more of a waste of time than money even.
Pros:
-Has replayability from a medal(achievements) upgrade system.
-Everything else is pretty much run of the mill.
Cons:
-Janky, unrealistic animations.
-Same models without any variation
-Uninspired, boring combat
-Early Flash Game level UI
-Nothing feels zombie-ish
-Survival elements are either limited or nonexistant.
tl;dr:
You can get the feel of the game under an hour, so it's safe to try then refund.

After three hours, I realized I was forcing myself to start this game up and play it in order to justify buying it.  I tried to push through that but I can't.  The outings into the zombie-filled wastelands are just too tedious.  It's more or less lots of the same fight over and over.  The enemies I faced didn't change anything regarding my tactics.  I was using the same sequence of abilities on every fight regardless of the enemy types....and it worked just fine.   On top of that, it takes a long time to get through them all, since exploration is just one fight after another until you decide to stop or you "arrive" at a quest goal.
Once or twice I did make some risky decisions and ended up fighting some enemies well above my level and they seemed to offer minor variation because they used guns and used their abilities more often.  But I can't force myself to grind enough to get into any kind of mid/late game.
The crafting is very run-of-the-mill.  I see other reviews listing it as a redeeming quality but I don't.  It serves it's purpose but it's not "fun" - it's very basic.
While you do make decisions about giving strangers food, etc.  It's just a true/false choice and I didn't see any consequences other than losing X food or the moral dilemma of letting some family go hungry.
I like progression and depth in strategy games.  I didn't get either of these things after four hours of gameplay, so I regret buying this game.  If you enjoy grinding, it might be fun.  If you like a game in which the world, your character and objectives evolve, don't bother.
