This review is written at the 2hr mark. I say this because soon, it will show that I have played much more than 2hrs.
Am writing a review NOW because of the steam refund policy. Those of you who love the Tales series know what you are getting into, but those who haven't played the last few installments or who have NEVER played a Tales game will want a review directed at them. So, here goes.
First off, I was spoiled to certain events before playing the game. So the entire time I was playing the prologue I knew what was instore. Which gives me a bit of an advantage in deciding whether to keep this game or not. IF you want to know what's to come and what features await you, there are videos on youtube and the like. If you hate cheesy do-gooders, and base your RPG purchases around whether or not the game's protagonist is one - I can first assure you that it isn't the case with this game. However, if you want more specifics do the research as I don't want to spoil anything with this review.
Graphics and Performance: You may hear people say the graphics are dated. That isn't entirely true. I think with a lot of Western RPGs and Triple A releases like FF 15 out there, people unjustly try to compare traditional or lower budgeted games.
I feel like there should be a scale. Suffice it to say, this game's graphics are an upgrade, however slightly, over Tales of Zestiria. In terms of quality, this game is above most indie and JRPGs you'll find right now. That isn't say the graphics are great. Merely decent.
Far as performance goes. No bugs detected yet. Clipping seems minimal. I run GTX 970 and am having no hiccups, and could easily see the older 700 series graphics cards handling this game as well. Doesn't seem very resource heavy.
Gameplay: No overworld map like what one might expect. Areas are similar. However, I find the places I have seen so far charming and unique enough to remember. As any fan of RPGs might attest, you DO remember the places your characters visit - IF they have personality. And so far, they do.
The battle system is what you'd expect from a Tales game. For those that don't know what that means - it's more or less a  fast paced brawler type. You set up combos, have a resource to manage, and just go nuts. Some fights require you to slow down and think. And there are various difficulty settings to play under as well that makes it more a thinking man's battle system.
The dialogue is better than Zestiria's, in my opinion that is. I have already recognized some voices. Shows quality. It pairs nicely with the facial expressions. Something you don't see too much in other JRPGs - the care enough to make facial expressions feel realistic. I'd say Berseria here did it better than FF 15 or even the new Resident Evil game. Again, my opinion.
Story: This game is going to have a darker tone to it. Probably the darkest tone a Tales game has ever had. Already witnessed child death in the game. Something you don't see much in games, but adds to the realism of the situation. Sadly, this version is the censored version. Japan's original release depicted events in more bloody detail. The way they have censored events however are acceptable. As in, the new version doesn't kill the moment by making it seem less severe.
The game does have a female protagonist this time around. BUT before anyone thinks this is an attempt to bow down to feminists or whatever, the main character is what you'd expect from a Japanese game. She is feisty, she is dark, and she is hot. Sexualized or, with outfit changes, less so - she reminds me some of Erza from Fairy Tail. Which in my opinion is a good thing.
I have detected no political agenda. Which is nice. Especially with having seen so many games trying to push one these days.
Now, in the first two hours, you see things start off dire and then calm down. The hero, or anti-hero as the case may be, starts off a well-mannered, responsible young woman. By the end of the two hours, she because the bad-@ss promised. So for those that want to try this game out, as long as you don't take as long to explore as I did lol, you can see the start of everything before the lockout window for a refund. Not that I think you'll want a refund. The game has promise, and I for one am excited to get back to playing it.
I will update this review once I have played more. For now, it is worth the $50 pricetag. As it is the first game in the series that truly appeals to it's adult fans. That and it seems like a very polished port.

And the combat? Oh, you'll feel like the biggest badass around when you make Wei Shen crush all that comes against him: "I'm Son On Yee, I break every bone in your body!"
You owe it to yourself to try this game. Better than GTA4, edging out over SR3 and coming close to the glory of SR2.

And the more upgrades you buy, the more powerful your weapons are. And the more powerful your weapons are... well, you get the idea.
Batla has a good feel to it and honestly could be an extremely good game. I can't really recommend it though. If you have some friends to play with, go ahead and download it. While commonly and quickly given the title "Terraria in Space," and yes it does appear to be that at surface level, Starbound is actually a fairly different game with some very different content and gameplay focuses. A large emphasis is the exploration. Millions of planets with their own unique climates and sub biomes are scattered around an infinite universe for you to explore. It also carries with it a good focus on combat, with many updates building and reworking the fighting mechanics to fit different styles and situations. My main gripe with the game is that it isn't updated as often as it should be (at least that was the case for a while), and when they do, hardly any of content added adds much to gameplay. While it may be nice to see new accessories and visual changes added as filler for smaller updates, it is a little more disheartening when they are practically all that makes up some major updates. Don't get me wrong, there are some kick♥♥♥♥♥things added to this game, it is just that there is a lot of filler that doesn't add much more than a few hours to gameplay.
Overall, I had really good fun with this game and would recommend it.

This game is loads of fun with a simple objective.. Stay alive as long as possible before you end up falling through outer space for eternity!  Yikes!
The world in comprised of nice looking reflective blocks and the outer space all around you is simply gorgeous.
Add in a very funky, fun, and fast paced musical background and you are ready for your attempt at surivivng as long as possible.  To beat your friends score, every second of surviving here is vital!  Where do you step?  Do you risk jumping the crumbling blocks to get to the other side where it looks safer and were you might live another 30 seconds?
This game offers two modes: Platform and Dash.  Platform is a big square area that is crumbling as red blocks smash into it from above.  In platform, every second you survive adds another point.  Dash offers a narrow, long base that you run back and forth on always trying to grab the blue score balls that will increase your score.  In each mode, the left mouse button will do some repair to blocks as they are falling apart, but once they have formed a hole, it's too late.  Each mode also offers three difficulty levels to make sure you are always challenged.  Other then that, the objective is to simply score as many points before you fal to your death!

I initially got this game for console as a gift a few weeks after it came out back in 2015. It was my first Fallout and I enjoyed it a lot. I probably spent hundreds of hours on it. Of course, with it being on console, modding was limited and performance sucked on those weak little toasters. Over the summer, I finally got a custom PC, and one of the first things I did was get Fallout 4 and start modding the ever-living hell out of it. I downloaded so many mods that I've nearly reached the plugin limit and have to start merging ESPs. It's because of these free mods that I bought the game all over again and why I've been able to drastically increase the replay value. Over the course of a few months, this game has become my most played game on Steam, and combine that with the amount of time I spent on console, probably one of my most played games of all time, behind the original Battlefront II (which until recently, I had only on the CD ROM), which was also kept alive for so many years because of free mods.
Fallout 4, of course, had some major issues. Removing skills, reputation, branching paths, the main story wasn't interesting, your choices very rarely had any impact, tons of missed opportunities, bugs, Preston Garvey's very existence, and a very weak DLC season. Automatron was okay, Far Harbor was actually quite amazing and addressed some of the game's major issues, and then everything else was just atrocious, and I liked settlement building! Nonetheless, I still really enjoyed the game, and that enjoyment factor was increased exponentially by mods. I've had two playthroughs on PC so far, and they've been totally different from each other. On my first one, I played as Nate and used ReGrowth, which overhauls the game by turning it from a dry, dead wasteland into a dense forest. It gave the game a whole new feeling. Now I'm on my second playthrough, I play on Survival (first time) with the Horizon mod. I play as Nora in a nuclear winter wonderland, where more often that not, it's snowing. Precipitation forces me to wear a gas mask most of the time thanks to the Gas Masks of the Wasteland mod, which make the game kinda like Metro. My game has gone from casual strolls in a dead wasteland, to an overgrown Boston, and now to a hardcore winter environment. Up next, I'm thinking of doing a much more silly playthrough with Dustbowl Overhaul, which changes the world into a desert environment.
This is the benefit that free modding brings. It greatly extends the lifespawn of a game. The original Battlefront games, World at War, Fallout 4 and New Vegas, these are all games that I've played that benefited greatly from free modding. Part of what gave these games such high replay value, aside from being excellent games on their own, was the constant flow of free new content. Quite simply, free mods are good for games! It doesn't just get you more money in the long run, but it also gains you respect from consumers and can bring in new fans that will buy your future games. As a sidenote, a lot of mods require DLC. If it wasn't for that, I would have only purchased Far Harbor and maybe Automatron when I got this game on PC.
So onto what this all leads up to. Creation Club, or as I prefer to call it, Plagiarism Club. By this point, most of us are aware that almost all the paid mods that were introduced to this had free alternatives that were objectively better. The Chinese Stealth Suit, X-03 Hellfire Power Armour to name a couple. Unlike their overpriced counterparts, they actually add new content to the game; you can customize them and find them in locations that make sense! These mods actually add content to the game! The Chinese Stealth Suit on Plagiarism Club doesn't even show up in the armour workbench and the Hellfire PA almost looks like it was ported directly from Fallout 3. Why pay for something when there's a free option that's superior in every way? And the worst part isn't the lazy and straight-up mediocre content or even that they update the game every time they release more "creations," it's the credits that you use to buy these outsourced microtransactions. For example: let's say you want to get one of those Pip-Boy paint jobs. The price of each one is equivalent for 50 cents. Well, if you want to get one, the lowest you can pay is $8 for 700 credits. You have to pay 16 times the value, and you don't even need the rest of those credits. Instead of letting you simply pay for whatever you wanted, you have to pay for more than what you wanted. Sure, they give you 100 credits for free, but that doesn't solve the primary issue with this. It's also worth noting that just a couple of these paid mods cost as much as some of the DLC released for the game itself, all of which add far more content than a terrible Doom armour and BFG with Gauss Rifle animations.
I don't believe for a single moment that Plagiarism Club will kill off free modding and anyone that says it will is completely out of their minds. Plagiarism Club has a hilariously low limit on the size of the files that are uploaded to it. There are some incredibly high-quality mods that have come out recently, like the Wattz 3000, and ones that will be coming out in the future, such as Fallout: Cascadia, which is basically a whole new game. Cascadia isn't alone in this, nor are massive projects like it exclusive to Fallout 4. The Frontier and New California are both massive projects for New Vegas that have been under development for years, and both will be completely free. The major issue with Plagiarism Club is its very existence. It's distasteful, it's disgusting, and it's a mistake. It's paid mods.

This game is a pinball game with RPG elements.  You have a variety of pinballs that represent different characters with different stats and equipment to upgrade them with.  You go through a variety of tables that represent a number of locations such as woods and towns and castles, following a more or less passable story.  It holds the story together well enough and the voice acting is actually quite good, which helps a lot.
There are two modes, campaign and arena (a challenge mode).  A full run of the game on Casual difficulty (the other being Hardcore) runs at just about four hours.  The pinball play itself was solid and there was only minor difficult in the switching-pinball mechanic when the ball is held on a flipper, where a multi-ball would block the switch.  Each character you meet and add to your party has their own specialized usages and also serve as extra lives, with the ability to revive your lost characters via mana (gained from hitting most things and more from some placements).   A few characters feel more interesting and unique than others, but I ended up focusing on some a lot more than others as well.
I think the main critique to be made of the game is that none of the boards have much individual depth because of the focus on the RPG elements and story progression.  That choice is fine, it just leaves the game feeling a little content bare because none of the maps feel replayable, so I don't have much drive to go back and play any more.  This might be solved in arena mode, but from the two arena mode tables I played it didn't really feel like it.  The variety between the characters feels both not unique enough and too unique at times, with some characters being specifically more important in some areas or not in others.  The last boss zone was especially annoying, but the game was kind enough to checkpoint on phase 3.
I got it in a humble bundle, but I probably wouldn't recommend it for more than $5 or so, and since it retails at $10 it seems likely you could pick it up on sale for that price.   The game's alright, I wouldn't object if someone asked my advice before buying it.
It is a raw diamond that is still being cut, but the gameplay experience is awesome and unique

Half-Life was included in the valve bundle when I got it. The game can be considered a piece of history. However, it doesn't hold up the test of time. When I played this as a child I could barely follow the story, and as an adult I still don't have a grasp of where all the forums gets their info from. The gameplay movement isn't too bad, but, there were times when a section loaded it would get me stuck in the world. Another issue that annoyed me was how long it takes to kill soldiers in the early game.
As a kid I was probably playing Half-Life on easy difficulty but as an adult playing on hard the soldiers are just sponges until you get good explosives. This leads to gun battles that are just spraying half a magazine, or hiding just out of sight to take them out. The soldiers voices sound like crap! It's like listening to that voice add on to an Atari for those old enough to know what that is. Limited capabilities of the time this game was created are not up to par with today's gamers standards. Friendlies just casually hang around a corner at times after you engage a gun battle to open that door, and that slope headed Neanderthal scientist model is funny to see.
In conclusion this game is a piece of gaming history and if you're young and interested in gaming history it's worth a play in that sense to see how good the games are today compared to early 2000's. Other then that, this game just doesn't hold up to today's standards. I hear Half-Life Source was pretty badly designed, but I haven't gotten up to that version yet. Personally, I think if Half-Life 3 ever gets announced Valve should take the time to remake/remaster the series to appease today's gamers such as: AI improvements, remove enemy sponges, fix soldier voices, and graphic updates. Until then just read the wiki pages if you want to know the story.

Road to Legend is simply one of the best "expansions" you can get for Descent: Journeys in the Dark 2nd edition. The fact that this thing is free with fully functional campaigns is absolutely mind-blowing considering the production value (there are actual voice overs for the story of the campaigns).
The app follows the core rule set of D2E, but has additional rules in place because it's fully co-op and thus no player will play the role of the Overlord.
There are many other great additions to the base game that improve the overall player experience, such as the examine feature (you can now examine objects - mostly different tokens on the map), a new traveling and campaign experience or side quests. In my opinion the addition of this app simply makes D2E feel more "alive" and it honestly just feels more enjoyable to play this way (at least for now).
Again, as this is free any new or veteran player of this "classic" board game should simply download it and check it out. The tutorial is a great way to get a feel for this new variant, while the PDF ruleset has all the nitty gritty details you might be interested in too.
The only downside is that this app was obviously optimized for touch devices. As I don't own a tablet and my TV is too far away from my table I've used a laptop so far. It works great, but misses a couple of things like mouse over texts for buttons and the likes. This is just a very small con though, so don't take this as a reason to not play the app.
TL;DR: 10/10 - it's amazing.

Marvel at your units falling through floors, and things disappear into thin air. Watch as your units shoot at an enemy, and a tree 20m to you side explodes from shear fear. Be left in awe as an enemy moves from far out of your line of sight, right up to your character and 1 shots them with a crit. Be prepared to have sub 60% hit chances from beginning to end of the game without being decked out in accuracy mods/PCs. For an extra challenege turn on ironmode and hope the game doesn't crash mid mission with various glitches like your characters or enemies trying to move through walls and onto unreachable spaces.
THE MECHANICS
A simple cover mechanic of 20% or 40% defence bonus that only cares if you are at a 90 degree angle or further to flank. You can hide behind a tiny object and leave yourself out in the open but still recieve that 20% bonus unless the enemy is 90 degrees to your side or behind you, despite having a clear LOS to you. There is seemingly no way to know if you will strike cover where you shoot, and cover is destroyed often at random nowhere near your line of fire. Giant robots and orbs standing out in the open frozen solid from a grenade might still give you a sub 50% hit chance. Absurd critical hit chances for yourself and enemies late game making 1 shots still possible against 15+ health units. The stealth system is ridiculous simple and, once revealed, even if 200 spaces across a map, the enemies know where every member of your team is permenently. You can be a sniper, in an elevated position, with an over 140% chance to hit an enemy, and still miss over half of your shots while in overwatch. The entire games mechanics are simpler than your average turn based flash game you can play in your browser, and so is the AI.
THE UI
I don't understand how the UI is so poor in this game. The Avenger UI and navigation works like you are using a controller and will give people prone to motion sickness a headache in no time flat. The UI ingame is completely arbitrary and gives you almost no dedicated keys at all. Things are stuck onto 0-9 keys at almost random, and if you have more than 10 have no hotkeys at all. Why not a dedicated reload key like R? Or a dedicated EVAC key like it has for placing an EVAC? There is absolutely no customization to make your gameplay smoother. Instead you have to stare at the tiny UI at the bottom of the screen and find what you want to do, having to micromanage even simple tasks as to not click an incorrect hotkey. To make matters worse, the hoykeys are reloaded VERY slowely. If you move a character, they update immediately to tell you that you can make a shot or whatnot, BUT, the keys do not actually update to what is now possible from your new position until over a full second AFTER you finish making your move. There is no planning which key to click ahead because it may be repositioned after you finish watching your character make their way to their new position. Even worse, if you accidentally click a hotkey or click on the UI with your mouse before a soldier has finished moving or reloaded the UI, they might randomly glitch out, and toss grenades into an abyss off screen, or use a combat protocol on nothing wasting the skill and your soldiers turn. Things that you literally CAN'T normally do. It makes you wonder if the game had any QA testing done at all.
THE CONCLUSION
I simply can't recommend this to strategy, or xcom fans at all. It pales in comparison to even the original Xcom release in 1993, or any other older strategy games like the Jagged Alliance series, or even new games like Mario vs Rabbids. I could probably rant on and on about how poor the game mechanics and strategy are for a AAA budget game. You feel like none of your strategy actually matters, and you will lose to completely arbitrary RNG bs a lot, especially on the 2 higher difficulties. This makes me truly believe that 95% of the budget was spent on art, visuals, cinematics, and advertising, while the last 5% or less was spent getting amateur college level designers and programmers to actually make the game, with 0% spent on QA. This was not a game that fans of the great Xcom franchise want or deserve.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

Serena is a wonderful game that is artistic within its own right.
The game is entirely played within the cabin, and the game is played by interacting with objects within the cabin itself via point and click. The point of the game is the story itself, so interacting with each object gives you parts of the story (make sure that you interact with each object multiple times, though!). As the story progresses, you are able to re-interact with objects to obtain more of the wonderful story. You're able to interact with each object through 3-4 phases, each one giving you completely different dialogue for each object. The end of the story was both expected and unexpected at the same time (more-so when you get further into the game).
The voice acting itself was alright. The sad emotions seemed lacking (which is important within a plot like this), but everything else was pretty solid. The music was good when it was there, and the silence also empowered the general eerie feel of the game.
The biggest thing with this game is that it makes you feel so mixed towards the character by the end. You spend so much time sympathizing with this character, feeling confused for him, understanding his rage, but then you become infuriated with him beyond belief. It's an emotional roller coaster in the simplest of forms, and it keeps you thinking for a while after you finish it.
For a free game, this is really solid. I'd pay a few bucks for it, honestly.

At its core, Batla is a generic and basic arena shooter with a kid-friendly theme. With the trash that comes with F2P games, however, it becomes an uninteresting P2W fest where those who spend more money gain the edge over those who don't.
The guns, movement, and maps are functional, at least. Most of the levels and the way they are designed feel like they would fit in Unreal Tournament or Quake; save for the childish decoration and theme, of course. Your arsenal is standard arena shooter fare; machinegun, rocket launcher, lightning gun equivalent, railgun equivalent, etc. The movement itself feels solid enough, but your options are extremely limited due to the exclusion of bunnyhopping, rocketjumping, or something akin to UT2k4 dashing. However, unlike most arena shooters, there's a slow but constant health regen effect, which I did not find to my liking.
Since it's F2P, there's a cash shop in which you can buy various passive abilities and upgrade weapons. "Paperclips" are the currency, you either get small amounts from finishing matches, or of course: buying them with real cash. This means that even if you're fairly experienced in the genre, you'll almost always lose to the other person if they've been playing long enough to grind for buffs or they paid for them; which in my experience, was the case in almost every match.
Imagine this: You land a direct hit with a rocket launcher on an opponent. You deal 35 damage, due to the opponent having purchased better armor from the store. You manage to strafe and hop around the stationary enemy, chipping away at what health you can. The opponent then lazily fires a rocket in your direction, dealing 150 damage off of some distant splash damage, because they bought rocket launcher upgrades. Similar situations happen very frequently in this game. Doesn't sound fun, does it?
The community is pretty small but big enough for a couple of games to be going at once. I assume most of, if not all, the players are little kids or people who have never touched an arena shooter in their life. I base this on the fact that a majority of them were only capable of standing still while loosely spraying in my direction with whatever weapon they had in their hand at the time.
To summarize, I can't recommend this. If it were completely free without the cash shop, I could see it as a basic but functional arena shooter. However, the inclusion of the cash shop and the pains that come with it make me give the game a negative.

I'm going to be up front with this: Town of Salem is a great game. That's not why this is a negative review, because everyone should play Town of Salem right now - in their browsers. The Steam version of this game is strictly inferior to the browser version, the only advantage I can possibly think of being that you'll know when your friends are playing without needing to login, assuming they ALSO have the Steam version, which is a $5 investment more than the browser version. As for what makes it worse?
Window settings are not saved when you close the game. It will launch in full screen each and every time. If you want to go into windowed mode, you either need to hit escape, or enter a game and press the full screen button. Upon entering windowed mode for the first time on a fresh launch, the window will be unimaginably tiny and must be manually resized to something functional. To go back to full screen, you MUST enter a game and press the fullscreen button. It cannot be done from the menu.
There is no way to back out of a game, even if you have no chance of winning (e.g. died during the night as a jester, lynched as an executioner). There is also no way to return to the login screen if you timeout.
There is no log out button. The only way to change clients is to exit the client and log back in.
The only instance I would recommend grabbing the Steam version of this game is if you were already planning on buying $5 worth of town points. Seeing as its a browser game to begin with, there's no particular convenience of having it on Steam right now, and the Steam version feels like it was rushed to meet a deadline without any actual attention given to justify its presence here.
Luckily, the devs ARE working on fixing these issues, and I'll be editing this review as they come, and once I feel like the Steam version is a worthwhile buy, I'll change the review to be positive.

This is a remake of the classic 4x genre, personally I didn't dislike this game, but I didn't get super excited about it either. Let's break it down quickly:
1. Need DLC to have more the races, without DLC, there's very few races in the game, that's feels like I've been had.
2. The tech advancement is good and well-planned and there's a logical development path.
3. The planet development is good and well-thought out.
4. The UI is easy to use, a plus for sure.
5. Several paths to victory is good.
6. Using stellar converters to completely destroy the planets of your rival is fun, wish there was multiple cutscenes to show the destruction though, as after seeing it for the 100th time, it does finally get old.
7. The space battles are great, with a movie mode or tactical command, watching the movie mode is simply cool with fighter or missile views as they're inbound to their target. Tatical decisions in the battle make a difference between winning and losing, usually the auto-resolve will cause you to lose when you would otherwise wipe them out when commanding yourself, making you having to nearly command every battle yourself.
8. Galaxy can feel small unless again you buy the DLC and have more races in the game, as the game will eventually be 3-4 civilizations vying for control and slugging it out with stellar converters.
Graphics: 7  (+1 Mini-cutscenes are a huge plus) : 8
Sound(Effects and Music): 8
AI: logical and makes sense; however, not easy to make allies even if you just declared war on their enemy and give them lots of tech to try to make friends : 7
Bottomline: Buy if it's on sale 50% or more off and the DLC's are too, otherwise wait.

Bought this game a couple years back because it was on sale for quite cheap and I had a bit of extra money in my Steam wallet. Let me break down what it does right and what it messes up.
The intro scene is extremely promising. You wake up alone on a stalled/crashed subway car in a dark tunnel. It's ominous and had me intrigued straight away because I tend to like dark/cryptic games like the one that was being painted by this scene.
Unfortunately, that's just about all that it does right. The rest of the game can be summarized more or less by aimless wandering. The level design is lacking, to put it gently. There's virtually no indicators in the world of where you're supposed to be headed. Even escaping the train car is a challenge, with the actual exit cleverly disguised towards the end of it. Once you get out, you're in a nearly pitch-black tunnel surrounded by fog. It's difficult to even tell which direction is up or whether you're still moving, and the tunnel is pointlessly long. When you do encounter the door you're meant to enter, you literally hit an invisible wall, which is a bit jarring to say the least.
Now, you're out of the tunnel and into a room with a couple of glowing items: a flashlight, and a couple of notes. I enjoyed this particular room, as it reminded me a bit of Amnesia and gave a small amount of insight into the story in a very enigmatic fashion. However, most of the rooms that follow are bone dry. At some point you need to enter some duct work, and then spend several minutes crawling through and hoping you're not about to hit a dead end. I stopped playing personally after spending more than five minutes wandering around the same small area with absolutely no notion of where to go next.
With that elephant out of the way, let's talk about minor issues:
- Batteries as a limited resource in a game where the level design virtually requires them
- Incomplete localization - the "batteries" indicator on the HUD is written in Russian despite the locale being set to English
- Failure to lock the mouse to the game window in full-screen mode
- I can excuse most technical goofs given the indie nature of this game, but this is just bad
It's possible I'm missing a good part of the experience given how little I played, but I feel somewhat confident in my overall judgement, as there was no indication that these problems would get any better as the game progressed.

First off, ignore the play time I have. I have played it for a long time while it was still browser-only.
Anyway, I don't write these reviews often, but I felt I needed to for Town of Salem.
The gameplay consists of a day-night cycle in which the players must try to complete their roles' objectives. The town players seek to kill evil players, mafia seeks to kill other evil and town players, and other miscellanous roles have unique objectives. Each role have specialized abilities to help accomplish their goals, whether the Medium that speaks with the dead or the Blackmailer that can keep someone from talking. During each day, the players can discuss and vote to hang someone. This bring the core mechanic of the game to light: lying. Lying to achieve your goal becomes incredibly important to your survival. After the day ends, the night phase starts and many roles have their abilities become useful. This cycle continues to a draw or one team winning.
Starting with the positives, TOS is free to play in the browser, and purchasing it on Steam nets you the game and $5 worth of in game currency. TOS, though having cosmetic items, does not have any gameplay features behind pay-walls. The roles the game includes all play differently from eachother due to their respectives abilities. Games are short, and are plentiful.
Ending with the negatives, TOS is plagued to be a browser-flash kind of game. It takes longer than expected to load into lobbies, but afterwards it is fine. The default music played is also loud and annoying, but there is an option to shut it off. Also, some rounds can be absolutley horrible if you don't like your role or are killed immediatley.
Final Verdict: Play the browser version, and if you enjoy the game and would like a Steam version, buy it here.

I have spent over $700 on Descent and my collection is short 5 out of print lieutenants. Ive been collecting long before the Road to Legend App became a thing and I do not regret a single penny. Ive also put in countless hours into the android app.
Descent is an asymmetrical dungeon crawl board game, much like a far more in depth, detailed and dynamic version of Hero Quest. One person plays as the Overlord and controls the games monsters, villains and traps, the other (up to) 4 players take on the roles of the Heroes.
The Road to Legend App replaces the Overlord player with a computer opponent so that all the players can work cooperatively. This means that you wind up in the situation where you have a physical game with a digital opponent and narrator which is an utterly unique experience.
Descent itself is a truly beautiful board game. The miniatures are pretty, the interlocking map tiles are pretty. Road to Legend follows a story with a laid out set of maps forming a campaign and the campaigns are offered for free. If you own physical copies of the expansions, Road to Legend will incorporate those new heroes, monsters, classes etc into the road to legend campaigns, keeping things fresh.
Descent is easily worth the $60 purchase price on Amazon. However do keep in mind that although the entry point may be low, if you start collecting things will get expensive quick. The base game and expansions are all great value for money. The Hero and Monster packs less so, but they do add a ton of variety. The Leuitenent packs (which act as playable characters for the overlord) are the worst value for money, but once you have all the rest you really dont want the games big bad guys being represented by a token. Its so more satisfying to slay the mighty dragon when its a gigantic figure on the board!
Road to Legend is a wonderful blend on Video game and physical board game. I cant recommend it highly enough!

This is the second game of the Atlus "Playing with balls" collection; the amazing Rock of Ages being the first in the series.
This game is a "Pinball and RPG hybrid", first of all, with the former being the core gameplay mechanic. As far as RPG elements, one can buy items that buff certain ball types (rogue ball steals coins and backstabs, knight ball can fight and defend, etc) at an in-game store. You also grind EXP to level characters. This is about as RPG as the whole thing gets.
Story is alright so far, but nothing amazing. As a pinball fan, I honestly don't care if the story turns out one way or the other. So no big deal at all there.
Experience and gold are gotten by hitting targets, or sequences of them, and hitting enemies enough times to vanquish them. As hinted at before, one has use of different ball types, or party members, to accomplish various goals. A rogue can backstab and pickpocket innocents by hitting them from behind. A knight would be a better choice if one is facing an angry mob of baddies, and so on.
Got this in a bundle, and I've seen enough to know that this will be a solid game. Avoid if you only want a quirky RPG game, because this is all about pinball with a hint of RPG. And that's just fine, because a similar system (albeit match-3 and not pinball) worked out pretty well for the first Puzzle Quest game.
Pros:
-Atlus
-Pinball
Cons:
-None worth mentioning if you like pinball.
Recommended.

It's no secret that I <3 pinball, and examples of video pinball that let you do things that can never be achieved on physical tables. This game takes video pinball into other genres of video game in a more in-depth way than I've ever seen before.
You control a group of people who are each represented by different pinballs; each one is made of different material and plays differently - your first ball is a "rogue" character who is a little polished wooden ball that moves fast. Your next is a "knight" character who is a large metal ball that often runs over enemies rather than bouncing off them. There are also water hazards that slow down the ball, which is interesting.
Each level is a table (or multiple single-screen tables), often containing wandering enemies to target, or little physical puzzles to solve, to get through. That's a bit like "Super Mario Ball" or the old "Crush Pinball" series by Compile.
There is also gold to collect on each level, with which you can buy new equipment to power up your characters between levels. This is something that's new to video pinball, as far as I know. It's an interesting addition!
The graphics are very nice, the voice acting is diverse and good quality, the music is grand but pleasant, and most importantly - the physics seem spot on.
There is only one issue with this game - it is too short! At least, it was for me. 6 hours and I've finished the game... and one hour of that the game was on pause while I took a phone call.
I would certainly like to see more of this game. :)

+ First Tales of game I've managed to stay hooked on since Symphonia, Vesperia, and Graces F.  Even with all the warnings, this is a surprisingly dark game.
+ Even though the story is rather dark, the familiar writing and skits and humor are all very Tales.

+ I'm having a lot of fun with the Break Soul combat system and chaining them together to create massive damage combos, a lot more fun once I upped the combat difficulty level. Once you figure out how to skip step to gain more souls and target dying monsters, combat is extremely fast.

+ I'm using a PS4 controller with my computer.  It's running great! The PS4 buttons are not shown in the game, however, but the button numbers are pretty easy to figure out if you have ever played a Tales game before or have struggled with button mapping in other games.

Story synopsis in the Tales games is always a life saver.  The story is not overly fluffy so far.  There are save points everywhere, and you can quick save if needed.

This is my first Tales game, and I am very much enjoying my purchase.
The graphical style is the kind that never really ages, at least  in my eyes.  So this sort of cell shaded, anime style has been used in just about every similar jrpg that utilizes polygons.  The key item in how the style has advanced is the environmental and the atmospheric effects.  So I'll be honest, you don't need a 1070 or the lates AMD card to run this well, but the art is very well done for the style chosen.
The characters are very well designed and thought out.  Each of the main characters have different quirks about their personalities that make them unique.  In other words, they really aren't a bore to pay attention to.
The game plays particularly well, though the optimization could stand for some improvement.  There seems to be a few instances of frame drops that seem to be in the game engine rather than an actual performance hit, as the fps reader does not seem to catch them.
The combat is fun and easy to learn.  It is not the usual cop out, turn based fighting mechanic used in many popular (and uprising) jrpg's.  It is free range, in a sense, and also allows you to button map different attacks with different types of damage styles and properties.  This will become very important when you are several hours into the game, as you will need to take advantage of your enemies' weaknesses.  There's also the very nice tag team system that comes into play when you get 4+ party members.  It allows you to take control of another character if your currently controlled character is near death or not working.

The equipment system seems to follow the standards for any similar game as far as gaining better weapons and gear is concerned.  You can enhance your gear, and dismantel gear you don't want in order to harvest their components.
One of the most important aspects is, the MUSIC!  Honestly, the music goes very well with just about everything it's used for.  It captures the mood of the different story scenerios, as well as just setting the tone of the different overworlds and dungeons you will explore.
Over all, I am quite comfortable having payed 50 dollars for this.  I recommend this to anyone who enjoys story driven games with a cast of uniquely entertaining characters, and an equally enjoyable combat/gameplay system, .
It's challenging, diverse, plays well, and has a fantastic physics engine

RNG the game. 1% strategy and 99% "I hope I get lucky". When the Mario vs Rabbids game has deeper strategy and gameplay mechanics than an Xcom game, there might be a problem.
It feels like an amateur flash game with a high budget for visuals. Everything is so incredibly simple and basic in terms of the game mechanics and horrendously buggy gameplay and UI.
THE BUGS AND RNG
Prepare to sit for 5-10 seconds staring at nothing after every action you take, or even sometimes a full minute or two while the game can't figure out what to do. Marvel at your units falling through floors, and things disappear into thin air. Watch as your units shoot at an enemy, and a tree 20m to you side explodes from shear fear. Be left in awe as an enemy moves from far out of your line of sight, right up to your character and 1 shots them with a crit. Be prepared to have sub 60% hit chances from beginning to end of the game without being decked out in accuracy mods/PCs. For an extra challenege turn on ironmode and hope the game doesn't crash mid mission with various glitches like your characters or enemies trying to move through walls and onto unreachable spaces.
THE MECHANICS
A simple cover mechanic of 20% or 40% defence bonus that only cares if you are at a 90 degree angle or further to flank. You can hide behind a tiny object and leave yourself out in the open but still recieve that 20% bonus unless the enemy is 90 degrees to your side or behind you, despite having a clear LOS to you. There is seemingly no way to know if you will strike cover where you shoot, and cover is destroyed often at random nowhere near your line of fire. Giant robots and orbs standing out in the open frozen solid from a grenade might still give you a sub 50% hit chance. Absurd critical hit chances for yourself and enemies late game making 1 shots still possible against 15+ health units. The stealth system is ridiculous simple and, once revealed, even if 200 spaces across a map, the enemies know where every member of your team is permenently. You can be a sniper, in an elevated position, with an over 140% chance to hit an enemy, and still miss over half of your shots while in overwatch. The entire games mechanics are simpler than your average turn based flash game you can play in your browser, and so is the AI.
THE UI
I don't understand how the UI is so poor in this game. The Avenger UI and navigation works like you are using a controller and will give people prone to motion sickness a headache in no time flat. The UI ingame is completely arbitrary and gives you almost no dedicated keys at all. Things are stuck onto 0-9 keys at almost random, and if you have more than 10 have no hotkeys at all. Why not a dedicated reload key like R? Or a dedicated EVAC key like it has for placing an EVAC? There is absolutely no customization to make your gameplay smoother. Instead you have to stare at the tiny UI at the bottom of the screen and find what you want to do, having to micromanage even simple tasks as to not click an incorrect hotkey. To make matters worse, the hoykeys are reloaded VERY slowely. If you move a character, they update immediately to tell you that you can make a shot or whatnot, BUT, the keys do not actually update to what is now possible from your new position until over a full second AFTER you finish making your move. There is no planning which key to click ahead because it may be repositioned after you finish watching your character make their way to their new position. Even worse, if you accidentally click a hotkey or click on the UI with your mouse before a soldier has finished moving or reloaded the UI, they might randomly glitch out, and toss grenades into an abyss off screen, or use a combat protocol on nothing wasting the skill and your soldiers turn. Things that you literally CAN'T normally do. It makes you wonder if the game had any QA testing done at all.
THE CONCLUSION
I simply can't recommend this to strategy, or xcom fans at all. It pales in comparison to even the original Xcom release in 1993, or any other older strategy games like the Jagged Alliance series, or even new games like Mario vs Rabbids. I could probably rant on and on about how poor the game mechanics and strategy are for a AAA budget game. You feel like none of your strategy actually matters, and you will lose to completely arbitrary RNG bs a lot, especially on the 2 higher difficulties. This makes me truly believe that 95% of the budget was spent on art, visuals, cinematics, and advertising, while the last 5% or less was spent getting amateur college level designers and programmers to actually make the game, with 0% spent on QA. This was not a game that fans of the great Xcom franchise want or deserve.

I played the famed Master of Orion 2 years ago, and was tempted to pick up 3 and never did. From what I can tell, 3 had many features that were poorly implemented, and a UI that battled the player in bloody conflict in whatever you wished to do.
I say this implying that I am familiar with the franchise and it's gameplay, even though it was many years ago. Interestingly I turn 20 in just a few days, it has been 20 years since the release of Master of Orion 2: Battle at Antares.
But with all that aside, I shall turn to what you desire to know. The game is overall decent, although a bit different from the franchise' 1997 entry. But that is to be expected and it is not necessarily entirely a bad thing. The gameplay works well although some features need a bit of ironing out as is unfortunately the norm for games today. The new developers took cues from Master of Orion 3 and have designed a UI so clean it could be comparitive to a Windex commercial. Everything I need to know is displayed in front of me, and anything else is a click away. There are a few things that should be clarified, i.e. espionage missions. "Hacking" does not stop all research as it tells you, it halves the output of a faction. Or "Destablize", it does not actually reduce relations with all other factions, only with one, and by small amounts.
I am in my third playthrough on "Very Hard" after finding "Hard" to be a cakewalk. I remember struggling with great challenge even on "Average" in Master of Orion 2. I have yet to experiment with commanding the battles, I leave them to an AI commander. But I have read from other players that they are dissapointing and poorly implemented overall. They are real-time instead of the traditional turn-based of the franchise, and were so buggy that they disallowed them in multiplayer altogether. That action is pretty sad considering I would think a large aspect of versus gameplay would be pitting your fleets against eachother to see who is the better commander.
Regarding the AI, I find it pathetic and hopeless. It is not hard for me to amass military strength so intimidating that all races feel "Threatened" by me, and bow down at my feet in worship. Also they handle finances without any intelligence at all. They are bad at making investments in the financial victory, just handing it to you every time. I always have to pay their part of the trade treaty, and I get the impression that they spend their money on things that are not very beneficial, wasting it.
The game is relatively enjoyable but needs some serious work here and there. I do find their move to add three of the classic races in 2 as DLC quite distasteful.
Pros:
- Extremely clean and intuitive UI
- Indepth but not complicated gameplay
- Customizable game experience, research speed, growth speed, etc.
- Interesting universe
- Ability to customize race
Cons:
- Information sometimes incorrect ingame
- Some bugs
- Three of the original factions from Master of Orion 2 have been chopped into a DLC
- Not challenging whatsoever
- Inactive servers.

Where can I start with this game.
This game has similar gameplay and functions to the well known Quake game and the Unreal Tournament game. This is why I played the game.
Your starting class is the Soldier. He (Or she) has no special abilities however has got more ammo than the other two classes. I will go over them later.
Your main weapon is normally some sort of SMG (If you are a soldier) and does pretty good damage.
You can pick up other weapons in game that have different functions or/and damage.
The main currency to upgrade gear, weapons, abilities and to purchase grenades are Clips (Or Paper Clips).
This is my problem with the game, It is so hard and tedious to get Clips. For a Ten min match with 27 Score (Kills) to 4 Kills (Deaths) I only got 34 Clips. This really annoyed me as I was doing so well and I got Nothing out of it. I understand for around £1.50, you can get 10,000 clips which I STRONGLY suggest you do, put in the long run, It does get tedious. And that word "Tedious" will come up often.
Now for the Optional 2 classes, The Tank and The Scout.
Warning: YOU HAVE TO PAY MONEY TO GET THEM!
The Tank has LOTS of armour and firepower however, the trade-of is Speed
The Scout has More speed and can dodge a lot of shots, However, he is weaker than the soldier and the tank.
Their Respective abilities (in order) are:
Charge: Very fast movement even in air, Can be used to (almost) do a 180
Shield: A shield to block incoming damage.
Both of these are good but to get them to their full potential, you have to upgrade them.
This uses Clips....
And as said...
Are tedious to get.
The game itself is almost superb in my personal opinion. I have not come across any hackers yet and that deserves some merit.
Overall, I highly suggest you try out that game and face off against some level 1's
If you are level 3 and you are facing someone of a much higher level, just leave as they will be overpowered.

Impressive police simulator! At least the idea of it!
Enforcer: Police Crime Action offers lots of possibilities and options and if you wanted to be a cop in real life, well you can get somewhat of a taste in this game.
I'd say more work in the visuals and the gameplay aspects (like car handling and on foot handling) would have made this a more appealing game. However, I don't have much the patience to do all the menial tasks there is and the gameplay puts me off.
PROS:
+Being a cop! Roaming the roads with the siren wailing and seeing the civilians respecting your authoritah!
+Fulfilling RPG progression system.
CONS:
-Not very engaging, gameplay wise.
-Unreliable controls (Gameplay could use refinement, especially in the car handling aspect).
-Outdated graphics and animation.
-Timers for food, gas and sleep are really annoying and goes way too fast.
-Game was unstable when I first gave it a shot. Granted it was early access so it should be improved by now.
OVERALL:
Game has lots of potential but to me, it puts me off. I'd like to give it another shot at it months later but by that time, GTA V will release on PC and that 'LCPDFR' mod will highly likely release too.
RECOMMENDATION:
I know this is more of a simulator than an action game so I'm not inclined to be too negative on this game. Still, I'd advise anyone with a more action-focused vibe, to seek out 'LCPDFR' mod for GTA IV instead.
Bluntly, get it if you are a sucker for simulators. If you seek an action oriented gameplay, give it a pass.
RATING:
5.0 / 10

As someone who plays little to no puzzle games; this game did a good enough job twisting the genre to excuse that bias anyway. I did not expect to like this game all that much; I had picked it up in a bundle this was one of the lesser reasons for me to want to pick up the bundle; at the time. After having played it to completion at least once; I can safely say that it feels like a more puzzily version of an old Legend of Zelda game, which is nice.
Pros
The Art Style - I really enjoyed the art style. It's very comically utitilized throughout the game, and suited the mood perfectly throughout.
The Difficulty - I felt the difficulty was really well realized. I rarely ran into puzzles or situations that gave me any significant trouble; there were a few times I felt challenged but overall the balance was well realized.
The Music - I liked the music. It was ominous where necessary, as well as jaunty where needed. Could get rather old if stuck on a puzzle, but otherwise it was utilized effectively.
Cons
The Gameplay - This is more a subjective gripe than anything else; I felt that the gameplay could be rather clunky at times. I think my major issue was more often related to the hit box of the character; there were times, especially when dealing with projectiles, where I would get hit and not feel like it was well represented. It was not common, but happened enough to be annoying. I think the perspective is what complicated it further at times.
The Puzzles - Once again, subjective gripe. I don't like puzzles. This game has them in spades. They're all right, but some were complicated enough to frustrate me and pull me out of the experience.
The Price Point - I hate bringing it up, but the "cost-per-hour" price point is rather lackluster here. True, you can always replay through the game and try to do so differently than before; but I personally don't have much motivation to do so. That said, if you don't mind the price point, you will be in for a good short experience; unless you're even worse at puzzles than I am, in which case you'll likely get your money's worth.
At the end of the day I do enjoy this game. It's surprising too given my lack of mirth for puzzle games as a whole, but at the right price point it's a nice experience. I wouldn't recommend this game over many others; but if you find it for cheap enough during a sale I wouldn't recommend against it. Cautiously recommended.

A bizarre concept in theory that works spectacularly well in practice.
Without a doubt, I recommend this game, likely even at full price.
The pinball mechanics are quite responsive, probably about two notches better than the level of frustration you'd experience playing real (or a more realistic digital equivalent of) pinball.
The RPG mechanics reveal themselves in the balls.  Every character is a ball, and they have stats such as size, agility, and damage, along with a mana-activated special ability.  This gives you a nice variety of tools to work with on most levels and provides some varying avenues of victory, which is always nice.
The look of the game is enjoyable, and it has a decent story without taking itself too seriously.
Again, I highly recommend this game, especially if you have even a passing interest in pinball games.

I would definitely recommend playing this game with a group of 2 or 3 friends to get the full experience. MGT is a really fun approach to game dev simulation games, You start on a small garage and can only build a couple different rooms, but after a while you will be managing a big office with +100 employees. You have to plan a lot of stuff into making each of your games. Early on, you will only have a small development room, with a few people that do most of the work, but as you grow, you will start getting new rooms for each specific part of development (music, graphics, gameplay, QA) working together to make the best game possible. After you grow enough, you can even start to produce the games, instead of relying on other companies to publish it for you (and you start getting publishing deals for smaller companies too).
It's still on Early Access, and it's getting weekly updates for most part. It still suffers a bit on the performance side, when you start growing up and using the bigger offices, you will get huge slowdowns, it gets a bit better each patch, but it's still far from good.
Pros:
- Engaging gameplay (Time flies while you try to make the best game possible, or organize your newly purchased office).
- Difficult early game (You're not a God sent developer, even more so in harder difficulties, this can be very frustrating or really interesting).
- As of the latest patch to date, you can build your own hardware, it's still in early stages and needs some work, but its fun to dig into the hardware market and try to make your platform the nº1 in the market.
- Building is not super indepth, which imo is fine, it works really well for what the game tries to accomplish.
Cons:
- Late game is far too easy, around year 2020, new stuff stops coming out, and by that time you start having enough money to completely monopolize the market, even in the highest difficulty.
- Changing to a new Office can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥when you have hundreds of employees and you have to manually assign each one to their position all over again.
- HUD could use some work.
- There are too many menus (e.g. To buy a chair you need to: Open the build Menu > Select the Misc sub Menu > Select the Chair you want), and while you're browsing the menus, the game completely stops, and slightly breaks the flow of the gameplay.
- The Market needs a huge revamp, a finite amount of buyers, and logic consumers (I've had a game, exclusive to my own hardware, and that game sold twice as much as the console ever did in it's life time).
Overall I'd say this game is a safe purchase if you're a fan of the genre :)

When I first heard About Sleeping Dogs, it sounded like just another GTA clone. I've never beena fan of the GTA series, as they tend to sell themselves as serious action games, but are often just as over-the-top and wholly unrealistic as Saints Row. However, as I looked into it more, the story and setting sounded interesting, so I gave it a chance.
Sleeping Dogs, to me, is everything GTA should be: An open world crime game with an incredibly gripping narrative and characters that feel like real people. The melee combat is precise and engaging, and while shootouts are rarer, the mechanics are excellent. Vehicles cotrol better than those in GTA, and each one has it's own individual feel and learning curve.
GTA may have reinvented the genre, but in my eyes Sleeping Dogs refines it to near perfection.

This is not exactly a game, it's more a work of interactive fiction. The 'gameplay' takes place inside a small cabin in the woods, where you basically explore memories by interacting with the scenery. As the character, you initially don't know what is going on, but as you continually click objects more of the story is revealed.
The emotions of the character go from confusion, to nostalgia, to anger; all contained within the singular eerie environment. The Walking Dead (Season One) is a game made by Telltale Games where you play as a guy named Lee Everett a former Professor of History. The game starts with Lee in a police car as he is being arrested for murder. You talk with the Officer in the car but then you end up hitting a zombie and crashing into a ditch. This is one example of how unpredictable this game really is. Be prepared for many twists and turns if you buy this game, there are more than I can honestly recall. The games story is great with many likeable and dislikable characters you will meet along the way.
The games structure is episodic and it has 5 Episodes each being about 1 and a half to 2 hours long. The game is about 10 hours to complete, if you include the 400 Days DLC it will be about 12. The games story can branch out in many different routes with the games choices, many choices can have severe consequences, while other choices can have barely noticeable outcomes.
The 400 Days DLC is not as great as the main game but I managed to find some enjoyment in it. The 400 Days DLC has you playing as multiple characters in little short stories. I would only reccomend 400 Days if you really want more and only have $5. 400 Days also has it's own achievements (I spent way too much time reloading Wyatt's chapter to get the 'Two Out of Three' achievement, I almost went crazy.
$25 - The Walking Dead (Season One) - 10/10 (Buy it if you like anything with a good story or zombies)
$5 - 400 Days DLC - 6/10 (Only get it if you want more or if you want all of the achievements)

Berseria is about what you always wanted the heroes to do to get out of a situation easily. Who cares about valiantly introducing yourself before a duel? Just attack! Need to get some fools off your trail? Let some worthless people become fodder for your assailants' blades. Velvet, the protagonist, will use any tool at her disposal.
Battles are fierce and have an interesting ebb-and-flow. You expend and extract souls from your enemies, allowing you to extend your combo lengths. Anybody who appreciates brawler and fighting games will feel at home, even if you don't normally play RPGs. While it's not quite as fighter-style as Zestiria's combat, it's still engaging and requires you to pay attention. Playing on Hard from the get-go felt natural and enjoyable.
If you didn't play the game before, Zestiria, you shouldn't be lost -- you'll miss out on some of the clever and/or harrowing realizations that come with having experienced Zestiria, but Berseria takes place a few hundred years prior. Strangely though, it does feel more like a sequel than a prequel. While chronologically this happened first, it's so connected that the pacing of the game's reveals is going to resonate more with Zestiria players than if you played them the other way around. Long story short, Zestiria showed you the most hopeful parts of this world's story. Berseria shows you its direst.
One of my only complaints are that while the main characters and the villains have great voice acting, some NPCs sound idiotic. My other is that dungeons tend to be lack-luster and kinda overused. Overall, I'd recommend this to anybody who likes jRPGS -- this isn't a Tales game, it's just a good jRPG with apple gels.

A poorly made Indie Horror game. That is how I will be reviewing Despair.
There is no introduction to a plot. All players start in a subway train, and from there on the player is left to do [redacted] all. There is no objective. I will be revealing spoilers here, for the sake of saving any future players from wasting their time on Despair: All that you do will only lead to a pointless and disappointing ending. You reach a loading screen, and that’s it. The end.
The controls were not established either, or where false. The latter is worse. In game, it says to “Enter E” to use or interact with an item, such as a flashlight. That key does not work. You need to use the “F” key …
The game play was as interesting as watching wallpaper dry. You can explore and interact with limited items. The map does include some form of direction by highlighting exits in red, but that seemed superfluous as they are not hidden or obstructed in any way. Now we go into the effects, which were also dull or poorly made or timed. Any game with the indication of “Horror” in it has some grim to it, but this game brought boredom. A little blood here and there, and that’s it. No enemies, pop-ups or other scare factors that are present in any decent Horror game. The only part that I remember, suspected to be a jump scare, was the clapping doors in the washroom. But in all honesty, it looked hilarious. I just looked for a second and continued on.
No music exist, which would explain the emptiness of the game. This feature could help bring about the atmosphere of the game, enhancing the mood and playing experience, if considered by the developer.
Settings exist, but are limited to Graphics, and Audio. You can adjust the Resolution, Full-Screen and quality of the graphics. The volume bar is there in the Audio. The graphics and art were so-so, and reminded me of a similar game: Devils Share was removed from the steam store a while ago. (With that in mind, who knows where this game could be headed in the future.)
Despair is one of those games where nothing is given, and nothing was received. Apart from the Trading Cards, it’s 0% satisfaction guaranteed, and I do not recommend playing this game.

A very endearing, traditional but fresh action adventure.
The gameplay is very Zelda with puzzle-heavy top-down rooms and palace-like dungeons for each tool you acquire. The tools are very different from what you'll find in Zelda games, though, and there's a lot of focus on having them interact with each other - one puzzle may have you freeze a block to let it slide across that spike wall and then freeze and teleport a bomb so its detonation syncs with you lighting a brazier.
Be aware that it doesn't take long to finish the game, but its replay value is high because the path through the castle is nonlinear, there's a lot of optional treasure/puzzles, and extra-hard shortcuts encourage challenge and speedruns. The limited game length also means that a lot of effort could go into each individual room - nothing feels rushed, and the puzzles use available game mechanics to their fullest potential.
Ittle Dew's strongest point of the game is the irreverent yet cute, self-aware humour. Quirky enemy design, expressive hand-drawn graphics and the music support the atmosphere very well.
Combat is rather basic and more about approaching strategically or outsmarting enemies than about the actual process of beating them up, but still a nice diversion between puzzles.
If you care about silly dialogue, clever puzzles and exploring different routes through the same dungeon, this is for you. If you like long, linear games with a focus on combat and are a dialogue-skipper or prefer serious storylines, you're looking in the wrong place though.

Police Quest meets SWAT meets GTA III.
This is the "right side of the law" simulator, I always wanted many other games to be.
The interaction and immersion is great. There is sooo much you can do, while capturing the day-to-day grind.  While this could become boring, it does a pretty good job capturing the realistic career-risk of any "routine", where even a routine traffic stop can turn suddenly violent and the player faces sudden and possible death.
It is not perfect.  There areas I wish would be improved upon.  My primary issue is, there is no, "backup" support.  You do not have a partner, and you can't call for backup.  I feel this, could be rectified in an expansion, which, maybe we will see some day.  This shortcoming, I was able to justify with the rationale, that, the town is pretty small, it "might" be possible, that you are the sole law enforcer on payroll (and of course dispatch).
Enjoyable game, does a great job of immersing the player in the atmosphere.  Visuals are well done in many areas.  The open-world, random citizen/criminal generation keeps the replayability going (and humorous at times... my first day on patrol, my first three suspects were woman truck drivers... immagine my shock when this cute girl in a sexy dress jumped out of her truck and pulled a gun on me...).
The realistic mode really draws you in to the life & death risks of the job... you learn to rapidly eject from your car in a chase, taking up cover behind your car, very quick.  My player has died in the line of duty four times (meaning permadeath-restart from scratch), before my latest actually has survived up to LT (and still going).
There is a more arcade mode... haven't played it, where death is not possible, but injury is.  This brings me to the 2nd issue I have with the game, I believe their should be a second mode, where both injury or death is possible (not always one or the other).
Great game.  Hope to see more from the developer.
Definitely recommend this game.

Paladin Danse looked at the advert for Creation Club filling the screen.
"It was corporations like this that put the last nail in the coffin for mankind. They exploited technology for their own gains, pocketing the cash and ignoring the damage they'd done."

Long story short: They pulled it off. It's a fun, unique, and interesting game.
The boards are fun and complex always with multiple flippers on each side.
Each might have different goals like some you might need to use the Thief ball to bump into the backs of peasants to collect some gold, others (quite a few) you defeat enemies, or you might need to make it to a different part of the board as part of the story.
The characters being represented by balls of different size and materials works well. They feel and play diferent, so where the small almost-too-fast Thief does a ton of damage from behind (much less from the front) and gets knocked around by the flippers easlily, the Knight is big, slow, heavy, does a fair bit of damage from any angle and can occasionally knock down enemies briefly. Meanwhile there's also the Ranger who pasively fires arrows when near enemies, or the Farmhand who wrecks objects and knocks over enemies easily.
All of the characters (balls) have an activate-able ability. The thief has an extra ball in play (her dog), the Knight blocks the balls from going down between the flippers for a short time. The character/balls can also be upgraded at the Port (a shop) buy buying them. Some may increase damage, lessen the special ability mana cost, modify their special in some way - usually making it stronger and/or last longer.
On a personal note: My favorite has to be the Barmaid, a hire-able side character who's good all around and can be upgraded to be able to heal the flippers on mana gain when her special is active which happens to make her more agile and do more damage to begin with.
"Not the kind o' spoonin' you were expectin'?"
There is some limited bad, however, in that several stages feel SUPER frustrating because there's too many enemies crowding the flippers so all your balls bounce off of them and in the hole. Perhaps the Farmhand is the character I was supposed to hire first so he could bowl through them.
As of yet, if you use a controller with vibration there's no way in game options to turn off the rumble so some stages I needed to take a break until my hands stopped being numb.

So after 1.0 all I can say is there's been a drastic change. The first is that crafting is still a focal point, but building is a secondary, very fun thing that is possible within the game.
Starting out there are tons of things you can do, build shelter, kill for meat, explore caverns, farm food, and much more for those starting. There's also been a shift from having to dig to the center of the planet to proceed to having to explore the caverns around the starting world, which I believe better introduces players to the exploration and mining aspect of the game.
It's much more story-oriented and forward-driving than the previous builds and has more to do with primary missions, but it's like the priorities split apart so much it gives a feeling of overwhelming options, and the new need to scan items to proceed is...sub-par. I enjoy learning more, but I don't really enjoy it being mandatory to continue with the story.
The lack of options when customizing your characters is also rather baffling to me considering how easy it'd be to simply expand the choices of hair or clothing starting out, but that's more of a nitpick.
What isn't is the frame-rate lag, the god-aweful frame rate lag! I had to go into my .config file to turn of vsync and other unnecessary options that created a terrible amount of lag with floating items and enemies, and even after there was still quite a bit of enemies randomly stopping in mid attack only to lag back to life seconds later. This game *seriously* needs optimization!
Regardless, the combat is fun and challenging, the different racial personalities are fun and the only thing I believe is missing that I'd (personally) love is more lore into the universe.
It's nice for a small indie title...but it needs work.

Below you'll find both a video and written impression on the game.
Rollers of the Realm takes 2 very different genres and mixes it up into one game. It takes the party building. character progression,  and narrative, of RPGs, and put it into a pinball setting. Each ball represent it's own character with it's own traits, stats, and specials. Each pinball table plays out more like an RPG quest than a traditional pinball table, where quest goals, and some times navigation are designed with precedence over classic pinball score attack.
The game looks great overall. Each table / environment are well detailed and stylized in the expected RPG motifs, with some pretty impressive art design and lighting. Though some of the character profiles, the 2D illustrations, I found to be not quite as strong as the 3D models. The sound design is what you'd expect from pinball games, but throw in some grunts as you hit enemy mobs, and other classic RPG sounds when you do RPG things.
As a game on it's own it's pretty enjoyable. The mixing of 2 very different genres itself grabs attention, and certainly playing an RPG based pinball game I was ecstatic at first! But as I played more I realized, through the blending of 2 genres, certain aspects of both were lost in the process. The character progression in the game is very simple when compared to other RPGs, while the tables are less exciting and creative than other pinball games due to it's need to be designed around a quest, or a goal, rather than score attack. So as a game on it's own, it's enjoyable, but when compared to either of the 2 genre it's blending it can leave a player wanting.
Overall Rollers of the Realm is a very curious game, that the idea of blending pinball with RPG alone should turn some heads. It's enjoyable in it's own right, but might not hold it's own when compared to either of the genre it's blending. But if you are looking for a pinball game with RPG elements, there's not too many other options out there, and you could do much worst than Rollers of the Realm.
Pros:
- A very interesting blend of genres
- Good Looking Pinball tables
- Enjoyable under it's own merit
- Easy to learn, very accessible
Cons:
- Good game overall, but doesn't excel as either an RPG or Pinball
- Simple progression system
- Some Awkward tables

It's a pinball RPG. No, seriously. If you hate RPGs and/or hate pinball, there's nothing about this that will convince you of the merits of either. However, if you love both types of games as I do, there's a lot to enjoy here. It's not a deep RPG, nor is it a particularly complex or fast pinball game but it's a lot of fun and something that hasn't been done before quite this way.
You use standard pinball mechanics but in a wide variety of levels that wouldn't be possible on a traditional pinball table and with a wide array of different characters, all of whom have different balls with different traits and special abilities. You swap them out during the levels and use their abilities as you see fit to accomplish your goals and get through the light story, using the spoils of your journey to unlock more characters.
Know what you're getting into with this game but if it sounds good, you'll probably like it. It's unique in what it does and is a lot of fun if you're into this kind of thing.
