Being more of an interactive story/experience rather than a true adventure game, Serena is presenting us with a mind of a man troubled by the past, wandering inside small cabin in the woods in thoughts of his wife. While only one hour long it is completely worth your time. The game achieves to tell quite depressing story of a relationship using subtle elements  like lighting, colors, sounds etc. to change atmosphere in the cabin as it progresses, becoming gradually darker and darker. The voice acting is pretty good for a free game, so we get some strong and believable emotions from main protagonist which helps you stay immersed more than anything.
When exploring the place you will start noticing a pattern in which things are changing to progress the story. Be carefull to follow that pattern not to miss anything because every detail adds to the story.
Warning: Some say the game should have save feature, but rather than that it is intended to be played on one go. There is no save, no menu so beware of pressing Esc unless you want to have to start back at the beginning.

I highly recommend it. It's not much a game as an interactive novel, though it's a pretty good one and free so you got no reason not to give it a shot. It's a low key horror story that will make you think about it much longer than it takes place. True to its Lovecraftian origins, the story does not involve direct i your face horror scares, but rather slowly grows on you in its eerie and chilling story. The writers got H.P Lovecraft's vibe correct - even the main protaganist has the same characteristics of the stories (don't want to give any spoilers, but read some of the original works and you'll see the similarities).

This is a Braid-esque platformer in that it relies around a novel mechanic and pretension to artistic statement. The story is hinted at and implied through collectible photo icons that contain snippets of text. Some are descriptions of a religious cult and some are mopey rememberences of a lost love. None are very captivating.
The gameplay is really good, though. The player can use a camera to clone certain parts of the scenery to create new platforms and solve jumping puzzles. That sounds strange, but it's a very intuitive and original mechanic. The difficulty scales gradually over the course of a robust 50 or 60 levels and many of the later ones especially are challenging and well-designed.
This is not a very polished game. The graphics are remarkably bad, although they are strikingly similar to some of the worst graphics from the 1990's -- a decade this game pays clear homage to. Is this some high-concept intentional design choice? If it is, it's too subtle for a philistine like me. All I can say is that many of the assests look like they were created at the wrong resolution and then stretched to the proper size at the last minute. Also there is a common "bat" enemy that looks like it was drawn by a child. The music, on the other hand, is amusingly relaxing considering it is often the soundtrack to you dying over and over and over agin.
Quibbles aside, Camera Obscura is a fun, creative platformer that kept me engaged for 10 or 15 hours. It was a great deal for the 50 cents or whatever I paid for it. Recommended for sure.

If you like 2D Zelda games, speedrunning and funny dialogue then get Ittle Dew. Its on here and the Wii U eshop for$9.99. Its hella nice. Yeah go get it. Unless you don't like any of those, then keep moving and ignore this review.
Alright, I'll actually talk about the game. So you're an adventurer named Ittle Dew and her sidekick Tippsie are on a raft when they bump into a rock and crash on the shore of an island. After going through a short tutorial cave, there's a big castle you come across filled with weird inhabitants who wear suits and tend to be wacky. Outside the castle is Itan, who runs a shop. You can find treasure chests in the castle with coins and you use those to go towards getting items from the shop. Well, you pay Itan and he launches you to a dungeon that the item is at (a fire sword in a fire cave/volcano, an ice wand in an ice cave/dungeon, and a portal wand in the woods). Each dungeon contains a shortcut that can help you get to the boss faster (most likely than not you're gonna use these if you're speedrunning but they do help you finish the dungeons faster supposing you can figure out the puzzle for each shortcut). Depending on the combination of the items you collect (you need at least 2 to get through the castle to the final boss), you can take different routes through the castle to get to the end.
Aside from the items I previously mentioned, there are also collectible cards you can find in chests throughout the game that have a picture of a character or enemy in the game along with info on them (they go towards an achievement) and you can find scraps of paper in chests as well that go towards increasing your heart count (4 pieces make a new heart a la Legend of Zelda heart containers, this is also for an achievement if you find them all).
This game will test you and your thinking skills. Sometimes puzzles are simple like press all the switches or kill all the enemies or hit switches. Other times, you might take a while to solve a puzzle only to be stumped by the next one. Gameplay - Bastion is a top-down isometric action game with an emphasis on combat.  You can equip two weapons at any given time and add one ability which often uses one of those weapons.  With 10+ upgradable weapons and 20+ abilities, you can experiment quite a bit and everyone will find something they like.  There are normal levels with enemies and the main story and challenge levels which let you unlock skills and items to help upgrade your weapons.  There are also a couple of side modes to help you get more money.  As you progress through the game, you also get to rebuild a little town (called Bastion) which adds new places to shop, upgrade weapons, etc.  Overall, combat is fast and fun and with short levels, the gameplay will hold your attention throughout the 6-9 hour long story.
Story- Bastion's story is a little weak though you have to play through a lot of the game before you start to realize it.  The Kid (the character you control) has no personality and the narrator provides all the informaion to you.  The mystery of the story is why the Bastion was destroyed and why the Ura hate you.  The game eventually tells you, but it isn't particularly interesting.  Playing the side modes like Who Knows Where do help you learn more information about the story and characters if you're interested or just are going for achievements.
Presentation (Graphics and Sound) - The top-down view makes this game pretty unique and the overall art style of the game is pleasing to the eye.  The music is great and has songs that really stand out from any other game I've played.  The announcer narrates based on your actions like if you kill something you shouldn't or use one weapon a lot, he will make a comment about it.  This feature is pretty cool and a nice gimmick.  The narrator becomes a little tiring by the end of the game because it seems like he is always saying the same things or saying he doesn't know about things in the story.
Overall Score - Bastion is a fun and relatively short game with plenty of action.  It is not too difficult to get all the achievemets in the game as well.  While the story was disappointing, I never got tired of running around and killing stuff or upgrading my character, weapons, or the Bastion.  This is a fun game and well worth getting when on sale.

This game is developing slowly, but steadily into the right direction. It's already completely enjoyable to play and feels feature complete for the price tag.
There are a couple of games similar to Game Dev Tycoon out there and this one has become my favourite, because it just keeps throwing features, genres, technologies and stuff at you all the time, basically incorporates the entire Game Developing and Console Developing features from GameDevTycoon while improving on it.
If you have played Gamers Go Makers or GameCorp DX you will realize that the genre actually offers a lot of possibilities in regards of adding rooms and facilities. Mad Games is the only game in the field that let's you create big teams doing different things in different rooms with a decent presentation.
In addition you get stuff like MMOs with a Server Room, Sequels for great games and Add-Ons for the MMOs.
The game development itself is pretty much the same in all games. You can use look-up-tables on the net to create the perfect game or stumble your way to perfection with your own table, or memory. With all the Genres and Topics in the game you will probably go crazy making your own table and definitely unable to remember everything that worked with all the sliders.
Mad Games not only takes the "hint" feature that Game Dev Tycoon introduced with a patch, but it also lets you re-apply the same setup from a previous project. The advantage being, that you can develop an RPG, then a Sports Game and then another RPG, load the RPG settings and re-adjust from there on out, instead of being forced to manually switch everything back from Sports to RPG. And thanks to the "hints" that appear, the more you develop within a certain topic/genre mix, the more of those hints you will see and the better your team becomes.
Is it the perfect game? Not by a long shot.
It's way too easy too be a successfull developer and the result is that I have no idea how platforms and genre mixes work.
Your workers don't age and their wages are quite low in comparison to what they start earning for you. This makes the game easier, but on the other hand you don't get the management horror of a Software Inc. , which is nice.
Once you develope a great MMO game you are done. It's GG. You could say that this is realistic and you are probably right. Just look at the history of Blizzard. If you are going for money, go for subscribers. You can also release a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sports game every year without learning anything in the process or improving the engine, so that's realistic, but also too simple.
Overall the best reimagination of the original GameDevTycoon concept by Greenheartgames. I'm sure we are going to see another one of those in the future that will surpass Mad Games, but for now I'm declaring it the best game developing tycoon out there.
I wish there were more games in that style. Especially if they could switch from Game making into a more detailed movie making simulation. A blend of the classic Molyneux' The Movies with the now 2nd Generation Indie Management games would be the best.
For the presence, we have to stick with Mad Games Tycoon.

I love Game Dev sims. Game Dev Story was one of those games that managed to burn away many hours of my life. It still is one of my favourite games on my iPhone. And for a long time, it was also pretty much the only game of its kind. Thankfully, Game Dev Tycoon came out in 2012. While it managed to be similar to the aforementioned game, it was also a bit more complex and supported mods. I played it a lot back in the day, but it never became an evergreen for me. Thankfully, Mad Games Tycoon has been in Early Access for some time now and I think it's the right moment to write this little review of it.
Mad Games Tycoon takes a similar, but more complex approach to the topic at hand: You start off in a garage, alone, with your new company and you immediately get to build rooms, Theme Hospital-style. You even get to buy furniture, which has some impact on hiring new employees for your young studio. More talented people only pop up, if your company has enough stars, which in turn are determined by the quality of furniture you have in your office. At the beginning, you won't have a lot of stars, since you need most of your money in order to finance your first games. While they are cheap to produce at the beginning, you have running costs, like the salaries of your employees and of course the upkeep of your studio.
Producing games is relatively simple at first. You define the name, genre and focus of your game. Each genre has a different focus, so you'll have to experiment and invest in a quality assurance department in order to find out what's the perfect mix. The closer you get, the higher the critics score your game and the better your game will sell. Later on, you can even combine some genres, but some combinations work better than others. You also take care of updating your games, which can have a positive impact on sales.
While this certainly sounds easy enough, there are additional things you can take care of. You can decide to develop your engines yourself, which has the added benefit that you can sell said engine to other game producers and get a fraction of the money they make with games that use your engine. This means you'll also have to invest time and money into research. Buying a licence for a third party engine is an option too, of course, but you'll be loosing a portion of your profits.
When your games start getting bigger, you'll need to invest in a quality assurance department and dedicated graphics, music and motion capture studios, in order to improve those areas of your games. This also means you'll need bigger offices quick and this is where one of my biggest problems with this game can be found: When you get a new office, you'll need to build all your departments from scratch and reassign your entire workforce. Now, this is manageable the first time around, but it gets tough quickly. In one of my games, I had a workforce of over 100 people and it was impossible to assign them properly in a timely manner. Sure, you have the possibility to arrange them by five different attributes, but that is not enough. The game lacks a filter for unassigned workforce, which makes life harder than it needs to be. Maybe this will be added at some point later in the development.
The latest addition to the game is console development. While it doesn't look like it's completely integrated yet, it is pretty awesome to research and develop your own console and push it on the market to let it go up against the NES. You can set the price for your console and developing for it is pretty cheap. Unfortunately, right now I haven't managed to develop an exclusive title that turned a profit...
While the gameplay is fun and the systems are comprehensive, the presentation still leaves a bit to be desired. Graphics are simple, yet functional and the music is ok for the first couple of hours but soon starts to get on your nerves. Some soundeffects are overused, especially the telephone, which thankfully can be switched off separately. Performance takes a notable hit too when there are more than 100 people working in your studio.
While these are some important complaints I have about the game, I'm also certain that at least some of those things will improve over time. But right now, Mad Games Tycoon is the Game Dev-Sim to go! It's more complex and more satisfying in almost every way compared to similar games.

First off, I'll admit that my review is somewhat biased because I have a nostalgic love of pinball games.
But to combine a pinball game with RPG elements, and story-telling, is pure genius.
PROs:
- good voice acting (really makes the characters come alive)
- excellent inclusion of story and story-telling
- beautiful integrated art style with pinball maps
- can swap between characters in mid-game to utilize character skills
- RPG upgrades to characters to increase skill set
- EXCELLENT boss battles (really need to be creative on how to utilize your characters)
CONs:
- very short game (spent 8 hours playing, but a good chunk of that time was spent grinding for gold in the arena maps)
- sudden arena "round change" pauses (game pauses in the middle of game to signify round progression, which sometimes blocks view of ball, and leads to frequent gutter balls)
- annoying menu navigation (switching between story and arena modes, forces you to wait for opening title screen to load every single time)
- limited RPG elements (RPG elements are a great concept, but having just a handful of pre-determined upgrades, and limitless gold to grind to purchase upgrades, limits a player's creativity on how to build class characters)
Overall, a very fun and at times challenging game, with LOTS of room to develop and grow.  I'm hoping that this is just the first of many RPG-Pinball games.

Searching the military tents or runways always had a chance to land you an AK, night vision goggles or other various military gear.
Dead Age strips away that excitement, and give you the chance to get materials, so tiy cab craft lame gear. So you have a chance to find lame crap, all so you can craft ever so slightly less lame crap. I think the devs really missed the mark on what made Zombie Apocalypse games so fun, and I am not saying they are alone, as I believe MOST of this genre's devs have sorely missed the mark. It's a cool idea, and maybe if they get the chance to iterate on it with another game it would be better. Unfortunately,  I don't think this game is going to make pinball fans or those looking for an RPG happy.
For starters, there's just not much there in terms of what you'd expect from an RPG. You can buy some upgrades that make very little difference to how the individual balls perform, and you cand spend a bunch of gold on buying another party member. That's about all. It's very thin if you're looking for any kind of character customization, which could be forgiven if the other aspect of the game - the pinball - was stellar.
It isn't. This game's idea of a good pinball table seems to be stationary targets that you have to hit over and over - and over and over- and when you finally "kill" one, another comes out to stand in the exact same place. Instead of interesting shots and modes like you'd expect in any real pinball table, you get to bounce off these targets a few inches from the flippers again and again. Honestly, the weakest tables in Pinball FX are more entertaining.
Like I said, I like the concept. I hope either these developers or someone else gets to take another crack at it, and before they do I hope they play some better pinball tables.

It has been sometime since I played XCOM 2 before I bought the War of The Chosen (WotC) package and I can honestly say that it is awesome to be back :)
The additions to the game that WotC brings is huge, starting with the Resistance Factions and Covert Operations, all the way to fighting Chosens and
.
The new classes are a nice addition though they don't feel very powerful in comparison to vanilla classes as they too received the point system to buff their skills.
The research options are more versatile and can actually make you sweat sometimes with breakthroughs and inspirations.
Adding The Lost to the game is a wonderful idea, I especially like using them against aliens by taking the fight to the roofs and letting the lost distract them below. They give the missions another kind of urgency (unless you take the "one shot lost" resistance order and a sharpshooter with face off can pretty much farm them :) ).
Soldier bonds are nicely thought as well, trying to keep bonded soldiers together to get the bonusses and using them for tactical advantage gives us another way of dealing with the aliens.
There are other aspects to the game that make it a much more beautiful one over the vanilla version, and I'm sure lots of reviews will talk about them :)
Overall, WotC is worth spending your money on if you love the XCOM genre, liked XCOM 2 but wanted something more.

This game is stupid fun. A real gem among it's early access peers. A game that is easy to learn, and even easy to master if you only account for individual ability. But this game is all about TEAM WORK. It's just you, your ship and your crew; every player must do their part. Or sink to the bottom of the sea.
Pros
- A visceral experience. The sounds of crashing waves, cannons firing, seamen screaming orders and the ambient sounds of warfare in the sea. All this in sync with the incredibly dynamic team-oriented gameplay; makes for some of the most immersive online experiences in recent memory(For me).
- Relatively polished for early access standards. In fact, in almost 10hrs of gameplay; I've yet to see a single bug. But it does have it's missing or lacklustre features, typical of EA titles.
- Easy to get into. Many competitive games have the tendency to have steep learning curves, this game can be learned in a matter of minutes. But that is not to say this is a simple and non-competitive game; BLACKWAKE is one of the most team-oriented strategy games I have ever played.
- Beautiful visuals. Glimmering seas, rain crashing on the deck, gentle snow in the midst of battle, thunderstorms complementing  cannon fire. It all looks great. Ship designs are very nice too, but I don't know♥♥♥♥♥♥about ships.
- The game inherently lends itself to friendly team-play. This not like casual DoTA or pub Counter-strike, where one man can carry a team. If the crew is not in sync, you will not win against a competent opponent. You work together, or you lose.
- Music and Sound. The music is fitting and a thrill to listen to during the heat of sea warfare. Sounds and voice acting also leaves little room for complaints. The British navy-men, in particular, sound hilarious. Though this may bother the more serious players.
Cons
- Character models and animations need work. Models(character) are ugly, in my opinion. And there are still many animations missing for certain tasks, e.g. using the pump, loading a cannon, steering the ship, and so on.
- As of right now, there is no ranking system, so there are really no stakes to winning or losing. But I am sure this will be changed in the future.
- Melee. The melee system is mindless. You board the enemy ship and awkwardly swing at anything that moves; that sums up the melee system. Awkward animations and no depth. Though this is easy to forgive as the game is in early access and melee combat is not central to the game.
Conclusion: A gem among the early access titles. And even with it's early access hindrances, it still feels like a bargain. It is THAT fun. A game where team synergy, and competently executed orders is key; BLACKWAKE is the epitome of team oriented gameplay.

Think of Serena as an interactive story: you need to click on things to collect info and, piece after piece, you'll begin to understand what's going on. If you enjoy reading and investigating, just download it. Otherwise, don't.
For the ones interested, this is what is going to happen: Serena will take about one hour of your time and you'll
leave the finished game thinking: "Well? Is this all? It's so obvious that things went THAT way..."
Then, you'll go back to your life.
Later on, you will remember one small detail and think: "But if things went THAT way, how should I explain... this?"
Another detail will haunt you. And another one will follow.
At this point, you'll realize there was much more depth in this
yet precious gem than what you first assumed, so you'll feel compelled to start all over and try to make ALL the pieces fit together.
At least, this is exactly what happened to me.
Serena is a wonderful gift to the community and I really recommend downloading it.

The Walking Dead (Season One) is a game made by Telltale Games where you play as a guy named Lee Everett a former Professor of History. The game starts with Lee in a police car as he is being arrested for murder. You talk with the Officer in the car but then you end up hitting a zombie and crashing into a ditch. This is one example of how unpredictable this game really is. Be prepared for many twists and turns if you buy this game, there are more than I can honestly recall. The games story is great with many likeable and dislikable characters you will meet along the way.
The games structure is episodic and it has 5 Episodes each being about 1 and a half to 2 hours long. The game is about 10 hours to complete, if you include the 400 Days DLC it will be about 12. The games story can branch out in many different routes with the games choices, many choices can have severe consequences, while other choices can have barely noticeable outcomes.
The 400 Days DLC is not as great as the main game but I managed to find some enjoyment in it. The 400 Days DLC has you playing as multiple characters in little short stories. I would only reccomend 400 Days if you really want more and only have $5. 400 Days also has it's own achievements (I spent way too much time reloading Wyatt's chapter to get the 'Two Out of Three' achievement, I almost went crazy.
$25 - The Walking Dead (Season One) - 10/10 (Buy it if you like anything with a good story or zombies)
$5 - 400 Days DLC - 6/10 (Only get it if you want more or if you want all of the achievements)

From the moment I booted it up, I knew Bastion would be one of the most amazing games I will ever play. Here are some of the things I love about the game; all are solid reasons to pick it up.
1) The art  - The brightly colored, oil paint style art mixed with the minimalist level design of only showing you areas you can explore make you want to explore and live in the world. The feeling of the art reminds me a bit of Braid, in that on the surface it seems childish and harmless, but also strongly hints at the darkness and uncertainty in the plot by painting in constantly shifting colors that vary in brightness and hue.
2) The gameplay - Bastion features an arcade style "weapon 1 / weapon 2 / special" button masher combat system which is both simple enough to completely understand by the end of the very well designed tutorial level and contains enough innovation to remain interesting through the end of the game. The variety of very distinct weapons (as opposed to gun 1, gun 2, etc that many FPS employ today) allows you to choose your own play style. The upgrade system for weapons encourages striving to find the material to upgrade your favorite, but doesn't require crazy amounts of grinding to do so. Finally, the base challenge level of the game is low enough that you'll be able to beat it, but early on you have the option to raise the difficulty in exchange for XP, (psuedo) money, and achievements in a variety of different ways.
3) The plot - Bastion has an unbelievable plot. A real plot, to the level of a fantasy novel. Early on, you are tasked with rebuilding the bastion, a safe haven in case of disaster that has fallen into disrepair in the wake of "the calamity". It seems simple at first, but wrinkles appear - what was "the calamity"? Who caused it? Who are the Ura? What are the backstories of the characters? And why repair the bastion, what will that do? I won't spoil any more, but suffice to say at the very end of the game you are offered two choices, and while I've played other games with choice systems, I've never thought this hard about which choice to make. The fate of the world that you very much feel a part of rests on your shoulders.
4 and my personal favorite) The sound - The entirety of Bastion is narrated by an old man who you meet very early in the game. He describes your character in the third person, as though all of your exploits are an old tale. And when I say all your exploits, I mean it - he narrates every blow you strike and boss you defeat in a fashion that makes you feel like you're writing history throughout your adventure. Interspersed in his narration are bits and pieces about the world that tie the plot together. The music, especially the bastion theme, perfectly complement the art style and the gameplay. The bastion theme starts out bare and thin, but as you rebuild it the music grows in strength and instrumentation in a rustic style, with a message of "it's going to be rough but we're getting through this". There are a few songs with words in the game that are used to great affect to drive a plot event home.
Overall, Bastion is unbelievable. It is a game that seeks to be more than just a game. It is gripping, dark, fast-paced, thought-provoking, and challenging in more ways than one. It is a masterpiece.

Drawn to it by its art style, the game won me by its quirky sense of humour, skillful breaking of the fourth wall and its soundtrack, seriously, the castle, where you'll probably spend the majority of the time, has a catchy tune, which, you know, is a good thing since spending an hour listening to the same thing can get a tad bit tiring. The makers said the game is designed in a way to allow speed running and it shows, with best times going as low as 10 minutes. This allows many modes of play, adding variety to playthroughs. The items you recieve can be gotten in any order, and you don't even need all of them to complete the story, although catching them all surely helps solving some puzzles. The bosses aren't really given much backstory, as any other character really, but this may have been necessary, seeing as having loads of story in a game this short would detract from the gameplay. However, tidbits of information are scattered throughout the game and reading them adds some depth to the world of Ittle Dew. Some of the harder puzzles can be a little tricky to solve since the game doesn't tell you a couple of abilities one of your items has, nothing that a little thinking wouldn't solve, but seeing each new skill having a small tutorial, one could get a slightly confused. Ittle Dew is an adorable little game that really shows the developers put a lot of care in making it as fun and endearing as possible, while maintaing its unique humour.

Mad Games Tycoon expands on this concept by adding in the capability to physically build the office you work in, assign space to specific tasks like R&D, Graphics, Sound, Motion Capture, Production, etc., and expands on the concept presented by earlier game development sims.
It's not an extremely difficult game, I didn't find it very hard to look up and have over $11Bn in money, and I'd love it if they had a larger top end building size -- I found it difficult to effectively set up a game development firm that was working on multiple games at a time, because of the size constraints near end-game.

This game is currently in early access and not all of the features that will be present in the final game are present yet. Most notably, the ability to develop your own console and the ability to make games in a Free To Play model.
Despite this, Mad Games Tycoon plays like a fully realized game. It drops you into a garage in 1980 (which is how most of these games industry tycoon things start) and tasks you with making your name. Features are gated behind fairly simple milestones, or alternatively you can have them all available at the start when you know what you are doing.
Once you make enough money, you can move out of your garage into one of a number of larger office spaces. This is actually one of the weaker parts of the game as rebuilding all of your offices and refurnishing them can get quite tedious. The UI also fails here as there are limited options for how you can sort staff in your staff list, so once you get to more than 60 staff members, re-assigning them after a move can be a pain since you can only see one of their stats at a time in the list.
While I'm on the topic of weaknesses in this game, once you get to later stages, again in the larger offices, micromanaging everything can get quite stressful. This is especially true if you choose to develop multiple games at once and self-release them.
The strength of the game is its willingness to allow the player to march to the beat of their own drum. If you wanted to, you could spend the whole game developing game engines and selling them to other companies with profit sharing clauses. You could spend the game publishing titles that other developers have made. Mad Games Tycoon allows you to do this.
If you want a game that explores every aspect of the games industry, look no further than Mad Games Tycoon.

I give Master of Orion a CONDITIONAL recommendation:
It's a good ENTRY POINT for people just getting into the 4x genre.
It seems that we can all forget about Master of Orion 3 now, right? But the question is: should we? The game didn't turn out well, but the things it tried to do were important to the 4x genre. It tried to eliminate micro-management and allow players to control a truly massive empire. It tried to focus most of the challenge and intrigue on the second half of the game, rather than it all being front-loaded into the early stages. These are valiant goals for a 4x to strive for. It's a shame that they didn't work out.
This rebooted Master of Orion is forgetting all of that and simply hitting the reset button. Though I had some fun, I don't see myself coming back to Master of Orion once I'm done with it.
Master of Orion: Conquer the Stars doesn't have any fatal flaws. It looks slick and has a lot of nice bells and whistles. It just doesn't do anything particularly well, and some of the systems and mechanics have annoying nagging flaws and feel a bit shallow. If anything, Master of Orion works well as a fairly gentle introduction to 4x strategy. It's easy to jump into, and games play pretty quickly. I actually completed an entire game in a single afternoon -- something that's nigh impossible in a game of Civilization VI. If you're new to the genre, then this is a great introduction. It has enough going for it to be interesting, but isn't going to overwhelm you in the way that a bigger 4x game like Endless Space or Europa Universalis or Stellaris might.
This is a solid successor to the classic Master of Orion games, and it's a great entry-point if you're interested in the genre. For experienced 4x players, there's bigger, better games on the market right now.

I like XCOM and have played the previous games in the series.
I was reluctant to buy this DLC because of 2K's pricing of it but, because I like these games, decided to buy it anyway.
Here's a list of noticable differences TO ME and what I think:
1. They've managed to iron out the creases in terms of performance. Now the game runs more smoothly and loading times have been reduced. HOWEVER, this should have been a free patch and doesn't justify the price of the DLC in my opinion.
2. Some of the additional content is fun and adds new stuff to the game that refreshes it. Some of the additional content, which seems to count towards the "loads of new additions that justifies the price" is stuff I can do on my mobile phone (messing about with photos and adding effects) which doesn't really have any effect on the game other than to perhaps build a bit of immersion in your own mind.
3. The game seems to be MUCH more challenging to me, which is good, but also a little frustrating at times when I try to be tactical. E.g. Discovering that I can still be hit (and killed) from a shot that came from across the map while I'm behind full cover, while all my shots seem to suffer a much larger penalty. I mention this here because I don't recall this happening in the base game. I could be wrong. There are plenty of new options available to customise your game.
All-in-all, I think many people will review this game based on their opinions of XCOM overall. The game is still as fun as it was before and the additional content does add to that.
But was it worth the full-game price? No, not at all, in my opinion. When I look at the additional content ALONE, and how it has been blended into the original game, I don't think they've done enough to justify making tens of millions of £/$ from this.
Should someone pay £60+ for the base game and the DLC if they want to get into it? Certainly not. Start with the base game and get the DLC later at a discount.
I've "recommended" this game simply because I'm enjoying it and whether you choose to pay the extortionate price for DLC is entirely up to you.

This is a great game, but wow is there a gigantic difficulty spike at the very end. They've added a checkpointing system to alleviate it, but the last boss is just
compared to the rest of the game.
See, for most levels you're able to use any of your characters, because they all have different uses. In the last stage though, there's a series of three different levels, each with three boss enemies - and only
of your characters is capable of dealing significant damage to them.
For the first two bosses, that's fine; you just clear out the board a bit, then pull out the special character and poke them until they die. If your special character dies, it's no big deal; you can just gather mana with someone else and revive them. It's not fast, but you make consistent progress.
For the third boss, though, you just can't
that. This boss has two special attacks: he does something which causes a lot of damage, and he does something else that drains your mana.
This means that instead of the normal repertoire of six or seven characters, you've only got three that matter: the healer, who restores your health; the ranger, who is immune to mana drain; and the special character, who's the only one that can significantly hurt the boss.
If any one of those three dies, you're boned. Healer's gone? Well, you're going to take a lot of damage, which means you're more likely to lose another character. Special character dies? Now you're playing catchup, because the person who does the next-highest damage to the boss deals 1/5th the damage. Ranger dies? You might as well give up. You're going to have a really hard time building up enough mana to restore another character, because there's no mana charms on this stage and to reach the mana gathering spots you need to go around the boss.
And going anywhere
the boss is super dangerous - if you ever make the mistake of hitting him head on, he smacks your character with a friggin Chaos Dunk and they go flying straight into the middle gutter. It's really, really hard to recover from that.
Overall though, this is a great game - it's just a pity the difficulty went from Super Mario World to Dark Souls over the course of one boss.

MOO CTS plays it safe by rehashing MOO2 with modern technology.  It's hard to fail at that but then it won't be anything revolutionary.   The most significant difference is that the map is a bit more like MOO3 with choke points - requiring more strategic selection of systems.  That's an upgrade.
The style and artwork of the game is great.
The game is much better balanced than MOO2 - but still stays true to the nature of each race (making some very OP - *cough* Elerian *cough*).  It's for the better IMO.  Where balance fails is with the fast pace of science (then you're greeted with science points contributing to nothing but score once completing the tree) and the slow pace of population growth.  Fortunately these can be tweeked in settings.  Set growth to fast and tech to very slow.
The biggest and most significant negative is how brain dead the AI is.  It is by far the most predictable and utterly ineffective AI I have come across.   It's at least better than the impossibly brutal AI of MOO3..
In the end it's good enough to be the MOO game to play for the modern gamer.  MOO2 is still amazing and you should play it but MOO CTS will probably get much more play time.   Definitely worth a buy if you like turn based strategery.

A fetus lookalike creature
A giant testicle that runs away from you after you damage it enough!

Berseria takes places in the Holy Midgand Empire, a powerful country that rules over this world's archipelago of a continent. The game's world is shared with Tales of Zestiria, although the events will occur in the distant past of Zestiria. Throughout the empire, a disease known as Daemonblight causes those infected to lose their humanity and sense of rationality and transform into monsters known as Daemons, who pose a threat to the world. Along with the rulers of the Holy Midgand Empire exists a theocratic order known as the Abbey, who are of great political and religious importance and are influential in imperial affairs. The Exorcists, soldiers from the Abbey, are tasked with bringing peace and order by purging the world of Daemons and are willing to go to extremes to reach their goal.
What I am saying is every single Tales game that have ever been released has always been NEW something that wasn't in a previous game, new characters in some of the sequels instead of focusing on the protagonists of the original.

Picture this:
You and 6 others are manning a small sloop. Wind whips through the sails, it's raining and you can barely see. In the distance, cannons ring out and you can see ship lights through the fog. Through the wind you hear your captain yell out, "Galleon incoming! Portside cannons ready!" You and your crewmates run to the cannons and ready your lighters. The galleon appears through the rain and fog, suddenly. She comes up alongside your tub, anti sail cannons firing upon your ship. "Fire!" the captain calls out. You all touch your fuses with the lighters, one after another. Boom, boom, boom, boom. Grapeshot fires from your ship and explodes into the side of the galleon. Bits of wood fly, intermingled with arms and legs. You look to your right and your friend has exploded into a fine red mist from an enemy cannonball. As the smoke from the cannon clears, you realize your ship has taken on damage as well. The captain calls to repair, and the 5 of you who remain rush to patch the holes. You're taking on water, and you rush to man the pump. Your ship, now upright, begins to turn portside to take another pass. You all begin loading the cannons, ready to do some more damage. The galleon however, is already upon you. You're not ready, and their cannons ring out. 6 holes, 7 holes, 8 holes in your ship. You all once again attempt to repair your boat. Even the captain has left his post to patch the holes. But it's too late, you've already taken on too much water.
"The Cuck Bucket has sunk" the text reads out as you and your beloved ship slip into the black, briny deep.

The object of the game is to win with your faction, Town, Mafia, or Neutral (dependent.) There are several game modes that affect the amount and roles of members in each faction, in custom mode the host chooses the roles and this can lead to some less than fun matches, BUT you always have the option to leave the lobby. The abilities differ from randomly selected role to role, you cna be a Serial Killer bent on murdering each and every member of the town, a crime boss leading a group of mafia members to become the last people standing, a kindly doctor whose goal it is to make sure your target survives the night, or even a madman whose soul goal is to be hung through the voting system in game, allowing him to "haunt" someone who voted him guilty.
The game has two sections, the day section where members talk to each other through an implemented text chat function (No voice chat, sorry!) and decie if someone needs to be hung by the town and if so the members vote on who is guilty or innocent once someeone is sent on trial. The night phase does not allow comunication (excpet through special roles and mafia members) and allows roles to use there special abilites, such as choosing someone to murder or protect (Whilst avoiding detection)
Each game is an entire different experience, and the game as a whole is very rewarding and msot certainly worth its miniscule $4.99 pricetag.

From the moment I booted it up, I knew Bastion would be one of the most amazing games I will ever play. Here are some of the things I love about the game; all are solid reasons to pick it up.
1) The art  - The brightly colored, oil paint style art mixed with the minimalist level design of only showing you areas you can explore make you want to explore and live in the world. The feeling of the art reminds me a bit of Braid, in that on the surface it seems childish and harmless, but also strongly hints at the darkness and uncertainty in the plot by painting in constantly shifting colors that vary in brightness and hue.
2) The gameplay - Bastion features an arcade style "weapon 1 / weapon 2 / special" button masher combat system which is both simple enough to completely understand by the end of the very well designed tutorial level and contains enough innovation to remain interesting through the end of the game. The variety of very distinct weapons (as opposed to gun 1, gun 2, etc that many FPS employ today) allows you to choose your own play style. The upgrade system for weapons encourages striving to find the material to upgrade your favorite, but doesn't require crazy amounts of grinding to do so. Finally, the base challenge level of the game is low enough that you'll be able to beat it, but early on you have the option to raise the difficulty in exchange for XP, (psuedo) money, and achievements in a variety of different ways.
3) The plot - Bastion has an unbelievable plot. A real plot, to the level of a fantasy novel. Early on, you are tasked with rebuilding the bastion, a safe haven in case of disaster that has fallen into disrepair in the wake of "the calamity". It seems simple at first, but wrinkles appear - what was "the calamity"? Who caused it? Who are the Ura? What are the backstories of the characters? And why repair the bastion, what will that do? I won't spoil any more, but suffice to say at the very end of the game you are offered two choices, and while I've played other games with choice systems, I've never thought this hard about which choice to make. The fate of the world that you very much feel a part of rests on your shoulders.
4 and my personal favorite) The sound - The entirety of Bastion is narrated by an old man who you meet very early in the game. He describes your character in the third person, as though all of your exploits are an old tale. And when I say all your exploits, I mean it - he narrates every blow you strike and boss you defeat in a fashion that makes you feel like you're writing history throughout your adventure. Interspersed in his narration are bits and pieces about the world that tie the plot together. The music, especially the bastion theme, perfectly complement the art style and the gameplay. The bastion theme starts out bare and thin, but as you rebuild it the music grows in strength and instrumentation in a rustic style, with a message of "it's going to be rough but we're getting through this". There are a few songs with words in the game that are used to great affect to drive a plot event home.
Overall, Bastion is unbelievable. It is a game that seeks to be more than just a game. It is gripping, dark, fast-paced, thought-provoking, and challenging in more ways than one. It is a masterpiece.

You will have some days on Duty where tons of action occurs. As soon as your day starts you get to a simple task like perform traffic stops, or road blocks and check drivers for vehicle problems, such as invalid license plates and drunken drivers. Or simple tasks such as ticketing illegally parked vehicles.
Other days you will get calls about robberies, injured people, people assisting in homicides. The game does have a customization menu for your vehicle and you can buy new weapons as well which is a nice feature however it is rather limited. You also do get promotions and paid more money with those promotions to buy new cars, customize them and also decorate your home.
You have 3 meters on your screen you need to keep track of.
-Energy (You need sleep)
-Hunger
-Stress (You reduce this by watching TV, showering, or hanging with family or friends on your time off)
The games major downfalls come in its outdated graphics as well as bugs. The AI can be very buggy at times and all over the place, also some of the options do not work so well. Such as obtaining a search warrant, I cannot seem to get this to work for the life of me.
All in all a great game, but it feels unfinished, it plays like it's early access and I wish there was a wider variety of jobs to perform besides ticketing, injured people, drunken drivers and fleeing criminals. I would love for the developers to bring new content to this game and address the issues with the bugs.
All in all I like the game game but I would NOT pick this up at full price. Wait for it to go on a major sale. STEP UP TO THE PLATE DEVS! Please fix this game.

This game certainly is more than just interesting. I haven't played a similar game before even though now I know there were games like this before. What at first seemed like a small little time waster, soon became one of my most played games.
In this game everyone in a village of 15 players gets a role which has each 1 special ability. You have 2 factions like Mafia and Townsfolk and certain unique roles like Werewolf and Serial Killer etc. This game is all about psychology and lying to others and finding out who is who because nobody knows for sure who can be trusted and everyone could be the serial killer, or belong to the mafia. During night time everyone can use their special ability, which can be anything depending on the role (kill someone, transport someone, protect, investigate, jail, douse, revive a dead, talk to dead etc etc).
Each day people can discuss about what happened, if they noticed anything etc. and then they can (but don't have to) vote to lynch/hang someone. But mind you, there is also a role called Jester, someone who's goal it is to get the others to lynch him.
Each round you play feels fresh and is fun as you usually get a new role each match. (there are 32 roles currently). Most roles are pretty fun to play.
I can only recommend this game. If you want to try it out for free there is a browser version free to play of this game. The steam version for 5€ is basically the same, but more stable since it's not browser related, no ads and you get 5€ of ingame currency for cosmetic changes like skins or pets etc.

For a new generation of MOM, this is a competent adoption, with some glaring issues. They aren't unplayable issues, but they do take some enjoyment out of the game.
The bright spots: The voice actors do a bueatiful job and were worth every penny. You may get tired of them after a while, but they are enjoyable, and it's worth the price of admission to experience them all.
The game hybrids between MOO 1 and 2 Economic model. You got population you can specialize in development and it has planetary surface development, but it does feel a lot like the Moo1 Sliders. None of this is a bad thing, and it feels nice wihtout having to micromanage too heavily.
Visuals are wonderful, and I tend to enjoy the colonization sequences. This might be a downside for others, but for me it doesn't get boring. At least not yet.
If you want to finish a game in a day or two, it is possible. Not a lot of strategy games lately can say this.
Downsides
Space Combat. OMG, you just have no control, it's almost worse than Moo3. It just is not servicable. I recommend skipping it. It's pretty, but not enjoyable at all.
Tech Tree : They get rid of the older system trees, and replace it with a singular development Civilization Style Tree. It's... okay. It has a few obvious paths through it. It's not as fun as Moo2's tree, but it serves welll.
Diplomacy - Yeah... it's... Well, it's not like they go to war at a drop of a hat, and the computer will work against itself, but if there is tech to trade, they'll trade it between itself before they'll trade it with you.
Overall, if you are new to the genre, and if you are an old fan, or if you just like space opera, this is a servicabe 4X game that honors it's sources well. If you are already a master of the genre and more complex space sims, you probably want to give this a pass. However, the voice performances are at least worth looking at.

As a fan who has enjoyed previous Master of Orion titles, I feel like I was duped into wanting this game.
What you get: some name recognition. Many of the races from the previous games are in this one. And it's a Master of Orion game.
What you don't get: anything like an enjoyable time. This game actually punishes you for playing it.
Let me lay out some of the features of this game:
1. Useless animations that can NOT be skipped.
2. The most pathetic excuse for a ship battle AI you will ever see from a fourth generation ship battle game. Even though the game penalizes you by making most weapons too heavy to be feasable for having anything but a forward-mounted gun, the AI rushes the enemy, forcing you to make wide sweeping turns to get a second shot in. But the enemy is now close on your heels, so that's never happening. Hope you only wanted one battle out of your expensive ship that took 20 turns to build!
3. Nonsensical diplomatic AI. On "normal" difficulty everyone you meet just can't wait to stab you in the back. This includes races listed as "pacifistic" in their descriptions. If the flavor text is all a big lie, why is there any flavor text at all? Really, don't bother with diplomacy unless you're going to be a bigger screwmeister than the computer.
4. None of the races act like they're supposed to. The Silicoids love diplomacy. The Psilons build up huge armies and shoot first. The Humans have the worst diplomatic skill I've seen in any science fiction setting that claims they have the highest diplomacy in the galaxy. The publishers didn't even try; again, nothing about these races but name recognition for players of previous games.
These are just some of the problems with the game. I'm sure you can read others and hopefully find reviews more insightful than, "This game sucks." Even though this software has more suction than a black hole.

There's DLC for it, but they seem to just add new races. I sure hope to hell that the DLC doesn't fix the above listed problems because that would turn a terrible game into the worst game ever.

Let me start by saying on real pinball tables I always prefered the older tables where you could control the launch via how far you pulled back the spring, and the buttons for the flippers you could somewhat control how hard you hit the ball, when tables switched over to the push button to launch and the flippers felt less controllable I didn't care for them. And that is how most all computer pinball games have felt to me, like they have all had the basic concept of pinball but lacking that feel and control of older pinball tables.
Does this feel like pinball of old? No, not at all, but it does feel really good. It contols smooth, the tables (or level's have you) all feel interesting, and its all around a good feeling game with some interesting mechanics to help it feel fun to control, unlike most digital tables and newer pinball tables.
Giving the game some RPG like mechanics is an interesting twist, and I enjoy the different abaliities the different classes have and how you switch between them. I think the only real negitive thing I have to say about this game is that the buying upgrades to make your classes stronger to "fight" harder enemies feels purely like a way to make people go back and play older tables again to grind some gold to add how long it takes to complete all the tables.  While it does give reason to play tables more then once as you go through the story it also makes previous tables more trivial as you get more and more stat upgrades, so it is kind of a double edge sword of forcing replaying slightly old tables while at the same time reducing the reason to play even older tables.
Adding RPG elements into a game just to add RPG elements can often end up being bad, but in this case it feels pretty good with how the different classes feel and what they do, its almost as if someone looked at Runespell :Overture and went "hey turning poker into a RPG when done right can feel really good, lets see if we can turn pinball into a RPG in a similar fation to Runespell Overture", and it worked out, it doesn't feel like a mechanic tacked on to have a  gimick, it feels like a legitimit mechanic with a purpose in the game to make it feel more enjoyable to play.
With that said, if you even slightly liked older pinball tables, or like the concept of digital pinball but don't like how most of them you don't feel like you have any real control, definitly give this one a shot.  At no point have I had a point where my death has felt like a "quarter eater mechanic" of having no control of the outcome, every death has felt like I just mis played it... And yes that is how I feel about older pinball machines compaired to newer ones, the older ones gave you better control, but as arcades started going away and as the fewer people playing pinball got better, they changed their controls to be "quarter eaters" much like how older video games where designed to have cheap deaths to eat quarters, on older tables I could play a single ball and earn extra balls for longer then all 3 balls of newer tables.

I would not recommend this game to anyone that is used to playing pinball games such as Zen Pinball, or any 'classic' RPG style pinball tables such as Pokemon Pinball, Sonic Spinball, etc. .
While this game tries to capture the spirit of previous games in the genre it completely fails to do so. Let's begin with some of the positives. It has some good voice acting, and an interesting design overall. Who wouldn't be stoked for an RPG pinball game? The RPG elements are incorporated into the playfields (more on that in a moment), and the idea is interesting.
I don't believe the execution was very good however. To begin with the most glaring issue, the controller support is awful, and feels terrible. A patch was issued so that some players not using Xbox style controllers could even play, but even with my 360 and Xbox one controller it still plays poorly. The menus feel horrible with a controller, there is no 'dead' zone, so the selection is bouncing all over the screen. On top of this there is a mechanic where you can select party members once in the game. This mechanic again suffers from the lack of dead zone. So you're trying to swap characters with a quick flick on the stick, and you just keep bypassing them in the list, hoping that you'll make it there eventually. There are also unbound keys by default, so only the flippers and launcher/special ability button work on a controller. Consumables cannot be used straight out of the box.
Once you get past the less than stellar controls, there are the mechanics themselves. You have some control over the ball when it is moving in regards to shifting its motion left or right. This is not done via bumping the table, but direct control on the ball which was extremely odd to me. After getting to the third area I've realized why they did this, and it's the biggest failing of the game. Almost every single level turns into a shooting gallery where you are attacking characters that stand in the middle of the playfield. There are three main types I've encountered: Guys that throw things/shoot arrows at your flippers, guys with shields you can only hit from behind, and guys with swords (sometimes with large healthbars), that try to knock your ball out. I wouldn't mind this if it wasn't the main mechanic for all but a few scant bonus levels but it happens all the time, and sometimes there are multiple waves of these enemies. It turns into 'get up around the side, try to cheese it by bouncing around on top of a guy using ball control, hope you do enough damage to kill them'. It's a poor design decision that leads me to believe they were unable to come up with more unique mechanics and tables that would enable such mechanics.
This frustration and boredom of the tables continues due to the size of most tables, they're very small, sometimes there are a few screens worth of areas, but often times those sections repeat mechanics. Additionally there are issues where special character abilities don't work, for example the knight character can block the main area between the flippers so you don't drain the ball, but the ball can bounce AROUND this area, and still drain, totally defeating the purpose of his special ability.
When looking at this game in a vacuum it might seem okay, but when you compare the mechanics here against older games in this genre, or even Zen Pinball tables, you can get more bang for your buck with a single table than I've played so far here (almost completed 3/6 chapters).
The physics feel bad and floaty, the tables repeat WAY too many of the same objectives (hit this thing, kill those guys), and it just doesn't feel great, especially with the poor controller support, which to me would have been essential for this sort of game.
I can't recommend Rollers of the Realm even on a sale, if you enjoy pinball you're not going to enjoy this game, it's boring, repetitive, and not challenging in a way that feels rewarding.

These fights are also very unrewarding, you might need to go through a dozen in 1 day, to get a bit more of materials - which may be around an hour in real time.
The characters themselves are shallow and generic: some sheriff guy, some army dude, some redneck with a feisty wife, some broad who gets saves on the road, some fatso who takes care of the supplies. I understand, that it's a sort of a comic RPG, but could I at least get some depth beyond two lines of text during the intro of a new character? And the hero himself? You can be joking around in a day or two with the new arrivals, even though your sister was gruesomly killed yesterday. How realistic is that?
At some point, 10 hours now into the game, I'm just forcing myself to continue because I (the further into the game, the less) want to see what happens when the military (supposedly) arrives, but if there's one word you can describe this game with, it's "repetitiveness".

Played this on Early Access and I was ... strongly ambivalent. Thought this was an exercise in futility back then.
Returned to the game since and -- it's GREAT.
It's not the most elaborate 4X game out there, but this game really manages to capture a perfect compromise between the original three Master of Orion games and comes up with a great niche spot in the current state of the genre.
Basically it has the simple elegence of MOO1 (and I mean this as a massive compliment), the colony building of MOO2 and the starlanes of MOO3.
I feel the starlanes are the most controversial feature of this game. I personally love them. To me they're a great way of keeping fleets sane, meaningful, and manageable. I like that you have fronts limited to a selection of systems. They make bases more meaningful too.
Overall simplicity -- I love games like Stellaris, but they're "big". I like that Master of Orion has everything on a boardgame-like board and I can understand what's going on in the big picture with generally understanded mechanics.
I still play Galactic Civilizations III and Stellaris regularly (and Civ 6), but Master of Orion definitely has a place in that echelon and I appreciate I can have a good solid campaign in 5-10 hours as opposed to 2-5x that...

It's a nice solo-RTS game with a great work on each scenario of the campaign. Once you setup your economy (growing fruits, feeding animals and selling them), there are various ways to achieve every objective, by using your special powers or sending a formation of soldiers.
Every aspect of the game stays simple. Don't expect a huge technology tree, just a few options. The same goes for creatures and units. But everything works together and provide a good experience.
On the other hand, the special powers got quite a lot of work, so you will be able to put monsters in a cage waiting to be killed, or expulse them from the islands with an explosion.
I really enjoy how each scenario is completely different from the others, and I'm glad to discover new ways to use the gameplay even towards the end of the game.
On the bad side, there is no save option mid game, so you will have to play several hours straight to complete each scenario (the game saves at the end of each scenario, and let you replay any previously completed scenario).
The overall pacing of the game is slow, but if you liked playing a Starcraft or Age of Empire map all by yourself, you will enjoy it.
Despite several crucial problems, I consider that this game is a true hidden gem so I recommend it.

I feel compelled to review this game as it was an instant-purchase and a subsequent let down for me. Firstly, I can see what the developers tried to do here, but imo they failed to produce a game thats fun to play for more than an hour. We want realism but we don't wan't constant frustration when it comes to difficulty, game UI and strange development choices - This is more of a resource management, strategy game, not an rpg, so why give us a main character who must survive or else - Game over! That's lame, especially considering we have no reason to care any more about him than the other survivors.
When it comes to the games difficulty, it suffers in the same way most similar games do, difficulty - building difficulty as the game progressed would actually give us a chance to learn how to play which would be far more preferable to just being dropped in the deep end, experiencing frustration and then dying. As a result of this, I have no motivation or desire to attempt the game again.
Sadly I have yet to find a post-apocalyptic survival game that is truly fun to play. (Not including zombie games of different styles/genres such as Telltales The Walking Dead, The Last of Us and Left 4 Dead - Zombie games done right in their own respective genres). In this genre, this is far from one of the better attempts I've seen which is sad because, for a game idea, this has practically unlimited potential but that is sadly missed once again with 'Dead Age'; Monotonous scavenging, pointless, reptitive zombie killing. I am a huge fan of the zombie genre when its done right, but this is not the case here. Refund requested.
TLDR - Another clone of a not-so-well thought out and repetive zombie survival / resource management genre. Not very fun to play and sporting a combat system that just doesn't suit the genre (Zombies healing each other - wtf?). There are much better similar games already on steam. The dialogue feels tacked on and we have a main character who we don't care about at all but must keep alive unless we want to start over.
Overall 5 / 10

A thrilling game that has provided me countless hours of fun, "Half-Life" is easily one of the best games I have ever played - and, I believe, perhaps one of the best games of all time. Being revolutionary at the time of its 1998 release, "Half-Life" isn't a pure shooting game full of mindless violence. It is something more, something much more. It has quite an interesting storyline, amusing easter eggs (I will let you discover them for yourself), quirky but loveable NPCs (the scientists and security guards), very interesting enemies and quite a few cases of truly fun problem solving. "Half-Life" is a game that requires you to think - that requires you to sometimes use the environment around you take out an enemy, rather than sheer firepower. And that, I think, is why I love "Half-Life": It's an intelligent game. I would warmly recommend it, maybe especially to those who are fond of shooting and problem solving, but generally to all who wants to play a really good game.

At first glance, "Serena" seems like a very bare-bones game. It takes place in a one-room cabin, with the drama supplied largely by voice-overs, music, and small changes to the cabin's appearance.  You can't navigate it with a mouse-WASD setup, only a basic point-and-click interface. You barely interact with the enviroment. It lacks even a menu, simply dropping the player into the game, and exiting when they hit "escape"... or when it's finished.  Yet within this meager setup, "Serena" delivers quite an emotional whammy.
The basic plot is that you are a man, who has been in a relationship with the titular Serena.  Now, in this cabin, you recall this relationship.  The plot is hard to describe in detail here, since a lot of what makes the game great is its gift for the slow reveal, but suffice to say that before the game is over, these recollections will take the player to a pretty shocking place.
The slow reveal truly elevates the game.  When I started playing, I was completely unimpressed.  The bare-bones set-up, combined with voice acting that doesn't do much at first, makes "Serena" feel like something hammered out by a couple of programmers and artists trying to make something "artsy." But the game acquires depth as it goes along.  There's a moment (you'll know it when you play it) when the game's sense of horror starts to creep in, and another (again, you'll know it) when it explodes.  The trick is keeping it steadily rising until then.
One consistent theme is the shifting nature of blame; the faceless protagonist goes back and forth between blaming himself for his relationship troubles, and vilifying Serena.  The game's ending twist, which is nicely foreshadowed, seems to upend some previous opinions about the real "bad guy", and yet you get the sense that neither character is really as good a person as they'd want to be.  They tried too hard to make a relationship last, and it drove them both a bit mad.  Isolation, another theme of the game's, may have something to do with that.  When you're in a cabin in the woods, and you slowly start to despise the only other person around, it might not be long before you do something crazy.

Picture this:
You and 6 others are manning a small sloop. Wind whips through the sails, it's raining and you can barely see. In the distance, cannons ring out and you can see ship lights through the fog. Through the wind you hear your captain yell out, "Galleon incoming! Portside cannons ready!" You and your crewmates run to the cannons and ready your lighters. The galleon appears through the rain and fog, suddenly. She comes up alongside your tub, anti sail cannons firing upon your ship. "Fire!" the captain calls out. You all touch your fuses with the lighters, one after another. Boom, boom, boom, boom. Grapeshot fires from your ship and explodes into the side of the galleon. Bits of wood fly, intermingled with arms and legs. You look to your right and your friend has exploded into a fine red mist from an enemy cannonball. As the smoke from the cannon clears, you realize your ship has taken on damage as well. The captain calls to repair, and the 5 of you who remain rush to patch the holes. You're taking on water, and you rush to man the pump. Your ship, now upright, begins to turn portside to take another pass. You all begin loading the cannons, ready to do some more damage. The galleon however, is already upon you. You're not ready, and their cannons ring out. 6 holes, 7 holes, 8 holes in your ship. You all once again attempt to repair your boat. Even the captain has left his post to patch the holes. But it's too late, you've already taken on too much water.
"The Cuck Bucket has sunk" the text reads out as you and your beloved ship slip into the black, briny deep.

If you like The Legend of Zelda then you will like this, as it's basically one big homage to the 2D Zelda games. It might be shorter than your usual Zelda game, but in return it gives a lot of brilliantly designed puzzles that genuinely makes you use your brain without relying on crazy-point-and-click logic. The combat isn't as good as in Zelda though, but it's decent enough to not be annoying, and the puzzles is the main meat of this game anyways. The artstyle and characters are also very enjoyable, mixing the best elements of Wind Waker with A Link To The Past vizually and having a colorful gallery of amusing enemies to fight, with a lot of fun references to the Zelda series scattered around for good measure. The music is also good, but not as memorable or brilliant as in the game it's based on, but it's cool still.
All in all, if you don't mind the game being a bit on the short side it's a great buy for any Zelda and/or puzzle fan.

This may be early access material, but it feels like very early access. More troubling is the fact that the developer suffers from a complete lack of focus on so many areas of the game (as others have mentioned).
Here's an example:
I get that toilets is a part of every day life, but when your little worker ants go potty as the game speeds forward at a pace where weeks are seconds, I see no reason why I should be treated to the view said ants taking a 15 second potty break, and then don't even wash their hands. That's right. After 15 weeks spent on a potty break (don't ask me what they ate), don't even wash their hands. Filthy animals!
I'm not saying I want the developer to add a new animation just to show me that my employees are wasting another couple of weeks washing their hands, I'm saying we're getting distracted by this whole potty nonsense to begin with! Just like the developer! There's no reason to even show such behavior at all, unless we're moving at a real time pace, in which case, those filty animals better wash up! A simple complaint notification about there not being a proper bathroom with a toilet and sink would be more than enough.
In Game Dev Tycoon, the employees need vacations now and again. That's fine. Perfect, in fact... because this isn't a real time kinda game. Focus on the big stuff, and not the potty. Please.
Another example of the developer wasting time:
There's no need for 3D models just to make a thumbnail representation of each individual worker ant. The 3D models currently in use are so badly made, I can't even tell race or gender most the time. I was playing the game, and it suddenly struck me that I only looked at the stats when hiring people. Go figure! My brain told me to hire the most skilled worker ants over the rest. I forgot all about being "politically correct" and trying to "diversify" my staff, so I decided - because I'm a perfectionist (and an idiot) - that I would make an effort to make sure my staff was in fact diverse.
That's where I ran into said problem, not being able to tell the one from the other. But it doesn't really matter. This isn't real life and I don't live in a country that's run amok with politically correctness. It's not even a feature in the game. I'm honstly just wasting your time with this rant, just like the developer is wasting their time making 3D models that suck, instead of making simple 2D graphics and focus their efforts on what this game is really about! Managing a game company! You'd think a game company would grasp this inescapable revelation.
The "tutorial guy" that pops up and tells you what to do talks too much, and doesn't really help that much. I was better off just clicking around and figuring things out on my own. There's no mention of how big a room should be in comparison to other rooms, or how many desks you would need to get a balanced workload.
In the smaller buildings, you'll want to maximize on what little space there is, but you can't create wall to wall rooms in certain scenarios because you're only allowed to have one door! That means you have to waste space on hallways, which really feel like undeveloped, empty space.
The gamebreaking fault with this game:
I spend hours and hours in my very first garage, slowly figuring out what was important and what wasn't. I ended up with a simple one desk office, a one desk research pit of despair, a bathroom which I'm having some kind of problem with (apparently), and I think that was about it. From these humble beginnings went from struggling to survive, to making millions of dollars! Then I bought a gigantic office space, spent half the day drawing up rooms and adding props. A few hours later I had 1500 Mill $ in the bank, a thriving MMO and the ability to produce and store millions of copies of my own games. That is to say: I was done. No new consoles coming out anymore. Nothing more to aspire to. Game Over!
It's like the game doesn't have proper stages for advancement. At one point, my worker ants were making a AA game. I clearly didn't have the staff for it, because it took about 20 years to finish, and every year I'd show up with a booth at the convention just to pick up more fans along the way. The fans stayed true and loyal for 20 years as I was promising to deliver. That aspect is something Game Dev Tycoon did really well. If you didn't publish within a certain timeframe after marketing your game, you'd lose fans so fast it looked like a snowball rolling downhill, heading straight for your office.
If I had to do it all again, I'm pretty sure I could reach the same level of success in half a day, and that's not a game worth money to me. There's not much replayability here. I know, because I don't want to go through this circus again. Besides, games like this are only really fun before you graduate to the big leagues, at which point it becomes a managing nightmare. This is why in real life we delegate! I don't want to have to tell that guy to do these same six things with every game I make! He should learn to do this automatically, because that's what I'd tell him to do if this was real life! I'm the boss! I don't wanna deal with all the little things. I have minions for that! I just wanna make the big decisions! There's management, and then there's micro-management.
When all is said and done, this game goes a smidge deeper than Game Dev Tycoon, but there are simply too many faults, missing pieces and lack of focus for me to think that Mad Games Tycoon will ever match the geniusly simplistic, polished marvel that is Game Dev Tycoon. Scrap this one. Start over. As for my recommendation: Don't buy! I want my money back, and this tragic game off my games list.

Guys I get it, it's been in early access for a while. It's not "completed" yet and that pisses a lot of you off. However, there are a LOT of amazing things about this game. First of all, let's get this out of the way. The art style is amazing, I absolutely LOVE the soundtrack and the game runs very fast. Second, this big update redid the whole progression system. I think that with a few more tiers, this could be a better progression than any other survival game, although it already surpasses most. When the update came out me and my bro immediantly downloaded it and thats where most of my time  came from. I also have a lot of hours in the unstable which I belive those are seperate from the hours I have here. I've done about 3 characters if you're including the two before the update, and I already have 66 hours. Also the looting system is AWESOME, it's not RNG unlike games like terraria. When you find a chest, which trust me you will find a lot of, you're almost guarenteed to find a weapon which power is determined by the tier planet you're on. The gameplay is ridiculously fun, although I'm not a huge fan of the missions. The game also has some big background lore if you're into that kind of stuff. There is an amazing crafting system with just so many options, espicially in the lategame. If you don't want to, you don't even have to build a base unlike most survival games, you can get the ship upgrades, which are all different depending on your race. Also let's not forget the sheer size of this universe. There are SO many planets, it forms in a certain pattern, and it would be simply impossible to explore the whole universe. You can fly anywhere inside your solar system for free, but you can hop to another system using fuel, which you will most likely use liquid etherium, found on moons. I could go on forever about this game, but there's too much to love. I know that the game isn't finished, but it's 15 bucks and you can get SO much time in it. Just try it, you won't be dissapointed.
