As far as Early Access games go...
I love this game!
TL;DR Scroll to bottom
-------------------------
Tired of CS:GO? Tired of the Halo's and the Team Fortresses? BUT, you LOVE Pirates?!
Get this game!
The action is fast paced, and teamwork is crucial, in this Pirate 3rd person shooter.
Join as a crew member of one of two different ships currently in-game.
Put your name into the hat to be considered Captain of the vessel.
Captaining the ship allows you to give commands to crew members (Other real life players!) as well as steer the ship as you please. Beware! Only the best Captains get voted in... in theory. Fear not, for there is the ability to MUTINY those scurvy dogs that aren't fit to walk land, let alone tame the high seas!!!
------------------------------------------------------
The game is fun with a good crew, tolerable with a bad one. But with a bad captain... unplayable.
So far I haven't had a bad captain... and if you do get one, the aformentioned MUTINY option is always popular. The community seems fun, role playing is a delight on most servers. There is, of course, still children... people that scream and swear and generally act a pirate every second of the match. Much like any game I suppose.
BEWARE, DEAD MEN TELL NO TALES! So don't be a dead man... speak up! Report bugs! Report problems! The game is under construction, and as such there are some... quirks to be expected. Server lag, ships crashing through rocks, through EACH OTHER, and other
things happen from time to time. But the only way the EXTREMELY ACTIVE developers will find out, is if you report it!
The game is being constantly patched and updated and improved. And I mean, daily. Sometimes multi times a day. The developers REALLY want this game to be fun, enjoyable, and PLAYABLE. So they have an ear to the discussion boards. Always paying attention.
-----------------------------------------------------------------
TL;DR
Buy the game if you like Pirate themed games. Especailly if you like Mount & Blade style combat, but Piratized.
You won't regret it. Worth 20 bucks, and on sale for $17.99 it's a steal!

I was pretty excited to see a god game pop up on steam.  Ever since Populus on the Amiga I've loved the genre but The Mims misses the mark for me.
Each mission takes place on a floating island, each of which contains new dangers to overcome.  The developers have clearly made an effort to give the game a semblence of plot although the transitions between missions feel a bit sudden with no real explanation of why the little aliens are choosing the next landmass or what happened to everything you left behind on the last one.
The gameplay for the most part is fairly simple.  Plants generate fruit, fruit gives you biomass and feeds your livestock and selling your animals gives you gems.  Both gems and biomass can be used to build and upgrade structures to further advance your camp with gems generally being your bottleneck.
Trying to over extend your production of fruit or livestock will result in pests coming to eat your resources or hostile life being attracted to your island which will attack your animals and Mims.  You need to balance production to minimise threats.  This system of discouraging over production is a really nice mechanic.
Sadly, the good news stops there.  The AI and some game mechanics feel poorly optimised which leads to more frustration than fun.
Mims get tired as they work and will need to rest up in a house to get their energy back.  On one level, despite having one house for every two Mims they just refused to rest regularly.  My guardians, essential for defense of my village are particularly guilty of not resting up when they have the chance and are frequently all out of energy when I most need them.
Despite being told early on that my Mims love nature, destroying trees is often the only viable way to get enough building space.  I could overlook the backstory hole here is the process of removing foliage wasn't so painful in it's own right; setting fire to some of the bigger trees just reduces their size, usually requiring three bursts of flame to get the job done.  The trees will grow back a bit though so if anything interrupts your pyromania while your Psi power build up (like needing to heal some guardians) you'll find the tree back to full height before you can have another go.
Plants can be a source of annoyance in other ways too.  Several of the fruit providing plants will throw their finished product across the island and despite my best efforts to ensure that they're aimed at a building or that they have plenty of space for the fruit to land, I frequently find my new fruit tree throwing their resources off the edge of the island.
A little trial and error with placement of my plants could maybe be forgiven if it was at least possible to sell my plants back or reposition after they've grown but this is sadly not possible.
The final straw for me though is the lack of a save feature.  Missions aren't particularly quick to complete and I've had a couple of occasions now where I've had to stop playing mid mission for one reason or another and have to abandon my progress.
Overall it's a game with some neat ideas and potential to be fun but seriously marred by it's shortcomings.

TL;DR: So, I got this game off humble bundle and wasn't particularly excited to play it. I started it up expecting to hate it after a few minutes and then just let it idle for the cards, but boy was I wrong. This game is really good. Probably among the most fun puzzle game I've played. Easy 8/10.
So in this game you play as an adventurer. Not much is known about your character aside from the fact that she's totally a girl. I mean, I didn't pay too much attention to the story, but that's basically all I know about it having completed the game.
You're off to get 3 magical items to help you solve progressively more complicated puzzles, a fire sword, a portal wand, and a ice wand thing. Different objects on the screen interact differently (or not at all) with each magical item. Conveniently, a local shopkeeper sells them and you're able to purchase them from him. Only, when you do, you're put into a puzzle series cave where you have to show somewhat of a mastery of the item to get out.
Some of the puzzles are really solid, making you somewhat frustrated after not getting them within the first 10 tries. Of course, there's also the others that are super obvious and take maybe 1 attempt, 2 if you pressed the wrong button. Good variety and the later stages of the puzzles make you think with portals.
Combat is pretty dull in the game. Though, admittedly, I totally died to a pancake out of recklessness more than a few times. Valv pls fix. You press x to do the damage, or you can be fancy and try to teleport mobs into spikes or something.
The controls either weren't given out in the game (I had to press every key on my keyboard to figure out how to use the stick to attack for a while), or I totally didn't pay attention to the tutorial. There is a 2 level tutorial.
Oh, I forgot to mention, the puzzles vary between push blocks into pressure plates, clear all enemies on the map, light all the things that need lighting, or burn out all the things that shouldn't be on fire. You might think that's pretty lame and hardly fun, but the quickness of the game definitely makes thing way less awful than they would be. Trust me.
Aside from combat, which really isn't even a big deal because the game isn't driven to encourage you to fight everything on the map except in a few area where you need to to open a door, the only real upset with the game is how fast you can complete it. Keep in mind, I had intended to just get all the cards in the game and then back out. I was sucked in and before I knew it, I finished the game. I mean, sure, I didn't 100% it, but I cleared the final boss. I didn't expect to because a certain key item given out at the end led me to believe that there would be some other areas to access, but that wasn't the case. In my first blind run, I finished the game in three and a half hours. I mean, sure, that's actually a pretty reasonable time for a game to take in a campaign mode anyway, but I really really wanted more. I guess that's a good thing, though.
So after getting here this far, you probably know that I'm going to rate this game pretty highly. I would put Antichamber and Portal above this game in terms of similar games that are more fun, but this game isn't too far behind! Easy eight out of ten. I would only dock points for not doing anything groundbreakingly new (which would push it over the top and is basically a requirement to get a 10. ♥♥♥♥ people who give every game 10s), and being exceptionally short. Though, the latter is likely not an issue because this game can be played on your phone.

.Story/Premise.
The Mims are strange, multi-eyed orange aliens who have landed on this scattered collection of floating islands as the result of a meteorite rain in space. You are their Saviour who will lead them to the missing parts of their space ship and their lost DNA Orb, which has the power to settle entire planets. The writing is amusing, though sometimes the humour felt a little forced.
.Game play.
In typical god game fashion, you have to plant, build, and use your powers in order to keep your little Mims alive.
Plants are important in both animal husbandry and building. Species require specific fruits in order to mature so that they can be sent to market and those same fruits can also be ground into biomass, which serves as a currency for creating animals and building structures. Gems also serve as currency and these can be gotten by selling adult animals or by breaking nodes found randomly around the map.
There is a total of 16 buildings, ranging from resource refinement to unit production. Placement is affected by the range of your Psi Tower, which acts as your HQ and allows you to launch rescue parties into space and recruit more Mims. The Psi Tower also allows you to use your powers.  Other buildings such as the Science Lab allows you to procure various species and the Port allows you to sell them for gems.
One interesting thing about The Mims Beginning is the smells system. By planting plants, you raise your plant smell meter and by raising animals, you raise your animal smell. As the smell level rises, critters both troublesome and deadly appear with increased frequency. The system forces you to pace your expansion and maintain a balance between production and military strength.
Your powers range from fire, which is primarily used for terra-forming, to speed buffs and debuffs, to spells that replenish your Mims' energy. You can use any of these powers as long as you have the energy to do so and energy replenishes naturally--though you can build electricity-producing structures in order to speed up the process. Electricity is also used to power your buildings and having enough means that everything will run efficiently.
.Graphics/ Art Style.
The Mims Beginning is cute. The art style is bright and colourful in a very family friendly way. The story is told in faux- cutscenes which are shown in the form of gameplay with a text box displayed at the bottom.
.Longevity/Difficulty.
I found that the difficulty spiked at random intervals during my play on the normal difficulty. Some maps took me near/longer than an hour to clear while others took only a few minutes once I figured out how to approach my objective.
.Pros and Cons.
+There are a host of abilities for you to use, which keeps dealing with the various problems that come up interesting.
+Clean, uncluttered U.I. Everything is clearly labelled and easy to access.
+Cute, sometimes funny story.
+Clear objectives, which are always available for you to review.
-The Mims very rarely clump together, which means refreshing their energy takes time and careful positioning.
-Limited structure selection.
-The Mims' artificial intelligence leaves a lot to be desired. I found that I had to do a LOT more micromanaging than I wanted (which means selecting Mims one by one and turning off their autonomy so that they'd do as I instructed) just to ensure things would run smoothly.
-Your godly powers can hit friendly units. This would be fine if it wasn't so easy to punt one of your workers off the side of the map while attempting to rid yourself of other enemies.
-No ability to select a group. Even when your warrior units are in formation, sometimes they won't all move together as one.
.Bottom Line.
Fans of god games and RTS will enjoy The Mims Beginning, and even those new to the genres could get their feet wet. Assuming you have patience, of course. I can't say I'd recommend it at full retail price, but if it sees a substantial (40~60%) price cut and you're really looking for a god game, then go for it.

Camera Obscura is a "puzzle" platformer, although the biggest gripe I have is that some of the "puzzles" don't feel very fair in their design, and where a simple mistake in later levels can force you to restart the whole level, like racing a slime to the end of the level, only to accidently kill it with your camera. How do you kill a slime with a camera, you ask? Simple: Using your camera (which, beyond jumping, is all you can do), you take a shadowy copy of the immediate surrounding landscape that is centered around you, and it follows you for a moment before freezing in place, which when combined with jumping and falling, can allow you to reach new heights, cross large chasms, or crush enemies between the shadowy terrain and the real terrain.
While you are able to prematurely dismiss the shadowy terrain you make with your camera, you have no way to deal with the few creatures in the game if encountered in large, open areas, to which most of the levels are designed as, and several levels throw sharp spikes in difficulty at you, like trying to jump from a higher, wider ledge down to a lower, more narrow ledge that is under the wider one, or like in the example in the first paragraph, racing a slime without killing it or letting it get too far ahead of you. There are three other incentives that will also demand perfection from you with the use of your camera; Photos, Flash medals, and Time trial medals.
Photos are the game's collectable and actually don't have any images on them, but rather they give details of the game's world and the protagonist's backstory, yet some of them require tricky or advanced shadowy terrain manipulation to reach. Flash medals are rewarded based on how many times you used the camera to make shadowy terrain; the fewer used, the better the medal. Time Trial medals are, well, rewarded on how fast you finish a level. Very straight forward for those. Between the three, they are ment to create replay value for the game, however the absurd increase in difficulty without proper tutorials creates frustration, especially when ingame text about your controls is spread few and far apart (which should be covered in like, say, a tutorial).
All in all, if you plan to pick up the game for yourself, pick it up only when it's on sale; The frustration induced by this "puzzle" platformer is not welcomed.

I want to like this game. I really do. However, in its current state, I just can't recommend it. Here are my thoughts (and for context, I have played MOO, MOO2, Stellaris, Endless Space, and Galactic Civilization, among many other turn-based games).
1. First and foremost, it's difficult to find information on many aspects of the game. For example, if you are trying to recall whether you can build an asteroid mine or laboratory in an uncolonized system, you have to send your space factory to a buildable location (like a warp point, and, presuming your build icon lights up, you can click on it and read the text. There's no way in-game (at least, that I've found yet) to call up this information. Likewise, want to find out what weapons your ship has? If you are in the main game interface, it's possible (although the easiest way is to click on blueprints). If you are in battle, also possible. But if you are on the pre-battle screen, you are out of luck. This lack of information (or lack of consistency) is so frustrating, that I really don't know if some of the problems I experienced were bugs or design features. For example, I can see all sorts of information regarding enemy fleets (including the weapons) but not why the hell the Space Dragon was apparently regenerating while I was shooting it. If that's just a feature of space dragons that is hidden from the player, then why tell me its health and attack strength?
2. The tactical combat system sucks. I reduced my turn length to 5-seconds so that I could have a semblance of turn-based gameplay, but the computer had no idea how to use my specialized combat designs, and quite frankly, neither did I. My escort class ships that sported a lot of point defense wouldn't stay formed up on my battleships and cruisers. And while they shot at missiles targeting them, they *didn't* shoot at anything targeting my other ships. Come on, the combat simulator in Gratuitous Space Battles is better than this, and you can't even do anything once the battle starts!
3. Why the hell can I rename planets but not ships? For that matter, why is my ship name limited to relatively small names? I wanted to create a "Light Carrier" class, but that was too long for the naming system.
4. I understand the blueprints and why the devs limited the number of designs you can have, but it would have been better to allow for a set number of designs PER CLASS. As it is, having specialist designs that you want to upgrade as new tech becomes available means obsoleting designs just to make room for new blueprints. Want to have a fast attack frigate and an escort class? Want to have a battleship that is primarily a missile design with plenty of PD and another that's a well-armored carrier? That's four of your designs right there. Want to tinker with a new prototype and see how it works? Sorry, that's not happening; again, unless you want to lose a design or two.
5. I had no idea that you could be attacked in neutral space by an AI opponent that you are at peace with and have friendly relations. The fact that my opponent could engage in a sneak attack destroying a colony ship (and presumably all of the colonists) without penalty surprised me; which is in itself, unsurprising, seeing as this "feature" isn't documented anywhere. Civilization, in comparison, makes you build privateers at least and not fly your own countries flag when you attack unarmed transports.
This game lacks polish, has interface, AI, gameplay, and other issues, and is equally frustrating and irritating. Someday, I will find a modern 4X game that has the just-one-more-turn playability of MOO2, combined with modern graphics and a gameplay equivalent of
meets
. But in its current state, I sadly give this game a  thumbs down.

Camera Obscura is a very simplistic looking side-scroller, that is reminiscent of something on the NES or Super NES. What makes this particular game different from other similar games is our ability to manipulate your surroundings by taking a photograph. When you take a photograph it creates an afterimage which you can then manipulate for a few seconds to create obstacles, bridges, stairs etc. There are 57 levels of the tower you must climb and each level contains photographs you can collect. The levels are timed allowing you to earn up to a gold star if you complete it withina certain length of time. As you progress the difficulty becomes greater with wild animals, and dangerous traps. For as simplistic as it looks, it is actually a lot of fun. You can really toy around with the afterimage effect and explore.
From what I understand there is also a custom level editior with this game meaning you can make your own levels and share them on the steam workshop. This would be very interesting to see how creative and insane of levels people can come up with. All in all, it is a decent buy. Probably best to buy it as part of the developer aliance bundle so you have a few other games to play around with as well,

Garbage. Broken gloss maps and insanely dark enviroment greet you, after which you find a flashlight. It runs on batteries that, like all horror game batteries, are out of power before you can say ''Wallmart''. This isn't a glaring issue, as games like Outlast managed to pull it off by having batteries be everywhere and the flashlight non-essential. All the English that IS in the game feels likeit was Google translated, and for the rest of the text in-game, it's in Russian. So if you actually want to know what's going on, you better start learning Russian today.
This game is absolute trash made to get a quick buck off the insanely abusable Steam Greenlight system. How this ever got through is anyone's guess, how it got trading cards is another, but how it actually sold more than 2 copies before it was taken down baffles me.

Town of Salem is presented somewhat in the style of an animated board game, pitting fifteen people against each other in a clever roleplay battle of wit, perception, strategy, and deception.
In a recent game, I was the serial killer. That means I can kill at night and can not be killed. All I have to do is keep killing people, keep deceiving them, and not leave any clues for them to suspect me. I won this specific game, because there was a player named Snoop Dogg and every time I killed someone, I would leave a "death note" with a vague dog-related reference on the victim - even some as obtuse as "Bow down before the Lion". This made people increasingly suspicious that this other player was the serial killer, without focusing any suspicion on myself. Yet, I (feigning to be a good guy) kept raising questions about yet *another* player, so that the town never had enough votes in agreement about Snoop Dogg to have him put on trial. Keeping Snoop Dogg alive meant I could keep killing with impunity. Until there were so few townsfolk left that I was able to kill Snoop Dogg, get away with it, and win the game.
When you start each game, you can pick new name. Some people choose generic and some are clever. It's the internet, so plenty are offensive. When the game starts, all fifteen players will be told what their role is. Each role comes with certain abilities, traits, alignments, and limitations. The goal is to play your role, while supporting your faction. Each role has different faction alignments. Some are aligned with the mafia and the town. Some are aligned with the town and witches. Some, like the serial killer, are aligned only with the survivors.
The game is broken up into rounds. Your activities are performed at night. If you're the serial killer, you kill at night. If you're the investigator, you investigate one person's information each night. If you're the mafia, you communicate privately with the other mafia and the godfather at night, about who to kill and then you kill them. If you're the jailor, you put someone in jail overnight. If you're the escort, you distract someone overnight.
Then there are limitations. For example, the serial killer can not kill the mafia's godfather. So if you choose to kill someone overnight, but are not able to, there's a good chance you (as the serial killer) have just identified who the god father is.
When the night is over, you get a tally of the dead and how they died. You can read their will (each player can write a will, which for some is just a clever or insulting quip, but for others is an on-going ledger of information they've gathered while playing, so that upon their death, other players are informed as to what that player knew).
Still in the day phase, everyone votes on who to execute, if anyone. If enough votes are tallied for an individual, that person has to plead their defense to the town (in their own words). The town can then determine if they find him guilty or innocent. If he's guilty, he is hung. After his death (as with all deaths), his name goes up on a visible list for all to see, along with their role. (As an aside, there are also mediums - who are the only players who can communicate with the dead players in chat, using their information for themselves or to share with the living to inform future judgments).
It will often play out something like this: Someone accuses a player of being the godfather. Everyone votes for that person. That person swears they are the sheriff and the town needs them. Nobody buys their lies. They hang him. Then the name and role appears on the grave sites... they were telling the truth! They
the sheriff! Uh oh!
And then night comes again and we carry out the rounds like this, until almost everyone is dead and the town, mafia, serial killer, or other faction is left alive and declared the winner.
First, this is a free-to-play browser-based game that is now also on Steam for $5 USD. Those $5 are converted to ingame currency to buy cosmetic items like death animations or houses. There is no pay-to-win aspect to the game; only cosmetic items. You also accrue currency simply by playing, so you could play with no disadvantage whatsoever without ever paying a dime.
Second, the game requires you to install Adobe AIR, so if this isn't already on your system, it will direct you to install it before the game runs. You'll also need to create a game account. Click "register" from the game's interface to be taken to the web page where you do this. The page it takes you to is a sign-up for a forum account, which may seem confusing. Just do it, as the account is directly tied to your game login. When you're done, login to the game with those credentials.
Third, when you go to play a game, you'll have the options "invite friends" and "solo". This is very misleading, but if you click "solo", you will actually be entering the online multiplayer, which is what you obviously want.
The game is addictive and allows for a lot of role playing and deception. Even with fourteen other total strangers. Depending on the mode you are playing, there are also somewhere between 15 and 30 different roles to be played. Vigilante, veteran, doctor, mafioso, framer, godfather, spy, jailor, sheriff, escort, serial killer, witch, werewolf, arsonist, executioner, survivor, amnesiac, forger, vampire hunter, vampire, janitor, disguiser, consort, consigliere, blackmailer, bodyguard, investigator, lookout, mayor, medium, retributionist, transporter, jester...
The game becomes a clever meeting of wits, suspicions, piecing together what you know about roles and how they interact with each other, lying, determining truth, banding together, and backstabbing. It is absolutely unique and so compelling that I played six hours straight the first time I launched the game.
The game is a no-brainer at the price of zero dollars, if you play the web version. Frankly, it's worth $5 USD for the Steam version, too. If you're unsure, try the web version and decide if you'd like to support the guys behind this game by kicking in the $5 on Steam and getting this version. It also doesn't seem like there are a lack of players. Even past midnight, there were more than 300 ongoing games being played by almost 4,000 players. I never waited to get into a lobby and lobbies are filled and launched into the game within about one minute.

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
The Mims Beginning reminds me a lot of the game "Spore", mostly because of the art-style, but also because they're both game about managing a tribe of alien lifeforms to complete certain goals. I won't reveal too much about the story but basically you are a god of some-sort going from island to island, creating living conditions, protection and technology for the lost Mims. You, as the god, have various powers and abilities to aid the Mims as well. Like most real time strategy god games, The Mims Beginning has other elements implemented into game like structure/city building, unit and resource management, as well as upgrading buildings and units. There are two game modes, the campaign and survival.
There are a few things I'd like to point out before I quickly break down the game into separate sections. Although the game is in early access, I encountered no bugs or glitches which is impressive. This is one of the only god games I've played that let you select individual units to perform tasks as well as letting them be autonomous, which I like, but other people might not agree with that. Lastly, with the easy progression and lightheartedness of the game itself, it's a good game for beginners who want to try to get into this genre of game or games similar to this one.
--------
The art-style is subjective, but I enjoyed it. It has a playful, colorful, fun vibe to the game. It wasn't too hard on my PC, and I'm running a mid-tier Nvidia Card and CPU. I do feel the animation quality could be a little better and smoother though, but it is in early access and I know everything has not been fleshed out yet. Although after staring at the game for awhile, it does start to get a tad monotonous, though that is to be expected with such games.
--------
The sound assets are fine, there isn't much that's extraordinary or below standards. I will say that I didn't get tired of the noises or background music, so that's good. However, there was this one theme in a cut scene, in between the campaign scenarios that I really liked, it was this gospel-ish tone and it was really soothing.  There isn't any voice acting in the game from what I can tell.
--------
The mechanics were solid, but there wasn't much that really set it apart from other god games or made it more enjoyable that others. That being said, like stated earlier, the mechanics are perfect for someone who would want to give this genre a try and then try other god-games. Aside from structure placement, there isn't that much customization in the game, the only terraforming in the game is burning down trees. There are however quite a few animal and plant types to mess around with, as well as cool abilities your Mims get as well as yourself as the god.
--------
The game is good for beginners in this genre, it's not the best god game ever created, but it's not terrible. It's impressive that it was done by two devs. The game is competent and does what it set out to do. This type of game didn't keep me hooked as it's not the kind of game I'm used to playing or have too much experience with, but I can see how some people would enjoy it. One thing I will say about this game, despite all that, is that I liked the narrative and although I've only played for 10 hours, I'm interested in the story, and would like to know more about the Mims, their homeworld, their experiences. The game did a great job of keeping me hooked into the story.
Thanks to the Devs for giving me the opportunity to review the game, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

The Mims Beginning is a real time strategic “God-Game”. There currently are not too many of those available on Steam which is really a shame. You play the role of the first powerful looking being the Mims have seen since they crashed. This causes them to assume you are their new God. Use your PSI powers and colony building prowess to aid the fledgling colony build up the resources needed to continue their trek to recover the fragments of their crashed ship.
The Mims are a rather cute looking alien race that sort of have the appearance of gloved hands. The way they speak and act further emphasizes the fact they are a charmingly sweet race. You want to do your very best to protect them from the nasty evils of the world. For the most part, those evils are pests that are either herbivores that try to steal the Mims food/building supplies or carnivores that attempt to eat anything meaty, including the Mims themselves, their livestock and the herbivore pests. Natural disasters can also plague the land from meteor strikes to earthquakes; the Mims sure have it rough. Luckily for the Mims, you are there to lend a hand. For example, you can put out the wild fires or help plants grow by making it rain, use PSI blasting or burning to take care of pests, cheering up the unhappy Mims or use some of your other “Godly” PSI powers to aid them. You also guide the Mims on how to build their colony in order to fulfill their objectives in that land.
There are two primary building supplies, biomass and gems. Biomass is produced from refining plant matter. Biomass is far easier to keep in stock than the gems. Gems can be acquired by mining any exposed gem deposits but those are few and far between. The best way to earn gems is through raising livestock and selling them off-world. This can pose a problem if you were not paying enough attention while building your initial colony. If you don’t ensure you have enough gems to produce the buildings required to produce and ship the livestock, you will find yourself having to restart the level. It would help if you could find a few gems laying around the map in areas you can hit with your powers or, if you have one available, are able to send a guardian to blast.
Mims can be classed into three main categories. Guardians are your main line of defense against the pests. They will shoot at any enemy near them and try to kill it. Unfortunately, if they are hunting alone, they tend to get scared and unhappy rather quickly. They may end up running around being attacked by the pests rather than focusing on trying to kill them. This often leads to your guardians dying. You can put them into a formation but that automatically disables movement autonomy leaving you having to manually control the formation. Workers build your buildings, collect the plant matter to make the biomass, and generally carry things from one point to another. Officers and other hero units generally have a special ability that sets them apart from a Guardian or the general worker Mims.
The building construction in the game is simple enough. There generally is one building to fit each of the needs and for the most part, that building can be upgraded to enhance its effect. Power generation is an exception to that rule. For example, you can build wind turbines that keep your buildings powered so long as there is wind (which unfortunately is often blowing too slowly to keep your buildings consistently running), or you can build a generator fueled by biomass (unfortunately it burns through biomass like crazy). Unless you have a lot of workers and biomass producing plants around, you will still often find yourself without power. There are enough building varieties in the game to satisfy those of us who like base building games. It isn’t the most complex building game ever, but it isn’t branding itself as an in-depth city builder. For a “God-Game” it is perfectly sufficient.
I mentioned planting extra biomass producing plants to keep the generator running and you probably were thinking, that seems simple enough, what could possibly go wrong with doing that? Ignoring any expense involved as most plants don’t need gems and therefore pay for themselves in time, the problem is they make your island smell. Livestock (the gem producer) also smell! Smell in this game is what attracts the pests. If your floating island smells of fruity plants too much, herbivores will show up and start eating your crops. If you smell of meat too much, carnivores will show up and snack on your livestock and Mims. This makes you have to carefully consider and weigh the consequences of your actions. You could change the tide of the game very quickly just by rushing your gem or biomass production faster than you can produce the guardians needed to defend it.
Even if you have a ton of guardians and workers, you may find yourself overwhelmed by pests. The reason for this is simple, as mentioned earlier; your Mims can become either unhappy or scared. Unless a Mim is happy, they will not do their job efficiently or maybe won’t even do their jobs at all. Workers not collecting biomass fast enough will cause even more pests to show up due to the smell. Guardians who are too scared or unhappy to fight will often find themselves being killed by the pests rather than clearing the pests out. You can use your PSI Power to cheer them up if you can target them and you have the energy available to do so, but that is highly inefficient and is really a losing battle. You can build houses to help make your Mims happy, and that works great… but I often found myself with multiple houses scattered around with a ton of unhappy Mims aimlessly walking about. The houses were turned on so I’m not sure why they didn’t really use them much. The ones that did though, came out of them chipper and willing to work. I’m thinking this is just an Early Access bug or perhaps I am missing something that I need to do to make them use the houses more often.
Overall, The Mims Beginning is a satisfying “God-Game” that I hope leads the way to a sequel or in the very least other developers jumping on the “God-Game” bandwagon.

Even though it's not finished I believe this game blows Game Dev Tycoon out of the water. The only thing GDT has on MGT is being able to build and distribute consoles, which could possibly be added in the future. (I'm not going to compare this game to Software Inc, because it's more about software in general and doesn't go into too much depth(yet) with game development like this and others in the genre).
Features
-Build each room within your building, giving you more control over your company (you can have 100's of employees if you want, it gets a little hard to manage in it's current state, but hopefully that will be fleshed out more)
-Employees skills raise by developing/working (Game Dev has this as a mod, but I feel it works better in this game) also the skills make more sense (GameDesign, Programming, Graphics, Music & Sound, Office Work, Speed, Work Will).
-Employee needs (Bathroom, heating/cooling, and furnishings)
-Research new genres, topics, engine features, game sizes (B - AAA), and game improvements.
-Has WAY more Genre and game topics than GDT, and there is no game genre/topic matching (which never made sense to me, there's no such thing as a bad genre/topic match in the real world, only bad games).
-Release updates/patches for your games after release. (In the beginning you won't be able to fix bugs during development, but you can after release by either patching the game, which will remove a lot of bugs. You can update the game and choose to remove some bugs while also improving the game, which will improve sales as well).
-Eventually you can have seperate rooms to improve your game:
~Game Design (Remove bugs during development and improve gameplay, also where you make game reports)
~Music Studio (obviously improves music/sound)
~Graphic Studio (dem textures)
~Motion Capturing (recently added, I'm not to sure on the specifics, but I believe it improves graphics/gameplay)

-Sell developed game engines and make money off games made with them (you can select the initial price of the engine and the % you receive from sales)
-Customer support room to keep your fans happy once you reach a certain amount. Can also run campaigns to increase fan base
-Publish your game through other companies (they will produce and distribute your game, and occasionally market it).
-Publish your own games! (To do this you need a production room and a storeroom. You can actually choose how many copies of a game you want to make, including the price and things like a t-shirt, game manual etc. You can also re-release older games and eventually release game packages)
-Marketing!
-Build a Server room and release your own MMOs! (Yes Game Dev Tycoon has MMOs too, but it works so much better in this game) You actually choose the Subscription price of your game and have to have enough servers to support your subscribers. Unlike other games, once your MMO stops selling copies it stays on the market, and you can release expansion packs. Expansion packs will act as seperate games (in terms of sales and marketing), but it will also make your base MMO start selling again. There is also a F2P option that is not usable at the moment, so hopefully the way MMO's work in general will be improved.
-Licenses for movies, books, or other games that you can buy. I honestly don't even use this feature as it's not necessary and there's always another game already released under every license anyway so I don't really see the point.
Possible negatives
-(This one really isn't a big deal, but it annoys me). I'm not sure if the Dev is foreign, but the FPS genre is called Ego-Shooter. Never heard this term before and I don't like it at all, I could see "Ego-shooter" being used for more arcadey style games like Doom, Serious Sam, and maybe even COD to an extent, but it's not a term used in the U.S.
-Managing huge teams can be annoying if you want to make sure you have the best people for each room. There is an auto-assign feature, but I'm not sure how it decides to assign employees.
-As I stated before, you can't create consoles like in GDT, but hopefully it will be added.
-The aspects of controling the way your game turns out (other than the skills of your employees) have specific settings for each genre that are considered "correct", but in my opinion GDT's sliders don't work much better.
-No real End game as of yet, and no New game+ like GDT has.
-Each genre has pictures for your game that depend on the level of technology applied used, but don't differ between topics. Ex. if you make a Fantasy Rpg and a Knight Rpg on the same engine, the pictures will be the exact same. Granted no other game in this genre has this from what I've seen.
If you enjoyed GDT then buy this game, it's way better IMO. I believe this game is worth the price even if it's not finished.

is a “god game” style real time strategy survival game where your goal is to gather up and maintain order in your civilization while you search for things from your old planet before you had to leave and inhabit new ones.  Once you can presumably find these things, you will be able to reestablish the old planet and once again live as you once did on your old planet.  You can use the mouse or keyboard to adjust the screen and angles as you play.  You’ll be building various types of structures to use resources, or create new things in order to make your area more stable and self-sufficient.  It reminds me of some other games I have played in the past, like Populous, Darwinia, or the Act Raiser games, for instance.  The gradual improvement system, and management of resources to continue to progress towards your goals is very fun in this game.  In story mode, there are factors that can really help or hinder your ability to get to the next steps, whatever they may be, depending on many different things that can happen.
Some good humorous dialogue, which is always refreshing for me to see in most games.
The seamless and gradual progression as far as putting different tools you have to practical use  is well done and I am enjoying it very much from scenario to scenario.
Creatures are interesting looking, and I like the artwork and graphics quite a bit.
The control scheme isn’t too hard to get used to, and quite friendly to someone not as familiar with RTS games.
This actually works well on my laptop with integrated graphics, which is really great!  I was not sure if it would be able to, but with enough memory, my laptop held up very well.  Some slowing when a whole lot of stuff was on the screen, but overall I was impressed at how well this handled on my weaker laptop computer.
I hope there will be more building types later, and extra variety in what all you can work with.  It’s still nice so far, but I do want more for such a great game.
I find it takes a while to get certain goals, and fighting and fending off some more trivial  things, or having slow production can cause me a bit of frustration.
The Mims themselves can be a little bit cowardly, and they are hard to control when their moods dip down.  They go into a chaos or fear mode, and controlling them can be a bit of a challenge sometimes.
It’s a bit strange how you end up with certain buildings up as you go through story mode, but your old structures are gone.  This kind of breaks up the story for me a bit, and I wish my gems and creations could carry over too.
Destroying things nets you nothing, as far as I can tell.  I think you should get some of what you used to create the structure back when you break it down.
I found the tutorial helpful at the beginning to get used to some of the basics.   Your Mims will move slower if they are tired, so ideally you want to keep them happy, or let them rest between work, so they can be productive and gather what you need to build whatever goals are set up for your colony.  Raising creatures up in the Lab can be beneficial to gain some gems by sending them off to trade, which can be extremely important for building and progressing.  If you run out of gems with a lot more to do, you might find yourself in real trouble.
I love RPG elements in games, and having perks or a carry-over sort of leveling would be great on this.  I’d love to have a bit more experimentation, or secrets or other things that contribute and possibly can change your overall progression depending on what you want to increase or focus on for a “build”.  Just a personal bias, but I think it would really suit the game well to have a little bit more of this involved in the overall RTS elements.

The Mims Beginning is a breath of fresh air  in an increasingly stagnate gaming pool. At first glance, the game may look light and simple but very quickly you begin to see that this is a deep, well-designed strategy/god-mode game. The graphics are very detailed, the artwork is beautiful, the mechanics are flawless. If you think that because its a god-mode strategy game that it will be boring, then guess again. There is plenty of action/activities to keep you busy without having to micro-manage your units and economy.  Research will increase the options and powers available during gameplay while continuing to upgrade and expand your alien colony. For any strategy gaming fan, I strongly recommend picking this game up. Most games are only moderately worth their sale prices, especially indie games. But this game is well worth the full price.
The big name gaming developers should take a few lessons from the Squatting Penguins Studio. This is how a game is supposed to be released. Out-of-the-box, ready to play. 100+ hours of gameplay and I have yet to experience a single bug. No glitches in gameplay, no graphics hiccups or units falling through maps, no game crashes. The game runs smooth and seamlessly like any released game should. Even more amazing is that this is still an early-access game so bugs and glitches are normally accepted and typically expected. A lot of care and effort went into this release and true gamers will notice and appreciate it right away.
Without going into a lengthy game description, The Mims Beginning will have the typical RTS simulation components, but with its own distinct approach. Expect a well-balanced economic system, a rich story to tie the campaign missions together nicely, an assortment of interesting buildings and units to build as you establish your camps, and a variety of research.
The one area that is lacking when compared to most games of this genre is the variety of units. In this game, you have only a couple of types to choose from. The basic, or generic Mim performs assorted tasks as you assign them rather than being specialized. Perhaps in the future more unit types will be added, but the game functions just fine with the current unit structure. The developer has stated that more features and game modes will be added as development progresses. As for the game's mechanics and features, here are some things that you should know:
Keep in mind that at the time of this review, the game is still in Early Access beta and will likely improve and include more features. Considering that, this game is very impressive. At first glance it looks like its going to be some simple cartoon-ish indie that will fill an hour or two of free time. But nothing could be further from the truth. Hours of challenging and entertaining gameplay awaits and a good bit of light humor is mixed into the storyline as well. Rarely do I enjoy an early access game this much. I anxiously await the final release.

After a terrible event the Mims find their home planet destroyed and all the little Mims scattered through space apart from the lucky few who managed to reach escape pods in time. But fear not! The Mims possessed an item which has the capability of restoring planets and before the horrific destruction of their home world they were able to jettison it to safety. Unfortunately it's ship was hit by debris from a meteor and all systems were shut down leaving it floating helplessly through space and no way for the Mims to reach it. With the help of you, their new God, the Mims must locate this if they ever want to flourish happily again and have any hopes of seeing their home rebuilt.
The Mims Beginning starts with an awesome little story and I found myself captivated right away. Your job as a God is to guide the Mims to safety and help them slowly rebuild and become prosperous like they once were. There are two modes to the game, the first and main being the Story mode. This is the mode that you'll want to start playing as not only does it contain the tutorial but also progressing through this this mode allows you to unlock the buildings and god powers in a specific order and will help you learn what they each do one by one. The Story mode follows the story of the Mims and you'll make your way through it by completing the objectives you have on each level/map which will in turn unlock the next. Survival mode on the other hand has all buildings, research and God powers unlocked and may be a little overwhelming or confusing to those new to the game. Survival mode has four difficulties that you must try to survive through starting at Easy up to Very Hard. You can also customize your own difficulty so you can choose if you want a relaxing sandbox style play, or something much more challenging to push yourself.
To help the Mims survive in either mode you'll need to guide them by telling them which buildings they need to create much like other God games. Your Mims will build what you tell them too and can also be told to go to specific places but other than that your Mims will carry out the task they most feel important. There are different types of Mims which you will encounter as the game goes on and these vary from Mims like Workers who do the day to day jobs, Guardians who patrol and protect the other Mims and even Shamans who can sense other Mim colonies that are in danger and allow you to help them. You also have various unlockable God powers to help you influence the Mim world further such as a group heal to revitalize and heal your Mims, fruit rain for when you run low on Biomass and things like a Psi cage used for trapping enemies and a Psi bolt for when you need to get offensive. All of these can be cast using Psi energy which is generated over time.
You'll need both Biomass and Gems to build/create in your world, the main being Biomass. Biomass is harvested from Fruit which can randomly be found growing in most worlds, but can also be created from your own fruit plants. Biomass is used for almost everything from building things to creating animals or powering buildings. Gems, however, are harder to come by as you can only receive them from a few sources. Buying and raising animals will be your main source of Gems but you can also find limited deposits on your island and some God powers will help you also but those these aren't unlocked right away. Once you've grasped correctly managing those two sources its up to you to build, survive and complete your objectives as you see fit.
The dialogue throughout the game is both charming and humorous and the cutscenes give the Mims  substance rather than just being 'things' you control like it is in most God games. I started to feel rather attached to my Mims and in one particular mission (I won't give any spoilers) I found myself heartbroken at my helplessness during a certain event.
As with most games The Mims beginning does have some little flaws. My two noticeable cons with the game are minor ones to me but some might find them much larger as they do impact the gameplay. The first is
. I'm going to repeat this as there are many negative comments I've found about this simple fact.
This applies to both story and survival mode so if you're looking for a game that you can come back and play the same save later this is not it. If you are like me, however, and enjoy smaller sessions you won't find any issues with this. This is something that'll not be added either as you can read
(the devs tried for a month and a half to implement it and it reaped no results and detracted from developing content). My second issue is more of a personal one but things can become rather overwhelming if you're not careful as there is a lot going on. Guardians are rather weak on their own so you'll heavily rely on using your god powers at first to destroy enemies so you'll constantly have to be checking your map for any new mob spawns. Speeding up the game increases the speed that enemies spawn so you have a choice between speeding through production and risk being overrun by enemies quickly or playing most of your game on a slower mode which can become a little tiresome especially since there is no save feature. You also have to produce animals manually one by one so you can't have the game running fast for any long period of time or you'll end up wasting time as you often forget to keep producing them. I did ask the devs if they plan to change this and they've replied saying they will look into it which is awesome! :D

The gameplay is pretty solid for the most part, while in combat it can feel a little slow to respond, but thankfully combat is generally used as a way to solve a puzzle. Most of the puzzles are pretty simple, with exception of the "expert route's" you find scattered (these are shortcuts but with puzzles that are much much more difficult.
My main issue with the game is it's length, in that it's completely feasible to complete the game in just under half a day.
I would recommend this game if it's on sale for £4 or less, it's just too short to pay more.

The Master of Orion series has been one of the most important in the turn-bsaed strategy genre since the first part. The second part has been a titan for a long time (and still is btw, so if you do not mind low resolution and do not have it already...). The 3rd part was so different in the planetary management that many players refused to accept it as a successor and some even lost trust in the frenchise. And for a long time a lot of what made the 2nd part so superior was still missing (character creation missing at all, then without MoO-essential traits like "creative"). But, with the last patches, the developers did everything of importance correctly.
The graphics are good, ships look quite nice (except the Meklar ones), the battles are auto-resolved or in pausable realtime (like in Baldurs Gate or Lords of Magic, which differs greatly from the turn-based battles in MoO2, but the mechanics are well adjusted and absolutely fine to play), the tech-tree is huge and the preconditions are well set, the race creation has everything it needs and there are even mods for that, the diplomacy is well done, the behaviour of the AI fits their traits, the travelling between solar systems now works with lanes (in MoO2 your movement was only limited by your engines/warp drives), so you can only travel to systems that are connected to your location now, which requires less strategy, but makes more fun for players who prefer the turtling-strategy in some way.
The only two downsides are that the buildings on the planets look oversized and are so scattered that it does not quite fit the detailed and nice style of the game, and that you have to buy the DLCs to have all races.
I'll give it a thumbs up because it definately is a worthy successor of the legendary MoO2 and makes a lot of fun.

This odd little indie game is both deceptively short and deceptively long. While the game itself can be beaten very quickly (there's an achievement for managing it in under 15 minutes), there are several routes you can take, of varying length. In short, this is a top-down game (similar to the oldschool Zelda games in terms of control), with a heavy emphasis on humor and parody, and there are different ways around puzzles depending on which items you buy. There are three items, and you can beat the game with any two of them. This is a game meant to be replayed several times, and each time should put a new twist on the same puzzles. Recommended for puzzle fans, or someone looking for a good change of pace for a little while.

This game is so fun and yet so frustrating to play.  The fun happens when when you get to take your squad out on missions and complte missions, then come back and promote your soldiers so you unlock new skills so you can take them out on more missions and rince and repeat.
The frustration comes with all the other stuff thrown at you.....
There are so many counters, timers, and mandatory events that, atleast for me, I do not feel like I have much control of the game when not on the batllefield.  Yeah, I can choose what to research and when and how to upgrade my headquarters, but when I do these it feels less like "Oh cool, a new X that I can use." and more like "well, what 2 things will I do without to get this margionally useful thing?"
The game is deceptive in that it makes you feel like you get to build and grow your command the way you want.  In reality, the game is on rails, with a few moments of "Choose Your Own Adventure" where you can do X or Y.  This is so infuriating because you find yourself either extremly restricted in what you can or cant do, or you become overwhelmed in what is available because you don't have enough time to get much of it done because this ride is on rails and it stops for no one.
So, I feel one part of the game gets in the way of enjoying the other.....in other words the game mechanics hold itself back.
I do recommend this game, but I would not buy it until it goes on sale.  War of The Chosen is not worth $40 and XCom 2 has been out so long that you should not pay more than $20 for it.

I was a really big fan of XCOM Enemy Unknown and the Enemy Within expansion. I played both all the way through and thought they were overall very fun. XCOM 2 is huge disappointment to me. For one there are lots of bugs, but what really killed it for me is panicked soldiers every mission. In both of my playthroughs of EU/EW I had a total of maybe 5 panic events (maybe 5) and in 6 or 7 hours of XCOM 2 (the "10 hours" pinned at the top of my review is not accurate)  I have not had a single mission without at least one soldier panicking. Sometimes it is three of them, and you only have four of them in a mission. I'm actually pretty good at the tactics in these games and I'm losing every mission, not because I'm making bad tactical decisions, but because the game engine in jacking me with multiple panicked soldiers every mission. Where is the resistance coming up with all these cowards? Don't they know the survival of humankind is in the balance? Wouldn't that give them a little more resolve? Wouldn't everyone who was still free at this point in the story timeline already be someone who was a survivor? Wouldn't they have to be?
It makes the game not fun for me: loosing every "easy" mission because ALL of my soldiers are complete cowards. It makes me not interested in what is going to happen when the missions are "hard."
Maybe it is unfair to the game as a whole for this part of it to ruin it for me, but it does. Panicked soldiers was always an irritation to me. It didn't happen much in the last game; happens ALL THE TIME in this game. Be forewarned: if you did not like the panicked soldiers in the previous game, the developers have increased its likelihood in this game by, seemingly, orders of magnitude. I'm really disappointed. I was really looking forward to this game and they took what was, in my opinion, one of the worst decisions from the last game and decided it was a great decision that needed to happen way more for this game and it ruins it for me.
The game is also quite buggy, which is kind of annoying, but would not have killed it for me.

the game itself plays well and is great and all but timers are ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
i'm sorry but if you think that it adds any tactics to the game, it just adds tension or frustration. that's it. I've had plenty of missions where by the time I can actually get to a VIP (after killing ballpark like 3-4 patrols, 1 of which usually flawlessly ambushed with a chain overwatch setup and the next aced by grenadiers, you usually have like 6-7 turns to get the VIP and extract whilst there's still more patrols on the map, and hello, you have reinforcements coming in on the next turn blocking you from getting to the extract.
The timers don't add tactical gameplay or tactical decision making. They add difficult gambling decisions based on luck and RNG. I've reloaded the same saves many many times (which is a poor way of adding game longevity) just to redo the same mission scenario over and over again, step by step- except this time cutting corners and avoiding elaborate tactics. Instead I'd try very risky luck-RNG based attacks and rushes just to shave time in order to complete the objective, or get lucky and walk out with minimal casualties.
The timers wouldn't be so bad if they weren't mandatory. You ran out of time on a VIP extraction mission? (which mind you doesn't offer you much turns to begin with) you lose ALL your soldiers that were on that mission. That's a stupid mechanic. It should just keep sending reinforcements, or make the mission harder. On a randomgenned map, with randomgenned enemies and randomgenned AI decision making, a timer doesn't make any mechanical or elaborate tactical sense in a tactical game. Because all it promotes (if you don't want to fail the mission or potentially lose a lot of your best units) is continuous repetition of the same save where you already pre-emptively KNOW what the enemy will do in that or the next following turns based off of your decision making. That's not tactical, that's just being able to read the person's mind without any intuition or raw talent.
The game clearly tries to stage itself as a tactical turned based game but with the timers, it severely negates this and becomes more of a luck-based shoot-em-up adventure to try and tell a story to those who get too far into the game's character.
And this is an experience played on the 'veteran' or regular difficulty. I'm sorry but if I run into impossible missions or have to redo a mission a million times to perfectly execute it, that's not a regular difficulty. That's an extremely challenging difficulty for people who want an un-necessarily difficult challenge that requires you to roll a die to win it.
Pick it up on a sale. It's still a good game and I don't have the DLC yet, and the DLC adds a lot of mechanics to the game to improve it. Especially settlement defense missions. But right now? It's not worth 80CAD or 60USD at all.

I am not a fan of the "Artistic" video game industry, as I feel video games are already a piece of art in their own way, just like any movie, song or painting. So when I saw this game, I was skeptical, as I was fooled once by Proteus.
However, I was not dissapointed this time.
Serena is quite a unique adventure, and although short, I believe it's one of the best stories I've seen in a game before. The fact that the game evolves, that things changes around you while walking around the room gives an impression of madness, and is superbly well done. The atmospheric music is beautiful and draws you further into the characters feelings, while the filter grain, lack of colors and disturbing paintings added to the eerie setting of the game.
There are a few ameliorations that could have been done gameplay wise to create even more immersion, like story branching, a couple of puzzles or maybe just a small inventory system, but maybe this would have caused the game to be less "artsy" and a bit more of a game, which was not the point.
Overall, it was brilliant, I do recommend it to anyone who would like to try the artistic game genre, as this is a fantastic experience. Definitely worth the look.

It would seem to the casual viewer that Starbound receives infinite hate because of its Early Access. I'm not very sure why this is, but I'll crush the reasons as best I can.
Currently, the top negative comment by Mandalorian addresses a few things, which I will counter-criticize with arguments varying in strength and relevance. Like people, sort of.
So now we know this guy's arguments are essentially troll quality with a cult backing as evidences by much of the blind upvotes.
This game has been compared to Terraria due to its 2D sandbox genre. Yeah, whatever, Terraria used to be considered a Minecraft rip-off. This is too cliché to be a respectable position anymore.
Starbound is an excellent space exploration-sandbox game. Starbound has many, many different types of planets and solar systems in addition to the spontaneous generation of creatures to inhabit them, meaning that it's a lucky happening when you find two planets with the same creatures. It doesn't use that as an excuse to stop. Starbound's planets are provided with a wide variety of biomes. There's no magicky filth biome that spreads through the planet. This is science. There's odd organisms, creepy, suspiciously familiar items and themes, and an amazing soundtrack that prompts the player to be brave and explore the stars.
I'm not a professional critic, so I won't provide a numeric rating, nor is that really what the Steam review system is ultimately about. It's about recommend or not, with an elaboration as to why. I recommend this game, but if you're so swayed by the naysayers, then I'll just assure you that you're gonna miss out on a spectacular experience.

Traditional Zelda is a style of gameplay that is near and dear to many people. The top down adventure makes for some creative puzzle situations and hugely detailed maps. After many years of tinkering with the formula, Nintendo is finally returning to their heritage with The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds.
What are gamers to do in the meantime, though? If one is not a fan of the 3D games or the DS titles, what kind of game will fill the void? Enter Ittle Dew, a top down adventure game from indie dev Ludosity. What the game lacks in innovative puzzle and world design, it more than makes up for with charm and game feel.
The plotline for Ittle Dew is incredibly simple. Your character washes up on the shore of an island and wants to get off. The caretaker of a shop will build you a raft as long as you go through some dungeons he has set up. You also need to pay him for the items he sells, so there is a main hub dungeon that will let you accrue some cash.
This is probably the weakest element of the game. While the original Zelda game did not really possess a story of any kind, forgoing a narrative in today’s age is a curious decision. One can personally believe that gameplay speaks above all else, but without a strong desire to continue, some gamers may not even be bother to check Ittle Dew out.
Thankfully, the puzzle designs in Ittle Dew are fairly strong. Stripping down the Zelda formula to its basics, Ittle Dew gives players very limited commands to deal with. Controls are essentially walking with the joystick, the four face buttons used for specific items and two shoulders buttons for a map and hint screen.
The hint screen is very nicely done, too. Instead of spelling out solutions or talking in cryptic riddles, the game uses the humorous character of Tippsie to lightly insult the player while giving some key hints. Things like, “You’ll only need your fire sword for this room,” are better tests of skill than detailing exactly where to swing your item.
The specific items collected are a teleport rod, a fire sword and an ice rod. In an interesting twist, there is no proper order of progression in the game. The best aspect of is how non-linear the design is. Upon completing the journey, I was under the belief that any player would have to acquire all three of the weapons to finish their quest. That actually isn’t the case. Some of the dungeons even have shortcuts direct to the boss rooms.
Along with shortcuts and paths for skipping items, the game also has hidden dungeons for collecting extra health and cards. The cards don’t really offer any purpose to the game, but their rooms have some insidiously obtuse puzzle designs. I was stumped in one room for a solid 20 minutes before stumbling upon the answer.
When you are transported to any dungeon for a specific item, you only need your wits to get through. No puzzles require another objects or skills you do not possess. This alleviates a lot of frustration from the proceedings.
There really isn’t much in the way of challenge, however. If you die, the game simply restarts you in the exact same room with full health. Other than how the sword’s arc doesn’t fully surround your character, the only time one will get annoyed is when they cannot solve a puzzle quickly.
A good mention must go to the writing behind Ittle Dew. Everything is very self-referential and parody laden. Genre tropes like collecting hearts and destroying pots all make some kind of appearance. Even the nonsensical nature of enemy placement gets mentioned for being so pointless.
Your main character revels in eating hearts and even wishes to just smack things around. The bosses utter some ridiculously incomprehensible catch phrases and then admit to not even knowing what they were talking about. One cannot help but crack a smile while playing.
Even the ending is funny. While a rather obvious plot twist occurs, when the final battle comes to a close, the game pokes fun at how most final bosses just kind of give up or don’t take a more obvious approach.
Sadly, while Ittle Dew might be great at questioning why adventure games follow specific mechanics, the game really does nothing to spice them up. One shouldn’t be displeased with a fairly high quality Zelda-
like game, but a lack of innovation really does hurt the final product.
There are some texture designs on the world map that are misleading, as well. For the most part, you cannot walk behind any of the trees in the game. Some of the hidden dungeons are behind them, though. Enemies also disappear behind the trees and are completely invisible to the player.
For that matter, the world map doesn’t really serve any purpose other than to move you from point A to point B. Hiding extraneous items behind puzzles is a great incentive for replay value, but giving players some other reason to explore would go a long way to creating a believable world.
There is a bonus dungeon hidden in the fields. This acts as the penultimate test of your skills, requiring every item in the game to fully complete. There are 12 rooms and each one gets progressively more challenging in skill. This serves as a nice little bonus to an otherwise very short game.
To sum everything up, while Ittle Dew might not be the second coming of adventure gaming or a masterpiece of epic proportions, the game provides plenty of wit and humor along with some decently mind bending puzzles. The game also controls nicely.
For $14, one could do much worse. Ludosity certainly does not get points for creativity, but their craftsmanship is noble. This game may not be Zelda, but Ittle Dew. (7/10)

This game has serious potential. The amount of people out there looking for a genuine (and playable) police simulator is a high number; this game is for every one of them. It is definetly a working progress, and the developers need to fix a lot of things and add more into this simulator:
- AI must be fixed... when someone decides to run away from you, your thoughts are "yes, finally a chase" and then they end up running into a wall or car and don't proceed. This ruined a fair few moments for me.
-More (and fixed) car chases. Car persuits are a big pro to police games, and this game just needs to up that. When a car fails to stop in this game, it drives far too slow, you want a car persuit to be fast and action filled, not at 25mph on a more or less straight road.
- Fixed sirens. The siren/ lights (on police vehicles) in this game is better than most others. Having said that, there could be A LOT more done to make this system more lifelike.
- Animations. The game is seriously lacking in animations when something happens in-game e.g. after you shoot and kill a suspect, or find any injured person, the protocol is to phone for an ambulance. Once pressing the ambulance button the cop states into the radio that an ambulance is needed. Then a still frame of the police station shows on screen along with the allocated points for what you have done. That is just one example of many animatons that are lacking.
- Fellow cops. For a POLICE simulator, there isn't enough police-you are litterally the only cop in the game. It would be nice to see other patrol cars patrolling and to be able to call for backup when you are under fire from multiple people.
- Different scenarios (and locations). After a while playing the game, the patterns are obvious, you do not even need to look at the map to find out where you're going because you already know where the developers have set that specific scenaro to happen.
To conclude, this game is very addicting, you can play for hours on end without getting bored. BUT, having said that, this game is 100% a WORKING DEVELOPMENT, only purchase this game if you are prepared to put up with some annoying bugs and repeated scenarios. This game definetly has potential. Lets just hope that the devs see what needs to be improved and act accordingly.

I played the original MOO 2 to death back in the day, more than Civilization even. Nostalgia is a hard thing to live up to. This remake succeeds in some points and falls flat in others.
While I'm not that bothered by star lanes, I am bothered by making the combat real time. The old magic of brooding over a map and planning the next turn just isn't there. Large battles are slow and chaotic and I just chalked this part off as "not worth the hassle". I simulate all but decisive battles and am actually glad this is the only option in multiplayer. From my rather impatient perspective, it's a good thing I don't have to slowly play out a battle against an outnumbered and outgunned enemy who just won't give up and needlessly drags the game out. However, it is definitely not, in any way, the "true MOO 2 experience". Far from it. I can see how this ruins the game for some people completely.
What does this remake do well? It's shiny. Oh my, is it shiny. The graphics are very polished, beautifully animated leader screens and 3D versions of the iconic races, along with top notch voice acting from several big names, starting out with Michael Dorn as narrator. All the races are there, though 3 (Trilarians, Elarians and Gnolam) are sold seperately for some reason, and they all look stunning.
Colony management is still the way it used to be, just shinier. You still get to assign your population to research, food production and work by dragging and dropping little avatars in slots. You still have the building categories and ability to buy or sell structures. The landing animations when colonizing a new planet are also very pretty, though they do get repetitive since every biome always has the same. The uber worlds (other than gaia) that some races have - Inferno or Grassland - don't have own animations, which adds to it.
The research tree feels more streamlined, but still has a few tough choices where the 'passed' tech has to be obtained via trade or espionage.
Ship design is also still the same; with a large selection of ship components, including the ever popular stellar converter. Visually, every species has their unique ship style and a small downside is that each class has only 2 models and 3 paint designs (that in many cases don't line up in any way with the hull). Still, it all looks very good in 'cinematic' battle view.
Colony leaders and fleet commanders make a comeback, after being absent for most of the Early Access phase. Their artwork (as well as that of Spies) is, as so many things in this game, simply beautiful. While the leaders and commanders are pretty straight forward, espionage works a little strange and it takes serious investment to have a decent success chance. There are different levels of infiltration and no such thing as 'spying a little bit'. It's all or nothing; either you go all out on it and prioritize spies over other areas, or you don't even try.
Custom races can pick from a long list of traits, advantages and disadvantages, just like in the good old days. They have to pick a race for appearance and ships, which is fine. But sadly, they will always be displayed as that race (i.e. Galatic News Network calls a custom race 'Klackon'). It's just a small thing, but I would like to name my race.
Diplomacy is straight up Civ V with aliens. All the options are there, trade agreements, non aggression pacts, open borders, demands, offers, annual payments, prisoner exchange of captured spies. And speaking of Civ V, that's also how the 'minor races' work. They are space city states who will provide their protecting race with food, money or research, and add their votes in the Galactic Counsil. I feel there was more potential in the minor races idea, like giving you tasks or trading with them, but maybe that was a little too Civ V.
Overall, I recommend this remake, though it isn't really "MOO 2 v.2". It is fun, it is - I can't say it enough - very pretty to look at, and it's a decent (though certainly not 'best' or 'deepest') scifi 4X game and worth picking up on sale.

Just a quick note, I never played the original Master of Orion games.
Master of Orion is a turn by turn strategy game with real-time space battles. There are multiple races to choose from each with their own special traits, voices and graphical buildings and ships.
The turn by turn based gameplay was a put off at first. But considering the amount of micro-management required in this game, I'm glad it's turn based. Space battles however, are in real-time. You can auto-resolve them, or play them out (Highly recommend playing them out most of the time you'd be surprised what you can win with just technology and tactics).
I appreciate how you can manually allocate population to certain tasks on each planet you have.
However, this is where the game requires time and patience. I can spend 100 turns just trying to develop new planets or even prepare the colonisation of new worlds. It takes time, depending on how you play.
I enjoy meeting the races and trading with them. One thing I love is that I can, with paticant even pushing wars onto each other only to sit back and watch them crumble at the same time.
I highly recomend playing this game if you are willing to give it a shot. I would suggest watching YouTubers playing this game first though. I watched the Mighty Jingles.
