Bastion was the first real indie game I played after moving to PC. At first, I played maybe twenty minutes of it before abandoning it - it was just too different for me, and this was a problem with me, not the game. I would not recommend buying this game, especially for a purchase price of $4.99 for a 1st episode. I was looking through bundles and this game seemed interesting. I think in total I spent about $2.50 for the entire bundle. After playing the game for a little while I wouldn't have bought this game for $0.50.
The good:
- Graphics look cool.
- There is a chance for a decent story but the gameplay itself makes the possible story not worth going after.
The bad:
- I hate this 1st episode crap, put the whole friggin game together and sell it. Make the first "episode" the demo and sell the completed copy. Not hard, easy to do and people get to test out the game before they buy it.
- Nothing is really explained.
- There is a pink orb that follows you around and spits out health boosts when your health gets low but no idea what it is.
- You need to chip away at glowing blocks so you can continue to see otherwise it turns dark after a bit but nothing told me that or why I just started hacking away at things and figured it out. Keep in mind, you're underground and it appears as though your people are used to this, so why do you need to chip away at stuff to help you see when it makes more sense that you just can.
- Nothing tells you what a save point looks like or how to find it. It's not in any place that is obvious.
- The abilities of each character aren't explained so you don't know what anyone can do until the girl's AI kicks in (sometimes) and does something new.
- There is a button that spits out monsters but no idea why. It really feels like the people who made this game were thinking "Crap, we need to put more monsters in to help complete the oil ingredients quest but we don't know what to do. How about we just say F*** it and put in a button. That should work."
- The level you start out in has very difficult monsters considering there isn't a way to expand your HP. If you run into 1 tough monster could die very quickly. After I found the save point I wasn't as upset but running into one monster that spits out multiple other monsters that kill you really quickly is annoying and irritating. While trying to defeat the monster with the most HP, I die in a matter of seconds without much of a chance.
- The girl's AI is pretty bad. It's really random about when she'll revive you but better for fighting. I was fighting the large HP monster and for the first 5 times through trying to beat it I died and she just stood there. The next couple of times she tried bringing me back once or twice then stopped. (Here's another bad thing, I kept dying because there was no way for me to get away from the green goo the other monsters were spitting out. I was brought back and instantly died again.) After a few more times of me dying the girl's AI kicked in a bit more and actually kept bringing me back until I was able to get away from the monster.
- This game feels very lazy and lacks substance. It's easy to get bored while going after the second goal. Basically you need to find ingredients to make an oil to visit another person. You have no idea how to get them so you kill monsters, monsters wind up dropping some of the parts but you have no idea what monsters will drop what. After you kill the large HP monster, the monsters it spits out no longer are spit out and will reduce your chance of getting one of the needed ingredients.
That's my entire review of this game. I hope it helps people avoid this game and I hope it helps developers realize that you can't just slap stuff together and expect people to love it.

I got this game from a Gem Auction during the Holidays from Steam because of all the negative reviews.  I'll be honest, I actually green-lighted this game personally on Steam.
The art style personally I couldn't really care too much for- it reminds me too much of those fairy stickers from Hot Topic but it looked well executed in the screenshots.  The story first impression seemed like "Ok, two characters- love...drama...bonding...possible use of double players in the moves." which by far isn't the most original thing out there.  But hey who does anything original anymore right?
Despite that it wasn't stylistically my cup of tea- I love platform/rpgish/whatevergameswithsomekindahotchickonit that this thing was seeming to market itself as... before I played it and confirmed what a lot of reviews already said.
THIS GAME IS A HOT STEAMING MESS
First off, great backgrounds and yes while I'm not totally into the art direction I like to give credit where credit is due.  Beautiful.  I can even accept the simplifi-wait why are the sprites so copy and their animations are completely inconsistent?  Why does my lil dude just seem like he pauses forever when he's attacking...
This game is bugged, unbalanced, the sprites are more or less seemingly rushed- it's like nothing was ever playtested.  Ever.  Did anyone of the Dev Team bother to even play this game?  Better yet did anyone outside of the Dev Team bother to play this game to let them know that some major game design sins are being committed here?
WHY DOES SOMETHING IN THE FIRST LEVEL TAKE 15+ HITS TO KILL? No this isn't even about "Difficulty" This is just downright negligence... there isn't any skill to fighting these things it's just walk next to them and...look frozen and stuck while this slug thing looks like it might be taking damage.
You have a partner from the beginning with the BEST dialogue that sounds as lifeless as some of those chat programs (hey I could go into detail about the voice acting, but I can't knock it for trying - voice acting is tough, I've personally failed out of a voice acting audition before for a cartoon because I wasn't British enough) and while she's cool in her own way I guess... she just kinda scurry around and gets in the way.  Heck even if all she did was just Mirror your movement that would be an improvement.  The partner system is more or less unpredictable and unreliable if you want them to do anything beyond rushing forward and taking damage when it's not necessary or just idling away while some monster has their way with you.
I don't understand some of the Interface, it's not anywhere near obvious or helpful whatever half of these meters are.  There is two sets and I'm sure one is my partners health? Maybe? Oh geez they have health great now I can look forward to them being useless and dying with the exception of them remembering to heal or rez me from time to time.
BOTTOM LINE -
Bottom line, these are just a couple examples of just how broken this game actually is.  I would have just been happy if it was just a mediocre game at this point.  No wonder why many people can't get past the first level- it's not actually fun in any way shape or form and if this mirrors what the rest of the game is like...who would want to put up with it?
Dev Team, or Person(s) - You owe it to supporters to at least try to overhaul this game.  You got the game completed as far as I can tell, hell even just tweaking the numbers of enemies and items will be a MASSIVE step up for this game.  Animation Hold Times do not need to be as long as they are.
There is a gem in here waiting to happen.

I've played a lot of this game and a lot of it (I mean A LOT) was just checking out newly downloaded FREE mods and playing around with the settlement building because I love building things in games. When they first announced that there would be settlement building in FO4, I was extremely excited, because I loved the atmosphere and lore of previous Fallout games and (as I said before) I love to build things in games. Unfortunately, the settlement building is pretty much useless as your settlements rarely get attacked, and since it gives you a misc quest marker everytime a settlement does get attacked, you'll usually wind up going there to wipe out any attackers anyway, making settlement defenses pretty much useless. Aside from defenses being effectively useless, the building system is clunky and doesn't really play any role except making a settlement look the way you want it to. No one really cares if their settlers are happy and have somewhere to sleep since their happiness doesn't really benefit you in you long run. You'll do just as well if they're mopey. Actually, you'll probably do better if they're unhappy because then you won't care if they get attacked because all they do is complain anyway. Leaves you more time to do other things in the game besides babysit your settlers.
Unfortunately, the story was extremely linear in comparison to previous Fallout titles and character creation was severely neutered. As thousands of people have said countless times before, you just can't really make your character in Fallout 4 your own like you could in the other Fallout games.
The locations were decent enough to keep me interested, but still felt pretty watered down in comparison to previous Fallout titles. One thing that bothers me with the world design that is also shared with the Elder Scrolls series is that you can leave a settlement, walk down the road for about 5 minutes and you can find, quite literally just off the road for a few paces, locations that predate the War and were clearly supposed to be high security and/or top secret. Call me crazy, but if I made a top secret facility or a high security military installation, I wouldn't just put it on the side of the road. I'd try to put a great deal of distance between it and civilization. Like I said, the same thing was done with ancient ruins in the Elder Scrolls series. Kind of takes away from the significance of a structure when you can literally come across it just taking a stroll down the road.
One thing that Fallout 4 had going for it was that the gunplay was improved upon from previous titles. However, ammo is very easy to come by, as well as more powerful end game weapons, so things like the pipe rifle or the 10mm pistol are only good for a couple of levels and then you can ditch them altogether. The weapon customization is nice and can allow you make a gun your own, but I usually just make the same type of modifications to my weapons every time. You can try different things with different guns, but why would you when it just makes them weaker? Basically, the weapon customization can lead to a strong sense of imbalance.
Quests in Fallout 4 are pretty much all the same, or at the very least feel too similar to tell a difference. They mostly consist of "go here, kill everything, come back". Even the more memorable side quests in this game (i.e. the Silver Shroud quests, USS Constitution quests, Vault 88 quests, etc.) were either the afore mentioned "kill everything" format or just fetch quests. The only thing that made them memorable at all either boiled down to comedic dialogue/actions or decent story. On a side note, as memorable as the Silver Shroud quests were, I can't bring myself to ever listen to the protagonist's dialogue from them ever again.
The only thing in this game that I really don't have any complaints about would be the graphics. Ok, so I may have two small complaints about them. 1) I understand that it's post apocalypse, but it's well over 200 years after the nuclear holocaust. You'd think some plant life would have regrown by now, especially if animals like deer and bears were able to survive (albeit heavily mutated). 2) The game was poorly optimized after release and even now in 2017 Bethesda still hasn't bothered to release any optimization patches, but sure were quick to put out DLC and release paid mods.
I'm not even going to mention all the glitches and bugs that were prevalent after the game's release (most of which are STILL a problem today). I'm just going to end this by saying if you play this game, it's extremely recommended that you google "Fallout 4 Nexus" and check out the FREE mods that are constantly being made for Fallout 4. Also, don't use the garbage that Bethesda puts in their Creation Club. You can get much better mods on the Nexus for free.
The game is fun, play with friends for more of fun experience.

As much as it pains me, I feel I have to give this game a thumbs down. Graphics and physics are great and with over 250 hours into the game, I can't say I havn't enjoyed it. But when taking all the negatives under consideration, there's really no way to recommend this game.
There are several reasons for this and the recent Creation club-stupidity is right up at the top, but my main objection is that Fallout 4 seems to be made for players with ADD  who can't play games that doesn't tell you what to do in every single situation. Oh, and just in case you were wondering, this is NOT a roleplaying game. Your role is set, your motivation is decided for you within the first 5 minutes of the game, and no matter how hard you try to ignore it, the limitations of a fully voiceacted character is shining through in the most menial conversations. Basicly, you are playing a movie that advances it frames when you click the left mousebutton.
Another major flaw that has to be mentioned is that there really is no way to fail. I've played on the hardest survivalmode settings and even though it at first seems challenging having to find food and water while being shot at by supermutants, you get past these fundamental issues within an hour or two if you know what you are doing. Fallout 4 has, as many other titles these days, implimented a lazy mans difficultysettings. Your enemies can take more bullets the higher you set it, but they really don't get smarter. Even in survivalmode, you can take out a deathclaw by standing inside a house shooting it through a window. It will take about 20 minutes to get him down, but you will still get through the fight without taking a single hit, all because Bethesda forgot to give the deathclaw the ability to crouch...
It's really sad to see a title with so much potential being wasted by a company that choses to focus on selling shiny things instead of making a game to be remembered.

As an aspiring game designer I find this game to be an inspiration. What better type of game to make than one about making games? Besides, I find this very type of game interesting as it allows me to simulate my dreams. This game is very much for the players as well, as any ideas or suggestions are considered by the development team. Although simple I feel as though it is the perfect game to begin your—Eggcode’s—development experience with.
Mad Games Tycoon starts you off in a garage in the 1980s where you must claw your way up through the game industry by starting your own company and making history. Creating revolutionary games is all the fun with this game. Being able to create a legacy for others to be inspired by as well as making the games which changed the industry in your own way are the reasons this game is so addictive. The game is quite easy as well, making all of the complex tasks very easy for beginners; of course there are exceptions further along in the game whereby the expansion of your company requires more elements to be available. The ability to unlock more aspects of the game in a more controlled manner by forcing players to earn money and play for lengths of time before they can move onto more complex tasks creates a buffer for new players to understand the mechanics of the game industry better. I did find however that when I began first creating my games they would usually go bust and I would have to rework contracts to regain money, I now realise that this game utilises the term you need to spend money to make money, and it works.
Their depiction of the tools available is quite well done in fact, it excites me. Being able to change and modify so many details such as the toilets for example captures the side of me that loves management games. The ability to develop patches, updates, language packs, sequels, as well as undertaking contracts tugs on my perfectionist personality when it comes to games, so making sure they’re ‘up-to-date’ creates the atmosphere of me almost being there. The endless immensity of content in this game leaves me wanting more, and the actual experience far outweighs the realistic visual quality some of today’s games may offer, especially for such a low price.
This game honestly propels my excitement for my own career through the roof. Being able to tell stories and make so many people happy in such an interactive way is thrilling. Mad Games Tycoon gives me encouragement to create games which can redefine gaming; a big dream yes, but at least I’m aiming somewhere. This experience provides me with insight into what can be done with a little work: being able to create worlds, or go back to different times, it’s all merely based on imagination and creativity and this game shows me that Eggcode has created a very tantalising experience—one that shows they create promising hope of future games as alluring as this one.

Ultimately for $8 there is plenty of play here.

More like Grind Age. Of Grinding.
There is far too much grinding involved for this to warrant a permanent place on my hard drive.  Early game missions like reparing the antenna turns into 10 rounds of the 3 same opponents with individual minor variations in level.  Special abilities that apply debuffs that do not make up for the damage not dealt that round... Maybe borrowing the turbo button from Doom & Destiny would help things feel less tedious.
Additionally, the leveling system is... odd?  Having every character have the same abilities available, with the same cost to invest in makes the characters distinctly generic.  Which is unfortunate given the good writing that went into introducing Trish and The Sheriff.  To be fair, I have not spent an over long amount of time with the game.  Nevertheless, tactical choices like a melee character using breakthrough or a regular attack is academic at this point of the game.  And wow was I already bored with choosing melee, attack, target.
Stats feel largely irrelevant.  For 7 character points, you can increase strength by one point with a melee character.  Although the tooltip reports a 7 point increase, the actual stat only changes by 1.  For 1 character point you can increase strength by 1 on a range focused character.  The marginal gain of abilities that don't feel worth using, damage that hardly seems to increase, and foes that only seem to be increased by between battle party skill checks and the grind becomes oppressive to me.  Those same skill checks make the frustration and loss of choice more apparent.  Approached by punks, apparently raiders have some kind of uniform, and ordered to murder one out of a group of survivors.  Only options available are agree or reject.  No options based on other skills, and certainly no third option like wiping out the opportunistic leeches that try to order your band of survivors to kill for them.
Trying to reach initial objectives or secure simple crafting materials ends up being more of a Skinner Box RNGesus crap shoot than product of player choices generating failure or success. The areas do seem to have distinct drop tables.  However when combat is against the same opponents round after round, it feels a lot more like playing a slot machine than a game.
Another gripe is the wording of the drunken soldier quest, send hunting within two days!  Send him on the hunting job his survival skill allows, and the mission does not resolve. Huh, well maybe Jack has to go hunting at the same time, it does say with him? Mission still doesn't resolve.  Ignore quest, and try to grind towards that AK generic NPC #2 mentioned?  After running into three bucks and successfully hunting them in the woods(day) area, then the mission resolves.
Another clarity gripe is job names like gunsmithing and blacksmithing.  How on earth does gunsmithing describe anything remotely related to crafting clubs?  Blacksmiths work metal into tools, not reloading ammunition.  What on earth does a hammer and anvil have to do with the hand loading of ammunition? If some idiot is working with primers and powder with a hammer and anvil, make sure they really don't need all 10 of their fingeres.
Ammunition is presented as being tremendously scarce.  There are 3 combat trees that rely entirely on distinct types of ammo.  Every weapon of a given class uses the same ammunition M1911 or Desert Eagle, same ammo right? If the player ever ends up with resources not panning out well enough, the character specialised in pistol attacks is going to be assigned to hunting or guard duty for the long haul.
I am no stranger to hard roguelikes, the overwhleming amount of hours on my steam account have been totalled up in Tales of Maj'Eyal.  Even won (without cheating) a few times. That said, this isn't hard in the sense of challenging, or difficult.  It is challenging to endure the repetition.
This game really should be taken back to first principles, or at least the design team should revisit their design priorities.  Take a look at Sonny 2 from Krin Studio to see how a far simpler interface and excellent design can produce a far more interesting, engaging, and most importantly fun game out of a zombie focused turn based combat RPG.  There is more character diversification, completely distinct combat roles to develop for each individual character, and special abilities that present meaningful choices on when and how to be used.  Equipment dovetails with abilities, or shores up weaknesses inherent to a particular build.  Combat meaningfully advances character progression.  Grinding is almost entirely optional.  When the player chooses to slow down progression, or wants to level a few times, they choose when and how to do so.  The player is not forced through at least 10 battles of the same opponents to reach a secondary plot point.
This has hints of good design, but present state loses badly when compared to an aged browser based game.

Was aiming for a technological victory, and I spot my oldest and dearest ally (little grey men) is closer to transcending this plane of existence than I, Humanity. This would not do.
1. Instigated a war between space cats and robots, so that little grey's military ally was preoccupied.
2. Massaged relations on my own borders with a bunch of lizards and birdmen so that Humanity could be left in peace for a while.
3. Solidified my own military fleet, kept far away from prying eyes, and maintained good relations with neighbours.
4. Gently rebuffed advances from the little grey men who were asking for free movement through my territory.
5. Gave away nearly all of my technology to a race of backstabbing shapeshifters so that they would start a war with the little grey men.
6. Waited until the little grey men had sent their deathstar away to deal with the shapeshifters before I opened up a warpway to their frontier, and piled every available ship I had through to attack grey systems.
As I shelled the very last member of their race out of existence and out of history, Humanity became a race of light-travellers, and got away to explore plains new - far away from the primitives. Humanity had been an entirely peaceful race up until that point - I debated with myself whether or not to get stuck into the action; the war was a drain on research resources for both the grey men and humanity. I could have kept our noses clean right until the very end, but I felt like the grey men were humanity's sick pet - it was our duty to put them down ourselves rather than leave it to the vet. Blasting their home planet from space with nukes was the equivalent of pulling the plunger.
See you in the next life, entire race of sentient creatures.
It took 15 hours or so to complete that one match. I still smile at the memory of how it ended.
Prepare to say "Just one more turn and I'll go to bed" and then look up to see the sun rising through your window. Fifteen hours goes *fast*.
I'm looking forward to playing it again with a new race, but I know I'll have to set a week aside to actually do it. Difficult to pick up and play, you really want to go at it for hours at a time instead of piecemeal. Thoroughly recommend it though. Excellent music and voiceover work, made me feel inspired in the way that space orchestra really should do - to put forth your most noble effort to expand your race's horizon. The mood shifted significantly when I declared war, and it had a feel of DEFCON to it; nobody truly wins. It was perfect.

the game itself plays well and is great and all but timers are ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
i'm sorry but if you think that it adds any tactics to the game, it just adds tension or frustration. that's it. I've had plenty of missions where by the time I can actually get to a VIP (after killing ballpark like 3-4 patrols, 1 of which usually flawlessly ambushed with a chain overwatch setup and the next aced by grenadiers, you usually have like 6-7 turns to get the VIP and extract whilst there's still more patrols on the map, and hello, you have reinforcements coming in on the next turn blocking you from getting to the extract.
The timers don't add tactical gameplay or tactical decision making. They add difficult gambling decisions based on luck and RNG. I've reloaded the same saves many many times (which is a poor way of adding game longevity) just to redo the same mission scenario over and over again, step by step- except this time cutting corners and avoiding elaborate tactics. Instead I'd try very risky luck-RNG based attacks and rushes just to shave time in order to complete the objective, or get lucky and walk out with minimal casualties.
The timers wouldn't be so bad if they weren't mandatory. You ran out of time on a VIP extraction mission? (which mind you doesn't offer you much turns to begin with) you lose ALL your soldiers that were on that mission. That's a stupid mechanic. It should just keep sending reinforcements, or make the mission harder. On a randomgenned map, with randomgenned enemies and randomgenned AI decision making, a timer doesn't make any mechanical or elaborate tactical sense in a tactical game. Because all it promotes (if you don't want to fail the mission or potentially lose a lot of your best units) is continuous repetition of the same save where you already pre-emptively KNOW what the enemy will do in that or the next following turns based off of your decision making. That's not tactical, that's just being able to read the person's mind without any intuition or raw talent.
The game clearly tries to stage itself as a tactical turned based game but with the timers, it severely negates this and becomes more of a luck-based shoot-em-up adventure to try and tell a story to those who get too far into the game's character.
And this is an experience played on the 'veteran' or regular difficulty. I'm sorry but if I run into impossible missions or have to redo a mission a million times to perfectly execute it, that's not a regular difficulty. That's an extremely challenging difficulty for people who want an un-necessarily difficult challenge that requires you to roll a die to win it.
Pick it up on a sale. It's still a good game and I don't have the DLC yet, and the DLC adds a lot of mechanics to the game to improve it. Especially settlement defense missions. But right now? It's not worth 80CAD or 60USD at all.

INTRODUCTION
The Mims Beginning, Developed by Squatting Penguins , Published by Squatting Penguins
Currently Early Access. How is the game? read this review and find out!
Plot/Storyline
The "Mims" a race of alien critters, with tentacles eyes and short orange bodies, crash on a strange island and need to find a missing part for their crashed freighter ship, they then discover "you" and decide to drag you into their turmoil and help them survive the harsh new world.
I like the story personally, and feel as tho others will too.
GAMEPLAY
"The Mims" play style is similar to that of populous or Godus (I know, The title we do not speak of)
but also brings its own unique style to the God game genre. Control are fully explained during the tutorial and are easy to learn and you will find yourself shooting around the map in no time.
The general gameplay is calm and you may start getting bored but the game always
has exciting moments just around the corner, such as predator attacks or harsh weather conditions (Some natural, others not so much).
GRAPHICS/TECHNICAL DETAILS
The graphics aren't marvoulous but they certainly give you the full experience of the quirky characters and bright alien worlds.
I had extremely fast load times, when first booting up the game and between levels. I also had a good smooth framerate
throughout all the gameplay, even when a lot of effects were on screen at once.
Some textures appeared blurry or low quality on menus but the game is still early access and they might get resolved by the time the game is fully released.
I didnt see any graphical anomaly throughout my playthrough, or any clipping issues.
SOUND
Overall sound quality is fantastic, the developers really put a lot of work into the sound effects,
you can hear wind turbines spinning or the spacecraft taking off. Ambient sounds are plentiful and add to the atmosphere
The Mims aren't voice acted in cut scenes yet but i could see at least their alien voices being added to the dialogue in the future.
MULTIPLAYER
The Mim's doesn't feature multiplayer at this time.
CONCLUSION
My final verdict is, Its worth the asking price for the amount of content and playability you are getting, the game is frequently updated and the developer's are highly active.Its far along in early access at this stage and i doubt the full version is far away. You can buy the game on steam for £14.99.
PROS/CONS
+ Funny dialogue
+ Well directed cut scenes
+ Good graphics
+ Unique setting
+ Unique and colourful art style
+ Informative tutorial
+ Good explanations of controls
+ Great environmental audio
+ Large building variety
- Not the best grammar during some cutscenes
- Can't save anytime

Camera Obscura is an earnest, well-conceived, enjoyable game that feels like it was the first effort of a new developer (which it was).
The game is a puzzle-platformer whose signature mechanic is the ability to create temporary platforms using a camera. Once they are there, the player can move for a bit before they solidify, and then jump on them before they disappear. Platformers with special mechanics tend to walk a fine line-either the mechanic makes the game too easy, or the developer overcorrects and it becomes too hard.
Camera Obscura leans on the "hard" end of that line but doesn't cross it, and I say this as someone who, as of the time of this review, was encountering a substantial ramp-up in difficulty. I do have to repeat that the game is indeed difficult. Probably to ensure the use of the flash-platforms, the main character cannot jump very high on her own, and many stages require careful environmental management to progress (both the stage I'm currently up to and the one I just completed require you to keep a fragile enemy alive to solve a puzzle).
The game just has a good "feeling" to it, the feeling of puzzle completion, the excellent soundtrack (which in my opinion is reason enough to buy the game by itself), and the sense of being seemingly stuck but knowing there just has to be a way out (which is what the difficulty entails).
However, the game also has some of the weaknesses one would expect from new developers. The flash-platform mechanic is imperfect and works a lot better in horizontal movement than in vertical ones, and making the right platform is often not a matter of ingenious puzzle-solving, but pure trial-and-error. The soundtrack and setting of the game imply a slower, contemplative atmosphere, but the frequent need for fast reflexes often contradicts it. Also, though not the fault of the developers themselves, the obscurity (no pun intended) of the game means there's little outside documentation. This, combined with the difficulty, means that a player may be forced to ask around should they be stuck (as I was)
The relative weakness of the main character without the camera and the fact that she slides a little too much can be a little annoying. Finally, without spoiling anything, the game has more of a plot than it actually needs, and said plot isn't the best-written (although it's a very small part of the game).
In spite of these, Camera Obscura is a worthy puzzle-platformer. None of the flaws are insurmountable, and none make the game feel tiresome to play, as opposed to just difficult. I got it for sale at a very low price, but it's definitely worth buying at its regular one. While one may be annoyed at how the door to the next level is so close but so far, and struggle with making just the right platform, once they reach the door, the feeling of satisfaction is all the sweeter.

2. Smoother transitions with weapons and aiming: I've died multiple times because the aim system is very odd. Also, you should be able to pull the trigger whether you're aiming or not. In real life situations, you aren't always going to be able to aim at your target if he/she is at point-blank range.
3. More frequent missions: I really can't express this enough. I don't want to spend my entire shift switching from giving parking tickets to taking people to jail for a DUI. That's not fun. I want to finish up with one call and immediately have to go to another call to take care of them.
4. Limiting players to one call on Normal mode is bad: The fact that I don't want to die permanently has no bearing on my ability to multi-task. I really don't know why they thought it was a good idea to only allow you one mission at a time in Normal mode. In an Easy mode, perhaps.

Straight up? This game is hot garbage.
As a side-scrolling action game (I don't use the term Metroidvania because this isn't one) Luna: Shattered Hearts fails to deliver the kind of fidelity and tightness in terms of controls you'd come to expect from the genre. The movement is very floaty, but the bad kind of floaty. I would describe Dust: An Elysians Tale's movement as floaty, but because you have so many movement options and aerial control it ends up working out. In this game you only have one attack and you pretty much stop when you touch anything in mid-air and lose all momentum. It's not fun.
Even if the controls were better the combat and other gameplay mechanics are pretty lame too. As I mentioned earlier, you only have one attack and it takes about half a second for it to actually get out once you hit the button. This would be fine if you didn't get knocked out of the animation once you get hit. It ends up with you having to just mash the attack button until the thing you're fighting dies. Which you'll probably be doing a ton of since the only "quest" in the game requires you to grind out a ton of items from enemies, which is extremely fun!
This game has a couple of "complex systems" in it but strangely enough the game doesn't actually tell you about them. There's a guide the creator has up for the game that you can check out that is extremely helpful and will probably answer every question you have about the game. The problem is it's not actually in the game. How is anyone supposed to enjoy the game to the fullest when they don't understand what any of the systems do?
All in all, this game feels more like a proof of concept than an actual finished product. If you want to play a good side-scrolling action game/Metroidvania check out; Dust: An Elysian Tale, Guacamelee, Hell Yeah! or Valdis Story: Abyssal City.

Ugh, I really wanted to like this, and I tried, I mean, REALLY tried to enjoy it.  I was looking forward to its release after seeing it on Greenlight.  I liked the look and the unique visual design, and it seemed like it had a lot of potential to be fun.
But it wasn't...
A lot of the problems seem to stem from the way it doesn't relay important information on how to progress to the player.  It seems to be left to chance to try and figure out what needs to be done in order to get what you need to progress.  I'm not saying things should be spelled out to the player; allowing them to discover things for themselves IS a good thing to do, but at the very least, you have to help them along in some way, like providing some kind of clue as to how they can obtain the resources they need.  Other things to take into consideration is just the tediousness of combat.  Maybe what you can do is make the beetle enemies significantly weaker, but provide more of them so its easier to make use of their carcass in order to actually get needed ingredients to drop from enemies, as its really hard to get some of the hive enemies in place.
Another thing that needs to be addressed are the loose physics.  It feels like the chracter slides around too much from the momentum.  Platforming needs to have precise control, otherwise the player will be constantly falling from ledges.  Also, more control in jump height would be beneficial, like shorter taps of the button for smaller jumps.
I'm not sure if this was a bug, but there was a frustrating instance during the major boss fight (with Chumbo?) where I would take constant damage for no discernable reason when I was at ground level.  At times I would get forced out of the room from the constant knockback after just entering it.  It's also too easy to exit that particular boss room by accident mid-fight.  Having the entrance/exit on an elevated platform would easily solve that issue.
As it stands, this still feels like its too early for release, and could really use more play testing.  There's a possibility of a good game in here somewhere, but it needs a lot of work before it reaches that point.

If you're looking for a horror game with jumpscares, loud sounds, and combat, "Serena" is not for you. The reason it's classified as "horror" is because of the way the player can perceive the story and events that take place. Immersing yourself in the story can and will cause chills to be sent down your spine, anxiousness, and maybe even fear. I would definitely reccomend this game if you're the kind of person more interested in the "psychological horror" category.

Ittle Dew is an action-adventure game heavily inspired by the Zelda games with heavy emphasis on replayability and speed-running. Mechanically, Ittle Dew works just about as well as you'd expect. You can walk around, hit enemies, but the real fun comes from the various puzzles. Like a Zelda game, Ittle Dew has an assortment of items that you'll utilize to solve puzzles. However, unlike a Zelda game, where you'll usually find yourself with 7-8 unique items, Ittle Dew only has. This isn't a major issue, for two reasons. Ittle Dew is a shorter game than Zelda games, and two the way that item's works together creates a large amount of replayabilty, due the game's design allowing for puzzles to be solved in multiple different ways. Ittle Dew's three items are a fire sword, which should be fairly self-explanatory, you hit things and light them on fire, a Portal Wand, which allows you to create blocks and teleport objects around and a Ice Wand which allows you to freeze objects. A large portion of the games puzzles are solvable in multiple different ways using any number of the game's items. Even beating the game only requires 2/3 of the items, this encourages exploration in the game world and experimentation with the game's mechanics as you figure out how to get to the end with a limited toolset, and I found doing so to be very compelling. There is also a fair amount of optional content, from hidden collectibles that require optional puzzles to be found, to a couple of optional dungeons. Competetive players will also enjoy trying to figure out optimal routes through the game in order to beat the game quickly.
While I can prise Ittle Dew puzzle solving mechanics and overall design, it's not a perfect game. There's some combat throughout Ittle Dew, and frankly it's not very fun. More often than not, I found that having to kill the enemies in a room detracted from the fun puzzles that I should be solving in the room. There's also bosses, but they're mostly one-trick ponies. You'll figure out how to defeat them quite quickly, and they rarely pose a threat. The combat is a minor part of the game, but I can't help but think it could of been more deeply intergrated into the best parts of the game, the puzzle solving.

It would seem to the casual viewer that Starbound receives infinite hate because of its Early Access. I'm not very sure why this is, but I'll crush the reasons as best I can.
Currently, the top negative comment by Mandalorian addresses a few things, which I will counter-criticize with arguments varying in strength and relevance. Like people, sort of.
So now we know this guy's arguments are essentially troll quality with a cult backing as evidences by much of the blind upvotes.
This game has been compared to Terraria due to its 2D sandbox genre. Yeah, whatever, Terraria used to be considered a Minecraft rip-off. This is too cliché to be a respectable position anymore.
Starbound is an excellent space exploration-sandbox game. Starbound has many, many different types of planets and solar systems in addition to the spontaneous generation of creatures to inhabit them, meaning that it's a lucky happening when you find two planets with the same creatures. It doesn't use that as an excuse to stop. Starbound's planets are provided with a wide variety of biomes. There's no magicky filth biome that spreads through the planet. This is science. There's odd organisms, creepy, suspiciously familiar items and themes, and an amazing soundtrack that prompts the player to be brave and explore the stars.
I'm not a professional critic, so I won't provide a numeric rating, nor is that really what the Steam review system is ultimately about. It's about recommend or not, with an elaboration as to why. I recommend this game, but if you're so swayed by the naysayers, then I'll just assure you that you're gonna miss out on a spectacular experience.

It may look and feel like The Legend of Zelda, but this is not your average Hyrulean adventure. What sets Ittle Dew apart from Nintendo's classic franchise are a willingness to make fun of itself and extremely streamlined gameplay. It's so streamlined, in fact, that you can easily beat the game in only a handful of hours. There is a deck of character cards scattered throughout the world that could potentially extend your play time, but they aren't very rewarding to collect. Plus if you wait until you are fully equipped, many of these optional puzzles are easier than they were intended to be. Speaking of equipment, Ittle Dew's arsenal would leave Link green with envy. The portal wand especially introduces some very unique puzzles that elevate the game above standard-fare LoZ block pushing and flip switching. There's still plenty of that, but the game is always aware of its source material and freely pokes fun of it. The first time I picked a heart up off the ground, I nearly fell out of my chair laughing. From the irreverent sense of humor to the squiggly hand drawn graphics, Ittle Dew is a charming game that holds its own against its apparent competitor.

Dead Age is developed by Silent Dreams and published by Headup Games. It’s still in Early Access, but the dev team has had their fair share of games launched on Steam. Most received a lukewarm reception, but as always practice makes perfect.

While video games and zombies have had their unholy matrimony in such a manner that few gamers haven’t played at least once such a title, it is also just as safely to assume that quite a large percentage of said gamers, have become bored by the never ending stream of digitized undead hordes. Afterall, there have been countless shooters and a few RPGs that have treated this subject and horror genre, in full detail. What more could be be said or done about it? I confess that zombies in general are a guilty pleasure of mine, so I couldn’t rate Dead Age any further down that I already did. It has a decent story to it. Is it revolutionary? Far from it and yet it’s certainly less generic that some of the zombie games I played in the past. Combining turn based combat with role playing elements and a randomized story, does prove to be a pleasant interpretation upon an almost stale formula. To spice things further, the permanent death looms over players at any given point. A threat which might be too much for beginners. The game has a tendency to save itself quite sparsely (and no manual saving option) which I did not apreciate at all. If you can turn a blind eye to the irregular difficulty scale and the visual issues below, Dead Age might prove to be a welcome addition to any zombie fan or game collector.

The sounds themselves no matter how subpar they might be, pale in comparison to the repetitiveness of the visual assests. The TBS combat scenery is just like the enemy variety itself, quite limited. And it feels like rinse and repeat, even after two hours into the storyline. Some antialiasing problems still linger, no matter how high, the resolution you are playing in. The game certainly deserved more, since the survival aspect has to be portrayed in some form other than through text. It doesn’t fail to deliver in the end. Not really, since the Early Access stage still gives me some hope that the dev team might iron out some of the issues mentioned above.

+ Mission and task variety
+ Open-ended storyline integrating permadeath
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards
- Repetitive combat scenery and a few glitches
- Random difficulty spikes
- Still in Early Access
Graphical hiccups aside, Dead Age proves to be a rather fresh take on the zombie survival horror. A type of game which refuses to die. Pun intended, though I have to admit that fusing more genres is the only way gamers won’t feel any dreaded monotony at this point.

It's a pretty realistic simulator, as you get rewarded in points for giving out tickets correctly, capturing criminals, and helping out people, and you lose points for arresting innocent people, police abuse, civilian casualties, etc. And as you get points you get promoted, which earns you a larger salary each time you complete a shift, and you can buy items for your house, cars, gas, food, and ammo. You have three meters (stress, energy, and hunger) which you can replenish while off duty or on duty, but you get penalized for staying off duty too long, and you can stay on duty as long as you want as long as you have enough energy. The animations are pretty good for each action like walking, asking questions, hand cuffing, etc. and the only bad part of the animations is the idle animation for you character, as he/she just stands there lik a ragdoll and slightly breathes, and some of the animtion transitions are jumpy but still pretty good. I pursued the male on foot calling out to him to him that I was the police and to stop!. Enforcer is one of those games you have to take a chance on to enjoy. The graphics are bad, its really outdated looking for a 2014 game and the driving engine is handmade in Hell. However, the gameplay is there in spades - fans of Maxis' SimCopter will be at home here.
You play a uniformed cop who simply works a shift and is faced with mundane tasks like setting up speed cameras to record speeding vehicles, or chasing down armed suspects after a botched home invasion. You can ask a suspect to comply while you check his ID, frisk him for weapons or arrest him, and use your radio to have him taken downtown or have his vehicle towed, all with an intuitive interface.
The missions are quite repetitive and if you're quick to complete them, you can face a boring period of wandering around looking for speeders or drunk drivers while waiting for an "official" mission. However, if you like police themed games, Enforcer is not too bad.

Got it for $25 on a Steam sale, and it is worth every bit of that and more if you are a fan of strategy games in general and XCOM in particular. It is a bit different as the Sectoids and stuff aren't the same standard X-Files aliens like in the original or anything like that, but there is a lot improved here as well.
It does feel more difficult than the original, and I've bumped back down to Rookie difficulty so as not to get totally murdered. Don't let that thwart you though. The new things like having a Ranger class that can go melee with a sword is a great addition to your tactical toolbox, as are the psionics. Those are actually quite powerful and I'm pleased to take them along now.
I haven't completed it yet, but I'm not in a rush to either. One thing I remember seeing was that there were time limits and it somehow ruined the game. Let me tell you that the turn limits in a battle are actually reasonable and logical: get X before Y happens, that sort of thing. A few of those were in XCOM and while you might want to play around on a map, frankly the longer you drag a mission out the more likely you are to end up with a roster of injured soldiers. Get in, get it, get out, just like you would if you were really doing this. As far as the campaign itself, that is no different than the Doomsday clock or whatever, except with the Avatar project you can actually take away the enemy's progress.
When you do have time to spare - and honestly you usually do - setting up ambushes is a super effective way to take out enemies quickly. Concealment and overwatch ambush is too good to pass up.
The storyline is interesting and I'm intrigued by the build-up to whatever this big revelation is going to be. They definitely have some neat ideas going.
The only negatives I might mention really are the interruptions. You're trying to scan or pass time on the map  but every few seconds there is a chain of stuff going on. Most of it is research or construction, sometimes notifications about new missions, other times required events that you need to handle. It's better than scanning for weeks and hoping a UFO comes down but yeah, just a minor complaint.
Overall: Seriously if you're wondering if it's for you, give it a try. Steam offers sales frequently enough that you could put it on your wishlist and grab it later. It is a good game, and it annoys me that I fell prey to negative reviews and held off. To be fair, it might have been rough before, and updates have patched various bugs.

For all those out there that are raging.
1) Kabam is not hogging your money. All these items can be earned. Remember, they are not selling UTs (untradables). If they were doing that then this game would be a real cash grab.
2) Don't mind my hours in this game because I play using adobe flash player with the .swf link. Within the past 2 years I have been playing 3+ hours EVERY DAY. Also all of you complaining about lag. Adobe Flash hardly every lags at all (only on US West servers nexus due to trading bots and swarms of traders)
3) Hacking IS NOT DEATHPROOF most of those *invincibility* hacks are because of your lag. There are some hackers who no-clip, autonexus, etc, however (after observing them for quite a while) no-clippers tend to disconnect after no-clipping too much (making them lose all their loot) and the autonexus does not protect against death. A good player WILL DEFINITELY be able to match the autonexus ability. The only hack I feel like is completely unbalanced is the Anti-Debuff hack.
4) All of you guys who think this is a pay to advance. IT IS NOT! All dungeons are complete able if you put enough time into it. Example, Assuming that you have breached the tier 6 boundary for your sword and the tier 7 boundary for your armor (both VERY easy to do) complete a snake pit dungeon to level up to level 10-15 ish then use the speed from the boss to buy you a dragonsoul sword (T9) from someone else. Then do another snake pit to buy yourself a desolation armor (T10). These items (and some skill) makes an abyss moderate-challenging to do but still very complete able. Then collect the def from the boss and buy yourself an archon sword(T10). From the archon and vengance armor up, your best chance at getting better loot is at oryx, however if you stay with the big mob getting through the dungeon is pretty easy.
So there you have it. Realm is not some type of cash grab, everything is obtainable through a little effort. I hope you realize that realm HAS given players free character slots, portal keys, etc before.

Master of Orion fails entirely as a good remake of the best entry in the series Master of ORion 2. Just buy Master of ORion 2. Costs 7 dollars and is mechanically better in literally every single way.
3's only good parts were an intensely more longer tech tree than 2, a more interesting galactic senate, a bit more options for racial picks, more factions, more starting empires in any single game, terraforming's increased complexity that's wholly ignorable, which I liked, fleet creation, designing starbases and the New Orions.
Otherwise it never happened, there's a reason why there's no officially titled Moo4, even if this game is THAT exactly.
First off, it's a remake, what I'm going ot say is already irrelevant due to that.
I've however played Moo 2 since it came out and I've never really stopped playing it for anymore than a week at any one time. I will be reviewing it as a remake of Moo 2, so the following will be a Pros and Cons list of simplified bullet points.
Pros:
- Most of the factions look really good versus how they were in 2. Save the Klackons, and (in my opinion) the Psilons. Klackons shouldn't have pupils and Psilons really don't need 4 arms.
- Voice work is great, save for the Klackons after a bit. 6 hours of playing as them, and now I want to burn them alive.
- System structuring is just fine. Not complex, which is good. Up until starbases.
- Trade Goods and Housing is here, though you gotta research Housing for literally no good reason. Gotta learn how to build houses in the age of space travel. Okay. Might be confusing it, however, for Trade goods, which makes just as little sense.
Cons:
- The Mrrshans are for no reason, entirely a female race. Who's idea was this?
- No Racial Specials.
- Less non-specials for Racial Picks, making this and the above point result in making custom factions almost totally pointless in a way.
- Real time combat with as much control if not a bit less so than Moo 3, which people often hated the most about it. People want control, and to be able ot walk away from combat to get water/food or do chores, or they want time ot think, hence why people kept asking for Turn-based combat.
- How you build starbases is just arbitrary, construction ship has no real point for that when the colony itself could just handle that directly.
- Freighters are a thing you can physically destroy, which sort of makes them a pain in the butt.
- Star Lanes. In short: They make Combat stupidly simplified, when it's simplicity, yet depth in MOO2 was it's main strength IMO. Oh and it's just lazy. Endless Space and Moo3 are not good games, mostly because of Star Lanes. Though ES's combat system makes that game worse than Moo3.
- Race pack DLC. Just why man. You can make your money, just make a good game FFS. World of Tanks probly pays enough to make a DLC-less game FFS. Worst part is, they aren't the Terran Khanate, but the Elerians, Gnolams, and Trilarians, which should be free, since those are base game races in Moo2.
- Morale is too hard to keep up. Moo 2 didn't have that and it was good due to it. Civ's design isn't strong and hasn't been since the very first game in it's series, irregardless of what "critics" say about it. It shouldn't scale off of population numbers, otherwise it gets too hard to manage, or harder than it really should be.
- 30 dollar price point. Moo2 is 7 dollars normally. I'm a firm believer that the age of a game should never deteriorate it's pricing if the price is good for what you get. Realisticlaly, this is more a 20 dollar game. Moo2 is a good 30 dollar game if not 35 or 40 for what it is.
- Ship design is just worse than in other games, including 1 and 3. It's not any better either.
- No miniturization from researching tech tree branches.
- You can't design starbases. The only weak point of Master of Orion 2 is this and only this. So what's the point of this remake's existence if not to just cash in on nostalgia?
All in all, versus Master of Orion 2, which is a superior game, still being patched (look up Master of Orion 2 1.50.8, it come with a launcher that allows online play without port forwarding, even if you are hosting), and on steam for literally 25% of the normal cost of this game.
For those that think ratings are a good idea, my rating for tihs game is a 2/10. You may think I'm judging it too harshly and comparing it entirely against Moo 2, but I'm a firm believer that remakes for video games is as pointless as "how to Breathe" seminars. Remasters? Sure, those make sense entirely, but Remakes, unless they do the same stuff as what was the best in the remade series, and do either as much, or even more better stuff, they justify their existence.
This game doesn't justify it's eistence, what it instead shows, is how absolutely lazy and terrible gaming has gotten in the last 20 years.
If you can't make a game in the same vein, and the same style and formula of a game series that is literally legendary, then you should just quit your job or not even bother.
Wargaming wasted their time and apparently the old MOO2 devs have no idea what made MOO2 so great and what made MOO3 so terrible.
After reading this, now you'll know more of why MOO2 was so great.
Would've rather we got a remastered version of MOO2 1.50.8 with star base designing and massively improved mod tools. Would've been easier for them to pull off in hte long run and the game wouldn't be at Mixed twice over for ratings.

Alright, Camera Obscura, where the hell to begin?
First and foremost this game looked liked it would be interesting it looked like it would be a lot of fun, a pretty cool side-scrolling platforming puzzler. Something that I had never experienced before and something that I thought, "hey, I can dig this".  On the surface, Camera Obscura, had everything I was looking for in something new and exciting, and then I played it.
A couple of things; you're a girl, which is awesome, I'm totally pro female protagonist. It's awesome we need more of it, but she's constantly staring at me, its kind of unnerving and a little frightening.  Why? Why are you looking at mt?  Look where your going, just look where you're going!  You're animating your sprite, which is awesome, just turn her head, just turn her head. She's always looking at you, judging you! "Why did you jump then? Why didn't you jump before? Huh? Oh, so that's how you're playing.  I'll remember that."
Camera Obscura's camera mechanic, what do you call this mechanic? I don't know but I love it.  I love the idea of it and everything that can be done with it.  It just needs a better game to better realize its potential, I see great things for this.  Remember Narbacular Drop?  It was an okay game, not a great game but a okay game with a great mechanic in need of a great game, Portal became its great game.  Camera Obscura is like that game, it has a great mechanic in need of a great game.
Camera Obscura, its a fun title.  The music was, a little repetitive, really repetitive, like super repetitive. It felt like a ten second clip looped ad infinitum.  It was... the music needed a lot of work, I'm not gonna lie.
Verdict?  Well if you want a challenge give it a go.  I may never touch it again, but then I really love the camera capture, so maybe I will.  I haven't a clue.

Camera Obscura is a cute little indie game that I admittedly had not had high expectations for.  Whenever you get a game for a quarter, you can't ever be sure of the quality. But I will say I was pleasantly surprised.
CO is a puzzle platformer that plays in the vein of games like Braid. It's only controls are jumping, movement, peeking your field of view ahead, and it's key mechanic: the ability to take pictures of the landscape, and as it "develops", it creates additional platforms to jump across. The soundtrack is soothing, the graphics are cutesy, if a bit uninspiring, and the story plays out in collectible pickups. The ambiguity of what's happening at first again strikes of Braid.
For this innovative mechanic alone, the game accomplishes a very tight level of game design. The difficulty curve is structured around gradually inputing more challenges that stretch your ability to use the mechanic in new and creative ways. A good puzzle platformer like Camera Obscura has very simple mechanics that extrapolate in complexity as the game goes on.
The game is not without its faults, however. The difficulty in the last few levels ramps up considerably, and the final level is excruitaitingly frustrating because of checkpoint drought. There are a few puzzles where you have to guide little mobs to hit switches for you, and it's possible for them to die and not respawn, so the puzzle becomes unsolvable until you die, at which point, you revert to the last checkpoint, and possibly, the beginning of the level. Another point of frustration is moving or timed levels, where you have to snap a pic at just the right time; a millisecond too slow or fast means starting the level over again.
All in all though, Camera Obscura is a solid game with a good bit of replay value. The level design is solid and the expanding complexity of the one simple mechanic is textbook game design. Camera Obscura is no gaming titan, but it is worth your time.

This was an enjoyable dungeon puzzle type game. You go through dungeons mostly solving puzzles, but there is a combat element to the game also. The combat is pretty basic, but you can freeze and teleport enemies in addition to slashing them with your sword. The puzzles are nicely balanced. Nothing was too hard to feel like giving up on and nothing was too easy to get bored on. The only thing I didn't like was the optional Master Cave dungeon. You basically needed a walkthrough to get through most of these. The solution to a lot of the puzzles require doing things that you never did during the main game, but are expected to know about somehow in this dungeon. A few of the puzzles also require fast reflexes instead of just puzzle solving like the rest of the game. It just all felt out of place to me. Overall though, the game was very enjoyable and I would recommend to anyone that likes the puzzle solving in something like The Legend of Zelda games. You can do mostly everything (minus the achievements) in about 7 hours, depending on how quickly you can figure out the puzzles.

This is a very colorful strategy game that I just fell in love with.
The Mims beginning tells a story about you being an invisible "god" helping the Mims to bring those planets back to life!
The Mims are funny little creatures that you need to use and to protect.
Know this, I am so very impressed of the fact that this game was created by 2 Developers, One for designing and the other one for Coding and a 3rd one working as a translator ( This is what i know ).
The character and level design reminds me so much of Spore as for the animations and sounds, And thats a good thing because Spore is a great game.
Bare in mind that this game is still on
so it gets updated every now and then and they are working very hard on it, so this is a + for the game, Even though its early access the game it still offers a lot of content, And many levels to play that gets harder every time ( And sometimes to the point of frustration but i will get to that later )
The music in the game is really beautiful I just gotta say 10/10 for that, Classic type of music that stimulates the need to play this beautiful strategy game.
Story so far is lovely, Every level you get a few objectives as main, And some secondary objectives to try to Achieve.
Gather Biomass and Gems to build your colony, Create more Mims Build Research centers, Spaceports, Windmills, And much more.
Upgrade your base and use your special PSI abilities to cast fire or to buff up your units or to defend them, Survive catastrophes, Keep your Mim's energy up and turn some of them to guardians to defend your base from predators and pests.
With various challenges to overcome, Surviving depression, A black-hole, Monsters and more this game brings out the need to strategies your movements carefully.
There are so many features that are just so good in this game, here I will try to explain the gesture of the game.
- You can speed up the game if you like ( normal , Fast, Fastest ) because the game progression is slow and sometimes if you want to retry a level faster its a handy thing to have.
- You create animals and help them grow to send them to the spaceship and sell them for Gems which are important to build and upgrade and research abilities.
- A lot of plants to place, They grow Biomass which your Mims take and throw at the Extractor so you get Biomass and use to build stuff ( The biomass is easier to get and used a lot , gems are harder to obtain and have certain uses ).
- Build windmills or Generators to create electricity (its not really that important, it just makes your Psi energy ( Mana ) refresh faster, and makes creating animals also faster .. and important in some objectives )
- Research center to research abilities and new stuff, Houses for Mim's to rest at ( you can also use abilities to replenish their energy ), Build Silos to increase your Biomass cap and other buildings to increase the electricity cap, and later on you get to build towers to protect your Mims.
- 3 Type of abilities ( Offensive , Defensive and global ) They are all explained from their name I hope.
Although the game graphics and details are spectacular it can also run on older machines, The graphic options can be reduced significantly so it would work on them.
After explaining all that, Going to the short point.

1 - Beautiful colorful worlds to go through and lovely design with characters and everything.
2 - Great music and sound effects in the game they are as good as the game looks in the screenshots.
3 - Challenging and funny story, The game requires strategy and thinking instead of just randomly building stuff.
4 - The fact that the game is created by 2 and still gave me that wonderful experience is a good thing because I know that they are hard workers who worked on this for so long, hopefully in about Six months it will be fully released.

There are 2 minor cons that exists in the game currently, They are so minor I am sure they will be fixed soon just thought i'd make this review completely honest and show everything in it.
1 - Remember when I said sometimes it gets a bit frustrating ? Well its a simple point that can be fixed easily (They are probably working on it ), You cant use the circle or square selection to select units in a group, and they keep wandering off sometimes if you don't put enough plants to give them a reason to stay to gather biomass.
2 - Sometimes when they pickup the fruit and throw it at the extractor just sometimes it would hit the edge and fall down on the floor again so they will pick it up and redo it , This mainly depends on where you put the extractor ( Make sure there are no tall trees next to it so it wouldn't bump into them )
So Considering this is an Early Access title it brings out a lot of game time, Internet goes off frequently because i have about 15 Hours so far,
There's a lot of content to go through the game does not feel completely polished but it is great for its current state.
I Recommend this to anyone who played Spore and enjoyed it and loves strategy games, And loves an adorable adventure that combines mystery and comedy.
Support those amazing devs for their outstanding work.

To address the elephant in the room: yes, this is very much like the classic Legend of Zelda games.  However, I would have to disagree with some other reviewers that this game is a rip-off of the Zelda series.
Surprisingly, I found quite a few of the puzzles to be more challenging than I've found in Zelda games (and yes, I remember the water temple in OoT.)  The developers did an excellent job of creating some difficult puzzles which take all of the available tools to solve (especially in the optional Master Cave.)  The interaction between the freezing rod and the portal rod was especially ingenious.  Plus, the game itself is quite tongue-in-cheek, which keeps it pretty lighthearted.  I was pleased to see the random commentary when walking up to some random objects throughout the game.
I thoroughly enjoy games that make me think, and this game definitely accomplished that.  Additionally, I found Ittle Dew to have decent replay value due to the added challenge of trying to complete the game with varying combinations of the tools (rather than all of them.)
In the end, if you enjoy puzzle-heavy games in the same vein as classic Legend of Zelda (and have a sense of humor), then Ittle Dew is worth the purchase.

The Mims Beginning is a god game, where you the player are basically God. Your job is to guide and assist a small race of beings known as Mims by directing them around the small asteroid on which they live. Gameplay is simple, just click on a Mim and tell him where to go. The game shares a lot of similarities with other genres as well, such as real time strategy and city builders. This is made evident by the building menus fulls of structures that you can have your Mims build to aid in their way of life. In addition to building, you also have a menu where you can use a number of "God Powers", known as PSI. These can range from refreshing your Mims' fatigue levels, or offering protection from outside threats.
The gameplay can be a tad slow, but the devs have stated that they are working on numerous fixes, including an adjustment to the camera controls (which are solely keyboard keys, no mouse involved). Anyway, once you select a building for your Mims to build, you choose where it is to be built. Once placed, your little alien friends will go and build the selected building. Thankfully, there is a meter when you click on a building in progress that shows how long until building is finished. There are 2 main resources: Biomass and Gems. Gaining biomass requires creating a garden, where food and organic material are harvested and then thrown into a machine to create biomass. Gems are acquired by selling things at the market, which comes bit later into the game. To do this, you need a bio-lab and a spaceport, but if you don't spend your starter Gems on these 2 items, you are pretty much stuck. Something that needs adjusted for sure!
Graphically, things are a bit behind for our standards in the recent year, but for a small indie studio they are quite impressive. Everything is also bright, colorful, and eye-catching. As for the sound and music, they are a bit bland but they work well for the setting in which they are used. The game just looks great and has a lot of personality. The Mims themselves are a comedic bunch, prefering to slouch around and eat instead of work, which I guess is why they need you around for guidance! There is a story as to why they are now stranded on this asteroid and repairing their ship, but it just serves to make silly jokes via dialogue. And that's not a bad thing. The game shines in it's gameplay, not the story.
Despite the many issues the game may have right now, the devs have stated that they are working on improving things.  It has potential, and it shows easily. With a patch or two this game can be great.

Town of Salem is a Strategic Elimination game that's set the the town of, well, Salem, back when the witch trials were very much alive.
This was a browser game in the past for quite some time, but December 15th is when it's mark on Steam came along. I played the browser version pretty extensively, and it's a very fun game to play because the outcome solely depends on player interaction and decisions.
See, you have these various roles, all with different alliances. Townies try and work together to survive and find out who the bad guys are. The mafia are their own group, trying to eliminate anyone who isn't them. And then the neutrals are people trying to achieve their own goal, neither with townies nor mafia. 15+ roles exist in the game, and they can all have a huge outcome on any game.
What's the catch? You have no idea who is what, so you need to use your smarts and think about whether to trust the people you're with or not. Each day, there's a discussion, then there's voting. If one person is voted to be lynched, they have a chance to defend themselves, then the town decides whether that person is guilty or innocent. The game then transitions to night, where the action happens. People can be stabbed, moved, killed, distracted, just about anything can happen at night, as careful as you may be. The game ends when either the Townies or Mafia wins (Neutrals are rare cases.)
This is why I like this game so much. Like I said, it depends heavily on human interaction, which is what keeps every game fresh and alive. You're always given a random role at the start of a new game. You can pick classic mode where there's a set list of roles, and all 15 players fufill one, or you can do "All Any" where you don't know what roles exist, and that makes it an even bigger mystery.
Overall, Town of Salem is an awesome game to play just for the suspensefulness and the fresh variety with every game, I really recommend this game.

Got it for $25 on a Steam sale, and it is worth every bit of that and more if you are a fan of strategy games in general and XCOM in particular. It is a bit different as the Sectoids and stuff aren't the same standard X-Files aliens like in the original or anything like that, but there is a lot improved here as well.
It does feel more difficult than the original, and I've bumped back down to Rookie difficulty so as not to get totally murdered. Don't let that thwart you though. The new things like having a Ranger class that can go melee with a sword is a great addition to your tactical toolbox, as are the psionics. Those are actually quite powerful and I'm pleased to take them along now.
I haven't completed it yet, but I'm not in a rush to either. One thing I remember seeing was that there were time limits and it somehow ruined the game. Let me tell you that the turn limits in a battle are actually reasonable and logical: get X before Y happens, that sort of thing. A few of those were in XCOM and while you might want to play around on a map, frankly the longer you drag a mission out the more likely you are to end up with a roster of injured soldiers. Get in, get it, get out, just like you would if you were really doing this. As far as the campaign itself, that is no different than the Doomsday clock or whatever, except with the Avatar project you can actually take away the enemy's progress.
When you do have time to spare - and honestly you usually do - setting up ambushes is a super effective way to take out enemies quickly. Concealment and overwatch ambush is too good to pass up.
The storyline is interesting and I'm intrigued by the build-up to whatever this big revelation is going to be. They definitely have some neat ideas going.
The only negatives I might mention really are the interruptions. You're trying to scan or pass time on the map  but every few seconds there is a chain of stuff going on. Most of it is research or construction, sometimes notifications about new missions, other times required events that you need to handle. It's better than scanning for weeks and hoping a UFO comes down but yeah, just a minor complaint.
Overall: Seriously if you're wondering if it's for you, give it a try. Steam offers sales frequently enough that you could put it on your wishlist and grab it later. It is a good game, and it annoys me that I fell prey to negative reviews and held off. To be fair, it might have been rough before, and updates have patched various bugs.

A high-quality knockoff, and I mean that as a compliment. Sleeping Dogs is a re-do of the blatant GTA-clone series True Crime, but while it keeps a few elements obviously lifted from Rockstar's series, it makes good on the attempt by actually doing a lot of things much better. Endless, ultimately-pointless side quests have been more or less abandoned, and what remains is pared down and tightened up. United Front knew they couldn't match GTA in sheer scope, so they wisely didn't try and instead worked a smaller batch of content over with a lot of extra polish. End result, while there's not as much stuff here, what is here is a lot tighter and honestly very fun. The story is engaging and moves fast and cool, though the second half has an emphasis on gunplay as opposed to the vastly-more-fun melee combat. The story also ratches up a wee bit *too* fast at times, making Wei's rise through the triad seem impossibly meteoric. Not necessarily a bad thing as far as making a game goes, though.

One of the best sandbox games in recent years. Has an amazing Kung Fu + Asian Crime action drama flick atmosphere ala movies like Kung Fu Hustle and stuff starring Bruce Lee, Jackie Chan and such, with a very lively representation of Hong Kong. As well as a mishmash of some of the best game elements from different video games, such as Batman Arkham Asylum/City's freeflow combat, Assassin's Creed's freerunning, Just Cause's stunt jumping of getting into different vehicles on the fly, a mix of GTA, Max Payne, and Saints Row gunplay, driving and customization.
The story is pretty good and well written, the fairly all-star cast of actors nails the dialog pretty well, mixing believable Cantonese & English. Most of the characters in the game are likable and the NPCs themselves actually feel alive, and you can catch them doing day-to-day routines in a realistic manner coupled with random events. Overall a huge recommendation to anyone who wants to break knees and feel like a dai-lo.

Secondly:
The only difference between free mods and CC mods (Mini DLC) is that Bethesda enforces a more professional pipeline for mod development with it's modders. In theory this is supposed to increase game stability, but the mods on the CC are small. The mods that tend to give players problems are larger mods that require the script extender, and I suspect that CC modders wont be allowed to use anything like the script extender. If I am right then the whole stability argument is a moot point. Which means I can't think of a good reason to fork out $15 for a mod from the CC when I can download a better mod for free.
