Astonishing!
I had no idea about this experience until yesterday. I noticed a free adventure game called Serena on steam and thought I'd give it a go so downloaded it.
Tonight I got back from work and poured myself a Dewar's whisky. I decided I would play Serena. The first thing I noticed was the name 'Agustin Cordes'. Hmmm, I heard that name before....ah yes....Scratches, a game I played about 5 years ago and really enjoyed, with its build up and thrilling climax. Then I realised 'Hey, that's the guy who is also making Asylum, with the scary youtube teaser.' Wow, and I've just stumbled upon this title tonight.
I started the experience. At first, it was a subtle tale of lost love. I poured myself another whisky and steadily explored more. The game mechanics became familiar. More whisky and a sudden drop in temperature in Hong Kong as the first cold front of the season just hit us suddenly and in the space of 30 minutes I switched off the fan for the first time in months, put on a t shirt and then got a dressing gown that had been in storage since last March.
I lost net connection for a while, perhaps with the weather change, but the experience continued, along with the whisky. Gradually, I discovered more and finally reached, what I expected to be the horrific conclusion. BUT, Serena is by the great Agustin Cordes and there was more; the experience progressed until suddenly one of the most amazing, unexpected and spine chilling twists I have encountered in my life occured.
Never has a pc (or movie, for that matter) title given me goosebumps so strong and really stunned me. An amazing work that is literally 'priceless'.
I sincerely recommend everyone to take up this experience, but do so when undisturbed and alone. It is way more chilling (and beautiful) than so many multi million dollar flicks.
I can't wait for the release of Asylum.
Thank you so much to Mr Cordes and the highly talented team that produced  Serena.

Not recommended right now, however has a lot of potential.
Pro's:
====
- Intent on telling a story, an absolute must-have for any aspiring RPG
- Mechanics are there for decision making
- The 3D environments really give you a feel of the atmosphere
- Still in early development, so plenty of opportunity for changes/improvements
Con's:
====
- Decision making is not *really* implemented. Yes there are scenarios where you have to make a choice, but all of them very much say to the player "Pick the option we want you to pick or you'll be punished." For there to be true decision making, the player should not be able to so easily tell that one choice will have a very positive outcome and the other will be very negative.
- Very little non-combat / exploration content. Yes, there is a map with locations on it but each of those locations represents nothing more than a string of combat encounters.
- Combat becomes very repetitive, very quickly. This is really driven home by the fact that you know every time you leave base you'll be fighting.
- Base management is currently quite basic.
In short, first reactions to the game are good, but once you get about 90 minutes in the repetitiveness of the combat system will start to overshadow everything else.

I baked this game on Indiegogo when it came out, and I have to say that, even if they are not that rapid, devs are truly making a great job about it. I'll try to make an extended "beta review", adding some personal considerations.
GAMEPLAY
The Mims is an addicting, funny game to play with elements that remember Black and White. In particular, you are in control of your own tribe of "mims", that are semi-autonomous (they can be controlled under a certain degree), and your aim is to make them evolve and colonize these islands.
I've seen much improvements since the first alpha version, and I have to say that the game is quite enjoyable, even if it needs in my opinion some fine tuning: scenarios are overly difficult at the beginning (and often make you start the scenario again just because you miscalculated the resources needed for a certain development), while become easier the more you develop them.
Something seriously lacking, as I have always said to the devs, is the ability to save game in the middle of a scenario (that can last even for some hours, if you take your time developing everything to the max).
The controls are quite simple and improved in relation to the alpha version. It takes a little time to get used to it (in particular it's not explained how to rotate the camera), but befor the end of the first scenario you can easly manage everything.
STORY MODE
The main feature of the game is the story mode, as opposed to the survival mode, that will be relased soon. My opinion is that during the alpha relase the story did actually make sense (it was about this mims lost in the universe, and every scenario was directly consequence of the last one, even if there were only three). As for now, i've played 5 o 6 scenarios (finding also the ones i played already) but the story was completely unrelated, just some random connection that doesn't seriously makes sense. I sincerely hope the developers work out something better for the story (even if it's not the selling point of the game).
GRAPHICS
Graphics are quirky and fun. They will surely not stress your video card, but despite being simple and cartoon-like, i find them very enjoyable.
MUSIC
Music also is simple and enjoyable. What seriously lack is the character dubbing during dialogues. Now it's only textuals, and they definitely don't exploit their potentiality.
FINAL CONSIDERATIONS
I think the price for the early access is definitely too high, for a game that is far from being complete, and will take at least another year to be. But in the end I reccomend it, because it is fun. Don't be fooled by the graphics, this is not a casual game: it requires patience and calculation more than quick wits, but it's not for everyone. I especially recommend it if you liked Black and White.

The Mims is a god-game where you play the mysterious creator who has ultimate power over an alien species who have crash landed on a set of floating islands. It's currently in early access and only the story mode is available, nevertheless I have not yet encountered any bugs and the game is very polished (short of a few typos) for day one early access.
You must harvest resources, create buildings, keep your Mims happy so that they can work productively, create and grow animals that you can then sell for more resources, defend your base, fight off creatures, and search for the parts you need to rebuild your spaceship and go home.
It starts off fairly simplistic but does gather depth as you progress. Problem is it takes a while to get there playing the story mode. If you're finding it too easy - it does get more complicated once everything is unlocked. I hope that when sandbox is implemented you can build on a much larger scope and hopefully set conditions that provide more of a challenge. I'll return to edit this once that is added!
I'd also really like an option to save in the story mode, especially considering some maps have a fail condition, ie. if your special hero dies - you lose a solid hour of play.
The (currently not rebindable) camera controls are the biggest negative and take some getting used to. I hope the developers consider reworking with the standard right click hold to rotate and tilt rather than having to move to the edges of the screen as well as adding bindings. Otherwise I can see the current system really holding the game back and frustrating players from the start.
Despite some negatives that need to be smoothed out, the game is charming. Beautiful graphics, runs very well, cute, entertaining and fills a niche in a genre which is sadly devoid of recent titles. I don't think this is the deep strategy god game some people are still hoping to appear in the genre, but it still has an absolute ton of potential at this point. Time will tell.

This has the potential to be a very good game. Unoftunately it's not there yet.  While the formula of mixing a bit of Populous with The Settlers, and adding the humor from Kerbal Space Program is a good one, and the game is fun to play, I can't recommend it for 3 reasons:
a) Non-intuitive keyboard controls with no way to rebind them.  Who uses the Q and E keys for zooming?  Every other game with a 3-d map uses them for rotation.
b) Lack of information.  There is too much stuff under the hood with no way to get to it.  The tutorial is 2 missions and just barely scratched the surface.  For example, it tells you that houses are the best way to c ombat fatigue and anger, but how many Mims does a house hold?  There is no in game or out of game documentation that I could find.
c)Most egregious, no in-mission saves.  There is one save slot, and restoring it takes you back to the start of the current mission.  Missions can take an hour or more, which is fine if you have the kind of time to play a single game, but for those of use who don't, it makes the game unplayable.

Dead age has a lot of elements I love. It's party turn based with rounds of incrememntal difficlty and story missions that do indeed challenge you. The need for good systematic attack patterns combined with random drop chances after rounds means you do have to think ahead in terms of not only battle strategy but also surrender. Alongside this, your active party size is small so you can dictate the behaviour of the survivors who remain behind to keep the camp afloat with hunting and guarding jobs. These survivors can also support those in your party by crafting ammunition, clothing, weaponry and medical supplies.
Speaking of the survivors, they can sometimes be a little... 2D (especially with almost every woman in the camp seeming to fall for you the second they walk in the door). But they arrive with suitable level to develp their skills and still be useful, and occur randomly in game so each playthrough you'll build a different party, adding a nice touch of novelty.
Overall, it feels like a good survival management game.
Of course with development builds there are always downsides. For example you currently max out XP gain & upgrades at level 10 and the game ends halfway through the story (both of these elements are being expanded and delivered in the coming update this september). The game is slightly unbalanced in places, like how the AP cost and gain of some skills means you can just spam some moves to keep bosses stunned and therefore remove the challenge. However, the devs are really listening to the players in the discussion boards and balancing things like rewards and enemies whilst also addressing bugs, which is really nice to see.
In short, the game is pretty good - take it's development issues and problems with a pinch of salt as it's going to be great when its finished.

The fear of the unknown, the fear of the unseeable or the unknowable. Things that go bump in the night, things that we don't see coming, or things that we don't understand. Dead Age:
~~~~~~~~
It is total darkness and your head is pounding with pain. It feels like an enormous effort to open your eyes. Then you remember driving on the road talking with your sister about the gravity of this terrible new infection which turns people into Zombies. . . Then the tremendous sound of the impact and now you are lying on the side of the road slowly coming back to your senses.  As you come around after the initial shock, there is no sign of your sister. You must find her before it is too late.
Dead Age is RPG/story rich/turn-based combat game.  As you launch the game, you will be asked to choose what the occupation of your character is. If it is your first attempt, you will only be able to select the student option. Four other classes are available to unlock later on.
As you progress through the story (very enjoyable so far), you will meet characters who will join your party and others who will give you quests to do. Very early on in the game, you will arrive at a survivor camp.  At the camp, you will be able to talk to people at the cantina and get quests. As you achieve them, your character will receive experience points. Apart from that, you can buy or sell items from the shop, check your inventory, decide who to add to your party (each day), and update your combat or jobs skills.
When you are ready to get into the action, just press on the map. From here you will be able to choose which destination you want to explore. In each destination, you can find specific items such as food, materials, ammunition and other goodies.
After making up your mind, you will enter the combat phase which is a turn-based system. You might have up to four people in your party and you might face between one to three Zombies or humans in each battle. Each day will consist of twenty battles in a row, if you can manage it. Each time you eliminate your foe, you will be awarded with items.
You can craft items when you have gathered the a specific number of appropriate materials during your daily activities. You will lose an entire day to craft an item, however.
Dead Age has nice graphics and the interface is really easy to get used to. I find the story really entertaining.
Positives:
~~~~~~~~~
-	Nice graphics
-	Entertaining Story
-	Good and easy interface
-       Achievements & trading cards
-	Fun and addictive gameplay
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Combat phase is a bit repetitive.
Dead Age is an enjoyable game and you should definitely have a look at it!
7/10
Key provided by developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

Sleeping Dogs is a re-do of the blatant GTA-clone series True Crime, but while it keeps a few elements obviously lifted from Rockstar's series, it makes good on the attempt by actually doing a lot of things much better. Endless, ultimately-pointless side quests have been more or less abandoned, and what remains is pared down and tightened up. United Front knew they couldn't match GTA in sheer scope, so they wisely didn't try and instead worked a smaller batch of content over with a lot of extra polish. End result, while there's not as much stuff here, what is here is a lot tighter and honestly very fun. The story is engaging and moves fast and cool, though the second half has an emphasis on gunplay as opposed to the vastly-more-fun melee combat. The story also ratches up a wee bit *too* fast at times, making Wei's rise through the triad seem impossibly meteoric. Not necessarily a bad thing as far as making a game goes, though.

I'm not sure where all of the hate comes from with this game: I actually think it's a pretty good, if standard 4x game.
Many of the reviews put me off of trying this, stating that Stellaris (which I also have) or  Endless space 2 are better.
That is where I disagree.
Stellaris is a very different game. In that, just like in MoO, you research and micromanage your empire, sure, but it has a completely different feel to it. Stellaris is a very slow affair and the AI cheats like you wouldn't believe. Great game regardless, but they are different games entirely.
MoO is much more like Endless Space 2, if only mechanically. Endless space 2, however, I feel is a let down. Combat is cinematic and the AI in battles is stupid to the point of frustration. In Master of Orion, you get full control. If you want full control that is. Then you have the trianglar textures, no doubt done for artistic purposes which make everything look like they are origami creations. You have the droning, depressing atmosphere of ES2, where the soundtrack was basically ripped out of Songs of Praise (google it if unsure what that is - choir singing. Horrible).
MoO is a worthy addition to the 4x genre and by no means the worst. If anything, it's standard. It doesn't add anything new, but that's hardly a crime if you go into it expecting a solid 4x and not a revolution in the genre. If you want something different, go for Stellaris.
Master of Orion is a bargain on sale. So is Stellaris. You could get both and have a very different experience. Just don't listen to the critics who praise ES2 and it's trianglar, choirboy cutscenes.
Master of Orion is also abbreviated as MoO. So when your friends ask what you are playing, you can just make cow noises like an immature man child. That alone makes it worth it.

This sequence of enticing experiences before me could not be categorized by any standard form of rating or critique. This is a simple, yet earnest game. It is powerful, and small, deep, and simple. It combines the greatest aspects of platforming -- running and jumping - with an innovative, practically unseen mechanic that allows new insight into level design. Speaking of which, these levels are simple, but designed effectively. This game was clearly created on a little-to-no-budget premise, and it delivers that small scope PERFECTLY.
Now, onto a bit more review:
The game itself involves a mysterious, unknown girl with an equally unknown past who must ascend this widely feared structure known only as "The Tower". Along the way, she collects old stock photographs, which contain the game's only exposition. These small bits of writing unveil the emotional journey of this girl, as she appears to be rebelling against the fears and doubts of those whoe have failed to ascend this "Tower". They explain vital moments of her life that tugged all of my heart strings.
The exposition compliments the key mechanic - which involves "snapshotting" or creating a "ghost image" of the platform sections in your immediate vicinity. These move with your avatar for a second, then become solid, allowing you to traverse unreachable areas.
This connection between the narrative and the gameplay mechanics is fantastically done. For a simple game, the designers truly took advantage of every pixel, every word, every platform and level tile. I've enjoyed it very much, but my enjoyment being conveyed through text on your screen won't be enough to convince you. The game is discounted to a VERY low price at the moment, so I must urge you to buy it with whatever pocket change you possess at the moment and try this masterpiece for yourself.
It is short, sweet, and to the point. The game is earnest and engaging. I am very proud of the developers for squeezing every bit of enjoyment out of what could have easily been passed off as a nameless flash game, were it not to be Greenlit on Steam. Do yourself a favor, purchase it before the price returns to normal. : )

I really don't understand why there's so much hate for this game. I've played all of the original MoO games, including the cursed 3rd one. I know that MoO 2 was the best of the series, and still play it on occasion. However, I've put in enough time for this game to get a good enough grip on how it is, and let me just say that this it is, in my opinion, the rightful successor to MoO 2.
That being said, I was very apprehensive about buying this one due to all of the negative reviews, but I decided to buy it since it was on sale. I honestly do not regret buying it, and I am willing to go as far as saying that it's as good as MoO 2, if not better. As much as I love MoO 2, I think it really is time to move on from it. This game has nearly all of the features of the original MoO games, and gives them a proper makeover.
Truth be told, I actually really like what they've done with the MoO universe. They made it a bit more light-hearted, and just made it seem a bit more vibrant. The GNN is much more fun to watch, the alien civilizations are much more dynamic and exciting to talk to, the terraforming is still there (and is even cooler), and you can still build doom stars. Another thing is  I used to kind of dislike the diplomacy in the original MoO series, but they managed to make it a bit more fun with this new game.
Really, I can only think of one flaw, and that's the fact that there're no turn-based spaceship battles. I'm fine with either real time or turn based, but I know there are people out there who prefer the old turn-based battles of MoO 1 & 2. Besides that, I can't really think of much that makes this game a negative experience.
Before you buy this game, just remember;
This isn't MoO 2 or MoO 1, and it sure as hell isn't MoO 3. It is its own game, and another wonderful addition to the MoO universe. I know I made a lot of comparisons to MoO 2 in this, but that's only because I know a lot of people are complaining about how unlike MoO 2 it is. I know MoO 2 is the best in the series, but please give this game a shot. It really breathes some new life into a universe I've loved for so long, and I've enjoyed every minute of it since purchase.

You will need to play frequently to "keep up" or fall into the loop of being behind, or worse, the "Pay to catch up" aspect.
Trion is all about paid options, and Trove is no exception. Services that were free/limited are now strictly pay.   It's not "P2W" however as someone can pay $0 and still be "End Game, Top Tier"  - they just have to focus harder to do it.
I Recommend this game ONLY to those willing to put serious time into pointless grind.     The "bosses" are a joke, there is still no quest/story line after over 2 years, and all drops are completely random.  Getting "better gear" simply means grinding more, be it to craft them, or to find them and enhance them.
You will quickly fall behind on the "current dragon unlock" unless you play everyday, even then you may not fully unlock the dragon before the next event starts - but at least you won't be paying nearly double resources after the event to fully unlock. The focus both in terms of development and in the game surrounds the hierarchal tier system. This is ultimately the game's Achille's heel since it revolves around boss fights and digging for ores on very specific, boring planets (even the most interesting one is made boring by the fact that we're forced into a specific activity) all so we can fight the next boss, who unlocks our ability to explore more boring planets. They took a Terraria stance on a game that isn't Terraria, whose goal should be to make you feel like this guy:
, but fails miserably at doing so.
Instead of locking the tiers behind bosses the game should be locking the tiers behind near completely random planets, resources, and exploration. We should be rewarded for exploring the unknown. Instead the game has us digging for oil on desert planets, for uranium on 'radioactive' planets, and for titanium on, I can't remember, but you get the point. The point is that it doesn't encourage exploration of the unknown or encounters with truly unique and interesting animals, planets, etc. Instead we're rewarded for completing 'quests' and beating bosses, which is a very minimal part of our game time.
This is made worse by the fact that they're constantly pumping out content that'll make you question spending a penny on the game. There are literally 9 different workstations to do the same d*** thing, but are there for ONLY because of the tiers. After replacing a work station the third time I got fed up with this. The life of a God doesn’t sound too action-packed. Probably pretty routine and slightly boring if you think about it. Then again, you’ve never lorded over a tiny alien sharecropper farm on a small slab of asteroid. Owned by a crew of crash-landed aliens called the Mims, you will soon be call to aid them in defending it from every other form of life out there. Once you’ve established your ramshackle farm, you begin to branch out. First a few more workers, maybe an upgrade to the city hall. Oh, you need to have a trading port! The game is cutesy, but much deeper than the child-friendly design would lead you to believe. Eventually an alien metropolis spreads out as far as the eye can see. Farm animals swarm the gardens, devouring anything they can in order to grow strong and be sold to what I assume is a cutesy alien slaughterhouse. The tiny Mim workers, and the tough Mim guardians, all working in harmony within the little slice of heaven that I’ve so benevolently created for them. Maybe you see a worker or two slacking off? You’d be perfectly within your rights to burn them with a fire spell. How else will they ever learn right from wrong? It feels good to be a God that’s so involved! Whether you are a benevolent ruler, or a vengeful one, The Mims Beginning is a real pleasure to play.
First off, I’d like to state that I’m quite impressed by the graphics that indie studios can put out these days. This game has been in development for 3 years, and while the age shows slightly, it is far above the average indie game. The buildings are strangely designed and outlandish, just like the little orange minions operating them. The multitude of pests and predators that will eventually make an appearance pulls it all together and makes for a nice comfy experience that is pleasing to the eye. I feel a lot more could’ve been done with the sound. The soundtrack is passable, mostly because I’m largely distracted by the beauty of my adorable alien empire. Don’t let appearances fool you though. This game doesn’t hesitate to teach you through pain. After building a village for thirty minutes, it is pillaged by spiders. How did this happen? Glad I asked. The gameplay mechanics at work here are intricate. To build almost anything, you need either Gems, Biomass, or both. Farming Biomass involves creating a garden, the fruits of which can be thrown into an Extractor. The resulting Biomass currency can be used for a multitude of things, but you will always be in need of more. So you plant even more fruit trees. Eventually the pests show up because fruit has been sitting under a hot alien sun, and pursuing the pests are predators which won’t hesitate to devastate your town. Predators can clear a lot of pests, if you have an infestation don’t hesitate to let them do some dirty work. They can also clear a lot of Mims, so keep a watchful eye and have a haste or heal spell handy.
The other form of currency is received by selling farm animals at market. This requires a spaceport and a bio lab, and if they aren’t built with your first handful of Gems it’s basically a game-over. I feel this requires reevaluation but tweaks and balance changes have been promised so I won’t judge that too harshly. Aside from all this farming business, sending minions to work or combat, controlling the electrical grid, and averting natural disasters with your ability to predict the future… A truly good God will find time to better his underlings, teaching them skills. He will bring new Mims to replace the ones that have fallen in combat or a misplaced PSI spell… Even if I did sort of do it on purpose. I’m sure even immortal beings are permitted a small giggle of laughter when watching an adorable alien scream as he plummets into nothingness. The Mims have some silly one-liners during cut-scenes that let me know this game has a good humor about itself. It also covers two genres that are sorely lacking, RTS and God-likes. I count The Mims Beginning as a cool breath of fresh air for lovers of both genres, as long as they aren’t afraid to enjoy some downright silliness.
On the negative side; the music seems quite generic, which simply shouldn’t be the case on an alien world. Survival mode is not yet implemented, and story-mode levels take a long time to beat. About or more than thirty minutes for each one, so not the type of game you can pick and and play if you only have 10 minutes (though this is likely to change with survival mode). The Mims have their own personalities, but as far as I can tell each one looks almost identical. Making them more individualized would add a great deal to the experience for me. Finally, the camera controls threw me off as well. Q and E are used to zoom in/out, while panning can only be done by mousing to the edge of the screen. Despite its few flaws, I found The Mims Beginning to be an extremely intriguing game that never failed to capture that “one-more-turn” feeling when close to unlocking the next structure or upgrade. Wonderful game, and a big thank you to the folks at Squatting Penguin. I hope that The Mims Beginning is just the start for you guys.

I've finally put in enough hours and a few playthroughs to feel competent enough to write an unbiased review.
First and foremost, to the developers, I would not advertise this as "Final Fantasy meets zombie apocolypse". As much as I have enjoyed the game, its a far cry from any FF game after FFXI. Character developement/customization/skill selection are too limited in their scope, as is the story, as it has been developed so far. I understand there is limited content right now, so no big deal there. But there is, so far,  only a handful of combat/noncombat skills to choose from.
I'll try to break it down into segments based on various aspects of the game.
Story: Assume the role of this vested protagonist, meet up with a camp of survivors, and try to survive by recruiting more people, boltering camp defenses, crafting, etc, and (wait for EVAC? I don't know yet.)
Combat: Combat can be fun and engaging, although once you start trying to crawl through 20 battles in a row, which can pit your 3 party memebers from anywhere from 40-60 enemies, all leading  up to a boss battle. You have to play very carefully, both with your supplies, and your character developement. I won't spoil it, but there are clearly a few skill builds that are optimal for combat and the "encounters" between fights. Once you figure our the meta build, the only thing that becomes a real threat is fighting the RNG with blocks/critical hits/status affects being applied. I was able to clear all available zones to area 20 and kill the bosses, which usually drop a nice piece of gear (green or blue is the best i have seen). Unfortunately, as the game stands now, your playthough ends once you reach 20 days and you are unable to proceed, therefore I cannot say what all they may drop and the rarity of the items, which we will segway into our next segment...
Crafting: It looks like the developers are putting a big emphasis on crafting and the need to craft gear/weapons/ammuntion/medical supplies/enginerring supplies, however, as of this current developemental build, its incredibly hard to focus on. I've done multiple playthoughs and the majority of my crafting has been ammuntion. Mainly because at best I've had 8 people in camp, which was not until day 15+, with 3 in a party to explore, that leaves 5 at camp, you'll need 3 on "guard duty" to keep punks from robbing your camp of your valuable tools (Don't even get me started on tools), and you need to hunt for food or everyone starts to lose health. I don't know if this will become less of an issue once you have access to more days/camp members, but as of right now its such a struggle to craft, and the payout is low low low. A piece of gear doesn't really make or break a character. In my combat party, naked party members with a decent weapon/ammo perform equally well as my main hero (named Rickster) who is decked out in all the best gear/weapons I am able to find/purchase/craft...needs more of an impact.
Tools....TOOLS TOOLS TOOLS...you need tools to hunt for food, tools to build lackluster gear, and tools are stolen by punks (both while out exploring, and when defending your camp). Needs to be more tools, more dependable ways to get them other than the occassional quest/event where you may find one in a crate somewhere/sometime.
I wish they would allow us to play past 20 days, even though it will not advance the story any, just to see what is possible once you pick up more camp members/able to craft.
That's all for now. Game has potential for sure. Would recommend.

Tower Unite is an experience that I would, frankly, like to see in more games. It is a fully social game, one that keeps getting better with every update. It is, of course, still early access, which does entail a few hiccups and bugs, but overall it's a very fascinating experience.
Social games are games that you don't really see much of anymore. Most games are too obsessed with stories, and quests, and goals. Not to say that this is a bad thing, on the contrary, a good majority of those games are fun experiences. But due to this, purely social-based virtual worlds have become, frankly, rather few and far between. A modern social experience like this is a breath of fresh air, giving the genre a taste of new life.
And it's not just a purely social game, though that is a big part of it. There's also minigames which give you in-game Units, which can be used to buy items to decorate your Condo, yourself, or make yourself look cooler. Have you ever wanted a gun that shoots confetti? Or a gun that shoots...bubbles? Or a gun...that shoots...potatoes?????
And the thing that ties the whole thing together? That little payment you make at the door is all you'll ever pay to this game, ever. Everything else is 100% free, all paid for by the Units you play games to get. So free, in fact, that it's literally impossible to, in any way, pay the game any sort of money for any sort of reward, such as Units, or whatever. Everyone acquires items the same way you do, the same Unit prices you do, and it's all for one simple payment at the door.
Would I recommend this? Hell yeah! Though, in all honesty, I wouldn't wait around for any kind of sale. As far as I've observed, this price doesn't drop for nobody, so there's at least that to concern yourself with. But hey, it's a great social experience, a great gaming experience, and an all around good time. I hope this helps you with your purchasing decision.

Recently purchased the game after reading some of the mixed comments and decided I would weigh in a bit.
I'm not sure how old any of you were when the original Master of Orion came out in 1994, many probably weren't even born yet, but this new overhaul of that game is basically the same.   I think that for us older gamers, we put a lot of nostalgic value on older games, often remembering them as being far greater than they actually were or are.
This game is a great overhaul of the original.  The graphics are smooth and beautiful.  The space battles are fun to watch.
As far as game play, it is basically the same.  You have colonies, three major categories (production, research, food), and you have to manage your empire through a simple diplomacy system and espionage mechanic.
While it is very true that since 1994 many other 4x space games have come a long that have done all of these things better, this version of Master of Orion is faithful to the original and contrary to popular belief, plays the same.  If you find this version boring  then I challenge you to go back and play MoO 1 and I am confident you'll find that just as boring.
We all know that MoO 2 was the pinnacle of the franchise and MoO has always been a lengthy game (I'd argue the same average length of game as any Civlization game).   It does take awhile to get your empire up and running and even longer if you start pre-warp, but it still is at its core a very solid 4x game with tons of customization in regards to races and ships, which is why we probably loved it so much back in the day.
DLC is a given nowadays, so no need to complain about it as is knowingly releasing broken games which they fix in a patch a week later, if we're lucky.  None of that is going away any time soon.
I think this version of the game is getting a lot of unwarranted flack.  Point is, if you loved the original MoO, then you'll love this game too with its updated graphics and look.

Camera Obscura is a small little indie title that I personally find equal parts charming and frustrating.  The puzzle mechanic here has a lot of potential, but the trailer is a bit misleading, as your after image moves with you for a second or so, then it stops, giving you lots of flexibility, but it can also be infuriating later on when you need finesse.
I like Camera Obscura.  The art style has a great deal of charm even if, in my opinion, the animation is a bit choppy here and there.  The story, hidden in the collectibles, is pretty moving and sad, equal parts a character study of our heroine and a look at the cult that built a tower to the sun.  The gameplay is surprisingly devious, to the point where it can get frustrating or be really innovative, depending.  I have spent some time yelling at my computer screen, but generally, it is pretty enjoyable.
Controls are fluid, but I HIGHLY recommend a usb controller, just for the difficult platforming sections.  The music is far and away the best part of the game, equal parts mysterious, calming, hectic, and adventerous.  This soundtrack is truly awesome.
The collectibles and the secret endings can be a bit frustrating as there are no guides to help with them, as of this posting, and the answers are seldom ever clear.  I got two of the three endings with a lot of experimentation.
I do recommend the game.  It's charming and fun, with a game mechanic that you will have to be really inventive with to use to the fullest.  As far as platformers go, it can be a bit frustrating, but as far as puzzlers go, it's deviously clever.
Camera Obscura.  Worth a playthrough, I think.

Now, with the Creation Club automatically downloading all CC mods onto your computer, (even if you don't buy them), I cannot keep this game on my PC. When you buy mods on the CC, you are only buying the ability to activate them, as a majority of the files are installed with game updates. Unless this problem is fixed, I'll be leaving Fallout 4, since I don't want company mandated bloatware hogging space on my SSD.

First Impressions:
I have to say, for an early access game, it's an incredibly solid experience.  It's essentially a strategic god-like game...that is, you can place structures and cast spells/enact powers that can both aid your minions and destroy pests and other nasty invaders.  The different structures and how they chain together can take some getting used to, but I was able to figure it out after a few playthrus on the first level.  The game eventually introduces a wave system and researching the appropriate tech will allow you to see farther into the future.  It's easily recommendable in its current state.

The game took about 3 hours to complete my first run through, but it will get faster with experience, and there are even achievements for completing the game within 15 minutes as well as doing it with 3 combinations of only 2 of the 3 items.
The game can be a bit frustrating at times, especially the final boss which was very little puzzle and a boatload of enemies that went on for far too long. The rest of the game on the other hand, was almost made up entirely of puzzles revolving around 3 items. A flaming sword, an ice wand, and a teleportation wand. The items can actually be aquired in any order if you know what you are doing, but it does a decent job of explaining each individually. By the end of the game, you have to use all of these items in conjuction with eachother. You can drop a teleportation block, freeze it, kick it across a spike pit, and then freeze the wall to shoot a teleportation beam that bounces back and hits yourself, sending you to where the frozen block landed. Now that probably sounds really complicated, but the way you are gradually led into single items and then combinations of two or all 3, you really get the hang of it by the end.
All of the rooms reset every time you go in except doors that have unlocked, so this cancels any possibility of brining things between the rooms, which makes it easier to work out the puzzles. The levels are very well designed. I felt that it was always introducing new mechanics, concepts, and ways to use the items together. I actually never had a single instance where I got stuck to where I couldn't get out of a certain spot. Although if that were to happen, there is a reset room in the pause menu. There are no consumable items of any kind, not even potions. I feel as if carryable items aside from the sword and two wands would complicate the puzzles and the game, so it is great that they aren't there. The checkpoint system is great in my opinion. If you die, you come back in just as you entered the room, with no penalties of any kind. It's really not an RPG, its more of a sliding block and combat puzzle adventure, it is only really styled after Zelda visually and thematically.
I encountered only a single glitch, and it was in the final boss stage. An enemy froze in its dying animation and stayed in place for a minute or so.
Overall I think this is a quirky, enjoyable, and decently challenging puzzle game, with tons of references to zelda, and a cute/unique art style. The game felt a little unfinished in a few areas. There didn't seem to be any music at all while the conversation with the final boss was going on, and it just wasn't as fleshed out as it could have been. It's not a must-play title by any means, but it will challenge you and give you a few good laughs. The puzzles can seem daunting or even impossible at times, but I urge you to keep at it. A bit of trial and error, and you'll figure them out. If you aren't willing to take a minute and think about things, you might not have such a great time...

A wonderful homage to the Zelda franchise. Ittle Dew features an amazing amount of well thought and tricky puzzles. A huge amount of time and love went into crafting and polishing this game.
Side note: Ittle Dew was actually submitted as an idea to Nintendo as a Zelda spinoff, but they turned it down. Which is really too bad for them as this would have fit in with any of the Wind Waker style of Zelda games.
Probably for the best really, a lot of the charm of Ittle Dew comes from the aesthetic as a Zelda parody, from poking fun at the goofy statues to the over the top silly monsters.
Really, the only thing I'd want out of Ittle Dew is a little more content, your first playthrough will top out at 90 to 150 minutes of play. However, there are multiple ways to finish the game, which can lead to a lot of replay value.
But that said, Ittle Dew is very much worth your time and money if you are a fan of puzzle games.

This has to be without a doubt one of the most try hard to be tactical failures I've ever seen programmed. Supplies and ammo is excessively scarce, which in a zombie style game is fitting. Unfortunately when you couple this with the games plethora of missions that -force- you to limit your party your already absurdly limited supplies is taxed further. You have toil through the same repetitive 20 levels you've been forced to repeat constantly for unrealistic missions like finding a spot for a date.
Situations give impossible odds, it's not tactical to increase difficulty; it's built on a foundation of absurdity. One mission I had a quest to visit the highway at night to find two characters and I was forced to have at it alone. First level I was given a civilian with 50 hp to protect versus three zombies. Nothing would have kept this person alive.
I acquired a soldier randomly through my playthrough whom required me to go on three hunting trips with him. The hunting bucks mission is random after each encounter, meaning you only encounter it a handful of times as you go through and repeat the same forest levels over and over. This soldier started with only a 55% chance of successfully hunting. Now if he failed it didn't count towards the 3 required. I had this fellow fail 6 of these hunting missions in a row. On the final day I was -forced- to go save the sheriff and liz, resulting in this solder to kill himself because I couldn't complete said mission.
Certain zombie types lay traps that if you attempt to attack via melee you take damage. Now you can bypass this obviously with range, however if you're out of ammo or if you have a character melee spec'ed without a ranged weapon you -have- to attack and take this traps damage. There is no guard or hold your action option I've happened across.
Each day you are nigh required to stick most of your party as guards or you'll be constantly robbed. There's little variation to speak of other than assigning guards and repeating the same levels over and over for loot.
I would not recommend this game until bugs is heavily ironed out and the level of absurdity patched.

I'm having a blast playing Camera Obscura. The unique art style is great and really gives me a fun and retro-indie feel, but with a professional polish. Combined with such an amazing sound track that's worth a purchase all on its own, this game experience has been exactly what I was hoping for. Immersive, challenging, lighthearted, and rewarding.
The learning curve does a wonderful job at consistently testing your perceivable boundaries and pushing you to break them over and over as new obstacles are tossed your way.
Each time I overcome an interesting hurdle in Camera Obscura I'm always left with both a rewarding feeling and the curious notion of whether or not that was the only solution to the puzzle. The snapshot "afterimage" mechanic is so clever in the unbelievable number of unforseen ways it can be used and in how easily it adapts to the user's play style. I found myself constantly discovering new ways to solve simple and complex puzzles, even surprising myself with solutions I hadn't seen at first.
The controls feel very smooth and play wonderfully with a game pad. Which is of paramount importance in a platformer that pushes you to break your limits. You can play with joystick or D-pad on a controller, or with a keyboard if preferred, the game doesn't limit you with any one option, but a gamepad definitely was a good choice.
The story is as much a beautiful puzzle as the rest of the game. I found it to be both mysterious and intreuging. At first I had the intention of speeding through the levels to prove that I could overcome each challenge, but after falling into the story I now want to revisit each stage to find the little missing pieces of the overall plot that are tucked in every corner.
Overall I feel that Camera Obscura really nailed the delivery with this fantastic Puzzle-Platformer Adventure.
I'd recommend this title to anyone looking for a high spirited and fun filled experience that will challenge them to think outside the box and push their limits!
Enjoy!!

Vanilla X-Com 2 is great within itself. IF you're familiar with the previous games of the same name, you'll drop right in to it like an old comfortable pair of shoes. There are differences of course, but without giving too much away, it's hard to detail here. One major mechanic's difference is with timers on nearly every tactical mission, it's one of those things you'll either love or hate, and there are mods to resolve the problem with it if you so desire.
If your new to the X-Com games in general, theres still an interesting turn-based game to be found. You have a global map that your overall stategic decisions take place in, with turn based tactical combat using a squad of soldiers that have varied skills and level up over time with a mild RPG sort of theme.
The story is solid and will having you pushing through with that "just one more turn" feeling, often resulting in late nights with several hours passing before you realise. Replay-ability is good, as there is a mild RNG on the strategic side of things making each play through have its own unique aspects.
Overall X-Com 2 is a great addition to the francise, and if your new to the genre or X-Com titles, you might find yourself becoming an addict rapidly. Value at the normal price, a must have if it's on sale. The DLC's aren't manditory to make it a good game, but if you do go for a DLC with it, Wrath of the Chosen is simply a must have imho.
8/10 - a game you won't regret having enjoyed.

Finally finished the game! This game is definitely very unique and really put in an amazing effort to incorporate puzzle and platformer to a new level. The game's difficulty had a pretty good progression and did really great job to make players think for themselves and find out themselves how to go to the next level - which, by the way, is very satisfying when you did figure it out.
The most fun parts are where there are more than one way to solve the majority of the puzzles. There are some where you can pretty much just solve it one way; however, these are essential "skills" (in terms of knowledge / know-how) that you would be using later on. It's very satisfying figuring out how to do it and then being able to use them on the levels later on.
This game also has a HIGH replay value! If you just initially went for the next level, you might want to tackle the game a bit differently the next time you try the same level by exploring more around the levels and finding mementos (sort of pretty much like item collection) which reveal more about the setting/situation. There are also medals where you can try to use the least amount of times you must use your ability(camera) which makes you view the game on more of a "thinking/puzzle" level. And lastly of course, there's also the finish the level as fast as possible medals. I can TOTALLY see this as a great game for Speed Runs.
Not to mention! They also have a level editor. So... you finished the game? Time to bust out some of what you've learned from just finishing the game and make your own level! Not very many games I know has this kind of feature that's something I would think only the developers would have and not share to people.
Highly recommended and worth the money.

Since the game's release I've put about eight hours into it, about split evenly between level progression and trying to get the various medals. It's proven to be a very addicting game, as I'm finding myself saying 'okay one more try' or 'let me see what this next level is' many times. It's also very fun, there's not much to it apart from the various platforming elements. There's still some stuff in the trailer I haven't gotten to yet, so the game doesn't throw everything at you right away, and each level is pretty different.
The platforming is nice and tight, as you're able to control how hard you jump, which comes in handy during speedruns when you just need to make a little hop. Respawns are quick, or if you want to restart the level, that's very fast as well. The camera element, or 'flashing', is interesting. Essentially, when you hit X, you make an afterimage of the background, which follows you for about two seconds before stopping, and then stays there for a few seconds more. You use this to create steps, lift enemies, and get to places you otherwise couldn't reach. It will take a bit of time to master this, as you'll have to learn when is the best time to jump before the platform halts its movement. But when you do you'll be able to move around levels like a pro.
Each level has a Time challenge and a Flash challenge. Bronze, Silver, and Gold medals for using the least amount of flashes possible, or beating it in the least amount of time. Sometimes getting gold for both happens at the same time, sometimes they're mutually exclusive. They're definitely challenging, but I wouldn't say they're unfair. Though it can be aggravating getting a time of 23.01 and you need to get a 23.00 to get the gold. But it's fun to see what shortcuts are in the levels. One that comes to mind can be completed in about five seconds, or over a minute, depending on if you know the trick or not. And when you're doing the speedruns, you'll often find the enemies are placed in juuust the right area to screw you over if you don't do it right. But then you get to do it and then you can laugh and laugh and laugh.
For the story, I haven't really delved into it yet. There are mementos you can find as collectibles. The main character is a photographer, and she's looking for somebody at the top of this tower. But anything other than that I either don't know or don't want to spoil. The memento give a history of the tower you're climbing, and what you're trying to accomplish, but it's not needed to enjoy the game. Only problem I have with this is there's no indication of what levels have mementos left uncollected, so you may want to write down what mementos you find in each level, as they're at least numbered.
The music is nice, I think there are about eleven tracks. They don't get repetitive and create a nice ambience for the game. Tempted to pick up the soundtrack myself.
I would estimate that if you were just going through the game, trying to get to the end, it would last you at least ten hours? I'm only at the halfway point myself, and it's definitely getting harder, so it'll take longer to beat the last levels. But it still hasn't reached unfair levels of difficulty, or Braid-level lateral reasoning to beat a puzzle. But then, that time doesn't count trying to get medals, or going back for mementos you missed. I did end up spending half an hour trying to get the two golds on one tricky level, but that feeling of satisfaction after I got them, oh, that was palpable.
There's also a level creator, but I haven't yet gone into that. But that's definitely something I'm looking forward to seeing after everyone develops some new levels. For the levels in the game, as I said before, there's a lot of variety. It changes the general theme of the level as you climb the tower, getting more mechanical as opposed to the stony architecture of the first levels, which is cool. There are moving platforms, switches you need to hit (or use monsters to hit), tiles that can't be flashed, tiles that need to be switched on to be flashed, and oh yes: no spikes whatsoever. If you die it's simply from falling down a pit or touching an enemy.
Definitely a good purchase, especially for the price. Absolutely recommended.

I would say it is appropriate for MATURE children ages 11 and up. Make sure that they know not to swear, act like the characters, or will be scared in any way by the content. If they want it, I'd advise a talk with them and a review of the game to make sure it is what you want them to be playing. Before anything else, yes, this is a good enough game to spend time and the cost money on.
Ok, now let's get to business.
My first impressions of the game (watching the first cinematics and playing the tutorial) was that it would be one of those generic hack and slash games you find on Google's Play Store. Well, I was wrong.
This game surprised me on many ways, first of all, it has a quite good and original soryline, it is not like a immersive story or something that really catches you like The Last of Us, but just enough for you to get interested and curious to finish the game. The second thing is that it has one of the best combat mechanics I've ever seen on a Hack n' Slash game; good spells, creative combos and the Rewind Time thing is pretty cool, and the most important thing: it is actually challenging, which is a big surprise for this genre. Although it's true you'll be most of the time pressing the left button of your mouse, this game requires a certain level of skill and smart thinking to defeat enemies.
Comparing this game's graphics to other 2012 games says it has a pretty mediocre rendering, but the environment's aesthetics and details really makes up for it, the game gets pretty creative on designing the levels. However, the characters' designs aren't really worthy of the amazing background. None of the characters (except the bosses) fit well in the scenarios, even looks like they just came back from a cosplay event (for the human characters) or from some kind of future apocalypse (for the "chaos" things, other enemies look good).
Anyway, this is getting too long so I'll end it here. I wanted to say something about the puzzles but they are just pretty plain, stand on buttons and time rewind sometimes. The thing is: this is a really good game with a nice challenge and I really recommend you playing it :D

The focus both in terms of development and in the game surrounds the hierarchal tier system. This is ultimately the game's Achille's heel since it revolves around boss fights and digging for ores on very specific, boring planets (even the most interesting one is made boring by the fact that we're forced into a specific activity) all so we can fight the next boss, who unlocks our ability to explore more boring planets. They took a Terraria stance on a game that isn't Terraria, whose goal should be to make you feel like this guy:
, but fails miserably at doing so.
Instead of locking the tiers behind bosses the game should be locking the tiers behind near completely random planets, resources, and exploration. We should be rewarded for exploring the unknown. Instead the game has us digging for oil on desert planets, for uranium on 'radioactive' planets, and for titanium on, I can't remember, but you get the point. The point is that it doesn't encourage exploration of the unknown or encounters with truly unique and interesting animals, planets, etc. Instead we're rewarded for completing 'quests' and beating bosses, which is a very minimal part of our game time.
This is made worse by the fact that they're constantly pumping out content that'll make you question spending a penny on the game. There are literally 9 different workstations to do the same d*** thing, but are there for ONLY because of the tiers. After replacing a work station the third time I got fed up with this. This also co-occurs with tools (drills, matter manipulator, and pickaxes all do the same job, but for some odd reason they decided to waste their time with remaking the same d*** tool). It would be lovely if they made it so that more meaningful resources could be gathered from plants, animals, etc that might encourage exploration into the unknown instead of the current system which makes a game that is supposedly open world feel like a hallway.
Here is my advice to the devs: GET RID OF THE BOSSES! They're a crutch for you at this point in the development. By revolving the game around them, you're actually taking development away from where it needs to be! Additionally, give players real reasons for exploration and interacting with plants and animals (and do away with the hunting tools). IE, tie it into the tier system in a meaningful way. I would also, while you're at it, nerf or reduce the number of combat meaningful metals or at least only make them available through animal or plant products. This way players aren't forced into only one form of planet exploration.

I really liked this game. To me, it showed a different method of telling a story. For instance, you did not really know what your character looked like other than what is shown in the photograph. You also knew how the character felt about the different objects due to his thoughts. It also intrigued me that you clicked on the different objects and your character would have a totally different opinion toward the end of the game than he had at the beginning.
It was also intriguing how everything was somewhat subtle. It was as though the creators of this game wanted the audience to solve the mystery for themselves with only the evidence that they had in front of them. It was like you had to piece together the story for yourself and figure out why everything went wrong. Why did everything happened? You keep asking those questions. This is the type of game that keeps you guessing, and that is the way that some stories should be told.
I also liked how the picture changed with the mood of the main character and the different things that happened. You can see the obvious changes in the pictures, and they match exactly with the obvious changes of mood within your character.
Now, I really did want to look more into the past of your character and Serena's relationship. I know that the game has Serena speaking at different points and that helps us grasp the different periods and feelings of the relationship, but I actually wanted to see more of the relationship. I wanted to see how it changed as time progressed forward.
I also thought that the ending went by way too fast. I thought there should have been a little bit more, but not too much. Maybe the ending should have shown flashes from the past. We, as the audience, could have seen the main character's memories before the ending ended.
I also did not like the fact that you could not save at anytime in case you needed to do something or complete the game later. If you exit out of the game, you have to do everything again. When I had to go through a part of the game again, it was somewhat nice to go through everything again, but at the same time, it was pretty tedious.
Despite those three preferences, I really think that this game was really good and more people should play it. It is for free, and it will only take forty minutes out of your day. It also has a really interesting story to tell where nothing is really expected.

I have one comprehensive criticism with this game. I don't think this will change, at all, although it's just in pre-alpha. And, that is, that they have this pop-up boxes PLUS they animate the entire screen once the pop up boxes are clicked off.
Why is this a problem? It is an epilepsy hazzard. Even though, I don't think I have it, I am very sensitive to screens flashing all over the place.
For instance, WoW had an animation whereupon if you were in a vehicle and you were taking damage, they made a red vignette flash around the screen. When I contacted Blizzard about it, they had already provided to completely remove it.
I understand that the pop-ups are there to create interest in the game, but literally, they could provide a side icon that is permanent, that could light up when whatever state is ready, lights it up.
I notice that if something small is on the screen, permanently there, and if it simply lights up, it doesn't cause so much eye stress.
Secondly, losing control of the game is terribly annoying to me. And, this is the 2nd complaint about these pop-ups.
Let's think about this for a second. If I am the executive director of a company, no one is going to send me a pop-up to tell me they are done with their poster marketing campaign. In fact, I find it highly juvenile that you don't have a queue of tasks for all departments.
Also, you have no feedback, nor projections of what tasks are hoped to accomplish by their monetary expenditure.
You've flushed out the other Game Tycoon games, but have left out the key components of why the successsful tycoons were so successful, feedback.
You can't have a game with the detail of self production and self publication and leave out any feedback of what you're going to get from spending any money or contracts, or campaigns.

Mad Games Tycoon is a lightweight management game focused on the games industry.
Lightweight in the context that the player is not flooded with analysis sheets left and right or financial reports but instead cuts through to the point - center attention on management and keeping the corner of the eye on the company liquid balance. Effective and fun.
_____________________________________________
[ early access review @ 20 August 2015 ]
The topic chosen is quite appealing and I must comment on the alter-names and logos of all the companies I know by heart given I went through them all during my PC gamer life and those that really made history like Microprose, Ocean and Activision just to say a trio.
The graphic department is competent. It does what it is intended - gives movement, colour and life to a "time sheet". There are some issues with colours but nothing that takes away value. My guess is some further work on it.
The sounds are there. Mechanic types and directed mainly to the alerts and to signal the progression of the tasks being performed. Would enjoy some variation and explicity especially on the events like the games conventions and marketing campains.
Mad Games Tycoon mechanics are good and open way to great diversity. We have all the technical departments in place, at least the major ones and the liberty to self manage a dynamic shift of responsabilities on the different offices is notable when compared to other tycoons where there are limits. For example I can build mini offices with all the necessary departments and develop several projects at the same time. Other tycoons fail at this. A plus on this mechanic.
The Marketing and Customer department mechanics need more depth, after all they ARE one of the most important aspects of the gaming culture :) Also it would be top work if we get the reports for the campaigns.
The Games Engines part is weak at best. While games can be buggy the engines are flawless. I bet this part will change for the best so we can develop a subsidiary dedicated to engines with their own issues, so better branching par with the Production mechanics are needed.
In the optimization side, the game can demand a bit from the shared graphics laptops. With a dedicated graphics everything goes very smooth. This being said and from a propective buyer point of view one would expect a average specs laptop with an SSD to run it okay especially with all blows and whistles turned off. It is early access and this can change as well.
To close it, this will be a entertaining game. Very fun at this stage already even with all the raw mechanics.
If attention is given to the core rules of the game in the upcoming development cycle we might have a lot more to review.
A great Indie project.

Telltale's The Walking Dead is one of the best games ever made. It's rich story, lore and characters really drew me into the game and made it one of the best gaming expieriences I've had.
As far as gameplay is concerned, this game is a point and click adventure game. Combat is made up of quick time events and some stealth segments. The rest of the story is comprised of exploration in small areas (you can explore/interact with your group's current hideout or wherever you are for your current mission), as well as dialogue via cutscenes (I'll touch on that later). It's basically what you come to expect from a point and click game, it's not a fps by any means.
As far as graphics go, it's pretty good. Telltale's engine has always been weaker, but they have taken advantage of this by making everything look more artistic. It's not bad by any means, but it doesn't look photo-realistic either. I don't mind it, but if you have to have everything look shiny and new then look at the screenshots and decide for yourself (That said, don't write off this game based on graphics alone. I was at a used game store once and I saw some guys pick up a copy of the game, laugh at the "2004 garbage", put it down and walk away. They missed out on one of the best games I've ever played, so you shouldn't make the same mistake).
However, the best part of the game is the characters and story. This game has some of the best characters in a game I've ever played. They all have their own arcs, motivations, and development which bring them to life and cause them to stick in my mind even years after I've finished the game. The story then takes these characters to new and dark places, and you'll end up hating some and crying over others (I have openly cried during every walkthrough of this game, and the only other game I can think of that does that to me is the sequel). The story is dark, sad, and well told with good dialogue and an engaging narrative.
However, this game is not perfect (It's close). There are two flaws that I have with it. The first is technical, however it is completely my fault. I am (as of writing this review) running a weaker Intel graphics card. It's good enough to run the game but suffers some occasional frame rate drops. However, the system requirements say that Intel graphics cards are not reccomended. If you have an older computer like me, you may have problems but it won't hinder the expierience too much. The second problem involves the dialogue and overall story, but is unavoidable to make a good story. I'm going to mark it as a spoiler. There are no spoilers in it but it could hinder your enjoyment of repeat walkthroughs, like seeing the "behind the scenes" of a cool movie scene and not being able to watch it the same again:
In conclusion, Telltale's The Walking Dead is one of the best story based games I've ever played, and is absolutely worth buying at full price. However, it can go on sale for dirt cheap so you may want to wait if you are nearing a sale. Otherwise, buy it now!

Starbound is a 2D-indie-sandbox-adventure game developed by Chuckle fish. Starbound opened up to Beta Testing on December 04, 2013.
Regardless of whichever race you play as, you're the sole survivor; depending on the race the background story is a little different, basically a tragedy happened to your people and now you're forced to explore the vast expansive universe.
The story is heavily gear based, first you need to collect a full set of this gear, before you can get the next quest. While this aspect does help give you direction, it is highly limiting and doesn't let you rely on skill, but forces you to farm materials to craft the necessary armor and weapons.
Starbound has a seemingly infinite set of galaxies, worlds, and moons for you to explore, gather materials, fight creatures, and just generally explore. There are 5 different star-types, each start type has a different mixture of elements and planet-types. Unfortunately once you explore several different stars with the same effect (for example, say you visit 5 different Gentle Star systems) you'll start to notice a theme among the planet land types. While this itself isn't necessarily a negative quality; it does take away some of the excitement of visiting other worlds near less dangerous stars.
There is a strong sense of progression within the game, you find/craft many different types of weapons and armor, upgrade your mater collector (Think “pickaxe”), upgrade your ship, craft interesting items with the materials you've gathered, and just generally hoard up tons of materials. (...and believe me, you will fill your inventory and dump it into a vault many times)
At this time there are no Starbound Steam Achievements, which is fine... but that means there's nothing else to add to this section.
Starbound is priced at $14.99 I quickly racked up 61 hours of game play within the first two weeks... the game was obviously worth it to me. However I wouldn't feel right without pointing out that
My good friend Cuteancuddly purchased it for me so we could play together.
To rephrase what I'm saying, “I would have preferred to wait for a steam sale, even though I knew I would put in more then enough time to make it 1 dollar per hour”.
Yessireebobberface, Starbound gets to have it's own warning category. There are a few hazards I should point out, and a potential solution.
Firstly, many Starbound players will complain about their data being reset in one update (I can't remember, I think it was in January 2015)... It's important to acknowledge it happened ...because it could happen again. It's forgivable because the game is early access... but no one wants to lose hundreds of hours because of an update.
Second, At one point my computer randomly crashed, after playing a good 20 hours into the game. I don't blame the crash on Starbound... HOWEVER, after the crash, I lost the starbound character I had been playing.
You might ask
It's because you can take steps to prevent it from happening to you. I strongly suggest you backup your character and universe every couple of days (or every 10+ hours).
There is so much more I could say about the game, I knew I'd enjoy the game because I have played over 500 hours of Terraria. Starbound is my types of video game. If you're not sure about this genre, I recommend trying out Terraria first, if you like Terraria you
like starbound, there are many differences that might put you off; if you'd like to know more specific things about the game or differences, feel free to ask in the comments.
I recommend this game for people who enjoy +indie +2D +Open world +sandbox, Thanks for reading my review.

Dead Age is a turn based zombie survival game.
When you start up the game and click to start a game you are greeted with the charecter creation screen. You pick a name limit@10 characters, pick a job and upgrade your starting stats
Only 1 of the 5 Jobs is currently available in early access, Student. You unlock the other jobs by earning medals during the game, which are awarded through random challenges most involving killing a certain number of enemies. In the upgrade screen you spend medals in a similar manner that you would spend talent points during the game to unlock boosts to 4 diffrent trees; Medical, Engineering, Close Combat, and Ranged Combat. At level 5 in each tree you unlock the corisponding job for your new charecter, Medic for medical Engineer for engineering Bodyguard for close combat and Soldier for ranged combat. To begin - even though many others have said this I feel every comment on it should mention - this is NOT a game in the sense you may be thinking.   It's an interactive visual story.
There is, unfrotunately, no save feature.  In fact there are no options at all.   Just the Esc key that will exit the game.
Tht being said... you should probably be able to finish it in one sitting if you're dedicated to thinking about what you haven't checked out.
The whole "story" takes place in a single small cabin.  You click certain items and pieces of furniture to trigger dialogue from the main character.  As you examine more things, he begins to piece everything together - dropping hints to the story as it goes.  Then a major change will happen - and you repeat the process, but this time with access to more places and items (a closet, a trunk, etc).
The music is incredible.  The art style is dark and atmospheric.  The story is, although maybe a little predictable, very emotional.
I have 1 complaint, really, and it's very trivial.   No real spoilers involved, but if you really don't want to know anything without playing the game for yourself, do not read on.   In short - I DO highly recommend "Serena"

Repeat.  I DO absolutely recommend "Serena".  Incredible work.

Dead Age is an early access turn-based survival RPG developed by Silent Dreams and published by Headup Games. It was released on 14th July 2016. Dead Age is set in a post-apocalyptic world filled by zombies. Your character partakes in a storyline to uncover the mystery of the whereabouts of your wife and to do so must engage with other survivors. The game is turn-based, labelled in days, so day one, day two, and so forth, and it has a current limit of 20 days. This review will cover Dead Age's content, gameplay, performance, and issues and developer engagement.

Dead Age incorporates both linear and freedom approaches to the game. To begin the game, there is a very solid prologue that achieves its task in introducing you to the setting, characters, and the gameplay mechanics. Furthermore, it allows you to transition into the main game, but it specifically lacks in teaching you the management aspect of the game of running your camp. The game acknowledges in the prologue that there is permanent death and death results in a restart. I personally like this approach to the zombie survival genre because it adds realism by fitting survival and one life. Each restart allows you to accumulate medals, which will help you level up skills to help with future restarts by making it easier. I digress, permanent death showcases the need for preparation as on my first play through I entered a battle, survived with 150 health and then was ambushed by enemy survivors. The game assists you with preparation through game mechanics. For instance, each day all of your camps will recover 20% of your health, which is very helpful. Lastly, there is a level progression tree. Currently there are 10 levels and each level gives you a skill point that can be spent on improving aspects of your combat or aspects of your personal job skills, such as improving melee or increasing your ability to craft various medicines. I personally enjoy the system as it adds variety and strategy to your survivors. Overall, Dead Age incorporates a lot of content that uses small game mechanics to balance out those features.
Dead Age features very refreshing and engaging gameplay. I have not played turn-based zombie survival combat so it is fun to play against zombies. Battles use action points (AP). AP accumulates per round in combat and you use AP to use your abilities that you unlock when you level up. Abilities have different outcomes such as breakthrough reducing the enemy defence, allowing for them to take more damage. Likewise, zombies possess different abilities as there are a variety of different zombies. For instance, nurse zombies can heal their team mates. I think that abilities and turn based combat add a new flavour into the game that differentiate from other games. For some context into my next point, Dead Age incorporates a map with five locations and each location has 20 areas. When you win battles you gain loot and you progress onto the next area in that location which makes the game harder by having stronger enemies. I think the loot system needs to be reworked because you gain too little for too much risk. It is all part of the early access process and the developers using feedback to improve the game.

As for performance, I maintain 60FPS while managing my base and when in battle around 38-45FPS. Regardless, 45FPS in combat is relatively good but it can be improved and I am sure it will over time. Loading times are surprisingly good as well taking about five seconds to enter the game and less to progress throughout the game.

Dead Age does not have many specific issues but broadly it can be improved. I encountered a game crash and I have noticed several spelling errors as I progressed into the game. Otherwise, I generally think the developers need to focus on balancing the game mechanics such as the rewards system because it feels uneven and sloppy in its current state. I can say that for a lot of other things. As I have said above, that's all part of the learning process of developers using feedback to improve the game in early access. In saying that, the developers are active on the Steam community hub, which means if you buy this game expect regular patches with new content and improvements.

Dead Age is a very solid early access title. It incorporates a fresh approach on the zombie survival genre through permanent death and turn-based mechanics. It features some fresh combat with level progression and abilities being a prime feature in combat. Furthermore, there is some diversity through the variety of enemy zombies. Judging by the Steam community hub, the developers are active with any consumer query, and performance is rock solid. There are issues with the game, but nothing that detracts from the experience. I think there needs to be improvements to game mechanics such as the loot system and the health system, but for a very new title, the game does a commendable attempt at those features. At USD14.99, it is currently light on content to justify the price tag, however, if you look at the long-term potential of this game, we may have a gem on our hands. Therefore, I recommend this game, particularly if you want to be involved in how the game turns out.
