In the short time I've played this, my initial thoughts are that this is a pretty decent title for early access. Its definitely playable, and somewhat enjoyable at the moment.
Given the simplicity of the gameplay, I believe that this game would
benefit from voice-over dialogue from the survivors. Being able to hear the personality of Trish, the Sherrif and others would go a long way in increasing the immersive factors of the game.
The quest system is really not that fun currently, but I do like that they are tied into other quests so that they can be completed simultaneously while exploring.
In combat, your first instinct will be to click on the desired power to use, then to click on the actual enemy... but you
to actually click on the enemy's name in the bottom menu. This is pretty minor though. Enemies seem to do absolutely minimal damage to your team, so the combat is really not that tough so far... which is maybe why they yeild minimal rewards. Seems like the game is geared up to be a little bit of a grindfest... but I expect changes that will directly influence gameplay in the coming months.
So far, the scenery is honestly abysmal. Its pretty much the exact same backgrounds, maybe 4 or 5 different ones, over and over. The graphics are decent I guess, but they aren't necessary when the gameplay is designed well enough.  As of now, its a little bit lackluster. There is no actual travel movement in the game whatsoever. Even the ability to see an avatar version of your party, physically move across the map as you select your destination, would be good. It'd also be nice to see visual changes whenever you equip new gear.
As of now, I can really only recommend the game on a heavy sale (which is how I got it.) With the current content, and lack of style in the gameplay, it is nowhere near worth the asking price of $14.99. Definitely more worth ~$5.00 - $7.00 in its current state... but it has enough potential that you should consider supporting the developers by buying the game during early access (at a discount.) The more people that buy it, the more likely (and quickly) the game will progress in development, and hopefully be fully released as a much more fully realized survival experience.
Thank you for reading my review!

Oh boy where do I begin?
Tower Unite is a casual social game where you can play minigames and earn money to spend on vanity items, upgrades, and furniture for your condo apartment.
This game was made by the same people who made the Gmod Tower gamemode on Garry's Mod. A game that I have currently somehow spent 4,100 hours in and probably still counting. For the game's age, this should not still be an early access public game. What is it with these backwoods developers that can't get their game out of early access within a years time? This game is still in early access after a bit over a year and a half and for how much this game is when not on sale, I wouldn't consider the purchase to be a viable addition to your game collection.
With the amount of time this has been developed, it comes just slightly further fleshed out than what Gmod Tower was and that's putting it a bit generously. There isn't a whole lot of character customization options, and for a social game that's a big problem. You can't customize your hair and there are very limited clothing options. The only thing you have a variety of options for is headwear, and you have to grind ingame currency to buy those. You can't even customize your hair style or facial structure and that's pretty sad.
The options of minigames you have to play is very limited, with about only 8 or so currently available, and even then they're not very good. Minigolf, Little Crusaders and Ball Race have very little replayability and a sparse selection of maps to choose from, and often are victim to bugs and glitches. After this, the rewards for them are pretty low, considering the price tags on ingame items and other purchasables.
The condos are more or less exactly how they were in Gmod Tower, with a few varieties of alternative condos, such as the underwater and high rise condos; and they're not exactly that great to build in. The Penthouse is massive and empty, and to fill it with furniture to make it seem somewhat 'lived in' (in lack of a better expression) is ridiculously hard. Especially considering the big empty basketball court type of area inside of it. Given the small variety and large price tags of these, players tend to keep to the default condo, which is arguably the best one available due to it's flexibility.
The selection of furniture is not much more bigger than what was in Gmod Tower, which is very disappointing considering this is now it's own standalone game that has had nearly two years on the market, let alone in early access.
The Casino is one of the main attractions to players, due to the fact that it is an undeniably better source of ingame currency than the actual minigames. Due to this, you can always find this area to be the most populated on the game server. The fact that this is such a good source of money makes minigames hardly populated, which takes away a big amount of content available on demand. Because of this, you would often have to wait for the peak population hours for that server to be able to play them.
The community is certainly not one for personal standards, as it is made up of a big portion of furries, bronies, anime fans, otaku, and other niche subcultures/fanbases. Fair warining: avoid this game if you do not want to have anything to do with them.
The one plus side I can give this game is it's very appealing looking user interface, reminiscent of the Xbox 360 interface. For those of you who have owned an Xbox 360 or currently owns one, you'll notice it's similarity.
I have a strong suspicion that this game was made solely because in the original gamemode on Garry's Mod you could play for free. However, some users could also donate to have access to a VIP status, not really offering much benefit than a badge of generosity to the server owner. The fact that you weren't obligated to purchase the VIP, and the benefits of doing so was very limited, it would seem the owner and developers were inspired to launch this into it's own game on the steam platform, effectively making players have to purchase the game.
To end this review, I'd have to give this game a 4/10, due to it's lack of improvement since the original version of this game, the lack of content and design flaws, the poor optimization, the amount of time this has been in early access, and the fact that the 'company' that owns this probably made it just to milk money out of players that loved this game when it was on Garry's Mod... For free.
This game isn't terrible for the $15 USD price tag but there is certainly better options available for the same price, or slightly higher. It certainly isn't my favorite but you could make worse financial decisions.

It's an understatement to say I was somewhat late to the party when it comes to
Valve's debut title was released back in 1998, and yet I only actually played the game last year in 2016. I wrote a review for it a little while after but I am not particularly happy with it, so here's the re-write of my Half-Life review.
Half-Life currently and always will occupy the grand title of my favourite game ever. Although that title is shared with a few other games (Hotline Miami 2, Kid Icarus: Uprising, etc) the position is not very easy to get to. Although my reviews may not make it seem this way but I am extremely critical of video games, making it very hard to actually title a game my favourite. Yet there's something so painfully gripping about Half-Life. From story, to gameplay. Level design to even graphics, the game really masters the FPS genre, especially for its time.
If you weren't aware - which is almost impossible - Half-Life follows the story of a scientist named Gordon Freeman. One day at work an experiment goes horribly wrong and a portal is opened to a dimension named
. Gordon then sets out on a 'quest' to escape the now broken facility, fighting both Xen aliens and a group of HECU soldiers who come to the facility to clean up any evidence of this incident. This story is further expanded in the game's expansions, Half-Life: Blue Shift and Half-Life: Opposing Force, and expanded further still in the sequel Half-Life 2. This story is conveyed completely without cutscenes. From the first moments to the last, every single part of the game you are in control of Freeman. You can also decide to kill whoever you like. Scientists and friendly guards are 100% killable and you can decide to either spare or destroy anybody who crosses your path. While it does not directly affect anything that happens in the game, it is still very interesting to have such control over what you do. Control taken out in many recent games.
One great thing about Half-Life is the range of weaponry available. Crossbow? Check! Pistol? Check! RPG? Check! SMG? Check! And it goes on and on, with even more added in the expansion Half-Life: Opposing Force. Some guns are completely made up, too, such as the Gluon Gun, a personal favourite. Along with this there are explosives such as grenades, trip mines and satchel charges. Each gun and explosive has a different use and a situation to use it in, making the play of Half-Life very easy to switch up and appeal to many different people.
Half-Life is a decently long game all things considered. 17 chapters altogether, some chapters longer than others, however all are a decent chunk of game. As most of the game takes place inside of the facility (named Black Mesa), most parts of the game are labs and rooms you'd find in a scientific facility. Parts are exploded or broken, due to the fighting that is taking place, along with various explosions. Enemy placement is done well, and the AI is also pretty good, some obviously smarter than others, the Black Ops being the hardest to kill in my opinion. With each scene change comes new scenery, always fitting the setting. I won't expand because I'd like to stay spoiler free, but the point is that all the level design is well done, from enemy placement to textures and such.

Ah, Master of Orion. Where to begin? This entry captures the spirit - if not the essence - of the timeless classic MoO2 without breaking many traditions but also without crossing many thresholds. It retains the simplicity of style and interface with the original two in the series and avoids the unapproachable complexity of the third, and it brings back the "cutesy" nostalgia feeling with the species' animations and voice-acting. Yet despite a familiar sense of nostalgia, it somehow does not compel me to stay up playing until 3am as I would have with the originals. (Of course, the originals were genre-defining in a day where there weren’t 10,000 gaming titles to choose from…)
The gameplay is solid - most things work and function as expected, and I've encountered no glaring bugs or crashes. Performance is great in saving, loading, and through turns even in the 400 to 500+ turn range. There are camera-focusing transitions that get annoying - zooming the camera for you when you click to change a "production finished" event - but sometimes that is actually useful (it does center the system, so you don't, for instance, blindly build a colony ship 25 turns away from your frontier where you need it.) Empire-management gets cumbersome by the mid-game, especially on larger maps, but I don't know many 4X games where this isn't true anyway. When you've got 20+ systems and 60+ planets with evolving technologies that improve what were once-worthless planets into impressive colonies, there's going to be some micro.
There is also an assortment of customizing options for how a game can play out; speed of research, growth, galaxy sizes and shapes, inclusion of pirates, random events, the traditional "Antaran" invasion, and various victory conditions. Standard fare while keeping with the MoO theme. These go along with the race options, where the game has the traditional races from the original series (although some are available only through DLC) and of course the ability to customize a race. Unfortunately the vanilla customize race option is weaker in terms of both variety of choices and overall points (default races have higher base points than possible with custom), but the choice is there to define your own style.
The graphics are good - I would say "great" but, let's face it, in 2017 how many space-based games don't look "great"? The galaxy map is solid with useful icon information, and zoom functions quite well to get a "god's eye" view or zoom into a system level. Planet screens are equally useful and enjoyable, although I do sometimes notice some input lag clicking-and-dragging population icons from different plots. The UI, overall, seems on the surface "simple" but is more than functional enough with only a few occasions of what I consider "excess clicking". It could use some improvement, especially with the leader screen (managing colony and fleet "heroes" and where they are assigned) but I haven't yet checked the Workshop to see if UI management improvements exist yet.
Audio is also fine - actually pretty solid. No glaringly obnoxious sounds, noises, or voices, and the music is a low-key ambient that fits right in with a relaxing gaming experience. Actually one of the few games I've played where I don't end up turning the music off after the first few minutes/hours. The fleet combat audio is also good - flowing in volume and special effect sounds based on where the camera is focused and/or how far in/out it's zoomed.
Strategically, my experience and from reading is that any degree of depth or difficulty is dependent on game-start settings, race options, and of course the random starting dice-rolls inherent to 4X games. I've played a few games on huge maps and I'm finding it's not too stressful, but not strategically "deep" except insofar as how to position my fleets to cover my increasing territory size while managing an ever-increasing system and planet sprawl. It feels tedious at times, but it satisfies that "relaxing, turtle-til-I-kick-your♥♥♥♥♥quot; mood. A smaller map, with faster "game pace" settings, is what I'll try next, and I should think it will be much more engaging.
Tactically, the combat system is - surprisingly - not the simple "watch it play out" cinematic of so many space 4X games, but, as this is not a sim, you are also not in complete micro-control. You can play it automatically, but with manual play you can still maneuver your ships individually or in groups and designate their targets. Designing ships gives you access to a variety of tactical choices - weapon types and focuses, specials and defenses, and even "roles" for general AI control - but, as with many 4X games, toward the end of the tech tree these choices mostly go away in favor of "the biggest gun". This is why I like to play with reduced tech development speed in the game start - so each tech advance feels "useful" for awhile instead of upgrading ships every 10 turns.
Overall, I've been really enjoying this game, but I will add the caveat that I am now playing using the 5X - Ultimate Balance Mod (by Spud Dastardly). The vanilla version, as I played the first time, felt not very polished or even unfinished/untested, and after my first game I set it aside for many months. Coming back to it with the 5X mod has made a world of difference. And the developers are still active in content updates, bug fixes, and perhaps more DLCs (not sure what could be added, though.)
It is not as deep (i.e., grand strategy) as other recent and popular titles, but the MoO series was never about that - it's a fun and engaging game that doesn't take itself too seriously while still providing the core elements of a solid 4X space strategy game. I heartily recommend it if you're a fan of the series or the genre.

I am nearly fifty years old. A sober grown man. With children. Children with whom I have now sat through hundreds of movies. Many of which I have enjoyed. And I am not completely hardened in my sophistication. The opening music to The Lion King brought tears to my eyes when my little ones were but wee tots. But still, these are after all just children's movies. In another life, I would never have seen them. And, really, one can't take such movies too seriously, can one?
And so, this summer, after the ritual badgering, I dutifully trudged into yet another Disney "adventure" movie. Named after that tired old ride in Anaheim I first went on in 1965. I mean really, how much can you expect?
And then, it happened. The swirling intoxication. The stunned feeling. What? Who? How? Was this a movie? Or a religious experience? Perhaps more like an addictive experience...
I cannot remember ever willingly paying to see any game not starring a relative of mine more than twice, and I can count those games on one hand. I have now played "BlackWake" four times. The only thing keeping me from playing it again is the sense that this whole thing is just getting out of hand. I cannot get enough of it. It's like walking into a painting that you never want to come back out of. My children ask, with a note of concern in their voices, "Dad, you really like Pirates of the Carribean game don't you", in before i would wip them and make them say Blackwake.
I often don't even watch the Steam Awards, and I certainly never have any emotional investment in who wins.
Except for this year.
Go Blackwake.
And, in a time when many big-budget games are little more than a hodge-podge of loosely- connected "money shots" this game puts all the pieces together, with a sense of fun and light-heartedness in special effects that are simply dazzling. I find myself laughing with dizzy appreciation when a pirate barks out, and the grinning captain comes into view, with Badelt's pounding score keeping time to the beat of their maniacal deck-swabbing.

And now to the music. I can just hear the effete aesthetes dismissing this score.
Well, perhaps it is, for those who spend their lives evaluating such things. To me, it is absolutely transporting. I first listened to it while doing a work-out on a rowing machine and found that I tripled my usual distance. It was like mainlining some hazardous tachycardic amphetamine.
Once again, the children were wondering, "What's up with Daddy? Is he OK?"
Perhaps I am just losing my grip, having an adolescent movie get to me this way. But when those final credits roll, and Captain Jack narrows his eyes and says, "Now, bring me that horizon. Drink up me hearties, yo ho" and the music swells ... it is difficult to put into words the effect it has.
At this point my children have to yank me forcibly from the computer, lest I persist in watching the credits to the bitter end, and bid good-bye to the little monkey once more, wiping tears of exultation from my eyes.
This is not just another "entry" in the summer blockbust sweepstakes. It is an exquisite work of fantasy and inventiveness, a true classic, on the order of "The Wizard of Oz." I cannot recall any game having such an effect on me.
I can't wait until we get lootboxes in our Fallout and Elder Scrolls games!

I cannot recommend this game in good conscience. I would give it a thumbs in-between if it was possible because there are aspects of it I liked which balanced those I didn't rather well but overall, I would not recommend it unless two things happen: price reduction... and you being bored out of your skull with nothing else to play. It's not either/or, both should be true. Please read below for a full review.
I'll begin by saying I completed the game on the Normal level of difficulty and found all the chests and notes.
Story: 5/10. It's nothing special but it's not bad either. I figured out what the journey is and even guessed the ending about two hours in so there was no surprise for me. The collectible notes you find along the way hint at what's going on which allows you to piece it together or at least form a couple of theories.
Art: 7/10. It's pretty awesome. I was surprised with the quality of the level design. Great architecture that fits well into the story. The various races you encounter are extremely well defined and quite diverse. Sound effects were decent enough but the music is completely forgettable. There isn't a single track that stood out for me. It just felt like background noise most of the time. Character design is well done. I believe the cover art speaks for itself but it's not all just skimpy clothes. Armors and uniforms are high quality, the artists have done a great job on those. And lastly, the voice acting. At times it's atrociously cringe-worthy and at times it's pretty decent. The wild inconsistency is a minus from my point of view.
Gameplay: 4/10. I cannot stress how repetitive the gameplay is. It starts with a short cinematic that shows you the room and the enemies. You walk in, do what needs to be done, walk to the next room. Rinse and repeat. It's painful how often this thing happens. The combat itself is no different. You're given all these different abilities, weapons and upgrades but you don't really have to use them until the last boss at the end of the game (and even then, you only use two). You can just pick one and plow through the entire game with it. It's ironic how this freedom of choice backfires because it actually limits you more. You'll figure out a spell you like or one that you think works better than the rest based on your talents and use that for the entire game. The time rewind mechanic is cool at first but then it just becomes a chore you have to use to kill or avoid some enemies who can't die normally or you'll use it to complete a puzzle. That brings us to puzzles. Puzzles are pretty much about standing on pressure plates. That's all there is to it. The enemies are very diverse so that's a plus but you'll cringe every time you have to fight yet another Skyguard Lieutenant or whatever they are. It's not difficult, it just takes a stupid amount of time for something you have to do a hundred times throughout the game.
TL;DR - For 14,99€ (which is the price of this game at the time of this review) you can play something much better instead. But if you can get it cheaper and you don't really have anything else to play or you think you'll enjoy some aspect of it based on screenshots/videos, go for it.

If you're looking for a positive review, then you're in the wrong place, HOWEVER, if you're here for a tremendous chicken Stir Fry recipe, THEN LOOK NO FURTHER!
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan and heat through. Serve with noodles.

Ittle Dew is an action-adventure game that is trying very hard to be a 2D Zelda game, and actually, it succeeds for the most part. Your goal is to explore the castle and use the riches you find to enter other dungeons and find tools that help you progress farther in the castle.
This game has two key strengths. The first is that the items are very interesting, and they each combine in interesting ways. The second is that this game has amazing replay value. You get three items, and you can use all three to win, but you only need two. For a challenge, try beating the game with each combination of two weapons. This game is also built for speed-running, and it will take a lot of planning to figure out how to get the speed run achievements.
I'd say this game's main weakness is the bosses. It's a big difficulty spike, and the method for defeating them is never straightforward. The hints help a lot, but the battles can still be tough even when you know what to do. That leads to the other weakness: the controls. They're not terrible, and you'll get used to them as you play, but there were too many times when I died in combat because I wasn't moving the way I wanted to, and many enemies aren't knocked back when hit.
A few other things to mention: the puzzles can get pretty tough, the death penalty is that you have to restart the room at full health (which isn't even a penalty most of the time), and the game has little story, but the humor was a lot better than I had expected from the previews. Also, the first playthrough will last around 3-5 hours.
So, despite this game's rather stupid name, I enjoyed it, and I'd say it's worth picking up if you enjoy Zelda-style games (try out the 2D Zeldas first if you're not familiar with them). I'd wait to pick it up at half price, though.

Interesting and challenging survival RPG with adventurous elements and a new perspective. The round based fighting system makes it far more exciting and harder to play, but it is still within a very fun range. Not only do you have to think your fights through with one to three active characters and calculate your opponents strength and your own teams strength and defences well, but you also always have to keep economics of your camp and the security of it in mind. Every level up of your characters, no matter if main character or surviver that joins your crew during the game, is desperatly needed in order to strengthen your group and to higher chances of your survival. Resurrection is impossible, so every hit point matters. And nothing is for free: guns, ammo, food, bandages, health packs, everything has to be made by your crew and specialization is for one of the many jobs is strongly advised since higher production amounts means you need more skill. Ultimately, this game is a 8/10 for me and if the start phase, the first couple of days in the game, get a bit easier then everyone will have a great time fighting the zombies and building the camp in this first class survival RPG.

Before anything else is said: This is free on the app store/ google play store, so before you spend 5 bucks on the PC version try it out on there to see if you like it.
Nimble Quest is a bit of an odd game because I did not expect it to be as good as it is. At all. It's a glorified free to play game of classic snake in which you progress through about 10 or so levels, but if you die once you are sent all the way back to the beginning. Sounds kind of dull and repetitive from that angle, doesn't it? I thought so too until I tried it on my phone a few years back and was immediatly addicted. The core premise on it's own sounds tedious but the devs obviously put a lot of time and care into this game and it shows. Not only does every section on your snake-train of heroes have a different power (there's a mage, a pirate, an archer etc.) but you are also rewarded with powerups as you go along making the game intense and strategic as well as insanely chaotic in the later levels. You can level up your characters which give them passive buffs and upgrade the powerups you find with gems you collect along your journey, as well as fight against tons of different enemies, from healers, to fast moving rats, to bone throwing skeletons. However as cool as this stuff sounds I did mention before that it was originally a free to play mobile game which, in this day and age, usually results in a paid PC port that costs 5 bucks and still has the absolutely terrible overpriced microtransactions. Thankfully, NimbleBit know exactly what they're doing and manage to balance the game by adding a type of gem to the game that counts as 10 instead of getting only the gems that count as 1 and occasionaly 5. Just adding this one type of gem makes the progression so much faster and, as an added bonus, they completely stripped the microtransactions. I personally was able to unlock as much as I did in 3 hours of gameplay on my phone in just one hour or so on PC.
So basically, if you are a fan of rouguelite games or snake from the good old days, I highly recommend you pick this up or at least give it a shot on your phone (it's free, what do you have to lose). The pixel art is great, the soundtrack is awesome, and I was happy to throw $5 toward a mobile dev that actually knows how to port a game to PC.

First, let me preface this by saying that I love the MoO franchise, as such my opinion is somewhat biased.
That said: If you enjoyed the first game in the series, this is a must buy.
Some things have changed in the past 20+ years since the original MoO was released.
Some things haven't.
Gone are several (sub)races introduced in MoO3.
Back is an updated version of the pollution system from the first game.
The star lanes introduced in #3 are back, so keeping an eye on the warp lanes at the edge of your terrirtory is needed, and allows you and the AI to funnel enemies into choke-points.
There is actually a lot to love about this game as it does a decent job of trying to mix the simplicity of the first game with a little bit of the additions and micromanagement of 2 and 3.
Be warned though, the community surrounding the game seems to be pretty split on the direction this addition to the franchise went.
Some like myself are fine with it for bein what it is and thoroughly enjoy it.
A fairly vocal number of players are anywhere from being disappointed to being totally outraged that in their opinions it isn't as good or better than another game in the series.
Then again, as I said to start with, I love the whole series so my opinion is just as biased as their's is.
Give it a spin, make up your own mind.
It isn't going to be the absolute best or most tactically intricate 4X game you've ever played, but if you give it a chance you'll see there's still a lot of fun to be had with it.

This is a fun arcade game, an interesting take on the old style Snake game, but with the snake being made up of a Conga line of RPG style characters. If you have Gizmo (bomb throwing) and the two spellcasters, then you might be maneuvering your snake for broadsides.
If you have a Merida the archer and Boomy the sniper then running at the enemy might work better.
A bunch of melee combattants may make you try to sidle up next to the enemy formations (usually 3-unit snakes) to let the swordsmen get in their strikes.
There's been some discussion about the price of this game, considering that the mobile version is free, but the in-game purchase of the red gems (an unlock that can only be done with cash for $3.99, and seriously lessens the grind because of their value in the game)  is included at the start of this game.  I haven't accounted for the remaining buck but given that I'm more than happy to pay money for this version of the game.

A building simulation with a little bit of skill building sims.
Like the game Theme Hospital but with computers instead and
the ability to upgrade your working conditions such as garage or office building.
You raise the stats of your people and produce a mass of games in hope of
being the best and keeping your business afloat. Story along the lines of
Game Dev Tycoon. All features of Game Dev Tycoon are in there including
Making your own system, doing side work, and  creating mass games that blow
peoples minds. Upgraded graphics and more open ended gameplay make this a
pretty good game. I like that I have a choice in what my people are going to do
and where. You can even pick employees with special skills and traits that you want.
I personally enjoy giving my employees what they need and even messing with them
when they do bad by taking away things like the bathroom. I love the new explination
system as it gives you more in depth information on things and offers beginners a
better understanding of what you are doing. I can't really say much about how to get
a perfect game but there are online  tutorials and such out there that you can look up.
You can  make the game easy or hard and cater to your desires of running a business
bankrupt or making it a success. I miss some of the cutesy graphics but I guess that the
new ones are just as good. I got frustrated at the move object function until I learned
how to turn it off as I kept selecting items I did not want and in a time sensitive game it
is not good for you to waste any precious seconds when in threat of bankruptcy. Also,
when you delete a room you get nothing for it. So if you spent 200000 on it and remove it
because it was too small, you lose 200,000. There is no way to enlarge or shrink a room.  So, in
my opinion it is just as good as their previous game but polished a bit for those seeking
better emersion and more stuff. I find myself stuck on it for hours when I play it and often
lose track of time as I micro manage my little simmies into an early grave.

#1 I've played all sorts of video games since roughly 1979. Do I sound like a pretentious old fart stating this (and all the below)? Probably, I do not care. I along with other dorks who still sit in the basement and play games made gaming what it was, made the classics "classics" and also helped inspire contemporary games of any salt, for the most part. So accept this fact and my word or bugger off, poseur.
#2 Many of the "classics" from C64 to early PC (up to mid-90s before games started to suck bad), I have played and loved as an original consumer.
#3 I like originality and creative especially pertaining to aesthetic - legitimate aesthetic - and admire some games that achieve this as well as stand on their own ground as unique visions.
#4 This game is tough as nails (you can view the walkthrough online) - I dare you to complete it. Does this mean that it is a bad game? NO.
#5 Is this the most legitimate true punk meets cybergame ever made? Along with the Trese brother's Cyber Knights RPG (Android) - ABSOLUTELY.
#6 Am I biased or serving an agenda in some way? NO. Have I even emailed the developer to only be ignored and did this bother me to the point of thinking the guy may be a jerk, when he's on youtube and simply could have replied? YES.
#7 Do I like this game? YES. Do I play it often? NO. Is is fantastic to put on once in awhile, get acclimatized to its bizarre environment and controls and give it a go in a gaming session? YES. Did I grab a copy of the posted walkthrough in my permanent vgame video archive - YES.
Like a great trash cult film, the developer has made a real and true original cyberpunk cult gaming classic that is top of the heap, truly. Unsurprisingly when many cult film classics came out they were considered trash, unwatchable or crap. Time and appreciation tells another story. This is the ultimate cyberpunk challenge or even a torturous, bleak, dystopian coffee break game.
I understand most games prefer another aesthetic or Green Day as their prefered poseur form of manufactured punk. I do not, and I constantly look for games in the weird or cyberpunk genres, this is a must --- even if you try to play it and give up due to its lack of instructions or confusion. Eh, it's alright. I know they were trying to capture the experience that was GMod Tower but there are a few fundamental differences.
First, the server sizes are vastly smaller. Along with this (and this isn't really the developer's fault), there are far less players. The lobbies are huge but they are sparesly populated because of both the smaller number of allowed connections to a server and the vastly smaller player base. This feels sad to me; the place should be packed with people flying around and having a good time.
Second, there's less personality I feel. I guess this goes with any 'game' that tries to recreate itself - it's never truly as good as the original.
Hits:
Huge, massive lobby with some things to do.
Self-Sufficient economy system that truly has no microtranscations which is very nice.
Various games to keep you occupied (shortly)
Generous starting condo space.
Vastly improved graphics over the original concept (GMod)
Misses:
Far less personality and player base than the original.
Less games (Early access, I know)
Less shops (Early access, I know)
(Personal Gripes, don't really count this in my review)
I don't like that you need to 'load' throughout the game (IE you have to load to the condo lobby and then, your condo isn't immediately accessible from the lobby, you have to be loaded to it, other players as well. GMod pulled this off, not sure why they couldn't here.
After an hour in this game, I have no desire to play more. Don't get me wrong, there's lots to do but with so little players and little player interaction, there's no motivation to play. If the community grows large enough, and server max sizes are expanded, the game could be enjoyable to me.
Microtransactions with lower quality than their free counterparts in a AAA game? No thanks.

The first couple hours in this game are similar to the first few hours of Terraria - filled with wonder and exploration, and with a few good mechanics added such as many worlds to explore and a good spaceship mechanic to jump between them.  There are occasion places where the game needs polish - where it isn't really clear what the game is asking you to do but with a little help from the Wiki you'll manage.  Eventually you'll arrive at the first boss fight - which is *really* poorly polished.
If you played before bosses were implemented and already have end-game equipment, this fight will be too easy for you.
If you don't have end game equipment but happened to build your character with exactly the same spec that the boss fight was tested with (and there seems to have only been one), it will be about the right difficulty.
In any other case, this will be the end of the road for you.  You will be two-shotted without getting close to finishing the boss.  You will then be forced to replay the same 15 minutes of content to get to back to the boss to make another attempt.  You will be two-shotted again.  You will look up strategies online - all assume end-game equipment or that you spent the only tech card available before the boss on a particular power.  After you repeat this process 10 times Starbound replaces Terraria on the shelf and you're playing more Terraria.
Or you could just skip the Starbound part and play Terraria.

Trove is a game that I used to love. I remember first playing it over six months ago, chosing the Ice Sage. I started it out with my friend, learning the mechanics and the controls of the game. I loved running through huge dungeons with my friend and loving it so much. It was actually a challenge; it took time and precision as I was a lower level. There was actual strategy; I'd use my 'Big Freeze' ability, while my friend would lash the enemy with fire and I'd throw icicles onto him. It was fun!
I then found out the Ice Sage apparently 'wasn't great' in solo play, so I decided to start using the Lunar Lancer. It was fun. I levelled up more, hitting level 30 and trying to get the best gems possible.
And now I'm sitting here with over 15000 power rank and I've realised that I've just had enough, and here is why.
Trove has, as most people know, become incredibly Pay-To-Win, making it very difficult for new players to get a good start. Making progression without things such as patron can be very difficult and easily causes lower levelled players to lose interest. Trion favours higher levelled players (a dying few) and endgame players more than the new ones, rewarding them for being a higher level with things such as contests that are only possible to get something decent from with a higher level, or higher mastery.
The item system is quite boring as well. Most classes need just damage, energy regeneration/attack speed, and some critical damage and critical hit. There isn't a fun system where you could spend hours coming up with the best build for your class to make it personalised and more fun. The weapons are mediocre as well, not giving any cool abilites or buffs/debuffs that could be used to the players advantage. This makes the game more redundant and repetitive.
And don't get me started on the gem system. This is possibly one of the worst parts of Trove; it's based completely around Random Number Generation and luck, not skill or level or time. I've played for six months and only ever gotten one perfect Empowered gem. I've also farmed over 1000 stellar gem boxes and gotten one perfect power rank gem, but with health regeneration. This is because it is based around luck, not time or skill put into the game.
I realised this only recently, but I've had enough of a game where RNG is the only way to succeed; not time played, not level, not effort, just luck. And this completely ruins the game. Trove has so much potential; the devs could add incredible updates improving the gem system, making the more farmable, improving the weapon system to make it a little bit more interesting, and fixing all of the things that are broken about the game, such as ridiculous store prices, stupid updates preventing different things being done and removing important things from the game. Instead, they're spending weeks on end just to add a minigame that is broken and doesn't even work properly.
I've just had enough of it. Sure, I might play to build things in my club and to spend some time messing around, but I've completely given up on everything else.
If you're looking to play this game because you want to play an MMORPG, I'd recommend playing another game. Sure, it can be fun at first but in reality it's almost wasted. I can suggest some other really good RPG's, such as the Borderlands Franchise or Terraria. But if you really want something this grindy and this repetitive, go ahead an play it.
Good job Trion, looks like you're planning to ArcheAge everything.
Anyway, if you got to the end of this review, good job. Hope it changes your perception of it all. Have a good day everyone.

In some ways, XCOM 2 is a step backwards from XCOM, but in other ways it's better, and overall it's a good game. XCOM 2 is set in a future where XCOM lost to the aliens and they're acting to perform and coordinate guerilla actions against their new alien overlords.
The strategic layer is substantially different in that you have a single ship that you can move around on a map. There are various things to do, but you can only do one at a time. Examples include scanning for resources, building radio towers to contact resistance forces, and performing missions. It's more interactive and offers more choices than the XCOM strategic layer (which was all about satellite rushing and base building), but there are more interruptions, which can be annoying. The base-building portion is similar to before but a bit better since there's less randomness that would require a restart of the game on higher difficulty levels. Satellite rushing is replaced with contact rushing, which is much easier. You can't permanently lose any regions of the world anymore either.
The basic tactical gameplay is much the same with the exception of a new concealment mechanic, but about half of the missions are timed, which forces you to advance quickly and decisively across the map. I know a lot of people hate this, and the negative reviews turned me off of buying the game at full price for that reason, but having played the game myself I personally think it's more fun this way, even if it's more stressful and victory is no longer assured. There are still a bunch of untimed missions, and you can really feel the difference when you switch between them. Going to an untimed mission and reverting to my strategy of creeping across the map in overwatch, I can distinctly feel "hey this safer, but it's actually a bit boring!" There is one type of timed mission ("defend device") that can become literally impossible late in the game; they made a mistake with that mission design, but you can choose another mission type and most missions work well.
The concealment mechanic has your squad semi-invisible at the start of most timed missions - effectively the detection radius is much smaller than normal - allowing you to move quickly towards the objective. This feeds into the new ambush mechanic where you can simultaneously attack a group of aliens while concealed (by putting multiple people into overwatch before starting the attack) to gain a high chance of instantly wiping out the first group of aliens. Some classes have the ability to do more with concealment, for instance remaining concealed even after the rest of the squad is revealed and gaining combat bonuses while concealed, making them great scouts or assassins.
Overall I think the timed missions and concealment mechanic are an improvement and they fit into the story of the aliens being in control and us carrying out guerilla warfare. The key thing to remember if you want to succeed in the timed missions is that you need to first make good use of the squad's initial concealment to move quickly and then once your cover is blown to kill aliens on the same turn you encounter them. You don't have time to sit in full cover and shoot at each other. To this end the game gives you various grenades and tools that will really help if you use them.
There's also a new hacking mechanic, which allows soldiers to hack mechanical units and control towers to gain advantages at the risk of some combat penalty for failing. On timed missions where you need to hack something, remember that the specialist can hack things remotely.
The classes are a bit less balanced now, with some classes being much more useful than others, but you're not forced into one way of playing and many strategies are possible. People say the sniper has been nerfed since XCOM and that's true, but in some ways they're way overpowered now, able to take up to six shots followed by six overwatch shots in a single turn and having squad sight from the start. Psi operatives are a completely separate class now and anyone can learn it. You can choose what class rookies will become, which is a welcome change. Overall the classes are a little different from what they used to be, but if you embrace the changes they're fun to play.
The aliens are a bit different too. Some have armor or shields, which you need to remove before killing them. Chryssalids are perhaps more deadly. In fact all the aliens are deadly, but the game makes you so overpowered that it rarely matters. In many missions, the aliens don't get a single shot at me. This is a bad thing, but that's how it is.
The graphics and sound are substantially improved, but that's not so important for a game like this. The user interface has some annoyances (especially with a gamepad) that they should have fixed but it's definitely playable. The game has been mostly stable for me, although I waited until recently to purchase it. Reportedly it was in a bad state on initial release. It does have some memory leaks and long missions (>40 turns) will begin to bog down until you quit and reload the game. It also crashed a few times, but I didn't lose much progress because of that.
Unfortunately, the DLC is pretty bad. While the Enemy Within DLC for XCOM was a great expansion to the game, the War of the Chosen DLC for XCOM 2 is ridiculous. It basically adds superheroes and supervillains to the game. In one of the advertisements for it they showed a single soldier moving almost all the way across the map and killing a dozen aliens on his very first turn. That's not XCOM. So, I'm not going to buy it, despite some interesting new mechanics. Even the base XCOM 2 game departs from the XCOM formula of weak humans fighting back against powerful aliens, since you can already overpower the aliens before the mid-game. But you don't have to buy the DLC and XCOM 2 is still a good game for any XCOM fan. I recommend it.

I'm a big 4X fan, I've been playing since 'Ascendancy' and I play most of the new space games.  I'm a huge Civ player nearly 1000 hours with CiV.    The two games I've been playing lately are this new MOO and 'Endless Space 2'.
'Endless Space 2' is a stunningly original and polished game with tons of depth and I strongly recommend it to 4X fans.  But know what?   Sometimes I prefer playing MOO.   I love the music, the art-work, the GUI, the really high production values.
And most importantly the gameplay is solid.  Every thing you want (pretty much) is there and it all works the way you think it should.    It's a relaxing game to play.   It's nice sometime to play a game that doesn't have a crazy high learning curve.  It's fun to play and what's wrong with that?
I like the Galaxy map, the research tree, the exploration, combat, ship design - it's all solid.   My first game I was in a big war with the Meklars.   I offered a truce and return of two of their planets if they voted for me.   They accepted and I ended up with a diplomatic victory.    It's nice to not 'be on a roadmap' you have to follow.
Strongly recommend you try this new MOO.   If you're a hard-core grognard who wants insane complexity this might seem slight to you.   But for normal folks who just enjoy relaxing with a good game this is worth trying.   You know how some games you just like the 'feel' of?   The music, the artwork, the story?   This is one of them for me.

Excellent game! This game allows you to simulate what it's like to run a video game starting in 1980 all the way to present times and beyond. This game has a lot of depth, and is loads of fun. At times, it can seem frustrating: Just keep in mind that starting out isn't always easy. This game is a bit of a process of trial and error, until you find that perfect balance of space and resource management. There are currently 6 save game slots (Awesome! Wish there was more tho). As of right now in Alpha, they are often needing to wipe saved games to accomodate for the new features that they add and change. I thought I would be more upset with the save game wipes, but it actually wasn't bad- It wasn't until starting over that I realized all the things that I could improve upon from my previous game. This game is not hard to figure out, but has lots of depth and thus takes time to truly master. As a musician and aspiring game dev, I found this game to be enlightening in some ways. Obviously it is "big picture" stuff compared to the day to day work of a single game dev, but it is interesting to consider all of the moving parts. It is astounding to see how time, society, console popularity, choice of game engine, marketing techniques and various other aspects all affect success or failure of a game.
Also, I wanted to avoid comparison, but I knew I couldn't. I own this and Game Dev Tycoon, both are excellent games. I feel that, at the moment, Mad Games Tycoon is a bit more complex and advanced. Both are truly awesome games in my opinion though.

Mad Games Tycoon is a pretty awesome game developer management sim. It's one of the few early access games I've bought, but I'm irrationally obsessed with Game Dev sims like Game Dev Tycoon and Game Dev Story. Eggcode's take on game dev management adds much needed customization options and depth to the experience by allowing you to build rooms and assign employees to specific rooms to perform specific tasks.
Before I get to the bad, I would like to say up front that I freaking love this game. I've had tons of fun and I think it's absolutely worth the purchase if you enjoy tycoon games or want another take on the Game Dev Tycoon style of management sims. The team at Eggcode is a standout example of how to do early access right and deserves recognition for their constant bug fixes and content patches that range from adding new rooms and employees to improving the UI.
That's also part of the frustration of this game. I'm sure that this was a gameplay choice, but having to build special rooms for certain tasks gets annoying. For example, the games core development all happens in one room. Bug fixes have to take place in a seperate room for QA. If it takes the QA team longer to squash the bugs than it takes for the core team to finish development on the game, the development room is rendered useless until you choose to launch the game. Not to mention, the development team can't help fix bugs unless they're dragged away from development and pushed into the QA room. I get that the music studio, art offices and motion capture rooms should be standalone, but why can't the core staff improve level design?
That is my biggest issue. Everything else is a minor problem. I don't like how many clicks it takes to assign tasks to almost every room except for the development rooms. The UI isn't that great. The art isn't terribly nice to look at and I wish there were more (or custom) logos to choose from. But the art didn't effect my enjoyment.
Like I mentioned above, I love this game. It's fun and I've lost afternoons to this game. I can't wait to see how Eggcode continues to improve this already enjoyable game.

Greed and lies in an otherwise mediocre Fallout title.
Lets get the greed and lies out the way quickly first: Bethesdas creation club is nothing like they promised with its "mini DLC" and instead almost entirely sells pointless skins and mods you can get elsewhere despite them saying they would not allow duplicate mods to go up. It is a deceptive, cynical cash grab, nothing more than the re-packaging of the reviled paid mods on steam.
Settlement system is pointless and annoying in the vanilla game, RPG mechanics have been almost entirely gutted in favour of becoming more of a shooter, weapon variety seems fairly low outside of the rare uniques and the base dialogue system is vague and unsatisfying with diaologue being comparatively gimped due to everything being voice acted.
The Good:
I liked most of the companions in the game and they seem like the NPC's who had the most work put into them. (Besides Preston "A settlement needs your help" Garvey who I honestly started avoiding after a while) The Affinity system can be quite annoying for players who want to play around however and it can make gaining maximum affinity difficult without avoiding doing certain normal things that your companion sometimes dissaproves of like lockpicking or hacking. That being said, they are all unique and have thier own backstories, voice actors, interactions and quests which are quite entertaining if you can look past all the games issues.
Sound design is pretty good. Not much to complain about here, ambient noise is good, weapons sound great and the songs are good too though the radio host will make you want to shoot him in his stupid face.
While the graphics aren't that much better than its predecessors, they do the job and are perfectly adaquate.
The Bad:
You better like your characters voice because you are going to hear that a lot, personally I hated my characters generic voice. With far less dialogue choice and your character saying whatever they feel like, sometimes nothing close to the couple lines they gave you in the choice, you may find yourself getting frustrated often with NPC interactions.
Maintaining settlements requires constant babystitting in order to stop the getting destroyed and when you have a high number of developed settlements it can start to feel like your never not going to save one settlement or another for almost no benefit.
The other problem with the settlement system is that NPC towns are few and far between and contain far less interesting characters and quests in order to leave room for player built settlements and space to expand and develop existing settlements.
The story is pretty tedious, boring, fairly predicatble past the first half and has more plot holes the more you think about it. More of a personal thing but I didn't find any of the main factions at all appealing; with my choices being genocidal racists, genocidal scientists, killer robot loving hippies and a man who up untill this point has spent his time constantly bothering me about settlements...
Variety is another problem that the game struggles with, both in terms of its abysmally low weapon variety, interesting perks and its enemy variety too. I assume the developers thought simple adding "Legendary" as a prefix was good enough without having to create new models, animations and behaviours. Overall though, both Fallout 3 and New Vegas shame this game in terms of the variety of things you'll encounter on your journey.
Conclusion: If this game looks interesting to you then buy Fallout: New Vegas. A game that is better in almost every way, is a hell of a lot cheaper, runs on newer systems without any extra effort and doesn't try to sell you micro-transaction mods.

Don't forget: this game is free! If you've got a spare hour, there's really no reason not to check it out.
It took me about an hour to finish this game. You can finish it faster if you want to, but I would recommend you take your time like I did, click on everything at least five times and read/listen to everything the narrator has to say. A lot of the good in this game is in the narration - the random comments are interesting and/or funny, and the voice acting is pretty decent as well. If you skip all that, you probably won't enjoy the game as much (judging from the other reviews).
I don't much care for jumpscares and luckily there are none in this game, even though that's what you would expect (what with the mood and the setting of the game). But I did experience a sense of dread, throughout the story as well as afterwards. There's this image that just keeps spooking around in my head (semi-spoiler: the last two versions of the photo). It's not even that scary, but I'm a scaredy-cat and it haunts me.
By the way, don't forget to click on the photo throughout the story! I forgot to click on it near the end, which led to the ending becoming a little bit more ambiguous (and vague) than the makers probably intended. At least I had an interesting discussion with my friend about the ending (and about the porn mag inside the bedside table, which my friend had completely missed out on - another reason to click on
).
There are some things which could've been done better; but again, this is a free game, so don't expect anything mind-blowing.
----
I enjoy it for what it is, but it isn't much. Having to go back and forth to click on the same objects over and over gets old fast. The story is interesting, but the ending is confusing - although that could be considered a strength as well: the first time I played this, I spent an hour debating the ending with a friend - at the same time, I assume the ending's openness is unintentional and that they did have a specific ending in mind.

So, to fully complete one playthrough of this, it took me about 13 hours. Most of the episodes are about 2-3 hours long, with the last episode only about an hour, maybe an hour and a half. For one playthrough that might not seem too long, but I definitely plan to do multiple more playthroughs and experience the game many more times before I'm through with it. The characters are easy to grow attached to (or grow to hate) and you definitely will want to see if you an have different outcomes and maybe make things better. Oh well, maybe I'll find out the next time I play.
For this time, I did do a let's play of it. Spoilers, I'm pretty sure that I got the darkest possible timeline. Maybe. I'll find out when I play again, eh?

You've got to like these kind of games. And, tbh, it's one of the same kind like many before. There must be an open source template for these kind of games, because the interfaces all look the same.
But still, I like it. The story ends at the moment at day 20, which is ok as it's just been released on EA.
The story is entertaining, no big text walls (which someone else stated in a german review). If 3 or 4 sentences to read are too much for you - ok, don't buy it.
The little tactical combat system is a nice idea, quite easy to handle. To get to the boss fight can be quite challenging if you don't have many med packs in your inventory.
The skill system should be finetuned a little bit in the future, but looks good. A nice touch would be to see how many skillpoints a character will get until max level for easier planning.
To swap people between camp and scavenging group could be improved a little bit with an additional button in the party overview.
There is no camp building. You just send people to guard the camp, later in game it happens from time to time that the camp get's attacked and you have your standard fighting screen.
So, if you don't expect miracles, it's a nice little game where you have to manage your survivors & equipment, go out on missions and kill quite some different kind of zombies ranging from cheerleader zombies to dog zombies, quite hard zombie bosses & npc survivors with a wide range of different skills. A nurse zombie which heals other zombies? Well, maybe not THAT common. But hey, I've never been in a zombie apocalypse, so who am I to say it's not possible ;)

Its hard to play right now.  And I wish it wasn't.  I really like a lot of things about this game but its just so hard to play.
I love how its you and beautiful women (and one fat dude and the sheriff) and all of the women are in love with you as you're pretty much the last man on earth (minus the fat dude and sheriff). Loot drops are plentiful, parts for all the weapons/items/medicine are readily available.  For the drop rate the consumption rate of medicine/engineering parts/ammo is incredibly reasonable.  Its got challenges, rewards for going 20 rounds endurance. You've got cool jobs like making weapons and armor and medicine and hunting.  Its just got problems.
First off challenges dont level up as you do in the game. For example you're level one, you find a chest, you have level 1 cunning you have a 40% + (1cunning x 5%) =45% chance of opening that chest. This makes random loot drops frustrating early game and more likely to sabotage you than help you.  So you think "If they never level up I'll get my cunning level 10 and forever I'll have a 90% success rate".  Well...  Its 1 point to get level 1, 2 more points for level 2, so its 55 points to get the stat to level 10.  This wouldn't be the biggest deal but they threw on a level cap so you get 60 points for the entire game.  Also 5% boost for going level 9-10 at the cost of 10 skill points is kind of painful.  But even all that isn't that bad....  You just need planning right?  one person dedicated to each skill type of thing.  I just feel like starting with level 1 chests which 1 cunning gives you 80% chance vs 60% with 0 or 100% with 2 or more and later level 5 chests which you dont have a 40% chance to open with 0 cunning.  Like more of a Wasteland system.
Next problem is scavengers.  They attack you every single night and take half your resources.  You post a guard with 3 cunning (yes it opens chests and helps you guard the base, most non combat skills have one adventuring perk and one base perk so you have to decide if you want to guard your base or open chests).  Now 3 cunning doesn't help.  It just doesn't.  They still hit you, you've posted one guard which is 1/4 to 1/3 of your group but scavengers dont start to not completely screw you unless you take a person, give them 5 cunning, which is 1/4 of your skill points for life and dedicate them forever to guarding the base.  Really, this person should have 10 cunning because they really cant do anything else or you'll lose half of your food/tools/materials(money) every turn. And once you run out of food you cant guard your base so you'll lose whatever you have left.  And loot doesn't seem like the biggest problem to get.  They'll give you lots for staying out for 20 turns.  Its just tax is the scavengers will take 50% in the morning.  Every day.  Part of the problem is without a graduated system you're not running into level one scavengers when you're level one and level 10 when you're level 10.  You're running  into the only level of scavengers that exists
The combat system is okay but its just okay.  Another guy points out its not really a "final fantasy" style combat system.  In final fantasy you start with 100% of your MP and your abilities consume your MP until you run out and are forced to use normal attacks.  This combat system has you start with 1 out of 4 AP and you get 1 AP every time you do a normal attack, or two if you use the ability and bide your time.  But with enemy hp and the limited boosts the abilities give (2 ap for 2 hits at 75% damage if you spend 28/60 skill points on melee).  And while ammo isn't incredibly uncommon it isn't common enough to use constantly, it really needs to be saved for fighting other humans so melee is your primary.
For resourves, its not really a significant investment to make medicine and weapons via parts but you have your 1 of 4 people guarding the base (the sheriff doesn't do anything) so making medicine or hunting costs an extreme amount of manpower.  And you can tell your other people to hunt and make armor (tell your main character what to do last, telling him to do anything in the base ends the day and everyone you didn't assign gets a vacation) but hunting consumes tools, which aren't incredibly common considering how much food you get relative to their cost.  You get them from quests but frequently you cant complete quests because scavengers are stealing all your stuff, and you're running out of medicine and while you have lots of parts its not really safe to send your main guy alone questing (as he has to be on any ranging team) and making your other people make medicine, hunt, Guard duty  and craft something.
So its kind of frustrating to play right now.

So hopefully I'm going to be able to write an in depth review on this game, probably not but here we go.
Recently the whole zombie survival genre has become very cliche with the same concept of game and very little changes in mechanics across like 20 different games. This has become very annoying as there is basically no new games coming out, the may all just be revamps of the older ones.
That being said, it is very rare that a new kind of Zombie Survival game is released that isn't a pile of crap; this game most certainly is not a pile of crap.
Dead Age is in early access state which most steam users will know is basically where most game developers just release something that isn't even near playable and just hope to get funds before they continue. Dead Age is already a well developed game with with a strong base for its Early Access to stand on.
However, this game isn't all sparkles and fairy dust; there are some faults with it which are understandable given it's current state. I haven't personally experienced anything game breaking as of yet I'm not aware if anyone else has but none the less.
So, let's get into the concept of the game;
At the start you're given a selection of characters to select from these being,
A Student,
A Soldier,
An Engineer,
A Doctor
and some other different roles, I can't remember them all but at the start all of these are locked except from the student. At first I thought this was because they had not been made/released but then I later realised that you actually unlock medals through completing achievements which you use to upgrade/unluck your character once you die. Yeah, once you're dead your character is gone for good. So don't get too attached.
Once you have made your character you're thrown into the combat almost instantly, they give you a nice cushty story line that you can't find your sister and you strole around trying to find her, upon your travels you find a Sherrif who helps you defeat your first encounter with the zombles and it teaches you how to whoop♥♥♥♥♥basically.
I could write about the story line but thats boring and I don't actually think anyone gives a crap about how I didn't give the little boy medical treatment and instead let him die. Hue Hue.
Anyway, the concept is very simple but boasts a lot of features which spice it up a little.
Long story short, you're in charge of a camp which hosts survivors; you have to maintain the camp whilst also exploring, scavenging and finding weaker peasants to recruits. That's no joke, some of the survivors are so weak they get one tapped by a Bitten Pedestrian. Lame.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Now, the features; everyones favourite bit.
The combat is turn based. 0_0 WHY WOULD YOU DO THAT? I'm sorry but I hate turn based combat and if it wasn't for my actual enjoyment of the game I would refund it to♥♥♥♥♥♥
Exploration, this is a very well thought out feature by the devs; I applaud you. So far there are 4 areas you can explore Woods (Day) Woods (Night) <-- (Don't know if this is right, I'm just assuming it is, I don't actually read things that often) Highway (Day) Highway (Night). Now this is where it gets fun, whilst you're out exploring these zones you go through areas, so far I think there are only twenty areas per zone and I think each of them has a big fat boss at the end of them. (ez to kill btw). After you have "beaten" up the zombles in each area there is a chance you will be met with random occurances. These can be anything from, "you found a hole in a cave, stick your arm in there" to "Oh look, a wild Gazelle; catch that♥♥♥♥♥♥and eat it". I probably shouldn't of quoted them because it doesn't actually say that but you get the jist. Each of the results from these have different outcomes depending on your attributes/skills/orbrainpower. SO for instance, if you have low survival you can kiss goodbye to those Gazelles because you ain't getting it. BUT DONT WORRY, if you suck at something but a party member is great at it, you can make them do it instead. There is more but this section is starting to look like my SAT's English paper. PARAGRAPHS!!!!!!!
Story Line/Quests, so far I have thoroughly enjoyed the story and quests, all from helping Liz get that AK47 (which by the way, there should be an option to execute her and take it for yourself) all the way to getting hit on by Lydia when her husband is right there. Sleeping Dogs is definitely a great game; set in Hong Kong, you play as an undercover cop trying to take down the Triad from the inside. The story is amazing, the graphics and sounds are amazing, but the need for the game to be open world is lost on me.
Though the game tries to be open world, it fails by limiting what you can do severely by making everything a "quest." There really is no reason for the game to be open world except to drive around fast in, as there is little reward or reason to go off the path of the main game. With that in mind, the game feels rather linear as there are only ever two quests open at any time. Small "favours" are available but do little to reward the player and feel tacked on. Essentially you have a large playground in which to do nothing in!
I’ve heard people compare Sleeping Dogs to Grand Theft Auto; sure, you could say that, but the only similarity is that they’re both in cities and you can drive cars. It ends there. In Grand Theft Auto, oddly enough, you can carry around a smorgasbord of weaponry. Sleeping Dogs, you can carry a single pistol and a melee weapon. Those weapons don’t even last either, once the situation you’re in is completed, away goes that pistol you picked up. Additionally, the melee weapons have limited uses, so hack and slash away but two enemies later, it’s done. Sleeping Dog’s combat focuses primarily on Kung Fu and Gun Fu. Most of your combat situations take place with your fists against countless enemies. Sometimes if you have a gun, you can vault over objects to enter a Gun Fu mode where time slows down and you shoot people in the head. I found the need for this limited, as most times I wanted to stay behind cover as there is no armor in the game.
The vehicles are all unique with motorcycles and cars to drive around with. They look very pretty and perform well, during the races you’ll see this first hand. I only managed to roll my car once during a police chase after I drove straight into a tree. You don’t get any God-like powers to turn the car back over. You get out and find another car.
I mentioned earlier that the storyline is amazing, and it really is. You play as an undercover cop and your role is to infiltrate the Triad and take them down from within. As you play, quests for the Police and Triad open up, but there is only ever one quest for each available at any time. So you can only kill your time by driving around aimlessly, doing one of the games “favours” (Which is just a tacked on side-quest that lasts all of eight seconds), competing in a road race or working your way up on the leaderboards of the Social Hub that they have. What I mean by that is… how long can you drive a car faster than 60 kilometers an hour without damaging yourself? People have done that for 30+ minutes, whereas I reached 3 out of pure luck.
While you’re gallivanting around the city of Hong Kong, you are picking up collectables of Lockboxes, Health Shrines and Jade Statues. The Lockboxes are just neat money bonuses, sometimes with clothing to expand your customization options. Health Shrines increase your health by 10% every five you find. Jade Statues are used for one of the game side quests to unlock new Kung Fu moves.
Unfortunately, I found Sleeping Dogs to be exceptionally short. I managed to complete all of the side-quests, road races and main quests in 20 hours. The only thing I have left to do is find all the collectables (Lockboxes & Health Shrines; I found all the Jade Statues to unlock all the Kung Fu moves.) Does this mean it’s not worth picking up? Absolutely not. But it does mean that you shouldn’t be stupid and waste your money on their idea of “DLC.”
These reservations aside, the storyline alone is amazing, combined with great voice acting and graphics, making Sleeping Dogs a must play! Pick it up, or rent it for the consoles at the very least.

XCOM2 is my all-time most disappointing gaming experience.
I am a decent chess player. I love chess. Playing XCOM2 is like playing chess with an opponent much better than you, but: A) he makes you play without your queen, and B) he uses yours. That is a reasonable assessment of how totally unbalanced this game is.
For a strategy game, there is nothing here other than trial and error. If you make a successful move, rejoice and save, save, save. Then it's your opponents turn. You get mind-controlled. You get stabbed. Your weapons become non-functional. A previously dead opponent is re-animated.  If you manage to survive this, rejoice. Awe, hell, now you have but two guys and the enemy called in reinforcements!? OMG, wow, you just manged to cut down the reinforcements! They just called in reinforcements AGAIN. And this is before you realize there are half a dozen undiscovered enemies who haven't joined the fight yet.
I played on normal mode. I breezed through the first few levels, and really enjoyed the game. I looked forward to playing all day. It was one of *those* games. I succeeded on some really hard levels and felt rewarded. Then I just got punched in the face. After reloading a level over 15 times, it occurred to me: this is not fun. This is the opposite of fun.
I wish I was part of some exclusive club of "hard-core" gamers capable of enjoying this game. My hunch is there are really only about 3 of them. They flood the message boards, eager to boast of their bona fides. Everyone else just effing HATES this game.
Before you call me "casual," I will mention that the notoriously difficult Dark Souls is my all-time favorite game, video or otherwise. The beauty of Dark Souls is that you can learn your enemy. Every time you face him you're that much more well-prepared. Also, in Dark Souls you get to react in real-time. The helplessness of idly watching as your crew gets wrecked is just.... the antithesis of fun.
Anyone who knows anything about writing knows that, in order to maintain the audience's interest, you have to give your protagonist(s) a chance in hell. This is a pretty fundamental thing for XCOM2 to get wrong.

I really hate to do this, but I'm changing my positive review of this game to a negative one.
I first reviewed this game about a year before it left Early Access, and at the time the game was fun. But since then the game's mechanics have changed, to the point where every game I create usually loses money, or at best breaks even. Seriously, I make more money doing contract work and licensing engines than I do making games.
The main problem here is that there are very few in-game cues to indicate to the player the correct settings for creating a successful game, and even these are vague. Add the fact that even if you use the perfect settings, your game might still fail depending on other variables such as the skills of your employees.
For example, in my last (and probably final) game, after creating ten failed games in a row, I checked out one of the community guides to find the perfect settings for  an RPG (leaving any game to check out a guide or wiki, just to progress normally in the game, is something that no player should ever have to do). Looking forward to a quick influx of cash to save my company from bankruptcy, I was dismayed to find that my game received a review score of 42% (only marginally better than before) and ended up losing over $50k.
Was it because of the skills of my employees? Was the failure of the game caused by something else? I have no way of knowing, and no way of finding out.
I'm sure that there are people who have the mechanics of this game all figured out, and I'm sure that many of them are willing to pass along their knowledge in guides and in the forums. But to me, not being able to figure these things out by myself (within the game) simply is not fun. And if I'm having these kinds of problems, with a couple years' worth of experience with the game, I can only imagine how frustrating it would be to a brand-new player.
This major, game-breaking problem (to me), is not likely to ever be fixed, as the game is finished and the dev has moved on.
TIP: If you do decide to buy this game, and if you happen to be a Game Dev Tycoon player, don't expect your knowledge of that game to have any bearing whatsoever on this one. The mechanics of these two games are completely different.
