You want a galactic civilisation game but lack the patience for the more complicated, sprawling titles.
I enjoyed my stint in Master of Orion, but can equally appreciate where a lot of the negative feedback is coming from. I think what works against MoO is ultimately that it looks like a AAA title but plays more like a strategic board game or indie title. Its gameplay just cannot live up to the promise that its graphics provides.
But truth be told, that meant it was right up my alley - filling a nice niche of a streamlined space-based empire game without demanding an obscene amount of upfront learning. The UI is exceptional and geared brilliantly to easily keep tabs on everything; making planet and ship management a cinch. This ultimately allows you to focus on the more fun stuff: Deciding what to build, where to allocate resources and when to invite the cat people round for a cuppa. It delightfully plays into the classic turn-based trap of "oh just one more turn and I'll finish up..."
The tech tree is well-designed and I like the pollution mechanic where it limits the ability to turn everything into a quasi super-planet/industrial war machine. You have to strike a balance in which roles your planets fill; a nice little touch indeed.
I also really like that there are multiple ways of winning... not just nuking everything into debris (fun as it is). The ability to acquire scientific or diplomatic victories really opens the door to broader styles of play, particularly making alliances quite valuable, as opposed to the temporary stop-gap before you get bored and have to kill each other anyway as in most other titles.
What lets the game down, however, are a number of weaker, fundamental game elements. The AI is quite basic and stops becoming a threat unless you let it cheat on the higher difficulties. Whilst the diplomacy is fun at first, the AI gets in a huff a lot and, truth be told, starts to come across as petty. Whilst I appreciate the idea is to create a somewhat volatile environment where superpowers may ultimately turn on each other... in practice it creates a very inorganic setup where factions oscillate between indifference and warmth - not really taking a stance either way. They seem to have a default baseline to each faction and, for the most part, gravitate towards this regardless of what you do - aside from the blowing the hell out of them... which obviously makes them a bit grumpy.
The combat certainly looks the part but, considering the speed and numbers of ships eventually involved, there's not a lot to actually
. Most fights are over within a minute, so it can feel a little shallow. The strategy comes more from the ships you bring to the fight and their respective loadouts, so plays more like Risk than an RTS.
Finally, there is no penalty for having multiple planets. Whilst this seems great at first... what I find is that this ultimately turns it into a numbers game: Whoever has more planets has more income, ships and construction to play with... so they can beat everyone else by pure attrition. Whoever gets the upper hand tends to keep it, particularly where the AI aren't sharp enough to gang-up on the stronger players. Each one generally sits back and gets picked off one-by-one by the dominant player, so grudgingly makes for a very linear single player mode.
And the advisors... ugh. If it's not the fan-service massive-chested lady in skin-tight uniform, it's the "oh great leader, that's a wonderful idea!", "oh honourable master, that is so clever of you!" and "I must say, Mr President, your willy is looking exceptionally large this morning"... The HR department who hired these people need some stern words or an ion cannon up their butt.
So yes, it's a bit rough around the edges and feels unfinished. But for the content that's there, it's proven to be enjoyable and engaging. It's not an outstanding or ground-breaking title, but it's good fun.

If your looking for a good police simulator then look no further. This game(as it is still in development) provides almost all the policing experiences a cop could experience in his every day life. However there can definitely be some improvements to the game as far as exanding the map to be more of an open world sandbox and have additional CPU police to patrol around as well and maybe even multiplayer. This game has a huge amount of potential to be the best police simulator out there but it still needs quite a bit of work to get there with minor bugs and a little bit more of a relistic feel. What I mean by realistic feel is when you play the game everyone and everything gameplay mechanics wise seems to be robotic almost, the civilians almost seem like they have no life to them at all, they look like robots walking around and the driving is a little unrealistic in the sense that if a car runs into you, it doesn't harm you but it harms itself by somehow flipping over and going out of control. Like I said though, this game is a great simulator because of the wide variety of missions and calls that a normal cop would answer to in real life. The basic concept of the game is fantastic, its working out great as far as how policing is done so far. If your like early development games and policing then I highly recommend this game, however if you like a full complete game and not something in development then I suggest waiting a little longer before purchasing the game however the price of the game may increase like almost all games that are in development always do.
My suggestions to you devs as far as making the game that much better is
1-Multiplayer. Co-op multiplayer and maybe even VS Drug Lords VS Cops/Swat
2-Implement more AI- patrolling around and busting bad guys and all is really fun but the lack of other police patrolling around and no backup seems a little unrealistic and a little dull, having a team to work with or maybe even command when your a high ranking officer can definitely spice up the gameplay and make it a lot more interesting.
3- Implement S.W.A.T- Everyone loves swat...No question about it. Swat is a huge help during tight situations and if there was even an option to play as swat and just go on raid missions, breaching and clearing, taking out High Value Targets and etc. that would probably spike this games badassery up by a ton. Everyone loves that feeling of being a badass S.W.A.T with a team about to breach and clear or just go into an area to raise absolute hell. Implementing S.W.A.T AI backup in the game and even a S.W.A.T mode would just be awesome
4- Connect the maps together to make one big sandbox- Instead of seperate maps, connect them! I think most people would prefer a sandbox rather than different sections, especially if the different sections of the maps can be really small in comparison to the main city.
5- Implement more traffic violations- I've noticed that every time I pull over a car for blowing a red light or even crashing into another car yields no bad outcome whenever they are pulled over and traffic stopped. I always mistake pulling people over for blowing through red lights and think I'm going to ticket them but the game doesn't pay attention to them blowing red lights, implementing that would be pretty cool too.
For all of those people reading this review all the way through good job! lol and thanks for reading. As for the Devs, nobodys expecting all these suggestions to happen in like one week, we can wait however don't blow the suggestions off otherwise the game will get dull very quickly because there is a lot more that you guys can add to increase the feel of being on the Police Force. Don't quit! This game has potential over all other police simulators to be the best because so far you can do a lot more in this game as far as policing than any other game made so far. You guys are doing a splendid job and I wish you the best of luck developing this game, I can't wait for the final product because if you guys can make it this good this early in development, you guys can definitely make it amazing with time. Don't quit! A lot of people will support this game to the end!

Starbound is a 2D-indie-sandbox-adventure game developed by Chuckle fish. Starbound opened up to Beta Testing on December 04, 2013.
Regardless of whichever race you play as, you're the sole survivor; depending on the race the background story is a little different, basically a tragedy happened to your people and now you're forced to explore the vast expansive universe.
The story is heavily gear based, first you need to collect a full set of this gear, before you can get the next quest. While this aspect does help give you direction, it is highly limiting and doesn't let you rely on skill, but forces you to farm materials to craft the necessary armor and weapons.
Starbound has a seemingly infinite set of galaxies, worlds, and moons for you to explore, gather materials, fight creatures, and just generally explore. There are 5 different star-types, each start type has a different mixture of elements and planet-types. Unfortunately once you explore several different stars with the same effect (for example, say you visit 5 different Gentle Star systems) you'll start to notice a theme among the planet land types. While this itself isn't necessarily a negative quality; it does take away some of the excitement of visiting other worlds near less dangerous stars.
There is a strong sense of progression within the game, you find/craft many different types of weapons and armor, upgrade your mater collector (Think “pickaxe”), upgrade your ship, craft interesting items with the materials you've gathered, and just generally hoard up tons of materials. (...and believe me, you will fill your inventory and dump it into a vault many times)
At this time there are no Starbound Steam Achievements, which is fine... but that means there's nothing else to add to this section.
Starbound is priced at $14.99 I quickly racked up 61 hours of game play within the first two weeks... the game was obviously worth it to me. However I wouldn't feel right without pointing out that

TL;DR: I feel like I wasted my 9 cents and time on this game. This screenshot sums up my feelings about this game:
Please proceed to summary.
The store page already shows broken English.
For example:
Some players offered to help out with translations and corrections but the devs never gave any reaction on that matter.
Following minimum requirement is false:
Steam items and trading cards aren't well-thought-out.
3 out of 6 cards show props you encounter in-game. You don't interact with those in any way and they don't have a meaning at all.
I am talking about the emergency exit sign, the padlock and the rope. The latter one may at least be good for atmospheric reasons.
The emoticon "weapon-axe" is weird because you will never get your hands on something else than the flashlight.
Take a look at the background "The Warehouse". The centered image will be hidden behind your profile and at the sides there will be nothing as that area is black only.
After starting up the game the camera is set in a moving subway wagon showing a girl facepalming, (supposed to cry I guess). Some words will fade:
(as seen above). The game may make you sad, frustrated, mad and amused about its poor quality. You probably will react as the girl did.
The game menu itself is quite small. The background still shows the wagon but it seems that it crashed and the girl disappeared. Looking close enough onto the moving door you may discover that its window frame isn't moving and floating.
You have three options. A major bug occurs when entering "Settings" > "Audio" as your mouse cursor will disappear. You will have a hard time to make any setting and may end up killing/restarting the game.
Another (working) section lets you chose between Russian and (poor) English. In game controls aren't mapable and not shown.
The description on the store page is pretty much the whole story. Any rising question will be left unanswered. I doubt that the planned sequels will come.
Basically the game won't tell you anything about the controls.
You can move with [W], [A], [S], [D] and use your mouse to look around, just as in most popular first person shooters.
First I thought that the blue bar that fills the bottom line of your screen would be a glitch. After I found out that you are able to run by pressing [Shift] I recognised that the bar shows your endurance.
Almost from the beginning you find a flashlight and a couple batteries. You can switch the light on and off by pressing [F]. Picking up batteries will pop up a message in the top left of your screen. It's easily missed as it is tiny and out of your center of view. You also have to figure out that the Russian word followed by a number is telling you how many batteries you have in reserve. The missing translation is still unfixed.
Finally you need to recognize that economising batteries is crucial and the most important game mechanic. Unfortunately the game won't tell you that either.
The flashlight itself is interesting. The power of your lightsource will decrease as the battery depletes. The game will prompt you to press [B] shortly before your battery runs flat. This is the only time that the game tells you about any control - besides quick time events.
There will be only one scene where you encounter quick time events. It is dull as you need to hit the same button two or three times and it won't even change on another playthrough.
Objects and passages you can interact with are glowing in red. Somehow that unnatural glowing in completely dark areas was the creepiest thing I encountered.
You will be able to pick up a few sheets of paper (also glowing) at several spots.
Warning: You can't read the notes ever again in that playthrough so make sure to read them properly!
I hate it to say it this way but the quality of the game may be the most horrible thing you will experience even though that isn't the kind of horror you seeked for.
On the other hand the game is at least able to create an uncanny atmosphere. The slow movement, your limited light source, being alone in in the dark underground.
The developer's name is "AGC", short for "Assets Games Company". The name basically says it all. You will play a Unity game where assets have been scrambled together. This is certainly the cause that some textures seem to be stretched to a point that they became blurry and ugly.
The props sometimes show great inconsistencies. For example you have a couple of pipes running along a wall. Clean ones are directly next to rusty ones.
It takes quite some time to load the game. At least you will encounter the most beautiful thing the game has to offer: The loading screen.
The sounds are acceptable and okay.
Unfortunately none. Run once through the game and you've seen everything. No real story, no alternations, no achievements, no collectibles, no progress percentage. It took me 30-40 minutes to complete. (I am a pretty slow paced player if the game allows to). Later I spent another 2 hours to fetch the steam trading cards by idling the game.
Sadly this review was more fun and more time-consuming than the game.
I felt despair because the game is bad, ugly, bugged and provides broken English.
The upsides are the interesting flashlight mechanics and the uncanny atmosphere.
It would have been nice if AGC at least replied to the biggest questions and requests. For example making a news announcement, giving some answers and telling what they are up to do. It doesn't seem that they work on that game anymore. I feel sorry that their project ended in a failure.
I can't recommend this game, don't buy it, except you are a collector or want to make profit from the cards when the game is on sale.

Sleeping Dogs is definitely a great game; set in Hong Kong, you play as an undercover cop trying to take down the Triad from the inside. The story is amazing, the graphics and sounds are amazing, but the need for the game to be open world is lost on me.
Though the game tries to be open world, it fails by limiting what you can do severely by making everything a "quest." There really is no reason for the game to be open world except to drive around fast in, as there is little reward or reason to go off the path of the main game. With that in mind, the game feels rather linear as there are only ever two quests open at any time. Small "favours" are available but do little to reward the player and feel tacked on. Essentially you have a large playground in which to do nothing in!
I’ve heard people compare Sleeping Dogs to Grand Theft Auto; sure, you could say that, but the only similarity is that they’re both in cities and you can drive cars. It ends there. In Grand Theft Auto, oddly enough, you can carry around a smorgasbord of weaponry. Sleeping Dogs, you can carry a single pistol and a melee weapon. Those weapons don’t even last either, once the situation you’re in is completed, away goes that pistol you picked up. Additionally, the melee weapons have limited uses, so hack and slash away but two enemies later, it’s done. Sleeping Dog’s combat focuses primarily on Kung Fu and Gun Fu. Most of your combat situations take place with your fists against countless enemies. Sometimes if you have a gun, you can vault over objects to enter a Gun Fu mode where time slows down and you shoot people in the head. I found the need for this limited, as most times I wanted to stay behind cover as there is no armor in the game.
The vehicles are all unique with motorcycles and cars to drive around with. They look very pretty and perform well, during the races you’ll see this first hand. I only managed to roll my car once during a police chase after I drove straight into a tree. You don’t get any God-like powers to turn the car back over. You get out and find another car.
I mentioned earlier that the storyline is amazing, and it really is. You play as an undercover cop and your role is to infiltrate the Triad and take them down from within. As you play, quests for the Police and Triad open up, but there is only ever one quest for each available at any time. So you can only kill your time by driving around aimlessly, doing one of the games “favours” (Which is just a tacked on side-quest that lasts all of eight seconds), competing in a road race or working your way up on the leaderboards of the Social Hub that they have. What I mean by that is… how long can you drive a car faster than 60 kilometers an hour without damaging yourself? People have done that for 30+ minutes, whereas I reached 3 out of pure luck.
While you’re gallivanting around the city of Hong Kong, you are picking up collectables of Lockboxes, Health Shrines and Jade Statues. The Lockboxes are just neat money bonuses, sometimes with clothing to expand your customization options. Health Shrines increase your health by 10% every five you find. Jade Statues are used for one of the game side quests to unlock new Kung Fu moves.
Unfortunately, I found Sleeping Dogs to be exceptionally short. I managed to complete all of the side-quests, road races and main quests in 20 hours. The only thing I have left to do is find all the collectables (Lockboxes & Health Shrines; I found all the Jade Statues to unlock all the Kung Fu moves.) Does this mean it’s not worth picking up? Absolutely not. But it does mean that you shouldn’t be stupid and waste your money on their idea of “DLC.”
These reservations aside, the storyline alone is amazing, combined with great voice acting and graphics, making Sleeping Dogs a must play! Pick it up, or rent it for the consoles at the very least.

I never feel great about giving a thumbs down to a game still in Early Access, especially when they're exactly the type of game that a 'Mixed' rating is crying out for. As it is though,
is lumbered with more ideas than it has any interesting prospect of realising.
The game's biggest flaw is also its unfortunate selling point. The touted 'Final Fantasy-like combat' is a little disingenuous in its advertising; it's more like the superficial surface controls of any JRPG driven by a frustrating AP system that chokes the fighting sections into a monotonous war of attrition. Your action points build gradually with each round of combat, allowing you to do little more than basic melee and gunplay. By the time your abilities of any tactical importance or nuance are available to you, it's either at the end of the battle or just too late to be any more effective than a simple swing of your bat.
This might not be such a huge deal if the fighting didn't feature so heavily in the game but it is literally the only live-action element of
. The rest is spent in menu micromanagement, assigning survivors jobs at the camp and noodling through the inoffensive but incredibly typical script. You quickly fall into a monotonous routine of delegating hunting, lookout duty and ammo/weapon/armour crafting (which CANNOT be done while you're on the road), thereby sacrificing NPC plotlines and story paths in exchange for having to leave them at base to perform scavenging duties that should REALLY be integrated into the main game for the sheer amount of time you spend drudging the highway for supplies.
There are a lot of very decent ideas in
but, at this point, it doesn't have the in-game scope to realise them.

Although pitched as a Zelda parody, dismissing Ittle Dew as such would be doing it a disservice. While the delightful art style and fantastic soundtrack both pay homage to the classic series, the similarities in actual gameplay are rather cursory and it turns out that's a good thing.
The emphasis here is entirely on the puzzles, more specifically, block puzzles. You'll spend nearly your entire stay on the island pushing, freezing, and teleporting blocks and enemies around, flipping switches and ultimately opening a ton of chests and doors on your quest for treasure. As the sole focus of the adventure the quality of the puzzles is paramount, and fortunately they happen to be supremely well designed and satisfying to solve, rarely crossing the line into overly hard nor easy. They provide an entertaining challenge as well as a bit of replayability with several different paths available for completing the game, something that's rarely seen in this genre.
All of this combined with the clever boss fights, tongue in cheek humor, and outstanding presentation add up to a very short but (technical hiccups aside) immensely enjoyable game from start to finish. Don't make the mistake of taking Ittle Dew at face value, for it has more than enough heart to breakaway from it's inspiration, and should not be missed!

Okay so, after completing the whole story on both normal and hard. Here's my opinion on this game:
Stats:
Voice-acting; 5.5/10
Story; 9/10
Gameplay; 10/10
Adventure; 9/10
Graphics (for 2012); 10/10.
If you're into Tomb Raider, Bayonetta and Skyrim games, this game is perfect. You get to explore a little and look for treasure, the fighting is amazing and as for Skyrim wise, the magic that you're able to do in this game.

When I first loaded the game, I was stunned - the game's art is just too captivating. I love how they made it look so gorgeous although the claim it's hand painted. The world is beautifully painted, the characters designs are cute and aptly made for the game, the animations are incredible. You owe your eyes to look at this game.
Bastion is a story driven game with great art and legendary Narrator. Yes I said it - legendary. I really like how the Narrator performs, he actually narrates most if not all Kid's (our protagonist whom we control) actions. His deep voice brings a new gaming element for real. The story itself is one kind of common topic - to restore the 'world' that's been destroyed by the Calamity. The combinations between the narrator, game's art, narrator and OSTs, though, make it feel different.
The OSTs themselves are ear-catching. Most platformer games I play I usually don't care about the OSTs, some even were so irritating I turned them off. In Bastion? I love every second the OST is played.
Gameplay is a mix between RPG and platformer. You can actually assign weapons/shields/power ups, have potions and the pure hack and slash aspect. You can't hack and slash your way, though, since it requires more than that. Evasion and blocking skills are also essentials, some enemies you can't just pew pew.
That said, playing with controller is recommended.
For people who love challenge, Bastion has plentiful for you. Starting from Hard difficulty, to New Game+, to Idols. Idols is a feature in game that actually tamper the situations of your choosing. If you want more exp but harder enemies, there's one feature for you.
Overall, the game's a bit short. Only 10 hours or so for normal to hard difficulty. For completionist it will take more hours. I'd love to get Bastion 2 to compensate this, but Bastion simply is a game that should end just there. You'll understand when you finish the game.
For 80% off, this is a steal. Shame the OST isn't on sale also.

New to the 4X genre? Loved MOO1? MOO2? Then this is a good game. It is basically MOO1+MOO2 upgraded. In comparing my experience with the PC Gamer review:
- PC Gamer basically knocked it for not doing anything to "shake it up" from MOO1 & MOO2. I consider that a good thing not a bad thing. I basically wanted to play MOO1 but not in VGA graphics (uggg), and this game does that no question.
- Some of the criticism of the AI or of dealing with pollution....MOO1 had that exactly. You ask the computer-controlled race to declare war on someone else, and they do, but they don't do anything for a lot of turns, maybe never. Pollution - yes, you need to think ahead especially on rich planets or certain races like Meklar. In MOO1 you had to divert a lot of resources to Ecology later in the game, and with technology you can do that more efficiently. Same here.
- Comparing an upgraded classic to the other 4X (eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate) style games that followed is bit unfair. If your expectation is to build on all 4X games that came before it, then yeah, you will be underwelmed. If you want to experience the classic that started the genre but beautifully upgraded with great personality (see the voice actors), fun but not overwelming, then you will enjoy this game.
- I like it as much as MOO1 and a bit better than MOO2 (I was not a huge fan of MOO2 but I enjoyed it). The only thing I miss so far, is that in MOO1 I could build a fleet of thousands of ships. This version is like MOO2 in that the fleet size is more limited. It's big, but not the thousands I used to use (e.g., 1000 small ships with shields, mass drivers mid-game....just decimate everything. Or each holding one or two bombs will elimintate a colony in one turn....)
The reviews seemed biased negative due to mismatched expectations. Also, I started playing May 2017, quite a few patches later, so if there were serious issues on release, I didn't experience them. So maybe I'm biased positive :)
Hope this helps and enjoy the game if you choose to try it.

XCOM2 is my all-time most disappointing gaming experience.
I am a decent chess player. I love chess. Playing XCOM2 is like playing chess with an opponent much better than you, but: A) he makes you play without your queen, and B) he uses yours. That is a reasonable assessment of how totally unbalanced this game is.
For a strategy game, there is nothing here other than trial and error. If you make a successful move, rejoice and save, save, save. Then it's your opponents turn. You get mind-controlled. You get stabbed. Your weapons become non-functional. A previously dead opponent is re-animated.  If you manage to survive this, rejoice. Awe, hell, now you have but two guys and the enemy called in reinforcements!? OMG, wow, you just manged to cut down the reinforcements! They just called in reinforcements AGAIN. And this is before you realize there are half a dozen undiscovered enemies who haven't joined the fight yet.
I played on normal mode. I breezed through the first few levels, and really enjoyed the game. I looked forward to playing all day. It was one of *those* games. I succeeded on some really hard levels and felt rewarded. Then I just got punched in the face. After reloading a level over 15 times, it occurred to me: this is not fun. This is the opposite of fun.
I wish I was part of some exclusive club of "hard-core" gamers capable of enjoying this game. My hunch is there are really only about 3 of them. They flood the message boards, eager to boast of their bona fides. Everyone else just effing HATES this game.
Before you call me "casual," I will mention that the notoriously difficult Dark Souls is my all-time favorite game, video or otherwise. The beauty of Dark Souls is that you can learn your enemy. Every time you face him you're that much more well-prepared. Also, in Dark Souls you get to react in real-time. The helplessness of idly watching as your crew gets wrecked is just.... the antithesis of fun.
Anyone who knows anything about writing knows that, in order to maintain the audience's interest, you have to give your protagonist(s) a chance in hell. This is a pretty fundamental thing for XCOM2 to get wrong.

Where do I start? How about with performance? The game launcher recommended ultra settings on my pc and I can run Skyrim on ultra just fine, so I gave it a try. Same engine. Should work out. Right? Nope. ~35 FPS out of the gate, and anytime I go anywhere like a city, it dips down to about ~5 and locks up for a minute or so, if it doesn't crash. So I figure, you know. Easy. I'll just lower the graphics settings. Boom. Problem solved. Only, it wasn't. On the lowest settings I can't get above ~15 fps and it instantly crashes anywhere near places like Diamond City. What the hell? What kind of blackmagicf*ckery is this? Seriously, how does that even happen? I don't know. This is the only game it happens with. So, you know, I thought, "Maybe it's mods. Yeah. Gotta be mods." Nope. Fresh install still runs like this. Every single play through also has me dealing with my grass textures eventually turning into brown, tin foil razor blades. Every. Single. One. Also, game reliably crashes about once every other hour. No matter what I'm doing.
That's the base game. What about the DLC? Never. Not once. Did I get to go into Nuka World and not have to pull up the console to get rid of monstrously oversized, incorrectly rendered Nuka Cola bottle statues. Then there's the Automatron DLC. Oh, the robot DLC. I've never been able to beat the final boss without using the tapes. Combat scenario bugs out no matter how many times I try it. A few times I couldn't even make it to the combat scenario, because my automatron follower just wouldn't open the doors. He's just like, "Nope. F*ck it, man. We've tried this a hundred times. I ain't even gonna do it. Not doing it. NO!" Far Harbor. Far Harbor was the one DLC where I actually had no gamebreaking problems. One out of three. You know, for Bethesda, that may actually not be all that bad. We might be setting records here.
I've got over a thousand hours of gameplay on record. Something's keeping me coming back. The Story? The RP elements? Gotta be, right? Nah. Those are pretty garbage. Why? You predefined my character. In an RPG. I HATE that! In Fallout 3, you start as a kid who's never seen the world, you know, an easily shapeable character. You're a little b*stard that can become anything you wanna be, just like your momma told you. New Vegas? Amnesia. Easily shapable. Don't remember a f*cking thing. Who knows? Maybe I was a serial killer. Maybe I was just some putz pulling my pud, like real life, but now I get to decide. FO4? Spouse, career professional, parent. Everything you were, already laid out before you. How the holy f*ck is a lawyer and housewife going to resort to drug use and cannibalism to survive in a post-apocalytic wasteland? How the holy f*ck is a decent parent going to waste time doing any other sh*t than directly searching for their kid? How are they going to become a blood thirsty, ruthless raider? Yeah. They're not. At least the male is a combat veteran. That's a somewhat easier stretch of the imagination when it comes to surviving and doing what it takes to survive, but again, if you go off and run side quests, isn't it sexist as all hell to assume daddy would care less about little Junior B*stard than mommy?
No. Nope. No. You can not make these characters satisfying to play. You just can't do it. They don't fit into this world and that would be fine if there was something to make that the center of gameplay, the focus, how you have to survive while being completely wrong for the world you're thrown into, but that's not even a side point. No. You just instantly adapt and you're just instantly the bad a*s hero.... you know, to everyone but your kid, who you just drag feet on finding. Who cares? Sh*tty parent is still a believable good guy, right? Pshh. Nothing fits in anywhere in this game. DLC's just feel worse. They just toss random storylines (your character also doesn't fit into, especially Nuka World), at you, with no cohesive connection to anything else in the game. Not even each other. Why not? Who cares? Right?
Still. I put a buttload of time into this game. Ulimately, I can't deny some kind of sick, twisted love for it. One word. Mods. The game has little charm to offer on it's own, but with mods? Loved it. Took away the voice acting. Made myself a ghoul kid. Dropped myself off in the middle of nowhere. Turned the story into looking for some mystery kid I learned about while out trolling the wasteland for food and sh*t. Focused on world exploration, fun quests, killing humanoids, and eating them; all while hopped up on Psycho. Throw in some sweet weapon mods, a good looking armor set, and the game was infinitely better than out of the box. Game was actually fun. A lot of fun. Unfortunately, never could find mods to fix my performance issues, but those became endurable when the game became about fun. That's the charm Bethesda fails to capitalize on. Give me no story. Just let me make a character and go nuts out there. Write my own story. That would have been way better than the story that came in the game. That makes the game so much more fun. They call this an FPS with RPG elements, anyway. If they hadn't forced the sh*t excuse for RPG elements, the game actually would have been a lot better.
Gunplay and combat? It was alright, but nothing great. Because, I didn't think it was much better than combat in the previous games, and if you're going to gimp the RPG people loved in New Vegas, you could have at least reinvented the wheel on the gunplay a bit. Hell, even just bring it up to speed with other FPS games. For example, the last Gears of War had better combat (cover system, for example) and a better story and it's meant to just be a multiplayer carnage fest. I actually kept trudging through frustratingly difficult racing elements in that game because I wanted to see the story's conclusion. Here, I had to trudge through the story, because I just wanted the sh*t to end. I got one ending and never touched the main storyline again. Oh yeah, and there's melee combat in this game. Why? I don't know. It's clunky and awkward. *Teleports behind you* "Nothing personal kid." I mean, literally. This is what you do, if you want a playable melee build. Shooting off someones arm or leg is great campy fun. Teleporting behind someone and stabbing the air in a buggy animation while having no control over your character until said animation is over, is just... dumb. Also, this world has freaking laser guns and mini-nuke launchers and you're gonna run around with a switchblade? Why? Just... Why?
I absolutely forgive Beth for making that element of combat an afterthought. Sadly, however, if I had one word, instead of this manifesto, to describe the game, I think that would be it; afterthought. I hate to bring up Creation Club. I do. That sh*t has already tanked the ratings of every Beth game on here. However, I feel like corporate greed might've played some part in this game. Most of it really feels like they sat down, said, "Hey. We got this newer engine in Skrim. It made a metric f*ck ton of money for us. Let's slap another IP of ours into it. Throw that sh*t out the door. Sit back while we drown in neckbeard money and gamer girl p*ssy." And Todd, aka God, said, "Let it be done."
The Creation Club and changes it makes to the game are still being fleshed out. Some are calling out that the sky's falling and free mods can't run with the Creation Club patch. I don't know if that's true or not. This game, with free mods, is absolutely worth playing. If they actually block old mods, forget it. The gamebreaking bugs alone prevent this game from being worth even $30, free mods or not. As for buying DLC, Nuka World and Far Harbor are the only two DLC of any decent length, and most of Nuka is busy work. Shame, because behind Nuka is a story with a lot of potential, but then they watered it down, made your choices meaningless, and again made it feel like just more rushed crap in an attempt to grab cash.

I downloaded this game recently and I have only played 4 hours at the time of this review. Never before have I given a review so quickly but this game deserves it. You play as either a captain or a crew memeber of the ship doing everything from loading/shooting cannons to fixing holes and putting out fires. This can lead quickly lead to chaos if there is no teamwork or communication. For that matter, I believe that a mic is almost a requirement for this game. It helps to be able to call out needs to the crew so that 5 people arent doing a 1 person job.
Community - I must say that this game has the best community. When I joined my first game I was greeted by the captain of the ship in full pirate accent. Everybody on board was talking in a pirate accent. They were all very helpful and patient with me as a new person. In fact, at the beginning of each game the captain would give a quick run down on how to succeed in the game for all the new people. It was the best online gaming experience I have ever had. Unfortunately, not all ships are like this. I played many other games where they spoke normally and didn't have a clue how to work as a team. I also just played a game where we destroyed them due to the leadership of the captain and the cooperation of the crew. While it worked, I switched to a different ship after playing on that one for two rounds because I did not have as much fun under the captain's strict rule. It seems that this game will foster both competative people and people who legitimately play for fun. Another note about the community is that most of them are adults. I only ran into one guy who sounded like he was under 18. Honestly this game is almost worth it for the community itself.
Gameplay - Terrific. Terrible. Exciting. Boring. It is all of those things and more. Above all I would use the word clunky to describe the gameplay mechanics. It works much like Mount and Blade: Napoleonic Wars, except less refined. The gameplay is also very unrealistic. Another negative is that there are minor glitches which can affect your ability to play well. Regardless of these issues, it is quite entertaining. There are so many tasks to be done in order to be successful and the only way to win is to work as a team. Many of the tasks are mundane, but even so they must be done and they are done with pride. Never before have I played a game where I felt that I was doing a small, but crucial, role in helping my team win. When it clicks you feel invincible. This game's gameplay gives a unique joy, one of team success rather than individual stats.
Note on combat - Player to player combat is pretty rare from my experience (if you are playing the game right). The guns are pretty accurate and rewarding to use. Melee is frustrating. I can be swinging my sword 1 foot away from a guy and miss him every time. Another difficulty is knowing who is who. There is no icon over the head of enemies. Instead you have to hold down 'q' to see who your allies are, then attack those who aren't indicated. As such, hiding on board a ship and killing their crew is a valid strategy. Even in the four hours I have played I was able to do it twice, scoring many kills before getting found out. Player to player combat is the only part of the game that feels like a solo effort.
Graphics - The graphics aren't bad for what it is. I seems like the same graphics as mount and blade. I must say that the fire graphics are pretty good.
Optimization and Playability - I have an i5 6600k processor, GTX 970 overclocked 34%, and the game saved onto a solid state drive. It runs with no framerate drops nor do I have issues with loading times or joining servers. This game runs flawlessly for me at max settings. I think the people who are complaining about optimization just have computers down with scurvy.
I would suggest getting this if you are a social player. I have actually been unable to speak during the time while playing this due to jaw surgery but I can't wait to dive in and eventually become a captain. You know what makes NPPD Rush great? It doesn't explain anything. What many will identify as negative aspects of the game, some will find to be perfect for the vibe the developers intended.
The game is confusing. The gameplay and core mechanics are not described, or taught to you through 'learning levels' like so many other titles. The teletype text and short 'scenes' don't give the player much more than nebulous hints, but encourage an imaginative player to read a great deal of the story between the lines. The crazy colour scheme, soundtrack and HUD make the game difficult to follow, and it will take you a number of playthroughs to figure out even the core mechanics.
The objectively great part of this game is the soundtrack. Fast paced, bumpin beats set the mood perfectly, and wouldn't be out of place at your next killer house party. Other than that, why was this game worthwhile to me? It's a game that you can learn on your own. It's a game you feel good about figuring out. It's a game you can beat.
Your friends might take a cursory glance and hate it. The negative reviews speak to that. Its a short game, and most won't think it worth the price. The complaints you might read in the review are not unfounded, but ask yourself: does this game deserve a place in my Steam library?
I say yes.

Let's cut to the chase here and say what has to be said: Good potential, bad execution. When I bought this I had expected they would bring me a reasonable 20 euros worthy product but what I got was a prodect that belongs either in early acces or in the "below 5$" section.
As I started playing this game I thought "seems to lead up to something" but slowly as I played more I had grown to hate it. It offers very little freedom in what to do as you can do almost nothing at all. There's very little missions to finish and not even super mario for the nintendo 64 is more repetetive than this game.
My typical day in a game like this is: I fill up the useless energy, food, and stress bar that are there for no reason by for one instance meeting up with friends (which you don't actually get to do, the screen just turns black for a moment) for no reason. I go to my closet and click on "on duty" below the 5 listed useless options of clothing you could wear when not on duty.  I walk out of my house and step in the car, look at the roads and see about 5 cars behind of each other of which 2 are halfway embedded into the ground, 2 are speeding in the most unrealistic way and 1 is driving like a total (ahum) "r'tard" because he/she is probably on alcohol.  I get a mission right away saying a drunk is behaving violently in the park so I go there with sirens and lights on. I drive over a steep mountain (cars in here are like horses in skyrim except they go 150 km p/h) and land on the dirt perfectly. I drive over a lantern pole (gta much) and get to the place. As always there is 2 witnesses and they describe the character, I see the exact matching description, walk up to the guy with my gun and turns out it isn't him, get a penalty for aiming at an innocent. I see the right person and walk up to them with a gun saying freeze and they pull a gun on me, by this time I start shooting the person and by 2 shots in the head the person lays down. Now apparently calling an ambulance will still work out. I get a bonus for shooting someone, and another bonus for shooting the ambulance.
There is about a variëty of I think 10 missions intotal in this game and bare in mind that this whole story is a more action packed optimistic version of the actual game, in that way I am making commercial for them for over-appreciating how broken it is.
Pro's:
-You get to be a cop
-Good concept
-Driving is so broken it's fun
Cons:
-Repetetive
-Looks like unfinished product (yet is not in early acces)
-Anything you do in this game raises no excitement whatsoever
Final judgement: 4/10

If you're a fan of the police and simulation thing do buy this game, you might actually enjoy it. (but don't get your hopes up) Best is to wait for it to go on sale. If this does not convince you here are some games that are cheaper and way better: Fallout 3, Fallout New Vegas, Mount and blade : warband. These are games I think you might enjoy if this game drew your attention.

Game should be placed under early acces if this is an unfinished product (and believe me it is). And if you do consider this product finished: Don't ask 20 euros for it, it's a far way from being worth 20 euros.

Recent changes have been made in this game, bugs have been fixed and playing it is not a general dread. Yet as I keep thinking this game should not cost as much as it does, it did turn out into a good game.
I did not expect the producers to adress any of the issues since it was never stated it was Early Acces, but I am glad they did it. This is a buy, but only if you like simulation combined with police.

Serena is a very interesting experience. I hesitate to call it a game since there's no real gameplay. You only interact with a small environment and learn the story of your unnamed narrator and his wife Serena.
I won't go into details about the story, but I will mention that the twist took me a second playthrough to truly understand. The first time through I pegged the game as predictable, but I didn't realize how much of the story I had missed. The second go round, I discovered the "real" twist ending (and felt quite stupid for having it fly over my head before).
Because of this, I definitely recommend you to play through slowly and carefully. Use the spacebar to highlight objects you can interact with and click through them until you've heard every story dialogue from them. There are small clues scattered throughout as to what happened in that lonely cabin.
If you pace yourself and listen through the whole story, the ending goes from predictable to quite rewarding (for you, at least).
But as I mentioned earlier, I can't really call this a game. If you're looking for a horror
, this isn't the title for you. If you want a tense, haunting
, you're in the right place. This would be a game worth a few dollars; the fact that it's free is icing on the cake.
The atmosphere is dark and moody, and the music and sounds really seal the deal; the songs will knock you off your mental balance, and the silences will raise your nerves on end. It's a short experience, but it's one that will stick with me for a while.

If it's a sandbox game where you can run people over, we call it a GTA clone. Well if it must be done, then Sleeping Dogs is the best GTA clone I've ever played. It's everything GTA IV should have been (good driving, well optimized, cohesive plot) evened out with some Batman Arkham Asylum style fighting. Anyone who knows me knows that I adore Arkham City so this one is an easy recommend. Only downside is the main story is over too fast, but 20 hours in and I'm not even at 50% of the side missions and collectables.

Every once in a while, you need to take a break from the crazy fast paced games that lack any plot. Serena is a great opportunity for that escape. A very beautifully created point and click adventure story featuring a very dirty and gritty but appropriate environment. The plot follows the main character trying to regain some of his memories about his lost wife. The game does a great job at carrying the player through a gambit of emotions as well as helping to progress the story at an increasing accelerated rate.
The game was created using a brand new adventure engine called Dagon developed by the Argentinian studio Senscape. Senscape was founded by the writer and creator of Serena, Agustín Cordes who also created the hit adventure game Scratches.
Overall, if you enjoy story driven adventure games, this game is well worth the time. It was very short but considering the story, the length was perfect. This was just like sitting down to read to a great short story.

I don't like this game at all. Now, I don't play a lot of MMOs, and therefore don't know anything about grinding, but I'm to assume it's not supposed to be this stupid. Because, at least in WOW, you stay in generally the same area killing enemies to grind, or you go through quests. In this game, there are no quests, there is no way to sit in the same area grinding at any amount that's relevant, and... Actually, even if you, say, played revenant, which was practically unkillable last time I played, and went in the highest world you had access to, and somehow managed to do dungeons without getting shrekt instantly, you wouldn't go anywhere. You might notice how you see people starting off in the ad with dragons, you actually have to either, 1, sit there and grind for years to get the worst dragon attainable, or 2, pay them a million dollars to get there. You have to pay the devs of the game if you wanna actually get anywhere. So, if you want anything good in this game, you'll have to give the developers your money, and a lot of it. Also, in regular or even good MMOs, there's characters to talk to, proper dueling, quests to get, and above all, there's things to do. In this game, there's quests, but that's about the tutorial, and past that, you have to climb to like uber 3-5 before the quests mean anything to you. Oh, and even the starting quests take ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t amounts of farming. For instance, the quest where you need a certain amount-a materials to get your forge... For some reason, the materials can't at all be called abundant. So imagine getting stuck on the literal beginning of the game. From here, how about we go in order of what the game does. So, first of all, you start out picking a class. Say you're an experienced player in this game, and know all of the classes. If you are, and do, then you know that it's practically impossible to pick one, at least, that's if you want a new experience, but with a good class. Almost all of them are great, and Revenant, if you go to worlds that match you, then you're untouchable. But, if you're an inexperienced player in this game, then you have no idea what to pick. For all you know, you'll land on the worst class ever. You can't even tell by looking at stats, because the best explanation of the class that the game gives is a joke or a summary of what this person would be like in real life. You pick, and get to the quests, like the first one that takes a second to do, the uh... The dungeon one, you have to do a bunch of dungeons. Now we get to talk about the gameplay. First of all, unlike WoW, there's no strategy or skill involved. Chances are, you'll rarely be trying to dodge. It's samey as hell, but see, in WoW, the beginning of the game is boring. Except, in Trove, the entire game is twice as boring. Seriously, with the quests in WoW, it was really simple. Go here, kill this thing, actually get far in leveling, go over here, kill more cool asf creatures with an actual clear sense of where you're going, continue. Now Trove's dungeons. With a map being your only guidance, go to a dungeon without any clear sense of what's stronger, more rewarding, harder, etc, and try not to get destroyed by your friendly neighborhood pound cake. Now, you've probably barely finished this quest, and you're probably bored out of your mind. Now, do what's practically the same thing, but you don't kill anything, and you can't find any of it on a map. Welcome to mining, something that, when I actually found what I was looking for, was quite literally more fun than the rest of the game. I guess this is because it's the ecstasy of a long journey coming to an end, and you finding what you've been questing for. Now you've got all the basic crafting things, and a forge and such. I'll explain why I hate these later. So, now, imagine you're on the first world, and you're just able to get to the next, because of power rank, which is literally the worst system for achievements ever, literally getting worse and worse as you go on in the game, but I'll explain that later. So you go in completely unprepared, and die. Yep, gotta go back and do the only mechanics of the game over and over, just clicking and pressing buttons. So, let's say you're bored of this, and wanna do pvp. Well, if you ever find it in the hub world, because you can't just click 'duel' on people, then good luck even figuring out how it works. I died like eighteen times in a row on my first and last time playing pvp in this game. I, at random points in time, just got oneshotted. Which is unexpected, because you'd think that they'd balance everything out. They don't. Let's wrap that part up. So, a bit of time goes by because apparently you're not bored enough to leave, and then you get to like uber 1, and everything just comes to a halt. Just, like that, you can't get any further. Here's where I'm gonna talk about a few things relating to power rank and items and the forge in succession. So, here's why the power rank system is horrible, at this part of the game: You get items that don't ever give you a higher power rank, or if they do, they're items that are missing out on a key feature, and now let's talk about the effects of some items. There are important, or really crucial, effects in literally only some items. That effect is mostly jump, but if you found an item that has really high health or something, you can never trade that away. So now you'll have to forge it until it's its best, which is something that the game really could've just done without. You don't need that part of this. If you'd removed the mechanic of forging altogether, you'd be left with items being much simpler, although there being less to do in the game. All it does is make it harder for you to say goodbye to that weapon if one with higher pr comes along. Now, I'll admit, every time you level up, you get a small amount of pr, and there are gems that can help you get further in pr, as well as make your items more effective. There are problems with this, though. Number one: If you get more pr from leveling up, why the hell does pr exist? Number two: At this point in the game, you have to reach levels that are so high that they give enough pr to jump a world up before you can get another gem socket. Number three: I've played 240 hours of this game, and I still have no idea how you charge gems. Number four: It takes a lotta♥♥♥♥♥♥nowadays to be able to pull gems out of their socket, at this point in the game. So, this is actually a point in the game that's brushing shoulders with the point that gems become really important, and pr starts getting sadistic and misleading. I got well over enough pr to go to the next world, and the world after that, but I can barely handle the next world, even on my Revenant main. This effect amplifies by the point that you can get your class gem. Somehow, you're a few worlds unprepared for the everdark, but your pr says you can get there, and probably get to the world that's 3 after it. Nope, still gotta do the same grinding thing for a million years, 'til you can finally get to the class gem. Now, when I talk about this game in this way, I make it seem really short, but in reality, it literally took a while for me to get a few levels further when I was a noob, with the help of my, like, 3k pr friend. I've seen in reviews that this game used to be great, and I've heard that server crashes happen all the time, and that they give crappy rewards for it. I'm still kind of a noob, so even if I'm wrong about most of the things I've said here, you still can't deny that the gameplay's repetetive, mindless, and grinding is incredibly annoying.

This is a tough one to review, especially as I become more and more convinced of just how insufficient the thumbs up/thumbs down review system really is. In my view, 89% positive just means that 89% of people found the game inoffensive, rather than the game being anything like a 9/10. In actuality, Blade of Time is probably worth about a 6/10. It certainly wasn't a bad game, but it's absolutely not one I'd go out of my way to play. The melee combat feels good, and many of the magic abilities you receive are tremendously powerful. However, dodging and countering can be a little finicky - so much so that although the melee was fun, I found myself using the machine gun in a tremendous number of encounters. Sometimes I'd stand in the door outside an area, sometimes I'd stay just out of range of all enemy attacks and kite backwards, and on one occasion I could tell that the game wanted me to come down at from a vertical height and fight on the enemies' level, but I declined. Although it almost always took longer to take out enemies using the machine gun, it was just so much safer! It's difficult to switch quickly between your melee weapons and your guns: on a 360 controller, you had to click in the stick to switch to your gun, and while in "gun mode" you move slower and are unable to dodge. In addition to your magic powers, guns, and swords, you also have the ability to "rewind" time. However, this is not a time rewind in the sense that you're thinking. "You" just stand still while time rewinds and another version of yourself emerges doing the things you did. So, it might actually be better described as a time-traveling cloning technique, more like an Ultra Time Force situation. Certain enemies require you do use this to stack up enough damage to kill them before dying yourself, or to have to use a clone to distract an enemy while you take care of a critical task. Some enemies have a bubble shield, and it seems that you must shoot the shield from two angles simultaneously to disable it. Another enemy requires one "clone" to attack his head while "you" climb behind the enemy to disable his mechanical health-regeneration packs. These encounters were neat, but the time rewind mechanic did take some getting used to. As a final note, the air targeting and dash moves feel very good, and the section of the game where your character can fly is an absolute blast. Either way, if you're looking for a neat action game off the beaten path, Blades of Time could be what the doctor ordered. However, don't go into it expecting a God of War or Bayonetta-quality game.

For me personally this is the best 'Game Dev' type game out at the moment. It builds further on the foundations laid by previous IP's in this genre. Compared to these previous titles this game offers a lot of personilization and offers deeper gameplay even at this early access stage.
You decide how to build your office as well as design it a bit by placing down various specific interior objects from a nice variety. There are various types of rooms which all help in the process of designing and developing video games. Including but not limited to QA rooms to improve game quality and remove bugs; sound studio for better game audio, marketing; customer support; toilets (when you gotta go you gotta go); development office and more.
Regarding the game development itself you research new technologies which you then implement by making new game engines for your own use or for selling it to your competitors for some extra cash. Although in the beginning you most likely have to purchase game engines due to shortage of cash. When starting development you have the basics such as the genres, topics, which engine to use, game size, etc. But also small extras such as licenses to purchase from movies/sports to give your game an additional popularity boost. Further down you choose with sliders where you want to focus your efforts on during development. The game can receive additional bonuses with the help of the QA room and sound studio at the moment.
Once ready for production you give can decide how many copies to produce and even decide what the package should be like. Want to give your new to be loyal fans a t-shirt and a manual? Or screw the manual! Let them find out on their own and just give them a nice one dollar sticker with the game! Set the sale price which can be adjusted and voila, rake in the profits .. or the losses.
This game also has some negative aspects at the moment. In my opinion the UI could be a bit better. Sometimes it feels you need to click couple times more in order to view what you want to view.
When building new rooms it's very difficult to sense the size of it. It would be helpful if there was some kind of visible tile/grid pattern to help visualise it. Because of that I often make my rooms too small because all the objects are not bound by the tile system that is used when creating a room. Desk 1 can be 1.25 tiles in lenght while desk 3 can be 2.2 tiles in lenght. Obviously it's somewhat more 'realistic' to not have everything the same size but it does not help with object placement at all.
Once you found the way to make money early game then you're launched and it will become very easy financial wise. You can get loans in case you're short on cash but they're paid off very quickly if you know the previous mentioned way to make money and the loan interests could be a bit higher as well imo.
Last but not least the game advances - at least in my opinion - rather quickly through time. So your play sessions could last a bit short.
All in all the positive aspects definately outweigh the negative ones. I highly recommend this game, not only for what it has right now but also for what will come. The developers give frequent updates and you can be sure that after an update or two/three you'll have some extra content to guarantee a new play session.

In short? Buffed up with the Chosen, XCOM 2 is the first game in a long while, which makes me go to bed at 1 am and get up at 5.
The base game of XCOM 2 is a meat-and-potatoes instant-classic. War of the Chosen makes it super-sized. With bells and whistles. If you like turn-base, you will like XCOM 2. If you already own the base game, get the Chosen. Now.
For people new to XCOM, do not, I repeat, DO NOT skip 2's base game.  XCOM as a series is merciless, even on the lowest level. There is no tank rush, but there is perma-death. Learn the ropes in basic, and only then proceed to the brave new world of the Chosen.
For XCOM vets, do not think your time-proven sequence in Avenger base-building still means bo diddley. And I am aware, it hurts, but learn to know when to skedaddle. Split and run, that is, for you merry folks north of the Mason-Dixon. Some scenarios are tailored ro make you cry like a little girl, if you don't.
So, what are the vast improvements by the Chosen expansion?
Lots and lots of little stuff, that will give you a hard time in a good way. The three most bombastic changes are mission numbers, bondmates, and squad tactics.
Mission numbers refers both to the choices available and to the campaign length. I always thought that the base campaign was too streamlined. Not any more, it ain't.
Bondmates are bitter sweet. In the base campaign I had long come to the point that I had some favorite names in the pool, but other than this I simply lived with whatever characters the game delivered. I told myself, that I let the game tell the story. In truth, I was tired of getting a character popped that I cared for individually. In the Chosen, characters eventually become so different, that you have to pay attention to their strengths. So you will catch yourself liking some more than others. After that, the lexicon defines "bondmates" as "Two characters, who are too frequently standing within plasma grenade radius distance from each other."
Squad tactics in the base game were not negotiable. There was a right and a wrong. Period. Against Advent, right is still right. The newly introduced Lost scenarios need different tactics. So far, so simple. Now picture Lost and Advent on the same map. Add to this half a pound of time pressure. No, not through a timer. YOU have to figure out, when to get rolling. Add to this a table spoon of vastly different skill sets. Add to this a knife tip of bondmates. Stir it until it bubbles, and now tell me the best tactics. Awesome.

Game is a polished, cinematic experience.  Connecting with your soldiers feels good, killing enemies feels good.  There's enough options to keep combat fresh.  This review will focus mostly on the meat of the game: combat.
However, the game is too hard.  The enemies are always 2 steps ahead of the player.  You can never catch up, even on the easiest difficulty setting.  You have to game the system by sacrificing rookie soldiers to complete objectives so your veteran badass soldiers don't die.
There are gimmicks in combat that the player can never account for - an issue with a strategy game.  Some random chance in how much damage enemies take per shot, accuracy, etc are all fine.  On the other hand, there are random enemies that spawn in melee range and can take a swing at the player's soldiers.  The player can never take into account where enemies will be on the map once they are out of conceal mode - often misleading the player into having an extra spawn of enemies because the player moved 1 square too far in a direction they couldn't have known about.  AI have more tools to control the players more than the player does.  And this is all on the easiest difficulty.
Overall recommendation: No.  The game is too frustrating, leaves real decision making out of the players hands, and punishes the player mercilessly with no counterplay and for no reason other than to make the game harder.

I downloaded this game recently and I have only played 4 hours at the time of this review. Never before have I given a review so quickly but this game deserves it. You play as either a captain or a crew memeber of the ship doing everything from loading/shooting cannons to fixing holes and putting out fires. This can lead quickly lead to chaos if there is no teamwork or communication. For that matter, I believe that a mic is almost a requirement for this game. It helps to be able to call out needs to the crew so that 5 people arent doing a 1 person job.
Community - I must say that this game has the best community. When I joined my first game I was greeted by the captain of the ship in full pirate accent. Everybody on board was talking in a pirate accent. They were all very helpful and patient with me as a new person. In fact, at the beginning of each game the captain would give a quick run down on how to succeed in the game for all the new people. It was the best online gaming experience I have ever had. Unfortunately, not all ships are like this. I played many other games where they spoke normally and didn't have a clue how to work as a team. I also just played a game where we destroyed them due to the leadership of the captain and the cooperation of the crew. While it worked, I switched to a different ship after playing on that one for two rounds because I did not have as much fun under the captain's strict rule. It seems that this game will foster both competative people and people who legitimately play for fun. Another note about the community is that most of them are adults. I only ran into one guy who sounded like he was under 18. Honestly this game is almost worth it for the community itself.
Gameplay - Terrific. Terrible. Exciting. Boring. It is all of those things and more. Above all I would use the word clunky to describe the gameplay mechanics. It works much like Mount and Blade: Napoleonic Wars, except less refined. The gameplay is also very unrealistic. Another negative is that there are minor glitches which can affect your ability to play well. Regardless of these issues, it is quite entertaining. There are so many tasks to be done in order to be successful and the only way to win is to work as a team. Many of the tasks are mundane, but even so they must be done and they are done with pride. Never before have I played a game where I felt that I was doing a small, but crucial, role in helping my team win. When it clicks you feel invincible. This game's gameplay gives a unique joy, one of team success rather than individual stats.
Note on combat - Player to player combat is pretty rare from my experience (if you are playing the game right). The guns are pretty accurate and rewarding to use. Melee is frustrating. I can be swinging my sword 1 foot away from a guy and miss him every time. Another difficulty is knowing who is who. There is no icon over the head of enemies. Instead you have to hold down 'q' to see who your allies are, then attack those who aren't indicated. As such, hiding on board a ship and killing their crew is a valid strategy. Even in the four hours I have played I was able to do it twice, scoring many kills before getting found out. Player to player combat is the only part of the game that feels like a solo effort.
Graphics - The graphics aren't bad for what it is. I seems like the same graphics as mount and blade. I must say that the fire graphics are pretty good.
Optimization and Playability - I have an i5 6600k processor, GTX 970 overclocked 34%, and the game saved onto a solid state drive. It runs with no framerate drops nor do I have issues with loading times or joining servers. This game runs flawlessly for me at max settings. I think the people who are complaining about optimization just have computers down with scurvy.
I would suggest getting this if you are a social player. I have actually been unable to speak during the time while playing this due to jaw surgery but I can't wait to dive in and eventually become a captain. Got this in Bundlestars' "Scorched Bundle" back in Aug '14. On a whim I decided to boot this up. 3 attempts and 37 minutes later I'm staring at a credits screen wondering what the hell I've just experienced. This isn't a game that goes down easy. N.P.P.D. Rush is confusing, violent, aggressive, and unforgiving. Yet somehow I enjoyed it.
The plot is given to you when you boot up the game; Nauseous Pines (a city) has a drug epidemic (Nox) by nightclub owner Ultra Violet. You're a surviving Nox addict, now berift of your limbs, grafted to a police motorcycle equipped with twin guns. You go around rescuing other drug addicts, saving them and quickly (30 in 5 minutes).
WASD and Left click, that's it. No remapping controls, no windowed / full screen, no resolution adjustment, brightness changes. What you get is toggling scan lines, toggling "chip fat" (makes things blurry if you do), volume control, and your Bike's color scheme (which is random and you won't see until you play).
Actual gameplay is five small levels of twin stick arena shooter. You have HP, which the drug addicts you rescue restore (10 per), and a timer that counts down from 300. Enemies drop money, which you use in the store area (that also contains going up or down floors) to buy a variety of things.
Graphics are super muddy and try to hit that retro aesthetic, gameplay is intense and you WILL need to retry (possibly many times), and the style really evokes that "Futuristic 80s" vibe really well. Or, it does when the camera doesn't leave you nauseous with the constant zooming every time you stop moving.
Things become a bit better when you rescue all 30; as soon as #30 is picked up you no longer have to worry about the timer. The enemies are much the same throughout, and the targeting reticule that follows you will continually attempt to summon what essentially are the Gradius fire worm creatures. These things are nightmares, avoid like the plague or face intense health drain.
Ultraviolet loses points for lack of optimization, lack of options, the god-awful camera, no Steam overlay or windowed mode (that I could find). But it is fun, it's not honestly THAT hard (3 attempts in 37 minutes) since you just need to remember where the rescuees are and beeline it for them (buying the gun on the 1st stage helped a lot), and it has such a unique flavor that it'll leave you thinking about it after you finish playing it.
Such is the flavor of the milk of Ultraviolet.

Graphics:
The art style is reminiscent of 80s arcades, but the execution isn’t near as crisp as many of those machines had. With a generally muddy palette in ones way, there are smog clouds that will obscure your vision of anything beneath them, including some of the more camouflaged enemies. Even in some of the brighter areas, of metallic and blue floors it’s easy to miss a lot of the information presented to you. The enemies are easy enough to identify from each other, but more often than not hard to identify from the environment. Other than the hard to distinguish enemies and muddiness, another issue with the visuals is the weird overlays that happen either when you’re hit or you kill an enemy. When hit the screen gets a lot of blue flashes, which wouldn’t be so bad if it were restricted to the edges but goes all over and makes it very hard to see. This also happens with a blood splatter overlay that happens when one kills an enemy. It’s horribly distracting and possibly seizure-rific.
The standard paint job of your Rush unit is very pink/purple, which makes it very easy to distinguish from everything else, and the junkies you are to rescue are bright purple, making them beacons for easy pick up. The paint job of your Rush unit however can be changed in the games ‘Config’ menu, if the standard colors just aren’t for you. That being said, the one time I changed the colors, I got set of grey and yellow, which got lost in the environment just like mostly everything else.
That being said, I hope you like the default resolution and quality settings, because you can’t change them what-so-ever.
Gameplay:
The controls of this game are just god awful, with WASD as your movement and mouse for aiming and shooting. While this doesn’t sound horrible at first, the spastic movements from both and the lack of any sensitivity options or even a calibration, will make you curse at the lack of controller support. Without the option to customize anything control wise, you’ll find yourself trying to hit escape to pause, which stupidly closes the entire game. The is no way to pause that I have found, and the only way to get any time to stop is get all the way to the stairs. The stairs are always at the beginning of the level but the maps are so confusing
The stairs, a static little hub, where shops and, for obvious reasons, the ability to go between floors lie. It’s kind of odd that you would use stairs though, as you’re kind of permanently attached to a motorcycle. The shops are pretty over priced for the amount of cash that drops from enemies, and unfortunately the only way to add time to the limit.
Audio:
Well at least the tunes are kinda cool. It does set up a hectic cyberpunk world with some decently executed buttrock. You can also adjust the volume mid-game which is a major improvement over any other setting. The stairs and other semi safe zones are calming, while the levels themselves are loud and hectic. The sound effects are not horribly distracting, but you will come to hate the sound of your weapon after a while.
Plot:
- The milk of Ultra violet is a 2D Twin stick shooter. In a cyberpunkish dystopia of an alternate 198X, where a designer drug called ‘Nox’ has completely screwed the city of Nauseous Pines. You play a former Nox addict who now has no limbs, due to said drug making them useless, who is plugged into some sort of battle motorcycle called a Rush. Tasked with rescuing other Nox junkies from the cities hellscape, where enough enemies lie in wait to make it a decently hectic bullet hell.
However rescuing other Nox junkies before it’s too late isn’t your only objective. Through play you will learn the origin of Nox and the identities and stories behind some of the games characters. That is if you can make it that far.
Verdict: I can actually see there being an audience for this, but for me, it’s not worth the 3.99 it’s currently selling for. I also cannot tell you what kind of mileage you’re looking at for completing this game. There are Steam Trading cards but I’m not sure who would really want a badge for this game other than some of the hardcore badge creators.
This is a solid Uninstall and forget for me.
