There is very little to fault with this game. For years, I avoided the "point and click adventure" genre thinking that it would be too restrictive, too linear, not in depth enough. But really what I was doing, was assuming that the only way to tell a great story was with an rpg with weapons, armours, multiple character, skill trees, crafting systems and all sorts.
What this game achieves though, is to take you away from the stuff that doesn't really matter and focussed you entirely on the story. It's a tough call, because a weak story with poor characters could have ended this game quicker than a horde of zeds chowing down on ones particulars, so it's a good thing this game has a great story and well developed characters! It plays like a well-written TV show as opposed to a videogame (as to be expected), so the storytelling pace is maintained at a decent rate, with only just enough time left between the crazy bits, to reflect on past choices. It really does make you appreciate each character, even the ones you don't like, and succeeds in maintaining a certain level of satisfaction that prevents you going back to replay segments just to get what you think may be the "optimum solution." In reality, there is no optimum solution, as whatever choices you make inevitably have consequences.
Graphically, the game has a consistent and attractive theme and art style. I think it fits quite well. For a game focussed on story, AAA graphics are not really required. In a way I think super realistic graphics could have spoiled the game a little, by overdoing the tension at times where it isn't really needed. In this department though, the game excels the most, in the facial expressions used by the characters. The are a wide variety of animated facial expressions that help you to gauge the intent of a particular character, beyond the basic words they are saying. The think I would say could have been improved is maybe the variety of zombies. They don't need special animations but I do recall seeing a lot of the same zombie model used over and over, which detracted a little bit.
In terms of sound, the biggest strength for me was the voice acting. Each actor played their parts well, and helped to define the characters in ways that text alone cannot do. Combined with atmospheric music and environmental sounds, this makes for an immersive overall experience. The rest of the sounds set each scene nicely without detracting from the quality of the voice acting.
Overall,  the game is very good. I paid £5 for Season 1, as well as £5 for Season 2 (also an excellent game), and completed both in 15 and 16 hours respectively. I'd say that is good value for money at just over 30p an hour per season. I'd say it is good value, even at full price.

It is important to tell upfront that this is not a game in the common sense of the word, there is no real gameplay here. This is an interactive story, so people not interested in that can walk along.
The whole game takes place in a cabin lost in the woods, where you unfold the plot by exploring objects and opening furniture. The main character is deftly voiced, his emotions are convincingly genuine. There is no jump scares, loud sounds, and so on, the fear comes from the well crafted story and presentation. The game world might be small, but each items hold lots of memories, and as the plot advances, you see them in completely different lights.
The length of the game is perfect (roughly 1h30) for what it aims to achieve, and the pace consistantly ramps up in tension. The writing is descriptive, metaphoric and subjective. The emotional side is highly nuanced, and despite the length, you will feel conflicted several times concerning the characters and the situation it presents.
In short: a free game with the quality content you expect from a commercial product. Be aware this is a condensed experience focused solely on storytelling.

There's nothing wrong IMO with interactive storytelling, but if you compare this to say, Gone Home, the quality in story telling is just so different.  In Gone Home, you explore a house and find stuff and eventually piece together a story.  In Serena, you're in a one room cabin, and you have you click on things in a certain order to get the story.
For example, you might want to open something and it'll say "No, I don't want to open it yet!  I just don't feel like it.  Maybe later." This is a small puzzle game where you traverse a few dungeons with a bunch of different mechanics and items that define what techniques and actions you can use to solve them. It took me less than 3 hours to finish it and get a majority of cards and other things, and I’ve spent over an hour after that finishing the collection. Haven’t decided if I should take the rest of the achievements yet or not, could be a fun challenge though. All in all I’ve spent about 5 hours on it and there’s still things for me to do, but mostly in the interest of completing the game without all weapons unlocked or speedrunning.
I have to say that its quite funny written, the characters and how they behave make fun of retro concepts, like eating hearts that fall on the ground. It doesn’t take itself very serious, which fits nicely into everything else.
So, gameplay! You solve puzzles by either hitting things, putting things on plates or killing things. Basically, if you have no items, you are limited to pushing blocks and finding fireplaces to light your stick on fire. But if you have a firesword you don’t need to find fireplaces, and if you have the icestaff and the firesword you can freeze blocks and then shatter them with your firesword. If you have the portal wand, you can solve even more puzzles, etc. Not only that, you can combine most of the tools in very, very interesting ways that wasn’t expected at all by me.
This works very well and the puzzles range from crazy obvious to "bweh?” making you feel very stupid when you don’t get them, and extremely clever when you finally do. In many cases you can leave it for later.
Every dungeon have a boss and they are ok most of the time. Personally I really disliked the last boss and the boss in the master dungeon (which were the only place where I eventually looked for help in solving the rooms). The last boss being annoying and the master dungeon boss being both hard and showing a lot of gameplay fallacies I dislike in 2D top-down games. Still the game is about solving puzzles first and the bosses come as a break that can be quite welcome.
It’s super pretty and animated in a way that completely fits the style. It very simply borrows a lot from Zelda games in how the graphics look, but have its own way of drawing it, which makes it more of a homage.
Anyway, if you like puzzle games and solving rooms zelda-style, get it!
If you want something more action-heavy, then you should probably look elsewhere.
Have a good day! :)

In short? Buffed up with the Chosen, XCOM 2 is the first game in a long while, which makes me go to bed at 1 am and get up at 5.
The base game of XCOM 2 is a meat-and-potatoes instant-classic. War of the Chosen makes it super-sized. With bells and whistles. If you like turn-base, you will like XCOM 2. If you already own the base game, get the Chosen. Now.
For people new to XCOM, do not, I repeat, DO NOT skip 2's base game.  XCOM as a series is merciless, even on the lowest level. There is no tank rush, but there is perma-death. Learn the ropes in basic, and only then proceed to the brave new world of the Chosen.
For XCOM vets, do not think your time-proven sequence in Avenger base-building still means bo diddley. And I am aware, it hurts, but learn to know when to skedaddle. Split and run, that is, for you merry folks north of the Mason-Dixon. Some scenarios are tailored ro make you cry like a little girl, if you don't.
So, what are the vast improvements by the Chosen expansion?
Lots and lots of little stuff, that will give you a hard time in a good way. The three most bombastic changes are mission numbers, bondmates, and squad tactics.
Mission numbers refers both to the choices available and to the campaign length. I always thought that the base campaign was too streamlined. Not any more, it ain't.
Bondmates are bitter sweet. In the base campaign I had long come to the point that I had some favorite names in the pool, but other than this I simply lived with whatever characters the game delivered. I told myself, that I let the game tell the story. In truth, I was tired of getting a character popped that I cared for individually. In the Chosen, characters eventually become so different, that you have to pay attention to their strengths. So you will catch yourself liking some more than others. After that, the lexicon defines "bondmates" as "Two characters, who are too frequently standing within plasma grenade radius distance from each other."
Squad tactics in the base game were not negotiable. There was a right and a wrong. Period. Against Advent, right is still right. The newly introduced Lost scenarios need different tactics. So far, so simple. Now picture Lost and Advent on the same map. Add to this half a pound of time pressure. No, not through a timer. YOU have to figure out, when to get rolling. Add to this a table spoon of vastly different skill sets. Add to this a knife tip of bondmates. Stir it until it bubbles, and now tell me the best tactics. Awesome.

Game is a polished, cinematic experience.  Connecting with your soldiers feels good, killing enemies feels good.  There's enough options to keep combat fresh.  This review will focus mostly on the meat of the game: combat.
However, the game is too hard.  The enemies are always 2 steps ahead of the player.  You can never catch up, even on the easiest difficulty setting.  You have to game the system by sacrificing rookie soldiers to complete objectives so your veteran badass soldiers don't die.
There are gimmicks in combat that the player can never account for - an issue with a strategy game.  Some random chance in how much damage enemies take per shot, accuracy, etc are all fine.  On the other hand, there are random enemies that spawn in melee range and can take a swing at the player's soldiers.  The player can never take into account where enemies will be on the map once they are out of conceal mode - often misleading the player into having an extra spawn of enemies because the player moved 1 square too far in a direction they couldn't have known about.  AI have more tools to control the players more than the player does.  And this is all on the easiest difficulty.
Overall recommendation: No.  The game is too frustrating, leaves real decision making out of the players hands, and punishes the player mercilessly with no counterplay and for no reason other than to make the game harder.

First, I want to mention that I NEVER recommend Early Access games unless the current product is entertaining, and well worth the price you pay. That is the case with this game.
I've played Game Dev Tycoon, and Game Dev Story (not 100% sure that's the name...I'm talking about the Kairosoft game), so I know this niche genre pretty well.
It will take a second to adjust to the way things are done in this game. The complexity I've always felt was missing from games like this is here in abundance. You need to manage how your resources are used to develope each game, and hire/fire employees...standard stuff. However, this game requires you to use the space you have to the absolute fullest. You need to section off areas of your garage/office into designated areas reserved for developement, quality control, research, marketing, bathroom, employee lounge, and much more! The game unlocks things as you play, so it attempts not to overwhelm you. I have to admit, even though I love these kind of games (and am pretty good at them) on my first playthrough I did find myself getting a little overwhelmed. I kept finding myself feeling like I was playing catch-up to the ever increasing demands of the game, and not in a good way.
EDIT: On my second attempt, things went MUCH better. I can honestly say that this game is the best Tycoon game I've ever played. I pretty much just lost an entire day in this game, and enjoyed every hour of it. It can be kind of complicated, but it's definitely learnable through some trial and error. If there are bugs, I haven't seen them. There's an element of Sims at play here, as it can be fun setting up your offices, decorating them, and all that. There is a lot to this game, but it's simple once you spend some time trying it out. Expect to fail at your first attempt, but just view it as a learning experience.
Long story short, this is the best game developer tycoon game ever made. Game developer story and game dev tycoon can't hold a candle to this game. Worth every penny. The best part is that it's still in Early Access, which (if the current state of the game is anything to go by) means it will get even better than it is right now.

TL;DR: This game is terrible.
Working from the tl;dr, the game has a clear aesthetic choice that is engrained in a retro, 80s-ish, cyber punk type design. The problem, is that the developer was so determined to stick to that artistic choice, that they sacrificed quality of life designs for the user's enjoyment. What you're left with is little to no information about how the game is controlled, or even how to start up the game.
You are given an almost non-existant config menu, with no choices for fullscreen/windowed, resolution, graphical options(other than scanlines, and something called chip fat that is basically just anti-aliasing), control customizations, and audio options(other than a 1 size fits all volume option that is little more than controlling the volume for NPPD Rush from windows audio volume). I will also add that when on the title screen, or the config menu, an invisible timer is counting down that after a certain time, will force you into the game. This means no walking off to do something else, nor idling at the title screen for trading cards.
Once you are in this atrocious game, you are greeted with once again, next to no information. WASD is used to move your vehicle around, and with the mouse you control a targeting reticule, and mouse 1 to fire bullets, with unlimited bullets at your disposal. There is a 5 minute timer that is counting down, and when it runs out, it's game over. In addition if I recall correctly you start with 200 health that vanishes pretty easily. It's to such a degree that often you won't even realize you are being hit by an enemies attack. This is thanks to the developers artistic choice in color schemes that makes it almost impossible to tell what's going on half the time(sucks for you if you're color blind, or prone to epileptic seizures), in addition to an abysmal view distance.
I will add, that even though the game appears to be full screen, there are black areas to the side of the playable area, that if my mouse cursor/targeting reticule made it into that area, I lost control of targeting, being replaced by a regular mouse cursor, and no longer the targeting reticule. This shouldn't even be possible with full screen, but you can thank the lack of options that I don't even know what the game is offering me in terms of window space/viewing options.
The controls, and game setup is simply no fun. As a developer you have free reign on how you design, whether to be user friendly, or to be rigidly stuck to an artistic design. The problem is that if your artistic design gets in the way of user playability, along with next to no information given to a new player, you WILL have negative reviews. You WILL be given little play time from the customers, and this may affect future game sales.
As it stands, the developer is stating in the forums that work is being done on a prequel, that will reveal more of the flimsy story, but if the game is anything like this game, you couldn't pay me to play it.

This game is a new twist on the old classic "Snake" but instead of a snake, you are a conga line made up of different heroes.  Heroes will randomly appear, and you simply touch them to add them to your conga line.  You die if you run into walls/monsters or if the health of your lead hero reaches zero.  The most exciting part of this game is trying to grow you line and finding the random power-ups.  You can be near death or overwhelmed and then suddenly a power-up saves the day.
If you sometimes just want a quick game to jump into, this game is perfect for a 15 minute session.  Also, there is an arena mode to this game where you can join a top guild to earn more gold.
This game taught me not to turn my nose up to mobile ports.  Fun is fun regardless of where the concept was first presented, especially if the controlls and price are fair.  8/10

Elements of team work include voice communications with captain and crew, repairs, and coordination just to name a few. This game is impossible to play without working together with your team.

I hadn't purchased a game for full price in a long while, but was itching to try this one after watching Robbaz's (YouTuber) playthrough for it. I saw that it was on sale via the Humbebundle store for $14.99, so I purchased it there.
The game is really fun, and if you like police simulators at all, you will enjoy this game - I will continue to play it and see how it develops. Unfortunately, however, I have to leave this at a "do not recommend," because I feel very disappointed at the product I was presented with. The simplest way for me to have given Enforcer a "thumbs up," would be for the developers to have this labelled as an early access/beta game. As an avid game reviewer, I CANNOT support this type of presentation. I have a fairly massive backlog of games in my library left to review (on top of my backlog of games to play), but I decided to bump this up to the very top, because I want as many people to avoid making the mistake I made in buying this game AND believing it to be a final, finished product. I went ahead and tried it out despite many of the negative reviews, but I implore everyone and anyone interested to wait to see whether or not the game actually develops further.
It both plays and feels like an early access game, and I would know, since I had a pretty potent early access game phase. Unlike the cesspool that is Starbound, I sincerely hope that the developers for Enforcer continue to work on the game, as it definitely has a lot of potential.
Now, on to the meat of the review.
The aesthetics are good, the detail in the environment and character models are decent. The rain effects are pretty weak, and there the vehicle damage is insignificant. There seems to be a very low pool of character models, with the main difference being the color of their outfits. The vehicle pool is also considerably tiny, and you will notice this very quickly. The sounds and music are average, but I prefer to play my own instead. While in your police cruiser, there will be chatter over the radio, but (again) that pool appears to also be small, so you will notice repetitions within the first hour of playing.
The controls may take a bit of effort to get used to - there is a pop-up help menu right when you begin, and a super quick tutorial after you select your character sex and name. The help menu also provides descriptions for most of the things you can currently do in the world, and I strongly recommend you take a look through everything to properly orient yourself in the Enforcer world. The learning curve is minimal to moderate, depending on your experience with police simulators. You can play the game on normal or realistic mode, the latter having permanent death and more rapid/frequent missions for you to do.
I've played this game quite a bit and enjoyed it a lot, however, many of the game elements show the unpolished quality common in early access game builds. For example, the AI is very basic, and many times you might ask a car to pull over, only to have them rear-end another car. Of course, the sloppiness of the AI will fool you, as this event will NOT constitute as an offence of any sort (at least on top of whatever offence that particular NPC might already have committed). I've seen a car speed through a red light and drive straight into a civilian crossing the street (not hurting the walker in any way, oddly enough) and - after pulling him over - the only recorded offence was speeding.
When you pull over vehicles - you can do so by toggling your cruiser's warning siren, or calling out on foot - you will be given a few options like: apply breathalyzer, write ticket, and check license and registration (this will show you any offences the driver has committed). Something I don't really like about the latter feature is that you can set up traffic cones to create a roadblock, then go through an endless lineup of cars and spam the "check license and registration" option. Even if the car had been speeding blocks away from you, you will magically know that they were speeding with your omniscient police powers. Note, that this is also a pretty cheap way to farm police points, which contribute to your police ranking (the higher your ranking, the more money you make after each shift, and the larger the variety of missions available to you).
After pulling people over, you can arrest drunk drivers and either put them in your squadcar (to take them to the police station), walk them to the station, or call a police van. Calling a police van, ambulance, or tow truck will bring you to a loading-type screen, and everything will occur behind-the-scenes, then bring you back to real-time. I don't mind this, considering how quickly you can pull over and check cars. Some NPCs might flee if you ask then to step out of the vehicle, and a quick taser shot will make them complaint again. Abusing your power (shooting them again with the taser, or even using your pistol) will cause considerable penalties to your police score.
One thing that really irritates me about this game is that it seems to only register "lethal force" as acceptable if the NPC shoots at you first. So, they can pull out and aim a gun at you, but until they shoot, you best use a taser, or worse - wait. NPCs commonly drop their weapons after taking one or two shots, and you MUST arrest them after this, or incur a penalty. I tried using a taser just to make sure they would remain complaint after the criminal dropped his gun, but received a heavy penalty for power abuse (annoyed me quite a bit). I also had a scenario where 2 NPCs were shooting at me (I still used only my pistol and not my sub-machinegun) - I killed the first person, and received a penalty for killing the second person because he hadn't fired at me yet. The crime/consequence algorithms can use a lot of refinement. It takes about two shots for you to die/be hospitalized, and the only way to heal is to sleep in your bed, or pay a fee at the hospital. Respawning (if you are playing normal) results in a considerable penalty to your police score.
I've taken a screenshot of a parked car hovering in the air, stuck in an odd position. I gave it a ticket and towed it - scoring some points. As I continued playing, I was disappointed to see so many cars randomly stuck in the air, at different elevations. Clearly, the bugginess throughout the game should speak volumes regarding its quality as a finished product.
You are the ONLY police officer in the small city (map is split into grids, and you can travel to each one by driving - or teleport whenever you leave your house).
There are three meters you must take care of - energy, hunger, and stress, You can eat while you are on duty (you must select "on duty" in your closet at home to start your shift), but you cannot sleep or recover stress. After enough time has passed, you will be able to end your shift by going to the police station and selecting that option. You can, however, continue to work, but your gauges will continue to fall. To fill these, you can sleep at home or eat at any place that sells food (you pay $5 when you interact with your fridge). Stress is recovered by going out with your friends or family, and each social call costs 4h of gametime. While off duty, you have a meter that will show you how long you can stay off for, and continuing to stay off duty after your time is up will cause you to progressively lose police points (you can get fired/lose the game if it falls low enough).
When you go for social calls, it will take you to a loading scene with a picture of whoever you decided to spend time with. A much more effective way (as of now) seems to be to buy a television in your house (use the online store on your laptop) and repeatedly watch tv. Doing so not only raises your stress, but also fills some of your energy (allowing you to skip sleeping in bed).

Review: An Epic Tale of Redwall : The Scout for the PC.
Soma Games has been working on their Redwall video game for a couple of years now, and anticpation is running high for fans of the series. Let's take a look at the final version of their take on the first official video game in the Redwall series.
It's tough to develop a great video game based on a book series, and games like The Scout are a good example of why.
I gotta say, I liked the setting of this game
The Redwall fantasy settings are rendered with glorious lighting effects decorating the terrain that is full of detail and hidden items. The creatures that you encounter are full of life, and I really enjoyed scouting the way and directing the Refugees to the abbey. The huge 3D areas are fun to explore, and you get to step into the feet (or paws?) of a mouse that lives in the Redwall Universe. Something I'm sure every fan of the series has wanted to do.
The story of the game is pretty good too, I mean, I couldn't get the full story effect with the available act but I feel like it that what I saw was a solid story with good characters that fit right into Brian Jacques book series. I'm really interested to see how the story progresses.
All that said, the Scout still feels like a sterotypical Adventure game with a Redwall theme. Which isn't quite a bad thing.
Sometimes it feels good to escape the rush and hustle of our daily lives and escape to the land of a fantasy land we have read so much about. I feel like the Scout does a great job encoprating the same feel I had when I first read the Redwall series.
Graphically speaking, this game has pretty good animations of the creatures, all of which is decently detailed and brings the characters to life effortlessly. I was able to put the character models to the test in the included Motions Lab, and I must say the animation did a pretty good job holding up.
This 3D world of Redwall comes to life in a cartoony-realisticy way, which is nice if you're a fan of the series.The visuals represent the objects they represent well.
All that being said, the game is still in Early Early Early access and has a lot of work to go. They will really need to improve generally every aspect of the game but that will all come in time.
In the end, if you're a fan of the Redwall Series I'd recommend this game. As long as you know what you're buying. It's not a AAA blockbuster video game, it's not a fully polished indie game that's blowing up steam, but it is a very interactive version of the Redwall universe, with a good story, that fans of the series will enjoy. If you're on the fence about this game I'd say go for it! It's a solid start from Soma Games that will improve over time.
Overall Score: 6.5 / 10

I will begin stating I have been following this project since nearly its inception and announcement to be funding via Kickstarter. This is for all intents and purposes an early access prototype meant to glean feedback from people like myself. Do not buy this game at this moment, if you are expecting it to be 100% complete and ready to play. It is early access for a reason. Giving it a negative review for being incomplete after willfully purchasing it as early access content is ignorant.
I do recommend it full heartedly for those who are willing to pick through, nail down details that can be improved upon, and are willing to provide that feedback to the developers. I've played through the polished level multiple times now. I still feel like I have missed things, and each time I have played I've found something new.
Positive for the polished level:
The lighting is stunning and gorgeous. The mystical feel creates a sense of things hiding in the shadows.
I am quite fond of the footprints (even if they do get left floating in the air after walking on a seesaw-ed bridge).
The physics are doing quite well, particularly when dashing, the mouse feels light on their feet and even skitters around corners as if they are trying to get a better grip while turning. The barrels have a hefty weight to them, and feel like they are as tough as the real deal.
The foley sound design is strong, though it could be toned down in some regards. I do feel that in the situation of the polished Old Moss Creek level, due to fleeing the village being raided, the music might not be quite fitting. It may be too easy listening, and there is no sense of urgency.
The enviroment does feel more grand and larger than Sophia, your playable character, and being that you are a mouse, I feel that is more immersive. Needing to have your companions help you with moving things feels like it is a natural need when you are so small.
The character models as design for anthropomorphic mice is a nice mesh of realism and cartoonish design. Sophia's clothing is quite intricate.
Currently as of Dec 18 2017 for suggesting to the dev team for improvements, here are the notes I took:
Sophia has a gaping neck where the polygons are missing while crossing balancing points
The dash x and y sensitivity of camera needs to be linked to normal camera
The dash animation looks more like "skipping" than dashing, I may suggest bringing the PC's head down more when dashing to avoid it looking quite so uncomfortable to run on all fours.
I would like the ability to scroll the camera out from the character more.
When walking, the tail looks unnatural being held up like a crook; relaxing it to a position more for just balance would suit the movement better.
Control bindings for interact are affected when dash was moved to left shift. Went from E to Space.
Jumping animation is jerky and cuts between launch and landing spots.
Footstep sounds could be brought down in volume slightly.
Is the pit under the logs you balance on supposed to be pitch black? I might add some depth to the rocks to make it feel more like a hole and less flat.

Take the original Legend of Zelda's level design and add a lot of clever puzzles and a sprinkling of humor and you have "iTTLE DEW." No, this is not a Zelda-like RPG. And, no, it does not try to be a Zelda-like RPG. Putting the graphics aside, this is it's own unique game.
The puzzles are worth the price of admission alone. They consist of pushing blocks, planting bombs, and and using your unique items to help you progress. Some of these puzzles can be quite challenging. One of the really clever things about this game is that some puzzles can be completed in different ways by using a different combination of your items. It makes for a lot of "ah ha" moments. There is also a real satisfaction in walking into a room that may seem utterly impossible only to discover the solution after reasoning things out.
There are enemies to fight, akin to Zelda, but they serve more to enhance the puzzle mechanic rather than offer an action spin. With that said, it does mix things up in the puzzle department and there are collectables that can be picked up for your efforts.
The only gripe i have with the game is that it is painfully short. It can be completed in a matter of minutes for more intelligent gamers out there; there is even an achievement for it. The average gamer will be able to experience most of what the game has to offer in two to three hours. The game does offer extras in terms of collectables that can be sought for completionists and a end game dungeon to really challenge your puzzle solving acumen. This can extend the game time some but over all it does leave you wanting more.

There are many 4X strategy games out there, but what any new player must realize is, Master of Orion is the father of all modern 4X space games. Since the first game, followed by the huge success of MOO2 (Master of Orion 2) and the mess the 3rd game was, this new one, is a modern copy of MOO2. Is that bad? Not really. While all the core concepts that made MOO2 the best 4X space game, Master of Orion is a gem. I played the old games to exaustion and do not let the low hours of play I have here on Steam foul you. I know this game very well.
Pros:
- A totally redesign of the old concept that works with new graphics and improved gameplay and new concepts that work.
- Total freedom of customization. You can setup your game in difficulty and the galaxy at your own taste.
- Many different types of victories
- Great implementation of Steam workshop and multiplayer.
- Great graphics effects and colors make the galaxy feel alive.
- Relaxing gameplay
- Real time battles, control your ships, give orders and let the AI take over but always ready for you to take control
- It's Master of Orion!
Cons:
- Game still needs some tweaking, since in late turns it takes some time to end a turn even on high end systems.
- DLC with extra 3 races that always were present in the franchise.
- Can be a bit repetitive in easy levels of difficulty.
About the DLC's I cannot recommend buying this game with all DLC's for full price. In particular the one that adds the extra 3 races since they were always present in the franchise.
If you really want to buy it now, go without the dlc's or wait for a sale and buy it all.
It is a great game with many different types of gameplay, the same tactics might not always work.
If you already know the franchise and still wondering if this is worthy, It is! imaging MOO2 with today technology.
If you never played the franchise and know some titles like galactic civilizations or Stellaris or even Sins of Solar Empire, then you really must have this game.
In other words, It is the epic Civilization in space!

The locations and the map and the designs are awesome, the enemies have fancy new moves and features on them and the companions are even somewhat romanceable. Apart from the main story, which kinda sucks hard after it reaches that certain point. The ending... is a mess, you only have about 2 separate endings with almost no variation, which feel unsatisfying. That is very ironic, since you have 4 different ways to finish the game. And as much as I appreciate the freedom of choice and the dialogue reactions which are quite impressive at times, just as much do I despise the lack of ending and drop in story quality.
If you wish to waste time, there are tons of ways to do so in the game with completely irrelevant settlements and crafting systems. Means: You can, at designated, fixed locations, build up a settlement with the materials that you find(aka collect all the trash that you see.. glue, bottles, cans...). You can copy pasta premade builds into the environment (which is a pain) and then have settlers move in there. The advantage that you get from this is... well... actually none apart from the possibility of sending artillery strikes onto a certain location. But that only works if you have collected all the trash that you needed in order to craft that stuff, gone through a lame quest line and a fatman can do the same... faster. Not as long though. Settlements have a border and a size limit. The building options are very underwhelming in terms of design and freedom. It's way too much fidgeting. Oh and they get regularly attacked. You have automated defense systems, but depending on your level, they dont do♥♥♥♥♥♥against the enemies unless you kinda hacked and spammed tons of them. So while youre in the middle of a quest, you often get the lovely notification that a settlement is being torn apart if youre not moving your♥♥♥♥♥there.
The weapon system works primarily with weapon modficiations. Which forces you, to collect even more trash(apart from the settlement). The design of most weapons that you can get in the start is questionable, since they look like a bunch of scrap metal taped together. The big disadvantage of the crafting and the settlements is that you need to collect ALL the trash that you can find in the game (plastic bottles, glue... really anything).  Considering that the trash weighs something and your inventory limit, you either die with traveling back and forth or you just cheat the hell out of this♥♥♥♥♥♥system.
Power armors are different now and need an exoskeleton (which you need to enter, exit, and park like a car) and fusion cores as 'fuel' to work. Since youre permanently digging through trash anyway due to the crafting system, youll find enough fusion cores. You can't put the exoskeleton in your inventory and you also can't teleport to your power armor. Have you ever wanted a Master Of Orion game that gave MOO2 the JJ Abrams treatment? Me either, but that's what Master Of Orion (4) is. It's got more than 2/3 of the features from MOO2, more than 2/3 of the playable races (by default), and over half the fun. It's the most logical reaction the developers could've had to the critical reception of the catastrophically boring, unpolished, yet innovative and deep MOO3.
I often get the impression that the voice cast is so great (you'll recognize voices from Borderlands and Invader Zim, for example) because of the development team's apparent "homage to MOO2" approach to designing this game. And you could say the same thing about the graphics. The musical score is forgettable, but importantly, fits the tone of the game and isn't intrusive enough to become irritating when repeatedly played. There was clearly a lot of thought behind the animating of the various characters, for that matter. The lighting, as odd as it is for a turn-based strategy game to have noteworthy lighting, adds a charming tone to the visuals. It's the most grandiose and beautiful monument to MOO2 that's ever been constructred... which is of middling consolation for its fans.
The gameplay, though, is functionally identical to Master Of Orion 2, other than the parts that were removed. Some of them are being added back into the game through patches. The tactical combat isn't as.... glaringly absent as before, due to a series of patches. The other races, evidently, are going to be added back into the game via DLC in 3-packs. No announcement (that I know of) has been made about the possible return of the Imsaes, Ithkul, or Evon to the game, or of any of the other races from previous MOOs. And the fun can be added back in through mods, to a surprising extent. There's a custom race option, but the balance is still botched (custom races are always objectively, statistically inferior to non-custom races, *which both sucks and blows at the same time), and hopefully will undergo yet another overhaul before a final version is settled on. And so far, we've got neither the delightful ground combat animations of MOO2 nor the delightful ground combat radio drama of MOO3.
So do I recommend this game? Sorta. This is a textbook example of a review that would've benefitted from a "sideways thumb" option. If you've got a lot of disposable income and you're sitting on the fence about this purchase, I'd encourage you to give it a chance. It's by no means a bad game. It's average. It doesn't make me worry for the future of the series, nor is it entertaining enough to compete with MOO2 and Sins Of A Solar Empire for my attention. It's definitely possible for a game with so much post-launch work behind it to eventually become even better than MOO2, especially with mod support (which it has), but it's clearly not there yet. For now it's a shallow but reasonably well-crafted Master Of Orion sequel. Its foundations are sturdy, its facade pictureque, and its insides unfurnished and empty. Yeah... that'll do. You get the idea.
*Edited for clarity

The developers are working very quick to patch and solve as many problems as possible. This is what an alpha should be, for developers to use for feedback from customers to improve the quality of the game.
Gameplay wise, the game is unique in its own way, I see a lot of potential for future updates to make combat a bit more fluid, especially during melee.
The atmosphere is amazing, some maps are snowy, stormy, or sunny, and the ambient sounds can really trigger some ASMRs if you are a nature lover like myself.
Graphically, the game looks beautifully, and same can be said for how well it runs. I have an EVGA GTX 1070 and an i5 Intel Core 4690k.
The mechanics revolve on team work more so than any other game I have ever played, and that includes CS:GO. The community seems to be inviting and very friendly. I see people help newcomers all the time. Every community has its share of toxic players, but I haven't encountered any so far. Elements of team work include voice communications with captain and crew, repairs, and coordination just to name a few. This game is impossible to play without working together with your team.
Overall, for 19.99, this game is a must, and they aren't asking to much unlike many of the discarded alphas we have seen in the past. This game has my full support.

If you love game development and if you love Theme Hospital then you will love this one. Given this is early access and room for heaps of improvement is brutally obvious, the game is shaping up to a solid management simulation in the likes of Bullfrog creations. It even sprinkles some humor over the game to keep things interesting.
There is depth in gameplay which is missing from Game Dev Tycoon (another good game in its own right). You need proper planning and the game, in its current state, is unforgiving. You cannot resize rooms! Choices like "should I place that expensive one star plant or the cheap one star plant?" become important as you grow a bond with your virtual employees. Sometimes you feel like rewarding them by throwing in an extra fan.
The game follows accurate history of game development and I felt nostalgic when I could easily relate to 16-bit graphics being a selling point.
I highly recommend you try it out and experience it for yourself but keep in mind : EARLY ACCESS

DO NOT WASTE YOUR MONEY. This game leaves a lot to be desired and honestly feels like an early release at best. It absolutely is NOT worth the $19.99 at this point in its production and will need many large updates to make it anywhere close to worth its asking price. I will list some pros and cons:
Pros:
-It's a police simulator and those are hard to come by, if nothing else it's an attempt to deliver a very demanded but rare game format
-It's ambitious: There are many features such as buying police cars, living life off work, etc. which are nice on first play
-Practial button layout
Cons:
-Really, really clunky - the car driving and handling may be some of the worst I've ever tried. Sure having features such as having to turn on the engine and the realistic idle movement of drive and reverse are fun in theory, but the steering controls manage to be un and/or late responsive while the gas and reverse are over-responsive. It's horrible. Running and crouching aren't much better.
-This game doesn't look pretty. I get that it's not a large studio producing it but if you're going to charge me $20 at least have more than five car and character models in the game
-Everyone in this game has a gun. I have done 10 missions and 9/10 ended with the suspect pulling a gun
-Shooting controls are very poor - the gun often will not fire the first few shots unless you zoom in, which can lead to getting you killed
-Boring mission types - There are a variety of missions and the idea of questioning suspects and searching nearby buildings is a great one, but the tips are only clothing descriptions and all the searches end in you having to gun down a pistol wielding suspect
-Simple features such as tow trucks, ambulance calls, and police pick up lack an animation and instead take you to a brief load screen before returning you to where you were witht he action performed - things like this REALLY make it feel like an early access
-Whoever developed it is not an English speaker and google translate is not flawless. Many spelling or wording mistakes really prevent it from having a professional, clean feal
In conclusion, don't buy this game. I was incredibly disappointed with this game. I was quite excited that a new police simulator was finally being produced as there are barely any available. Don't get me wrong, I know it is a small project and wouldn't be upset if this were an early release, but I paid a decent price for it for far from a decent product. On the very bare outside it looks similar to LCPDFR, but don't be fooled. This game is far from being worth its asking price and will need some serious updating in the control, mission, and visual department before it comes close its asking price.

The gunplay can get a little wonky when foes get up close, and getting into cover can be a bit hit and miss - but these are small gripes really when most of the gameplay is kung fu brilliance.

- The review should come after I finished everything, even improvements! Now it happens immediately after I selected 'release game'.
- I am not sure, but it seems that even if I started repaying my bank loan, when I have enough money to repay the whole amount, the original amount will be taken from my account.

- There are tons of topics to research. With a 4-member-team I can easily reach a point when I do not really have anything to do just reasearching new topics. Rating: 7/10
Overview: Third Person Hack and Slash
The Good
+ For a budget title, the graphics look good with some decent graphical options
+ Every level has a different environment and atmosphere. The levels have good pacing, providing a good mix of combat and puzzle solving with some minor exploration.
+ The gameplay mechanics are solid. You can rewind time, allowing you to create clones of yourself. This ability can be used in combat to defeat enemies or used to solve some of the puzzles. The puzzles themselves are not terribly difficult.
+ Equip different equipment providing different bonuses to stats
+ Controls well
The Average:
Story, characters, voice acting are all average. The story is decent enough but the characters are boring and its hard to care about what is going on.
The game controls well enough but combat is lackluster. The biggest negative; your attacks have no weight or feeling to them, nor is there any good feedback when you or an enemy attack. There are no combos to speak of so you just mash the same two buttons over again.
The Bad:
- vsync is broken
- fell through the floor a few times.
Conclusion:
If Devil May Cry and Bayonetta are summer blockbuster movies, than Baldes of Time is the straight to TV movie on Lifetime network. It borrows different elements from different games and puts it together but doesn’t do it well enough. It’s a fun game for what it is but don’t expect much more.

I was skeptical about XCOM2. The notion that the alien won the war lead me to suspect the game was taking a dramatically new direction, and I wasn't sure that the developer could do so effectively. There was no underground base anymore: you're on a ship, travelling from region to region - even that worried me. When I saw that the game was no longer "spooky" or intimidating, I was very much dissapointed. When I saw many of the enemies had been reimagined, I was troubled again. When I saw that completely new enemies had been created, which look less classic alien lore than they do irrational scifi fantasy molded to appeal to teenagers (Shieldbearer, Avatar), I was greatly concerned.
Watching gameplay, I observed that units look more like teenage fashion models than soldiers. That the customization options concentrated on teenage apparel and exotic fantasy appeareances. There were no standard kevlar helmets, but there were dozens of mohawks to choose from. I saw that the game's launch was plagued by bugs. I saw that the DLC concentrated on additional non-militaristic apparel, and "rulers" who were players weren't entertained by but instead immensely frustrated with, to the point of disabling the DLC which they had purchased. I saw the mission timers and was frustrated by the idea of being forced to abandon the tactics of scouting and bounding in favor of sprinting blindly into the unknown, because there's no time. I saw the doomsday clock, wasn't sure what it was about or how to deal with it - it was less straight-forward than the previous XCOM incarnation. I saw the immense number of complaints in the forum, and I saw the developer responding to many of those complaints with bans, not solutions. I was very worried that the game was bad, and that it wasn't going to be improved.
Then I saw the game on sale, at a substantial discount. I hadn't even played the game, but I felt that I already disliked it. I decided to give XCOM 2 a fair chance. I bought the game. After installing and starting XCOM 2, it crashed on the strategy screen, before even my first mission. That was absolutely not the last crash. I found myself disappointed again and again. "Soldier" appearances were even worse than I had I believed. Graduating beyond the basic gear, the armors and weapons look increasingly ridiculous, and are unmistakably ridiculous by the final tiers. Mods were absolutely necessary to remedy this, because with all the DLC offered, it was apparently never thought to offer realistic kits beyond the basic gear.
In a game of tactical warfare, emphasizing the use of cover and concealment, one would think a larger emphasis would be placed on gear which looks like what you might expect the soldiers of the future to wear. After all, several counties are already developing full armor suits, combat robots and so forth - one need only look at these publically viewable protoypes to estimate what the future of combat will look like. Instead, they abandoned realistic gear and camoflage for elaborate fantasy appearances, with even an assortment of lights on their gear to ensure any enemy would see their soldiers long before the player's soldiers see the enemy. Instead of looking at military gear for inspiration, they looked at Fallout, teenage fashion and cartoons.
None of the improvements I would have expected were present. An entirely different direction was pursued. The developers didn't increase the spooky atmosphere to an experience of sheer horror, but the spookiness was instead abandoned entirely. They didn't better embrace alien lore to produce enemies with appearances and behavior comparable to the decades of UFO/abduction reports, or classic alien films. They didn't offer a uniform manager, so that, as military organizations do, the player could quickly equip every member of his/her squad with the same appearance - a uniform. Luckily, there's a mod for that. The game doesn't inform the user of the environment the squad will be deployed into, so that appropriate camoflage can be utilized. Luckily there's a mod for that too. They didn't make it so that there's bonuses based on the camoflage/colors used in unit appearances, for example a concealment bonus when wearing black at night. There's no reconnaissance drone allowing for constistent observation of the battlefield, despite that the game's Gremlin drones could have offered such a capacity very easily, and in fact nearly do - except the Gremlin can only surveil once per operation. Being able to scout ahead consistently via UAV would have been a great improvement. Luckily, there's a mod for this.
In general, the story's short and it's not very interesting. The ending is disappointing, but I won't spoil that. However. The game is very familiar. It's also entertaining. With the aid of mods, one can overcome the majority of this title's shortcomings. There will still be crashes. You can even mod out the doomsday clock and battle timers, but I've found they're nothing to worry about. I've never lost a battle because of running out of time, and I've never lost the game because of the doomsday clock, or at all, for that that matter. The maps are now generated randomly, which means that sometimes they will be greatly unbalanced, if not impossible. I've played at least one impossible map, where after landing my soldiers, I was surrounded by an extensive horde of powerful enemies. Three "pods," to be exact. They each had cover nearby. My soldiers didn't. It was near the beginning of the game. It was, I believe, four squadies kitted with basic gear, standing in the open, with no cover available, against nine entrenched adversaries, in the first turn, on Rookie difficulty. I've played several battles which were ridiculous, on Rookie, Veteran and Commander difficulty, but that none were ever as bad as that one. Many were difficult, but none were impossible, aside from the one which I just described.
If you're skeptical about XCOM 2, don't be. It's very similar to the previous incarnations and if you enjoyed those, you'll like this. Whether or not the DLCs are worth buying, however, is another question entirely. Definitely buy the base game. If the game's bundled at an amazing discount, then go for the bundle. You can disable to DLC if you find that it's frustrating for you, or you can avoid the leaders without disabling the DLC by never bothering them in the "nest" mission. They won't appear in any of your battles if you don't. If you're a fashion minded teenager or a kid who things gothic style weapons are cool, then the DLC is definitely for you. The base game is definitely worth buying for anyone who was interested enough to read this full review. If you read all of this, I guarantee you won't regret buying this XCOM 2. It's fun, despite its many problems.

Despair is a cheap horror indie game, but will you want to play it ?
Story doesn't really make sense. You play as a woman who walks around a subway station to find out what happened to the other passengers on the train.
The game is a walking simulator. All you do is walk around in dark tunnels and that's it. There's no jump scares and there's nothing that can kill you.  There is one puzzle in this game, but it's not even really a puzzle.
Audio is pretty normal things you hear in a horror game. Footstep noises, door creeks and stuff like that. There's no music to speak of what so ever.
Graphics are a bunch of slapped together Unity assets. There's not much to speak of. The entire game looks bland and really dark. You use a flashlight that can run out of batteries and if you do, you're pretty much screwed cause you can't see anything.
The game is incredibly easy. There's nothing that can hurt and the only thing that can actually make you restart is running out of batteries.
Level design is this games biggest flaw (out of all of the flaws). During the game you enter a warehouse and it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to navigate, cause everything looks the same. The level design is an absolute mess.
Despair took me 30 minutes to finish. There is no replay value what so ever. I got the game for 9 cents so I didn't get ripped off, but no matter what don't get this game at full price. If you do want to check it out only buy it during a sale.
The game is pretty buggy. I once bugged the game out and it took away all of my batteries and gave me one that never ran out until I went into another section of the game which took away the never ending battery and gave me one battery.  The controls are also a problem. You have to press B to change the batteries in the flashlight and the character doesn't always do what you tell her to do.
Overall Despair is a really bad game. If the game is anything to go by there's also a sequel in the works. The game is boring, not scary and just down right painful.  I really can't recommend the game to anyone. Don't waste money on this game. Just skip it. I give Despair a 2/10

Good enough to play for around 100 hours as it is. I wouldn't probably play it for more.
Each one of the currently existing gamemodes just has a small gripes that make them something wouldn't want to do forever.
Bowling is slow - yeah, real bowling is slow too, but bowling in Tower is reaaal slow. There's no reason for the score card to not be on-screen UI to avoid having to show the bowling monitors so often. The strategy is thin (the spin meter goes too fast and makes it feel weird), and the bowling alley just feels kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥, it's not very well lit and it doesn't loolk all that great. It also doesn't make much money considering how long it takes.
Laser Tag is often unbalanced, hard to find games, similar to Trivia and Bowling because everyone is busy gambling on populated servers, and the arena is too big so you run around for ages trying to find each other as soon as it gets down to 2v2 or less.
The casino seems to be the most popular area by far, but all the machines except Double or Nothing go excruciatingly slow and just destroy your soul. I wanna waste my money fast, damnit! Also, you'll basically never win any of the wheel games except the knight one which is just a slog of hoping the dragon dies soon as you pour more and more money into the machine hoping to get to the end already.
Also, people are probably botting everywhere in casinos because the bot check is easily bypassed by smart bots, AND it messes up sometimes causing real humans to have their machines stolen.. by someone who's just going to run a bot on it!
Ball Race seems to have a bad host advantage and also is one of many games where you literally do not interact with players except trying to get more bonuses than them. In minigolf this is expected, but it'd be nice if Ball Race had an  'enable collision' modifier for messing around? In mingolf too, why not?
Minigolf has... problems. Many of the maps are inconsistent and will just screw you over randomly. Getting balls stuck under moving objects, getting a ball up against a rotating circle causing it to not even allow you to put anymore (just gotta wait for the afk timer to give you extra strokes. there is no reset ball or undo stroke button at all!! christ just give us one per game or something for when it breaks). Cannons will shoot you into the ocean repeatedly. Taiko drums will bounce you out of bounds. Ramps will let you phase through them. These problems are exacerbated when connected to a host with a bad framerate and/or ping I believe.
Virus is a bit too thin, it can be fun and intense but it just feels.. lacking. Also, I hope you like shotguns and entire teams managing to stay in one spot and camp the only virus player for most of the rounds.
Typing Derby is fun but if you win early it takes forever to end and you cannot do anything until the game ends. Can't get up, walk, talk over voice, etc..
Ultimate Chimera Hunt is fun but it's not for everyone. It's also very latency-sensitive, like most games in Tower Unite.
Speaking of voice, it's awful. It's like they decided to take the worst parts of GMod voice and intentionally recreate it. Some players are ear-hurtingly loud somehow, but other players are too quiet to hear, and the voice quality is less than Speex/Discord by far, so just use discord with friends and turn the ingame voice way down. Unfortunately this means few people actually use voice ingame in public spaces and when they do it's mostly just kind of grating and hard to understand.
The best thing by far is the furniture and condo decorating. Honestly the minigames are just sort of a distraction and this is the meat of things. The character customization is also still fairly basic but has potential even in its' current state with no custom haircuts at all, and 5 sets of clothing for both models. There are a fair amount of hats, some glasses, a wristband, a watch and a tie at least, and all colors can be customized freely.

So, after my disappointment with The Prodigy, I was set to never touch this series again - once I had gone back and finished it, of course. A family member assured me I was wrong and that the series got better in The Hero Project - to their credit, they were right.
However, even in that case, THP barely struggles to make *average*. The writing style continues to be quite sophomoric and not in the entertaining sense of being young. It's sophomoric in the sense of awkward phrasing, juvenile handling of sex and bizarre, immersion-shattering rants about correct gender pronouns. It's immature and banal. Look, I get that more games should deal with sex and gender, and I get that interactive fiction is one of the best genres for it, but Zachary Sergi needs to handle it with a bit more deftness. Credit for attempting it.
To Sergi's additional credit, there are some interesting choices in this game. I thought many of the ones relating to Null and Lucky were quite good and hard to choose from. Unfortunately, much like the previous entry in the series, THP suffers from the stark feeling of being stuck on rails with an author that's waiting to jump out and go 'aha!' at you for not picking the right choice (while giving you no indication of what might be the right choice unless you *pay for it as an in-game app store-esque purchase*. THP, however, seems to have less of those ridiculous options like The Prodigy had (infilrating and forgetting to take off your hero costume, anyone?) - so, that's some improvement. But it's still not embracing the strength of an interactive medium because good IF rewards choices and does its best to disguise the rails (eg; Choice of Robots).
Much of the worldbuilding and setting continues to be a bit on the nose - again, it's very sophomorric. The fact that Sergi continues to interject 'slugger' into so many sentences as a catch all term that seems to be a general epithet, noun, verb, adjective and so on is lazy. Honestly, if there is one thing I could remove from this whole trilogy, it's this word. As a whole, the world feels very derivative of superhero comics and doesn't offer much in the way of originality.
For a simple premise (superhero reality TV) the plot has too many characters (of course, expecting you to remember/care about all of them) and a slow development where things just seem to happen. I'm not sure how much control over my story I actually had, thanks to the aforementioned of feeling like I'm on rails. What's worse, is that the characters aren't particularly likeable - again, due to the writing style.
So, what's good about it? Well, there's a fair bit of customisation. If you're looking to feel like you're in a superhero story and you want a bit of a self-insert fantasy where you can craft your dreamworld to exacting specifications then this is for you. If you want something that advances the medium of IF, offers interesting, branching choices with clever writing and wit - avoid. As someone who looks for the latter, I cannot recommend THP.
Additionally, I ran into a bug near the end that caused me to need to restart my entire story. I won't mark the game down for that but it was quite unfortunate.

Mad Games Tycoon starts off just like GDS and GDT, you start off in a garage and it's a struggle to release a good first game, however once you have had your first good title, the game seems to get too easy, you just get better and very rarely fail, which is a shame as it would add to the realism if you made bad games as well as good ones.
Mad Games Tycoon has all the features you love from GDS and GDT, but expands up on them, not only do you make games, you also build the studio and you can become an exclusively Production compay only company, which is a really good feature, you build a Production facility and a Store House and then you can make money from selling other companies games and with this you can fail if you don't pick the right game to publish.
There is a feature that allows you to buy rights to Movies and Books and then produce a game from that book or movie, they have their popularity and also have their funny parodies of other Movies and Books, which some of them are quite funny and relevant to todays Books and Movies.
The work spaces you get to buy and occupy are pretty big and fairly cheap as well, the only problem is when you get to the final Office, it becomes a little laggy, this is especially noticable in the Hire menu, but this is the only lag that I have spotted so far.
The menus are easy to navigate and simple to use, though they do look like they have been pulled from a mobile game, the scrolling is a little slow though, but this is by no means an issue.
After roughly 6 hours of playing I seem to have done everyhting in the game, it progresses a lot faster than GDT and GDS, which I hope is by design for future features.
You can buy out your competitors which allow you to publish their games if you want or you can let them continue as they are, though they don't seem to make you money unless you publish for them.
Pros:
Cons:
Overall I find Mad Games Tycoon a very enjoyable game, I will be looking forward to what the devs have planned in the future.

First off: this is a great game, ignore all the naysayers.
This game maintains the ambience and feel of the old Master of Orion series whilst still providing a much improved and modernized UI.
A lot of people criticise the choice to use star lanes from MOO3 instead of the fly anywhere  within range ability from MOO1&2.  Since most people skipped MOO3 this is a departure from what they remembered from MOo2.
It's neither a superior or inferior solution but presents a different set of strategies.  With star lanes you can set up choke points, you can build military outposts and more physically define your species borders.  It's not "realistic" but neither are space bears, it's a game and it adds an interesting strategic layer.
The graphics, the voice acting, the humour is all there; although seeing the same joke for the 3rd or 4th or 100th time loses the eventual appeal.
The AI isn't the smartest, but there are multiple difficult levels and for anyone wanting a real challenge they can create a custom race and give themselves any handicap they like.
For those coming from MOO2, the AI is no worse than in that game.  It is a lot more trusting than the AI in Civilization and a lot less likely to act in bizarre random ways.   Unlike civ if you've got a good relationship and a non aggression pact, trading and research agreements in MOO you're not likely to be declared war on by that species.
I've not encountered any bugs in two play throughs.

I have a feeling this will be one of the games I keep replaying over the upcoming years, always on rotation.

I don’ t think I’ve ever written a review of a space strategy game without mentioning Master of Orion, the granddaddy of the genre  and a title which it’s illegal to look back on without wearing rose tinted glasses.
There’s a reason everyone has fond memories of MOO, it was a great game in its day and deserves all the rosy hued love it gets, of course if you played it now you’d struggle to get past its aging graphics and dated game play, but who’d want to risk tarnishing those memories by playing MOO again now anyway?
It’s not like there aren’t plenty of more recent space 4x titles out there to scratch your galactic empire building itch.
Elton John and the Lion King had it right, what goes around comes around, it's the circle of life.
When you lived long enough you'll notice songs that you remember from years ago being re-released by "modern artists" who'll inevitably have fiddled with the track and aren't singing it properly.
There'll be movie re-makes which just aren't the same and worse, movie re-inventions where they get it wrong on purpose!
Clothes, hairstyles, the economy, war and peace, it's all cyclical.
If you wait long enough, what's old will inevitably be new again and it seems we've waited long enough in the case of Master of Orion, because it's back!
The first thing you're going to notice when you fire up Master of Orion: Conquer the Stars (to give it it's full title) is just how glossy and polished everything looks.
From the beautifully rendered opening cinematic to the animated menu backdrops , your initial moments with the game are so shiny you can't help but have high expectations of what's to come.
If you're old enough to have played the original Master of Orion (but young enough to still be able to remember it!) you should recognise the ten races available to you when you set up your first game.
The cat-like Mrrshan, the robotic Meklar and the insectoid Clackon. they're all back and all looking better than ever.
It's a nostalgia kick and will bring a smile your old gamers face.
Although when it's time to choose your galaxy size that smile may fade a little (depending on your expectations), even the largest option seems a little on the small side compared to other recent space strategy releases.
Stellaris gives you a galaxy comprising of one thousand star systems, Galactic Civilization III can give you a maximum of around 1500 Stars (although I haven't counted, so that might be a bit off).
So What's the largest playing area in new MOO?
A measly 100 systems!
Now don't get me wrong, if you're looking for a quick game (relatively speaking) then this is absolutely fine, but if you're the type who sets your research speed to slow before settling down for the long haul in a vast galaxy then you're likely to be disappointed with your options here.
Once you've set your galaxy size and starting options there are other issue which gamers looking for a sense of realism might find annoying.
Star systems generally don't have enough orbital bodies, systems can only handle a maximum of 5 planets plus the odd moon or two if you're lucky, It's not a huge issue but unfortunately it's also not the only one.
If you play a sandbox game as the humans,  you'd at least expect Sol to be a yellow type star right?
Well don't get your hopes up,  you could just as likely end up with a red or blue sun as a yellow one, it seems to be a random element during galactic generation.
There isn't even a nod towards any sense of realism in the generation of the planets either. You'll get a continental class planet, Earth, not that it'll be called that, orbiting in a random position around a randomly coloured Sun.
As I said earlier, MOO can only handle a maximum of five planets around a star, so you'd think we'd at least  get Mercury through to Jupiter in the Sol system, but again no.
There'll be a few random planets labelled Sol 1 through Sol 5 (if you're lucky enough to get 5 planets that is.)
This isn't an issue if you're playing an alien race or the alternate Terrans available in the collector's edition of the game, but play as vanilla humans and this is very jarring.
So after taking a deep breath and reminding yourself it's just a game and doesn't need to acknowledge realism,  it's time to actually play it.
Starting out is pretty standard for any turn based Space 4x title, we all know the drill by now. You send out your scout ships to explore your neighbourhood, you build colony ships to grab any nearby planets worth having and send out your construction ships to build "stuff" to give you an edge, stations, mines, surveillance outposts etc.
It's worth noting here that MOO takes the star lane approach to interstellar travel. Whilst it will occasionally let you head off into empty space with your survey ship to investigate the odd anomaly, for the most part you need to stick to the space roads provided.
Planetary construction also follows a familiar vein.
Click on a planet you control, Pick the building you want to construct and wait for it to finish building to get the relevant boost to food, research, production etc. then rinse and repeat.
This isn't a critisism, this is how all these games play, and "if it's not broke don't try to fix it"
It's all generic  4X fun.
The ship design mechanics are well presented with a polished interface which looks great.
Each hull type has a maximum capacity which you can fill up with a variety of core systems (engines, shields etc), weapons systems(pew, pew) and specialised systems (magic gadgets which tinker with your weapon damage and shield strength, that sort of thing). It's all done through a simple, clean drag and drop mechanic, it's not revolutionary but it does the job well enough and as I said, it looks pretty good too.
Of course you're going to need to research all these fancy gadgets before you get to play with them.
The research interface is a glossy affair which also looks great. It's presented by a chatty advisor who (if you're playing as the human empire) peers at you over her glasses expectantly whilst you peruse the options available from the 70+ technological advancements you'll eventually unlock.
There are some important decisions along the way too, research a technology and you may be given an choice regarding which benefit it unlocks, whichever one you don't choose could well be locked to you for the rest of your game, it's a nice touch and adds to the replayabilty.
The diplomacy interface is highly polished and looks great (noticing a trend yet? ).
From the diplomacy menu  all the races you've met appear as holograms with some basic information about their colonies and fleets if known.
Click for an audience and you're welcomed into the aesthetic halls of your chosen races leader where you can negotiate trade deals, treaties or wars.
It's worth noting that all the races (just like your own advisors) are superbly voiced.
There are some big names behind the voices in Master of Orion. Worf son of Mogh, Luke son of Anakin and Lieutenant Barclay from Star Trek (or Murdock from the A-Team if you prefer) are but a few of the actors onboard, even John de Lancie has been let out of the Q Continuum to voice the human emperor.
It adds a huge amount to the quality of the experience having genuinely talented actors lend their voices to the game and fits with the cinematic polish perfectly.
It always pays to keep an eye on your neighbours too and that's where your spy network comes in.

I've been playing Master of Orion games since the original came out in 1993.  Since then, I've always had a copy of MOO & MOO2 on every computer I've owned.  I still have the original manuals as well.    I, like almost everyone else, experienced the extreme disappointment that was MOO3.   So, I wasn't overly optimistic for a reboot.
That being said, I must say that overall I am pleasantly surprised by this game.  Yes, it does have some flaws which I'll get into later, but what struck me the most is that it feels like I'm playing Master of Orion.  You can tell the developers put a lot of love into this game and tried to recapture the magic of the originals, and I think they succeeded.  The iconic races are all there, and have their own unique flavor.  The soundtrack is a delightful remake of the original's.   And the technology tree contains the advancements we all know and love.
Outside of that, they've also managed to improve the managementment aspects of the game without overly simplifying them.  Planet management is smooth and easy, the sitrep updates let you know what's going on, and my favorite aspect is the game will warn you if you have any outstanding actions to address or ships that need to be moved when you click the End Turn button.   It reminds me of the simplicity of MOO1 where you can just sit down and enjoy playing the game.
The game however, is not without some flaws.   It still has balance issues and bugs that need to be fixed by the development team.  The combat, while enjoyable to watch the first few times, quickly becomes repetitive - as you lack a lot of fine control on the 3d battle map.   Many die hard fans (myself included) had hoped NGD would include a turn-based tactical combat option, similar to the originals.  But alas, that was not the case.
Another complaint is that the game uses star lanes, where MOO1 & 2 did not.  This doesn't bother me as much as I like the idea of choke points. However, I wish they did include an option to turn them off and play without them for those that  want it to feel more like the originals.
Lack of race customization is another complaint I hear often about the game.   On the surface, you get similar customization to Master of Orion 2 where you're able to take any race in the game and tweak them as you see fit.    What you don't get is the ability to create an entirely new custom race.    This seems to be because each race is tied to its associated ship models.  Ideally, I'd like to see you be able to create a new race and choose the ship model family you'd like to use for it.
So, to sum up - I feel this is a fine successor to Master of Orion 1 & 2.   If you're looking for deep strategy and tons of options - check out a different game, like Stellaris.   But if you're looking to curl up with a relaxing game on a Sunday afternoon and just have a good time - I'd highly recommend this game.   Especially if you're a fan of the originals.
After today's update I'm glad to see the developers haven't given up hope and are still working on fixing and improving this game.  I hope they continue to improve and add new (desirable) features to the game in the years to come.  With a bit of work and polish this game has the ability to (one day) become THE Master of Orion game.
