Bought this game as soon as it hit early access, gave feedback during its developement, read the forums constantly for the last year or more.... hugely disappointed.
To be fair, I think the theming is excellent.  I like the stupid robot news anchors.  I love the voice acting.  The graphics are wonderful.  The space combat LOOKS really interesting and fun (gameplay wise it is atrocious though).  The music fits really well.  Each of the alien races have a leader and an advisor, all of which are very interesting and fun (though don't play the bird people, because the advisor is unbearable).  Every race has a set of spies and leaders you can recruit which give you that XCOM feeling of attachment.  I love that each race has its own feel to it, sadly the GAMEPLAY of each race plays almost identical.
The first wrong step for the game was not doing Turn Based combat, every other decision from then on was totally botched.  Trying to fit a real time combat system into a game that was ENTIRELY designed around having turn based combat just didnt work.  Every tech upgrade you could get just felt like getting a +1 to the end of the last technology (or a -1 if you don't pick missles, which are the only worthwhile weapon).  Nothing that you research/trade/steal signficantly changes the way you play the game.  Nothing that your opponents do significantly changes the way you play your game.  Essentially, once you have defeated your first neighbor, the game is over, as its just a repeat of defeating each neighbor until they are all dead.
Another huge misstep was going away from an open universe design with fuel restrictions to limit your ship travel distance.  In this game you are able to map out nearly the entire universe with your very first scout.  There wasn't any mystery as to where something important might be hiding, or what interesting thing you might find on the other side of that alien territory once you defeated them.  After about turn 100 you've seen everything (in a 500ish turn game, depending on universe size).
If only they had hired someone who knows how to make actual turn based games.  Perhaps even hiring someone from the board game industry to iron out some of these obvious problems.  The GAME part of this game is bad.  They tried, they really did - but they either didn't have enough time, or simply didn't have the talent to pull it off.
I would give this game a 3/10.  Wouldn't recommend anyone buy it, even on sale.  I think, if you can stand the oldschool graphics, just buy MOO2 - you won't regret it.

The perfect example of a cash grab using a famous series. Not sure if Master of Orion series will ever recover from this one, sadly.
Original Review 3/1/2017 :
I'm going to have to go ahead and say I don't recommend the game at its current price. While it is an honorable start to being a glorious 4x space stategy game, and it does feel a lot more like MOO to me than MOO 3 did.... overall the experience just kind of peeters out after an unsatisfactory amount of time.
Pros :
- Most of the UI functions smoothly
- A good deal of MOO lore is included
- FPS is good and stable on a mid-range machine, even with all graphics options turned up
- The graphics are acceptable, but nothing special
- MUCH less buggy than 1 year ago, but still very buggy
Cons :
- I think "terrible" is actually a poor word to use to describe the AI. The right word is "ridiculous." Nothing they do makes sense
- AI uses cheats instead of tactics at higher difficulty levels to become harder
- The opening video seems to lag for me, not sure what that's all about
- Turn length increases far too quickly
- Workshop community, as always, is trying its best... but the game has design limitations currently which are severely limiting the depth, functionability, and compatibility of the mods.
- Community agrees that game is only about 1/2 done, at most, but updates have screeched to a halt in the last few months. Furthermore the devs have been in much less communication with the community than they had been.
- The pirates function way too shallow fo my taste. They essentially just attack as soon as their ships are spawned. They do not at all feel like their own hybrid civilization. No way to form diplomacy with them either. I know this is uncommon in 4x games anyway, but it really is a feature that would add depth... if you could have a back-door way of getting on the good side of pirates, but bad side of everyone else in doing so.
- Random pauses between screens at time, especially when entering a battle.
- Tech tree is too short, too shallow, too streamlined, too everything that makes a tech tree unexciting
- Very limited customization options for galaxies. Even with mods.
- The largest galaxy type that comes with the game would be considered medium in most 4x games.
- Can't rename planets/star systems
- Quite possibly some of the most underwhelming paid DLC I've ever seen for this genre of game
- They made all the leaders/species look way too cartoony in most instances. I think using these graphics but sticking to MOO 1 and 2 lore (it seemed like a rather rustic, raw, and Babylon 5-ish universe did it not? Now it feels like Shrek in Space)
The game felt like it was progressing quickly until the fall so perhaps the devs are just working on something big, let's hope so. But until then, thumbs down.
Also, I have quite a bit more experience than the 8.5 hours recorded on steam.

Not sure why there is all these negative reviews.  Is the game worth $4, no.... Worth a buck on sale, maybe.
Whether this game is worth having depends on whether you like retro top-down twin stick shooters---you move using WASD and have 360 degree range of shooting using your mouse to direct endless stream of bullets.  The shooting goes off screen, so one of the basic strategies in this game is to shoot as much stuff as possible off screen, which requires keeping a bit of a mental of map of the area since you only see a screenful at any one time.  It does remind me of some old NES games, but has a different flavor, given the subject matter that is a bit dark.   Also to be honest, this game is little more than running around shooting and collecting things.  The story, as it is, is infinitely ignorable.
Granted the game is not the latest greatest twinstick shooter, but unlike many of that genre, this is relatively easy to play for some mindless fun.   While this game has the tag of bullet hell, it does not really fall in that subgenre, since you can generally avoid being immersed in a screenful of bullets, which is typically not an option in a true bullet hell shooter.
The game lacks basic stuff like configuring options, and even quiting (use Q) is initially obvious, but looking past these minor shortcomings, this game can lead to a few hours of mild enjoyment for those that appreciate mindless twin stick shooters.

For anyone with an interest in police work, this is a fairly good game. The calls are varied and the situations feel organic with the suspects reacting in a believable manner. For example, drunks and thieves are unlikely to pull a gun on you (but much more likely to flee) while hardcore criminals with drug raps and worse tend to violently object to your stopping their crime sprees. Also, the locations of the criminals are not automatic and sometimes you just have to go around looking for them either from witness descriptions or behaviour described in the initial call (example: rowdy drunk). The game does give you hints after a time in the form of radio updates about the rough location of the suspect(s), if you are worried about never finding the perps.
The police procedures are sometimes a bit off (you generally want to cuff the perps before searching them, devs...) but overall the basics are there. Note that this game is meant for people who WANT to follow police procedure. If you want to mess around, the game basically ignores it and it will feel weird. But then again, if you just want to mess around in an open world, why are you here? GTA series are that way --->
The game has problems too. The driving model is wonky and there are some glitches and bugs around, some amusing (like trucks launching in to orbit) and some not (a car parked 10m in the air....).Its not the prettiest game in any way, shape or form either.
In the end of the day, this is a game for cop fans and no-one else. Being one, i recommend it. If you have no interest in patrol police work then this game is really not for you.

Absolutely worth it. I love beautiful games with rich lore that reward you for exploring many environments, and Starbound has that in spades. The devs care about making this an amazing game, and that enthusiasm really shines through. "Terraria in space" isn't quite an adequate description, but it'll get you ~70% of the way there. There aren't as many bosses, since there's more of an emphasis on exploring the cosmos, though you may encounter procedurally-generated minibosses on any planet. You can do things like capture and train native monsters to be your companions and bodyguards, and finding procedurally generated weapons can be hilarious (personal highlights include a wooden hammer named Poop Smacker and a pastel pink shortsword named Miss Dudedicer).
I've been mostly happy with where the updates are taking the game (this review was written during Stable version Spirited Giraffe), and what few tweaks I haven't liked I got over within 5 minutes because the new way was overall better. For instance, I like the current food system better than the old one (hello, buffs!) and am glad they replaced the old hot/cold system with nanosuits - give up almost all my armor rating for the only clothing set warm enough to explore a frozen planet? Nope, sorry.
There are still some minor details that don't make sense, like torches functioning in oxygenless areas, but I know the devs have been working on that. My one major complaint is that there's currently no ingame way to search for items. There comes a point where you have to perform some fetch quests before you can get the next starship upgrades. Nothing inherently wrong with that, but when you have to locate said items on procedurally generated planets... and have no radar or quest markers for locating quest items... and can't even look up coordinates for planets containing the item out of game because structure generation is different across OS's... it can become quite an exercise in frustration if you're unlucky.
Chucklefish has a blog where they post daily about what they're working on, and you can opt into the Unstable or Nightly builds if you really can't wait for them to release Stable updates. If you're the kind of person who doesn't mind playing an unstable version of the game for the sake of helping them balance and polish whatever they're currently tweaking that much faster via additional feedback, that may be the option for you.
I don't know why everyone complains so much about it still being in early access. A good game takes several years to make, and Starbound literally has an entire universe's worth of potential to work with. Would you rather they rushed to release an ultimately shoddy and untested product at the impatient urging of fans, as so many devs have done to the detriment of their reputation, or would you rather they took their time to polish everything to a shine? Have some patience, friends.

Some of the reactions from "My" character feels closer to watching a character, instead of controlling myself. This adventure takes you into a reality TV show for superheroes, though I'm not sure I would want any of these heroes saving me.
One of the biggest issues I have with "my" adventures up to now are the romantic options. Maybe spoilers, but the romantic choices suck. At least, during my adventure they have. I think the writing overall was better then the first story, I wasn't pulled out of my adventures as much as I was in Prodigy. After seeing where Prodigy took the storyline, I was extremely curious to see where the next adventure took me. I'll be honest, I was a little disappointed with a reality show setting, but after finishing the adventure I can at least see why it was chosen.
Some of the most important choices during my adventure though felt emotionally powerful, but it wasn't always my emtions that were moved. As I had mentioned, sometimes I'm watching this lead hero react not in a way I would have in the same position. Also, with the given choices, more then a few times during combat I feel like there is no gray area between "nuclear bomb" and "don't move". When this occurs, I tend to take into account how angry I am at the target, or how serious they have attacked me.
Overall, I would say I enjoyed this adventure and where it might lead too, even if it was a little obvious from the begining. I was never really invested into the reality show's antics, and I was so unwittingly thrown into the event that I was completely suspicions of the thing the entire time. Though, I never really had an option to express this feeling. How much love will I find next, i'm starting part 3 now!

This is an amazing game that is quite literally 'infinite.' Here are some of the many reasons this game appeals to people who like sci-fi games (and terraria).
First off, you get your own ship that you can upgrade and build anything inside! As far as I know there are 8 ship upgrades to make your ship bigger.
I have a generator that turns on all of the lights in my ship all at once!
Second, there are an overwelming amount of guns that aren't available to starting players, but you can easily obtain as soon as you fix your ship's thrusters! (They use energy that is displayed below your health bar)
Third, there are 7 different species to choose from listed below!
Human: just a normal human
Avian: bird-like humanoids who believe they lost their wings because of their god, Kluex
Apex: a knowledge driven ape-like creature who are led by the (possibly corrupt) Big Ape
Floran: plant based creatures who are extremely primitive, however they are cannibalistic and will try to eat you
Hylotl: a fish species that evolved to come out of the water and thrive
Glitch: (by far the coolest(opinion)) a robotic race that are controlled by the hivemind and are locked in the midevil era. For example, they live in large castles and their ship has large stone castle "turrets" on it
Novakid: a strange race mase out of stellar gasses in space. I have the least amount of info on this one.
Again, the game is infinite! The star systems keep going on forever in every direction, and each ave anywhere from 5 to 18 planets orbiting them! (the range that I have found) Furthermore, on those planets there can be settlements made by any of the species above! (Apex laboratory, USCM prison (for humans), glitch castles, Floran village, ect.)
Also, if you want to play the game for fun and just build with no restraints! Simply type the following command into chat: /admin
You get instant acess to all craftable items, infinite pixels, infinite energy, invinciblity, and some other stuff that you can figure out! =)
Yet another amazing feature, you can use the money in the game, called pixels, to 3-d print any item in the game! Right in the comfort of your own ship!
Thanks for reading and please remember: this game isn't even finished! There will be MORE!

Well, what people say is true. The developers abandoned a relatively big name title that I think everyone was hoping would slowly be patched back to life. Maybe we can hope they're working on a DLC? I'd buy it, strategy games are still mostly niche so I'd rather support them and see if they can fix this game even if it costs more.
Does the game stall for long times between turns? Yes. Are some parts completely broken? Eh, yeah kinda I suppose. Is the realtime combat part a piece of utter♥♥♥♥♥♥ YES YES YES IT'S LIKE SOMEONE'S FIRST GAME THEY EVER MADE. It's bizarre and jarring since the rest of the game is so polished visually, and then you have this early access looking thing for ship combat. You have to nurse it as if you're playing League of Legends, constantly clicking the mouse and repeating orders. It sucks because even though you can skip the realtime parts entirely, the automatic calculations aren't in your favor even when you should win a battle, so it's better to do it the realtime way.
One of the complaints I hear the most that is more subtle, is that the game just isn't very strategic. Funny for a strategy game. Well, this is VERY TRUE. It's much more like an arcade game in a strategy game's clothes. The planning and thinking are as shallow as dish water, it's mostly just about gathering up the strength to throw all you can at the enemies, and with mind control letting you steal a planet instantly with one click, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ monkey smoking a hookah could beat this game.
BUT ... it's a pretty dang fun arcade game. The news broadcasts are funny, the lines the characters say are filled with cute geek references and stuff like that, and the visual polish feels like watching an animated movie at its best moments. I think the problem is that too many hardcore strategy fans bought this and thought it was bad, but it's more for someone who wants a relatively simple stress-relief game that they don't have to think too hard about when they're playing. It's cheetos, not filet mignon.
So, uh... honestly, for that, I recommend it. It's great to blow off some steam and play something that has the dance moves of a more complicated game but goes easy on you even at the highest difficulty levels. Hah, I just realized something while writing this - you know what it's like? One of those clicker games, like Cookie Clicker and all of those! Just with a bit more structure. You click your way to victory meeting funny characters along the way. Is it worth $30? For the amazing animation quality and beautiful music I say yes, yes it actually is.
Insanely high production values black-sheep game that everyone hated, would play it any time I need something simple and stupid. 10/10 for what it actually is (instead of what it was hyped to be, mostly by the fans). The performance issues on computers with slower CPUs probably didn't help either, but if you keep it down to 5 opponents or so and have a recent i7, it's fine. If it's okay for a chess simulator to take a while to decide on a move, it ought to be okay here too.

When you first play the game, it looks very polished. Many of the characters are well voice acted and all have interesting animations. You feel like you're playing something that COULD have been a AAA title.
Sadly, that's not the case.
As I explored the races and played the game quite thoroughly I found that in the combat aspect, most play pretty much the same as the others. On the economic scale, there are differences. On the colonization aspect, there are differences. But in warfare, which ends up being a significant portion of the gameplay? Almost none.
I began to realize that the given assistants you have aren't as charismatic as the race leaders, and some are down right so annoying with their overly cartoonish actions that I began to avoid specific races.
After trying almost every race, I began to realize the game felt essentially the same. The long campaigns often ended similarly. There was nothing guiding me to different victories. Win or lose, it always happened in the same way.
I thought the game would have new life with its expansion, but I realized after its release that it was essentially content that SHOULD have been in the game from the start, and this might be another case being fed an unfinished game in order to get you to buy the rest of it later.
The initial bundle pack wants you to pay quite a bit for very old previous games and a new race which is even more "more of the same" in that it's just humans with a meaner leader and no new ships, technology, etc.
Then I looked to multiplayer. My friends enjoy games similar to this. It could be fun working together or against each other!
The multiplayer is completely gutted, for reasons I don't really understand. Although the team tried to fix some of the issues with the game, this was never anything more than numbers fiddling, and resulted in many people on the forums reporting that the game was virtrually unplayable.
I want to note that I never had an issue monitoring pollution, and thought it was an interesting aspect. But I may not have played it since the last patch.
The multiplayer also lacks actual combat. Your fleets autoresolve their battles off screen.
The combination of poor AI (reportedly going from offering no challenge, as I often experienced, all the way up to utterly unbeatable, with little to no middle ground), lack of combat, and generally poor management pushed me slowly from being super excited about this game to realizing that I was offered something shiny.. but that was just the wrapping, and underneath was a rusted hunk of junk.
I can not strongly enough push the importance of this to you. They made it look good, but only enough to sell the game and keep you playing just long enough that you can't get a refund. By the time you've explored the game, it's too late. They have your money.
IT IS LITERALLY A TRAP.
I held out. I hoped. But it's been 3 months now since the Devs left with out a word. This game is dead and despite its real potential, it will never be allowed to become what it should have been. I'm not angry just at my money lost, but at the potential tossed to the ground. It COULD be SO GOOD. You can see it while you play it... but they won't let it be. And that disrespect to both the customer and the product they themselves created is why they don't deserve your money.
That is all.

The graphics certainly haven't aged well for this game, but nevertheless Half-life has held my attention from beginning to end. As someone who did not play the game in those almost 2 decades, and only up to now did I play it, I can see why it was deserving of all those awards. It is quite the product for its time, and while the graphics haven't aged well and some irritating grab mechanics with crates being wonky, I still had fun from start to finish (except maybe near the final part).
Aside from the outdated graphics and audio, level design was pretty linear but clever. Like, it's not always going down a striaght hallway, there are moments you're going in vents, going down railways, fighting your way outside, etc. You just have to think about how to progress, and the game presents this without some marker pointing it out to you, and the levels themselves get more distinct as you progress, so I can give a lot of respect to this game, that while graphics and audio haven't aged well, the levels have.
Enemies as well are unique as you fight them, you get the famous head crab zombies, then you got some monsters spitting acid, some shooting electricity, some that go to herds ready to do a kind of sonar blast at you, some with a sort of bee tracking gun, some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t flying monsters and some typical soldier enemies. The way they are uniquely designed and how they attack you makes you sure you never forget them or confuse them with some other enemy.
Storywise, its more or less of you trying to get out of a labortory in an experiment gone wrong kind of sci-fi story, which is all I can say. And I can say that it works with the environment the game has built.
A complaint I can say nearing the final part. I'm not gonna spoil much except that there are boss fights, and the final one is where it gets frustrating. It gets points in its creativity in the battle field being with how I can say as vertical and some creativity in the way it attacks. But that creative way it attacks is what makes it frustrating. All I can say is save often in that fight, and get ready to load when you get hit by that special attack, because its not worth getting hit by it, oh and it can follow you.
Now another criticism I could say with this game would have to be lack of indication of an enemy's death but I think I could chalk that up for being the product of its time, because the way they die is animated, not physics based and with some enemies being close to ground already you may waste some extra ammo on their dying animation. I wouldn't say its a really big complaint, but in my playthrough I did lose precious explosive ammo on that.
Overall this game was fun from start to finish. I was still captivated to continue on in the game, finding new areas to shoot down enemies in, exploring the different areas to keep me in the game. Now graphics included it hinders the game as the textures and sound again, haven't aged well.
But considering those being the parts of its time, I say the game deserves.

As many other reviews have already stated, this is a 'beat-em-up' in the vein of Devil May Cry or Bayonetta. Unfortunately, it cannot live up to that legacy. The story is not memorable (borderline terrible), the amount of times you're given the same information over and over becomes ridiculous, and odd pacing make it hard to appreciate any positive aspect of the game.
Graphically, it's decent enough to look at but not something to write home to Mom about. The controls are serviceable, but oftentimes I found myself targeting an enemy and falling to my death, or attempting to hit the button prompt and instead getting beaten to death by the enemy that shouldn't have been able to hit me in the first place.
And man, they really need to work on their character work. Supporting characters would show up with no introduction, yet we as the audience are supposed to understand who they are. None of the characters were intriguing, and the interaction and introduction of the characters was extremely sloppy.
If you can get past all of that, then you have a serviceable beat-em-up. However, if you have any others sitting in your backlog, think twice before picking this one up.
Final verdict: if you enjoy games where every single character is annoying and terribly written, bad guys that spout dialogue that is so muddled in post-processing that you need subtitles to just understand the (threadbare) storyline, and semi-janky controls then this might be up your alley!

I can't really recommend a game that's unplayable. How is it unplayable? Well, the game's purpose is the simulate a game development studio. The main mechanic of the game is the allotment of resources to the different aspects of a game. Should you focus more on game depth or beginner friendliness? What percentage of the budget should you devote to graphics vs. sound? etc. Apparently, the game favors particular combinations of the sliders which represent these values. Thus, to create a successful game, you need to randomly guess what would make a game of that genre and of that topic successful. Good luck with that, as after an hour of trial and error I have yet to come up with anything. There isn't even a good wiki or forum to reference (although I am a big believer that a game should never require you to utilize outside resources in order for you to play it). The locations and the map and the designs are awesome, the enemies have fancy new moves and features on them and the companions are even somewhat romanceable. If you wish to waste time, there are tons of ways to do so in the game with completely irrelevant settlements and crafting systems. Means: You can, at designated, fixed locations, build up a settlement with the materials that you find(aka collect all the trash that you see.. glue, bottles, cans...). You can copy pasta premade builds into the environment (which is a pain) and then have settlers move in there. The advantage that you get from this is... well... actually none apart from the possibility of sending artillery strikes onto a certain location. But that only works if you have collected all the trash that you needed in order to craft that stuff, gone through a lame quest line and a fatman can do the same... faster. Not as long though. Settlements have a border and a size limit. The building options are very underwhelming in terms of design and freedom. It's way too much fidgeting. Oh and they get regularly attacked. You have automated defense systems, but depending on your level, they dont do♥♥♥♥♥♥against the enemies unless you kinda hacked and spammed tons of them. So while youre in the middle of a quest, you often get the lovely notification that a settlement is being torn apart if youre not moving your♥♥♥♥♥there.
The weapon system works primarily with weapon modficiations. Which forces you, to collect even more trash(apart from the settlement). The design of most weapons that you can get in the start is questionable, since they look like a bunch of scrap metal taped together. The melee weapons are however really cool in this game and stay relevant through it.
The big disadvantage of the crafting and the settlements is that you need to collect ALL the trash that you can find in the game (plastic bottles, glue... really anything).  Considering that the trash weighs something and your inventory limit, you either die with traveling back and forth or you just cheat the hell out of this♥♥♥♥♥♥system.
Power armors are different now and need an exoskeleton (which you need to enter, exit, and park like a car) and fusion cores as 'fuel' to work. Since youre permanently digging through trash anyway due to the crafting system, youll find enough fusion cores. You can't put the exoskeleton in your inventory and you also can't teleport to your power armor. Fortunately, enough exoskeletons can be found.

While it has a lot of fun things to do, it currently is quite buggy, which the developers have promised to fix in patches, along with new features in the next few months. So here are the pros:
- Has a fun concept; patrol the town and surrounding country looking for criminals or traffic violations.
- Different dispatch missions; various calls like drunks causing trouble, robberies etc.
- Multiple ways of catching criminals; tasers, guns, shout at them to surrender etc.
- You can kick people's doors in an arrest them with a warrant (this is buggy at the moment tho)
Cons:
-VERY buggy and not very user friendly at the moment (probably fixable in patches soon though)
- There's no backup system, so ATM you're the only cop in town
-animations, drivng physics and pursuits don't really work properly.
-tasers make people hover in the air for a minute (???)
So overall, if you're a fan of games such as SWAT 4 and GTA 4's LCPDFR mod, i'd recommend you give it a try after a few patches. For the dev's first PC release, it's pretty decent, with a good graphics/sound options menu.

This is clearly a game with a relitively low budget, but still is a very fun police simulator and, in my opinion, worth the money. In this review I will assess the positives and negatives, explain some of the features and finally give my verdict on the game.
Positives:
- Variety of different missions (passive and direct).
- 7 regions to explore.
- On and Off Duty modes.
- Level up / Ranking system in the police force.
- Can interact with every NPC civilian.
- Police cars have warning sirens, full sirens, and lightbars that can be customised.
- Variety of clothing and vehicle paintjobs.
- Realistic feel of policing.
- Can storm buildings, make civilians surrender, stop fleeing vehicles by hitting them with yours.
- Has an easy and hard mode.
Negatives:
- At the time of its release, it is quite buggy.
- When an ambulance / police transport / tow truck is called, they are not actually seen.
- Car physics are not very realistic.
- You get reduced career points for actions such as breaking down doors even if there is a criminal inside.
- You are the only patrol officer in the game.
- Fleeing NPCs act as if they were not being chased if they get clear of you a few metres, then run again when you get close.
- Limited things to do Off Duty.
- Does not have a very comrehensive help / controls screen.
PLEASE NOTE MANY OF THE ABOVE WILL MOST LIKELY BE IMPROVED / FIXED AS THE GAME DEVELOPS!
Suggestions:
- Could have custom loadouts (e.g. different weapons).
- Could call backup such as a SWAT team.
- When the player reaches a high rank, they could command other officers.
- Needs more vehicles and Off Duty activities (could maybe respond to specific emergencies).
Analysis:
I am someone who is a big fan of police simulators. Arma 3 Altis Life was great for this, and Enforcer: Police Crime Action is quite similar, only it is single player. You can drive around the town centre looking out for speeders (cars drive around 20mph and around 30mph is considered speeding) and you can pull them over, use the breathalyser or frisk them if you feel it is necessary. On the start of every shift there is a passive mission to complete by the end of the shift, for example setting up a roadblock with cones and checking 6 drivers for faults on their cars. There are also dispatch calls with generous time limits such as finding a person wanted for assaulting passers by. For this you would go and talk to the victims to get a description, then wait until there is intel about where the person was last seen. You would then go to the scene, find the person matching the description, and park up. Normally when you call out for them to stop, they will run off. You can pull out your tazer, and when you get close you fire. After that you can arrest the suspect, take them to the station or call for a transport. You get career points which help you rank up after completing every mission.
Off duty mode is really unique, and has a lot of potential. When you have enough money you can buy a car, and you can also customise your home with new furniture. It is also possible to level up your stress level buy going out with friends or your mother, and other people. Instead of actually interacting with your friends or mother, the game teleports you to their house and puts the time forward a few hours, and says that you have spent time with your friends / mother, without you actually seeing anything. Physically doing activities may well be something the developers add in the future. When off duty it is also possible to fill up on food and replenish your energy by sleeping. You have to be careful though as spending too much time off duty will reduce career points.
Conclusion:
This game as mentioned earlier has obviously been developed on a low budget, but they have made that budget stretch as far as possible. The gameplay is enjoyable even though the graphics and physics are not fantastic. I bought this game for $0.49 a while back.  I haven't finished it yet, but I think I have a pretty good idea for this recommendation.  Ctrl+F "TL;DR" to skip reading.
Nimble Quest is also available as a free-to-play game on mobile devices, and that's where I'll start.  Your purchase on Steam gives you the "Red Gem" DLC from mobile for free, and there are no microtransactions after that.  You can't pay real money to unlock additional heroes or to buy more tokens.  There isn't a demo of this game on Steam, but you can try it for free on iOS/Android if you have a compatible device.
The gameplay is pretty simple.  You start with a small roster of three heroes, of which you pick one to be the leader.  You start in a field and your ever-moving hero runs near (not into!) some enemies and starts attacking until they explode and vanish, leaving behind a gem you pick up.  Or maybe there's a powerup that gives you a temporary boost.  Or another hero.  Picking up the hero adds one 'car' to your train and also amplifies your attack power, but also gives you a tail to worry about.  This is an arcadey RPG Snake mashup.  Kill enemies, gather heroes, get gems and tokens, power up, and die.  Aim for the highest kill counts and gem collections!  Clear stages to unlock more heroes!
Since this is a game of Snake, you have to mind the walls and your own tail.  If you run into a wall, an enemy, or if your leader gets hit too many times and runs out of health, you die and Game Over.  Assisting heroes have the same mortality concerns, so it's very possible that an enemy train can cut through yours and kill several allies.  And your leader running into your train will kill the assisting heroes you touch, so careful maneuvering is key.  I found keyboard controls much better than swiping on mobile, and you can even use a controller if you wanted.  Controls were WASD or the arrow keys to move, Enter and Escape to pause.
The big part of the game is killing things to get gems.  Clear a stage, get a small bonus of more gems.  Green gems are worth one, blue five, red ten.  Gems go to boosting powerups, giving heroes permanent upgrades, and buying tokens.  Powerups range from instant enemy-killing bombs to freezing all enemies in place to a potion to heal allies of damage.  All of these upgrades are pretty costly, but that's the name of the game.  And having the Red Gem DLC already means it's going to go somewhat faster than F2P.  Tokens are used for buying continues when you game over, entry to the Arena, buying buffs that last the current run, buying random unlocked heroes in the between-stages screen, and to skip stages you've cleared already.
The stages are square for the most part, with some exceptions like Graveyard having some obstacles or Courtyard having small alcoves, but the enemies are more interesting.  You have damage-sponge knights with big swords, or stationary archers that'll shoot arrows at your allies, or healers who don't attack but will heal enemies you haven't killed, or fast-moving rats or so on.  You have the same if smaller variety of heroes, though they shine a bit more with upgrades since they can do different things like explode and take out enemies on death, or soak even more damage, or heal on dealing damage.  There don't seem to be any boss battles in this game.
Difficulty is pretty linear.  The game starts out slow with spawns and introduces new enemy types at a decent rate, but you'll quickly have to learn how to manage multiple enemy trains and your allies' HP.  You'll run into some cases where you just can't advance through a stage without spending gems on upgrades or tokens on buffs, but in the latter case, the game at least is pretty generous on its drops.  You can also earn tokens through the game's only form of 'multiplayer' in the Arena.  You're put into a Guild to start, which is nothing more than "#NAME" or whatever, but the game autopicks a hero you may or may not have and then a set of enemies and you just aim for the high score.  You don't play with anyone, but it's a form of co-op if you think about it.  Depending on how well you did in your guild and how well your guild did worldwide, you get a payment in tokens.
I also thought it was a cute touch with the descriptions you get on how you died, like "Merida tried to knock over a healer and lost" or "Uther made friends with a hairy rat" or so on.  There seems to be a death description for every stage and every enemy, possibly for dying to its attacks and for running into it.  It was also a nice touch how the hero sprites change slightly with each upgrade, like Ulrich's armor getting golden additions and his sword getting bigger or whatnot.
TL;DR:  For 49 cents, this game was a steal.  $5 may not be so bad, too.  It's got pixel graphics, tight control, decent music, and there's quite a bit of replay value.  There is a good variety of enemies to kill and be killed by, and buying upgrades does have a noticeable effect on your heroes and powerups.  It is admittedly grindy and can be repetitive, but I don't think it's a game you can just sit down and play for hours on end.  It's perfect for if you have to wait for another game to install or update, and you might find yourself playing a little longer than you expected, trying to beat your last high score or get just enough gems to get that upgrade you've been wanting.  I know I didn't pay much, but I really got my money's worth out of the game.  And I'm still not done.

If you’ve played previously games like Game Dev Tycoon or GamersGoMakers then you already know what to expect.  If you haven’t, then this puts you as a game developer, starting out in the early 1980’s.  You begin small, producing small, simple games, from small, simple premises with appropriately early gaming technology.  As time goes on (assuming you don’t go bankrupt) you have the opportunity to expand, by hiring more people, researching new technology and moving into bigger premises.
Visually, Mad Games Tycoon is better looking than those other games.  Another area where this differs from the aforementioned games is that with Mad Games Tycoon, you have to manually create each room and place the appropriate furniture in it.  Over time, your staff will complain about wanting things, like plants or heating, which you’ll have to place in the room, so you’ll need to make sure you create a room big enough.  Not too big, though, because in the early stages, you only have limited space for your rooms.
Eventually, you’ll have the opportunity to produce and distribute your own games instead of going through a publisher, as well as creating MMO’s hosted on your own servers.
This game is still in early access, and while it should be obvious what that means, it’s apparently not obvious to some.  Early access means the game is still in active development.  So, new features will be added and existing ones may be altered or even removed.  You might even find your save games get ruined sometimes, forcing you to start again.  The game is NOT a finished product, which is why it’s in early access.  You’ll almost certainly run into bugs from time to time, and features that aren’t available or aren’t working as intended.  The most important thing to know about early access games is this: are the developers actively working on it?  The answer for Mad Games Tycoon is definitely ‘yes’.  Updates are regularly being released, which are usually both fix bugs as well as adding new features.  This is important, because I’ve seen early access games where the updates concentrate on one but not the other, causing the game to suffer as a result.
The game is still very much playable in its current state, but it’s by no means finished, and nor is it perfect as yet.  It would be really good, for example, to have better feedback as to why your game was terrible, or indeed why it was so good.  It’s not necessarily easy to work out exactly why your previous game did as well, or as badly, as it did.  Hopefully that aspect of the game will get worked on in time to come.  I know too many early access games have died or taken forever to do anything, but I’ve seen nothing so far to suggest that this game will be the same; on the contrary, I’m confident that we will indeed see a finished product in time, and a damn good one.  But please keep in mind, if you buy a game in early access then you’re paying money for something which may or may not actually get finished, or finished in the way you were expecting.  It’s always going to be a gamble, but in this instance, it’s one I was happy to make.

Blades of Time is an action-adventure hack-and-slash video game.
It is a discount Devil May Cry/God of War but it doesn't mean it's a bad game. The plot is very simple, the voice acting of everyone but the protagonist is pretty good, there are a couple of collectibles, fun times with the Rewind ability. Has several puzzles and interesting boss battles. There's no Guard/Defense button but you may heal quite often so it's ok. Took me 'round 10 hours without DLC. Got it at a Humble Store sale.
Good:
+Rewind ability. You can copy yourself multiple times and punish enemies. Some enemies/bosses in fact need you to abuse the Rewind.
+The voiceacting from everyone but Ayumis is fairly nice.
+You can choose different weapons and accessories as you progress. They will give you different strengths.
+The puzzles are simple yet need timing or some trial and error.
+A pair of boss battles are interesting. The rest are blunt and direct.
Bad:
-Her voiceacting. Even if she's strong willed and stubborn, I can't stand her voice.
-If you don't try different combos or don't use the Rewind much the combat turns very repetitive.
-Sometimes gravity betrays you and you turn heavier than usual, giving you no chance to recover from a fall.
-The plot is simple. Adding a subplot or something would've been nice.
-The ending.
Overall is a decent game. Not worth full price but a good choice for a sale.

This game is pretty middle of the road.  If all you're looking for is a mediocre 4X space game, this is the game for you.  For me, it was a bunch of annoying little things that really brought down the whole experience.
First of all, there's not a lot of information on how the mechanics work.  I guess I'm just used to civ games spoiling me with the civilopedia.  There is nothing like that in this game.  Confused about how pollution works?  Too bad, figure it out yourself.  Want to know what a leader's Disposition skill affects?  Time to Google it!
There is also no way to broker a peace agreement between two other warring races.  Basically, once they're at war, they will always be at war.  And therefore if you're trying to be nice to everybody, you'll keep getting diplomacy penalties with each of them for deals with the other.
That's not the only problem with diplomacy.  To trade multiple technologies, you have to use the dropdown menu multiple times to select them.  And it doesn't tell you anything about those technologies, like what they do or how much they cost to research (and therefore how valuable they are).  So you either have to do it blind; or write down what they have and you have on a piece of paper so you can exit out of diplomacy, go consult the tech tree, calculate what you need and what you think is a fair trade, go back to diplomacy, talk to the other leader again and try to work out a deal.  Far too much work and screen switching.
A similar problem arises with espionage.  Not enough information about the empire you're trying to spy on.  You can try to steal a technology, but why bother if the target race doesn't have a technology you don't have?  How do you find out?  Back to the diplomacy screen again to go through the several steps to reach the trade screen to see if they have any technologies listed for trade.  There's also only a few options available for spies to take.  You can't steal money, only technology.  I found most of my spies to be pretty useless.  I either let them sit at home doing counterepsionage, or sent them off to another race and just let them sit there and hide.  Also, when you detect a foreign spy, you have the options of capture, deport, or kill.  Why would you deport them when you can capture them?  I don't know, there doesn't seem to be any negative diplomatic consequences for one over the other.  Another case where having an in-game lookup for information would have been helpful.
I personally had a problem with pop-up tooltips.  As in, they wouldn't always show up and I'd have to keep moving my mouse back and forth hoping that they would pop.
Even if you get them to pop-up, there are places where there is no information that there should be.  Like over the size/biome/resources for a planet.  What are they, how do they affect things?  Can I at least click on them to learn more?  No?  Well, I guess I'm flying blind again.
I didn't really play a military-type game, so I can't comment on the combat.  I tried it out and it seemed stupid and boring, (and, again, suffered from lack of information) so I just used Auto-Resolve for any other battles.
Planetary management was mildly interesting, but it mostly just involved choosing whether citizens worked on research, food or production; and what the colony was going to build.
And how about a timer that lets you know when the galactic council is going to meet again?  Don't they schedule these things in advance?
So to sum up, this game would be a lot better if the developers had spent more time on making sure the player had easy access to the information they need at any given time on any given screen.  The bones of a great game are here, but that's about it.  I was just never able to find the fun.
Edit: Oh, I almost forgot how annoying and unfunny GNN is.  The news scroll at the bottom seems like it might be funny but it scrolls by too fast to read so I have no way to tell.  And most of the time it just pops up to give you useless "State of the Galaxy" reports, which show which three races are leading in a particular victory option.  Why is that useless?  Because there is a management page that lists all of the victory conditions and all of the civilizations progress in them all the time.  So...  yeah.  Annoying AND useless.

The game is almost a true sequel to Moo2.
here are the problems:
1. real time combat just doesn't feel right. You never really know what is going on or if you're going to win.
2. The game gets REALLY slow late game. I'm talking, hit the 'next turn' button and go get a coffee slow. Games literally take  tens of hours where really nothing is happening. It's hard to understand why this is so bad, except that it has to be a complete lack of optimization by the devs. I actually like playing moo2 over this simply because you can play a game in a few hours intead of days. 3. Slightly watered down gameplay. Moo2 had a level of randomness that made games really play out differently. This version has some of that but not enough. Pirates are a weak mechanic and not very interesting.
4. The AI. The scourge of modern gaming. It's not good. It can't fight, it has no strategy in terms of fleet positions, it doesn't even seem optimized much on the planet dev side, which is where you'd think some math and perfect knowledge would help. :\
It's really a shame too, so many things in this effort done right. The art direction is a massive leap forward over what's been done on MOO before now. The sounds and vocalizations are enteraining. I'd be willing to overlook all the other problems if it just played faster.
At this point get this game on sale if you're a fan. Don't expect to enjoy the end game unless you like to watch your life pass before your eyes with nothing to show for it.

This is the first review I've ever written on Steam and I'm doing it because I feel like, for the first time in a long time, I FINALLY made a good decision buying an Early Access game.
Now don't get me wrong, this game lacks polish, optimization, servers, and all that, but the core gameplay is there and it is fun.  I haven't found anything game-breaking yet.
Also, this game is played in first-person, but it is by no means a twitchy shooter.  I am a middling CS player at best, and I constantly get slaughtered in Rust, but on this game there have been several rounds where I am in the top couple players on the server because this game rewards my playstyle.
If you want a game where you can be the guy who just fixes the ship and pumps out water, while someone else has all the fun swashbuckling in PvP, and yet you outscore them, this is game for you.  Especially because if they entire other team screws around like that the whole time, your team will win by a landslide.
My recommendation for new players - start out on the smaller ship.  Not because it's easier (it's not, they sink quicker and you have less cover), but because it is mostly wide open and you will get a good feel for what is going on.  I played my first game on the big ship and stayed below deck and I felt really lost and disconnected from the action.  After getting a feel for battle though, playing below decks on the galleon is now my favorite thing to do.
Lastly, I have to give a shout out to the devs - there are just two of them, and this is obviously a labor of love.  I love paying indie developers for a fun concept thoughtfully executed, and this game is exactly that.  Thank you also devs for making the playing field level.  No micro-transactions, no pay to win, not even skill unlocks as you level.  The only thing you get for leveling up is cosmetic stuff with no impact on gameplay.  You pay the $20 for the game, and you have access to everything and can compete on equal ground with the guy who has dozens of hours already sunk into the game.  That's exactly how it should be.  You guys rock, looking forward to more updates!

This being my first entry in the Fallout  series, I thought the game was decent for what it is. I've played mainly TESV: Skyrim from Bethesda Game Studios and absolutely loved it. However, lets get a couple of things clear:
1) Bethesda Game Studios Q&A is a joke. The community that surrounds these games have had to go in with the creation kit and fix a majority of the bugs and glitches in the game. Any other developer would catch a bunch of flak for this, but with BGS, its just a given.
2)The community (including modders) are what allow the game to stay relevant for years on end. The only reason games like Fallout New Vegas, Fallout 4, and Skyrim are still talked about and played has to do with the ability to mod and customize the games.
Now, with the implentation of the Creation Club, what started as a means for mod authors to be recognized for the work they have done and receive compensation for it has turned into an avenue for the empty suits to profit for a game that they've already received the asking price for. The content on CC is subpar with what is available on other mod hosting websites and even on
. Bethesda Softworks has retroactively added in microtransactions and have willingly engaged in shady business practices that the gaming community at large are against. You aren't allowed to directly purchase the items you want, you instead are forced to purchase a virtual currency, which are sold in tiered packages. Then they price the most engaging pieces of content on CC (DOOM armor and BFG) just outside what you would receive from one package, forcing you to purchase the next one up and essentially give Bethesda Softworks more money.
They won't call this paid mods (even though thats what it is) and stated they are more like mini-DLCs. Then those that have the season pass ask if they will receive this, and are told no. Guess why? They aren't DLC's. This type of corporate double talk can only come from people motivated purely by profit. This is just semantics. The content that has been offered on the Creation Club are the same things you would find on mod hosting website such as the Nexus, and those mods are of higher quality, greater variety, and FREE!
Bethesda Softworks created a wonderful game in Fallout 4. I've put hundreds of hours into the game and loved every minute of it. However, with the implementation of the Creation Club and the willingness by Bethesda to engage in shady microtransactions, going out of their way to nickel and dime the customer and reach the levels of EA, Activision, and now 2K Studios, I can't rate this game above a 4 out of 10. To Bethesda Softworks, realize your error. You've used up a lot of the goodwill you had with your consumer base with this latest debacle. Please remove the Creation Club, and focus on giving your customers quality games like you have in the past. If you insist on pushing the Creation Club to your future games, I for one will not be a part of it.

Let me start off by saying this game shows potential, however with that beign said, this game is not a finished product.
The game has a number of problems that need to be fixed before it can truly be considered a worthwhile purchase
one of the first problems I noticed while playing the game is that, at least in the starting region, driving onto the platform for the gas station will damage your car, there is literally no way around this from what I have seen, this also occurs in other locations around the city such as the repair station (or whatever it is called). Furthermore the missions are often rather repetative as the criminals will often spawn in the same locations every time. In addition there is literally no incentive to bring the criminals back alive (if they have their gun drawn) you recieve the same points for killing the criminal as you do for brining them back alive (unless they dont have their gun drawn, points are lost for shooting at them).  As well despite the several distinct regions in the game, they all feel almost entirely bland as they are rife with either unenterable buildings, or land with nothing on it. Another thing that I must complain about is the fact that shooting vehichles does literally NOTHING, if you shoot at a vehichle it will not do any damage to the vehichle or the driver, also problamatic is the fact that if you shoot at a civilian vehichle, no points are deducted. Another problem is that if you simply quit and reload your game, your stress level will be reset and your sleep and hunger levels are also almost enitrely reset, which removes the necessity to take anytime off. There are also rampant glitches, such as the fact that the main city (or at least the one your house is in the region of) is rife with invisible potholes on the streets that will do damage to your car if you go over them at too high a speed and possibly even send your vehichle flying. As well I have noticed sometimes that there will randomly be vehichles just sort of floating in the air. I have also noticed that sometimes in the city various vehichles will run into each other for no apparent reason, maybe it is just the drunk drivers but I dont know.
Overall, I think that if the problems with this game are fixed it could be a good or maybe even a great game, I really do like the concept of a game where you play as a police officer as it has not been done very often, however until they fix the problems listed and the many more that I probably didnt notice or think to write about, then it is not really a worthwhile purchase
UPDATE: they are improving the game however, so hopefully soon they will fix the bugs that currently plague the game

I supported Enforcer during its infancy, when it was actually known as Police Tactics. The developers were friends of mine on a forum, and I eagerly expected the release. The trailers provided a great insight into what we could be doing when the game was officially released; however, it seems the actual product wasn't really portrayed very well.
Enforcer: Police Crime Action delivers a fun and different experience with its gameplay:
You have an off duty lifestyle, tied into the game with an actual need (Stress level). While it's not really superbly fun and you can't spend more than a few hours off duty before getting bored, it's a cool feature.
Being on duty involves multiple 'tasks' in which you do not have to finish but increase your career points, leading to promotions. These tasks can be anything from pulling over a required amount of vehicles within a certain amount of time  to call-outs, robberies and drunks being just a few.
Vehicle customization is a neat addition, offering four different vehicles (two are unlocked via secret codes, obtained by registering your game) all with their own liveries. Lightbars, light colours and wheel types are also some of the changeable options.
To experience the features, you really must watch a gameplay. Of course, being a police officer, a day is never the same, and you have to watch someone play it to see this.
Of course, as it's only a first release, bugs are to be expected, but this game has started very poorly. Driving needs a hell of a lot of fine-tuning, it feels clunky and not at all fluid. The entire game is sort of clunky; it plays very much the indie game it is. If you're looking for an LCPD:FR contender, you're not going to find it. LCPD:FR expanded on a triple A game engine, fully developed and rounded off by Rockstar; Odin Game Studio has built this game from the ground up and it stands as a completely different game. LCPD:FR has the advantage of calling in backup, more vehicles, an urban environment, backup, etc, whereas Enforcer is somewhat primitive in this approach, featuring no backup and only a crude radio to call in prisoner transport (this is executed via a loading screen), but I feel after many updates the realism will shoot up, making the game a more immersive experience than it currently is.
The usual bugs are found, odd animations, cars flying everywhere, but these don't really affect gameplay too much (they did on the first release; gunfights were a mess!),, and provide a few laughs. It is a bit annoying, though.
As it stands, Enforcer: Police Crime Action needs a lot of work, but if we do get that, it could easily be worth its £14.99 asking price.

I believe the price they are asking is still too much (currently almost $32 CAD - Expansion is $54((!!!)) CAD), and Canadians especially have to pay more on top of the exchange rate for absolutely nothing extra.
It's only a few dollars, but it made the difference for me between buying and waiting until later.
There isn't much story to the game really. The Commander character is not defined as a real character in any meaningful way, but this may be in line with earlier iterations back in the 90's. I really didn't care for that aspect at all.
The rest of the characters in the ship, Bradford, the Central Officer, the heads of research and engineering are also quite flat characters with basically no history or development.
There are threads of backstory about how they came to be where they are on the ship, but nothing is explored in depth. None of the missions have anything to do with the current characters or the old characters from the original games which haven't strictly been ruled dead and gone. I was disappointed about this.
I never found the turn limits on any of the missions to be particularly bad. They were challenging, but not as bad as many of the other reviews made them out to be. Many of the missions do not have this condition, so it is definitely not something you're facing constantly.
The Avatar project is rather ill defined and throughout the game, you never really figure out what the true plan of the Elders is. They have something that they need to solve, but you never really get an idea of what they plan to do when that is complete. You never see them until the end game cinematic, there doesn't seem to be that many of them, and they really don't seem all that powerful given the reasoning for the Avatar project, and the consequence of the end game cinematic.
Psionics are a somewhat Deus-Ex-Machina/Mary Sue type of story element that are the cause of, and solution to, all of humanities problems, not unlike Beer.
Playing the game and strategizing tactics during missions is a lot of fun though, and basically encompasses why I recommend this game. The story is weak, but the gameplay is strong. The strategy layer with contacting rebels in other regions is good and I think the expansions elaboration on this part of the game will prove to be quite good. I can't speak to that though. As it stands in Vanilla, it's rather simplistic, but I still feel that it adds a fair amount to the strategy requirement as it means choosing to do certain things while passing on other things.
For the most part, doing the Dark Event pop-up events is pretty much required, or you will suffer pretty large consequences. This isn't a really bothersome thing. There aren't that many of them really. They are pretty managable.
If you're interested in the game and haven't played it yet, I'd wait a little longer for an expansion sale, buy both, play the game in Vanilla, and then play the game with the "Long War 2" expansion. By the time the expansion goes on sale, I'm sure Long War will be fully integrated with it.

Chucklefish, realising how toxic the survival game community is (equal to how toxic the MOBA game community is), have decided to change their game around from being a survival game to being an exploration, creative building, puzzles, and platforming game.
Do you remember how Notch had to disable the comments on his blog because the people posting there were just so terrible? Using racist slurs and cusses that no one should ever have to see. And to think, Notch wanted his blog to be seen as family friendly. For those not in the know, Notch was the lead developer of Minecraft. He was so fed up of it at the end that he simply sold Minecraft to get out of the business. He did this out of spite, sick of how utterly awful, narcissistic, and egotistical the community was. To the point of sociopathy.
Chucklefish, the developers of Starbound, discovered the same thing.
The survival game community is matched only by the MOBA community is how it tends to house some of the worst aspects of humanity. The dregs, if you will, of society. The potty mouths, the idiots, the aggressors, the manipulative sociopaths, and so on. They love survival games, especially survival games with PvP, and it's not at all hard to understand why. Is it?
When Chucklefish decided to leave that community behind by revitalising their game with a new public image, there was a backlash. The top 'most helpful' comments are poorly written, ill conceived, misinformation-laden and FUD filled works upvoted by that community out of sheer hatred. They hate Chucklefish now. And considering how bad that sort of community is (the worst of the 'gamer' community, the most GamerGatey of them all), I wouldn't mind betting they've even had death threats over it.
If a guy working on Star Wars: The Old Republic got death threats for rebalancing a couple of classes...
Anyway, Starbound's not a survival game any more. Good riddance to that aspect. As I said, it's a game about exploration, creative building, puzzles, and platforming. It's far, far better for it. When a person like me pulls out a text based game, they are looking for an adventure where the world and story is interesting, decisions are impactual, good decisions and insight are rewarded, and there is freedom of choice to make your character into whatever they may become.
Before I get into specifics, here's the short rundown of my thoughts.  The choices feel constrained as you need to choose a role and stick to it, this is bad.  The hero feels like a buttmonkey, getting the short end of every stick regardless of your choices.  This producer has better text based games, so don't get this one.  Why they chose the Heroes Rise, one of their earliest works, to put on steam over their better products, I don't know.  Check out their site, choose a different game.
The Hero Project has a nice world, if not a tad overused (superhero metropolis city). The story however, is lacklustre, in my opinion worse than that of The Prodigy, this game's predecessor.  I won't go into more detail than that.
Like it's predecessor, the decisions do not feel impactual or rewarding beyond juggling you're alignment "meters" of loyal/soloist, popular/underdog and the like.  Unlike the previous game however, this game makes your choices seem constrained, telling you what kind of decisions you SHOULD make, and even MUST make in situations where it may not make sense.  Having your options limited to "insult him", or "insult him in different words", when I felt no desire to do so, or having the game tell me, next time be more "Justice" hit my enjoyment of the game pretty hard.
In addition, the low level of detail in descriptions, and the lack of impactual additional reading meant that I was not invested in finding out more about the world.  The way the game played out saw me caring less and less about what happened, a deadly feeling to any story based game.
On the positive side, depending on the roles you choose, there are a ton of different endings.  This game is pretty long for a text based game, and there are some wacky decisions you can make that work in the game's framework.
Even so,
I recommend getting a different, better text based game.

This game is much like the first in the series, and you can play it without paying the first one but I wouldn't recommend it. After the fame generated from Prodigal and her Deathwave, you are trying to find a way to keep your legend level high. Your best idea to do this is to join a reality TV show called the Hero Project, which the top six winners will join a team of superheroes supported by the government. Black Magic, Jury, Mayor Victon, Jenny, and your Grandmother all make appearances. You can continue your relationship with Black Magic, if your were in one, or you can start a relationship with Jenny or another Hero named Lucky. Black Magic is pretty jerky in this one, so I went with Lucky, who is sweet. At the end you can import your save file into the third game, which some of the romances in the third one require the romance to have been completed in this game. Also you do not have to import a save file from the previous game and you can start fresh.
Some of the bad things were: you cannot save and load in the game, so if you do not like a choice you made, you are stuck with it, the legend guide that you unlock isn't that helpful, they could have added more achievements, and sometimes it was hard to tell how a choice would affect your stats. Overall it is a good game that is well written. Some complain about ending up at the same place regardless of the choice you make, but that is sort of the point to keep the story moving, and it being written out. Sometimes you'll unlock scenes you didn't see on a previous playthough.

While I'm glad i did finally finish, I'm also dissapointed in the overall experience. First off, getting this damned game to work on a 3440 x 1440p screen is an unneccesary chore. I ended up using flawless widescreen along with changing the settings in Geforce exp. Bethesda for some reason almost neglects any resolution above 2560 x 1440p, yet their games would widely benefit from the exrta screen space showing more of the landscape you need to traverse. With both employees focused on producing a game of epic proportions history would be changed forever. The release of their game generated nearly 500 million dollars in revenue for the company, thus expansion began. APS became a titan in the gaming world almost over night with over 30 employees on staff 24/7. Reed decided it was time to unveil the real reason he started APS in 1980, to take over the gaming industry. With all staff members devoted to one project they created a monster, a hellish beast. Critically acclaimed and winning game of the year this game pulled in over 10 billion dollars in revenue and stayed on the market for 20 years. With such a large income Reed purchased all competitors and forced them to close, making Angry Panda Studios the studio of the year, every year.

Half-Life was voted 1998 Game-of-the-Year by over 50 publications, and it has received various other awards as well.
Deep in the confines of the Black Mesa Research Facility, a top secret project results in disastrous consequences, and a portal to another dimension was accidentally opened. The entire Black Mesa facility is destroyed, with few survivors. Many of your former friends have mutated into alien slaves.
You are Gordan Freeman, a survivor of the Black Mesa accident. Caught in the middle of the destruction, you were saved by your safety suit. It is your job to escape, but with limited security clearance, and most of the access ways destroyed, you will have to fight your way out.
You are almost out of the Black Mesa facility when you come upon a soldier. Without a thought, they shoot at you and kill numerous scientists. The government has sent in troops and sharpshooters to eliminate everything in the Black Mesa facility, including you.
Half-Life is an action packed first person shooter, with a great storyline and very realistic characters. The thrill exists from the beginning, and players will be deeply involved with numerous storylines and lots of surprises. Players must seek out scientists and security guards to gain access to restricted areas of the Black Mesa facility, even if this includes rescuing them from dangerous situations.
Want to learn the functions of Half-Life? Well, hop into the Hazard coarse, and an automated tour guide will show you what you will need, including weapons training, tricky maneuvers, and co-operating with security guards. This is a great feature, and makes it easy for beginners to jump right into the game.
The graphics of Half-Life are indescribable. The levels are incredibly detailed, and almost everything is modeled. Even the small details, such as breaking glass and smashing the covers off vending machines have been modeled. The textures used in the levels are superb. Valve has done an outstanding job modeling the objects as well. When you hit the wooden crates, they will break into chunks of wood, and those crates filled with explosives will explode into a huge fireball. Don't want to get too close or you will end up like burnt toast. One great thing about Half-Life is a 3D Video card is not required, and because of a new technology, the game will run excellent with great framerates without a 3D video card. Although, if you have a 3D video card which supports OpenGL, Direct3D or MMX Rendering, then, the game will look extraordinary with it.
The characters in Half-Life are incredibly modeled, and their animations and movements are very realistic. The scientists and security guards move like real humans. If a security guard comes upon an alien, he will raise his gun and help you out, attempting to blow it to pieces. Many times however, they are not so lucky, and the alien will rip the guard to shreds. The movements of the military personnel are very good. They move like a solder would, quickly and deadly, carrying a load of ammunition and other supplies on their back. The aliens in the game are one of the best aspects. They come in all different shapes and sizes, and are all modeled differently. The all move in different patterns, and in different ways. Half-Life's creatures have the highest polygon count in a action game to this day. We have screenshots of the many different creatures which roam around the Black Mesa complex, which are listed at the bottom of this review.
The assortment of weapons is Half-Life is astounding. Many different types of weapons are present, including shotguns, tripmines, magnums, rocket launchers, crossbows, grenades, and many others. Each weapon has its own unique handle and sound. The rocket launcher makes the player feel as they will blow back when they fire it, and the magnum can blow through almost anything with its pure power. For the diehard Half-life fan, some other weapons are available for certain tasks. Some examples include military style turret machine guns, and the good old fashioned tank arsenal.
Half-Life also features a state of the art multiplayer feature, which allows up to 32 players to connect into a game, and fight in a battle to the death. Although to play effectively online, you may require a fast connection, as multiplayer can be rather slow.
The sound in Half-Life is one of its best features. The sounds of shells firing, and those lethal explosions are just the beginning. You know a military solder is nearby, as you will hear them contacting each other through radios. Scientists and security guards will approach and speak to you. If you get electrocuted, you will certainly know about it, as you will hear the electric current flowing through your body. The sound is one of the games strongpoints, but its best feature is is outstanding artificial intelligence.
Half-Life features some of the most elaborate and realistic computer controlled opponents ever created. Throw a grenade at a soldier, and not only will they avoid it, they will unleash a grenade and a ton of ammunition back. The aliens will not give up in killing you, and no matter how fast you run, you will not escape them. The AI is fast, and will work together to destroy you. The soldiers will attack the alien slaves, and they will fight back. The battles are very realistic, and the AI can usually think faster than you. Aliens will work in packs to try and kill you, and the soldiers will call in backup if you attempt to attack them. This game is one of the best.
Overall, Half-Life is one of the most enjoyable games released to this day, and the Half-Life saga will continue to get better over time. Everything in this game is perfect, including the excellent characters and graphics, and the realistic sound effects. Half-Life is not a game, it is an adventure.

I spent a LOT of time playing MOO2, and think it's one of the best PC games ever made.  I also consider MOO3 to be one of the worst PC games ever made.  That said, I find this newest iteration to be a good, but not great game.  I bought it on sale for $14.99 and am quite happy with my purchase.
The Good:
The graphics, soundtrack, and general atmosphere of the game are great.  The dev spent alot of money on the voiceover work and it shows.  The game is quite pretty, and really has a lot of polish.  The game mechanics are solid and fun, and the UI is very functional without getting in the way.  Combat can be underwhelming, but unlike alot of RTS space combat, ship design actually matters quite a bit - which was one of my favorite parts of the previous games, designing ships.  The tech tree is well thought out, and the way the Creative/Uncreative racial trait works is fun and IMHO, better than MOO2.
The Bad:
I had to restart several times in the beginning to get to know what I was doing.  There is a tutorial, but it locked up on me the first time I tried it, and I prefer jumping in with both feet anyway.  There are nagging little bugs also, the UI does funny things sometimes, and late-game the time between turns can get a little long.  Combat is pretty, but the camera needs a couple more modes and some tweaks.  The "tactical" side of the tactical combat is a bit weak.  My favorite race, the Elerians were, locked behind DLC which I bought on sale, but those 3 races should have been in the base game  Also a race (the Terrans) and a couple of features are DLC-locked for the collectors edition only - which I didn't buy because I already owned MOO1-3.
Other:
Be sure to download the manual for the game, I didn't realize it was an option at first and was annoyed at the lack of in-game help.  The game also seems to have a little more of a MOO3 influence than I'd like - starlanes are back, and the Antaran victory condition has a MOO3 feel to it.  However, the classic races are back, including the Mrrshan, and the MOO3-specific races are gone (thank goodness).
Verdict:
All told, I'm pretty happy with this game.  It's fun, it's pretty, and it's MOO.  There are things that could be better, sure, but it's fairly solid in its own right.  At 14.99 I feel like I got a pretty good deal, and even at full price I think I'd still be happy with it (except the DLC - $5 was ok, but $10 is too much imo).  I'd give the game a 7/10 overall.
