I do not write a lot of reviews, but I feel this simulator needs one. I'm not going to review the story line, but just the gameplay itself. Enforcer: Police Crime Action centres around a single municipal police officer in a small desert town. You respond to call the dispatch informs you about and you have the options to respond to the calls or not. There is also real-time events happening in the city as well. It likes to focus mostly around the every day duties of a police officer and it does this very well. The simulator also goes beyond the duties of a police officer and you have to maintain you social and home life when you are not on duty, like manage your stress, eating, sleeping, and spending time with friends and family. Now that I have vaguely explained the game, I'm going to go into pros and cons of the game.
Pros:
-The simulator/game, or whichever you prefer to call it, does an amazing job of immersing you into the life of a police officer. The lackluster graphics still do not get in the way of making you feel and believe you are the law enforcement of this town and tries to make you thorough in your investigations and arrests, making you feel like you want to make a difference in the one-cop-town.
-The callouts. There is, at this stage of the game, quite a few different types of callouts that dispatch will give you while you're driving aroung town, looking for any law breakers. You can do simple things like, stopping some delinquents from vandalizing a public building to solving a kidnapping and finding the kidnapped and taking out the kidnapper and calling in an ambulance to take the kidnapped person from the situation.
-The rank up system. There is a huge list of different ranks to go through, from just a simple patrol officer to the chief of police. The list is quite large and every crime you solve and even just giving an illegally parked car a ticket helps you earn points to rank up and earn new things, like different police vehicles and customization items to them, as well as making your paycheck at the end of each shift more bountyfull.
-Being able to make vehicle roadblocks and checkpoints, for example, like creating a drunk driving program where you stop vehicles and perform breath tests to catch drunk drivers and even inspect vehicles to make sure they are road-worthy. Even just doing this can add enjoyment of feeling like a police officer and busting those damn drunk drivers a ticket and time in the slammer.
-The game does balance the action and simulation very well. I have had to chase down many suspects that attemted to flee and deploy the tazer on them, watching them get the jitters and then give themselves up after one hell of a shocking. You are equipped with a pistol and a SMG when there are those times that you just can't take them down the nonlethal way. I found myself hiding behind my vehicle helplessly as the offender continues to sling lead my direction and found myself trying to figure out how to take him down and end the situation.
I could name many more Pros to this game, but I may edit those in at a later time, but let's address the obvious Cons of this game now.
Cons:
-The graphics are horrendous, but given the small team that made this whole game themselves, you find yourself not caring too much, but this is a Con because the optimization is pretty bad. For a game that lack a lot of detail in the town there shouldn't be an excuse why I only get less than 20FPS on the medium settings on my system. The optimization is really bad and I run a pretty good system, so I should get 30FPS or more on the medium setting.
-Physics are non-existing. You are, what feels like, stuck to the ground, like your car is a giant magnet and stuck to the ground. There's really not much else to say about the physic-less world, but let's hope there is some sort of physic engine added in later, probably much later.
-The controls, oh the controls, they are awful, with no sensitivity sliders, or custom key options. You turn your car almost 90 degrees by just barely tapping the "A" and "D" keys. It makes it hard to stay to one side of the road and you find yourself all over the damn road and crashing into everything.
-Damage system. Your car takes way too much damage easily. Just by bumper tapping or hitting curb, you'll find yourself repairing you vehicle up to 3 times a shift and the shifts are very short. To get to parking lots, or the gas pump, and the garage have no slope on the curb, so you always take a lot of damage by just trying to get into the gas station. It's extremely frusterating and annoying. This huge flaw needs to be addressed immediatley. Like, now, seriously. It almost ruins the game for me.
-Your food, sleep, and stress bars. They deplete waaay to fast. I think they have been fixed, but they still go down way too fast. They need to be slowed down by 10x or more.
Okay, so I hope this review helped people deceide whether or not to invest in this game. Is it worth $16 on sale? Maybe, but maybe not. If they release a MAJOR and I mean, MAJOR update soon. Then hell to the freaking yes it's worth it, but as it stands no. Helping this small team of developers is worth it, though. This game has AMAZING potential and I'm so damn excited to see what they have in store for this game. Personally, I give this game a 8.5/10. I love this game. The police simulation games come in a small amount, like Police Force 2 or the LCPDFR mod for GTA IV, so I welcome this game and I am happy to support the developers. Keep it up, so far this game has me hooked and I can't wait to see what you all have in store for this.

The biggest problem I have with the game is how much grinding you have to do in order to get anywhere.
It is another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mobile port so what did I expect? The options menu has only; sound on/off, music on/off and tutorial on/off. So make sure your screen can handle 720p because that is what the game is looked at. You can't run it in full-screen or rebind the controls (only arrow keys and WASD) because that will ruin the idle way of playing the game through the developer's eyes.
Shame on you Nimble Bit!
It does have support for the Logitech F710 out of the box, so that is something nice I guess.
The game-play is simple, but punishingly hard, after two hours of playing I only got to “castle 1” which is the fifth level out of 14? The problem is that the enemies have too much HP so I can't kill them fast enough until the whole map is swarming with them and I just die.
It is possible to level up the heroes, but that too takes ages to do because of how little experience point they gain each kill. It is possible to bypass it with gems (in game currency), but it costs a lot. They have three levels each, which will increase attack speed, strength, range or add a special passive ability like HP drain or stun.

The levels are not that big so it's a bit annoying that the game can't be set to a higher resolution so the whole level can be viewed at once. Therefore, it is very easy to walk into enemy archers or mages and end up dying because they can't be seen.
You can continue form where you died, but it costs a special coin to do so. Which you can gain as a random drop or buy them in the shop for 1000 gems each. The gems can also be used to upgrade the heroes if you don't want to grind for enemy's over and over. It costs 1000 gems the first level and 10.000 gems for level two, don't know what it is for level three since I only have played it for about two hours.  You can also buy increased time for some of the item the emery's drop at random at the shop for 320 first tier, 720 for second tier, 1520 for third tier, and 2530 for fourth tier, and the last and fifth tier I don't know. (the prices may be off, but you get the idea of how they increase.) I got around 1000 – 1300 gems (depended on how many chests-drop I got) before the fifth level and died.
So you are better off starting from level one and using the coins in the arena or buffs before a level. The arena it's a 24hour, one life, clan war fight. You have to have gotten to “courtyard 1” before you can enter and spend your coins on it, then you can choose a clan to join or make a new one by typing it in the box that shows up. The arena is a one life, daily challenge, where you get one random hero to use.

So a lot of people say that this game is "unfair" or that the timers are just not cool bro. While in some cases I do think the game is unfair, and that the timers definitely force you into an uncomfortable style of gameplay, that is kind of the point.  You will always lose troops over the course of the campaign no matter how hard you plan it out. This was true for me in my first game and even now as I write this I currently have 3 KIA in the late game. The main concept of this game is risk/reward coupled with the soul tearing unfairness where the situation goes entirely out of hand and all you can do is hold the line and do your best. For me, I both love and hate this game- The same went with EU/EW- and I love to hate it because every failure presents a personal challenge and when your troopers get powerful in the late game, the satisfaction of taking all of these once intimidating aliens out to the trash is one of the best feelings in gaming imo. Also the graphics are nice and as far as turn based strategy components go with limited base building, this is some of the best ever done.
TL;DR
Looks good, plays good, dont be turned away by all the poor sports. Understand what this game is and you will have one of the most satisfying gaming experiences.

Ever since I completed Game Dev Tycoon in a few entertaining evenings I have longed for something more.  I waited with much eagerness for some kind of update or sequel but sadly none was forthcoming.  Well thankfully this game came along and I really couldn't be happier.  My review will compare it to Game Dev Tycoon.
PROS:
Game is slower - it really allows for you to get stuck in and enjoy all the little components that involve running your company.  Also allows for you to keep up with the market instead of being one step behind all the time.
More to develop - Not only can you develop games but you can also develop game engines (which is a great way to make some money) this is a lovely touch.  There is also more to develop in terms of what you want in your game.  Plus when you come to produce your own game you have some freedom to decide what to include in the box and how much you want to sell it for.  There are also many more genre's and topics
Buildings - it's refreshing to be able to build and equip your own offices.  Much more freedom to decide how much you want to spend/how many people you want working on something.
Staff Training - much easier, much quicker and much more effective
CONS:
Can get annoying when people won't work for you because you don't have a certain fridge or seat.  In some cases I have had the luxury version but people won't work for me because I didn't have the cheaper version.
UI can get a little annoying.  I can't think of how to describe it but the expanding boxes type of thing becomes monotonous and you have to go through a few boxes sometimes to get what you want.  Be good to be able to pick multiple things too, especially when selecting platforms.  The screen can become a little cluttered also.  Be nice if the full screen would work but I can't seem to get it to do so.
No ability to develop your own console (at least not that I have found).
No tutorial although it is easy enough to figure out.
OVERALL:
This is a really good game and I'm sure it will continue to improve.  It is far better than Game Dev Tycoon and provides an enjoyable gaming experience.

It's a good game, but I'd wait for a sale. This includes the new expansion, which I haven't played yet. I only played the game over the free weekend, and I completed it during this time (on regular difficulty).
I believe the price they are asking is still too much (currently almost $32 CAD - Expansion is $54((!!!)) CAD), and Canadians especially have to pay more on top of the exchange rate for absolutely nothing extra.
It's only a few dollars, but it made the difference for me between buying and waiting until later.
There isn't much story to the game really. The Commander character is not defined as a real character in any meaningful way, but this may be in line with earlier iterations back in the 90's. I really didn't care for that aspect at all.
The rest of the characters in the ship, Bradford, the Central Officer, the heads of research and engineering are also quite flat characters with basically no history or development.
There are threads of backstory about how they came to be where they are on the ship, but nothing is explored in depth. None of the missions have anything to do with the current characters or the old characters from the original games which haven't strictly been ruled dead and gone. I was disappointed about this.
I never found the turn limits on any of the missions to be particularly bad. They were challenging, but not as bad as many of the other reviews made them out to be. Many of the missions do not have this condition, so it is definitely not something you're facing constantly.
The Avatar project is rather ill defined and throughout the game, you never really figure out what the true plan of the Elders is. They have something that they need to solve, but you never really get an idea of what they plan to do when that is complete. You never see them until the end game cinematic, there doesn't seem to be that many of them, and they really don't seem all that powerful given the reasoning for the Avatar project, and the consequence of the end game cinematic.
Psionics are a somewhat Deus-Ex-Machina/Mary Sue type of story element that are the cause of, and solution to, all of humanities problems, not unlike Beer.
Playing the game and strategizing tactics during missions is a lot of fun though, and basically encompasses why I recommend this game. The story is weak, but the gameplay is strong. The strategy layer with contacting rebels in other regions is good and I think the expansions elaboration on this part of the game will prove to be quite good. I can't speak to that though. As it stands in Vanilla, it's rather simplistic, but I still feel that it adds a fair amount to the strategy requirement as it means choosing to do certain things while passing on other things.
For the most part, doing the Dark Event pop-up events is pretty much required, or you will suffer pretty large consequences. This isn't a really bothersome thing. There aren't that many of them really. They are pretty managable.
If you're interested in the game and haven't played it yet, I'd wait a little longer for an expansion sale, buy both, play the game in Vanilla, and then play the game with the "Long War 2" expansion. By the time the expansion goes on sale, I'm sure Long War will be fully integrated with it.

Pirates of the Caribbean is a series of fantasy swashbuckler films produced by Jerry Bruckheimer and based on Walt Disney's theme park ride of the same name. Directors of the series include Gore Verbinski (1–3), Rob Marshall (4), and Joachim Rønning and Espen Sandberg (5). The series was most notably written by Ted Elliott and Terry Rossio (1–4); other writers include Stuart Beattie (1), Jay Wolpert (1), and Jeff Nathanson (5). The stories followed the adventures of Captain Jack Sparrow (Johnny Depp), Will Turner (Orlando Bloom), and Elizabeth Swann (Keira Knightley). Characters such as Hector Barbossa (Geoffrey Rush) and Joshamee Gibbs (Kevin McNally) follow Jack, Will, and Elizabeth in the course of the films. The fourth film featured Philip Swift (Sam Claflin) and Syrena (Àstrid Bergès-Frisbey), while the fifth film will feature Henry (Brenton Thwaites) and Carina Smyth (Kaya Scodelario). The films take place in a fictional historical setting; a world ruled by the British Empire, the East India Company and the Spanish Empire, with pirates representing freedom from the ruling powers.
The film series started with their first release on the big screen in 2003 with Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl, which received positive reviews from the critics and grossed US$654 million worldwide. After the first film's success, Walt Disney Pictures revealed that a trilogy was in the works. The franchise's second film, subtitled Dead Man's Chest, was released three years later in 2006; the sequel proved successful, breaking financial records worldwide the day of its premiere. Dead Man's Chest ended up being the number one film of the year upon earning almost $1.1 billion to-date at the worldwide box office. The third film in the series, subtitled At World's End, followed in 2007, and Disney released a fourth film, subtitled On Stranger Tides, in 2011 in conventional 2D, Digital 3-D and IMAX 3D. On Stranger Tides succeeded in also grossing more than $1 billion, becoming the second film in the franchise and only the eighth film in history to achieve this.
So far, the film franchise has grossed $3.73 billion worldwide; it is the eleventh highest-grossing film series of all-time and it was the first franchise where more than one film grossed $1 billion worldwide.
A fifth film, subtitled Dead Men Tell No Tales, is set to be released on May 26, 2017.

So, it's ostensibly a "retro" shooter, in the twin-stick style, comeplete with odd colour palletes and scanlines, but "N.P.P.D. RUSH" (I'm not typing the full title) has some major issues.
Old/retro games had to work with hardware limitations, like the nunber of colours which could be displayed at once and per sprite, scanlines on the display hardware and so on, and this tended to lead to cleaner but more abstract display. Unfortunately that's not the case here.
While the noisy display this may be the art style, its done terribly. What you get is a confusing mess which means you can't instantly tell enemies from the backgrounds. The scanlines don't help, either - they seem to be applied on the display when its being rendered, and then again (optionally this time) on the final result, leaving a terrible moiré pattern mess.
Add to this a camera which zooms out slowly when you move, but almost instantly snaps back to a close up (meaning you can't even see the thing you were shooting at any more), and the mouse movement being locked to the player, so you need to constantly make adjustments, and you have something which is unfortunately signficantly sub-par.
Nice concept, poor execution.
All I can say is that this is the best. Ever.

A Must Own for the First Person Afficionado
I will say this, I have never experienced an FPS campaign as great as Half-Life's. You play as physicist Gordon Freeman as he attempts to not only escape the facility known as Black Mesa, but right the wrongs of his experiment gone wrong. What sets this apart from most FPS games is that you're never taken out of the action. There are no cutscenes, the story unfolds right before your eyes, keeping you completely immersed. There is a slight exception for the loading screens, which are common, but they are brief and don't overstay their welcome. It was a great experience to see how this disaster unfolded and how it would be corrected. My only complaint, though, is the lack of any real characters. Don't get me wrong, its shocking to see your fellow scientists killed by enemies, but none of the scientists or human characters ever really stood out except for one in particular near the end, which I won't spoil here. However, the overall story as well as the progression of it makes up for this complaint. Gunplay is, well, great. This is the gunplay which helped model our modern day FPS games. Enemies are only slightly varied, with the Xen creatures having their differences, such as the Head Crabs, Bullsquids, and Gargs, and the human enemies are pretty much the same. However, their AI makes up for this lack of variation. They'll team up on you, attack each other, hide from attacks, the whole bunch. The AI is impressive, especially for the time it was released. The puzzles in this game can be tricky, but are never too difficult nor impossible. The only true thing which is difficult is the combat, which is a series of trial and error segments, seing which strategy will suit you the best. Be wary, however, that you will die alot, so use that quick save button like your life depends on it. The graphics are slightly dated to today's standards of gaming, but this was not too much of a distraction given the impressive gameplay and story.
If Doom is the father of all FPS, then Half-Life is the son which helped paved the way for all FPS. It is a classic and a must own for all FPS lovers. Although better characters might have been needed, it's tense and thrilling story and gameplay will keep you satisfied from begining to end.
Final Score: 9/10

I want to point out that Enforcer: Police Crime Action is like calling the Half Life Series Scientist: Atoms Destruction Wait. And yet it is still a much better title (and game) Then any of the "Simulation" Games released for the purpose of a quick cash grab.
It's simple. You play as a police officer, male or female, and are tasked with the daily routines of being said police officer. You go do a shift by beginning with a mundane mission and will either get interrupted with a more exciting mission or just simply go through the mission and gain points. Points mean you are promoted and get money, thus allowing you to spend it on your house. The closest comparision I have is True Crime: New York City in terms of random missions and being tasked with being a police officer.
The game doesn't look impressive, but it get's the job done. It has good character and vehicle animations that allow you to tell what a character is doing and what they plan. The appeal of just going through the daily life of a police officer is a welcome compromise between the hardcore idea of being an officer (Swat series) To the matienince of health and hunger levels (Deadly Premonition).
The worst part about this game is that it feels cheap. The love for this game the developers gave to it is clear, and I enjoy the experience thus far, but there are a lot of times where I find cars flipped over for no reason, the camera constantly get's stuck to one position and once someone screams you will hear that scream throughout your shift like that victim is haunting your soul. If given more assets and time, this game could honestly be as good as Euro Truck SImulator in providing for a niche audience.
WOULD I RECOMMEND THIS GAME: YES
Despite the cheap look this game has, it is a game with a lot of love and detail put into it that already feels like a unique experience.
SUGGESTIONS TO DEVS: Focus more on bringing in the social life for the protagionist; I actually felt like this town could be given a lot more history and more characters that you could interact with.

I feel like this game is now at a state where it's fair to leave a review, so here it goes.
This game is awesome, and deserves to be considered the successor to Gmod Tower, even though it's not perfect. I'll just briefly go over some pros and cons and let you make the decision for yourselves:
Pros:
+ Widely varied content: There's something to do for pretty much every kind of person. The game features several full gameworlds, and many plaza activities that you can play in a central hub.
+ [Most] current gameworlds are awesome and very well made. I say most because games like Planet Panic are still in alpha, whereas games like Virus still need some tweaks and bugfixing.
+ Very fun with friends: This game is totally designed to be played by groups of people. It's still fun solo, but interacting with friends and messing around is where it really shines.
+ Lots of building capabilities: You're able to customize and furnish your very own condo (of which, there are many different choices), in many ways. With advanced condo tools on the way, and workshop support allowing for further customization, the possibilities are pretty amazing.
+ Dedicated developers: While just a small team of devs, updates are pushed out pretty frequently, and the best part is how transparent they are with their work. On their forums, they post daily about everything they accomplished, and interact with the community pretty often too.
+ No microtransactions / DLC: When you pay for the game, you unlock everything the game has, and everything it will have in the future.
Cons:
- Best with friends: I mentioned that the game is very fun with friends, but I feel like the downside is that you it doesn't hold up quite as nicely when playing solo.
- Low activity: On most days, the playerbase is rather low so at times it can feel barren or be hard to find others to start a game with. However, they have been working on features to better connect the many servers and that seems like it'll make it feel quite a bit busier.
- Lots of unfinished content: Granted this game is in early access, but for new users it might come as a shock just how many buildings or gamemodes have a 'Coming Soon' sign posted in front. The content is coming, but if you were really excited for the Nightclub or something, it might be a while until it actually comes out.
- Kinda laggy: The servers can sometimes feel pretty jittery, and the game does have framedrops when loading some parts of the plaza. It is being optimized slowly over time though.
I think that sums up most of the points off the top of my head. Overall, I find the game to be worth it, especially since it carries the promise of much more content to come in the near future.

While not perfect this game is fantastic. I say this because rarely does a game make me lose all track of time. I grew up with the Police Quest series and until recently, I've played the Police Force series from Excalibur Publishing  (makers of Simulator games). About a year ago, the maker of Police Quest, Jim Walls, was trying to revive the Police Quest series and bring it into the 21st Century but sadly it left Kickstarter and ceased.
If you've played Police Force, there are some things alike. You can walk around, accept emergencies, and use the number keys for "actions," Enforcer definately uses Police Force as a foundation but expands on it greatly and whoever put it all together definately should get a raise!
I have to say that the devloper and his team really did a great job. You are able to have a home and when your shift is over, you can spend time there eating, watching TV, showering, sleeping, and/or taking a nap. Any of these things can help your stress, hunger, and alertness. All of these can have an affect on your aiming in sticky situations as well as your life ( you can die if you don't eat). You can explore any of the 7 regions but your patrol area is within Mountain View. You can buy furnishings for your home and at a higher rank, you can upgrade your patrol car as well as buy a car while off duty. Your home is kind of bland. I wish that my house looked a little nicer than the shack it resembles. I do find it odd that when I'm off duty, my patrol car seems to be parked at my house. I though I would have to drive (walk, or take a cab) to the Police Station, and get to my patrol car. When I go to the Police Station it's void of any NPCs. Your main reason inside the Police Station is too check email, ask for a warrant, or go off duty. When you have suspects in custody, all you do is click the police station door (without going in) and a window pops up asking if you want to put the suspects in jail. Clicking the window, tells you how you did (giving expierence). You also get expierence putting tickets on illegally parked cars and towing them away when a driver fails a breathalyzer test.
While on duty, dispatch will squawk emergencies and you have the option of excepting. If you do, dispatch alerts other officers that "26" (your call) is in route. It would of been nice like in Police Quest, to be able to click a button to alert dispatch og your whereabouts (ex. "dispatch, 26, is heading south on main or dispatch, 26, is on scene or requesting backup. I found that when a suspect raises their gun, you don't have much time to react which in real life is true but there should be something that allows you to walk up to the suspect and if he/she pulls out a gun, how can you survive.  I have to say that the game makes you learn. If a murder suspect or drug dealer is your emergency, you bring your car close enough, and if things get hairy; jump in your car for a better strategic location. I did find that outside, the perp runs and you can command them to stop. The one in the mini-mart only allows me to take him down. I wish there was an other way instead of killing the suspect. By the way, the mini mart only had a counter.
Your patrol car is fantastic. I love how you can get in, turn on your lights, (high beams also),  turn in the warning siren ti pull people over, turn on the emergency lights for persuit, and siren. You can set up speed traps and road blocks to check traffic. The help screen is a nice touch. I wish that there was a quick tutorial that goes thru it by putting you in each situation.
I love how this game is open ended on the realistic side. It won't end unless you retire. You can rise through the ranks from patrolman to trooper captain ( I think, I would habe to look). Rising through the ranks seems to allow you to be able to buy a car, upgrade your patrol car and/or buy another. That seems it.
I wish we were able to see other cops, mingle with them as well as call for backup. In Police Quest, you would be at the Police Station, shower, change into your uniform, go through a briefing with the captain, grab your walkie and patrol keys. I see the speed limit signs which is realistic, however, when I was not called to an emergency, I find that me speeding, had no effect as well as running red lights. I thought when you don't respond to emergencies, as a police officer, you still must obey all traffic laws.
All in all, for $19 (from the release date till Oct. 31st, it's $15) this game is really good. Yes it has bugs (cars parked 5 ft. in the air), poor path finding by NPCs but the game has already been thru 2 patches so it will be interesting how this game evolves. I'm hoping it's constantly supported with added DLC and expansions. This game has the potential to be fantastic. Now while this game has some bugs, it certainly doesn't make this game unplayable. It's still very enjoyable!
Interstingly, a patch came thru during the weekend. Cudoes to the developer for working "after hours." Don't think it's not appreciated!

Have you ever asked or been asked if video games are art? Look no further than this game to seek your answer. This game's beautiful art-style and stunningly moving (and reactive) narration is so powerful it will bring tears to your eyes, and is by far the best written game I have ever played (and I prefer games that focus on storytelling).
Don't let the cute art-style or isometric perspective fool you - this is a tragedy set in a post-apocalyptic world (that's right, a post-apocalyptic world featuring every colour of the rainbow) that will have you battling both your conscience and fate through a linier narrative. The battle system may be simple, but there is enough variety of both melee and ranged weapons, stat-boosting tonics and difficulty-enhancing totems that you will find exactly the kind of game you are looking for, regardless of your tastes. Unusually for a linier story replayability abounds as this game features a 'New Game Plus' mode, 'Score Attack' mode, in-game challenges and multiple endings to the 9-hour story for you to sink your teeth into.
If ever you have bought a game out of curiosty or on the word of another, let it be this one - you will not be disappointed.

Before I started playing, I wasn't expecting much (it's obviously a port of an Android/iOS mobile game, so nobody would reasonably expect great things).  To my surprise, this title is great fun and I've found myself wandering back to it time and again.
I won't bother to describe the basic gameplay, as everyone's already done so and it's exactly what you'd expect.  There is a bit more strategy to the game later on.  The non-upgraded characters are mostly fairly similar in terms of usability and only when fully powered-up reveal their respective strengths in play, with previously-entirely-unwanted healers and freezers becoming surprisingly useful as leads.
The game is not without fault: collecting the sizeable numbers of gems needed to upgrade all characters to level three and complete the last levels is taking a very long time.  I assume this reflects the pay-to-play nature of the original, but these character upgrade costs definitely need to be reduced for the desktop game.  On the plus-side, as grindy as it is, I'm still enjoying just playing towards the finish, as much as I would have liked to get there sooner.
The developer is NimbleBit, although they're strangely shy about putting their name on Steam.  This seems to be the only thing they've ported so far.  I hope we see more of their work in future and I hope especially for a bigger, better sequel to Nimble Quest, which very much deserves it.
On the whole, this is very much an underrated title - I recommend it highly to anyone who appreciates this kind of old-school gameplay.  Kudos to NimbleBit, for creating a game that is far better than its humble mobile origins would suggest.

You reasearch technology and genres while doing contracts in between for extra cash so that you can eventually release big titles, gain fans, and maybe even take over the world? The not so fun thing about these games was that if you got lucky and managed an amazing score on a certain game, future releases would be forever held to that standard which in turn made it very tedious to try and stay afloat while releasing a quality product that your fans would like. Half of the time the score would seem a bit random even if you did all the right things like combining the right genres and putting your strongest team to work on the more dificult parts. It would get frustrating when you would lose power or your machines would break down, ruining all progress on any of the titles you work on. This isn't so bad at first, but it happens more as the game goes on which effectively makes the time and care you put into making a good game title pointless. You also had to grind out 'Research Points' to be able to learn about anything which took valuable time away from making money among other things. In short, while fun at first, but was hurt by seemingly RNG mechanics and too much micro management which I never thought possible.
Still research everything from technology to genres but it only requires money. You can actually design your game company with special rooms just for your developers, researchers, marketers, customer service reps, etc. You can even build a warehouse/production area so you can publish all your games in house and watch them fill the shelves! It made it really easy for me to keep track of who does what and making sure they were on task. You don't have to worry about a previous game's high score effecting future releases with unrealistically imposed standards. You don't lose power or progress and your employee stats are much clearer and easier to gain. You don't have to grind research or any other kind of currency besides just money which allows me to spend my time doing other things to help my company thrive. Training your employees is much less costly and everything from their stats to the game creation seems to be a lot more streamlined. I also love that you can change where any of your employees are working with a simple click and drag.
As far as early access titles go, this product is pretty polished! My only gripes are that once your company starts to get REALLY big the game starts to struggle with the load. I had the big 2 room office which is the largest one you can get and while most things were still running smoothly, the hiring window was really laggy. I also wish there was a way to hit pause on the game time while a dialog box is open notifying me of something so I don't lose time in between tasks.
This game, like its predecessors, can be very unforgiving at first til you learn how everything works. Expect to restart your game a few times within the first hour of playing as you get the hang of it.
Don't be afraid to exlpore and make mistakes. Try new things! When in doubt, save first! You can reload if things go badly.
You have toggles on the bottom of your screen in case you keep accidentally picking up furniture when trying to click an employee.
Keep an eye out for a sad face icon on the lower left hand side of your screen. That is your employees trying to tell you they need something to thrive. It's usually shelves or fire extinguishers so fix it. Otherwise they work at half their normal speed.

I will give the game's creators a great deal of credit for their attention to gender and sexuality - it gets a little hamfisted at times, but allowing a player to set their gender and sexual preference seems like it should be a given in 2014...

Here are my thoughts and feelings about Heroes Rise: The Hero Project. (Spoilers ahoy)
The story is even better than the last one, with twists and turns that will keep you guessing on your first time playthrough. It has a feeling to it that really gets you tense and pumped up for what happens in the story.
The characters have varying types of personalities and most have semi-realistic personalities.
Even though the story is better this time round it has even more problems than the last one. While the first one felt linear it wasn't glaringly obvious, unlike in this one. Never before have I felt that the choices I made had no impact to the game. Everything I did just felt like poking a wall, it changed nothing. No matter what you do you will ALWAYS get as far as the final eliminations and all that changes is how the ending starts off.
Although I said most characters feel semi-realistic it is not the MAIN characters that feel that way, tis the side characters. Jenny has a "My way or the high way" attitude and she will force you to leave the competion just so she can do her investigation, even though she clearly states that you are also apart of it and can continue it without her. However you never can and don't even get the option to look into it YOURSELF!
Black Magic has a complete personaltiy reversal! In the first game he/she is kind, caring and can be a bit forceful in her methods. But overall she/he is a good person. In this story she becomes narcisitic, confrontational, manipulative and even cruel. She/he goes out of her way to stay in the competition and will pit you against another potential love interest, even if you say that you aren't interested in her/him.
Rexford is played like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like ALL the obvious bad guys are, its like the writer didn't even try to hide the fact he's the bad guy. His stat is useless and changes nothing so don't even try to pander to him.
In the last review I said that the choices were biast to one specific style of play, going for the "Correct" options. For example saving a reporter or your Sidekick, saving the reporter was seen as only wanting fame and saving your Sidekick was the "Hero" way. In this story its even worse, as the types of play actually have catergories now! Which makes them even more narrow minded than before! It makes it feel like you are meant to play the game ONE way and if you try to do it another way prepare for so many penalties you'll feal like Oliver Twist asking for more food. "CHOICES?! How dare you ask to be different and do things your way! GET BACK TO MY WAY OR GET OUT!". Why can't you get the teams to work together to get Culic or save the people in the Tunnel? Why is stoping Culic, a Leader of super-Terrorists, consider pandering to fame when stoping him there might stop the current attack AND save lives!? Why do you always get low scores when you actually perform the best you can actually do at a trial?! The max points you can get is 90 when doing a team training trial and even if you get perfect scores for each you will always be at the bottom! So you are forced into the situation of either leaving the finals or outing your friend to get further in the competition. Why can't I actually get past this with good points?! Even though I got my Gold key at the near the start I still come at the bottom, exactly the same outcome if you take the longer "Correct" way! What the hell is this?!
There's also the fact that most of the statistics for stats and relationships don't matter for most of the characters it shows! Rebellion's stat does nothing, Rexford's Stat does nothing, and Grandma's stat does NOTHING! Why are they even there if it changes nothing story wise, gameplay wise, or even freaking conversation wise?! What's the point of the Control and Unleash guage when going either way does NOTHING! Being in complete control of your powers does nothing, so if you think it means that when you use you Infini powers it isn't as bad as if you didn't. You will ALWAYS fail at evacuating everyone at the Castle with infini powers.
This is meant to be a Text adventure GAME, but it really just feels like a story with slight variations in what happen. If you have played text games you should now that it has much more freedom in what you can do and actually feel like you choices matter. Here its just a story with fake options that do nearly nothing.
Overall even though this game is better than the last it has even more problems that nearly negate every gain it has made. Even though I reccommend this game I still caution you on buying it. If you like it when most of the control you get does nothing and only want to see a story play out then by all means buy this. But if you want a Text adventure GAME than I'm afraid this isn't up to snuff yet.

Yes, it obviously is very much based on that other game dev tycoon game. The title is a bit underwhelming, and I expected a pretty bad rip-off. At first, I thought I was right, as the starting situation, with your company in your basement and a car next door reminded me quite a bit of a certain other game.
However, soon you realize that this game has more features. You can design your office, controlling the size of each room and what is being worked on in that room. You assign dev- or research projects to a room, and the more people work in it, and the more advanced they are, the faster the result is done.
You can even start to produce the games yourself, which requires a manufacturing room with CD presses and a storage room (make sure you get both, they dont need employees in them, but before you have both, production won't start, and you wanna have the game available as soon as it was developed).
Moving to a bigger space requires a bit more work... you sell old office stuff, move into the new space... and it's all empty. So you have to build those walls, decorate and furnish the rooms and assign your workers, which of course still get paid while you build, so it helps to go room by room so you can assign people quickly.
In general, the game has more detail than that other game (Which I enjoyed a lot as well, btw!!), has more options and features which DO make sense, and seems to be shaping up quite nicely. My first play-session lasted for 3 hrs straight with no break, and I am looking forward to continuing. Not sure how much replay-value the game has once you have become the big and rich tycoon, but until then, its a very enjoyable and slightly addictive game.

-Early Access Review-
Well, where to begin with Mad Games Tycoon? Would I recommend it in its current state? Yes. Yes I would.
I bought this game today, I played it non-stop and have now ran out of content after building my one man in his garage into an enormous empire with around $2270m. More content will be added in the future as a few rooms are locked and I assume more techonology advancements and the likes will be added, so fun fun!
Pros:
+Its addicting, seriously.
+The customisation for the rooms is interesting.
+Plenty of choice and competition.
+There is already a fairly large amount of content, even for an EA.
+The graphics are nice and fit in well with the theme.
+The choices when making a game are pretty cool and varied.
+The different stats on your workers allow for some tactical placement early game.
+Updates appear to come quickly and in response to community demand, which is nice for an EA! (Cough, Starforge, Cough)
Cons:
-The music. God damn. I had to mute it after about 20 minutes as I felt an urge creeping upon me to douse my computer in petrol.
-Placement of items is still a little so-so, I've bugged it a few times and had desks stuck in walls and objects placed over the tops of each other. (Just another minor issue with EA)
-The MMORPG's subscribers drop off in drones randomly you are also unable to make expansions at the moment, if I'm wrong correct me. ( I just didn't see a way)
-Once you have money, it is beyond easy regardless of difficulty.
-Needs more level 3 publishers to allow for greater yeild on your prefered games. (Current set-up makes RPG's less than profitable)
Interesting bits!
* The random speech is quite fun actually, with strange little references to other games.
* Some of the current bugs can be funny and are not particually game-breaking. (one of my workers was typing on a plant and cupboard)
*The names - Seriously - They are great little knock offs. I love it!
To sum up, even in its current state it is well worth the purchase and the time. The developers are community-centric and update often with bug fixes and content. There is much more to come so pay up, support the developers and reap those rewards!

Pirates of the Caribbean is a series of fantasy swashbuckler films produced by Jerry Bruckheimer and based on Walt Disney's theme park ride of the same name. Directors of the series include Gore Verbinski (1–3), Rob Marshall (4), and Joachim Rønning and Espen Sandberg (5). The series was most notably written by Ted Elliott and Terry Rossio (1–4); other writers include Stuart Beattie (1), Jay Wolpert (1), and Jeff Nathanson (5). The stories followed the adventures of Captain Jack Sparrow (Johnny Depp), Will Turner (Orlando Bloom), and Elizabeth Swann (Keira Knightley). Characters such as Hector Barbossa (Geoffrey Rush) and Joshamee Gibbs (Kevin McNally) follow Jack, Will, and Elizabeth in the course of the films. The fourth film featured Philip Swift (Sam Claflin) and Syrena (Àstrid Bergès-Frisbey), while the fifth film will feature Henry (Brenton Thwaites) and Carina Smyth (Kaya Scodelario). The films take place in a fictional historical setting; a world ruled by the British Empire, the East India Company and the Spanish Empire, with pirates representing freedom from the ruling powers.
The film series started with their first release on the big screen in 2003 with Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl, which received positive reviews from the critics and grossed US$654 million worldwide. After the first film's success, Walt Disney Pictures revealed that a trilogy was in the works. The franchise's second film, subtitled Dead Man's Chest, was released three years later in 2006; the sequel proved successful, breaking financial records worldwide the day of its premiere. Dead Man's Chest ended up being the number one film of the year upon earning almost $1.1 billion to-date at the worldwide box office. The third film in the series, subtitled At World's End, followed in 2007, and Disney released a fourth film, subtitled On Stranger Tides, in 2011 in conventional 2D, Digital 3-D and IMAX 3D. On Stranger Tides succeeded in also grossing more than $1 billion, becoming the second film in the franchise and only the eighth film in history to achieve this.
So far, the film franchise has grossed $3.73 billion worldwide; it is the eleventh highest-grossing film series of all-time and it was the first franchise where more than one film grossed $1 billion worldwide.
A fifth film, subtitled Dead Men Tell No Tales, is set to be released on May 26, 2017.

Sometimes it's a problem to be a massive fan of a game like Terraria, the 2D RPG-Platformer-Building masterpiece. I say this because the hunger for more similar games that meet the expectations often leaves me disappointed. There are so many Terraria clones out there that, plainly, suck balls. So when Starbound came along and it seemed to not suck like most clones, I really wanted to try it out.
Turns out that this clone does not suck, at all. It's difficult to innovate in this genre, because there is not a lot more to add to what Terraria has done. Starbound takes this to a new level: there are virtually infinite worlds to explore, as opposed to the one in Terraria. Granted, these are smaller, but the variety in them makes it incredibly satisfying to fly from one planet to another and find a completely different place, with different enemies and different loot to find.
The RPG aspect of Starbound is also top-notch. You can choose what race you want to be from a wide pallet and based on that the quest system and the upgrades for your equipment will be different. So yes, you have to play the game from scratch several times to enjoy all the content it has. And keep in mind that this version is still early access. It only gets better from here on.
I have to address also the fact that this game has been in early access for almost two years now. The developers are taking it slow, perhaps too slow. Take that into account when buying this game: the released product may be very different from what you will get now. But in the mean time, you can enjoy a game that takes Terraria and expands it to a whole universe. It's the same, but different at the same time. If you love Terraria, you will love Starbound. Maybe not as much, but it sure is enjoyable.

Honestly, I get the hate. The game is not finished (that's why it's early access, people), but it has been around for a while and I understand why people are getting fed up. However, I really do think that it's worth the purchase. It's a fun game (especially with friends), and if you enjoy games with sandbox elements like Minecraft or Terraria, you'll enjoy Starbound.
The first thing I'd recommend is not to let yourself get burnt out. The quest-upgrade-rinse-and-repeat system gets very repetitive, and mining does get old after a while, but if you set up some pet project like a house or something (and not in your ship; you'll just get fed up with moving things around again and again), you'll feel more invested.
If you play with friends, it makes the experience ten times better. Have someone set up a Hamachi server and play in a small group of your friends; when it's just you, the quests seem to be all there is, but when there's a friend or two around, you can go off on adventures (even mining is more fun), and you can finally put those silly facial expressions (try pressing the arrow keys some time!) to use.
Don't buy this if you don't understand what early access means. This game is not finished. I do, unlike some other people, believe in Tiy and the other developers, and I think once this game hits release it'll be a masterpiece--but right now, it's still a work of art, and I wholeheartedly recommend it.

One day, you and your friends are enjoying an excursion in the woods when you stumble across a solitary cave. Outside stands a fish; he chuckles and beckons you closer. When you approach, he regales you with stories of adventure and of entire worlds to discover beneath the depths of the earth. What mysteries does this cavern's depths contain? What secrets could you unfurl? You and your crew could know, for the low price of $15.
Titillated, you hand over the money one person at a time until you've all entered the cave. Heart pounding with excitement, you light a torch and hold it aloft, illuminating the cavern with a saffron glow. Grinning, you stalk into the darkness, and grinning grins of their own, they follow you.
Several feet in, you come to descry the visage of what appears to be a solid rock face; a dead end. Obfuscated, you give it a nudge. It doesn't move. You try again with your shoulder, but this attempt is just as futile as the last. You issue a mighty roar, bringing your foot against it, and a patina of dust glides off the surface. You watch the wall with expectance. Nothing. Sighing, you motion to your friends, and they approach.
You and your friends spend the next several hours pushing, kicking, and attempting to shove the wall down. At one point you hear the din of metal, and look over to see your friend using a pickaxe; you don't remember where or when he got it, but ultimately he's not making any progress - the wall is completely indestructable. Finally, you decide to take a break. You lean back against the cool stone and squeeze your eyes shut, the sweat trickling down your face. You're beginning to realise that it was all a farce. There was no adventure, nor mysterious depths, nor secrets to be uncovered here - and there never was.
You call to your friends to cease their efforts, and grudgingly they comply. When you again reach the outside, the sky has grown dark and there's no trace that the fish had ever been there. Furious, you squeeze your hands into fists until your nails bite into your palms, until you can just begin to feel your warm blood beginning to trickle.
"Are you alright?" your friend enquires, placing a reassuring hand on your shoulder.
"Yeah, it's nothing," you reply, avoiding his gaze.
Turning away from him, you gaze off into the woods. Somewhere out there in that ebon expanse is a fish, chuckling merrily as he's several dollars richer and your group is several dollars poorer. In your mind, you can still hear his chuckle; it repeats itself endlessly, and you know from this moment on, that sound will haunt you for the rest of your life. You'll wake screaming in the dead of night, the sound limpid as the memories of your crushed dreams harry you again; you'll be sitting by a pond on a sunny day when the sight of a lone fish sends you sprawling away in terror; you'll be telling a joke and one of your friends will laugh, and that laugh will remind you of that fateful day - that one fateful day, where you and your friends were blithe and stupid enough to listen to that fish...that one...sordid...
EDIT:
As to my actual reasons for why I dislike this game, read on:
I found it to be a shallow, poorly balanced experienced. Terraria benefits from having everything hand-crafted, making it a game with a lot of depth and replayability; you can always come at it from a different angle, find something new.
In Starbound, depth is a veneer of procedurally generated content often with no rhyme or rhythm. In Terraria, what you choose to pursue in terms of armor, weapons and accessories is a strategic decision: Do I want to be a tankier, more melee-oriented character, or do I want to be more ranged-based -- maybe I could be a mage? In Starbound, it's a roll of the dice: Does this randomly-generated shotgun named 'The Poopstick' that I could purchase for several hundred coins have better stats than my starting sword? Usually, in my experience, the answer is no.
I've also found exploration to be lacklustre. I can dig all the way to the center of the planet and find basically nothing, or if I do, it's a tiny little cave with some pixel containers in it. Never do I find chests containing valuable loot, or dangerous dungeons with some high-tier rewards at the end.
Once I dug down really far and found an underground temple/pyramid-type structure, and inside I found absolutely nothing; some breakable pots and a container that was totally empty. I once flew far away to this snow-covered planet, finding a high-tech base with a laser-guarded room, guards that had automatic rifles and snipers that could one shot me, et cetera. I made my way around this base, sneaking past the guards, opening all the containers I could find. You know what I got? Some furniture and some stims, and some other miscellaneous stuff that's basically useless. Terraria rewards exploration, but in Starbound, you might as well not even bother.
There's also no reason to do any base-building, as most planets are identical. And most of the time you're going to be flying around in your ship anyways, so it's not like there's a reason to settle down. You go to a planet, find what (little) there is to find, and move on. The game allows you to collect furniture and materials to build with, but gives you nothing to do with them. Why am I going to settle down on one planet as opposed to another? I might as well just throw everything in my ship; at least the game spawns me there.
There's a whole bunch more stuff; I could talk more about the lack of interesting procedurally generated content, the floaty combat, the starting quest you have to do that takes way too damn long (a good sandbox game should just drop you in and allow you to do whatever you want; forcing you to do this tutorial quest where you've gotta go through this colony and then fight this giant boss at the end is extraneous and tedious).
Anyways, that's just my opinion and it's all right if people dissent. It's been several updates since I've played, so maybe they've fixed some of the issues I've listed. I can just say that, for me, I've not found it to be a worthwhile experience.

The experience playing through again revealed that the dialogue and decision choices, while varied, did not drastically affect the outcome or create new subplots. Other than getting different reactions from the NPCs, the experience becomes very repetitive. All in all, I would not hold that against what was otherwise a great interactive story.

The map is split into tiny sections you have to drive through checkpoints to get to different parts of the map, there are so many loading screens in this game for pretty much everything you do.
All the above points are things that are core parts of ther game and will probably never be changed/fixed at the time of writing there are many other issues too such as bugs (cars floating in the sky), I feel like the duty time is too short it makes you rush to complete the day, buying yoyur own car is far too expensive compared to how much money you make, you have to get a taxi home because home is too far from the station. Hopefully the modding community will come to the rescue of this game but at the moment i wouldn't recommend this game, ive played played games that cost £4 - £5 that have been more polished  and genrally better games.

I traded a game I would never play to get this one. I felt the name alone would make it good blindstream bait. As such, I booted it up yesterday to show my friends. I went in with neutral expectations, keeping an open mind.
1.4 hours later, which is how long it took to finish You Are Not A Banana, I had three words to say about it: "Screw this game."
First, let's give credit where it is due. There are a few legitimately amusing moments in You Are Not A Banana. Some of the humor in it does work. It's not a logical game in any sense, but frankly, if you went into a game called You Are Not A Banana with hopes of logic being present, you need to check your expectations. So it did make me laugh a few times, and that is more than I can say about some games.
With that out of the way, it's time for all the things I can use to discredit it. The game's title is a bloody lie, and it took me a few tries to even figure out what I was supposed to do. After that lie is unveiled, there is no mention from any characters about bananas. This is extremely depressing.
Okay, let's be serious for a moment. The gameplay is awful. I don't mean the parts where you walk around as the main character from room to room, because that's your basic movement scheme. What I'm talking about is the "gimmicks" present. For example, you have two race sequences on a bicycle. Controlling that stupid bike, and moving it quickly enough to pick up the wrenches you need, all without crashing into random nonsense, is absurdly annoying. There are a few times where you need items, and those items are unintuitive in how they are gotten. On top of that, there isn't really anything to examine. Your character will comment on certain things when he is close to them, but there is no way to specifically trigger those comments beyond hoping you are in the right area, and you can't make the stupid speech bubble go away if it does pop up unless you get away from said location.
The protagonist, by the way, is an utter loser who I gladly ran into several cars. This unlikeable waste of data space gives no incentive to help him get what he wants. Every time a character made his life more difficult, I was quite happy, because he deserved it. None of those characters have names, for the record, or if they do, I sure as heck didn't see them.
Oh, and speaking of running into cars, here is one of the few things I can say this game did right. If you die, you spawn nearby. No progress is lost, unless you're in the race, in which case you restart the race (which honestly is not a huge deal, even if it is annoying). And thank everything it does, because this flipping game does not have a save system. It's a short game, yes, but come on now. After how awful some of these segments were, I really wanted to save, quit, and come back to it later. But no, I had to do it in a single sitting, and that was just bad.
The music is mostly meh. I didn't particularly like any of it. The graphics? Also meh. I mean, some of the items look like what they should. Others... I thought I had gotten soda instead of milk, let's just put it that way. The protagonist also looks obnoxious, which is fitting, given that he is, but still makes him blah to continuously look at.
But all of this pales in comparison to one flaw I have not yet mentioned. I probably would not have recommended the game even without this flaw, yet I could have at least said, "If you can get it for free or something, sure, give it a go for a few quick laughs." With this? I don't recommend it even for free. And what is it?
The graveyard puzzle.
The graveyard puzzle is one of the worst experiences I have ever had with video games, and that is saying a lot. It is an infinite cemetery that has you constantly at crossroads with four paths. You have a heartbeat/music to follow, with one randomized path having a slight variation. You take that path, and then do it again, and again, and again, constantly wondering if you are getting anywhere, until you finally find something different.
This bloody puzzle took me somewhere from half an hour to forty-five minutes to complete, and not because it was particularly mind-challenging. No, it was because the sound differences are so subtle that it is nearly impossible to figure out where to go. I couldn't hear any difference 90% of the time, and the people viewing my stream couldn't tell, either. You know what's not fun? Randomly picking paths and praying they work, and then banging your head against a wall when you find out you've actually made things worse. To add icing on the cake, your character's footsteps are so stupidly loud that it's ridiculously annoying to try and hear the heartbeat over them. I honestly had no idea if I could ever get through this segment, and when I did, I could not wait to finish the game just so I could rant about how horrible it is and delete it off my computer forever.
Fun fact: the developer has evidently said this is an "experimental puzzle." I've got news: that experiment failed. NEVER DO THAT AGAIN.
After that puzzle, I finished the game in about five minutes, give or take. So yes, a total of 1.4 hours, with most likely over half of that being the awful graveyard part. I have 3.6 hours because I left the game running when I was done to collect the trading cards. But not for a badge, because I don't want that shameful thing in my profile. I'm trading/selling/doing SOMETHING with the cards to get them out of my life, and only got them so I would never have any reason to download this game again (barring something highly unexpected coming up, such as having a gun pointed at my head and being threatened to be shot unless I play it again).
Is this the worst game ever? No, but it sure as heck isn't a good one. That you have to pay anything for it is a crime. Even if it was a free game, I wouldn't recommend it, but at least it would only be ripping off your time and not your wallet. Thank goodness I got this for basically nothing. It did at least make for an amusing blindstream at parts, but I will never let that graveyard segment go, and I will be referring to it from now on as a fantastic example of what NOT to do in a game.

Really nice little arena based FPS with short intense action, persistent weapon upgrades which combines with learning the game and the enemies to make a nice smooth difficulty curve to work your way up as you improve your gameplay and your arsenal to enable your expeditions to last longer.
Your task is to drop into a crater and follow around your automated mining robot (FRAND) and pick up the gold he mines from the crater (and the occasional gold from the gold coloured skeltins that sometimes appear). The main thing that really makes the game is the greed mechanic - the first gold you pick up is worth 5, the next is worth 6 (for 11 total), then 7 (=>18) and so on. However if you die before depositing this gold back in the middle of the arena where you started, you get nothing, so you have to balance the risk of losing everything to the every increasing rewards for staying out longer.
As your expeditions last longer more enemy types appear, each with their own gimmick (green skeltins explode when you kill them, which is good, red skeltins move very fast, which is very bad, etc.), but the key is all of them can be killed by one shot (except maybe the boss at the end which I haven't reached), so the difficulty is in numbers and the special abilities some have, which I always find much more rewarding to prevail against than just endless amounts of tanky enemies that you need to empty entire clips to kill each one.
Another nice touch is the start menu - instead of being in a traditional menu system, all the features you would normally find in a game menu are laid out on the interior of the ship, so to turn the in game music off or to a different track, you go over to the radio, or to upgrade weapons you go to the upgrade machine in the other corner, and to start a game you drop through the hole in the floor down to the crater. You even have some motivational posters in there which explain the key mechanics of the game you might otherise miss (how the gold system works, why wraiths appear, how to kill the ball enemies in one shot).
The only down side I really found was once gold is no longer useful and you have no more upgrades to buy it takes away quite a lot of what this game work so well, but before then you will probably have a good few evenings blasting skeltins and being run over by balls while chasing after that big score.
Overall this is highly recommended, and is perfectly suited to lots of short five minute gaming sessions whenever you get time, or longer "just one more expedition, I promise I won't get too greedy this time"

Even in its current unfinished state, Mad Games Tycoon is a great game! Initially I thought it looked like a Zynga-esque rip-off of Games Dev Tycoon, but I took a gamble on it during a sale and to be honest I find MGT is the better game! There are very many similarities between MGT and GDT but Mad Games feels like the less mobile-version game of the two. It has a watered down, but still enjoyable, Sims-ish building/management component that GDT does not. But the best element about the game in my opinion is the actual game making itself. I found it infinitely more enjoyable and transparent than GDT, where the quality of your games feels like a crap shoot and you are not penalized so harshly for being imaginative and drifting from obvious genres. Instead of the Tech/Design ratio thing GDT has, MGT has a numerical graphics/sound/controls/technology pool which is influenced by the visible stats of your staff, making way easier to understand where you game succeeded/failed. Similarly, any feature extras like 'sprites', 'vibration controller support' etc contribute directly to the game in transparent ways that make sense, such as 'sprites' contributing to the graphics quality of the game, 'vibration' improving the controls, etc.
Also, every update the dev releases (which is about 1 a month or less) has been excellent and not just bug bashes, and he seems very responsive to feature requests on the Steam forums. He has also been very cooperative about making the games files available for modding, allowing us to rename companies and products to their real-life counterparts.
So if you like GDT, I recommend this! I find it like a less mobile, more in-depth and (most importantly) more transparent version of GDT, and even then it is still an early access with features being added to it!

I like this. I've been playing a lot of 4X, starting with MOO1 waaaay back. MOO2 and Alpha Centauri were my favorites, and I still play a game of Alpha Centauri every now and then, since it is such a stroke of genius.
Anyway, this new MOO somehow just works for me. It copies a lot of things from MOO2, but that's not a bad thing. I don't know what the exact reason is, but MOO2 was always more FUN than other space 4X games. For me, at least. I have not played a whole lot yet, but so far it's been a very fun experience.
Also, they didn't just copy the game, they made lots of little changes too. For instance, they switched to star lanes, which I like, because you can no longer just attack the inner planets of an empire, without going through the outer ring first.
If you put too much population into one field, you get diminishing returns, which is a change I especially like. When you take all your nerdy researchers, give them a pickace and tell them to slave away at the new spaceport, it's not exactly efficient. :)
One thing which they both kept and improved is the research system of MOO2. You still have to pick between technologies, which is probably why MOO2 was so awesome in the first place. In this game, there's a baseline of technologies you always get, which is a bit sad, but I guess also makes things easier to balance. Anyway, you still have to make lots of tricky decisions.
On the technical side, I have not had any difficulties , but I've only played a few hours so far. Anyway, it ran for 6 hours without ever crashing, which is a plus. ^^
I've only bought this game now because I read mixed reviews and was burned by MOO3, but now I bought it on a sale and am definitely not regretting it.
P.S. The new Trilarians are awesome. Ph'nglui mglw'nafh Cthulhu R'lyeh wgah'nagl fhtagn! :)

I thought I'd recommend this game in spite of its problems. It does have some, but it's worth getting anyway. If it were 60 dollars, no, but at its current price, it's good value. I'll spend this review going over what's wrong with the game (IMO), and in some cases, how to get around those problems.
Firstly, one issue is how the pollution system works. It IS a problem. Pollution is tied to both production AND population. Larger planets can handle larger populations. But larger planets dont seem to handle higher levels of pollution. The pollution problem doesn't scale with the planet, but the population does. As a result, larger planets become utterly useless for production. Some of my 20 pop planets could only handle 2 pop units on production. The rest had to be placed on research or food. Counter-intuitively, this means that having LESS than max population on a planet actually makes it BETTER for production in some cases.
There are a few solutions to this problem the devs should consider, and one solution already in game. Firstly, one of two things should happen. First, the devs could make pollution not tied to population. Second, and something I like the most, is they could actually make putting pop units on food production REDUCE pollution levels. If your planet is producing pollution because you've maxed out production, you could put some of your research pop units on food to compensate.
I struggled for a long time to get any meaningful ship production out of my empire, particularly because i was researching new buildings faster than I could build them. But with the pollution system the way it was, my bigger planets, which rightfully should be the production powerhouses, couldn't produce much. I made the mistake of choosing the core drill research when I came to it in the tech tree. This made a lot of pollution, and limited me to just 2 pop units on production on most of my fully populated planets, even with all pollution countermeasures built. I later made a trade for the core dump research with another empire... This was a god send. CHOOSE THAT INSTEAD. Even with all the production buildings researched (core drill included), and even with maximum population on production, so long as you build a core dump and the other pollution reducing structures, it ELIMINATES pollution from being a problem. I was pumping out fleets at incredible rate end-game.
Secondly, I'm not a huge fan of the way end-game works. Basically, when you fulfill a certain criteria, the game ends. You can keep playing if you want, but then it feels like there's no point. You can't continue to win in another area (with the exception of domination, where you eradicate all other species). I won my first game on the galactic counsel. I was looking forward to moving on to fighting the Antarens, but once you win in one area (such as the counsel), the antarens dissappear.
This is a missed opprotunity. The counsel president is just an empty title. I was hoping that being elected would give some sort of special power in the galaxy, such as influencing the actions of other empires. I was hoping to use it as a weapon against the Antarens, by unifying the 5 other species against this greater common threat. THAT would've been an epic way to end the game.
I get that the "criteria" method is how most games like these judge who "wins"... But honestly, I think that should be changed, particularly in Master Of Orion's case.
Thirdly, the AI has issues. I discovered one of these issues when I made the mistake of destabilizing an enemy with espionage. I destabalized them a few times, and then asked my ally to go to war with them. A few turns later, after I'd gotten rid of their colonies in my territory (my end goal there), they offered peace, which I took... My ally continued to fight them because they had been so destabilized.
This was at the beginning of the game... By the end, they were STILL FIGHTING. My ally was bent on exterminating an entire species just because I destabilized them over a few colonies. A third species started fighting them too for NO REASON, simply because I had made the mistake of lowering their galactic standing with espionage several hundred turns before that. It made relations and alliances really difficult. My relations with that ally kept dropping because they'd give me an offer to go to war with that species, and I'd refuse. It also hurt my alliance every time I had diplomacy with the species they were at war with... Which was unavoidable since I was trying to get enough votes for the galactic counsel.
By the end of the game, that species was nearly extinct, unintentionally, over a spat about colonies at the very beginning of the game. I was left dumbfounded. There really needs to be a way in the game to broker peace between 2 species. I basically used espionage to break the game, and it made diplomacy a pain all the way till the end. This is just one example of how the AI needs work (though to be fair, this is true of a lot of games like this. Gandhi, anyone?)
Fourthly, I've read that multiplayer doesn't allow tactical combat... Why? I would love for nothing more than to try out the tactical interface against a human opponent. I'd vastly prefer doing that than using auto resolve vs human opponents. That's when tactics could actually matter in the game. In fact, I think the whole tactical interface needs love. There should be more ways in the game, using cunning tactics to defeat bigger opponents.
There's also a method of simultaneous turn taking in multiplayer, which is cool (and would be perfect for the tactical interface). What's uncool about it though is that, if any single player clicks "next turn", all other players get a 60 second timer to finish what they're doing before the game finishes their turn.
It seems like a lot of their decisions about multiplayer are driven by wanting to move the game as long as fast as possible... I think wargaming fails to realize that unlike with WOT, strategy players LIKE to take their time, and manage their empire... Or at least, I do. I don't like pressing "next turn" without knowing that I've done everything I possibly can in that turn. There should at least be the option to turn on tactical interface (rather than auto resolve), and turn off the 60 second timer in game options.
Fifthly, there's an issue with performance. AI players take a while to take turns, and I've noticed my character desyncing with their audio a lot when talking, because the animation gets stuck. I have a good computer, so I doubt the issue is my end. I hope they work on optimization in future updates.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I know that sounds like a lot of negatives. The reason I recommend it anyway is because despite all of that, I found it very enjoyable. Furthermore, this game supports mods... And if you can name a problem, odds are, someone's made a mod to fix it. Steam workshop does a lot to massively improve the games on steam, and I fully support any game that takes part in that program. It's vital to beta testing and inspiring potential changes, allows players to customize their experience, fix things they see as problems, and makes it easy for the community to interact with a game through mods.
If it weren't for Master of Orion being a part of the workshop, Id hesitate to recommend the game, because of it's problems... But where the price is at, and with the game being extremely customizable with the workshop, it's WELL worth the 30-40 dollars. I never played the original games, so bare that in mind. My review is purely from the standpoint of this as a standalone game... And as a standalone game, it's pretty good.
