//N.P.P.D. RUSH//- The milk of Ultraviolet is a very, very weird game! It's mostly a top-down shooter of sorts, with some light rogue-like and bullet-hell elements. It's a game that you can pretty much beat in less than 10 minutes, but it may take a couple of hours to understand what's going on and be able to beat it.
Basically, you're dying. You've been in some sort of accident, lost your limbs, and are now attached to a motorcycle, with guns for arms. Badass, huh? Everything has a decayed, drugged feel, in a good way. Your task is to collect girls for an unknown purpose (later revealed), and try to survive while you're at it.
You kill enemies that drop money, and you can use that money to upgrade, sell your organs (and be left bleeding out), buy girls, buy more time, etc. Have I mentioned it's a crazy game?
After Uriel's Chasm, Rail Slave Games seems to have become the developers whose games people just get for very cheap, and then do joke reviews on. While there are many legitimate flaws in this game, it certainly does not deserve the way people look at it as.
I played his other game yesterday, and while I recommended it for people who owned it, and wanted a completely crazy experience, I do not think it is a very good game, even at its core. The cryptic biblical theme didn't help either.
With this game, however, while it's full of huge flaws, design-wise, it's also something very unique at its core, and I actually enjoyed it! Think dark Hotline Miami, on steroids. This is pretty much that, although in a smaller scale.
I've bought it for less than 40 cents, and it gives you 3 cards, which you can sell for 9 cents each, so half of the game pays for itself.
Alike their other game, there are steam reviewers saying the game's
is badly done and very ugly.
Well, the ugliness is completely intentional, and it gives the game a very personal vibe, in my opinion. It's a weird mixture of
. It's gritty and cheesy, but it definitely sets the tone and carries the experience almost by itself.
Mind, however, that the game has many faults when it comes to feedback, and part of it comes in visual form.
This is because you get blood on your screen when you kill enemies (the one introduced after release doesn't, due to a bug...). This would look like you're the one being damaged.
However, when you're damaged, the screen gets blue, and can often pass unnoticed.
It's ... not good. You'll often die because you didn't realize how close you were to death. It's unfortunate...
Thematically, it's very cool looking!
The
aren't very high quality, but again, help to set the tone. Didn't find them very good at all, but hey...
The
is also a mixed bad. It's mostly an amateur industrial metal. It's
noisy and low-fi, and I'll definitely not listen to it on my own time. Yet, it adds a lot to the experience. Most people will find it completely awful at first listen... the whole game feels like that. But if you can put yourself in the right mindset, you'll find that it's a very cohesive experience, design-wise, and thus creates a great atmosphere to visit for a short while.
, it's pretty horrible. Besides, half of the things do not exactly work as intended. Your preferences always reset when you get to the menu (either by starting the game, or finishing a run), the timer starts counting on the menu rather than when you start a run, etc. Still, the most important option for me was the game's volume (no separate sliders either), and that could be changed at any time, by pressing "+" and "-", so that's fine.
You always have to click when the cursor is on "back" to go back. Many people, myself included, simply press "Esc" to go back, and that closes the game immediately. There isn't any sort of saving, so you may lose a few runs by mistake like that.

The game didn't feature any menu, initially, but it was updated after release to have

In this game, you need to save 30 girls, spread through 5 floors. After that, a passage on the 5th floors opens up, leading you to the final Bossfight.
It's a simple twin-stick shooter. You move with WASD, and aim/shoot with the mouse. The menus are the same.
I don't know why people mention the controls as being bad. I thought they were fairly good. Sure, it does not have gamepad support, but it's no the end of the world.
Perhaps people didn't notice that you're on a motorcycle, so you move as in such. It felt pretty good, to me!
Besides, your guns have a very high rate of fire, and make the enemies seems like butter, at times.
The camera is also very close to your character, which may
gameplay for most people. Honestly, I was waaay past that when I played this game. It's the kind of thing you can play for 10 minutes, be challenged, and then put it down.
Each floor has a different configuration, and you'll have to learn their layout to plan accordingly. You have a time limit (which you can increase with money), so it's important to know where to go. The levels are also full of enemies, some of which have a very bullet-hellish pattern. There are only 3 enemy types, though.
There's a shop in the begining of the level, and it's also your "staircase" to change floor. In the shop, you can buy
weapon upgrade, time, girls, and then there are 2 things with a heavy penalty to them. One, is buying health, but losing time. The other, selling your organs, for a big amount of money. Time doesn't tick when you're in the shop. However, once you sell an organ, your health starts to decrease, as you're bleeding out.
While the intention would be for the game to have a very subtle balance between what the player buys, it can be cheesed (haha, obviously!). While that may seem a bad thing (and yes, it is bad design), it opened up a speed-run competition on the Hub, where people are trying to cheese the game faster. It's amusing.
When I first beat the game, I beat it normally, by using the shop only to buy the weapon and time. I explored the levels thoroughly, and collected the girls. It took me more than an hour to understand what was
going on, haha! After that, I cheesed the game, and half cheesed it a couple of more times. It was fun.
The last Boss is in a small screen, with bullet-hell patterns. It only has one phase, and there are situations where you can't avoid to take damage. Still, I never died against it, and I'm not particularly good at these games... The Boss fight is also independent on the rest of the game, so no need to worry about health or anything else.
The game is very, very imperfect, and really bad at times. However, if you manage to ignore that, and even the sub-par design, you'll be left with a
, and quite fun at its core, I've found! I won't play any more than these 2 hours, but it was almost free... Besides, if you're into getting into the highest scores, the game is quite fun to play with.
For the vibe alone, recommended! Otherwise.. don't.

I had read the reviews on this game, but I have to say that I was lucky enough to have a good experience of this short horror adventure. I got up at 5 o'clock in the morning to go to to loo (by torchlight). On the way back I thought that I should idle this game for the cards. I found myself in an almost blackened room with headphones on playing this game. It was the perfect environment for this type of thing.
I didn't mind the slow walking speed as I fumbled my way in the dark, briefly turning on my flashlight to survey a room and then shutting it off to conserve the precious batteries. It was quite tense balancing the need to see now with the fear that I might run out before I found the next stash of batteries. Of course, by immersing myself in this playing style completely, I ended up with quite a supply of unused batteries by the end, but I enjoyed it more that way.
I didn't realise how tense I was until I
and felt a huge relief, only to get me hopes dashed when
.
I tend not to get scared in games, as I tend to find efforts to scare us to be contrived, but there was one moment in this game that genuinely got me. As I kept hitting the F key to turn on the flashlight trying to see
, I could almost feel myself hitting the torch trying to get it to work before creeping forward cautiously to figure the shadows were playing tricks on me.
The only thing that spoiled this for me was that I managed to end it with a bug. I got caught in the middle of door unable to move. Judging by the reported play times of others, I think that I must have been near the end. I knew ends in a "to be continued" message so it wasn't too disappointing. Maybe if I get up in the middle of the night some time in the future, I will try playing this again.
This game really isn't a story, and if you play it wanting to rush through it then you will not have a good time with it. But if you can get yourself in the mood for playing a game that is just about finding your way through some creepy areas in the dark then you can get some enjoyment out of it, but even then you are going to want to get it on sale.
I should point out that I managed to play the game and write this review while being lit by my (real life) torch, which still hasn't run out of batteries. I guess life isn't as scary as the game!

Bastion is a good game ... but not a great one.  Lets get to the good stuff first.  The first thing most people will mention is the narrator and with good reason.  Everything you do in Bastion is narrated.  Whether you are fighting monsters, buying upgrades, or just standing around, the narrator always has something relavent to say.  The voice actor has a great voice for the part and he helps make something that could have been gimicy a stand out feature of the game.
The art and look of the game are excellent.  Vivid colors, unique art design and locals, and a cartoony look make the game look and feel unique.  When you aren't being attacked just wondering through the different locations is a treat.
New enemies, new upgradable weapons, dreams (arenas), and boss fights keep the game feeling fresh.  Getting stuck at a certain spot, find the location to upgrade one of your weapons and go through the trial there to see if you unlock new items and upgrades.  The dreams are a good places to rack up money and face a good challenge as combinations of enemies attack you in different rounds.
The music is simple but effective.  It never gets overly complicated or stands out, it just accompanies game play and it does that well.  It may not be for everyone but I enjoyed it.
The control scheme with a keyboard and mouse was a little cumbersome.  It felt hard to be precise with my movements using the WASD for my movement keys.  The mouse gave me good accuracy for targeting but given a choice I think the game would feel better being played on a controller.
While it was fun upgrading my weapons, I would have liked to have ablities to unlock or upgrade on my character that would make combat even more fun and varied.  This could have lived up some of the boss fights which devolved into run far away as possible and use a missile weapon, rinse, repeat.
The very end isn't a traditional boss fight.  I won't spoil it here and some may have been put off by it but I liked how it finished the story and did something other then kill the boss, roll credits.
I would recommend this game for most people to try out.  Watch the videos and if you are intrigued give it a try, I don't think you will be disappointed.

There is no denying that this game has taken a huge amount of inspiration from Game Dev Tycoon. The game feels similar due to a similar layout, a lot of similar functions, and even the music is oddly reminiscent of Game Dev Tycoon. The thing this game does well though, is that it locates a lot of the flaws in Game Dev Tycoon and fixes them. This could easily have been called Game Dev Tycoon 2 and no one would have doubted it for a second.
I personally love that this game lets you have more than one development team, more than one research team, etc. It increases the pace at which your company grows immensly and it gives you more to do while waiting for a game to finish developing. The production element is also quite interesting, as you can print your own games and determine price, rarity and more. You are also able to buy other gaming companies, and release their games as your own, where you take the majority of the profit. While it's a fun element at first, it can get quite demanding if you own a lot of companies, as they produce a lot of games! If you're like me, you'll even forget to release your own games and instead just rake in 100+ million every year releasing other companies games.
Overall, the game runs extremely well for an early access game. It has a lot of cool features and expands brilliantly on top of an already terrific design by Game Dev Tycoon. It'll be interesting to see what other features they have lined up for the completed version, but so far I love this game!

Fair warning, I am one of the testers, but in the event my review seems at all biased, I'd like to point out that I would not have continued testing the game if it was one that I did not enjoy to play.
Pros:
-Simple, easy to pick up and play concept.
-Good system of progression. New weapons exist not to make the game easier (as each new weapon comes with it's shares of weaknesses to balance out it's benefits), but to add variety to the gameplay.
-Fantastic soundtrack by Aethernaut.
-Charming art design.
-Light, easy gameplay quickly becomes difficult and chaotic about 2 minutes in, providing a nice challenge after a decent length warm up.
-Time consuming achievements. Some may see this as a con, but I see it as an excuse to keep me playing the game until I can 100% it, and as a general rule of thumb, if a game can keep you playing it, it's doing something right.
-Quick rounds of gameplay. I like that I can queue up for a dungeon in a game and then play a few rounds of this while I wait out my timer.
-Moon physics. The game adds some additional difficulty through use of low gravity/friction. It's a bit difficult at first, but once you have it figured out it adds satisfaction to being able to navigate your way through a swarm of skeles.
Cons:
-Some minor movement issues. While the moon physics don't bother me, I find myself dying a lot due to getting stuck on skele corpses and having my speed drastically slow down. While that does add some realism, it's somewhat frustrating to lose 100g because you get stuck on a body.
-Lack of controller support. This is a minor issue, and I can understand it being difficult to enable since I tried to juryrig it using DS4Windows and it failed horribly (the right thumbstick could not come close to matching the sensitivity of the mouse movement).
All in all, an enjoyable experience. It does have it's flaws, but they're all minor and can be worked around with practice.

Let me start by saying I am a mad tycoon fan!
(failed pun, right?)
Not going to say the game is great, it isn't. But it will be. It's not another of the "had potential" games. This game HAS potential, and its developers know how to get there.
Despite having some really bad grammar issues, which are being solved, there are frequent updates, and they're reasonably active around the forums, which is a big plus for any game, especially an Early Access game.
I don't like mentioning other games during reviews, but you can't help but sort of compare it to the likes of Game Dev Tycoon, which is far simpler, and probably easier on the eyes, since Mad Games Tycoon has the ability to build rooms, furnish them and even decorate a bit (wish you could turn the fan movement off, though). Since you can build rooms, it's easy to imagine that you can build them to any size you want, while having a big variety of office sizes to choose from, as well as a big variety of rooms to build, from Development Rooms to Research, Marketing, Server Rooms, and even a couple more that are still not active.
Not a fan of branding a tycoon game by its graphics, soundtrack or even story (since there's hardly any), since the gameplay is pretty much the important part of any tycoon game, and oh boy, does this one have it.
I do recommend this game, not only for what it is right now, but for its actual potential, its active development team and its active community.

As should be fairly apparent at first glance, Nimble Quest is a re-imagining of Snake, only instead of the focus being on collecting pellets and avoiding your own ever-growing body, for the most part your body remains at a manageable size and the object of the game is to skillfully avoid enemies while coming close enough to get them in range of your attacks.
The game is originally from mobile devices, and to a degree it shows. Options are minimal, barely acceptable. UI is clearly designed for touch and though functional with a controller, really works better with a mouse. As a personal preference I prefer a d-pad for the game itself, though I'm sure the keyboard works just fine. It also has mouse controls that mimic the touch controls from phones.
The gameplay is pretty dull at first, to be honest. Playing it for than fifteen minutes at time before boredom sets in is impossible. The game was clearly designed as a grindfest. However, once you've done that grind, gotten your upgrades, and worked your way to the higher levels, the game becomes far more enjoyable. The levels are hectic and engaging, with enemies galore and items all over the screen, a far cry from the more sparse environments of earlier levels. Your line of heroes should be longer at this point as well, meaning you need to pay more attention to your own movements to avoid running into yourself. All the same elements are present, but the increase in the amount of things you need to process keeps you from just sitting and staring at the screen and lets you get immersed in split-second reactions. It's a great experience and a shame it's hiding behind the dull grind that may scare people off before they ever see the more interesting later levels. If you do wish to cut right to the chase and get to the good stuff though,
(as far as messing with your registry goes, anyway, which isn't for everyone), and I wouldn't really blame you if you wanted to go ahead and skip the grind.
All in all, the game's got a good set of underlying mechanics hidden behind some unfortunate vestiges of mobile design. On sale though it's hard not to recommend, especially at the $0.49 I paid for it (and card sales bring that number down even further). If you're looking for a fast-paced arcade action game, this one does a pretty good job of it.

You want to concentrate fire on the big bad battleships coming in? I'll start out by saying that this game isn't as horrible as the reviews might suggest. But i still wouldn't recommend it.
It is made by the same developers who brought you the infamous "Uriel's Chasm". That in of itself is a red flag. But NPPD RUSH is actually a whole lot better than Uriel's Chasm. it isn't exactly down there with E.T and Bad rats as many people would lead you to believe.
But the game is simply too difficult and eccentric for the avarage consumer.
Here are the main problems:
-Barebones mechanics, No powerups or anything like that. Just WASD and Mouse1.
-Camera is too close to the character compared to how fast you're moving, Making the time to react to a threat very slim. And enemies can also shoot you off-screen.
-Art style is very cluttered and could cause problems for some
-Game is timed, and the timer starts as soon as you launch the game. This means you can lose just by idling in the menu
-Options only contain Volume slider and two toggles for the visual effects "scanlines" and "chip fat". No resolution or control options.
-You're constantly being chased by a target reticle that will drop bombs on you if you stand still. The explosion animation of these bombs decays slowly for some inexplicable reason, and continues to damage you long after they initially exploded.
This is very frustrating as there seems to be nothing you can do about it other than to avoid it. Even when all enemies on any floor is cleared, the reticle remains and continues to bombard you. As if the timelimit wasn't stressful enough.
-Enemies can fire "bullethell patterns" simultaneously, Making their patterns overlap and becoming effectivly undodgeable.
-Store prices are unbalanced, Buying extra time (1minute) for example costs 3000 in-game credits. Which is a way offset price compared to the rate you are gaining credits. Getting 3000 isn't really that hard, But 1 minute is simply not worth the price and effort. The same kind of ridiculous price ratios are present in other store items as well.
-When you get damaged the screen gets covered in blue blood, Making you unable to see your character and potentially causing you to bump into more enemies, further damaging yourself.
-You have to find 30 "junkies" that are spread out and hidden across 5 huge levels. And finding them all within the timelimit on your first try is next to impossible. The game therefore requires you to remember all the positions of the "junkies" and leads to a lot of trial and error. Which isn't necessarily a bad thing, But is worth mentioning since trial and error-style gameplay isn't very popular.
The Positive aspects of the game would be its experimental and eccentric vibe. It works if you look at it as a piece of art. However, that might not be something very sought out for here on steam, and would probably fit better on a place like Newgrounds.
NPPD RUSH feels like an experiment made by an art student, which is not aimed to be an insult. But might put many people off.
My recommendation would be to ONLY buy it if it's on a huge discount and you're intruiged by the concept. EVEN after reading this review.

According to Steam I have now played this game for a 153 hours. Here is my impression to date:
When the game works this is a noble and fantastic remake of Master of Orion 2. Unfortunately,  the problems I have experienced have occurred many, many hours into the game. The problems have  made completing any game I start impossible so far. From reading the forums the game appears to have other bugs that appear at unpredictable times.
In my first game, after 400+ turns, I still could not travel through unstable star lanes. This after researching the technology to traverse the lanes. I did report this is a bug but I did not have the time to keep following up with tech support on the issue. In my second game I installed a mod that did not have unstable star lanes. That game was going well although  some turns were taking half an hour to complete. My laptop would also sometimes overheat and freeze between turns. However, my desktop did not lock up. Unfortunately, the mod creator updated the mod this week and now I receive an error trying to load my save games. I manually loaded the old version of the mod and unsubscribed to the newest version of the mod. However, I still cannot load my save games. After 153 hours of play time I have been unable to finish a game due to bugs.
I see that many others are not having these problems. Maybe I received a bad copy or something else is buggy or not configured on my end. I hope that is the case because the creators did a really great job of modernizing MOO2. However, again, just browsing through the comments there appear to be many bugs that pop up.
Bugs aside, I stress this is a MOO2 remake. I spent probably over a year of my life playing MOO1 and I have conceded that no one will ever make true remake.  MOO1 had a simple interface using sliders from the main screen that controlled almost everything.  I found that interface much easier for controlling an empire than having to open up each planet individually. This remake does help in that regard by allowing the user to click through planet to planet without going back to the main screen. That is a time saver but I still wish the planets could be controlled in a way similar to Moo1.
I can nitpick a small book for everything I want to see in the game but I think they did a good job overall recreating MOO2 minus the bugs.  Unfortunately, I do not have the time in my life right now to keep trouble shooting my games.  The really frustrating part is spending two weeks, dozens of hours with several hundred turns getting into the game I cannot complete. Feels like a huge waste of time.
I am going to wait a few months and to see if any of the upcoming updates solve these issues. My recommendation is not to buy this right now unless you enjoy the possibility of becoming a beta tester.

BETA REVIEW:
Starbound is a wonderfully, magnificent game. Starbound is a game where you can choose your species, design your character, and then destroy entire worlds because you want some fuel for your ship. It's Genocide SImulator: 2013. You spawn onto your world for the first time, and you decide to get a simple establishment going so that you can survive. But after a short while of playing you've built your small establishment into a giant building or set of buildings and have killed thousands of the natural inhabitants. You decide to go adventuring into the unknown universe and that's when you happen to come across a village. What do you do? Murder them all, murder every single one of them. And this is why I enjoy this game so much, because no other game lets me destroy the universe because I'm bored. 9/10
BIG UPDATE REVIEW:
A long time has passed since this review has posted. The devs didn't update this game for an extremely long time, and that was a problem. There was a large amount of hype towards the "big update" when they announced it. That update ruined this game. Now the whole purpose of the game is to complete "missions" for people and to conquer certain buildings or whatever. This makes the game way too linear, forcing you to do specific things to further advance in the game. One thing that made this game great was the fact I could go wherever when I wanted to, I could just destroy random planets. The update made it so it was highly linear and you had to do these tedious tasks in order to upgrade your ship enough to leave the solar system. I enjoyed this game a lot, but the updates completely changed that. 4/10.
FULL RELEASE REVIEW:
It's been a long time I last updated this review. I saw the final release was coming out, and I was excited. I was hoping that they had fixed some of the problems I had with it. They didn't fix a thing. What they did was make it worse. The entire story is boring, lame, pointless. It makes the game feel extremely linear, repeptitive, dull, just overall lackluster. The only way to progress through anything is by completing dull missions that have no real meat behind them. They're dull and repetitive. The armour and weapon progression is the same way. You get these materials to craft things to get to new planets to get new stuff to craft more things to go to even newer planets. It's the same thing over and over again. I was hoping that they would add something that gave this game some replay value, or just something that didn't make it repetitive. The plot is the entire focus with things you can do to distract yourself. Like building a home, pointless, your ship can do that all. Pets, crew, useless. They even got rid of some of the customization that made it nice. Different races have the same weapons now, the tiers are the exact same weapons so you can't decide anything. You can't choose to make a dagger or a sword or an axe like you could before. If you want a new tier weapon, you have to get that one type. It's ridiculous. A game like this was never meant to be linear. It feels like it's trying to be something that it never wanted to be. It was open and nice in the beta, now it's pointless and repetitive. There's no replay value. The game has no point anymore. I loved the beta. Those 300 hours were in the beta. I don't love anything about this new game. (I'm not even going to get started on the terrible optimization and lag problems. I hoped those were going to be fixed through beta. They got worse.) 0/10. I'm done with this.

I'm writing this review from the perspective of a person who gamed on Playstation his entire life, having barely played PC games and buying Half Life only because of the huge praise it got. After finishing the game, I have to say, this is one of best first person shooters I've ever played.
Everything it does, is great; gameplay, level design, atmosphere, story, platforming and on. The first hour was boring for me, but I instantly fell in love with the clever level design of having to utilize vents and your trusty crowbar. From there on, it was a beautiful tale of Gordon Freeman and his tale of escapade from Black Mesa.
This game did not need amazing CG cutscenes or an intricate storytelling narrative or overutilized/overly complex elements of the AAA games we get nowadays. All Half Life gave you was a tram to sit in that escorts you to work and as a very polite lady introduces you the science facility of Black Mesa, the safety guidelines of the workplace and a crowbar.
The thing that I find impressive the most is how this game was able to set itself apart, take a more slow, strategic and tactical approach to the FPS genre compared to Arena shooters at the time. With that said I can say, I have never played a game like this.
The atmosphere is dripping with story, asking the character: "What happened here?". From the moment I pressed an elevator button and that action alone had consequences, I was hooked. There are gray areas, different characters have their own agendas, and by the end you might be asking yourself: "So..who was in the wrong?"
This is a must buy game.

Regardless of whether or not you watch the show (or even play games), Telltale’s The Walking Dead is a masterpiece of interactive storytelling that everyone should experience.
The gameplay is simple, you solve some puzzles, make dialog choices for your character, and point and click your way through its surprisingly emotional story. Because it takes place in the comic book universe, but does not follow the main characters (sorry, fans, no Carol or Michonne here), you don’t have to worry about knowing anything from the series. Just kick back and enjoy.
For fans of the series worried that the game focuses on characters they’re not interested in, worry not, Lee & Clementine will grow on you quickly and by the end you’ll be aching to see more—which is convenient, because the story continues (complete with the choices you make carried over via your save file) in further separately available seasons.
A rare game for those who both love and have never played games, as well as both love or have never watched the show, Lee & Clementine’s story in Telltale’s The Walking Dead is a must buy. Grab it right now for whatever they’re asking (it’s worth it), or add it to your wishlist and wait for a price drop; it’s actually frequently on sale.

'Serena', like its character namesake, is by no means perfect. Its major downfall is the impassive voice acting. In the game, you play as a man walking around a cabin, who tells you the story of his life with his missing wife, Serena. As you click on different items in the room, he ponders their connection to her. His mood flips from loving to angry and confused as the story progresses, but this isn't displayed much in the voice acting at all. I feel like a game that focuses so much on spoken narrative (there's really no other aspect of the game - click, hear story, click) could afford voices with a little more feeling. Even Serena's voice actor struggled to portray strong emotion.
Still, having said that, I'm going to recommend this game on the basis that despite the shortness (roughly 1hr from start to finish) and mediocre voice acting, you will think about the game long after you've finished playing. The game ends with some unanswered questions and you will likely find yourself wondering about them, as I did! The game has interesting themes and is honestly mildly disturbing in parts. Would I pay for this game? Unlikely. But for a quick fix of mild horror, tragedy and an hour of entertainment, 'Serena' is definitely worth a free download.

Blades of Time was a gem that I did not expect it to be. Blades of Time is a completely linear style third person game about a blonde female character, Ayumi, and her journey in an alternate land. The story is a little mroe intriguing than I thought although there were certain parts and characters I was expecting more development on. In Blades of Time, you are able to freeze attack, fire attack, strong attack, and dash as some of the abilities you can use. Your main weapon is a two katanas and you are also presented a gun later which can be used strategically.
However, the most appealing part of the game is the time rewind part. Time rewind allows you to create essnetially "clones" of yourself that fight while you can still fight. In one semi-boss, I just kept creating more and more clones onto the semi-boss to the point where I had enoug damage to kill the semi-boss in the eqvuialence of 5 seconds. Obviously I had a lot of clones hitting him, but you get the point. Time rewind is also necessary to complete some puzzles that advance the level and some enemies actually require you to time rewind to kill. It is such a unique and interesting concept that I'm surprised Blades of Time 2 hasn't come out yet.
The graphics of this game are pretty beautiful although some things get repeated a little too often. But other than some repated things (doors, enemies, and lever like things, etc), the environment is beautiful and the world is very beautiful as well. However, the graphics can be a little intensive to computers that cannot handle high demanding games. I have a gaming laptop and sometimes it still lagged hard.
Overall, I highly recommend Blades of Time for anyone who likes to play third person games. Also, just on a side note: you never actually have to pay full price for this game because there is a perpetual bundle on bundlestars featuring this game and some others for only $2.99 which you can find here:
For a small $2.99 price, whoever doesn't buy this is losing out largely...

In a short summary, you play games to earn units (the currency in-game) to buy anything you want or to just have fun and play with random people or with friends, you could even play them by yourself. Still not sure if you want to spend your hard earned cash or money you've received from your parents? Well here are some more details about the game if you're interested.
=================================================================
SOCIAL/APPEARANCE:
This game revolves around social activity and interactions with other people, which is pretty good if you're trying to make some online buddies. Just like in reality, some people are painfully toxic (thank god you have the option of muting/blocking them, too bad you can't do that in real life though), and some are pretty cool and chill. Like any other online multiplayer game, it's always fun to play with friends or make new friends if you're a social butterfly.
You have the option of changing your appearance, although most of the items require you to purchase them with units. You can buy other items for your character in shops that are in the plaza (for example: a jetpack, confetti gun, potions to change your character's size, and even pets that roll around and follow you everywhere).
CONDO:
You start off with just one condo, but you can eventually buy more than one once you're rich enough. Decorate your home however you like using furniture and other items. Put whatever images on the internet onto canvases by providing links. If you need ideas, inspiration, or if you're just bored and curious, (as I said earlier) you can visit condos owned by other people. Look at their stuff or what they could be watching or listening to on their in-game televisions. Oh yes, you can watch youtube videos, twitch streams or listen to soundcloud tracks on media players with other people in-game.
GAMES:

Blades of Time was a rough play for me.  There was obviously an attempt to make a solid action RPG here, but the game is bogged with problems!
- Enemies attack you through combos with no real recourse except to range them.
- Combat is "feathery", lacking any weight or strength.
- You spend a good portion of the game using the same combo attack over and over followed by a few exection skills to   finish off foes.
-The aming is loose and floaty, never feeling like you are actually aiming anything.
- Sound production is horrible, giving little feedback to the world and your interactions with it.
- Interactive Objects are covered in the same grey/brown-mid-2000's color scheme making them easy to miss.
-The camera has a mind of its own, often swinging around awkwardly and hiding enemies from view.
- I stopped caring about the story ten minutes in.  It's cliched and typical and the stilted dialogue is entirely exposition.
- Blades of Time is an attempt to blend God of War with Tomb Raider and fails to capture any of what makes either of those games great.
- Enemies lack personality and originality
- The jumping is quick and hard to control
In closing, I couldn't do it.  Everything wrong with the first few minutes of the game is everything wrong period.  The camera, the controls, the uninspired world, the lazy enemy concepts, the bad combat, the terrible writing, the odd and exaggurated physics and the horrendously-bad Lara Croft impression was enough to make me put this one down for good.

This review was made after the update that fixed FPS problems, and this patch has made the game run flawlessly (90+ FPS) on my mid/low-end PC (on low settings).
Outside of the normal bugs found in Early Access games, this game has a very promising concept, and already provides a large amount of fun. The current gamemodes allow from 16-54 player battles of 1-3 ships per team.
Communication is key in this game, so if you are playing solo (or with friends), be ready to use your microphone or at least follow commands of your captain. If you enjoy team-based combat where proper coordination is rewarded, this game is for you. If you prefer to "carry" your team, this game will become very frustrating for you.
TL;DR if you don't want to listen to other people, don't buy the game. If you enjoy team coordination, buy this game.

Regardless of whether or not you watch the show (or even play games), Telltale’s The Walking Dead is a masterpiece of interactive storytelling that everyone should experience.
The gameplay is simple, you solve some puzzles, make dialog choices for your character, and point and click your way through its surprisingly emotional story. Because it takes place in the comic book universe, but does not follow the main characters (sorry, fans, no Carol or Michonne here), you don’t have to worry about knowing anything from the series. Just kick back and enjoy.
For fans of the series worried that the game focuses on characters they’re not interested in, worry not, Lee & Clementine will grow on you quickly and by the end you’ll be aching to see more—which is convenient, because the story continues (complete with the choices you make carried over via your save file) in further separately available seasons.
A rare game for those who both love and have never played games, as well as both love or have never watched the show, Lee & Clementine’s story in Telltale’s The Walking Dead is a must buy. Grab it right now for whatever they’re asking (it’s worth it), or add it to your wishlist and wait for a price drop; it’s actually frequently on sale.
*Please note: I played this game on the PlayStation 4

Presentation is top notch, and I often find myself lost in the environment. While the game is much more simple than others in the genre, it still presents quite a challenge. Some reviews mention the game crashing at ~500 turns, but i've never experienced anything more than a couple of extra seconds. I enjoy the pace, espeically if you decide to crank up the game speed. All in all i would give it an 8/10. If you enjoy 4x space games, and want something new, I would recommend.

While I've seen more than a few rather negitive reviews on this game, I'd like to add to the growing pool of positive ones.
This game lacks a certain polish -- it almost reminds me of the old GTA or Driver games, yet has a sincere charm to it. It's a great concept (as mods for GTA V such as LCPD:FR have shown with their massive fanbase), and this actually isn't a bad excution of it, while it needs some serious bug-hunting and polish, the potential is certainly there.
Problems:
1.) Days are way too short, you don't have time to do much, then your character is clutching his guts in agony while standing in the road.
2.) Time compression is extreme, gas runs out, hunger sets in, and your character becomes lethargic all while driving to work.
3.) Physics are non-existent, one stop light in particular sends cars flipping across the road, good entertainment value, but certainly immersion breaking.
The good stuff:
1.) I think a game like this has had a demand for some time now, while we've seen a few teasers over the years they've often turn to little more than a flash in the pan, unless you count the CoD clone SWAT games (police=FPS... wut?).
2.) The game-play is rather straight forward, and the Sims-esque needs give you a break after putting the hurt on drunk drivers for a couple hours. I know after playing GTA V with LCPD:FR for a couple hours, I often got bored and started a massive killing spree -- no reason to do that here.
3.) Options: car liveries, and player clothing. You have several asthetic options right off the bat, all of which seem to have had work and thought put into them.
4.) The future -- I think this game will get the polish it needs, the devs are small enough to work with their potential fanbase, and although I haven't had look at the files yet, probably has a good modability factor.
I know what you're asking and why you're reading this: "Red, should I buy this game with my hard-earned money?"
Well, I really couldn't tell you -- while the potential is there, it isn't yet. Is it worth $20? Probably not.. not yet anyways. Do you have $20 you want to spend and help a small company along the way? Then buy it. But if you don't want to spend $20 just to see if you like it, then I wouldn't recomend it, you'd end up hating it like the rather harsh people who've commented before me because now you think you "wasted" $20 on "this".
Give it a shot though, and keep an eye on it, I know I will.
-RedHorizon

Saddens me to leave a bad review after enjoying it so much.  The first 10-15 minutes of the game were spectacular, then the milk scene happened and I had to quit as I thought there was a game breaking bug.  It turned out that I needed to fetch the milk from the shelf and continue my game.  I was so excited to play again after being so sure it was broken.
That's where my frustration began to incline.  Now, here's my thought process:
You start off the game in your house, hearing music playing, and as you walk around there are little hint bubbles above your head.  I would even say that 75% of the floor area is covered in triggers that make hint bubbles appear above your head.  They are extremely clear.  You will soon figure out how to stumble your way out of that first scene, I really enjoyed it.  Bravo.  Then the bike level, pretty tame, but I also enjoyed the challenge of how difficult it was to complete without error.  Bike level 2, even harder, same thing, I get it, it's challenging, I win, go me.  It's very clear what you need to do.
Then this graveyard level.  I gotta say, no one should ever experience that.  My cat was even starting to worry about me after playing that level for an hour straight.  So luckily I saw a thread in the discussion area that
in order to navigate the graveyard.  Cool!  So I do just that, go out there with that in mind, trying to feel my way around listening very carefully.  Walk a few blocks in one direction, few in another, always going back in alternate directions to make sure that I didn't potentially walk past any point where I was supposed to turn.  The tone never changed for me.  You can walk for 10 minutes in one direction, 10 minutes in another, zig zag around, doesn't matter.  The whole area is infinite, there is no way to reach any corner of the level, it's a giant loop.  I literally walked around trying different directions for an hour straight, not even the slightest change in the tone.  I don't get it?  It's the most maddening experience.  I don't wish it upon anyone.  So let me just GUESS at random numbers here:  let's say you walked 100 graveyard blocks to the right, and then went 20 blocks up, did you miss it right at the beginning?  Then from this point is the only way to go back to where you came to retrace those steps?  I can't tell if the tone changes if you are within 5 blocks or 1 block or what.  It's just dumb.  You can spend your whole life in there bumping around.
How would you ever start from the beginning again?  You can't.  The only way is to press the escape key.  What happens if you press 'escape'?  The game terminates immediately, without warning, no dialogs, settings, anything like that.  The game instantly shuts down.  You can't resume where you left off.  You have to start the game back up and play through ALL of the previous levels each time you play.  So if you were frustrated at a few of the previous levels, well surprise surprise, you need to go back and beat them all over again just to have another chance at perhaps walking in the right direction on the graveyard level.  It really wouldn't be so bad if you could resume at the last checkpoint, similar to how when you die in other levels it just restarts from a checkpoint.  There is no way to restart the graveyard.  You get lost, well, game over.  Start the entire game from scratch again.
Can I remind the reader once again that the first stage has popup hints almost 75% of the time while you walk around, very clearly telling you EXACTLY what to do.  Then when you are shopping at the store level, it's up to you to figure out that there are 1000 things in the store and you have to know which button to press at which wall.  The only way to do it is to know in advance where to go or to button mash every key and walk to every single corner and eventually you will find it.  Not really a puzzle!  Just seems like lazy game design.  Put all of the effort in the beginning and then send the player out to button mash.

The narration of Bastion is, as advetised, the strongest point of this game. In fact it's so good that you will lose track of whether  or not you are learning anything at all about the driving points in the story. Coming out a first playthrough I don't think I learned very much at all about the world Bastion is set in. The thin story is allieviated however, by the small number of characters involved in it. I found myself caring about the few characters I interacted with, but they were the only characters in the entire game. So if I didn't care about them at all there would be a massive problem. For a game that has nearly zero meaningful player choices though, I found myself caring about the choices I did make just because of single lines of dialogue by the game's narrator. The game is not advetised as having a character driven story line, so this was actually an endearing addition to me. This again shows the strength of the game is primarily in the narration.
Bastions combat systems leave very little to complain about. My one complaint is that certain weapons are either really effective or nearly not effective at all based on what control setup you use. This caused my to switch between keyboard/mouse and gamepad often enough that it was a bit of a nuisance. Other than that the combat is simple enough to be easily understood, and dynamic enough to take time to master. The accessibility of challenge modes comes at a nice pace to aid in the learning of these mechanincs but there are moments when I felt overwhelmed by the sudden change in combat. Mostly this is caused by the way the game replaces one of the two weapons you choose to bring into an area with any weapon you happen to find, and unlock, in the area.
The final, and really the main selling point to me initially was the soundtrack. Recently I have been listening to a lot of game soundtracks while doing coursework and ever since I picked up the Bastion soundtrack it's constantly been in my playlist for occasions when I want music to relax a bit to. It was so good that out of all the games I have picked up from Steam sales and Humble Bundles in the lasst few years, this is one of the first ones I have set aside time to really play through since my courseload increased a few years ago.

The game is hard.  It's damn hard.  I died a lot.  But god damn, this game is good.
The story is fantastic and takes us on a journey with The Kid and the few people left alive in the world that he meets along the way.
The music is top notch.  If you buy this game, you might as well buy the Bastion Soundtrack Edition.  Matching the music's tone with the game is a hard thing to do right, but the creators did that perfectly.
The RPG elements in this game are not traditional.  You don't level up, but rather you find parts you can apply to your many weapons.  For each quest/mission/level, you choose approximately three weapons to take with you.  Each have their own properties, and some are better specialized against certain monsters.  Throughout the game, due to your play-style, you'll likely find a set of weapons that you enjoy using the most.
There is much replayability.  Whether wanting to discover all alternate endings or just wanting to complete certain challenges, you'll get hours of enjoyment out of the game.

There's still a lot of work to do, but this concept has got a lot of potential to become a knock-out fun time consumerer. It already is in a sort of way, but it's still a short-term addiction.
The interface is a shameless copy of Theme Hospital. Let's just be honest about that. But why not use something that has proven to be solid instead of reinventing the wheel? There's something very appealing in being in charge of a gaming company. You start from your garage, being small time and struggling to keep the annual figures in green colors. You have to work a way through developing games, hiring staff, expanding your business and getting fans.
The strength of these 'tycoon' games, is that they don't demand much graphical attention. What does demand attention, is detail. I want to have to make important decisions: do I take out a loan? Do I invest funds to reignite a game? Do I have to cut the budget by firing staff? Some elements of a typical Tycoon game already show, like deciding to take part in a yearly game convention and expanding your fanbase or the endlessly staring at figures and gauges towards planning your next move.
If you're a fan of tycoon- or simgames by any stretch of the imagination, you'll like this game. There's a satisfying depth in developing your own games and there are a lot of possibilities to do so. I can only recommend to the creator to add more depth. As much as possible. I mentioned Theme Hospital. Remember how you were able to turn up the heating at a certain expense? More heating means the people will feel better, but it presses on your budget. I want to be thinking about these managerial decisions. If that can be provided, this game can become a long-term addiction.
Some advices for enhancing the game: add a toggle gridline, show the measurements of rooms when designing them, add the option to redesign a room without having to delete it, being able to take out a loan, easy dispatch of staff (not having to pick them up one by one), more gamespeeds (the first speed still feels a bit too fast, especially later on in the game).
Keep up the good work!

If you're a fan of Game Dev Tycoon, this is a must-buy.  Especially if you can get it when it's on sale..  Just make sure you can set aside a few hours first.

There have been significant additions, updates, and various items cleaned up since my initial review.  The developers have been making those improvements steadily, and have been communicative about issues that have arised.  The price of the game has doubled since I initially purchased, but I would say that I would gladly purchase it at the $14.99 US price poitn that it's currently at, given how much enterainment it's provided.  Original recommendation stands, if you liked Game Dev Story, this is a must purchase.

Wow!!! Even by 2012 I thought it was impossible to innovate a hack and slash adventure game. I love the genre, but I just like the colors and combo strategy, I thought God of War covered the good stuff. And then I found this. Another lost gem that faded into non-existence because it's not a major AAA developer. Let me explain myself...
The best part about this is the time warp system. This is TOO FREAKING COOL! I'd suggest buying this game JUST to experience this mechanic. It's difficult to be innovative in modern gaming, so it's possible it had been done before and I just missed it, but either way it is incredibly fun. Basically you can reverse time in fairly short increments, but your "past avatar" will still exist doing what you just did while your "present  avatar" is free to do whatever. You can make several of these avatars at once to fight alongside you or help you solve puzzles. It's a bit confusing at first, but once you get the hang of it you can't wait to use it again.
How it works is say you have a group of 3 enemies. You can take out your gun and blast away for 5 seconds at one of them while they charge you. Reverse 6 seconds. Your past avatar will now be there shooting at that same enemy. So now you have a few choices. You can use your present avatar to keep shooting at the same enemy, reverse time 6ish seconds again, shoot at that enemy, repeat however many times you want, and then suddenly have 5+ people blasting this enemy away in 2 seconds. Or you can use another avatar to shoot a second enemy, making them stumble or holding them back. Now you have 2+ avatars distracting two enemies, so you can charge in with your main avatar using swords and melee on the third. To top it off, after, say, 3 seconds of meleeing that third mob, you can reverse 4ish seconds, and now you'll have both your past and present avatar wailing away at this mob. Repeat however many times you want. You now effectively have 4+ warriors on the battlefield attacking at the same time, and even though the process took place over 20 seconds, once you reverse to the very start of the battle and continue time, all 3 mobs will drop dead in an instant.
It's awesome.
The next best thing are the puzzles. FINALLY I find another game with unique puzzles that actually make you think without being outrageously difficult just for the sake of being difficult. And it's none of the usual "do this kind of puzzle once then use it a bunch more times." Instead, they draw elements from previous puzzles but add a twist or two to keep it fresh. I still haven't beaten it, but as of now I've encountered 3 different "types" of puzzles and each one has been expanded upon later in the "level" to make it feel new. Well done.
The next best thing is the graphics. Graphics are normally the least of my worries and something I'll glance at, appreciate, and move on. But considering the time period and developer, this game is INCREDIBLE! It absolutely stands up to some of today's games but is beautifully optimized. It baffles me how a game from 2012 can look, and more importantly run, 1000% smoother than a game from 2015.
Third I'll go with the boss fights. Again, FINALLY a game that has unique bosses that, again, require you to think and stay focused. Not every single one, some are the typical slash away without getting hit, but others do require specific strategies. And hey the strategies aren't always necessary either. You CAN slash away at this boss for an incredibly difficult 20 minutes, but if you learn how to exploit weaknesses, you can take them down in a few attack runs.
Next would be the combat. Not the most innovative aspect of the game, but still a tried and true method that is just as fun as it always is. It starts off pretty generic, but once you start unlocking combos it exponentially increases the fun and some are unique enough to make Blades of Time stand out amongst its God of War and Dynasty Warrior peers. And this is where the time warp mechanic comes in. Just like I was saying with the puzzles, it takes an old mechanic and makes it new again. It's also a good balance between simple and difficult. You cannot just stand there and spam left mouse button. You will die. Though you don't necessarily have to be constantly in motion 100% of the time either...in a good way. You CAN be and it makes it that much more fun, but it isn't completely necessary, which I prefer. I like to jump around a bit and get in hits here and there, then wail away at a single enemy, then jump around a bit more.
However I'll finish off with the voice acting and story. To be fair I actually do enjoy the storyline. Maybe it's not pulitzer prize winning, but it is somewhat unique compared to most fantasy games. Unfortunately, as others have noted, the voice acting is horrendous. I actually laugh pretty much any time anyone says anything because it feels so...fake and out of place. You can tell this is where they cut the budget from. If you've ever played an Oblivion or Skyrim mod where the creator did their own voice acting...it's kind of like that. Just awkward with mediocre writing where it's almost difficult to actually pay attention to what they're saying and not how they're saying it.
But overall I recommend this game to anyone who likes action games, and DEFINITELY anyone who loves hack and slash games. I am actually quite stingy with prices, so t's difficult to say if it's worth $25. I almost NEVER spend more than $15 on a game. Though $25 on Steam for a 4 year old game is somewhat of a testament to the game's quality. However if it's on sale under $15 I wouldn't even hesitate to add it to your cart. If that extra $10 isn't a big deal to your wallet, then yeah I'll definitely give the go ahead for $25.

Edit: Patch 2/27/2017 Added custom servers and more global servers. The developers are doing an excellent job responding to customer feedback and actually fixing the game quickly.
This review was made after the update that fixed FPS problems, and this patch has made the game run flawlessly (90+ FPS) on my mid/low-end PC (on low settings).
Outside of the normal bugs found in Early Access games, this game has a very promising concept, and already provides a large amount of fun. The backbone of the game is in place, and in it's current, somewhat barebone state, the game can provide hours of fun. The mechanics within the game feel very well thought out, and provide a good amount of balance to the game. Your ship doesn't just instantly die if you fail in one situation, but you don't have infinite health and repeated mistakes will cause failure. Customization within the game is limited in its current state, but I am sure there will be plenty of additions in the future.
The current gamemodes allow from 16-54 player battles of 1-3 ships per team.
Communication is key in this game, so if you are playing solo (or with friends), be ready to use your microphone or at least follow commands of your captain. If you enjoy team-based combat where proper coordination is rewarded, this game is for you. If you prefer to "carry" your team, this game will become very frustrating for you.
TL;DR if you don't want to listen to other people, don't buy the game. If you enjoy team coordination, buy this game.

So far this is the best *dedicated police sim* available. If you are a fan of LCPD:FR, you'll love this - it's more refined and less glitchy. It is not without bugs and glitches however, but once you accept that 1. It's the first day of release, 2. It's their first PC game on the market and 3. The team consists of 4 devs you really appreciate the work that has been put into it (especially if you've been following the game since it was first announced like I have).
Some feedback I would like to give the devs:
1. Currently certain areas in the roads are buggy, making your car flip at high speed, or just hit invisible objects.
2. The cars could be a bit more durable - police cruisers (particularly the Crown Vic) are known for their ability to take a lot of punishment, at current time i lose about 2-4% of vehicle health by going over small bumps at the gas station.
3. I'd love to hear more variety in the police radio clips, currently the clips are from the NYPD and as such reference New York locations, it'd be awesome to get voice actors in to record some radio, or at least grab a few more clips.
4. Change the hunger animation, or remove it. I don't have a problem with the animation, but it'd be better if it only played once - when the hunger bar drops right down and from then on only having the text notification. I get what it's trying to achieve, and i like it: but at crucial times (foot pursuits, shootouts) it's annoying to have to stop for 3 seconds for the animation to play, leaving you very vulnerable.
Some things I'd like to see added in the future:
1. More player customisation (especially some kind of Sheriff / State Trooper uniform)
2. More NPC variety
3. An extra civilian car or two (perhaps a charger for about $25,000)
4. Perhaps a police motorcyle (and proper uniform of course) for more highway patrol type players.
For anyone who has actually read this far, you should definitely get the game if you're into police sims - the devs are very open and actually listen to our feedback, so give it a play and tell them (constructively) what you think - at $14.99 until the end of October you really can't go wrong!

Couple this with incredible voice acting and a diverse race roster and you have a really really fun game.
There are problems though, some of the stronger ships really aren't worth the cost. In a game like Stellaris or Endless Space, the largest ship classes in those games can EASILY destoy several dozen of the smaller weaker ships if they are built correctly, with good upgrades whereas in Master of Orion the stronger ships are only better because they have more slots, they don't have that much more HP than smaller ships to justify the cost, so it's generally better to just mass an absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of smaller ships with good upgrades, than rush your tech for the "powerful" large ships.
For example I built a Doomstar (A thinly veiled Deathstar reference), the largest ship in the game, and even with all of the  most incredibly expensive upgrades I had, with technology that was FAR superior to the enemy, I still lost a battle against only 24 frigates (the second smallest ship class).
That is ♥♥♥♥ing stupid. And this isn't Star Wars where your Deathstar has a critical weakness ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that only a small ship could exploit, it's just massive wall of health, and it doesn't do nearly enough damage to justify it's INSANE cost.
Other than the balance issues listed above the game is great, It's only 30 bucks and it's essentially CIV in space. So If you like strategy games with a very streamlined, easy to pickup style, then look no further.
But if your looking for more in depth gameplay, with complex systems and a cluster♥♥♥♥ of a UI, then go play Stellaris or Endless Space(both excellent games).

This is very underrated game, probably because it was made by Russian developer. Most hack and slash games at these times were available only on consoles. Fact that this game is obscure does not mean it is bad, it is like rhodium (very rare noble metal from platinum group). X-Blades has similar aesthetics like Heavenly Sword by Ninja Theory (also non-Japanese developer) and similar main protagonist (both heroines have even Japanese given name, Heavenly Sword - ナリコ, Nariko, X-Blades - 亜由美, Ayumi). Mechanics from these two games are entirely different, X-Blades is dynamic hack and slash with character development system. Ayumi can not only fight with swords but also shoot enemies on sight and cast spells. Combat system in X-Blades is clever designed, some monsters are immune to specific attacks and you have use to proper combination of enhancements to defeat them. Fights in this game are also bit difficult, especially fights with bosses. Graphics in this game is very good and also game is well optimized (I've seen games with bad graphics and poorly optimized, for example Dreamfall Chapters). Sound is also good, especially music, crossover of heavy metal and hard techno which fits to this game very well (it reminds me old game by Ritual Entertainment Heavy Metal F.A.K.K. 2 also very underrated). I can recommend this game to fans of hack and slash, X-Blades is good alternative of Devil May Cry series for less money.

Where to begin? This game is absolutley beautiful, from the soundtrack, to the different regions/"worlds", the art style, the very vibe it gives off; it is amazing. There is something so mystical and vibrant about the environment that I just can't put my finger on. The Narrator's voice also adds a lot to the game; he is the one who walks you through vivid memories and reflections of the characters in the game, and without hardly any clips or unskippable sequences to accompany it. No other speaking voice besides the Narrator's is used, and I honestly wouldn't have it any other way; his descriptions and story-telling is really all you need, and adds to the feel of the game in a very positive way.
The story of the game itself feels fresh, and is very interesting if you can keep up with listening to the Narrator while trying to fight your way through intense enemy sequences, which is my only real gripe. Then again, its best to save time and works more fluidly for him to explain while you are fighting in the area he is explaining. If you want to know the fine details of the story, you really can't afford to zone out for too long, because he describes things in simple sentences (that do the job and do it fantastically), but make it all the more harder to refocus and understand what just happened.
The gameplay is very smooth and just works. No complaints there. As you travel through each region, the ground literally places itself piece by piece out in front of you, adding to the beauty and mystical vibe of the game. I love all the different weapons and skills you can equip and upgrade to use in battle; it makes everything more diverse and suitable to your playing style, which is kind of a standard for an RPG, but the game has its unique twist all the same. A drawback is that if you die, you have to start that region/level all over instead of having a checkpoint to teleport to. The enemies are varied, but they seem to have the same themes depending on which part of the game you are in and/or what region/level you are playing. They are not too difficult to defeat, but you can make it more challenging by using Divine Idols which can make enemies more resistant to attacks, hit harder, etc.
Overall, this game is simply gorgeous and all-around fantastic, involving some of the best art styles, music, and usage of a Narrator I've ever seen. I would definitley reccomend to anyone who wants a great adventure with a good story.

Tower Unite is an odd sort of game. Many people compare it to games like Second Life or PSHome. I can't say how similar this is to either of those; I've never played them. What I did play was GMod Tower, an old mod that this game is the spiritual successor to (complete with the same dev team). If you're here from GMT, then you already have a very good idea of what to expect and if you'll enjoy it.
That said, comparisons won't tell you much about a game if you haven't played the similar games. So what can you expect if you decide to purchase this game? As an overarching title, it's mainly a selection of decently fleshed out minigames. They've got enough depth to keep you entertained, but no one part has the polish that focused development would give. Each major minigame (known as "Gameworlds") take place on separate servers, while many smaller minigames are available in the Lobby (more on that later). As of writing, many areas of the game are still under development and clearly show the need for more work. Time will tell if the devs have bitten off more than they can chew, but at the moment what is present is quite enjoyable.
By playing the aforementioned games, you earn a universal currency known as Units. These can be spent on just about anything, but purchases generally fall into one of two categories: Cosmetic or Condo. Cosmetic items are pretty self explanatory: these are the hats, accessories, and other visual flare that makes your character stand out from everyone else. Condo items are used for the second major portion of the game: your condo.
Your condo is a little place you can spend time relaxing in. Using the items you've purchased, you can decorate your condo to suit your needs. Maybe you want a relaxing atmosphere for friends to hang out in. Maybe you're looking to build a theatre to watch YouTube videos in. Maybe you've got an idea for a little minigame you want to make, or a spectaular build to impress people with. You can color pretty much any wall, adjust just about any light, and even set the weather to your liking. If you're looking to be alone, you can keep your condo restricted to just allow you. Otherwise, you can let your Steam friends in or even open the place up to the public. Another nice feature is the ability to save these layouts, so you can rearrange everything to a completely different build with only a few keypresses.
This is a game that does a lot, but it's also a very social game. The minigames and condo can be accessed via the menu, but they can also be accessed via a "Lobby." These lobby servers act as a sort of social hub that connects all these features as well as provides its own unique set of distractions all under the guise of a tropical island resort. The minigames have queue hubs you can beckon people to join, each shopkeeper runs a uniquely decorated shop and comes with their own personalities, and the lack of loading screens keeps everything feeling interconnected (though freezing may occur when areas load in).
Perhaps the biggest issue with this game is that it is quite taxing on your computer. Mid to high end gaming rigs can certainly handle it at a solid 60 FPS, but lower end rigs and certainly anyone on integrated graphics will feel the framerate drop. The lobby is the worst with this, what with its interconnected and networked variety of games all running at once. Luckly, there are plenty of graphics options to help you squeeze out every frame. If you're really desperate, you can turn the resolution down; this will make everything look extra pixely, but it really helps if you need more frames. My laptop's graphics card recently died on me, so I've been playing with integrated. At the minimum possible graphics (excluding window size), I can still get 30 FPS in games and 15 FPS in the lobby.
If the store page hasn't already screamed this in your face, you'll be happy to know that this game contains no microtransactions. All non-backer items must be earned by the players, so you can rest assured that no one forked real money over to get that fancy crown. $15 is also the final price of this game, so if you'd prefer you can wait and see where the development of the game goes before making your investment.
At the end of the day, I recommend this game. It's a fun collection of various activities; you're almost always in the mood to do something that Tower Unite has to offer. From its gameworlds to its condo and everything in between, it's quite the enjoyable experience. Just make sure you're willing to deal with unfinished content and have a decent rig to run it on.

I'm warning you now this contains spoilers. This is for you sake more than it is mine, because I'm saving you an hour of your time. So this game started oit incredibly weak, then built it's way up. I started to geuinely enjoy it. There were mysteries to be solved. It gave you just enough information to begin piecing things together, but not so much that you had your answer. You play as a writer, name not given, as he patiently awaits his wife at the cabin. The thing that kept me playing was the thing where he would talk about patiently awaiting the love of his life, and occasionally break off into how he missed her so much... How he'd do anything to see her again but realistically knew it couldn't happen. It reminded me a lot of Silent Hill 2, and as a very avid fan of the orignal Silent Hill games, it gave me a damn good feeling. Another thing I enjoyed was the fact that after a while, all this untapped love and immense amounts of nostalgia turned into bitter hate. He talks about burning her clothes, how much he hates her and how vein she is. It turns violent. Fast. Something happened between the main character and his wife Serena. They never really tell you what happens. He talks about pouring salt down her throat until she vomits. Throwing entire bookshelves into the damn lake. You hear the voice of Serena once you look at certain objects; going from sweet and loving to angry and hate filled. Now, before long, after finding a jewelry box in a trunk and setting it down on the wooden table, you have to go to the ama- amair- dammit I don't speak French. You go to the big old dresser right next to the bed and there's a dead body. By the way, Mr. "I'm a writer so I have to use unnecesarrily big words" Goes into a horrible fit of rage earlier in the game, the likes of which are usually reserved for insulted Russians and Patrick Kane after a cab driver forgot to give him the extra $0.25 to his change from cab fare. (I wouldn't lie to you. Look it up.) So, you hear voices and there's a dude and a chick. They talk about bulldozers taking down the cabin and how the female left something in the cabin. (I thought it was the body but she said she wore it. I dont think many people can slip into a dead body like it were some type of dress.) The female voice is very obviously Serena. They then set the place on fire and the credits roll, leading to a more disappointing ending than Arkham Origins. It also leaves a lot of questions unanswered. Who was the dead body? Who was the stiff Serena was talking to? Why did they set the cabin on fire? Why didn't the main character remember anything? Why was he even in the cabin in the first place? Did Serena invite him there so she could kill him? What bulldozers? Why bulldozers? Why does the same damn spot on the floor make an ungodly amount of creaking sounds? Is there a sercret there? I'm not just being dumb and skipping over things here. I spent an entire hour exploring every possiblity in the game. These questions and more are left unasked. I'll hand it to them though. The creators did do a pretty good job of making an overall somewhat creepy atmosphere. It'd grow oddly darker for no reason. There is a picture of Serena on the table, the face is first scratched out, but before long you can see her face there. Soon, the face is scowling. Noises, whispers, voices; whenever you make some type of revelation. But besides that massive♥♥♥♥♥♥♥don't waste your time.

As someone old enough to remember the first-hand buzz over Half-Life in highschool, but never having played it until 15 years later, I'm very glad I ignored the voice telling me it'd have dated gameplay mechanics and be dated and weak by todays stanards because I was 100% wrong and enjoyed it from start to finish.
I remember kids at school talking about how amazing the graphics were more than anything else and so I was scared that this was most of what the game had to offer, and by playing it in 2015+ it'd be just plain visually uninteresting, and that the physics engine Valve is so lauded for would be boring. I was completely wrong and while Half-Life certainly has fairly bland graphics and visual palettes by some standards, it's still artistically appeasing to look at, particularly in the intro but even the level designs and contrasts of later levels are striking at times and the physics engine is no longer impressive by todays standards, but strengthens the gameplay rather than being a dependent part of it.
What all this means is that this game hasn't aged in terms of fun gameplay and has barely aged in terms of visual style and it still felt impressive to play through. I'm sad I didn't get a chance when it came out, but I haven't missed out and I'll be revisiting this game every few years to come.
If you're one of the handful of people on the planet like me and visiting this game for the first time more than a decade and a half later- don't delay, the first play-through is every bit as fun, thrilling and impressive as it was on release.

Sadly I cannot recommend this game, though it has many pros.
It is surprisingly complex for it's price-point, and has a reasonable amount of depth to really go for many different playstyles and strategies.  The tech-tree is pretty deep, and the micromanagement of planets definitely makes large impacts.  It is also simple and easy enough to jump in and start playing after watching a 15 minute youtube gameplay video, unlike games like EUIV where you have to basically watch 8 hours of tutorial to know how to do everything.
There are a variety of races, good graphics, and the combat/battle system seems fairly complex with different weapon types, armor categories, engine and speed differences, as well as weapon facings.
So why don't I recommend it?  It's unnecessarily long and poorly designed for conquering enemies.  I like to play all grand strategy games as a warlord who defeats and conquers my opponents through military force.  This game allows you to easily destroy all of their fleets, but you can almost never destroy or annex your opponent's planets.  There are limited ways in which you can even harm their planets, infrastructure or population.  You need specific technologies and specific ships with specific weapons, and even then you cannot take over their planet as your own.  You need further research of a specific far-teched military troop invasion, and must spend dozen[s] of turns getting an army from one of your worlds to one of theirs.  I played my first game on a cluster based galaxy, this was probably a mistake because the ONLY way to travel between distant star points is again a very specific technology far down the tech tree.  I rushed this, as was able to invade multiple enemy cluster areas, and none of my enemies researched this technology so I never had to defend or worry about being invaded or counter attacked.  It also took several turns to send reinforcing fleets, and is a poorly thought-out travel mechanic imo.
So after dominating my opponents' armies and fleets, and attempting to conquer the galaxy, I realized how slow and tedious the process was.
