Gameplay:  Similar to Guns of Icarus but more straightforward as ships are smaller. There is one captain and everyone else is crew. There is resupplying, repairing, reloading cannons, shooting swivel guns, shooting cannons, repairing sails and of course onboard fighting and shooting.
Ive sniped a captain before with the musket and its very satisfying. You can choose 4 different guns with diff reload times (musket, bludnerbuss, etc), 4 diff pistols, 4 diff melee weapons etc.
Balance: It's a concern if one team has teamers or a clan that all log on together but there's so much chaos that you don't really get that as much. Compared to Guns of Icarus, where one ship could just dominate because there's only 4 roles and there were definite clans, Blackwake has a galleon with 16 people, then 2 sloops with 7 people each.
It's much more chaotic but when everything comes together and you sink a ship its super satisfying.
Community: Roleplaying is also fun. And many of the captains pretend to be pirates, which is so much fun.
Every captain has a mic, which is a MUST. You can mutiny and replace with another captain if you wish as well, but I've never had the need or seen it happen.
Feeling: You dont' really feel bad when you lose. I've had a couple big comeback games where we were down 20 tickets and came all the way back. But if you lose it's not a big deal. Kinda like Battlefield where you play the game to play not for the result/score.
I am pleasantly surprised by this game. My main concern was trolls/idiots but I haven't run into any so far. All the captains have tried their best and some have been really really good. There is vote kick and muting VOIP if someone decides to be a troll.
Performance: Runs good on 390x 4690k. 54 man servers but I get 90 fps on a 144 hz monitor. Very satisfied with performance.
It has 4 different voip options too.
And I think devs are adding more servers so that is good too.
Basically, this is the game Guns of Icarus should have been gameplay-wise, because clans/teams can't dominate and ships aren't locked behind leveling. The only thing GoI has better was finished polish and cosmetics and main menu.

Where to begin? This game is absolutley beautiful, from the soundtrack, to the different regions/"worlds", the art style, the very vibe it gives off; it is amazing. There is something so mystical and vibrant about the environment that I just can't put my finger on. The Narrator's voice also adds a lot to the game; he is the one who walks you through vivid memories and reflections of the characters in the game, and without hardly any clips or unskippable sequences to accompany it. No other speaking voice besides the Narrator's is used, and I honestly wouldn't have it any other way; his descriptions and story-telling is really all you need, and adds to the feel of the game in a very positive way.
The story of the game itself feels fresh, and is very interesting if you can keep up with listening to the Narrator while trying to fight your way through intense enemy sequences, which is my only real gripe. Then again, its best to save time and works more fluidly for him to explain while you are fighting in the area he is explaining. If you want to know the fine details of the story, you really can't afford to zone out for too long, because he describes things in simple sentences (that do the job and do it fantastically), but make it all the more harder to refocus and understand what just happened.
The gameplay is very smooth and just works. No complaints there. As you travel through each region, the ground literally places itself piece by piece out in front of you, adding to the beauty and mystical vibe of the game. I love all the different weapons and skills you can equip and upgrade to use in battle; it makes everything more diverse and suitable to your playing style, which is kind of a standard for an RPG, but the game has its unique twist all the same. A drawback is that if you die, you have to start that region/level all over instead of having a checkpoint to teleport to. The enemies are varied, but they seem to have the same themes depending on which part of the game you are in and/or what region/level you are playing. They are not too difficult to defeat, but you can make it more challenging by using Divine Idols which can make enemies more resistant to attacks, hit harder, etc.
Overall, this game is simply gorgeous and all-around fantastic, involving some of the best art styles, music, and usage of a Narrator I've ever seen. I would definitley reccomend to anyone who wants a great adventure with a good story.

I initially had high hopes for this game. For the longest time, I ignored new games because they just didn't suit me (CoD 4, Bayonetta, Fallout 3, Oblivion), and at the time I haven't played 6th gen beat-em-ups in a while (Rise to Honor, Path of Neo, Treyarch's Sam Raimi Spider-Man games), so when news came out that a sandbox game was coming out that focused on martial arts, one of my favorite things of all time, and taking place in Hong Kong, one of my favorite cities, I was thrilled.
I played it and thought it was the greatest thing since sliced bread, but upon reflection I couldn't be more wrong.
Here are some of the things you can do in Sleeping Dogs:
-Fight Close Quarters
-Do parkour
-Shoot guns
-Hijack cars
-Hack security cameras
-Take down drug operations via sofa
-Take down crime operations via combat/guns
-Pick locks
-Play Mahjong
-Bet on cockfights
-Compete in melee matches
Sounds like a hit, right? Well, no. The fact of the matter is that most of these mechanics are used either exclusively in story missions or just exist for 100% completion, and are never seen again.
Going back to Sofa Cop, what you do is spot the drug dealer via cameras you hacked from your flatscreen TV. However, the drug dealer IS ALWAYS THE SAME GUY, as is the situation itself.
The game also features an upgrade system that's partially based on a tired moral choice system, where you get different upgrades based on your actions during story missions; not actions during overall gameplay like in inFamous, but story missions, to tie in to the story of Wei Shen, our protagonist, being caught between the loyalties of the badge and of his Hong Kong childhood friends-turned Triad (more on this later).
This system, along with the aforementioned drug stings, are very poorly made; the cop upgrade tree is situational and doesn't have anything to do with actual cop operations. The Triad upgrades, however, are completely close-combat oriented, a.k.a. focused on the most flesh-out system of the whole game. The rest are based on collectibles, such as health upgrades, extra moves, etc.
There are also vendors who will give you health refills with temporary buff effects, stores that have clothes that can give you additional buffs of their own, but it's all for naught because it ties in with the game's biggest problems:
1. It is extremely shallow
2. It is JUST TOO EASY
1 is a result of adding all of these mechanics and not bothering to give them a concrete place in the game's world. Once you complete the story missions and collect everything, there's nothing cop-related to do. The parkour is restricted to story sections, and the world overall has way too many invisible walls.
2 is where everything loses momentum: The enemies flash red when they're about to hit you, you regenerate most of your health on your own (so vendors are almost completely useless), and worst of all is that you can't change any of this, and as a result the game becomes very boring.
The DLC is what you would expect out of modern games: Extra costumes/missions that would last you a lunch break.
The story in itself is ok, as it kept me interested enough to see it end, but the fact that you don't lose cop upgrade points during sandbox mode makes the story hard to take seriously during gameplay.
There are 3 things UFG could've done to improve SD:
1. Cut out all mechanics pertaining to cop work and other secondary actions and just focus on the combat: Have it be a linear action game, and restrict story development and cop stuff to cutscenes.
2. Flesh out everything: Open up the world so that we can parkour more, give us different/more collectibles, and have us do more cop-related activities.
3. Make it a semi-nonlinear, Action-RPG like Deus Ex: This would give the gamplay more depth, and provide us a greater choice on the good/bad cop dichotomy.
As it stands, Sleeping Dogs is functional, somewhat unique, yet very shallow, and perhaps too much like Assassin's Creed. It could've been so much more.

As far as I am concerned XCOM 2 did the previous installment justice. They didn't innovate the game onto a new level but they polished the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of what framework they previously had. XCOM is they type of game that scratches a particular relaxing strategic itch and has plenty of out of no where game changers (often game enders lol). If you don't like the idea that 99% chances still have a 1% chance to fail you better be ready to load save files. That said, save often (unless you are iron-manning, in which case, best of luck commander).
Pros:
Great graphics and scenery and the overall package of the environment is really sharp.
Customization, although each customization is rather skimpy, it allows you to customize a lot of different things.
Gameplay requires you to do some planning and also to react on the fly, a well balanced amount of challenge.
Mission variety and every upgrade feels important to life or death
Cons:
Basebuilding doesn't feel as rewarding or varied. You will end up with everything by the end.
Timed missions are sometimes a few turns too short to approach without excessive risk.
Gameplay gets redundant near the end game, battles become trivial.
Some character development is really luck dependent. If your hacker gets enough +skill, they can basically do anything.
Psionic Characters are too powerful. Some of the specialist talents feel useless.
Overall I would give it 8/10

There are few sequels that can build from the ground-up into a completely new experience. Where XCOM: Enemy Unknown was a modern interpretation of the original XCOM, XCOM 2 is anything but iterative as it takes the general framework and ramps up everything, good and bad, into one of the most highly polished, modern turn-based tactics games of all time. The amount of blockbuster levels of polish for a niche audience is legendary; it’s a strategy game that cares to include a narrative beyond its basic premise, official mod-support on day one, and systems for attachments that becomes a meta-game that could rival The Sims.
Quite frankly as someone who only became a fan of XCOM within a year, XCOM 2 might be one of my favorite games of all time. Whether you are a die-hard who hasn’t gotten into the Long War or a newcomer who should start with Enemy Unknown before thinking about its sequel, XCOM 2 is an experience that should be played no matter what your preferences are. That last statement is important because XCOM 2 expects you to have finished the previous game beyond its narrative expectation to brave the new challenges.
Similar to the changes of Darkest Dungeon during Early Access, many of the complaints about XCOM 2 are how Firaxis trimmed away cheaper, cautious tactics that rewarded players mainly with their time than their strategy.
Enemy pods and the lack of timers created scenarios where players creeped forward with reaction shots, so X2 added missions with turn-limits and a stealth system to promote ambushes. Maps in Enemy Unknown became way too familiar and prone to optimized paths, and X2 created randomly generated maps. Base-building for airships, satellites and waiting out research trees are now geared towards stopping advancements in the enemy’s development with modifiers (Dark Events) and the Avatar Project (the losing condition). This new condition, however, can be stalled by players much more easily than satellite-coverage and the three-mission structure of the EU. Even the cosmetic options are cranked up in terms of its depths, which some view as needless additions, but the “Character Pool” mode helps players invest into their individual troops without worrying about their deaths.
All of these changes, even the infamous ones such as the timers and the Alien Hunters DLC “Ruler Reactions”, feel far more balanced than in EU. As someone who is stressed out by timers, the turn-limits of XCOM 2 are very generous on Normal, which can be modified and the new expansion offers a Second Wave option to double the timers. However, it’s important not to be turned away from these additional challenges as there are new features to balance X2 such as concealment that promotes a quicker pace along with the Specialist’s Gremlin that can reach objectives from far away. Changing one of these features will disrupt the careful balance of the game, robbing the guerilla warfare experience X2 wants you to believe it is, and it’s ultimately the mods themselves that question of how successful Firaxis was.
Mods are never something to be considered a negative except when their additions showcase an issue with the base-game itself, and XCOM 2 is one game that becomes too close to the Bethesda standard. Mods should tailor games to fit the needs of the player that designers cannot account for as it makes for an experience more personal at no cost of the developers other than making the tools. This isn’t concerning overhauls such as Long War 2 that arguably creates a more authentically classical XCOM experience with X2’s guerilla warfare tone with additions like multiple squad deployments and an insane, though fairer, campaign that pushes its challenge to one extreme audience.
What I am referring to is when mods are filling in the gaps the developers should have addressed that start out as small omissions like Free Map Rotation and the EVAC All button, yet then showcase far larger issues such as “Neutralize All Enemies Optional” for missions that require you only to steal something for success or a silencer/suppressor mod to make concealment have more depth behind its base-game implementation. (Even LW2 has the optional objective enabled by default, and that game is a far harsher experience.) Some of these additions like Perfect Information or Numerical Health Bars are only for people like myself who want to know all the calculations in a clearer manner, yet these additions show small issues like UI concerns that shouldn’t be fixed by modders. Even when it comes to some of the cosmetic options, perhaps the pettiest of issues, modders have to make simple changes like making an eyepatch option for the other eye.
The question that all these mods bring up about a game’s quality is this: “How many mods are acceptable to make a game play the way it was intended to be played?” For most people, I imagine the number is zero. In my case, I feel that some of these oversights are the result of making an experience that doesn’t alienate too many newcomers from the overcomplexity of XCOM 2.
You might find it absurd to suggest XCOM 2 considers its casual audience in mind when the series is a ball busting affair that can kill players in a moment and result in game-overs after 15 – 25 hour campaigns that result in having to start over. However, it’s evident by how the game calculates its difficulty and how the game simplifies its additions from EU with a few lessons from Long War 1 that Firaxis attempted to build a game that appears more difficult than the first game, yet it really is pulling cheap tactics without the player being aware of them like an invisible crutch to create challenge.
When it comes to the differences in difficulty options, the main culprit is the config file and how the early game is structured. Below Commander, these changes add a bonus chance to hit after numerous missed shots, training players to play poorly, while also increasing the percentages of the enemies’ health and aim. These modifiers wouldn’t be so egregious if the early game wasn’t designed to kill off your troops because they are lucky to survive a hit due to their low HP and lack of options. Troops in the early game are more like pawns in chess for the queen; throw-away expenditures until you can finance resources and train some of them up to an acceptable level to avoid further losses. What always amazes me about the Long War mods is that low-rank soldiers are not worthless as they can be equipped with Carapace Armor to take a safety-hit and they can equip more than one item to allow more depth in the combat. Difficulty in the Firaxis games is largely stat-based, not RNG, and it’s something I wish they would learn is an illusion of a hurdle.
However, what made me realize that XCOM 2 was tailored for new audiences—not a negative—was playing Long War 2 itself to see how the guerilla warfare tone of the base-game could have been more demanding with its constant enemy reinforcements on top of the timers along with the convoluted infiltration system and multiple squad deployment. This epitome occurred to me when I realized the 75+ hour campaign of LW2 was too much of a commitment, and the general length of the base game was better paced for accepting failure. All these concessions showcase how even niche AAA games are somewhat constrained by their userbase to make experiences that appear and feel challenging yet can never become too much for the player. In spite of this concern, of all the glowing praise I could ever give X2, it’s an experience where accepting failure is part of the entertainment, even when it manages only to be difficult when it takes a cheap-shot at a blind spot you never knew.

Since my previous review was from February last year, I thought that it was time I updated my review.
Mad Games Tycoon (MGT for short) has seen a lot of progress in the last year. This early access titlle is one of those pears that will continue to see updates until it is finished. The developer continues to improve the game and has on ocasion fixed reported bugs within twenty four hours.
Admittedly, that doesn't happen often, since it's better to do a lot of bug fixes in one then dozens of patches to fix single bugs, but it HAS happened. The game supports many languages which is mostly done by other people. That being said, Stefan (that's the dev's name. I think.) could definetely  improve his English. It's a world language and if you release a game on Steam then it's first language should always be English. Well, in my humble opinion at least.
My opinion of the game hasn't changed. It is definetly worth purchashing and if you have doubts... Watch a let's play. That should at least show you what the game is like.
Now, there are a lot of people who compare MGT to other titles. I'm not going to name those titles here, I don't want to start yet another bash fest, but keep in mind folks, there are only 'so many' ways you can do a game like this.
While the art is simiilar to some titles, that could be because of how the game is made.
As always, this title is in early access, so some features are still missing, incomplete and there may or may not be imbalances. Always keep early access in mind, because it is ALWAYS a risk and the game can ALWAYS be abandoned mid development for various reasons.
Trust me, I know. If and when you buy any early access title, and it goes sour, then you don't have basis to complain. You knew what you were getting into, and the risks you were and are taking.
Anyway, buy or not buy?
Definetly. BUY.

Stare at an Salvador Dali painting. Now read a Tolkien book (just parts of it). What would happen if the two works of art come together? Say, Dali painted a scene from the Lord of the Rings series? Or if Tolkien could put in words a Dali painting? Give either concept the most basic of Action RPG mechanics, with a old west kind of sound track and BAM, you just made Bastion. One would think that two great masters of different mediums working together on the same project would create a stellar result. Few times, it works, but more often, it does not; Bastion is the latter.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is basic, nothing more. It uses standard action RPG mechanics played on an isometric map. Like a lesser Zelda game. The weapons are broken, favoring all ranged weapons. I know that there are those that prefer melee, but it is pointless when a fully upgraded shotgun or blowgun can cut down anything and everything. The weapon challenge mode can easily be exploited. An endurance challenge can be fun in early gameplay but when a myriad of perked up ranged weapons are used, they become pointless. The difficulty can be adjusted to give more of a challenge. But this is pointless when a game should have natural challenges inherent to each enemy and enemy type. The payoff is adding a percent increase to currency and XP which can be beneficial from early to mid game, but becomes pointless end game. The dodge mechanic is similar to jumping in Portal: it can be used for its intention, but its just a faster mode of transportation as the Kid’s runs painfully slow. One interesting feature was how the narrator, Ruckus, sometimes narrates the actions the Kid makes, like rolling too often, destroying scenery pieces, defeating a boss, etc… It is a unique quirk that gave it some depth, and could have made the story much better, but it’s noting too special. Rather than using traditional RPG character stat leveling, Bastion uses weapons upgrades and a perk system. All of the perks, stats, weapons, upgrades and currency carry over in New Game+. This makes pointless gameplay even more pointless.
Rather than standing up to the big time RPG's, the game takes a safe approach. It feels more like "baby's first RPG."
Story:
The world of Bastion can summarize the whole story; it is a pretty world that feels loose and is fabricated on the spot but has no real understanding about what’s under the Kids feet. In the world of Bastion, an event called the Calamity happened which reduced the nation of Caelondia (but I presume a world) to a series of floating islands in the sky. Now the player, the Kid, has to piece together the remains of the world in hopes to save… something; the Bastion, probably. It’s really cryptic and really has no grounding. If you are going to destroy a city or world, then it would help to have some context as to what is being destroyed. The game is centered on rebuilding the Bastion by collecting crystals that restore buildings to their former state and finding any survivors. And because of this lack of context, there wasn’t any sense of urgency. Reading the Wikipedia gave more story than what was delivered. But  what’s even worse, is a (spoiler) moral choice ending. It’s kind of hard to make a moral choice when there is nothing to compare it too.
The whole story is told though the perspective of the narrator called Ruckus. It is an interesting narrative method for games. The story felt as if someone is sitting down and telling player a story. However, there is little disposition to character depth, world settings, and overall no relations other than with Ruckus. After all it is told from his perspective so it feels appropriate to him. This would make a good story to read, or listen to, or watch as an animation. it does serve it’s purpose. The flip side to this is that there is a level of disconnect with the Kid. The player is watching the Kid’s actions while being told a story along the way. The story might make sense in Ruckus' head, but it doesn't translate very well.
As a whole, the story is forgetful. It involves a lot of piecing together what lead up to the Calamity. It’s a post apocalypse, centered on a world that really has no reason to exist. It’s hard to save something when you don’t know what you’re saving.
Art:
The art of Bastion is one of its, both in sound and artwork. The sound track is somewhat of a hybrid of folk music with and old west. The artwork has a very vibrant pastel appearance that brings a softness to the world. The music fits with the tone of the world, but the artwork clashes too much with the gameplay.
The music is nothing spectacular. It does what music is suppose to do in a game, set the tone. It does a good job of setting a soft tone and has the feeling of sitting around a campfire. The music is combines well with the gameplay and story. The sound effects have an unusual and other world sound which makes it unique to the game itself. There could have been more variety of sound effects to distinguish between some enemy types, but this is only a small part.
The artwork is bright, colorful, and very detailed. Like the music, the artwork is also designed to set the tone of the game. However, this artwork clashes with the game too often. Having the floor build under the player is no different than lighting a preset corridor. The Kid can fall off the edges but not on the sections being built. Too often the borders are vague and clashing or the holes in the floor are small and hard to see when fighting in a fast paced battle. Paths can feel vague and unknown even though they are prebuilt to “light the way.” Buildings and structures have a shanty town appearance that feel like Megaton in Fallout 3 with a vibrant paint job. If this is a post apocalyptic world, then it doesn’t appear that way. If this is a western, it’s too green and vibrant. Many of the enemies blend too well with the environment and it can be difficult to detect where the attack is coming from. The Bastion’s art work should have taken much more of a minimalistic approach to designing the game that could match the gameplay and or story.
Bastion’s sound is good for setting the tone but it is not worth listening to on an MP3. The artwork is too much and too colorful to create an effective setting and world. On the surface it carries the appearance of a bright colorful world with a simple story like with a Mario game or Zelda: Wind Waker. But to use their color and design choices to tell a story in a post-apocalypse setting really does not do it justice.
The Bastion could be best summarized by eating a homemade sandwich at work. The gameplay is like store bough deli meats, with regular cheese, maybe tomato and lettuce, and a hint of pepper with a light mayonnaise. The artwork is equal to having handcrafted artisans bread that has a unique flavor and texture. It might have some variety and looks pretty, it might taste different, and others may call it the best tasting sandwich ever, but all it can do is satisfy the hunger to get though the day. Eat this sandwich along with hearing some slow western country song while the old raspy co-worker tells a story, and that is the experience of playing the Bastion. It is a treat for some but not for those looking for more substance.

As far as I am concerned XCOM 2 did the previous installment justice. They didn't innovate the game onto a new level but they polished the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of what framework they previously had. Timed missions are sometimes a few turns too short to approach without excessive risk.

Overall I would give it 8/10

There are few sequels that can build from the ground-up into a completely new experience. Where XCOM: Enemy Unknown was a modern interpretation of the original XCOM, XCOM 2 is anything but iterative as it takes the general framework and ramps up everything, good and bad, into one of the most highly polished, modern turn-based tactics games of all time. The amount of blockbuster levels of polish for a niche audience is legendary; it’s a strategy game that cares to include a narrative beyond its basic premise, official mod-support on day one, and systems for attachments that becomes a meta-game that could rival The Sims.
Quite frankly as someone who only became a fan of XCOM within a year, XCOM 2 might be one of my favorite games of all time. Whether you are a die-hard who hasn’t gotten into the Long War or a newcomer who should start with Enemy Unknown before thinking about its sequel, XCOM 2 is an experience that should be played no matter what your preferences are. That last statement is important because XCOM 2 expects you to have finished the previous game beyond its narrative expectation to brave the new challenges.
Similar to the changes of Darkest Dungeon during Early Access, many of the complaints about XCOM 2 are how Firaxis trimmed away cheaper, cautious tactics that rewarded players mainly with their time than their strategy.
Enemy pods and the lack of timers created scenarios where players creeped forward with reaction shots, so X2 added missions with turn-limits and a stealth system to promote ambushes. Maps in Enemy Unknown became way too familiar and prone to optimized paths, and X2 created randomly generated maps. Base-building for airships, satellites and waiting out research trees are now geared towards stopping advancements in the enemy’s development with modifiers (Dark Events) and the Avatar Project (the losing condition). This new condition, however, can be stalled by players much more easily than satellite-coverage and the three-mission structure of the EU. Even the cosmetic options are cranked up in terms of its depths, which some view as needless additions, but the “Character Pool” mode helps players invest into their individual troops without worrying about their deaths.
All of these changes, even the infamous ones such as the timers and the Alien Hunters DLC “Ruler Reactions”, feel far more balanced than in EU. As someone who is stressed out by timers, the turn-limits of XCOM 2 are very generous on Normal, which can be modified and the new expansion offers a Second Wave option to double the timers. However, it’s important not to be turned away from these additional challenges as there are new features to balance X2 such as concealment that promotes a quicker pace along with the Specialist’s Gremlin that can reach objectives from far away. Changing one of these features will disrupt the careful balance of the game, robbing the guerilla warfare experience X2 wants you to believe it is, and it’s ultimately the mods themselves that question of how successful Firaxis was.
Mods are never something to be considered a negative except when their additions showcase an issue with the base-game itself, and XCOM 2 is one game that becomes too close to the Bethesda standard. Mods should tailor games to fit the needs of the player that designers cannot account for as it makes for an experience more personal at no cost of the developers other than making the tools. This isn’t concerning overhauls such as Long War 2 that arguably creates a more authentically classical XCOM experience with X2’s guerilla warfare tone with additions like multiple squad deployments and an insane, though fairer, campaign that pushes its challenge to one extreme audience.
What I am referring to is when mods are filling in the gaps the developers should have addressed that start out as small omissions like Free Map Rotation and the EVAC All button, yet then showcase far larger issues such as “Neutralize All Enemies Optional” for missions that require you only to steal something for success or a silencer/suppressor mod to make concealment have more depth behind its base-game implementation. (Even LW2 has the optional objective enabled by default, and that game is a far harsher experience.) Some of these additions like Perfect Information or Numerical Health Bars are only for people like myself who want to know all the calculations in a clearer manner, yet these additions show small issues like UI concerns that shouldn’t be fixed by modders. Even when it comes to some of the cosmetic options, perhaps the pettiest of issues, modders have to make simple changes like making an eyepatch option for the other eye.
The question that all these mods bring up about a game’s quality is this: “How many mods are acceptable to make a game play the way it was intended to be played?” For most people, I imagine the number is zero. In my case, I feel that some of these oversights are the result of making an experience that doesn’t alienate too many newcomers from the overcomplexity of XCOM 2.
You might find it absurd to suggest XCOM 2 considers its casual audience in mind when the series is a ball busting affair that can kill players in a moment and result in game-overs after 15 – 25 hour campaigns that result in having to start over. However, it’s evident by how the game calculates its difficulty and how the game simplifies its additions from EU with a few lessons from Long War 1 that Firaxis attempted to build a game that appears more difficult than the first game, yet it really is pulling cheap tactics without the player being aware of them like an invisible crutch to create challenge.
When it comes to the differences in difficulty options, the main culprit is the config file and how the early game is structured. Below Commander, these changes add a bonus chance to hit after numerous missed shots, training players to play poorly, while also increasing the percentages of the enemies’ health and aim. These modifiers wouldn’t be so egregious if the early game wasn’t designed to kill off your troops because they are lucky to survive a hit due to their low HP and lack of options. Troops in the early game are more like pawns in chess for the queen; throw-away expenditures until you can finance resources and train some of them up to an acceptable level to avoid further losses. What always amazes me about the Long War mods is that low-rank soldiers are not worthless as they can be equipped with Carapace Armor to take a safety-hit and they can equip more than one item to allow more depth in the combat. Difficulty in the Firaxis games is largely stat-based, not RNG, and it’s something I wish they would learn is an illusion of a hurdle.
However, what made me realize that XCOM 2 was tailored for new audiences—not a negative—was playing Long War 2 itself to see how the guerilla warfare tone of the base-game could have been more demanding with its constant enemy reinforcements on top of the timers along with the convoluted infiltration system and multiple squad deployment. This epitome occurred to me when I realized the 75+ hour campaign of LW2 was too much of a commitment, and the general length of the base game was better paced for accepting failure. All these concessions showcase how even niche AAA games are somewhat constrained by their userbase to make experiences that appear and feel challenging yet can never become too much for the player. In spite of this concern, of all the glowing praise I could ever give X2, it’s an experience where accepting failure is part of the entertainment, even when it manages only to be difficult when it takes a cheap-shot at a blind spot you never knew.

c. Or you fortify the areas that you own
In my opinion the way they need to improve this game is to overhaul the microtransaction ystem and add an anti-cheat system even VAC will work. As of right now I wish I could reccomend this game as it has a good idea but the way it looks right now I just cant.

The story is really meh, it has many cliche or simply boring moments, and overall it's not a very strong, memorable one. However it's not the worst story ever. The combat is fairly well done, though the execute animations can sometimes feel a bit long and enemies rarely ever interrupt you when you're executing enemies, leaving you feeling invulnerable during an execute. Shooting is really bad, honestly. But it's third person shooting so yeah...
Overall this game was pretty good and if you see it on sale, get it and give it a playthrough.
If you like God of War or any third person hack and slash games, this may be for you.

I was positively surprised by this game. Whenever a female character is presented in a certain way, there is always the suspicion that the developers are trying to sell a game based on that presentation. While I dislike that cynical view, it isn't like it came from nothing, sadly.
That said, this game has some interesting combat mechanics, and overall, I found the combat fairly enjoyable. The most notable element is a sort of time-rewind mechanic, but the way this works is it leaves a clone of you that does whatever it was that you did up to the point you started rewinding time. They use this well in puzzles, and it adds quite a bit to combat, allow for you to unleash intense burst damage. There is also a sort of magic system that works very well for this sort of action game. Basically, attacking enemies builds up a meter that allows you to use magic at certain points. It also gives you an extra-health potion (essentially) when it overflows.
The story is OK, the dialog is often cringeworthy (though I felt it was more from the writing than the voice acting personally, others may feel differently, though). The locations are varied and interesting enough.
Also, for some reason, there is basically a MOBA mode, not unlike that random Guilty Gear MOBA. I have no idea why, and I find it most perplexing.
To recap:
+ Solid Combat
+ Interesting Time Mechanic
+ Nice Locations
= OK Plot
= Random MOBA mode?
- Bad Dialog

Wow, for an Early Access game this is quite good and one of the few Early Access games I haven't felt "burnt" by.
The Naval Battles are really satisfying and the game is heavy based on Teamwork. You will need to repair, resupply, load cannons, time firings with the ships movement, dodge cannonballs, not dodge cannonballs, musket people, stab people with broken bottles, drink tea, pump water off the ship, try not to catch on fire, swim, and blow up the other ships.
Working together as a crew and as a fleet is a great feeling when everyone does it. You will vote your captain in at the start of a round (and if they suck you can mutiny against them). A good captain certainly makes a difference with guiding the ship and barking out commands.
The game /is/ early access though. I've not experienced any game breaking bugs, but I have seen some hilarious rag doll bugs as people go FLYING from cannonball hits or bodies stick weirdly into the ship. My friend did "fall" into the ship and get stuck once. He suicided and we moved on. Graphics look good, although AMD users may experience an issue with "Christmas lights" in the water as the Devs described it, but they offer a workaround.
There are more gameplay modes coming as well according to the Devs.
You also level up and get a top hat. If you're the captain, you can color the ship neon pink and name it childish things.
I do recommend this is you're looking for a fun Naval Battle style game. There's nothing else out there like this that I know of and it's a blast.

This game is visually gorgeous and with some exceptional sound design and voice acting. However, at least in this current patch, the game is numerically slightly imbalanced. The rate at which enemy civilizations can accrue vast armies whilst maintaining strong infrastructure is simply too fast even at low difficulties such as Easy and Normal. At its heart, I believe the reason for this to be that population is weighted too heavily in terms of its utility in the early game. Because a fast population growth is essential for Research, Production and Expansion, civilizations that should be able to go aggressive early are hamstrung into playing extremely conservative, base-building strategies because their homeworld has a biome unfit for growth (looking at you, Mrrshan...). Despite this, the game has enough positive qualities that I would happily recommend it to a friend. I'd just advise staying clear of playing Mrrshan as a new player until the game has undergone some balance adjustments.
One idea: Give Mrrshan a Destroyer to start instead of a Frigate, allowing them to farm pirate bases, because Fieras is garbage to start.

The freakin' timer (which kills you when it runs out) counts down on the pre-load screen! You can Game Over before you even begin playing!
It's difficult to tell what is an actual hazard and what is merely part of the trippy background, and you don't seem to have any mercy invulnerability, so you can take a massive amount of damage in a short period of time when your screen gets "splattered" with pixels, which it constantly will. The camera itself barely lets you see ahead of you, too, so if you try going faster than a snail's pace, you're going to run into enemies or their projectiles. things with it until you've moved the arrow

XCOM 2 is one of the best games I have ever played. In the past I used to hate turn based strategy games because they felt like they were slow and boring to me. Everything changed when I received a free code to redeem XCOM: Enemy Unknown. I did know nothing about the franchise and decided to look for reviews on YouTube. I found an Angry Joe Show's review and his final verdict was an 8. I decided to give credit to Joe (as I always do, because he makes honest reviews) and bought the expansion, Enemy Within, for a few euros.
That's when the love started. XCOM was perfectly paced and absolutely not boring thanks to the fact that no outcome is completely predictable. The game offered a story-driven experience that was able to capture the player and keep him in-game to see how the story would be going to evolve, what new research would have been available, what kind of new alien foe would come out next. XCOM 2 takes all that was good in its predecessor and brings it to a new level. Better movie-like cutscenes, amazing voice acting (in English at least) and epic soundtracks.
The game starts after what happened in XCOM: Enemy Within (and that's why I recommend you finish that one first) and introduces an XCOM that despite all the efforts failed to defend humanity from the overwhelming alien invader's force and is now in disarray, transformed into a small guerrilla force. You need to take command again, aided by the good old Bradford (codename "Central" now), Lily Shen (old Dr. Shen's daughter) and Dr. Richard Tygen and rebuild the XCOM once more to take back the Earth from the so called Elders, the most powerful and intelligent alien species known. To do so, taking good care of your new base of operation will be crucial. Unlike XCOM: Enemy Within, XCOM 2 puts you in command of the Avenger, a stolen alien ship modified to serve as a mobile centre of operations (in XCOM: EW a classic underground secret base was present). This offers a new challenge for the commander that needs to choose where and when to go wisely. The game features again the "doom indicator", now called "Avatar Project", that can be brought back, unlike the XCOM: EW one and separates you from the alien's victory. Yes because you can lose the war against them once and for all.
Since the XCOM is now a guerrilla force, it acts like a guerrilla force. For this reason, a new game mechanic has been introduced: ambushes. Choose well how to spend your action points, commander, to make more damage as possible before the enemy knows to be under attack by your forces! ;)
The game features four basic classes for soldiers that can be improved through promotions that will give them new powerful abilities plus a psionic class available later in the game.
With the Shen's Last Gift DLC a new class will be introduced: SPARK, big robotic soldiers (XCOM: EW had MECs, human-mechanical hybrids) that look pretty cool and can pack a punch.
XCOM 2 will also feature a new big expansion being released on 29th Aug. 2017, "War of the Chosen", that will add a new bunch of mission kinds, maps, techs, enemies, playable units and a new quest storyline for each alien chosen (that will be three in all).
I preordered this last DLC and I advise you do the same. It's going to be worth the money for sure.

I sold my organs after being told of a pre-Robocop Murphy in the factory like loss of limbs and function. I drove around "saving" those too reliant on junk to function whilst suffering from the extreme blood loss I tried to profit from.
I bullet hell-ed my way around a 5 floor mall of a Verhoeven-meets-Scott future.
I put 90 minutes into a game which lasts 5 minutes before you lose without even realizing time had slipped from my mind, like the abstract concept that time is. I was lost as the window of the game warped like an age old CRT monitor, as layers of pixels and painted on cars stopped me speeding away from natural and mechanic, brutally harmful enemies shooting lasers and pins and rolling thunder, the dialogue of characters that headed over 2 screens max told me who they were, who I was, what this world was within 5 easily lost minutes.
Play it, if you get as much fun out of this as I did you'll be playing again in future, it's more than a retro-kick back, it's more than an aesthetic...despite being all about the aesthetics and aural sensations. It's entrancing. Illegal rave just outside of Bolton in a half abandoned industrial estate feelings.
And I've not completed it! I've warped the marketplace -sell organs/buy a good time via escort to up my diminishing health/buy a few more gameplay minutes from what's left of my organ-fund/get out and try to collect more addicts-, I've driven around every floor...I always die or JUST run out of time.
In that way NPPD Rush makes me recall legendary flight/trading sim Elite or its sequel Frontier, there's no winning without manipulating the game's mechanics in stores. It's simple in every element, but put together like two dozen basic melodies in hardcore pop-punk perfection, which is anything but simple.
Don't ever buy this game . Just don't.

Nimble quest is an unique game. It's basically a snake game with cute graphics and RPG-ish features. You start with a few heroes and each have different attacks. You pick your leader and join the fight against the various creatures the game has to offer. As you fight through the level and you kill the monsters, some will drops buffs while others will drop other heroes. As you collect more heroes your snake will become bigger and bigger. As you go through the level your heroes will get hit and eventually die like you. However the game only ends if the leader dies (the hero you start with).
Overall i think the game is fun for a few minutes and then it'll just be boring. You're basically forced to upgrade your heroes to beat the levels and you can only do that if you kill X amount of monsters with the leader (10k monsters for level 2 which is A LOT!) OR get enough gems in a SINGLE run to level up a certain hero. I haven't played the mobile version but i'm sure the tokens act as a P2W thing which you need to buy with real money. That doesn't happen in the PC version but they are very hard to get. Tokens give you powerful bonuses that turn the game into an easy mode pretty much.
I'm going to recommend this but it's pretty boring after a while and the only thing unique about it is it being a snake game.

How to sum up this game? if you enjoy ye olde pirates, ships, gunpowder and old school weapons then this is the game for you. It's simple, effective and fun.
There are a multitude of actions you can do in the game such as:
-Take control of the ship by nominating yourself as captain to get votes from other players and then colour your ship
-Load and fire the cannons with various ammo such as (Grapeshot, Cannonballs, Grapplinghooks)
-Fix the holes from enemy cannons
-Pump water from the ship due to said holes
-Repair sails when they get damaged and shoot enemy sails when you get the chance with the swivel guns
-Put out fires with buckets of water when one erupts on deck
-Board enemy ships and watch hilarity ensue as you fight to kill enemies desperately trying to pump water from their ship
-Grapple enemy ships to lengthen respawn timers and fight to the death with the enemy, when all enemies are killed the ship is downed and you steal their supplies
-Equip varying ye olde guns of varying effectiveness
-Drink tea or rum to heal yourself
-Throw oldschool grenades and watch enemies blow up into pieces... or yourself if you hold the fuse too long.
-Mutiny your captain if you don't like him then throw him overboard (I wish the last part was a feature for the pirates at least hehe)
There is always something to do in this game, it might seem repetitive and it is kind of but you are always in the thick of action and there's always something to do which makes it less repetitive.
There's nothing like blowing another man away with a cannon ball and watching his body fly away.
There is a barebones level system and customization system that allows you to change your clothes and character which will be improved upon as the early access continues.
The leveling system is for cosmetic items only so you can look a bit different as you level up, i think this is way better as it does not create any imbalances in the game system by including actual character buffs for the leveling system like so many other games do. (Many people might disagree with this but it's a fact that games that include item unlocks and other things in their leveling systems create an unfair advantage to those that are higher level "Usually")
The game itself is simple and not "too" hard to get into but it's also complicated enough for it to be a fun learning curve.
Fun Wanted Features: I am leaving this here in case any devs read my review, it's a list of features i thought might work with this game.
- Walk the Plank Ability to make the captain walk the plank or throw him overboard after you mutiny him without a ticket loss just for a funny effect on the actual mutiny function.
- Throw them in the Brig Ability to throw toxic players into the brig (And add said brig) by using the voting system for kicking people, if a person is being toxic on voice chat against his team and purposely being destructive and negative we should have the ability to throw him into the brig instead of kicking him you should force him to leave on his own accord.
The Brig could basically take away all his rights and he would be stuck in a cage unable to use voice chat or do anything, a far more fitting punishment for somebody who is going to be kicked anyway.
The downside of this is obviously he would take up a server slot but perhaps you could simply move him to an observer slot and allow another player to enter (Quick fix)
You could also have the toxic players walk the plank as an option as well.
- Bigger Ships - Boy would i love to see a Man-O-War in this game
- Ship to Land Combat modes - A mode where we have to besiege an island with a fort or otherwise and capture the flag or something using the ships cannons on the fort and the fort has cannons as well. You could do a lot with this basically making a land mass that the ships can sail around and the enemy team has to defend and attack. Perhaps even having a larger map where you have to force your way into the land attacking with the ship at first, docking then pushing in with troops to take over the town/fort ect. (You guys ever watch Black-Sails?)
- Small Ships Vs Big Ship Boarding (King of the Hill) - You could have a king of the hill mode where a team has to defend a large man-o-war type of ship from an attacking fleet and the defenders have a slower respawn rate then the attackers.
- Sloop Race - You could have a sloop race mode where people race their sloops to the finish lines using any underhanded tactic to get to the end goal.
- Rowing Ships - Adding some rowing boats might be fun as well although you would have to figure out what modes they would fit best into.
- Explosive Barrels and Fire Ships - Adding a function to use a ship as a fire ship by lighting it on fire and ramming the enemy ship to spread the fire, Adding explosive barrels to the ships that we can throw into the water like mines that either have a fuse or explode upon impact with enemy ships
- Breakable masts - Having destructable masts might bring more dynamic to the game as you would need to repair them like the nose when you ram, perhaps requiring a few cannon shots to actually break them (Maybe a 0/2 Repair instead of a 0/3 like the nose)
- Rope w/Grappling Hook - A function would be to use the rope while you are in water to grapple and get aboard enemy ships from water (Sneak attack) this would be a very appreciated feature as boarding enemy ships from water now is almost impossible.
Perhaps using the Rope to lock the enemy ship wheel while you are boarding them that they need to remove to be able to actually steer the ship other then forward.
Maybe you can add a weapon to knock people out and take them captive with the rope as well if you added a brig.
- Destructible rudder - allowing the rudder to be blown off so you can no longer steer the ship and you have to actually get on the back side to repair it.
- Multiple Matchlock Pistols - Allowing us to go full blackbeard would be super fun although i guess you would have to balance that somehow in the end and it might be difficult. (Maybe a delay timer when picking up the next one).

It's no Stellaris when it comes to complexity, but the last time MoO tried to be complex, it ended up killing itself and the genre for the better part of a decade.
It's no Homeworld when it comes to tactical real-time combat, but at least they tried instead of shoving in autoresolve and calling it a day.
It's no MoO 2 when it comes to be the untarnished, shining image of literal perfection that will absolutely never be surpassed, but not being perfect doesn't equal being a bad game.
It has a certain charm of its own, the late game tedium is kept to a minimum and, somewhat unusually for a Wargaming title, there seems to have been some actual, rational thought put into the UI this time around.
Most importantly, its developers
. Patches are rolled out at regular intervals and include new content in addition to bug fixes. Community feedback is considered and acted upon - many of the early grievances, such as spies, pollution and leaders were corrected. The DLC, while priced perhaps a little too steeply, does not contain anything essential to enjoying the core gameplay to its fullest extent.
It could still use some polish. Tactical combat needs to be introduced into MP first and heavily rebalanced second, as the current go-to strategy is "MIRV missiles, loads of 'em". Racial traits could use some work. The manual needs to be updated to account for new mechanics. A little more variety in anomalies and random events wouldn't hurt.
Still, as of now, MoO 2k16 is a perfectly adequate, enjoyable and accessible game well worth its price.
Oh and there's stuff voiced by celebrities. This is supposed to be a selling point, but I'm rather confused as to how the voice of
Luke Skywalker makes for a better gameplay experience.

I had been looking around for a new 4X style space strategy game, and I ran across this one. I had my doubts, but upon playing it I've been nothing but impressed. This is a very polished game, the game feels colorful and vibrant and even immersive. The planets and other races are detailed and interesting with great animation and voice acting, and the humorous space news segments really gave me a chuckle.
I think it strikes a nice balance between simplicity and complexity. It's not too simplistic, and it isn't overburdened by ridiculous levels of micromanagement like some 4X style games. This is a game I think can enjoy sinking a good deal of time into because it has a relaxing and atmospheric quality to it.
More random events and a more diverse tech tree might be nice, however. Definitely recommend.

Really, if you buy a game built in the Unity engine for 7p with a logo of this quality you shouldn't be expecting anything amazing. Despair, truly, isn't amazing. The absolute epitome of generic horror walking simulators, Despair is an incoherent mess of wandering around confusingly laid out corridors and vents for just under an hour doing absolutely nothing and with absolutely nothing happening, hoping to scare you by simply making everything really dark and really quiet apart from the occasional spooky banging noise, finishing up by feeding the player the most underwhelming ending conceivable and not even bothering to truly answer the question posed at the beginning. No tension is built whatsoever during this aimless meandering about, the devs not really understanding that horror games have to contain some kind of, y'know, horror, outside of a spooky face shoehorned in at the end once the game has actually been finished. The bog standard flashlight mechanic, complete with amusingly untranslated cyrillic lettering in the top corner, just completes it. Considering the miniscule price I paid on sale it's hard to act like I was ripped off and act as if I didn't know what I was getting into, but the full price of £1.59 shouldn't be bothered with. Get yourself a bacon butty or something.

Essentially a remaster of Master of Orion 2, this new game delivers the sequel we all wanted.
Master of Orion is the turn based strategy game that has you up light murmuring, "just one more turn." The interface is simple and most commands are intuitive, making it easy to govern your space faring civiliation. Where graphics is the most obvious improvement over the originals, the primary innovation rests in three areas: research, espionage, and combat.
Research is simple and not nearly as punishing as in the past. In former games, you would research only a single tech from a category and then move on (unless you had the creative trait). Now you ae only occasionally faced with that choice (thus curbing creative). Instead you are choosing research based both on what it gives you now, but also what it may unlock in the branching and twining tech tree.
Espionage now feels like its own minigame, where spies gain experience and go on specific missions to help you achieve your goals, rather than just charging into the enemy state and flipping desks for enemy research or propaganda. It at least feels like a vital part of the game now instead of something bolted on.
Combat is not as user friendly as the game's namesake. It is closer to MOO3 with a three dimensional map that has shipps rushing towards each other in defiance of logic and tactics. It sure looks pretty though.

XCOM 2 is one of the best games I have ever played. In the past I used to hate turn based strategy games because they felt like they were slow and boring to me. Everything changed when I received a free code to redeem XCOM: Enemy Unknown. I did know nothing about the franchise and decided to look for reviews on YouTube. I found an Angry Joe Show's review and his final verdict was an 8. I decided to give credit to Joe (as I always do, because he makes honest reviews) and bought the expansion, Enemy Within, for a few euros.
That's when the love started. XCOM was perfectly paced and absolutely not boring thanks to the fact that no outcome is completely predictable. The game offered a story-driven experience that was able to capture the player and keep him in-game to see how the story would be going to evolve, what new research would have been available, what kind of new alien foe would come out next. XCOM 2 takes all that was good in its predecessor and brings it to a new level. Better movie-like cutscenes, amazing voice acting (in English at least) and epic soundtracks.
The game starts after what happened in XCOM: Enemy Within (and that's why I recommend you finish that one first) and introduces an XCOM that despite all the efforts failed to defend humanity from the overwhelming alien invader's force and is now in disarray, transformed into a small guerrilla force. You need to take command again, aided by the good old Bradford (codename "Central" now), Lily Shen (old Dr. Shen's daughter) and Dr. Richard Tygen and rebuild the XCOM once more to take back the Earth from the so called Elders, the most powerful and intelligent alien species known. To do so, taking good care of your new base of operation will be crucial. Unlike XCOM: Enemy Within, XCOM 2 puts you in command of the Avenger, a stolen alien ship modified to serve as a mobile centre of operations (in XCOM: EW a classic underground secret base was present). This offers a new challenge for the commander that needs to choose where and when to go wisely. The game features again the "doom indicator", now called "Avatar Project", that can be brought back, unlike the XCOM: EW one and separates you from the alien's victory. Yes because you can lose the war against them once and for all.
Since the XCOM is now a guerrilla force, it acts like a guerrilla force. For this reason, a new game mechanic has been introduced: ambushes. Choose well how to spend your action points, commander, to make more damage as possible before the enemy knows to be under attack by your forces! ;)
The game features four basic classes for soldiers that can be improved through promotions that will give them new powerful abilities plus a psionic class available later in the game.
With the Shen's Last Gift DLC a new class will be introduced: SPARK, big robotic soldiers (XCOM: EW had MECs, human-mechanical hybrids) that look pretty cool and can pack a punch.
XCOM 2 will also feature a new big expansion being released on 29th Aug. 2017, "War of the Chosen", that will add a new bunch of mission kinds, maps, techs, enemies, playable units and a new quest storyline for each alien chosen (that will be three in all).
I preordered this last DLC and I advise you do the same. It's going to be worth the money for sure.

Thanks for forcing me to reinstall the game NOT on my SSD, Bethesda.
I will simplify my disappointment in three groups:
1. All "Creation Club" content is predownloaded on the PC, no matter if I paid for it or not. As a person who had this game on an SSD, I was not happy with this. Even if I doubt the content will even come close to destroying an SSD, such uncontrolled bloating is bad in general and should not be endorsed.
2. Paid Mods 2.0, NOW WITH EXTRA OVERPRICING!!!!!! Let us be honest, no matter what fluffy name they use, it esentially comes down to the CC content being "official" paid mods. Mods, in general are DLC(Downloadable Content), so it is silly trying to categorize it like that. I will say it now, I am FOR supporting game modders one way or another. The problem comes from the implementation. I don't think Bethesda Softworks is thinking "Let us fund the next Falskaar" or such. They have money in their mind. They are not stupid, so I expect that they will pay modders well, but this whole not getting a cut of the pay after that clearly speaks of "We care more about the money than the content". The other big problem that one can easily see now is that, using their current price plan for Creation club content as a base, large Official DLC sized content will probably come close to Retail game prices(expect the occasional exagerration in order to make a point).
3. Micro transactions in a Retail game. I understand clearly that there is an issue with the game prices. In an inflationary economy, where everything is getting more and more expensive, including the cost of making games, gamers expect and some even demand the same retail price that has been there for almost 2 decades(that I can remember). I also am not a person who normally complains/♥♥♥♥♥es/cries about bugs on release because of cost cutting(less QA). What I do not like is when a company is obvious in it's money grabbing scheme. Day One DLC, while I don't like a lot, I understand. Same with releasing the game in parts. Microtransactions in a retail game? WHY?! I don't want to deal with ANOTHER fake currency that I can only use in one place. I don't want to pay for an armor or a weapon that I can get in 5-10 gametime. If I am going to pay for something, I don't want my character to magically know about "Epicly Unique" power armor that is in the middle of nowhere, that ONLY I WILL ENJOY! In online games, I buy custom armor/weapons/skins/whatever more for bragging rights or because I want to show off in front of friends. If I buy an offline armor that looks cool, I want a quest attached to it. It would make a player a lot more attached and satisfied to the content he paid for, if there was a cool and maybe challenging quest attached to hearing about the item and going out to find it. Some people would call that immersive. I, on the other hand, will call it getting my moneys worth in entertainment.
Entertainment is what it all boils down to. "Am I entertained by the content that I spent money for?" I personally was not entertained by what the game was originally and none of the DLCs were that entertaining in my oppinion. For me, ever since Morrowind, All Bethesda Game Studios games are basically frameworks for the modding community to create a lot of content. Some of it was glorious, others demanded holy purging. But all mods were made around the core of the game. Fallout 4 had an interesting core and mods made the game glorious. People made amazing free mods that I would gladly pay money for. I wanted the Creation club to be different. I wanted paid mods that were done well and tested well. I got that. I also wanted the mods to be faily priced for the entertainment I got. This I did not get. The final and, to some, most important part was that I wanted the moddders to be well compensated. I have no idea if they are paid well or not. We are lead to believe that they get paid well for the mods, but get no cut from the profit. This leads me to one simple question for people. You, person who decided to read this, tell me. Do you trust that Bethesda will fix the CC content if there is a bug there? My answer wilth a rethorical question. Does Skyrim Special Edition STILL have the same bugs the original game did?
Now let me make this clear. I love Bethesda Game Studios games. I hate the decisions Bethesda Softworks makes because of lack of understanding or care. These are two different entitites and treating them as one is insulting to Beth Game Studios. We. ofcourse can always "insult"(jokingly) Beth Game Studios because of Todd Howard(I choose not to use his nicknames).
If, by chance, I misunderstood everything the CC is about or Beth Softworks changes their mind and actually manages to fix this system, that I will happily update this review. Until then, I am officially writing Bethesda Softworks on my Whiteboard of Shame(actual whiteboard), where other proud companies, like EA, Apple and Ubisoft lie, among others I doubt any would understand.

Sometimes you will be scavenging for enemies and junkies, sometimes you will be overwhelmed and, if you're quick, rich. The ability to move about the five levels freely is a false positive; you're always asking yourself if you grabbed the last one at the last level you were at, and, having to go search for that final junkie is killer. Literally.
Everything scales well on a CRT monitor; looks exactly as it should. I can't speak too much on the graphics because of my weird setup and the nature of the game. If you're still rocking a CRT, you're in for a retro treat. Flatscreen 16:9? Don't know; hopefully it scales okay.
This game is the price of a bag of candy, or a big box of Pop-Tarts. I can say that this is a much better value than either if you like twin-stick shooters. Or arcade games. Or if you ever had a Sega Genesis. Or if you're a person.

If you are EASILY CONFUSED or looking for something "modern", then you won't be satisfied. HOWEVER, if you ARE looking for a game that puts you right back into the 199X era shareware feel or know what a ZX Spectrum is, then you must try this out!
The developer has created a gaming experience which harkens back to an age where most of the games were brutally difficult and those of the weak of heart dare not tread. The game is best described as cyber-trash punk (or glitch punk), a style which is hard to pull off considering trash-punk, by nature, looks unfinished.
The game also does not hold you by the hand. You learn how to play from both failing and trying things out. If you fear failure, this game is not for you! (and frankly, neither are most games pre-2004). As you play more and begin to understand what is expected of you, you begin to delve deper into the world that RailSlaveGames has created for you, and you begin to love the experience even more.
You play as a Junkie yourself... salvaged from the streets. What was left of your mangled and torn body has been merged with a high-powered police vehicle and sent on a mission to recover others who are on the brink themselves. You might be horrified by what you've become, but you have no time for that. You just focus on your mission and all will be revealed.
The game consists of 5 floors each with their own badass music track. The key to enjoying this game is to understand that each of these floors can be explored in any order. Floors do not need to be cleared sequentially. In fact, the key to beating the game is to find your own paths to acquire the NOX Junkies, collect the cash and get out!
By the time you're good enough to finally challenge the boss, you're sucked in and digging every moment!
This game would fit right in at the Data East arcade featured in Robocop 2, a gritty reminder of exactly the type of world which resides just outside the video arena.
Still not sold? Well, you can watch me play around 2 hours of the game and decide for yourself! You can even challenge my score if you think you're RUSH enough!                  See you on the other side, NOX Junkie!

This is the classic Snake game with a twist. Instead of a 'snake' that get's longer when you eat a pellet, you're an adventurer/warrior, and the 'pellets' which drop fair rate are warriors that you collect and 'add' to your party. Your adventurer, and you party both attack the various enemies that run around the levels.
Each warrior is unique in their appearance, stats, and the way they attack sometimes. The Mage is squishy but hurls powerful fireballs. The Knight has a lot of health, damage, and armor, but attacks at a somewhat slow rate. The 'Gizmo' is a little dude with goggles that hurls
powerful bombs with a large radius at a
slow rate.
Each warrior can be 'leveled up' 3 times, each level giving new stat increases or sometimes even benefits. The Knights first level increases his attack speed, while his second and third levels increase his armor, which makes him very difficult to kill unless you decide it would be great to punch that 30 foot ogre with your face.
There are about 7 different arenas for you to progress through. You start in a forest, go on to a sewer, etc. When you reach the final area type and beat it, it loops back to the first forest, though the difficulty increases continue. And while I never done it before, I believe beating the final area the second time 'wins' you the game.
Each time you beat a level for the first time(including the second trip levels), you unlock a new character. All characters you unlock can be picked up and added to your party during the game, so your 'length' get's quite long. For example, if you have 5 characters unlocked, your line can only get 5 long, and you continue to battle through the levels. If you only have 2 characters, then the line will only be 2 characters max. There's a total of 16 characters, which equates quite a long line if you can keep them all alive, and each one of them has a unique attack to add to your parties killing machine prowess.
Along with the characters and their 3 levels, there are power-ups that defeated enemies drop, and they do temporary effects like giving your a damage shield, freezing all enemies for 5 seconds, increasing attack speed for 30 seconds, replenishing health, etc. You can upgrade these items multiple times, 10 times I think, and each time increases its potency/length/radius depending on the item.
All in all, this is an amazingly fun game that I believe all should play. If you ever loved the classic Snake game, then this is absolutely a must buy even if you are bored with the original. I got this on a sale where it cost $0.50, but I would happily pay the full $5 for this great game.

"Blades of Time", a 3rd person hack & slash in the manner of "Devil May Cry", is a game where nothing feels quote right.
You are a scantily-clad blond treasure hunter named Ayumi (I guess the developers where watching watching/reading too many animes/mangas), who is transported to Dragonland (because magic) where there's untold treasure (because ancient legends), and of course, a warmongering Chaos demon (because ancient prophecy). And you are sort of in the middle of all this, and hack & slash your way through without true reasons.
Extremely crappy story aside, there's much wrong with this title.
First, the visuals. What seems a lush and vibrant world at first glance, is really just a stiff, brightly-colored jungle. Ayumi just clips through the greenery, the leaves and grass are mostly static. Dragonland felt like a colorful dead world. Character animations are stiff, too. What look like detailed models from afar are revealed to be really mediocre ones. But, this is a budget title, so the graphics issues are truly the least concern.
What is a huge issue are the gameplay and the controls.
Ayumi moves too fast. She jumps too high. Controlling her never feels alright. Precision jumping is almost impossible. Even walking narrow ledges is a challenge due to speedy movement. The enemies have no "meat". Ayumi's swords just sort of pas through them, and then they eventually fall down. The combo system is poor, and the melee deteriorates into mindless button mashing. The shooting part of combat seems tacked-on and minimally refined.
Add to all this the fact you have to constantly bear with Ayumi's babbling, presented via poor and annoying voice-work...
Ugh, There's much to quit "Blades of Time", and very little to stick to it.

Before this I'd never played Master Of Orion but I'd certainly heard of it. People speak of the original MOO like it was some kind of videogame Messiah and many game mechanics that 4X games take for granted these days can supposedly be traced back to this series in some way. So does this remake hold up?
The gameplay is your usual space 4X. You start off with a single planet and a few ships and from those humble beginnings you must forge an empire and then decide how you want to conquer the galaxy. This can be through peaceful means like science and diplomacy or you can just decide to blow everyone up with space lasers. The presentation is great with the stars, planets and fleets all beautiful and shiny. The alien leaders look great too with some well known voice actors. Ever wanted to be shouted at by a birdman voiced by Mark Hamill? Your wish is granted.
Many have criticised the game for oversimplified mechanics and they're not entirely wrong. The game seems to lack depth compared to other games like Civilization and never quite pulls off the 'Oh crap it's 3am' kind of immersion you usually get with a 4X. It's still entertaining however and I'll play it when I want a more relaxed strategy game, and it could be perfect for introducing someone to the genre. Not the videogame Messiah I was promised but still fun. Any game where you can build a Death Star(ok Doom Star but screw copyright) is gonna keep me entertained.

Okay, going to say this, first and foremost: DO NOT BUY THIS GAME! IT IS NOT WORTH IT!
The game is horrible. Without hardly any deviation, this is how the game goes: You start off in this room where you have to kill all these enemies until the game tells you to stop and move onto the next room, where you have to kill all these enemies until the game tells you to stop and move onto the next room, where you have to kill all these enemies until the game tells you to stop and move onto the next room, rinse and repeat, RINSE AND REPEAT, OVER, AND OVER, *AND OVER!* Repitition is the name of the game, here.
The ruins where you "explore" are interesting to look at. Wanna learn more about them? Too bad, the game doesn't explain them! And Ayumi, the lead character, is nothing short of obnoxious! I HATE HER! I hate her personality, I hate how she dresses like a street walker, I HATE HER! And, yes, she is a BLATANT rip-off of Lara Croft, without any of the latter's charm, explorative abilities or puzzle-solving antics.
The enemies are dumb as rocks, and while that can be dealt with easily, there is one kind of enemy that you face early on that is a pain to deal with, as if you're getting swarmed by ground-based enemies and five of these special enemies circle you, then there goes half your health and no, I am not kidding.
I also had MAJOR lighting issues while playing it, at least on some stages. It was like the camera had its own shadow. And speaking of mechanics, swiping or shooting at destructible items is counter-intuitive. You need to break all items in the game to get 100%, but you can stand in front of a pot, hack and slash at it for about five or six swings, but it'll break at the sixth or seventh swipe. Stone coffins do show you hitting it, but nothing else does.
Finally, something worth noting, this version was played on a Mac. I am aware that the Mac isn't a good system to play on, except I also owned this game on the XBox 360, which is said to be the best version. That's not saying much - I had the exact same issues with that version. However, as I mentioned, this was on a Mac, so, instead of doing a different port, they just made what is called a Wineskin (for those who don't know, it's an application that allows programs that were made for Windows to be played on Macs.) They did nothing to enhance the game in any way for the Mac.
In the end, there is no possible way I can recommend this game. It's like they tried to make a game, like Golden Axe or Streets of Rage, but ended up sucking all of the charm out of those kind of games.
In the end, I had more fun playing Superman 64.
