At first Master of Orion IV feels like Master of Orion II with a lot of window dressing slapped onto it; and it is in many ways. I read the reviews and stayed away from this game for the longest time because of peoples' complaints. However, after playing through a few rounds I feel that some of the negative reviews were completely unjustified.
One of the common complaints was the addition of warp points, since the old games allowed you to fly around the map at will. In some ways I miss the old system, but seeing how other games have gone this way I can understand it. If you’re looking for examples look at Sins of a Solar Empire and Endless Space. Both games are fantastic and they use warp points, jump points, hyper points, whatever you want to call them. A lot of hard military science fiction uses jump points in them, usually because it’s suggested that gravity plays a role in how ships are able to move between star systems (see The Lost Fleet books) or there’s gravitic waves between them (see the Honor Harrington books).
The ship design system can be a little annoying at times. Namely the auto-upgrade for your blueprints can oftentimes take a weapon off that you really want to keep and replace it with a newer one that sometimes reduces your DPS! You have to be mindful of this as you’re designing your ships. Yes, I know, this seems like an unnecessary step but you could just skip the auto-upgrade and use your best judgment.
One thing I will agree with other reviewers on here is the need for DLC. I simply can’t believe how the gaming industry is going this way. Everything is coming down to micro transactions nowadays. It’s horrible. In order to experience the “full” game you have to pay additional money for something that should’ve been included to begin with? Bull****! The developers did this with the Elerians, Gnolams, Trilarians, and the Terran Khanate. In addition the developers made an unforgivable sin in my book, packaging the Khanate into a “Collector’s Edition” that included Master of Orion I, II and III for an exclusive price.
I can’t justify paying that. Not when I was able to download Master of Orion I and II from
for a lot cheaper and both still play on Windows 10 through their system! Although, to be fair, Master of Orion I looks absolutely terrible when stacked against Master of Orion II.
The industry is going this way with DLC and will continue to do so as long as we the People are willing to go along with their shenanigans. It’s either they nickel and dime us that way or they get us with “early release” versions (see beta versions) or pre-ordering.  I for one won’t pre-order most games because I know that buyer’s remorse may be just around the bend. I’ll wait until reviews come out before I buy a game. The only company that has my trust for pre-ordering is Blizzard, and that’s because they consistently make a good product every time.  Say what you will about Diablo III or World of Warcraft, but both have been solid products since their beginnings and I trust Blizzard to continue delivering solid products.
It will take we the People to stand up and say, "No more DLC!" for the industry to change their ways. But as long as gamers (who are supposed to be the most unforgiving people on the planet) are will to go along with the industry's ways they'll keep right on doing it.

X-Blades is a very hard game to review. It's a mixed bag of great ideas with somewhat poor execution. Visually environments look stunning but there is no cohesive artstyle. Menus and graphical effects cheapen the games look. Animations are far too simple, bland and don't feel rewarding when you land a hit. This is something that is crucial to the success of a hack and slash game. There is no audio-visual feedback and there are times where your attacks will miss easy stationary targets
I bring up these issues because with a more cohesive artstyle and an animation overhaul X-Blades could have become a cult favorite. The gameplay itself is standard. It's a level based hack and slash game with slight free-roaming elements as you swap between areas. Most levels involve hoardes of enemies rushing at you, but unlike in other games such as dynasty warriors. The lack of feedback or spectacle make things teadious quickly. Some bosses and enemies require special strategies but have no visual way of iterating that to the player. This forces you to read the in game hints on the pause menu.
X-Blades has a lot of small gameplay issues, but the problems above are the big dissapointments. It could have been a good game with annoying faults but is left utterly mediocre with so much wasted potential.

A different take on the classic snake game, Nimble quest is a simple yet sometimes difficult game where you take lead as one of several heroes, collect heroes, treasure, and defeat enemies. Go to the bottom for TL;DR version.
This game has a lot of Theme Hospital inspirations. Like how your staff needs radiators to be productive or how certain staff members can only be hired when you have certain items. The game's atmosphere is nice on its own and it has a lot of topics and genres and features for your development journey.
Now, let's talk about the downsides of this early access. First of all, there isn't much of a tutorial on how things work, the only tutorial you're given is at the start and it's pretty simplistic. After that you have to unlock certain stuff by doing other stuff. Researching a feature to be able to make your own engine for example. However, the buildings that you unlock have no tooltips whatsoever and you can only go for a trial and error approach. They do have tooltip boxes though so they're sure to be explained later on in an update. There are also some minor grammatical errors or typos but nothing too bothersome.
Now, if you have bought the game and you're just starting out, don't invest in the last 3 skills. They are only ever useful for research, marketing and support. Get skills other than music, sound and graphics since those are the first few employees available to you and you can just get one if you need.
TL;DR version: This game is like Theme Hospital meets Game Dev Tycoon. It is in Early Access but it doesn't have any bugs that I can see. Only issues are, late game lag (can be solved by lowering graphics etc.) and npcs getting stuck (can be noticed easily) and some minor typos. The game deserves its current price tag. As an Early Access game it gets a 9 out of 10.
-----------------------------------------------------------

Master of Orion (4) seems like a reasonably faithful update of MOO2.  The major difference is that combat is real-time rather than turn-based (though through strategic pausing and direction of ships this can be somewhat simulated).  Gameplay and ship design also have been steamlined a bit so you don't have to spead so much time micro-managing things (which could be a plus or minus depending on whether you you enjoy complexity or not).  Mostly the overall game experience is very much like playing MOO2, which is also an excellent game despite it's age.
Overall I don't have any major complaints about what overall is a really good game. The worst thing I can think of is that "Heavy Gravity Homeworld" is a 4 point "advantage" when it no longer allows you to settle the much more numerous normal gravity planets without a penalty (For obvious reasons, the Bulrathi are one of the worst races to play because of this), which all things considered is a fairly minor complaint.

This is a buggy, annoying game, that could have been great, but it's not.
It doesn't work with multi-monitor setups, unless your main monitor is to left. It also just assumes your monitor is 16:9, and looks horrible and stretched if it's not. When I first tried to switch to window mode to changed monitors, it glitched and I had to kill the process. I had to disable my second monitor to play at first. They have since fixed the window mode freeze, but it still doesn't read settings correctly. I have to switch to window mode, move it, switch back to full screen, switch to another app to fix the scaling, and then switch back. I don't know if this is only on Linux, but multi-monitor setups are almost common now days, and it should work correctly.
The tutorial is extremely poorly designed. In one of the first steps it it tells you that you can click a fleet and select individual ships to split them off. You can't. The ship window doesn't show in this part of the tutorial. Next it will have you explore planets in the system. Then the adviser will recommend that you not place a colony on the planet, except you have to place a colony there for the tutorial to continue. At this point, trying everything but what I was supposed to, I thought the game had frozen, and I killed the process. It hadn't. All clicking is disabled, including the menus, so you can't quit, enter the settings, or start a new game, or even exit. Huge design flaw.
The entire time I was TRYING to play through the tutorial, and getting extremely aggravated, the voice of the tip adviser kept going off, saying things like "Excuse me, Mr President." There are even more of these alerts than during normal game play, due to it being a tutorial. If it was not possible to turn off voices, I may not have continued to play. I have not become so aggravated with a game for as long as I can remember. Frustrated, sure, but not aggravated like I was due to the tutorial. It's also not actually a tutorial. You simply follow the instructions, with little or no choice in your actions. You're better watching a video. It's way less aggravating.

This game is not all bad. If you have a kid that likes sci-fi and you want to introduce him to 4X games, this might be a good choice. The graphics are remarkable, and they have an all star cast of voice-overs. Because the game-play is a bit lacking though, all the fancy graphics and voices just felt like shine to me. I honestly don't think the game was ready to come out of Early Access. They have a very fancy start to a good game, with a few poor choices that nearly cripple it.
Most of your time will be spent choosing the next thing to build. The auto-build also disables itself any time you add something to the queue. You can definitely start to feel like you are simply micro-managing through much of the game. It gets really boring. I don't think I've finished a single game yet. The page to manage multiple colonies at once, the "Empire" tab, is crippled, so you're constantly going through every planet, which is annoying. The research suggestions however, are one of the best changes they made, and really help speed up your choices in research.
The auto-turn is also very poorly designed, and it can blaze past important things, including hostile forces. It only stops when you NEED to do something, so you have to keep your mouse hovered over the button.
The ship combat AI is a pain. Trying to control a fleet with a mouse sucks, so you'll likely just click to auto resolve it most times. It is nice that they have multiple ways to resolve a battle though. I would have liked to see it further developed, but that's unlikely.
One of the things that is very subjective that I disliked is the races. They're a bit too heavily modeled after real animals. Some of the choices seem straight out of a kids movie.
There's also DLC races available. I think their presentation was a mistake. I would have preferred a button to get additional races. This would have also allowed them to add additional races at a later date. The way they did it makes it look like the game is incomplete, when not everyone will even want those additional races.
The GNN news updates are just plain stupid. In previous games they were a little silly, but nowhere near as bad as they are now. At one point, when talking about a population boom, the male robot actually asks "You do know where babies come from, don't you?" Seriously? WHO thought that was a good idea? Who thought that was funny? The whole game has a very cartoonie and kiddish feel to it.
The research tiers are almost exactly the same as from previous games. It is likely that they took the exact tiers and simply made some minor alterations. Some of the alterations are nice, others not so much. I would have liked further expansion. I also would like whoever decided to change the colony base to get a boil in an unpleasant area.
This game was released before it was ready, and abandoned. The production company should be ashamed.
